0.title: In the Beginning Was the Word
0.overview:
The Gospel of John is the most theological document ever written. Where Matthew presents Jesus as the King of Israel, Mark as the Servant-Son, and Luke as the Saviour of the world, John presents Jesus as the eternal Word of God who became flesh and dwelt among us — the visible form of the invisible God. John wrote last, having lived longest with the mystery of God become man, and every sentence carries the weight of that lifelong meditation.

John's purpose is stated with unusual precision at the end of the book: "these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name" (20:31). Two things: belief and life. Not merely agreeing that certain facts are true, but trusting a person; and not mere existence, but the eternal life that is knowing God and knowing Jesus Christ whom he has sent (17:3). The entire Gospel is an extended argument for this faith, structured around seven signs and seven "I AM" declarations.

The seven signs escalate in power and publicity: water to wine (private), healing the official's son (at a distance), healing the invalid (Sabbath controversy), feeding five thousand (crowd), walking on water (disciples alone), healing the blind man (Jerusalem), raising Lazarus (public, four days dead). Each sign is a window into who Jesus is; together they build the case that "no one can do these signs that you do unless God is with him" (3:2) — and more than that: unless he is God. The greatest sign of all is the resurrection itself, towards which the whole Gospel moves.

The seven "I AM" statements run through the Gospel like a spine. Each one takes up the name God gave himself at the burning bush (“I AM WHO I AM”, Exodus 3:14) and joins it to what Jesus does to save us: I am the bread of life; the light of the world; the door; the good shepherd; the resurrection and the life; the way, the truth, and the life; the true vine. They are pictures, but not a merely human teacher’s pictures of himself: in them the Son of God tells us who he is. When Jesus says "Before Abraham was, I am" (8:58), his hearers pick up stones to throw at him: they know he is claiming to be God.

Who wrote it? The Gospel names its author only as the disciple whom Jesus loved, who is bearing witness about these things, and who has written these things (21:24; cf. 19:35). He was one of the inner circle at the Last Supper, and he never names himself or his brother James, though he names almost every other disciple. The early church, from Irenaeus on, identified him as John the son of Zebedee, writing in old age at Ephesus, probably between AD 80 and 95. Some scholars think the beloved disciple was a Jerusalem follower other than one of the Twelve, or that the Gospel was finished by his community. But the internal evidence fits John, the son of Zebedee, best, and the church’s testimony is early and consistent.

Why is it so different from Matthew, Mark and Luke? John has no parables, few miracles and long discourses; much of his story is set in Judea and Jerusalem, across at least three Passovers; and the great “I am” sayings are his alone. He was not correcting the others but completing them. He chose his material deliberately, so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God (20:30–31), and says plainly that he left out much more than he included (21:25). Where the others mostly give the Galilean ministry, John adds what happened in Jerusalem and what it meant.

Unique to John is the Farewell Discourse (chapters 13–17) — five chapters of intimate instruction given to the disciples on the night of his betrayal. Here Jesus gives his most extended teaching on the Holy Spirit ("another Helper"), on union with him ("abide in me"), on the world's hatred, on the coming joy, and on the prayer that will sustain the church to the end of the age. The High Priestly Prayer of chapter 17 — Jesus praying for his disciples and for all who will believe through their word — is among the most treasured passages in Scripture. John’s Gospel ends not with a great commission on a mountain but with a question on a beach: "Do you love me?" Everything hangs on the answer.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–18 — The Prologue: The Word Became Flesh
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before anything existed, the Word already was, with God and himself God, the maker of all things and the source of life and light. The world he had made did not recognise him, and his own people did not receive him; yet all who received him were given the right to become God’s children, born of God. The Word became flesh and lived among us, and the only Son, himself God and closest to the Father, has made him known.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Word is not an abstract principle but the personal Son of God, through whom all things were made and in whom life and light reside. Jesus is fully God, eternal with the Father, the one through whom all was created and the source of life, and becoming man did not make him any less God: the Word became flesh while remaining the Word. The Word simply was, while all things were made, and in verse 14 the Word himself became flesh: he never became God; he became man.

The new birth of verse 13 is denied three sources before its one source is named: not descent, not natural desire, not any human decision. A place among God’s children is given, not earned. The right of verse 12 is a standing God grants, and believers are called children (1:12; 11:52), while the Son is kept for Jesus alone; that keeps Christ unique, and shows the size of the gift: we are brought into the family of the one who is Son by nature.

Grace and truth (vv. 14, 17) echo the name God proclaimed to Moses at Sinai (Exodus 34:6), so verse 17 does not set Moses against Christ, a reading Jesus himself forbids (5:46). What Moses was shown in part has now come in person. And verse 18 closes the prologue: no one has seen God as he is, and the only one who has never left his side has made him known, by a life rather than a lecture.
verseByVerse.examples:
Whoever grasps from the prologue who Jesus is will read every later sign rightly. The Word was God, not a god, is one of the clearest statements of Christ’s full deity in Scripture.

The darkness has not overcome it is the sentence a reader in a dark season needs. It does not promise that the darkness will feel defeated; it says the dark has not put the light out.

Because nothing in the new birth was contributed by the one born, there is nothing in it he can later fail to keep up. That answers the Christian who cannot locate a moment of conversion: no one remembers being born, and the evidence of a birth is not a memory but a pulse, and the pulse is believing in Jesus now (1 John 5:1).

verseByVerse.quote: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. The Gospel of John was written by the apostle John, the son of Zebedee, the disciple whom Jesus loved (21:20–24), probably in Ephesus late in the first century, so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and by believing have life in his name (20:31). The prologue (vv. 1–18) is the overture, introducing the book’s themes: Word, life, light, darkness, witness, belief, glory, grace, truth. Its first two verses take us further back than any other page of the Bible, to the Son before the world, face to face with the Father, himself God.

In the beginning. The words deliberately echo the first words of Genesis 1:1. John begins a new Genesis, a new creation. But he goes further back than Genesis. Genesis says what happened in the beginning; John says what already existed in the beginning.

Was the Word. Not came to be, but was. The tense (imperfect) means continuous existence: there was never a moment when the Word was not.

Why the Word? Of all the titles available to him, Son, Lord, Christ, King, why open a Gospel with a noun that sounds like a piece of grammar? Because a word is the thing that comes out of a person and tells you what is inside him. You can watch a man for a year and learn very little. He says one sentence and you know something about him you could never have worked out by looking. God is not visible. But God has an eternal Word, not a sound he makes but a Person, his own Son, and that Person has now walked into a room and spoken to people who could hear him. A word expresses what is in the mind; Jesus expresses who God is.

A word for Jews and Greeks. A Jewish reader hears Genesis, a world that exists because God spoke (Genesis 1:3; Psalm 33:6), and the prophets, where the word of the LORD does the thing it was sent to do (Isaiah 55:11). A Greek reader hears logos, the reason holding the universe together, the thing his philosophers had been reaching for. John takes the noun both were straining after and does something neither expected with it. He does not say the Word is a principle. He says the Word had a face, and we ate with him.

And the Word was with God. “With” (pros) means face to face with, turned towards, in relationship with. The Word is distinct from God the Father, in eternal fellowship with him. Two persons, and between them not distance but communion. The wonder of it is this: love did not begin when God made someone to love. Before the world was made, the Father loved the Son (17:24), so love is not something God learned from his creatures; it is what he has always been (1 John 4:8).

And the Word was God. Not a god, not divine in some lesser sense, but fully God, God by nature. In Greek, “God” comes first for emphasis (theos ēn ho logos): God was the Word. The Word is distinct from the Father, yet himself God. Here is the foundation of the doctrine of the Trinity: not yet named, but already present.

Where Christians differ, and beyond. Jehovah’s Witnesses translate “the Word was a god”, arguing from the absence of the article before theos. This commentary’s view: this is grammatically mistaken. In Greek, a noun placed before the verb without the article usually stresses the nature or quality of the subject; here it does not mean “a god”. John means the Word was fully divine, all that God is, without being the same person as the Father. A “god” alongside God would be polytheism, which John, a Jew, utterly rejected. The church confessed it at Nicaea (325): true God from true God, of one substance with the Father.

The grammar in plain words. A reader may well have had this disputed on his own doorstep. John needs to say two things at once: the Word is not the same person as the Father (the Word was with God), and the Word is nonetheless everything the Father is (the Word was God). Had he written “the God”, with the article, he would have said the Word was the Father. And the very next verse closes the door: all things were made through him, so the Word cannot be among the things that were made. He stands on the Creator’s side of the line.

Watch the verbs. In these two verses the Word simply was, four times, in a tense with no starting point in view. From verse 3 the verb for everything else changes: all things came to be; there came to be a man sent from God (v. 6). And in verse 14 that second verb is finally used of the Word himself: the Word became flesh. He never became God. He became man. The whole passage is built on that switch of verbs.

He was in the beginning with God. Verse 2 is not padding but a guard. The Word was God, standing alone, could be heard as saying the Word simply is the Father under a second name. So, having said that the Word was God, John says once more that he was with God, so that neither truth cancels the other: there is one God, and the Son is not the Father. All this is in place before a single event has been told.

Does this mean there are three Gods? No. Christians believe in one God, as firmly as any Jew (Deuteronomy 6:4). But this one God exists eternally as Father, Son and Holy Spirit, three persons who share one and the same divine being. The Son is not a part of God, or a third of God, or a junior God; he is wholly God, as the Father is, and he is not the Father. No picture from creation captures it fully, and most attempts (water, ice and steam; one man as father, son and husband) end up teaching an old error: that God is one person wearing three masks. It is better to say what Scripture says and stop there: the Word was with God, and the Word was God. We do not believe it because we can picture it, but because God has said it, and because only a Saviour who is truly God can bring us to God.

If Jesus is God, who was he praying to? To his Father. Prayer between the Son and the Father is not God talking to himself; it is the eternal conversation of verse 1, overheard on earth. Before the world existed, the Father and the Son were face to face in love (17:5, 24). When the Son became man, that relationship did not stop; it was carried into a human life, so that the Son now prayed as a man, depended on his Father as a man, and obeyed as a man. The prayers in the Gospels are therefore not a problem for the doctrine of the Trinity. They are one of the clearest windows onto it.

The alternative is silence. The alternative to this sentence is not a neutral universe but a silent one. If the beginning was matter alone, the deepest thing about reality is force: impersonal, uninterested, and very old. On that view, which many thoughtful people honestly hold, everything warm arrives late and by accident, and will go out. John says the deepest thing about reality is a conversation. Before there was light or time or air to carry a voice, there was a Father and a Son, and they were not sitting in silence. Before anything existed that could hear him, God was speaking, and what he was saying was a Son.

In everyday life. Ask what you picture God doing before he made anything. If the honest answer is waiting, a solitary figure with nothing to occupy him until the world turned up, then you are praying to someone who needed you, and you will never quite shake the suspicion that you are a disappointing return on his loneliness. The God of this verse was not lonely. He made you out of a fullness already complete without you. He is a Father who had a Son to love before there was a universe, and who has decided to bring you into that love. Pray to him like that today.
verseByVerse.note: “In the beginning” deliberately echoes the first words of Genesis. “The Word” (Greek logos) was a term both Jews and Greeks understood: God’s self-expression, through which he created and revealed himself.

verseByVerse.quote: "All things were made through him, and without him was not any thing made that was made. In him was life, and the life was the light of men."
verseByVerse.commentary:
All things were made through him. The Father created all things through the Son (Colossians 1:16; Hebrews 1:2; 1 Corinthians 8:6). The scope is deliberately total: nothing that exists came into being apart from the Word. There is no eternal matter independent of God, and the Word is not one creative force among many. If all things were made through him, he himself was not made.

And without him was not any thing made that was made. John says it twice, once forward and once backward, and the second clause is a fence. There is no back door into existence: no raw material lying about, no dark thing that got in by another route. And it refutes the ancient heresy (Arianism) that the Son was the first and highest created being.

Everything that was used against him. That means something bracing about the world you woke up in. He made the wood the cross was cut from, and the ore in the ground that became the nails, and the hands that would drive them, and the breath in the lungs of the men swinging the hammers. Nothing was ever used against him that he had not first supplied. That is simply what all things means once you follow it into the story this Gospel is about to tell.

Why does my Bible punctuate this differently? The oldest manuscripts carry no punctuation, and some early readers ran the sentence on: without him was not anything made. That which has been made was life in him. Your Bible may carry a footnote to that effect. The difference is real but small: on either reading the Word is the Creator, and on either reading the life is in him. It is a question of where the full stop goes, not of what is being claimed.

In him was life. “Life” (zōē) occurs 36 times in John, and it means the life of God himself, eternal life. Everything alive has life the way a room has light at four in the afternoon: on loan, from elsewhere, and shortly to be withdrawn. In the Word life is not on loan. He does not have it; he is it (5:26), and he gives it.

What do you have that you did not receive? Nothing: not even your next breath (1 Corinthians 4:7). Whether that is terrifying or restful depends on what the giver is like, and John has twenty-one chapters to show you. (See 1 Corinthians 4:6–7 for the fuller answer.)

For the one sitting with a diagnosis. Say this carefully to the reader who has been given bad news, or who is watching someone thin out in a bed. The Christian hope at that point is not that life is generally stronger than death; it plainly is not, and pretending otherwise is cruelty dressed up as comfort. It is that there is one place in the universe where life was never borrowed and therefore cannot be called back in, and that this Gospel exists to tell you he has come within reach. He does not offer to extend the loan. He offers himself (11:25).

The light of men. How does life become light? In this Gospel light is the revelation of God, truth and salvation, as opposed to the darkness of sin, ignorance and death. It is what lets you see where you are, and, less comfortably, what shows up whatever else is in the room. By chapter 8 Jesus will say it outright: I am the light of the world (8:12). The light is not a body of teaching he brought with him but the overflow of the life he is. Nobody is illuminated by studying him from across the room. People are illuminated by being near him.

If he made everything, did he make evil? No. He made all things good (Genesis 1:31). Evil is not a thing God created but the ruin of good things he did create: a creature turning its God-given powers against him. Darkness is not a rival substance; it is what results when creatures turn from the light. That is why the next verse speaks of darkness opposing the light and failing. Nothing the Word made is evil in itself, not the body, not food, not sex, not work, not the material world, and nothing evil is outside his rule. He who made all things is able to remake them, and that is exactly what this Gospel is about to show him beginning to do.

For worship. The only one in the universe who has life in himself chose to die. The spring of all life went down into death, and on the third day came up out of it still the spring; and the life that is the light of men now shines on graves, because he has been in one and come out.

all things were created through him

verseByVerse.quote: "The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it. There was a man sent from God, whose name was John."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The light shines. The verbs in the opening lines are in the past: was, was made. This one is present, the first present tense in the passage, slipped in at the exact point where the darkness enters. The light is not afraid of the darkness; it shines into it. Whatever else has finished happening, this has not. It is going on while you read. It has been shining since before the first night fell. It shone in the garden after the fall, in the promise of a serpent-crusher. It shone through the long night of Egypt and the exile and the silent centuries. It walked into the darkest Friday the world has known and let the dark close over it, and on the third morning the dark gave it back.

And the darkness has not overcome it. The ESV notes that “overcome” can also be rendered “understood”. The Greek (katelaben) means to seize, to lay hold of, to take something and have it. It is used of an enemy overtaking a man on the road, and it is used of a mind finally getting hold of an idea. So the King James read it as comprehended and most modern versions read it as overcame, and both are honest translations of the same word.

Both meanings are true. John almost certainly wants both. The darkness in this Gospel tries to put the light out, and that is what Good Friday is, and it fails. And the darkness repeatedly fails to understand what it is looking at: a teacher of Israel who cannot follow a sentence about birth (3:10), Pharisees asking whether he means them (9:40). The sentence was built to carry the two. And its verb looks back on something settled: the dark is real and present, and so is the light, but the dark has already had its verdict handed down. It failed.

What it does not mean. A sentence this confident can be turned into a cruel demand that sufferers feel victorious. This verse does not promise that the darkness will feel defeated, or that the light is winning by any margin you can see from where you are standing. It says the dark did not put it out. If you are reading this in a season where God seems to have gone quiet and the light appears to be one candle in a very large room, you are not failing to believe the verse. You are living inside its first clause: the light shines in the darkness. It asks you only to notice that the light is still lit, and has been through much worse than yours.

If the light has won, why is there still so much darkness? Because the victory is decisive but not yet complete. At the cross and the empty tomb the darkness did its worst and lost; its defeat is settled. But God, in patience, has not yet ended the age, so that the light may go on shining into the dark and drawing people out of it (2 Peter 3:9). We live between the decisive battle and the final day, when there will be no night at all (Revelation 22:5). That is why the Christian is neither naive about evil nor despairing in front of it. The darkness is real, it is still dangerous, and it is already beaten.

A man sent from God. With no warning, we are out of eternity and in a wilderness with a man who has a name. This Gospel never calls him the Baptist. It has no need to: he is the only John it names, since the author never names himself. Sent from God marks a true prophet; a man, in contrast to the Word who was God. And the verb changes: there came to be a man. He has a start date. The Word does not.

The eternal with an address. Put verse 1 and verse 6 side by side: the eternal Word, and a man with a name and a place. The eternal has come to an address. Christianity’s strangest claim is not that God is eternal but that the eternal turned up in a particular decade, in a specific stretch of river, and that a man with a job and a diet was sent from God to point at him. After centuries of prophetic quiet, the first voice God sends in this Gospel is a man saying: look over there.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “overcome” can also be rendered “understood.” The John of verse 6 is John the Baptist.

verseByVerse.quote: "He came as a witness, to bear witness about the light, that all might believe through him. He was not the light, but came to bear witness about the light."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He came as a witness. “Witness” is one of the load-bearing beams of this Gospel, turning up with its related words nearly fifty times: John the Baptist, the Father, the Scriptures, Jesus’ works, the Spirit and the disciples all bear witness to Jesus (5:31–39). John is writing something shaped like a trial, and the reader is addressed not as an audience but as a jury. The Greek word is also the one from which we get martyr, because of what testimony repeatedly cost. The man in this verse would lose his head for it (Mark 6:27).

That all might believe through him. “Believe” (pisteuō) occurs about 98 times in John, but the noun faith never. For John, faith is an action: believing, trusting, coming, receiving. The goal of all witness is belief (20:31), and all the signs, discourses and encounters in this book are designed to produce it.

Through him. God could have arranged for people to believe without an intermediary, and he did not. He appointed a man with a strange diet and a rough manner, standing in a river, and routed faith through him (Romans 10:14). Almost certainly you can name the person it came through for you, and almost certainly they were not impressive.

He was not the light. Why would that need saying? Because John’s influence outlived him by decades: Paul met about twelve men at Ephesus who knew only John’s baptism (Acts 19:1–7). This flat denial is very probably a correction to a movement the author knew was still alive, and John himself said the same (v. 20; 3:28–30).

The signpost. John’s whole identity here is stated in negatives: not the light, and in a moment not the Christ, not Elijah, not the Prophet. That is not a diminishment. A signpost that people admire and stop at has failed. A signpost they walk straight past, on their way to where it pointed, has done the whole of its job.

A lamp and the Light. Jesus will later call John a burning and shining lamp (5:35): lit from somewhere else, burning itself down giving what it was given. The light in this prologue has no source behind it. The Baptist lost his head testifying to Christ; Christ gave his life testifying to the Father (18:37), and his death did what no witness’s death could do. He is the faithful witness (Revelation 1:5), and the truth he bore witness to was himself (14:6).

I am no John the Baptist. Can I still be a witness? Yes. A witness is not someone with special training but someone who tells what he knows to be true. You may not be able to explain the Trinity or answer every objection, but you can say who Jesus is, what he has done, and what he has done for you. John himself was simply a man sent from God to say what he had seen (vv. 6–7), and the man born blind did the same with almost no theology at all: one thing I do know, that though I was blind, now I see (9:25). Witness happens over a kitchen table, in a hospital corridor, in an honest answer when someone asks why you still go to church. And the results are not yours to produce. A witness is responsible for the truth of his testimony, not for the verdict of the jury.

parallels.desc: he was a burning and shining lamp

verseByVerse.quote: "The true light, which gives light to everyone, was coming into the world. He was in the world, and the world was made through him, yet the world did not know him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The true light. “True” (alēthinon) means genuine, real, as opposed to imitations and shadows. It is a favourite word in John: the true bread (6:32), the true vine (15:1). Jesus is the reality to which all other lights point. Every human experience of light, beauty, reason and goodness is a dim reflection of the one who is the source.

Which gives light to everyone. Every human being receives some light from the Word: the light of reason, conscience, and the knowledge of God through creation (Romans 1:19–20; 2:14–15). Not that everyone is saved, but that everyone is accountable. Theologians call this common grace: God’s kindness to everyone, believer or not, which does not save but gives all people some knowledge of God and of right and wrong, holds back evil and makes life bearable: he sends rain on the just and on the unjust (Matthew 5:45).

Was coming into the world. The Word’s coming as a man. The phrase can attach to the light (the true light was coming into the world) or to everyone, as the older versions read it: the light that lights every man that comes into the world. The Greek allows both, and the difference is not doctrinally serious.

What it does not mean. Gives light to everyone has been made to carry a great deal: that all people are already savingly enlightened, that every religion is a road up the same mountain. But John settles it in the next breath: the light shone on the world, and the world did not know him. The sun rising over a city is not the same thing as the city waking up.

No one outside its reach. What the verse does secure is real and worth having. There is no human being who is simply outside the reach of this light. Every flicker of conscience, every ache after beauty, every stubborn refusal to believe that cruelty is merely a preference: all of it is light, and it is his, and it is falling on people who have never heard his name.

So what about people who have never heard of Jesus? They are not without light: creation and conscience speak to them of God, and they are accountable for what they know (Romans 1:20; 2:14–15). But that light, by itself, has never saved anyone, because the human heart suppresses it. Scripture teaches that salvation comes through conscious faith in Christ, for there is no other name by which we must be saved (Acts 4:12), and faith comes from hearing the word of Christ (Romans 10:14–17). That is not a reason for despair but for mission. God is not limited; he has sent his gospel to the ends of the earth and saves people in every nation through it. The right response to this question is to pray, to give, and to go.

World three times. He came into the world he had made. John says world three times in a single sentence, and each time it turns the knife. There is no villain named, no plot described; the tragedy is done entirely with a repeated noun.

Did not know him. “The world” (kosmos), about 78 times in John, here means humanity in rebellion against God. Isaiah had found the image: the ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master’s crib, but Israel does not know (Isaiah 1:3). The creation stood in the presence of the one who specified every atom in it and registered nothing. And this is said before any hostility begins. The first thing said about the world’s response to God arriving in it is not that it fought him. It is that it did not notice. The Maker walked into his workshop and the tools did not know his hand. He came anyway, knowing he would be unrecognised, and he came for the very people who looked straight at him and saw nothing.

Would I have known him? Almost certainly not. That is the plain sense of the verse, and it is meant to land. The people best equipped to recognise him, the ones with the Scriptures, the calendar, the prophecies, the daily sacrifices, are precisely the ones this Gospel will show missing him. If recognising God depended on being religious, well taught or sincere, the record of the first century is against you. Which is exactly why the next few verses do not go where you expect. Having established that nobody recognised him, John does not turn round and urge the reader to look harder. He says something else entirely, and it arrives in verse 13: those who did receive him were born of God. Recognition was never going to come from the side of the ones who could not see. It had to be given.

parallels.desc: a light for the nations

verseByVerse.quote: "He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him. But to all who did receive him, who believed in his name, he gave the right to become children of God,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
He came to his own. John changes the gender of a word halfway through the sentence, and the tragedy is in the change. The first his own is neuter and plural in Greek: his own things, his own home, Israel, to whom he had given the law, the prophets and the promises.

Did not receive him. Now the word is masculine: his own folk, the household. He came home, and the family would not let him in. The verb is the one used for welcoming somebody in off the road. He was not turned away at a border by strangers; he was left standing at his own door by people who knew the address because it was theirs too.

They were not badly prepared. They had the Scriptures, the temple, the calendar, and a national hope built around his arrival. The failure did not happen for want of information. It happened because a Messiah who came to rule them, and not to approve them as they were, threatened what they already had: their standing, their righteousness, their control of the temple (11:48). Religion can be the best hiding place from God there is, and the first to shut the door on him were the people most at home in his house.

When your own family will not receive him. Some who follow Christ pay for it at home: a father who stopped speaking, a family who treat the faith as an embarrassment, a husband or wife who did not sign up for this. If that is you, this verse puts you in company you did not expect. He knows what it is to be the odd one in his own house, from further in than you do, because his own people eventually killed him. Keep loving them, keep praying, and keep the door open from your side (1 Peter 3:1–2).

But to all. Then but, and the sentence turns. Some did, and all means whoever they are, Jew or Gentile, from anywhere.

In his name. To receive him is to believe in him: the same act described from two angles. To believe in his name is to rest your whole weight on Jesus as the one he says he is (20:31): not admiring him from a distance, but trusting him with yourself.

The right. The word is exousia: not power or ability but authority, legal standing. God does not merely make it possible for people to be his children; he confers the standing, and it holds because of who conferred it. That is worth having on a day when you do not feel like anybody’s child. Your standing was not issued by your feelings and is not withdrawn by them.

Children. Across this Gospel, Son of God is Jesus’ title alone; believers are called children of God. That takes nothing from the gift; it keeps clear how we come by it. Jesus is Son by eternal right; we are children by gift, by adoption through faith in Christ (Galatians 4:4–7; Romans 8:14–17).

Become. Not discover, not realise. Something happened to them that had not happened before. In one sense God is the Father of all: he made and sustains everyone (Acts 17:28). But John means more than that. By creation everyone is God’s creature. Only by a new birth does anyone become his child.

Is believing then my contribution? A careful reader will feel the pressure here, and ought to. If the right is given to those who receive and believe, has the believing not just become the qualifying act, the one contribution that is finally mine? Verse 13 exists to shut that door, and John shuts it before anyone can get a foot in it. Those who believe are those who were born, not of the will of man, but of God. Faith is truly yours: you believe, and you are commanded to. But it is never a payment you hand over. It is the empty hand of a child who has already been given life.

In everyday life. Ask what word rises first when you think of God, and be honest. Judge. Employer. Landlord, keeping an eye on the property. Distant relative. Or Father. Not which word you can defend, but which one your stomach reaches for at four in the morning when something has gone wrong. When you pray today, begin with Father: God has sent the Spirit of his Son into your heart to cry it (Galatians 4:6).

If my own father failed me. Say the plain thing to whoever needs it: if your own father was absent, or frightening, or simply never much interested, you are not disqualified from this verse; you are its natural audience. The word Father is not being defined for you by the man who taught you to flinch at it. It is being defined by the Son who is going to spend twenty chapters showing you what his own Father is like.

For worship. He came home and was shut out, so that strangers could be let in. And on the morning he rose, the Son who alone is Son by right sent word: go to my brothers and say to them, I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God (20:17).
verseByVerse.note: “His own” is Israel, God’s own people.

parallels.desc: sons of God through faith

verseByVerse.quote: "who were born, not of blood nor of the will of the flesh nor of the will of man, but of God. And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not of blood. John says the new birth is God’s work three times in the negative first, and each denial closes a door people have actually tried to get in by. Not of blood (the Greek is plural, bloods, from the thought that a child came from the mingled blood of both parents): not descent. Being born a Jew, or into a Christian family, does not make you a child of God. A godly mother is one of the great mercies of God, and she is not a birth certificate. Grace does not travel down a bloodline.

Nor of the will of the flesh. The second door is natural desire, the bodily desire by which children are conceived. Nothing we have by being human can produce this birth.

Nor of the will of man. Here the word is the specific one for a male, a husband, a father. In the Greek and Roman world the head of the house decided whether a newborn was acknowledged into the family at all. John says: not that either. No one can decide you into God’s family: not your father, not a minister, not a church roll, and, hardest to hear, not you. The decisive vote is not yours to cast.

But of God. Three closed doors and then one open one. Becoming God’s child is a new birth, and its source is God alone (3:3–8; James 1:18; 1 Peter 1:3). As in verse 3, John shuts out every other source, so that the birth can be credited to no one but God.

Where Christians differ: faith and new birth. Arminians teach that a person, enabled by grace, chooses to believe, and is then born again; on that view “not of the will of man” rules out only natural descent and human effort as the source of life, not a free human decision to believe. This commentary’s view: Reformed theology reads verses 12–13 together: those who believe are those born of God, not of the will of man. The new birth is God’s sovereign work, which produces faith (1 John 5:1, where “everyone who believes … has been born of God”, perfect tense). We believe because we have been born of God, not the reverse. Yet we truly believe, and are commanded to.

Then why should I preach, or call anyone to believe? Because God gives the new birth through his word (James 1:18; 1 Peter 1:23). The same Jesus who says no one can come unless the Father draws him (6:44) stands and cries out, if anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink (7:37). The call is sincere and it is for everyone. We do not know who God is bringing to life; we only know that he does it as the gospel is spoken. A sovereign new birth is not a reason to keep quiet. It is the only reason to expect anything when we speak, because we are talking to people who cannot raise themselves, and we know who can.

When you cannot find the moment. Some Christians go cold at this verse, because being born again makes them look for a date, and there is no date. They have believed as far back as they can remember, and they conclude that whatever happened to others has probably not happened to them. But nobody remembers being born, and nobody treats that as grounds for doubting it happened. You establish your birth not by memory but by breathing. John gives the present-tense evidence in his first letter: we know that we have passed out of death into life, because we love the brothers (1 John 3:14). Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God (1 John 5:1): if you are believing, you have been born. The birth is behind the faith as its cause, not in front of it as its reward.

A pulse, not a feeling. Run the honest test. Do you want things you did not use to want? Has sin you once enjoyed gone quietly sour on you? Do you pray when nobody would know if you did not? Have you had every reason to walk away from Christ and found that you could not? None of those is a feeling. All of them are a pulse. But this must not become a false comfort. If nothing in that list is true of you, the news is not that you should look harder for a memory. It is that God gives new birth, and that you may ask him for it.

And the Word became flesh. This is the heart of the prologue, and of the Christian faith. The verb of beginning, used until now only of created things, is at last used of him. The eternal Word became a real human being, with a human body and soul. Not merely appeared to be human, as the Docetists, an early group who thought matter beneath God, taught (1 John 4:2–3). Not changed into a man, ceasing to be God. He took human nature to himself while remaining what he was. He did not visit flesh, or wear it like a coat and take it off again. He became it.

Flesh. Look at which noun John picks. He does not write that the Word became a man, though that is true. He does not write that he took a body. He writes sarx, flesh, which is the crudest, weakest, most mortal word available to him. It is the word for what a man is when you consider that he gets tired, gets hungry, gets thirsty, bleeds when cut, and dies: human nature in its weakness and mortality. John, who has spent thirteen verses climbing to the highest claim in the New Testament, sets the two words side by side without a cushion between them: the Word, and flesh. Many of the great errors about the person of Christ in the next four hundred years were attempts to soften that collision, and John’s own letters show him already fighting such attempts (1 John 4:2–3).

Make it concrete. It is meant to be. It means he had to be taught to walk and fell over doing it. It means teeth coming through, and splinters in a carpenter’s hands, and sweat, and the particular kind of tiredness where you fall asleep in a boat in a storm. It means that at some point somebody changed God’s nappies. God did not send a message, or a projection, or an appearance. He arrived in a body that could be hurt. God became what we are, so that we could become what he made us to be.

Did he stop being God when he became man? No. The Word became flesh by taking human nature to himself, not by setting aside his divine nature. He did not exchange one for the other, and he did not blend them into something in between. He is one person, truly God and truly man, the two natures joined without confusion and without separation (the Westminster Confession 8.2; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 8.2). As man he grew tired and wept and died; as God he upheld the universe throughout (Hebrews 1:3). He laid aside his glory’s display, not his deity. That is why his death can save: it is the death of a real man, in our place, and the life of the one who dies is the life of God.

And dwelt among us. “Dwelt” means literally pitched his tent (eskēnōsen), tabernacled, and John reaches back to Exodus. Israel in the wilderness, with no land and no temple, builds a tent to God’s specification, and the glory of the LORD fills it so completely that Moses cannot go in (Exodus 25:8; 40:34–35). That is where God chose to live: in a portable structure of goat hair and dyed skins in the middle of the camp, moved when they moved. From the outside it was the least impressive dwelling imaginable. Inside it was unbearable with glory.

This time the tent was a body. Outside, a plain exterior that nobody in Nazareth found worth a second look; inside, the glory. He is the true tabernacle, the place where God meets his people. And it is a tent: thirty-odd years is a short stay. But the Bible ends with the same word coming back: the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them (Revelation 21:3). The tent was temporary. God’s living among us was not.

And we have seen his glory. “We”: John and the apostles, eyewitnesses who kept looking (1 John 1:1–3). “Glory” (doxa) is the visible radiance of God’s presence that filled the tabernacle. The apostles saw it in his signs (2:11), and supremely at the cross, which John calls his glorification (12:23; 17:1). John never even narrates the transfiguration. The glory these men saw was chiefly a man dying a shameful death in public, so do not look for God’s glory only in whatever is going well.

The only Son. “Only Son” (older versions, only begotten) means unique: he is the Father’s Son as no one else is, sharing his nature (see v. 18).

Full of grace and truth. This phrase unlocks the verses that follow. Go back to Sinai. Moses asks, please show me your glory, and is put in a cleft of the rock while God passes by proclaiming his name: the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness (Exodus 34:6). The last two words in the Hebrew are hesed and emet: covenant love and covenant faithfulness, the two things you most need to be true about anyone you stake your life on. What Moses was given a fraction of, from behind, through a crack in a rock, these men watched cook breakfast on a beach (21:9–13).

Why does grace come before truth? Because that is how God revealed himself on Sinai: steadfast love first, then faithfulness. In Jesus they are never separated. His grace is not soft on sin, and his truth is not hard on sinners. He tells the woman caught in adultery that he does not condemn her, and then that she must go and sin no more (8:11, in a passage missing from the earliest manuscripts, as most modern Bibles note). Grace without truth would be sentiment that leaves us as we are; truth without grace would be a sentence we could not survive. In him we receive both whole, and we are meant to carry both into how we treat one another.

For worship. The tent he pitched among us was meant to be taken down: destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up (2:19, 21). The Son took flesh so that it could be torn for us, and then raised, and it is flesh still, at the right hand of the Father. God has a human face now, and he will keep it for ever.
verseByVerse.note: “Dwelt” means literally “pitched his tent” — God’s presence among his people, as in the tabernacle.

parallels.desc: that I may dwell in their midst
abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness
born of the Spirit

verseByVerse.quote: "(John bore witness about him, and cried out, 'This was he of whom I said, "He who comes after me ranks before me, because he was before me."') For from his fullness we have all received, grace upon grace."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Cried out. Loudly, publicly, like a herald. Twice now the great poem about the eternal Word has been interrupted by a man with a name and a location: this Gospel refuses to let the Word float free of history. And the Baptist has probably been dead some sixty years by the time this is written, and the testimony is still ringing.

Three time-words. The riddle packs three different time-words into one sentence. Later in arrival. Ahead in rank. Earlier in existence. The middle claim is explained by the third, and the third could be said of no one else in Israel. Jesus came after John in time, but ranks above him in dignity, because he existed before him, eternally (8:58).

An older relative’s claim. John the Baptist was born about six months before Jesus (Luke 1:26, 36), an older relative. So here is a man pointing at a younger relative and saying: he existed before I did. There is no polite way to hear that sentence. It is either the claim of the prologue or it is madness, and the man saying it staked his life on it.

His fullness. The word is plērōma: everything that is in him, nothing held back (Colossians 1:19; 2:9). And the word that governs it is all. The oldest saint you know and the person converted last Tuesday are drawing from the same supply, and neither is drawing on a smaller tap.

Grace upon grace. Literally grace in place of grace. The picture is not a heap but a succession: grace giving way to grace, the way waves arrive. No wave is the last one. Nobody is on their last grace: there is another one behind it, and behind that one a fullness that has not been touched. Some read it as the grace of the new covenant in place of the grace of the old (v. 17). Either way, endless grace. Wave after wave it comes, and the sea is not lowered.

Am I running out of grace? Most of us, somewhere in the middle years, quietly start doing arithmetic: I have confessed this same sin so many times now, I have had my share, whatever I was given at the beginning must be getting thin by this point. That is the arithmetic of a fixed quantity, and it is the wrong arithmetic entirely. The grace you are living on this morning is not the grace of your conversion, stretched and rationed and going grey at the edges. It is a new one. The old one did its work and was replaced, and this is what has been happening every day since, whether or not you noticed a single one of them.

What it does not mean. Grace that keeps arriving can be misheard as grace that does not mind. A wave is not a shrug. The supply outlasts your failures; it is not indifferent to them. The man who concludes he may now sin comfortably has missed whose fullness it is coming out of (Romans 6:1–2).

How do I actually receive grace? By coming to Christ himself, again and again, with empty hands. Grace is not a substance stored up in sacraments or earned by effort; it is the favour and help of God given to us in his Son. We receive it as we trust him, and God has given us ordinary means by which he keeps feeding that trust: his word read and preached, prayer, the Lord’s Supper, baptism, and the fellowship of his people. None of them is magic, and none of them is optional for a hungry soul. Go to them not to earn anything but to receive, the way a child goes to the table.
verseByVerse.note: John was born about six months before Jesus; “he was before me” points to Jesus’ existence before his birth.

parallels.desc: in him all the fullness of God was pleased to dwell

verseByVerse.quote: "For the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ. No one has ever seen God; God the only Son, who is at the Father's side, he has made him known."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Given through Moses. The law was a gift of God, good and holy (Romans 7:12), revealing God’s will and exposing sin. It was given: God was the giver, and Moses the one through whom it came.

Came through Jesus Christ. Here is the prologue’s own verb of arrival, used when the Word became flesh. The law was handed over; grace and truth walked in. Not that there was no grace in the law, but that the fullness of grace and truth came in Jesus. The law could command but not give the power to obey.

Moses is not the villain. Jesus in this very Gospel forbids setting the two men against each other: if you believed Moses, you would believe me; for he wrote of me (5:46). Moses is a witness on Jesus’ side. And grace and truth echoes what God called himself on Sinai (Exodus 34:6), so the sentence is not saying Moses got the rules and we got the kindness. The same grace and truth have now come up the road on two feet. Moses had the account. We have the person the account was about.

Does this mean Christians can ignore the Old Testament law? No, but we read it through Christ. The law still shows us God’s holy character and our sin, and its moral heart, summed up in the Ten Commandments, still describes how love for God and neighbour behaves (Matthew 22:37–40; Romans 13:8–10). What has changed is our relation to it. We are not justified by keeping it, that is, we are not declared right with God on the basis of our obedience, because Christ kept it for us and bore its curse (Galatians 3:13). The ceremonial laws of sacrifice and cleanness were shadows, and Christ is the substance (Hebrews 10:1). And now the Spirit writes the law on our hearts, so that we obey from love rather than fear (Jeremiah 31:33).

Jesus Christ. A small thing worth noticing in passing: this is the first time the full name Jesus Christ appears in the Gospel, and one of only two places John writes it. He has spent seventeen verses on the Word, the light, the life, the only Son, and then, at the moment the eternal meets the historical, he puts down a man’s name and his title, as if to say: this one, the one you have heard of.

No one has ever seen God. God in his essence is invisible (Exodus 33:20; 1 Timothy 6:16). But a reader who knows his Old Testament will object: Moses and the elders saw the God of Israel and ate and drank (Exodus 24:9–11); Isaiah saw the Lord high and lifted up (Isaiah 6:1). John means that nobody has seen God as he is in himself, unveiled. And he says more later: of Isaiah’s vision, Isaiah saw his glory and spoke of him, meaning Christ (12:41). The Old Testament sightings of God were not exceptions to this verse. They were early appearances of the one this verse is about.

God the only Son. The ESV notes the readings “the only One, who is God” and, in some manuscripts, “the only Son”. The best manuscripts read monogenēs theos, God the only Son. Either way the sentence teaches the same thing, and the older evidence points to the reading that calls him God, so the prologue ends as it began: the Word is God.

Begotten, not made. Begotten does not mean Jesus had a beginning. The Greek word means one of a kind; Isaac is called by it in Hebrews 11:17, though Abraham had another son. It speaks of uniqueness of relationship, not origin in time, which is why the Nicene Creed insists on begotten, not made: he was not created. He is, and always was, the Father’s own.

Who is at the Father’s side. Literally in the bosom of the Father, the place of closest intimacy. John uses the word once more: at the last supper one disciple is lying at Jesus’ side, the same word, kolpos (13:23). The position the Son eternally occupies with the Father is the position John found himself given with the Son.

He has made him known. “Made known” (exēgēsato), from which comes exegesis, the explaining of a text: to draw out into the open, to tell in full. In the Greek the verb has no object. The sentence ends: he has explained. He himself is the explanation. The one person in existence who has never been anywhere but the Father’s side has come out and told us, and the telling was a life. Jesus is the explanation of God: whoever has seen me has seen the Father (14:9).

If Jesus shows us God, what about the hard parts of the Old Testament? They are not a different God. The same Lord who drowned Pharaoh’s army wept over Jerusalem; the same Jesus who welcomed sinners overturned tables in the temple and warned of hell more than anyone in Scripture. Jesus does not cancel God’s holiness and judgment; he reveals them at their most intense, at the cross, where God’s wrath against sin fell on his own Son. What he shows us is that God’s justice and his mercy meet in one place. So read the hard passages in the light of Christ, not against him. Where they puzzle you, trust the character of the God you have seen in Jesus while you keep studying.

In everyday life. Most of us carry a picture of God assembled out of odds and ends: what our father was like, our temperament, the last sermon that frightened us. Take one thing on that picture you are fairly sure of: that he is disappointed in you, say, or reluctant, or hard to get hold of. Now ask where you would find that in Jesus Christ. If it is not in him, it is not in God, because he is God’s own explanation of himself, and there is no other.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes the readings “the only One, who is God” and, in some manuscripts, “the only Son.” “At the Father’s side” is literally “in the bosom of the Father” — the place of closest intimacy.

parallels.desc: no one may see me and live
whoever has seen me has seen the Father

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–51 — The Testimony of John and the First Disciples
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The week of witness begins. John the Baptist tells the delegation from Jerusalem what he is not, and calls himself only a voice preparing the Lord’s way. The next day he points to Jesus as the Lamb of God, on whom he saw the Spirit come down and remain. Then the witness bears fruit: two of John’s disciples follow Jesus, Andrew brings Simon, and Philip brings Nathanael, the sceptic who confesses Jesus as Son of God and King of Israel. Jesus promises greater things: heaven opened over the Son of Man.
verseByVerse.theology:
This section shows how testimony works: John testifies to Jesus, Andrew to Simon, Philip to Nathanael, and each one who meets Jesus points another to him. The titles accumulate (Lamb of God, Son of God, Rabbi, Messiah, King of Israel, Son of Man), each true, each partial, each pointing to the one who exceeds them all. Faith begins with testimony and ends in meeting him: Come and see.

Two cautions belong here. The Jews, first used in this section, usually means the Jerusalem authorities, not a people: the author, every disciple and Jesus himself are Jews, and salvation is from the Jews (4:22). And the Lamb should not be tied to one background: John’s frame is Passover (19:14, 36), but takes away the sin echoes Isaiah 53, the only lamb that bears sin.

The call by the Sea of Galilee in Matthew and Mark is not a rival version of this meeting but a later summons: here men meet Jesus and begin to believe, and later they leave their nets for good. Faith by stages is the normal pattern, which is also the point of verses 50–51, where a man who has believed for minutes is promised greater things, and the greater things include a cross.
verseByVerse.examples:
Behold, the Lamb of God gathers the Passover lamb (Exodus 12), the daily sacrifice (Exodus 29:38–42), the servant led like a lamb to the slaughter (Isaiah 53:7) and the Lamb who alone is worthy (Revelation 5) into one person.

Nobody in this section recruits by argument. Andrew fetches his brother with a five-word sentence. Philip’s testimony is incomplete twice over (Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph), and Nathanael came anyway: nobody waits for a witness to be finished before he is useful.

Two cautions. Andrew won his brother the same day, but that is the exception; Jesus’ own brothers did not believe during his ministry (7:5), and this chapter does not rebuke anyone who has prayed for a relative for decades. And I saw you under the fig tree comforts the believer whose faithfulness nobody is counting, and exposes the one with something to hide; but the one who sees everything is the one who came to take away the sin of the world, and he mentions the tree and says nothing else.

verseByVerse.quote: And this is the testimony of John, when the Jews sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to ask him, "Who are you?" He confessed, and did not deny, but confessed, "I am not the Christ."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The narrative begins. After the prologue, John’s Gospel opens with a week of testimony (1:19–2:11), ending at the wedding in Cana, and it starts with an interrogation.

The Jews. This phrase turns up some seventy times in this Gospel, and because it has been put to appalling use it is worth stopping over at its first occurrence. In John the Jews often means the Jewish religious authorities in Jerusalem who opposed Jesus: the men who send delegations, convene meetings and eventually take a case to Pilate. Sometimes it simply means Jewish people or customs (2:6; 4:9), but it is never a verdict on a whole people. John was a Jew. Every disciple in this book is a Jew. Its central figure is a Jew who keeps the feasts and says that salvation is from the Jews (4:22).

What it does not mean. What is being described is an argument inside a family about the family’s own hope, which is the sharpest kind of argument there is, and the moment it is read as one people’s verdict on another it has been turned inside out. Christians have done that, at scale, with results that do not bear describing. The term must never be used to justify hatred of Jewish people. Read the phrase as the Gospel uses it: the authorities in Jerusalem, and not your neighbour.

Sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem. An official delegation, perhaps from the Sanhedrin, the ruling council, to establish by what authority an unlicensed man is conducting a religious rite in the open country. Levites assisted the priests and also served as temple police. Inquiries are opened when something has grown large enough to be a problem.

Who are you? It is the question the whole Gospel is about: who is Jesus? First they ask John. It is the right question, asked of the wrong man, by people who will shortly be standing within a few feet of the answer without recognising him.

He confessed. Emphatic and freely given, though the moment offered him a real opportunity. People were questioning in their hearts whether he might be the Christ (Luke 3:15); the delegation had come to him, and a career was available. He puts it down in the first sentence he speaks in this Gospel. The word is the one used elsewhere for confessing Christ publicly when it costs you. Here what he confesses is what he is not.

I am not the Christ. “I” is emphatic: I am not; someone else is. John shines only by reflected light.

The question comes back to Jesus. The same men will put the same question to the right man: who are you? (8:25); if you are the Christ, tell us plainly (10:24). John answers by stepping out of the question. Jesus answers by saying openly who he is, often to people who had not asked: I who speak to you am he (4:26). And in the end it is his claim about himself that they will take to Pilate (19:7).

In everyday life. This temptation usually arrives as an offer: somebody credits you with more wisdom or spirituality than is true, and the correction would be awkward. John corrected his in front of an official delegation, at the height of his influence. You are already accepted in Christ and need no one’s overestimate, so when someone leans on you this week as if you were more than you are, say so, and point them to him.
verseByVerse.note: In John’s Gospel “the Jews” often means the Jewish religious authorities in Jerusalem.

parallels.desc: whether he might be the Christ

verseByVerse.quote: And they asked him, "What then? Are you Elijah?" He said, "I am not." "Are you the Prophet?" And he answered, "No."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Are you Elijah? Many expected Elijah to return before the Messiah. Malachi, the last of the prophets in our Old Testament, closes by promising that God will send Elijah the prophet before the great and awesome day of the LORD (Malachi 4:5): the last word of the prophets before some four centuries of silence, and therefore the thing everyone was still waiting for when the silence broke. John dressed like Elijah (2 Kings 1:8; Mark 1:6). Jesus said John was Elijah, in the sense of fulfilling Elijah’s role (Matthew 11:14; 17:12–13). But John denies being Elijah literally returned.

I am not. Watch the three answers shrink. I am not the Christ: a full sentence. I am not: three words. No: one. By the next verse he will not claim to be a person at all, only a sound.

One says I am not, so another can say I am. John has said egō ouk eimi, I am not (v. 20). Jesus will use the formula again and again without the negative: egō eimi, I am the bread of life, the light of the world, the good shepherd. Before Jesus says I am, the greatest of the prophets says I am not, and so leaves the phrase free for him.

Are you the Prophet? The Prophet refers to Deuteronomy 18:15–18, the prophet like Moses whom God would raise up, to whom Israel must listen. Peter later identified him with Jesus (Acts 3:22). The delegation is working through the list of expected figures, and John answers with a single word: no. He refuses every title. All the titles he refused belong to another, and that other wears them all: the true Prophet like Moses, the Lord whose day Elijah heralded, the Christ. Every crown John set down, Jesus picks up, and they fit.

So was John Elijah or not? Yes in role, no in person. The angel had told his father that he would go before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elijah (Luke 1:17), which is exactly what Jesus later says he did (Matthew 11:14). Jesus is describing a role; John is refusing a reputation. What John will not accept is the popular version: the returned prophet as a figure in his own right, with his own following, around whom a movement could be built. His denial is not a contradiction but humility. He will not allow the crowds to construct an identity around him that would compete with the one coming after.
verseByVerse.note: Many expected Elijah to return before the Messiah; “the Prophet” is the prophet like Moses whom Moses promised.

parallels.desc: I will send you Elijah
a prophet like me
he is Elijah who is to come

verseByVerse.quote: So they said to him, "Who are you? We need to give an answer to those who sent us. What do you say about yourself?" He said, "I am the voice of one crying out in the wilderness, 'Make straight the way of the Lord,' as the prophet Isaiah said."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who are you? Again, and the pressure in the question is very human. We need to give an answer to those who sent us: they have to file a report. Somebody in Jerusalem is expecting a finding, and this man keeps saying what he is not. Give us something to write down.

The voice. What he gives them is barely anything at all (Isaiah 40:3): not a person with a title, but a voice. A voice exists only while it is being used, and then the words it carried go on without it. Jesus is the Word; John is only the voice.

Isaiah 40, the turn to comfort. Isaiah 40 is the great turn in that book, from judgment to comfort, addressed to exiles who have concluded that God has lost interest. Comfort, comfort my people, it opens, and then a voice: prepare the way of the LORD. The picture behind it is a road gang. When a king was coming, the road was made ready: hollows filled, rocks cleared, because a monarch does not pick his way over broken ground. John is not the king or the escort. He is the man out in front with the news that someone is coming and the road is in no condition for it.

The LORD himself is coming. In Isaiah the one announced is the LORD himself, and John applies it to a man who will walk up to him next morning: so, like the prologue, he is saying that this man is the LORD. And this comfort was spoken to people who had been waiting so long they had stopped expecting anything. That is who the announcement is for.

Make straight the way of the Lord. Prepare the road by repentance, and preparing the way is not decoration; it is demolition and haulage. In the sermons John actually preached it turned out to be quite specific: what you do with your coat and your food, how you handle money, whether you use your position to squeeze people (Luke 3:10–14). He did not tell them to feel differently. He gave them roadworks.

What does making straight the way look like for me? It means clearing out of the way whatever you know Christ would have to step over to reach you. Name it specifically: the grudge you are nursing, the money you are handling dishonestly, the habit you keep hidden, the relationship you know is wrong, the apology you owe. Confess it to God, and where it involves others, put it right. You do not do this to earn his coming; he is coming anyway, and he comes to sinners. You do it because a heart that is busy defending its rubble cannot welcome a king.

parallels.desc: the voice in the wilderness

verseByVerse.quote: (Now they had been sent from the Pharisees.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sent from the Pharisees. A single verse, and it changes who is in the room (the Greek can also mean that some Pharisees had been sent, a second group). The first delegation was the temple’s clergy; this note names a different group behind the sending, one we will meet throughout the Gospel.

Who the Pharisees actually were. They were not the temple establishment, which was the wealthy priestly families, mostly of the rival Sadducee party. The Pharisees were a lay movement: a few thousand men, many of them tradesmen and teachers, who took the law of God with complete seriousness in the details of an ordinary week. They tithed their herbs, knew the Scriptures by heart, and believed in the resurrection and the coming Messiah. Ordinary people admired them enormously. If sincerity had been enough, or knowledge of the Bible, or moral effort, they would have been first at the river. It was not enough.

The righteousness they were missing. What the Pharisees wanted was right: a people fit to stand before God when he came. Every tithed herb was reaching after a righteousness that would at last be enough, and the only righteousness that ever was enough was about to be lived out a few yards away by a man from Nazareth and then counted to sinners who trust him. A Pharisee of the strictest kind said so later: not having a righteousness of my own that comes from the law, but that which comes through faith in Christ (Philippians 3:8–9).

What it does not mean. When a Christian says Pharisee he almost always means someone stricter than himself, and that is nearly the opposite of the truth. The Pharisee problem is not strictness. It is being so certain you are on God’s side that there is nothing God could do that would surprise you, and therefore nothing he could do that you would recognise. That condition is available at every point on the scale of strictness, and most available to those who have been right about something for a long time.

Should I then distrust every careful, serious Christian? No. Taking God’s word seriously in the details of life is good, and the New Testament commands it. Nicodemus, a Pharisee, came to Jesus (3:1), and Paul was one before Christ found him (Philippians 3:5). The danger is not seriousness but self-trust: relying on our own record to stand before God, and refusing to be corrected by him. The cure is not to become careless but to become humble, to keep your Bible open in front of you rather than behind you, and to keep asking God to show you where you are wrong.

verseByVerse.quote: They asked him, "Then why are you baptizing, if you are neither the Christ, nor Elijah, nor the Prophet?" John answered them, "I baptize with water, but among you stands one you do not know."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then why are you baptizing. Baptism was associated with the cleansing God promised for the messianic age (Ezekiel 36:25; Zechariah 13:1). Ritual washing was ordinary in Judaism, but one washing marked entry into the covenant people from outside: later Jewish sources describe Gentile converts being circumcised and immersed, washed clean of their paganism. Whether that practice was already established in John’s day is debated, but the offence was felt either way.

Jews washed like outsiders. John is baptising Jews: sons of Abraham wading into a river to be washed as though they needed to come in from outside. Hence the question: by what authority do you treat the covenant people as outsiders? It was a sermon preached without a word: your ancestry will not do it; you need cleansing, in public.

I baptize with water. Only water: an outward sign. His answer does not defend his credentials at all. He changes the subject to the only subject.

One you do not know. Among you: in this crowd, not somewhere else. Stands: present and settled; he has been here while you were asking your questions. And these are the best-informed religious men in the country, standing within yards of him, investigating the wrong man. The Lord of glory stands among ordinary people, unannounced, unhurried, waiting to be known.

Was John’s baptism the same as Christian baptism? Not quite. John’s was a baptism of repentance, preparing Israel for the coming one; Christian baptism is into the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, a sign of union with the Christ who has now died and risen (Matthew 28:19; Romans 6:3–4). That is why the disciples Paul met at Ephesus, who knew only John’s baptism, were baptised in the name of the Lord Jesus (Acts 19:1–7). What the two share is the sign of cleansing and the call to turn. Like John, we hold that baptism belongs to those who repent and believe (Acts 2:38; 8:36–38), as the 1689 London Baptist Confession teaches, because in the New Testament baptism follows repentance and faith. Many faithful Christians baptise their children, seeing baptism as the covenant sign given to believers’ children as circumcision once was, and we honour them as brothers and sisters who do so in good conscience.

verseByVerse.quote: "even he who comes after me, the strap of whose sandal I am not worthy to untie." These things took place in Bethany across the Jordan, where John was baptizing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sandal strap. Untying a master’s sandals was a slave’s job. A later rabbinic saying gives the sentence its edge: a disciple served his teacher in almost every way a slave would, except the one duty with the feet, untying and carrying the sandals. So John does not say he is unworthy to be the man’s disciple. He says he is unworthy to do the one job a slave’s list contained and a disciple’s did not.

The King with a towel. Twelve chapters later, the one whose sandal strap John was not fit to loosen ties a towel round his waist, kneels, and washes the feet of men who will every one of them fail him before morning (13:4–5). The task too low for the herald is the task the King performs, and this verse gives the measure of how far he stooped in chapter 13.

In Bethany across the Jordan. East of the Jordan, not the Bethany near Jerusalem where Lazarus lived. Its location is uncertain; some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read Bethabara, but the earliest read Bethany. If, as many think, it lay near the crossing opposite Jericho, this is where the nation came out of the wilderness into the land, and where Elijah went up in a whirlwind (2 Kings 2:8–13). John is standing at Israel’s front door, on the outside, telling the covenant people they need to come in again.

Is it healthy to think of myself as unworthy? It depends what you mean. John’s unworthiness is not self-hatred or low self-esteem; he spoke with great boldness and never doubted his calling. It is simply an accurate measurement of himself against Christ. Next to him, the greatest of men is not fit to touch his feet. But the gospel does not leave us there. The same Christ who is infinitely above us kneels to wash us and calls us friends (15:15). Humility is not thinking badly of yourself; it is thinking truly of Christ, and then receiving gladly what he gives to the unworthy.

In everyday life. Consider the lowest job in your church, the one nobody puts on a rota: stacking the chairs, the bins after the meal, the lift home for the person who talks too long. Would you be glad to be known as the person who does that and nothing else? Then go and do it, for the one who washed your feet.

For worship. The feet whose sandal the Baptist was not fit to loosen walked to Calvary and were nailed there. Years later, on Patmos, the apostle who wrote this verse saw those feet again, like burnished bronze, and fell at them as though dead; and the Lord laid his right hand on him and said, fear not (Revelation 1:15–17). This is our Lord: majesty that kneels, and glory that lifts the fallen to their feet.
verseByVerse.note: Untying a master’s sandals was a slave’s job. This Bethany lay east of the Jordan — not the Bethany near Jerusalem.

parallels.desc: where John had been baptizing at first

verseByVerse.quote: The next day he saw Jesus coming toward him, and said, "Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world! This is he of whom I said, 'After me comes a man who ranks before me, because he was before me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, the Lamb of God. The next day, John says, marking off the days of this first week (vv. 29, 35, 43; 2:1). This title is the key to the whole Gospel: Jesus is the sacrifice God himself provides. There were four lambs available to a Jewish imagination, and they are not interchangeable.

The lamb of Genesis 22. Isaac carries the wood for his own sacrifice and asks: where is the lamb for a burnt offering? God will provide for himself the lamb (Genesis 22:7–8). And then a ram is caught in a thicket, and the promise of a lamb is left standing, unfulfilled, for two thousand years.

The daily lamb. A lamb every morning and evening in the temple, for centuries (Exodus 29:38–42), which was its own testimony: a sacrifice you have to repeat tomorrow has not dealt with anything permanently (Hebrews 10:11–12).

The Passover lamb. A year-old male without blemish, killed at twilight, its blood on the doorposts, and the destroyer passing over that house (Exodus 12). The Passover lamb was not, strictly, a sin offering. It marked a house as belonging to God and turned aside the judgment falling everywhere else.

The lamb of Isaiah 53. Like a lamb that is led to the slaughter, he opened not his mouth. And this is the only one of the four in which a lamb bears sin: the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all; he bore the sin of many (Isaiah 53:6–7, 12).

Let John decide it. Two things in his own account are decisive. First, he alone dates the crucifixion so that Jesus is condemned on the day of Preparation of the Passover (19:14), when the Passover lambs were being killed. (How this fits the other Gospels, where the Last Supper is a Passover meal, is long debated; careful harmonisations exist.) Second, he alone tells you which Scripture was fulfilled when the soldiers did not break his legs: not one of his bones will be broken (19:36), the Passover rule of Exodus 12:46. So John’s frame is Passover. But who takes away the sin of the world echoes Isaiah’s sin-bearing servant. The Baptist has put the Passover lamb and the sin-bearing servant into one person and pointed at him.

The whole doctrine in one lamb. Isaiah tells you how it works: the iniquity is laid on him and he carries it in our place. Passover tells you what it does for you: judgment is real, and it does not come into the house marked with blood. Genesis supplies the question, and the daily lamb explains why there had to be a last one.

Takes away. “Takes away” (airōn) means to lift up and to carry away: he takes sin up onto himself in order to take it away (Isaiah 53:4, 11–12; 1 Peter 2:24). The form of the verb describes what he is: the one who takes sin away. Then the noun: the sin, singular, the whole mass of human guilt treated as one object that can be picked up. And “of the world”: not of Israel only, but of people from every nation (11:51–52; 1 John 2:2).

Even my sin? People rarely doubt that Christ takes away sin in general. They doubt whether he takes away the particular thing they have never told anyone, the one that feels too shameful to sit beside ordinary sins. Look at the grammar again. If he had said sins, you might wonder whether yours was on the list. He said the sin, the whole weight of it, lifted as one load. Whatever yours is, if you come to him it is not too heavy and not too dark for the Lamb to carry; it was laid on him with all the rest (Isaiah 53:6). None who come will be turned away (6:37).

Where Christians differ: “the sin of the world”. Arminians (Christians who hold that God’s grace enables everyone to believe but leaves the decision with each person) take “the world” to mean that Christ died for every person equally, making salvation possible for all; they point to 3:16 and to 1 John 2:2, for the sins of the whole world.
