This commentary’s view: in John, “the world” usually means humanity in rebellion against God, not every individual, and the point is the scope of Christ’s work: not Jews only, but Gentiles from every nation (10:16; 11:52). Christ’s death actually takes away sin; it does not merely make removal possible. It takes away the sin of all who are his, from all over the world. This is often called definite atonement: Christ died to save his people for certain, not merely to make salvation possible. The reason is that this Gospel speaks of a death that accomplishes what it sets out to do (6:37–39; 10:11, 15; 17:2). Faithful Christians read these verses differently, and they preach the same Lamb. The gospel is offered freely to everyone (3:16), and none who come will be turned away (6:37).

Breaking the fence. The men listening had come from Jerusalem, with the categories Israel and everyone else. John says world, the word that breaks the fence, and the rest of this Gospel keeps breaking it: a Samaritan woman, a royal official’s household, some Greeks who ask to see him (10:16).

He was before me. The Baptist repeats the riddle of verse 15. The man walking towards him is still the one who existed before him: becoming man did not make him less than God.

The Lamb on the throne. On Patmos John looks for the Lion of the tribe of Judah and turns to see a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain, and the whole of heaven falls down before it (Revelation 5:5–6). The title is not a stage he passed through. It is what he is called in glory.

Is the whole idea of sacrifice not primitive? It looks primitive only if sin is small. The sacrifices taught Israel two things a modern mind finds hard to hold together: that God is holy, so sin cannot simply be waved away, and that God is merciful, so he provides a way for the sinner to live. Every lamb said that sin is deadly serious and that a substitute could die in the sinner’s place (Leviticus 17:11). The animals could never actually pay (Hebrews 10:4); they were pictures. The Lamb of God is the reality: not a human gift bribing an angry God, but God himself providing, and in his Son becoming, the sacrifice. That is not less civilised than our ideas of forgiveness. It is the only kind that takes both justice and love seriously.

In everyday life. The first word is an imperative: behold. Look. Not understand it, or feel it, or resolve to do better: the one instruction a man carrying something too heavy can still obey. When guilt comes back today, do not argue with it from your own record. Look at the Lamb, and say: he took that away.

For worship. Every morning and every evening, century after century, a lamb died in Israel, and not one of them chose to. This one does, walking down the riverbank to become the last, of his own accord. The one who put the ram in the thicket is walking toward the altar himself. He did not have to be caught. All that blood was rehearsal. The Lamb of God carries away the sin of the world: there is nothing left to bring, and nothing left to pay.
verseByVerse.note: Lambs were offered daily in the temple and at Passover; Isaiah’s servant goes “like a lamb that is led to the slaughter.”

parallels.desc: the Passover lamb
God will provide the lamb

verseByVerse.quote: "I myself did not know him, but for this purpose I came baptizing with water, that he might be revealed to Israel."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I myself did not know him. The two men were relatives (Luke 1:36), so this need not mean he knew nothing of him. He did not know him as the Messiah until God revealed it (v. 33). Knowing Jesus as a kinsman is not the same thing as knowing who he is. He had to be shown.

For the one raised in a Christian home. To the one who has heard it all since infancy and wonders whether familiarity has spoiled it: a prophet sent from God was in exactly that position and needed God to reveal it anyway, and God did.

For the one who distrusts his own certainty. John’s certainty did not come from inside him. God told him in advance what sign to watch for (v. 33), and he saw it, outside himself, on a particular day, in front of witnesses. That is where yours rests too. The events this book reports did not happen inside anybody’s feelings, and they do not stop having happened on the mornings when you cannot feel anything at all.

For this purpose. The baptising was never the point, nor the crowds. The whole operation existed to create an occasion at which one person could be identified. It was scaffolding, and scaffolding is judged by the building. Every ministry exists for the unveiling of Christ, not the establishing of the minister.

Revealed to Israel. The verb, phaneroō, to make visible, becomes this Gospel’s word for what Jesus does: at Cana he manifested his glory (2:11), and by the Sea of Tiberias he revealed himself again (21:1, 14). No one stumbles on the Son of God merely by being near him. He makes himself known, to people who did not know him.

But in Matthew, did John not recognise him? In Matthew, John protests: I need to be baptized by you (Matthew 3:14). The two fit together. John knew Jesus as a relative and a righteous man, and in Matthew he senses that Jesus is greater than he. What he did not know until the sign was given was that this was the one who baptises with the Spirit (v. 33). His protest in Matthew came at the baptism itself; his certainty came with the descending Spirit.

verseByVerse.quote: And John bore witness: "I saw the Spirit descend from heaven like a dove, and it remained on him. I myself did not know him, but he who sent me to baptize with water said to me, 'He on whom you see the Spirit descend and remain, this is he who baptizes with the Holy Spirit.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Like a dove. At Jesus’ baptism (Mark 1:10), which this Gospel does not describe, giving instead the Baptist’s testimony to it. The dove may evoke the Spirit hovering over the waters at creation (Genesis 1:2) and the dove that returned to Noah (Genesis 8:11): new creation and peace.

It remained. “Remained” means abode, stayed. In the Old Testament, the Spirit came on prophets and kings for particular tasks, and could depart (1 Samuel 16:14). On Jesus, the Spirit rests permanently (Isaiah 11:2; 42:1; 61:1). He has the Spirit without measure (3:34).

The first abiding. The verb is menō, around forty times in this Gospel, the word behind chapter 15: abide in me, and I in you. Its first appearance is not about us at all but about the Spirit settling on the Son and not lifting off again. The abiding does not begin with your effort to hold on to Christ. It begins with the Spirit resting on Christ permanently, and our abiding in him is a share in that. The Spirit who rested on Jesus without measure has been poured out from him on all his people, and he will not lift off from them either.

He who sent me. God. John did not work it out or sense it. He was told in advance precisely what to watch for, and then he stood in the water and watched, perhaps for months. God gave him a sign specific enough to be checked, and then honoured it.

The Trinity at the river. Here is the whole Trinity without the later vocabulary: the Father who sends and speaks, the Spirit who descends and settles, the Son on whom he settles. The definitions came centuries later to protect the report.

Baptizes with the Holy Spirit. Water is applied from outside; it goes on you, and it comes off. The Spirit is given, and he stays, because the giver is the one on whom he has been seen to stay (7:38–39; 20:22). Fulfilled at Pentecost, and in every believer’s new birth (3:5).

Have I been baptised with the Spirit? If you belong to Christ, yes. This phrase has been used to make Christians anxious about whether they have had a second experience they may have missed. Many Pentecostal and charismatic believers, whose love for Christ is plain, speak of a later baptism in the Spirit, and we gladly own them as brothers; we read these texts as describing how every Christian begins. The New Testament’s own position is blunt about it: anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him (Romans 8:9), and in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body (1 Corinthians 12:13). There is no category of Christian who is still waiting for the Spirit. If you belong to Christ, the thing John is announcing here has already happened to you, whatever it felt like at the time and whether or not there was anything to feel. You may and should ask to be filled afresh, to walk in step with him and to know his power more (Ephesians 5:18), but that is growth in what you have, not a gate you have not yet passed.

parallels.desc: the Spirit of the LORD shall rest upon him

verseByVerse.quote: "And I have seen and have borne witness that this is the Son of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have seen and have borne witness. Perfect tenses: a completed action whose result is still standing. He is not describing a moment of enthusiasm but giving sworn evidence that cannot now be withdrawn, which is what a witness does in a Gospel shaped like a trial.

That this is the Son of God. The ESV notes that some manuscripts read the Chosen One of God (Isaiah 42:1). If so, John is echoing Isaiah: behold my servant, my chosen, in whom my soul delights; I have put my Spirit upon him, exactly what has just happened, and the servant of Isaiah 42 is the one who by Isaiah 53 is led to the slaughter. Either way, this is the climax of John’s testimony: Jesus is the unique Son of God (v. 18), the one this Gospel was written to make known (20:31).

What would they have heard? It is worth knowing what the title would have meant to the men standing there, because it did not yet mean to them all that it means in the creed. In Israel’s Scriptures son of God could be said of the king: you are my Son; today I have begotten you (Psalm 2:7). So the crowd would have heard a claim about the Messiah, the anointed king. John, writing decades later for readers who have now read his first chapter, means all of that and the thing verse 18 said as well. The title grows as the Gospel goes on. It does not change its mind.

He came, he pointed, he went. After one more pointing the next day (vv. 35–36), we hear from the Baptist only once more, in chapter 3: he must increase, but I must decrease. His arrest is mentioned in passing (3:24), and he gets no death scene.

What if my faithful service seems to have come to nothing? You are in good company. The greatest man ever born of women, on the Lord’s own assessment, has a public career of perhaps a year, spends it telling people to look at somebody else, is imprisoned on a private grudge and, as Mark tells us, executed to keep a promise made at a birthday feast (Mark 6:21–28). From the inside it can have looked very like a wasted life. He had seen, and he had borne witness, and it turns out that is the whole job description. God does not measure faithfulness by visible results, and he forgets nothing done for his Son (Hebrews 6:10). Your testimony, too, once given, still stands.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “the Chosen One of God.”

parallels.desc: my Chosen One

verseByVerse.quote: The next day again John was standing with two of his disciples, and he looked at Jesus as he walked by and said, "Behold, the Lamb of God!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two of his disciples. Andrew (v. 40), and probably John, the author, who never names himself. Something easy to miss is happening here, and it costs the Baptist everything he has left. He is not preaching to a crowd this time. He is standing with two of his disciples, his own men, the ones who had attached themselves to him, who fasted when he fasted and prayed the prayers he taught them (Luke 11:1). And as Jesus walks by, the Baptist looks at him intently (emblepsas). He is not gesturing vaguely down the road, and that is what the two of them notice first: not the words, but where the man is looking.

Behold, the Lamb of God! Shorter, repeated. John points his own disciples to Jesus, knowing they will leave him. He does not soften it or ask them to stay in touch. He simply says, behold, the Lamb of God, and the next verse is the two of them walking off after somebody else.

The same sentence, again. The second day running he says the same thing (vv. 29, 36). The pressure to say something not said before is very often vanity; the preacher’s task is not novelty but faithfulness. This man had one line and used it until it took his followers away.

The Lamb worth leaving for. Why would two men walk away from a prophet they loved on the strength of a handful of words? Because the day before, John had said what this Lamb does, and nothing in John’s own ministry could do that: his baptism could call for repentance, but it could not lift anybody’s guilt. So he is sending his disciples to the only person who can give them what he has spent his life telling them they need. He is not losing them to a rival. He is handing them to their Saviour. This is the glory of the Lamb: he is so worth following that the best of men counted it joy to lose his disciples to him.

The friend of the bridegroom. The cost is what makes it remarkable. He is not resigning at the end of a full career; he is at the height of his influence, and he is dismantling it deliberately, one pair of disciples at a time. When people came to him later complaining that everyone was going over to Jesus, he gave them the image of a best man at a wedding: the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him and rejoices greatly at the bridegroom’s voice, and whose joy is now complete (3:29). The happiest man at the party is the one who is not the groom and never thought he was. He must increase, he said, but I must decrease (3:30).

Is it wrong to want to be appreciated in ministry? Not in itself. Paul longed to see his converts and rejoiced in their love (Philippians 4:1). Wanting your work to bear fruit and your people to flourish is good. What John shows is where that desire must be held: under a greater joy in Christ himself. The test is not whether you ever enjoy being thanked, but whether you can rejoice when people outgrow you, leave for another church, or never mention you again, because they are following him. If that is hard, tell the Lord so honestly and ask him to make his glory sweeter to you than your own.

verseByVerse.quote: The two disciples heard him say this, and they followed Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Followed. The first use in this Gospel of the verb that will describe the Christian life to the last page: literally walked after him. At this moment it means nothing more spiritual than walking behind a man on a road. It does not mean they had settled anything. They got up and went the same way he was going, with no idea what to say.

How following usually starts. They have no question prepared, and it is Jesus who turns round and breaks the silence (v. 38). Say it plainly to anyone whose beginnings were unimpressive: the first conversion in this Gospel was a sentence overheard, two men walking off after somebody without a plan, and an awkward silence broken from the other end.

So little to go on. No miracle had happened, and nothing had been explained. Everything in the next twenty chapters, the water into wine, the raising of Lazarus, the upper room, the empty tomb, follows from two men taking one sentence seriously enough to move their feet.

The voice behind the voice. They heard John, and followed Jesus. Later Jesus explains what was happening on that road: my sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me (10:27). They follow because they know the shepherd’s voice, and they know it because he knew them first.

What does following Jesus mean today? It means more than believing things about him; it means going where he goes. We follow him by trusting him for forgiveness, by listening to his words in Scripture and doing them, by taking up the life he gives us among his people, and by going his way when it costs us (Luke 9:23). It is a whole life, but it is lived one step at a time: the next obedience you know about, the next sin to turn from, the next act of love. You do not need to see the whole road. These two did not. You need to keep him in front of you.

verseByVerse.quote: "Jesus turned and saw them following and said to them, 'What are you seeking?' And they said to him, 'Rabbi' (which means Teacher), 'where are you staying?' He said to them, 'Come and you will see.' So they came and saw where he was staying, and they stayed with him that day, for it was about the tenth hour."
verseByVerse.commentary:
What are you seeking? These are Jesus’ first words in John’s Gospel, and the fact matters before the content: the first thing the Word says once he has begun to speak is not a statement. It is a question, and it is a question about what you want. He does not ask what they believe. He does not ask what they have done, or whether they are sorry, or what they understand. He asks what they are looking for.

The question the whole book asks. It is the same word (zēteō) Jesus uses in the garden when the soldiers arrive: whom do you seek? (18:4, 7). And on resurrection morning, to a woman crying at a tomb: whom are you seeking? (20:15). Nobody in this Gospel gets to Jesus without being asked it.

What if I came for the wrong reasons? Most people do. The question is aimed past the disciples at whoever is reading, and it is worth answering honestly rather than piously, because the pious answer is often not the true one. Most people come to Christ seeking something other than Christ: relief from a fear, a way out of a mess, certainty, respectability, a marriage saved, the return of a peace they remember having. Look at what he does with that. He asks the question, and then he does not screen anybody out on the strength of the answer. He does not say, wrong reason, come back when your motives are pure. The question is not a filter. It is the beginning of an education, and this Gospel is largely the record of people arriving with a small want and being given something they had not known to ask for. Come as you are, and let him change what you want.

Rabbi, where are you staying? John translates Rabbi, Teacher, for Greek readers. “Staying” (meneis) is the same word as remained (v. 32), abiding. They want to be with him, to know him, not just ask a question. And they duck his question. Asked what they are seeking, they answer with a question about an address. That is exactly what people do when a question goes too deep too fast: they change it into something practical. He lets them. He does not force the deeper conversation; he answers the question they were able to ask.

Come and you will see. An invitation to discover him for themselves. Not an argument, not a leaflet: an address and an afternoon. Philip will repeat it (v. 46). It is not a recommendation to stop thinking; this Gospel was written from evidence deliberately selected so that you might believe (20:30–31). Come and see is an invitation to examine the case from close up rather than from the road.

They stayed. The verb is the same one again: abode. They asked where he abides, and the answer turned out to be that they could abide there too. The teaching of chapter 15, abide in me, is already present in this conversation, and nobody in it knows (15:4). The eternal Word, who was with God in the beginning, opened his door to two strangers on an ordinary afternoon and let them stay.

For it was about the tenth hour. About 4 p.m., as the ESV notes. Why is that in the Bible? Because the man writing it was very probably the unnamed one of the two, an old man now, and he still knows what time of day it was. He does not tell us what was said in that room. He remembers the hour, as you remember the afternoon that divided your life in two.

Does John use a different clock? Some think John counts hours from midnight, Roman style, which would make the tenth hour ten in the morning. That question matters chiefly at 19:14. Here the natural reading, counting from sunrise as Jews ordinarily did, is about four in the afternoon, which is why they stayed the rest of the day.

How do I come and see today, when Jesus is not physically here? Through the means he has given. He is present by his Spirit, and he speaks in his word. Read one of the Gospels slowly, from start to finish, asking at each page what it shows you of him. Pray, speaking to him as someone who is listening. Go where his people gather and his word is preached, and keep going. Ask honest questions and bring them to Scripture and to mature Christians. The disciples spent an afternoon in his company; you can spend your mornings there. The invitation has not been withdrawn.

For worship. They asked where he was staying, and he gave them an afternoon. Later he gave them the whole answer: in my Father’s house are many rooms (14:2), and the word for rooms is built from the very verb they had used. Come and see was the first word of an invitation that ends in a room prepared for us.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the tenth hour was about 4 p.m. — late enough that they stayed the rest of the day.

verseByVerse.quote: One of the two who heard John speak and followed Jesus was Andrew, Simon Peter's brother. He first found his own brother Simon and said to him, "We have found the Messiah" (which means Christ).
verseByVerse.commentary:
Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother. Always known in relation to his more famous brother. This Gospel gives him three scenes, and he does the same thing in every one. Here he brings his brother. In chapter 6, with five thousand people to feed and the disciples calculating what it would cost, it is Andrew who says there is a boy here with five barley loaves and two fish, and then adds, honestly, but what are they for so many? (6:8–9). In chapter 12, when some Greeks come asking to see Jesus and Philip does not know what to do with the request, he takes it to Andrew, and Andrew takes them in (12:20–22). Every time he is bringing somebody to Jesus: his brother, a boy with a packed lunch, and foreigners nobody was sure were allowed.

The connector. He never preaches a sermon in the New Testament; every recorded saying of his is an introduction or a question. But the whole of Peter’s life, the denials, the restoration on the beach, the sermon that added three thousand in a morning, enters the story because his brother could not keep quiet for an afternoon.

His own brother. His first act as a disciple: tell his family, the nearest person and therefore the hardest. Nobody is less impressed by your spiritual development than the person who watched you grow up.

What if my family has not believed after years of prayer? This verse gets used to prod people who do not need prodding. Andrew found his brother the same day, and it worked. That is not the pattern; it is the exception, and the New Testament knows it. Jesus’ own brothers did not believe in him during his ministry (7:5). Jesus himself, who grew up in the same house, did not win them over in those years, and they came in later, after the resurrection, in God’s time. If you have been praying for a brother, a son, a husband for twenty years and nothing has moved, this verse is not a reproach. It is a reminder that Andrew’s job was to fetch him, not to convert him, and that the fetching is the only part any of us has ever been responsible for. Keep praying, keep loving, and leave the hour with God.

We have found the Messiah. Messiah (Hebrew) and Christ (Greek) are the same title; only John uses the Hebrew word in the New Testament (also 4:25). And there is an irony in that we. By themselves they found nothing. A prophet was sent to tell them where to look, Jesus turned round and spoke first, and in the next scene it is Jesus doing the finding (v. 43). Every person in this chapter who says they have found him was found.

The Anointed One. Israel’s kings and priests had oil poured on their heads; Isaiah promised one on whom the Spirit of the LORD would rest (Isaiah 11:2; 61:1). The day before, the Baptist had seen the Spirit come down on Jesus and remain. Andrew’s word was exactly right: the one anointed with God’s own Spirit without measure, the King every earlier anointing had been waiting for, now sitting in a room on a riverbank, being introduced to fishermen.
verseByVerse.note: “Messiah” (Hebrew) and “Christ” (Greek) both mean “anointed one” — the promised king.

parallels.desc: Andrew and Simon called by the lake

verseByVerse.quote: He brought him to Jesus. Jesus looked at him and said, "You are Simon the son of John. You shall be called Cephas" (which means Peter).
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus looked at him. “Looked” is a penetrating gaze, seeing who he was and who he would become, the same verb used six verses earlier of the Baptist looking at Jesus: a deliberate look. Simon is being examined. And what comes out of the examination is not a verdict but a name.

You are Simon the son of John. Jesus knows him already. Watch the tenses. You are is present: an accurate description of the man as he is, known without being told.

You shall be called Cephas. Future tense, and between the two tenses is the rest of Simon’s life. Cephas (Aramaic) and Peter (Greek) both mean rock, as the ESV notes. The name stuck so hard that Paul, writing to Greek-speaking churches twenty years later, still calls him Cephas by reflex (1 Corinthians 1:12; Galatians 2:9). A new name, as God renamed Abram and Jacob, signifying a new identity and calling.

A name before the evidence. At this moment Simon has done nothing: confessed nothing, left nothing, promised nothing. The name is handed to him before there is a single piece of evidence for it, and when the evidence comes in it runs the other way: he will swear he is ready to lay down his life, and hours later deny three times that he is a disciple (13:37; 18:17, 25–27). The name says not what he was, but what grace would make him.

Names are declarations of intent. The names God gives are not descriptions of performance. Gideon is addressed as mighty man of valour while hiding in a winepress (Judges 6:11–12); Abram is renamed father of a multitude while Sarah is still barren (Genesis 17:5). The name arrives first and the man walks toward it, usually badly, and usually for years. You have been told you are a child of God, a saint, a new creation, and the daily evidence is someone who lost their temper before breakfast. The gap is not proof that the name is false. It is the normal condition of everyone God has ever renamed.

Does naming Simon the rock make him the first pope? Roman Catholic teaching reads this with Matthew 16:18 as the founding of an office passed on to the bishops of Rome. The name is real and prophetic; Peter did become a foundation stone of the church. But Scripture says the church is built on the apostles and prophets together, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone (Ephesians 2:20), Peter calls himself a fellow elder (1 Peter 5:1), and nothing in the New Testament speaks of his office passing to successors. Peter’s foundation work was done once, through his preaching and his letters, and we stand on it whenever we believe the gospel he preached.

In everyday life. Ask what name you would give yourself this morning from the evidence, and then which one God has used of you: forgiven, child, saint, beloved. When you fail today, do not rename yourself by the failure. Confess it, and walk on toward the name.

For worship. Simon, son of John: that is what Jesus called him on the first day, and it is what he called him again at the end, on the shore after the denials, three times over (21:15–17). The Lord who named him Rock before he had done anything did not withdraw the name when he had done the worst. He came back for him by his old name and gave him sheep to feed. The one who calls into existence the things that do not exist (Romans 4:17) is faithful to his word about us, and he finishes the people he names.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that Cephas (Aramaic) and Peter (Greek) both mean “rock.”

verseByVerse.quote: The next day Jesus decided to go to Galilee. He found Philip and said to him, "Follow me." Now Philip was from Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Peter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To Galilee. North, from the Jordan to Galilee. And John has been counting days since the delegation arrived: the next day (v. 29), the next day again (v. 35), and now the next day once more. And then, at the start of chapter 2, on the third day there was a wedding at Cana. Add them up and John has laid out something very close to a week, which is difficult to read as an accident in a book that opened with the words in the beginning.

A new week of creation. The exact arithmetic is debated; commentators reach six days or seven. But the shape is unmistakable, and so is where it lands. A week that begins with a man announcing that the light has come into the world ends at a wedding, with water turned into wine and his glory manifested (2:11). Genesis brings its week to man and woman made in God’s image and joined as husband and wife; John’s week ends at a wedding. The same person who made the world is now at work making it new.

He found Philip. Here the verb turns round. Everyone so far has been finding somebody: John points, Andrew finds Simon, and in a moment Philip will find Nathanael. Here, for the first time, Jesus himself does the finding; nobody fetched Philip. Ultimately it is always Jesus who finds us (Luke 19:10).

Follow me. The call to discipleship, and the first Follow me in this Gospel. Two words, no explanation, no terms offered, no indication of where. It is also, and this is worth carrying to the end of the book, the last thing he says to Peter on the last page, on a beach after breakfast: you follow me (21:19, 22). The first Follow me and the final one are the same. Everything in between is what it looks like to obey it. The Creator who began the first week by speaking light has begun a new week by speaking to a man from Bethsaida, and the same word that made the world is now making disciples.

From Bethsaida. A fishing town at the north end of the Sea of Galilee (Mark says Peter and Andrew lived at Capernaum, Mark 1:29). It is also one of the towns Jesus later names in a lament: woe to you, Bethsaida! (Matthew 11:21). Three of the twelve came out of Bethsaida, and the town itself did not believe.

A comfort and a warning. If you have come out of a family or a church or a town where the gospel was heard for years and did nothing, its unbelief is not a verdict on you; three men walked out of Bethsaida and followed him. And if you have grown up inside a great deal of exposure to Christ and have never actually moved, this verse says that the exposure is not the same thing as the following, and that being near where God is working is a more dangerous position than being far from it, not a safer one.

If Jesus finds us, do I have any part to play? Yes, a real one, but it comes second. You respond: you hear his call, and you follow. The call does not wait on your seeking, but it does summon you to act. When Jesus said follow me, Philip did not stay where he was and wait to be carried. Yet the order matters for your peace. You did not stumble on Christ by your own wisdom or hold on to him by your own strength; he came looking for you, and he will not lose what he has found (10:28). So follow him gladly, and when you feel your grip weakening, remember whose grip it really is.

In everyday life. He found you before you followed, and no one follows him without stumbling; your standing rests on his perfect obedience, not on the straightness of your steps (Romans 5:19). So ask what following him would mean in the specific decisions in front of you this week, a conversation, a temptation, the use of an evening, and take the step.
verseByVerse.note: Bethsaida was a fishing town at the north end of the Sea of Galilee.

verseByVerse.quote: Philip found Nathanael and said to him, "We have found him of whom Moses in the Law and also the prophets wrote, Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Philip found Nathanael. Philip has been a disciple for perhaps an hour, and the first thing he does with it is go and find somebody. He was found by Jesus in one verse and is finding a friend in the next. Nobody has taught him to do this, and nobody has told him he is allowed to. Nathanael is not named in the other Gospels; he is often identified with Bartholomew, who is paired with Philip in the lists of apostles (Matthew 10:3). He was from Cana in Galilee (21:2).

Moses and the prophets. That is not a vague religious phrase; it is a claim that can be checked. The whole Old Testament points to Jesus (5:39, 46; Luke 24:27). Moses had written of a seed of the woman who would crush the serpent’s head (Genesis 3:15), of the offspring of Abraham in whom all nations would be blessed (Genesis 22:18), of a ruler from Judah to whom the obedience of the peoples belongs (Genesis 49:10), of a star coming out of Jacob (Numbers 24:17), and of a prophet like himself whom Israel must hear (Deuteronomy 18:15). The prophets had written of a virgin’s son called God with us (Isaiah 7:14), a child on David’s throne called Mighty God and Everlasting Father (Isaiah 9:6–7), a servant pierced for our transgressions (Isaiah 53:5), a ruler from Bethlehem whose origin is from of old (Micah 5:2), a king coming humble and mounted on a donkey (Zechariah 9:9). And on the Emmaus road the risen Jesus does exactly what Philip has just done, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets (Luke 24:27).

Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph. How people knew him, and in two respects incomplete. He was not from Nazareth in the sense that mattered prophetically; he was born in Bethlehem, which is the very thing Micah had specified and which the crowd will throw at each other in chapter 7 as a reason he cannot be the Christ (7:41–42). And he was not the son of Joseph by birth, as the Gospels insist (Matthew 1:18–25; Luke 1:34–35). Philip may not yet have known of the virgin birth; John’s readers know more. John does not correct him. The mistakes stand on the page, and Nathanael comes anyway, and by the end of the conversation he is confessing more than Philip knew how to say.

What if I get it wrong when I talk about Jesus? This is for you if you have ever kept quiet because you were afraid of getting it wrong. The first missionary sentence in this Gospel is incomplete twice over, and God used it to bring in one of Jesus’ closest followers. Philip’s grasp of Christ was partial, second-hand, an hour old, and expressed inaccurately. What he had was true enough to be worth passing on, and the passing on is what he was asked for. Accuracy grows. Nobody is waiting for you to be finished. Say what you know, admit what you do not, and point the person to the Gospels, where Jesus can speak for himself.

In everyday life. Read the Old Testament as Philip did: it is about Jesus. When you read it this week, ask of each passage what it promises, what pattern it sets up, or what longing it leaves open that Christ fulfils.
verseByVerse.note: Nathanael is not named in the other Gospels; he is often identified with Bartholomew, who is paired with Philip in their lists.

parallels.desc: Nathanael of Cana

verseByVerse.quote: Nathanael said to him, "Can anything good come out of Nazareth?" Philip said to him, "Come and see." Jesus saw Nathanael coming toward him and said of him, "Behold, an Israelite indeed, in whom there is no deceit!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Can anything good come out of Nazareth? The remark is funnier and smaller than it sounds. Nazareth was an obscure village, probably a hamlet of a few hundred people, up a hill off the main road. It is never named in the Old Testament, nor by Josephus, who lists dozens of Galilean towns and knew the region as a commander. There is no prophecy attached to it, no history, nothing, and the Messiah was expected to come from Bethlehem (7:41–42). And Nathanael, we learn at the very end of this Gospel, was from Cana (21:2), a village a few miles off. This is not lofty prejudice from a man in Jerusalem. This is one small place being rude about another small place a few miles away, which is a thing small places have always done.

The ordinary form of unbelief. That makes the objection more useful than a grand one would be, because it is the ordinary form unbelief takes. Some honest unbelievers have looked long and hard. But many people do not reject Christ after weighing the evidence. They decline to look, on the grounds that nothing worth having has ever come from that quarter: that sort of church, that kind of person, those people, that book. It is not an argument. It is a reason not to have to make one.

Come and see. Philip does not argue. He invites Nathanael to meet Jesus himself, using Jesus’ own words (v. 39): the invitation is being passed on exactly as it was received. He could have started a debate about origins, and he would have lost, because he had his facts slightly wrong. Instead he offers the man a look. The best answer to objections is often an encounter with Christ.

So should I avoid giving reasons when people object? No. Peter tells us always to be prepared to give a reason for the hope that is in us, with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15), and Paul reasoned in synagogues and marketplaces. Learn what you can, and answer honest questions honestly. But arguments are not the goal. Philip’s instinct is right: the aim of every answer is to bring the person to Christ himself. So when the objection is really a reason not to look, do not get stuck defending Nazareth. Invite them to read a Gospel with you, to come to church, to see for themselves.

An Israelite indeed. A true Israelite, honest, sincere, without guile. There is a wordplay in it that a Jewish ear would catch instantly. The word for deceit is dolos, and it is the word used in the Greek Old Testament at Genesis 27:35, when Isaac, shaking, tells Esau what has happened to his blessing: your brother came deceitfully, and he has taken away your blessing. So: here is a true son of Israel, a man descended from Jacob, with none of Jacob in him. Jacob, whose name was heard as deceiver, got everything he wanted by deception and spent twenty years running from the consequences (Genesis 27:35–36). Jesus looks at Nathanael and says: not this one. Psalm 32:2: blessed is the man in whose spirit there is no deceit. And having opened with Jacob, he will close the conversation four verses later with the night Jacob slept on a stone.

Honest, not sinless. It does not mean Nathanael is sinless, and it does not mean he is nice. The last thing out of his mouth before this was an insult about Jesus’ home town, and it is precisely for that, in a sense, that he is commended. Here is a man who says what he actually thinks. There is no gap between what is in him and what comes out of him. Even his objection was honest. He was rude, and he was honest, and Jesus prefers that to smoothness by a wide margin.

For the awkward one. That is worth saying to the Christian who has always felt himself to be the awkward one: too blunt, too doubtful, the person who asks the question everyone else is too polite to ask, and who has quietly concluded that the smooth people are the spiritual ones. It is not a smooth man that Jesus stops to praise here. It is the sceptic from the next village who said the wrong thing out loud.

The Israelite with no deceit at all. Nathanael is without guile in the sense that he says what he thinks. But the same word is used in the New Testament of Jesus himself: he committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth (1 Peter 2:22, quoting Isaiah 53:9). Nathanael is an honest son of Jacob. The man speaking to him is the one Israelite in whom there was no deceit at any depth, the faithful servant Isaiah saw, who would be numbered with the transgressors and bear their sin. Nathanael’s honesty brought him to Jesus. Jesus’ sinlessness is what makes it safe for a sinner to come.

For worship. Good did come out of Nazareth: the best that ever came out of anywhere. The Lord of glory grew up in a village no one thought worth naming, and he kept its name to the end; over the cross Pilate wrote, Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews (19:19). The despised hometown was written above his head in the hour of his glory, and the slight became part of the title of the King. He is not ashamed of small places, or of the honest sceptics who come out of them.
verseByVerse.note: Nazareth was an obscure village; it is never named in the Old Testament. “No deceit” may contrast Nathanael with Jacob, the deceiver who became Israel.

parallels.desc: your brother came deceitfully
in whose spirit there is no deceit

verseByVerse.quote: Nathanael said to him, "How do you know me?" Jesus answered him, "Before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I saw you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
How do you know me? Nathanael’s surprised question is already halfway to a confession; they had never met, and he suspects something extraordinary. And Jesus’ answer begins, before Philip called you, stating the order deliberately. Before the human contact, before the invitation, before Nathanael had the first idea that anything was happening, he was already the subject of attention. Everything Philip did was second. The word before holds a whole doctrine, with no technical term in sight: Christ knows his people before they ever turn to him.

Under the fig tree. This is a verse people fill in. Sitting under one’s own fig tree was a picture of peace in the messianic age (Micah 4:4; Zechariah 3:10), and later rabbinic stories picture teachers studying under one. Preachers have supplied the scene for centuries: that he was praying, or reading Genesis 28 about Jacob at Bethel, which would explain the answer Jesus gives three verses later. Any of those may be right. The text says none of them, and the honest thing is to say so.

What the effect proves. Whatever happened under that tree was private enough that being told I saw you turned a sceptic into a confessor inside a minute. A man who had been mocking Nazareth moments earlier now says, Rabbi, you are the Son of God. Something under that tree, known to no one else, had just been referred to by a stranger. Jesus saw him, supernaturally, and knew what was in his heart (2:25).

For the one who feels unseen. This verse comforts one reader and undoes another. To the one who feels unseen, the years of praying in a room nobody knows about, the caring for someone that nobody is counting, the faithfulness that has produced no visible result and no acknowledgement: this is the verse. He saw you. Not deduced you, not was informed about you: saw. And he does not say what he saw, then or now. He simply lets you know that the private place was never as private as it felt.

For the one with something to hide. To the one who has something under his own fig tree that he would rather were not seen, the same sentence lands as exposure. He saw that too. But look at what he does with what he saw. He does not use it. He does not name it. He mentions the tree and stops, and the whole weight of the encounter is not accusation but welcome. The one person who has complete access to your private life is the one who came to take away the sin of the world, and he does not use what he knows to shame those who come to him. He uses it to prove he knows who he is talking to. Whether being seen frightens or comforts depends entirely on the face of the one who was watching, and we know that face now: it is the face of the Lamb of God, full of grace and truth.

Does Jesus know everything about me now? Yes. He knew what was in man (2:25), and as the risen Lord he searches minds and hearts (Revelation 2:23). He knows your thoughts before you speak them, your sins you have hidden, and your sorrows you have never voiced (Psalm 139:1–4). For an unbeliever that is a solemn truth, because nothing will be hidden at the judgment. For a believer it is the ground of deep rest: you never have to pretend before him, and you cannot surprise him into rejecting you. He took you knowing everything. Bring him the truth, because he has it already.
verseByVerse.note: Sitting under one’s own fig tree was a picture of peace and security.

parallels.desc: every man under his vine and under his fig tree

verseByVerse.quote: Nathanael answered him, "Rabbi, you are the Son of God! You are the King of Israel!" Jesus answered him, "Because I said to you, 'I saw you under the fig tree,' do you believe? You will see greater things than these."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A great confession. The fullest so far in the Gospel, and it comes from the sceptic. Son of God and King of Israel were both messianic titles (Psalm 2:6–7), and Nathanael may not yet understand all that the first one means. It is true in the fullest sense the prologue has already given: not only the anointed king, but the only Son who shares the Father’s very being and was at his side before the world began (1:1, 18).

King of Israel. This is not a devotional phrase but a political claim, and in an occupied country it gets people killed. A crowd will shout it with palm branches (12:13), and Pilate will have it written in three languages above his head and refuse to change the wording (19:19–22). The title Nathanael gives him in a field in Galilee ends up on his execution notice. He is right, and he has no idea what he is saying, and the man he says it to knows exactly what it will cost. The King of Israel wore his title on a cross, and then rose to wear it on a throne.

Because I said to you, I saw you under the fig tree, do you believe? This could be read as a mild reproach, that faith resting on one impressive moment is a thin foundation. But nothing in what follows sounds like a rebuke; it is a promise. Jesus does not tell Nathanael his faith is inadequate. He tells him it is small compared with what is coming, which is a different thing entirely and much kinder.

Jesus does not despise small faith. That distinction matters, because Jesus in this Gospel is notably unfussy about where faith starts. He will tell a royal official that people will not believe unless they see signs and wonders, and then heal his son anyway (4:48–50). He will invite Thomas to put his finger in the wounds (20:27). He never once turns away a small faith for being small. What he does, repeatedly, is refuse to let it stay that size.

Greater things. The signs of the Gospel, and the glory of the cross and resurrection. Not different things; greater. The direction is set: whatever brought you in is the smallest thing that will ever happen to you. And the honest word on the other side, which the verse also requires: the greater things promised here were not more moments of being privately known. They were a cross and an empty tomb. What Nathanael actually went on to see included the worst week of his life. Greater does not mean more pleasant. It means more of who this person is, and there are parts of who he is that can only be seen from somewhere painful.

What if my faith has gone flat since the beginning? Some Christians have a moment they have been living off for thirty years: a conversion, an answered prayer, a week when God seemed close, and everything since has felt like a slow decline from it. The moment has quietly become a museum rather than a beginning. This verse says the moment was never meant to be the peak. It was the fig tree. It was the thing that got you to look up. Jesus promises greater things, chiefly a deeper sight of himself, and he gives them through his word, through suffering, and through the long faithfulness of ordinary years. Ask him to show you more of himself, and go looking where he has promised to be found.

parallels.desc: my King, my Son
the King of Israel, the LORD, is in your midst

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to him, "Truly, truly, I say to you, you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Truly, truly. Amen, amen: a double truly found only in John (25 times), and this is the first. Amen is what you say to somebody else’s statement: yes, let it stand. Jesus puts it in front of his own sentences, twice. That is either extraordinary presumption or a claim about who is speaking. He never argues for his authority in this Gospel; he simply talks as though it is not in question.

I say to you, you will see. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, add hereafter; the earliest do not. The ESV notes that “you” is plural: he turns from the one man to the whole group, and by extension to everybody reading. The fig tree was for Nathanael. This is for all of us.

Heaven opened. Genesis 28:12, Jacob’s dream at Bethel: a ladder set up on the earth, reaching to heaven, and the angels of God ascending and descending on it. And the circumstances are not respectable. Jacob is running, having cheated his brother out of the blessing by lying to his blind father’s face, with Esau intending to kill him. He sleeps on a stone in open country, alone, guilty, and about as far from a holy place as a man can be, and that is where heaven opens over him, with the LORD himself standing above it, promising to be with him and bring him back.

Surely the LORD is in this place. Jacob wakes up afraid and says the sentence that names the place: surely the LORD is in this place, and I did not know it. This is the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven (Genesis 28:16–17). And he was afraid: how awesome is this place. That fear was right. Where heaven opens, the holy God is near, and no sinner stands there casually. What makes the open heaven of this verse good news is the one it opens over: in the Son of Man the holy God can be approached by guilty people, and they live. Read that against verse 26 of this chapter, where the Baptist tells the delegation from Jerusalem: among you stands one you do not know. It is the same discovery, centuries apart, in strikingly similar words. God turns out to have been present in the place where nobody thought to look for him.

On the Son of Man. Jesus is the ladder. He is the meeting place of heaven and earth, the true Bethel, the house of God, the gate of heaven. The way between God and humanity is open through him alone (14:6). Nathanael, the true Israelite (Israel was Jacob’s new name), will see what Jacob saw, fulfilled in Jesus. And there is even a translator’s question in Genesis that Jesus may be settling here. The Hebrew says the angels were ascending and descending on it, or on him; the word is ambiguous, and the ancient rabbis discussed both. Jesus says: on the Son of Man. Jacob thought he had found a place. Jesus says the point of contact is a person. “Son of Man” is the title Jesus uses most often for himself, from Daniel 7:13, where one like a son of man comes with the clouds of heaven and is given everlasting dominion.

Ascending first. The order is odd in Genesis and odd here: ascending first, then descending. Angels are presumed to live in heaven; you would expect them to come down before they go up. They start at the bottom. Wherever the ladder’s foot is, that is where the traffic begins, and Jesus has just said where the foot is standing: on earth, where the Son of Man is.

The ladder has legs. That is the whole point, and the reason this verse is the right end to the chapter. Jacob stumbled on the gate of heaven by accident, in the dark, and marked it with a stone and poured oil on it and called it Bethel, house of God, so that he could find it again. Many religions since have tried the same thing: locate the place, secure the access, mark it so it can be returned to, whether a shrine, a practice, or a state of mind you were in once. Jesus tells a man who has been a believer for a few minutes that the ladder has legs. The meeting-point between heaven and earth is not a site you have to find and not a condition you have to achieve. It is a person who walks about, and who found Philip, and who saw Nathanael under a tree before anyone called him. Jacob was terrified of the gate he found. This one goes looking for men under fig trees, calls them by name before they have been introduced, and invites them to come and see. Heaven is open, and it is open over him.

Does this mean I will see angels? Not necessarily, and you should not go looking for visions. Jesus is not promising the disciples a literal sighting of a stairway; he is telling them that in him the traffic between heaven and earth is now open, and that they will see it in what he does: the signs, the cross, the resurrection, the ascension. Angels do serve those who will inherit salvation (Hebrews 1:14), usually unseen. But the wonder of the verse is not the angels. It is that you have access to the Father through the Son, right now, in ordinary prayer, wherever you are, because heaven is open over him and you are in him.

In everyday life. Wherever you are today, the kitchen, the office, the hospital, the place you feel far from God, say what Jacob said and mean it: surely the LORD is in this place. Then pray, not as someone trying to climb up to God, but as someone for whom the way has been opened in Christ. You do not need a holy place. You need the Son of Man, and you have him.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “you” is plural: the promise is for all the disciples. “Truly, truly” is a solemn formula found only in John.

parallels.desc: Jacob’s ladder, angels ascending and descending

1.title: The Word Made Flesh
1.text: <sup>1</sup>In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.<sup>2</sup>He was in the beginning with God.<sup>3</sup>All things were made through him, and without him was not any thing made that was made.<sup>4</sup>In him was life, and the life was the light of men.<sup>5</sup>The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it.<sup>6</sup>There was a man sent from God, whose name was John.<sup>7</sup>He came as a witness, to bear witness about the light, that all might believe through him.<sup>8</sup>He was not the light, but came to bear witness about the light.<sup>9</sup>The true light, which gives light to everyone, was coming into the world.<sup>10</sup>He was in the world, and the world was made through him, yet the world did not know him.<sup>11</sup>He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him.<sup>12</sup>But to all who did receive him, who believed in his name, he gave the right to become children of God,<sup>13</sup>who were born, not of blood nor of the will of the flesh nor of the will of man, but of God.<sup>14</sup>And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth.<sup>15</sup>(John bore witness about him, and cried out, “This was he of whom I said, ’He who comes after me ranks before me, because he was before me.’”)<sup>16</sup>For from his fullness we have all received, grace upon grace.<sup>17</sup>For the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.<sup>18</sup>No one has ever seen God; God the only Son, who is at the Father’s side, he has made him known.<sup>19</sup>And this is the testimony of John, when the Jews sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to ask him, “Who are you?”<sup>20</sup>He confessed, and did not deny, but confessed, “I am not the Christ.”<sup>21</sup>And they asked him, “What then? Are you Elijah?” He said, “I am not.” “Are you the Prophet?” And he answered, “No.”<sup>22</sup>So they said to him, “Who are you? We need to give an answer to those who sent us. What do you say about yourself?”<sup>23</sup>He said, “I am the voice of one crying out in the wilderness, ’Make straight the way of the Lord,’ as the prophet Isaiah said.”<sup>24</sup>(Now they had been sent from the Pharisees.)<sup>25</sup>They asked him, “Then why are you baptizing, if you are neither the Christ, nor Elijah, nor the Prophet?”<sup>26</sup>John answered them, “I baptize with water, but among you stands one you do not know,<sup>27</sup>even he who comes after me, the strap of whose sandal I am not worthy to untie.”<sup>28</sup>These things took place in Bethany across the Jordan, where John was baptizing.<sup>29</sup>The next day he saw Jesus coming toward him, and said, “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!<sup>30</sup>This is he of whom I said, ’After me comes a man who ranks before me, because he was before me.’<sup>31</sup>I myself did not know him, but for this purpose I came baptizing with water, that he might be revealed to Israel.”<sup>32</sup>And John bore witness: “I saw the Spirit descend from heaven like a dove, and it remained on him.<sup>33</sup>I myself did not know him, but he who sent me to baptize with water said to me, ’He on whom you see the Spirit descend and remain, this is he who baptizes with the Holy Spirit.’<sup>34</sup>And I have seen and have borne witness that this is the Son of God.”<sup>35</sup>The next day again John was standing with two of his disciples,<sup>36</sup>and he looked at Jesus as he walked by and said, “Behold, the Lamb of God!”<sup>37</sup>The two disciples heard him say this, and they followed Jesus.<sup>38</sup>Jesus turned and saw them following and said to them, “What are you seeking?” And they said to him, “Rabbi” (which means Teacher), “where are you staying?”<sup>39</sup>He said to them, “Come and you will see.” So they came and saw where he was staying, and they stayed with him that day, for it was about the tenth hour.<sup>40</sup>One of the two who heard John speak and followed Jesus was Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother.<sup>41</sup>He first found his own brother Simon and said to him, “We have found the Messiah” (which means Christ).<sup>42</sup>He brought him to Jesus. Jesus looked at him and said, “You are Simon the son of John. You shall be called Cephas” (which means Peter).<sup>43</sup>The next day Jesus decided to go to Galilee. He found Philip and said to him, “Follow me.”<sup>44</sup>Now Philip was from Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Peter.<sup>45</sup>Philip found Nathanael and said to him, “We have found him of whom Moses in the Law and also the prophets wrote, Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph.”<sup>46</sup>Nathanael said to him, “Can anything good come out of Nazareth?” Philip said to him, “Come and see.”<sup>47</sup>Jesus saw Nathanael coming toward him and said of him, “Behold, an Israelite indeed, in whom there is no deceit!”<sup>48</sup>Nathanael said to him, “How do you know me?” Jesus answered him, “Before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I saw you.”<sup>49</sup>Nathanael answered him, “Rabbi, you are the Son of God! You are the King of Israel!”<sup>50</sup>Jesus answered him, “Because I said to you, ’I saw you under the fig tree,’ do you believe? You will see greater things than these.”<sup>51</sup>And he said to him, “Truly, truly, I say to you, you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man.”
1.overview:
John opens not at Bethlehem but before creation. The prologue (vv. 1–18) is the overture to the whole Gospel: the eternal Word, who was with God and was God, has become flesh, and in him the glory of the Father’s only Son has been seen, full of grace and truth. Its themes run through the whole book: life and light, witness, the world that does not know him, and the gift of becoming God’s children by a birth from God.

Then the story begins with a week of witness. John the Baptist refuses every title and points to Jesus as the Lamb of God. His disciples follow Jesus, and each one found becomes a finder: Andrew brings Simon, Philip brings Nathanael. Title after title is given to Jesus, Word, Lamb, Messiah, King of Israel, Son of Man, and the rest of the Gospel shows what they mean.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The Wedding at Cana: Water into Wine
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At a village wedding in Cana the wine runs out. Mary brings the need to Jesus, he answers that his hour has not yet come, and she tells the servants to do whatever he says. The water of six purification jars becomes the best wine of the feast, known only to the servants who drew it. This first sign reveals his glory, and his disciples believe in him.
verseByVerse.theology:
John calls the miracles of Jesus signs: not mere wonders but pointers to who he is. This one shows him as the one who brings the new wine of the kingdom, turning the old into the new, scarcity into abundance. His hour, the hour of the cross and glorification, has not yet come, and every sign points toward it.

What Jesus uses for the sign is part of its meaning. He does not smash the jars of purification; he fills them. The old order of ritual washing is turned into joy, and there is far more wine than the wedding needed. That abundance is the message.

A sign is a signpost, worthless if you stop at it. In 1:14 John wrote that we have seen his glory, and he manifested his glory is the first sight of it: a wedding present given almost anonymously in an unknown village.
verseByVerse.examples:
Jesus honours marriage by performing his first sign at a wedding, and the abundance of the wine pictures the generosity of the kingdom.

The Son’s first miracle was done because somebody was going to be embarrassed, so no trouble is too small to bring to him, though most of our praying assumes otherwise. Mary states the trouble and proposes nothing: They have no wine.

The world serves its best first. The gospel runs the other way: You have kept the good wine until now. What is promised is a better end, not an easier road, and that is why it speaks to the reader who has concluded his best years are behind him.

verseByVerse.quote: On the third day there was a wedding at Cana in Galilee, and the mother of Jesus was there. Jesus also was invited to the wedding with his disciples.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. The wedding and the temple belong together, and together they say who he is: the bridegroom who brings the wine of the kingdom, and the true temple where God meets his people, whose death and resurrection will replace the whole old order of cleansing and sacrifice.

On the third day. John has been marking off the days (1:29, 35, 43), and this is about the seventh day of a new week, though the arithmetic is not certain. A book which opened with in the beginning has laid out a week and arrived at the end of it. And many have heard in on the third day a hint of the resurrection.

Where the week lands. Genesis runs six days of making, crowned by man and woman made in God’s image; John’s week ends at a wedding, with more wine than anyone could drink. The guest at that wedding is the Word through whom all things were made (1:3). The Maker of the first week has come into his own creation to begin it again, and this time the week ends not with a garden but with a feast, and the one who brings the wine is himself the Bridegroom (3:29).

A wedding at Cana in Galilee. Cana was a village a few miles north of Nazareth, so small that no other book of the Bible mentions it. At the very end John notes that Nathanael was of Cana in Galilee (21:2). So the man who had asked whether anything good could come out of Nazareth is very probably standing at a wedding in his own village, watching Nazareth’s carpenter make the best wine anyone there had ever tasted. Jesus told him he would see greater things. It did not take long.

What a wedding was. Weddings lasted up to a week, with the whole village invited, and the groom’s family had to feed and supply them all. Hospitality was not a courtesy but a duty, and failing in it brought public shame.

The mother of Jesus. Perhaps she was helping, as a relative or friend of the family. She is named first; Jesus also was invited, and his disciples with him. The text does not say so, but Jesus’ five or more disciples, as extra guests, may be part of the reason the household ran out of wine.

Two scenes, one thread. John, who names Nathanael and Nicodemus and Lazarus and even Malchus the servant, never names her; she is always the mother of Jesus. Apart from a passing mention (2:12), she appears at only two scenes in the whole book: here, at the first sign, and at the cross, where she is standing when his hour finally arrives (19:25–27). Both times he addresses her the same way: Woman.

Jesus also was invited. Jesus’ first sign is at a wedding. He honoured marriage by his presence (Hebrews 13:4). He was not an ascetic; he came eating and drinking (Luke 7:34), sharing in human joy. He who would walk the road to Calvary first walked the road to Cana, and sat among ordinary people on the happiest day of their lives. The eternal Word who was with God before there was light spent one of his first recorded days as an incarnate man at a village party, and stayed long enough to notice the drink running out.

Are holiness and enjoyment at odds? Say this to anyone who has quietly come to believe that the serious Christian is the one who does not much like anything. Some piety would have been more comfortable if the first sign had been performed in a synagogue. It was performed at a wedding, for a family who would have been embarrassed, and it produced more than a hundred gallons beyond what the occasion strictly required. God gives us richly all things to enjoy (1 Timothy 6:17). Food, friendship, music, marriage and laughter are his gifts, and receiving them with thanks is not worldliness but worship (1 Timothy 4:4–5). What turns a gift into an idol is not enjoying it but loving it more than the Giver.

What does this say about marriage? That God honours it. Marriage was his idea from the beginning (Genesis 2:24), and Jesus chose a wedding for the first display of his glory. Scripture will go further: marriage between a man and a woman is a living picture of Christ and his church (Ephesians 5:31–32), and history ends with the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:7–9). So a Christian wedding is not merely a private celebration; it is a small sign of the great one. And if you are single, widowed, or your marriage is hard, the deepest wedding is still yours: the Bridegroom has come for his bride, and you belong to her.
verseByVerse.note: Cana was a village in Galilee, a few miles north of Nazareth. A wedding feast could last a week.

verseByVerse.quote: When the wine ran out, the mother of Jesus said to him, "They have no wine."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wine ran out. By our standards it looks like nothing: nobody is ill or in danger. But in a culture built on honour and shame, with the whole village present, the shortfall would be talked about for years: a social disaster for the bridegroom, and a humiliation that would last.

An embarrassment, not a tragedy. Most of our troubles are of this kind, though most of our praying is not about them: the thing that will be noticed, and remembered, and told about you, the moment everyone saw you had run out. Jesus could have opened his ministry by raising a dead child. He opens it by rescuing a family’s reputation at a party, and that tells us no need is too small to bring to him.

They have no wine. Mary states the problem and stops. No request, no suggestion, no reminder of who she is, no proposed method. She brings the need to him and trusts him to act: a model of prayer.

What it does not mean. Mary’s way is not a technique. There is nothing wrong with asking God for specific things; the Psalms are full of it, and Jesus told us to ask (Matthew 7:7). But a great deal of praying is really the presentation of a plan for approval, and the anxiety in it comes from having already decided what the answer must look like. She lays the problem down and leaves the method with him, which is wise, since what he does is not remotely what anyone would have asked for.

Faith in his character. There is no evidence she had ever seen him do anything of this kind; verse 11 says this was the first of his signs. She has thirty years of knowing him and no track record of miracles. Her faith rests on who he is, not on any assurance that he will do what she asks.

The wine the prophets promised. In the prophets, abundant wine is a sign of the messianic age: the mountains will drip sweet wine (Amos 9:13–14; Joel 3:18), and on Mount Zion the LORD will make for all peoples a feast of well-aged wine and swallow up death for ever (Isaiah 25:6–8). A wedding where the wine has run out may picture the old order at its end, its religion run dry. Then the Messiah arrives, and the first thing he does is supply the wine. Isaiah’s feast and Cana have the same host. The one who fills the jars here is the one who will swallow up death, and he will do it by going into death himself.

Is it really all right to pray about small things? Yes. Paul says, in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God (Philippians 4:6), and everything includes the small. The God who numbers the hairs of your head (Matthew 10:30) is not bored by your car, your exam, or the awkward meeting on Thursday. Praying about small things is not trivialising God; it is acknowledging that nothing in your life is outside his care. And it keeps you honest, because the person who only prays about emergencies has quietly decided he can manage everything else on his own.

For worship. The Lord of glory began his signs by lifting a small shame from a bridegroom in Cana, and he finished his work by carrying the great one. He who would not let a village family be disgraced at their feast endured the cross, despising the shame (Hebrews 12:2), mocked before a whole city, so that no one who trusts in him would ever be put to shame (Romans 10:11). The wine at Cana cost him a word. The covering for our disgrace cost him his blood. Nothing that troubles his people is beneath his notice, and nothing that shames them was beyond his bearing.
verseByVerse.note: Running out of wine would have shamed the family publicly.

verseByVerse.quote: "And Jesus said to her, 'Woman, what does this have to do with me? My hour has not yet come.' His mother said to the servants, 'Do whatever he tells you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woman. A respectful form of address in the first century, not a rude one, but not the word a son would usually use for his mother. It creates a gentle distance and signals a change: in the work his Father has given him she does not direct him. He is still her son, and he will care for her to the end (19:26–27), but in this work he answers to his Father alone.

What does this have to do with me? Literally what to me and to you? It is a Hebrew idiom meaning: what do we have in common in this? This is not your business to direct. Jesus acts on his Father’s timing, not his mother’s, however well meant (Luke 2:49). In English it can sound like a brush-off, and coupled with my hour has not yet come it seems to be a refusal, after which, puzzlingly, Jesus goes ahead and does exactly what the situation required. Did his mother change his mind? Did he decline and then relent?

Why does he refuse and then act? Two things dissolve the difficulty. First, the idiom’s force depends entirely on tone: it can be a rebuke, as when demons cry it at Jesus (Mark 5:7), or it can be gentle, meaning this is not for you to arrange, said by one who is about to act in his own way and time. Paired with the courteous Woman, the softer sense is very probably meant. Second, my hour everywhere in this Gospel means one thing, the hour of the cross and the glory that follows it. So my hour has not yet come does not mean ‘I will not act now’. It means ‘the hour when I am fully revealed is still ahead’. That is exactly why the sign is done so quietly that only the servants know how the wine came to be. This is a veiled foretaste, not the public hour itself.

My hour has not yet come. Everything in his life moves toward that hour, set by the Father (7:30; 8:20; 12:23, 27; 13:1; 17:1). At Cana he gives a sign of the abundance of the messianic age; at the hour he will give the thing itself, through the cross, when his blood is poured out and the new covenant is made. The wine of Cana is real, and it is a foretaste. The feast it points to is bought at Calvary.

The two ends of his ministry. At the cross, when the hour has arrived, he says: Woman, behold, your son (19:26), and arranges her care with almost his last breath. But from this verse on she has to learn to know him as the one whose hour is coming, one of the hardest things a mother has ever been asked to do.

Do whatever he tells you. Mary’s last recorded words in the Gospels, and advice worth a lifetime. She does not take offence or argue; she points others to him. And the sentence has a precedent. In the famine in Egypt Pharaoh says: Go to Joseph. What he says to you, do (Genesis 41:55). A shortage nobody can fix, and the answer is to go to the one man who has what is needed and do what he says without asking how.

Where Christians differ: Mary’s intercession. Roman Catholic devotion has seen Cana as a picture of Mary’s power as intercessor, obtaining favours from her Son. This commentary’s view: the passage shows the opposite emphasis: Jesus gently declines her direction, acts in his own time, and Mary directs the servants to him: do whatever he tells you. She is a model of faith and of pointing to Christ, not a mediator between us and him. There is one mediator (1 Timothy 2:5).

Honouring Mary rightly. Jesus’ answer is no snub: he honours her faith and grants the need. Scripture calls her blessed among women and favoured by God (Luke 1:28, 42, 48), and Protestants have often been too shy of saying so. But her best word points away from herself: not do what I tell you, but whatever he tells you. The way to honour her is to take her advice.

How do I know what he is telling me to do? Chiefly from Scripture. Jesus’ commands are written down, and most of what he asks of us is already plain: love God, love your neighbour, forgive, tell the truth, be faithful in marriage, give, pray, gather with his people, make disciples. Begin there; most of us have more than enough to obey before we need any further guidance. In decisions Scripture does not settle directly, such as which job, which house, whom to marry among believers, ask for wisdom (James 1:5), take counsel from mature Christians, and choose what best serves Christ and others. You do not need a voice. You need to do what he has already said.
verseByVerse.note: “Woman” was a respectful form of address, not a rude one. Jesus’ “hour” in John is the time of his death and glorification.

parallels.desc: “Go to Joseph. What he says to you, do”

verseByVerse.quote: Now there were six stone water jars there for the Jewish rites of purification, each holding twenty or thirty gallons. Jesus said to the servants, "Fill the jars with water." And they filled them up to the brim.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Six stone water jars. Everything in this sign turns on what the water was for. Stone jars, not pottery, because stone did not become ritually unclean the way earthenware did, so they held water for ceremonial washing (Mark 7:3–4): hands before and during the meal, vessels, the removal of whatever defilement a person picked up in an ordinary week. Six, perhaps because it is one short of seven, the Bible’s number for completeness, though John does not say so. They stood for the old order of ritual purification.

The machinery of cleansing. That is what Jesus makes the miracle from: not a well or an empty wine jar, but the equipment of a whole system for people who were not clean enough to come near God. In his hands it becomes the wine of a feast. And he does not smash the jars; he fills them. The washing-water is not condemned but fulfilled and turned into joy, because the one who fills them will himself make the cleansing they could only point to. The long centuries of washing and sacrifice end not in a smaller religion but in a feast.

Was the Old Testament law then a bad thing? No. The purification rites were God’s own gift, given to teach Israel that he is holy and that sinners need cleansing before they can come near him. They were good, and they were temporary, like a signpost that is meant to be passed. They could make the body ceremonially clean but never cleanse the conscience (Hebrews 9:9–14). What they pointed to, Christ provides: the blood of Jesus cleanses us from all sin (1 John 1:7). So we do not despise the jars. We thank God for them, and we drink what they were waiting for.

Each holding twenty or thirty gallons. Literally two or three measures: between 120 and 180 gallons (450–680 litres) in all, six to nine hundred bottles, for a village wedding late in the feast. The need was for enough to get through without disgrace; what arrives is more than the family could have drunk in a month. The lavishness is the message: in his kingdom God does not give just enough.

Fill the jars with water. And they filled them up to the brim. An ordinary command, with no explanation, and obedience, as Mary had said. Full to the brim, so nothing could be added to the water: what follows is no trick. They could not make wine; they could only fill jars, and they filled them until the water was level with the rim.

Does the size of the miracle mean God will always give me more than I need? Not in the sense of more money or easier circumstances. Paul knew hunger and need as well as plenty (Philippians 4:12). What the sign promises is the character of God’s grace: it is never measured out grudgingly. In Christ he gives forgiveness that covers every sin, a Spirit poured out without measure, an inheritance that cannot fade, and a love that surpasses knowledge (Ephesians 3:19). Your circumstances may be thin. His grace to you is not, and it is always more than enough for what he calls you to bear (2 Corinthians 12:9).

In everyday life. Think of something you were asked to do and did only adequately: the visit kept short, the apology with a qualification attached, the giving calculated to be defensible. It is not open defiance; it is simply not to the brim. He has filled you from his own fullness, so obey him in the ordinary instructions, all the way, before you see how it helps. And where your obedience stops short of the rim, as all of ours does, his did not: his perfect obedience is counted as yours (Romans 5:19).
verseByVerse.note: Stone jars did not become ritually unclean, so they were used for purification water. The ESV notes that each held two or three measures — twenty to thirty gallons: well over a hundred gallons in all.

parallels.desc: the washings of the Jews

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Now draw some out and take it to the master of the feast." So they took it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now draw some out. No prayer, no touch, no word over the water. Somewhere in that sentence the water became wine, silently, by his will, and John refuses to describe it. He is far more interested in what a sign means than in how it looked. The Word who spoke the world into being needs no ceremony to change water into wine. He wills it, and it is so. And he chooses, out of sheer kindness, to work through the hands of servants who trust him.

The master of the feast. Probably a trusted guest or senior servant in charge of the food and drink.
