So they took it. More obedience, and a real risk. If nothing has happened, they are handing the master of ceremonies hand-washing water in front of the party. Nobody had told them anything had changed. All they had was a sentence from a guest, and a woman’s instruction to do whatever he said.

The proof comes after. They do not taste it first in the kitchen and then decide whether to carry it out. That is what trust is: acting on his word before seeing the result.

Does faith mean acting without any evidence at all? No. The servants were not leaping in the dark; they had a word from Jesus and the testimony of someone who knew him. Christian faith rests on solid grounds: the eyewitness record of his life, death and resurrection, the fulfilled Scriptures, the changed lives around us. What faith does not have is a guarantee in advance of how each step of obedience will turn out. We trust the person, and then we act, and the confirmation often comes after. That is not irrational. It is how every relationship of trust works.
verseByVerse.note: The master of the feast was the guest put in charge of the celebration.

verseByVerse.quote: "When the master of the feast tasted the water now become wine, and did not know where it came from (though the servants who had drawn the water knew), the master of the feast called the bridegroom and said to him, 'Everyone serves the good wine first, and when people have drunk freely, then the poor wine. But you have kept the good wine until now.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The servants knew. The water had truly become wine. The steward tastes it and cannot account for it. The bridegroom gets the credit and has no idea what for. The guests drink it and never learn anything happened. The only people in the building who understand are the ones who carried the jars. The knowledge went not to the man with the office, nor to the one being honoured, but to the servants, who obeyed a strange instruction and therefore found out (7:17).

Where from? The word is pothen, where from, and it is going to follow Jesus through the whole book. The crowd in Jerusalem will say they know where this man comes from and that settles it (7:27). A blind man will tell the authorities that the remarkable thing is precisely that they do not know where he comes from (9:29–30). And at the very end, Pilate, out of his depth in his own judgment hall, will ask him straight out, where are you from? and get no answer at all (19:9). The first person in this Gospel to taste what Jesus has done and be unable to account for it is a wine steward at a party, and he will not be the last.

The bridegroom praised by mistake. The bridegroom is praised for the one thing at his own wedding he had nothing to do with. Within a chapter John the Baptist will use that word of Jesus: the one who has the bride is the bridegroom (3:29). The real bridegroom is standing in that room, and the compliment goes to the wrong man from a man who does not know what he is saying, as it will when a high priest explains that it is better for one man to die for the people (11:49–52).

The good wine until now. The world puts its best first: the advertisement is better than the product, youth is spent early, and almost every pleasure is best at the start and then fades. God works the other way round. The old covenant was good, but the new is better (Hebrews 8:6), and Scripture ends with a wedding, the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:9). The steward’s compliment describes how God runs the whole of history: he keeps the best until last, and for his people the best is still to come.

What it does not mean. The best wine last is not an assurance that your circumstances will improve, and it must not be handed to someone as though it were. Plenty of Christian lives get harder; health goes, and the people you love are buried one at a time. What is promised is not a better stretch of road. It is a better end, and that end is not an ending but life with him for ever.

Where Christians differ: wine and alcohol. Some Christians argue that biblical wine was unfermented grape juice, and that Christians should abstain completely. This commentary’s view: the wine Jesus made was real wine, as the master’s comment shows. Scripture praises wine as God’s gift (Psalm 104:15) while forbidding drunkenness (Ephesians 5:18; Proverbs 23:29–35). Christians are free to drink in moderation, and free to abstain; they must never get drunk, and must be willing to abstain out of love for weaker brothers (Romans 14:21). Abstinence is a wise choice for many, but not a command.

Not a killjoy. The steward’s remark about guests who have drunk freely makes no sense of grape juice. But nothing here licenses excess, and nothing shames the Christian who abstains. What the sign does say is that the God who came among us was not a killjoy: his first miracle was a wedding present, and an extravagant one.

What if alcohol has been a problem for me or my family? Then abstaining is not legalism but wisdom, and often love. Freedom to drink is not an obligation to drink, and Paul says it is good not to drink wine if it makes a brother stumble (Romans 14:21); the brother may be you. If drink has a hold on you, the gospel offers forgiveness and real help: confess it honestly to God and to a trusted Christian, get practical support, and remove it from your home. And if a parent’s or spouse’s drinking has wounded you, this passage does not ask you to celebrate wine. It shows you a Lord who brings joy without ruin, and who can heal what drink has broken.

In everyday life. If you have begun to suspect that your best days are behind you, that the years when you felt most alive and most in love with God are in the past, say the steward’s sentence over your life. In a life without Christ that fear would be right. For anyone in Christ the order is reversed: the best is still ahead.

For worship. The good wine kept until now is the Son himself. Long ago God spoke by the prophets, and he kept his best until these last days, when he spoke to us by his Son (Hebrews 1:1–2). The one who made the wine at Cana would give his own blood for the new covenant, and every cup of grace since has come from that store. Glory to the God who kept the best until now.

parallels.desc: a feast of well-aged wine
the mountains shall drip sweet wine

verseByVerse.quote: "This, the first of his signs, Jesus did at Cana in Galilee, and manifested his glory. And his disciples believed in him. After this he went down to Capernaum, with his mother and his brothers and his disciples, and they stayed there for a few days."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first of his signs. John calls Jesus’ miracles signs (sēmeia), pointers to who he is. Matthew, Mark and Luke commonly call them dynameis, mighty works; John never uses that word for them.

A signpost, not a show. A mighty work invites you to be impressed. A signpost has no interest in itself; its whole value lies in pointing somewhere you have not got to yet, and a traveller who praises the carpentry has missed the point. That is what will go wrong with the crowds in chapter 6, who came looking for him not because they saw signs but because they ate their fill of the loaves (6:26).

Seven signs. John records seven signs before the resurrection: water into wine (2:1–11), the official’s son (4:46–54), the paralysed man (5:1–15), the five thousand (6:1–15), walking on water (6:16–21), the man born blind (9:1–41), and Lazarus (11:1–44). The counting is debated at the edges, but he tells us at the close what he was doing (20:30–31). And the word for first is the one he opened the Gospel with: in the beginning was the Word; this was the beginning of his signs.

And manifested his glory. His divine glory (1:14), hidden in his humanity, shone through: we have seen his glory, and here is the first instalment. The Creator, who turns water into wine every year through the vine, does it in a moment. Glory is the shining out of who God is. When Moses asked to see it, God made his goodness pass before him and proclaimed his name, merciful and gracious (Exodus 33:18–19; 34:6). At Cana that same goodness is seen in a man’s kindness to a bridegroom in trouble.

The glory in clay cups. The glory of God, the thing that filled the tent until Moses could not go in, that drove the priests out of Solomon’s temple so that they could not stand to minister (1 Kings 8:11), that Isaiah saw for one moment and cried out that he was undone, was in a back room in Cana, quietly seeing to it that a young couple were not humiliated on their wedding day. Nothing shook. Nobody fell down. The steward went on doing his job and the bridegroom accepted a compliment he had not earned, and the glory of the eternal God went round that room in cups.

His disciples believed. That is the purpose of the signs (20:30–31). They had already believed (1:41–49); now their faith deepened. Faith is not a switch thrown once; it grows, is tested, and grows again. The same men will be scattered on the night of his arrest, and one will refuse to believe the resurrection without touching the wounds. If your faith is larger or smaller than it was five years ago, that is not instability. It is the ordinary condition of everyone in this chapter.

Should I look for signs and miracles today? Look for what the signs were for. They were written down so that you may believe (20:31); the record of them is God’s chosen means of bringing you to faith now, and Jesus pronounced a blessing on those who have not seen and yet have believed (20:29). God still answers prayer, and he can heal and provide in ways that astonish us; we should ask him freely. But the apostolic signs belonged to the founding of the church, and we do not need fresh wonders to confirm a gospel already confirmed. That is the view called cessationism, held because the New Testament ties such signs to the apostles’ own witness (2 Corinthians 12:12; Hebrews 2:3–4). Many faithful Christians, in Pentecostal and charismatic churches among others, believe these gifts continue, and we honour them as brothers; all of us agree that every sign points to Christ. A faith that keeps demanding new signs has missed the one they all point to. You have the signs, in writing, and the Lord himself.

His mother and his brothers. The first mention of his brothers in this Gospel, and John will tell us where they stood: not even his brothers believed in him (7:5).

Who were the brothers who went down to Capernaum? The natural reading is that they were sons of Mary and Joseph, born after Jesus, and so his half-brothers; Matthew names them (Matthew 13:55–56), and Paul met James the Lord’s brother (Galatians 1:19). Roman Catholic and Orthodox Christians, holding that Mary remained a virgin, take them as cousins or as Joseph’s sons by an earlier marriage. But Scripture never says so, and the plain reading is the more likely.

For the one praying for family. This is for you if you have been praying a long time for someone in your family. Living with Jesus did not convert his brothers. A flawless life lived in front of them for three decades did not convert them, and neither did this wedding. And yet James is later found leading the church in Jerusalem, called a pillar by Paul, and writing a letter that is in your Bible (Acts 15:13; Galatians 2:9). What changed them was not more exposure. It was the resurrection: Paul records that the risen Christ appeared to James (1 Corinthians 15:7), and what thirty years under one roof had not done, the risen Lord did. Keep praying.
verseByVerse.note: John calls Jesus’ miracles “signs” — pointers to who he is. Capernaum was a fishing town on the lake shore.

parallels.desc: these are written so that you may believe

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–25 — The Temple Cleansing and the New Temple
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At Passover Jesus finds the temple court full of traders and money-changers and drives them out: his Father’s house is not a place of business. Asked for a sign, he speaks of a temple destroyed and raised in three days, and John explains that he meant his body. Many at the feast believe because of his signs, but Jesus does not entrust himself to them, for he knows what is in every heart.
verseByVerse.theology:
The temple cleansing is the Lord coming suddenly to his temple (Malachi 3:1). The zeal that consumes him is the Son’s passion for his Father’s honour, and my Father’s house is the claim that gives him authority there.

The temple thread runs the length of Scripture and this passage is its hinge. In 1:14 the Word dwelt among us; here John says the temple is a body (v. 21); and the Bible ends with a city with no temple at all, for its temple is the Lord God and the Lamb (Revelation 21:22).

Verses 23–25 must not be used to unsettle the wrong reader. They describe faith produced by spectacle and not yet tested, like the crowd who turn back in chapter 6 (6:66). Anxiety about whether one’s faith is real is not a symptom of this condition; the people described were untroubled. And when Jesus does not entrust himself to them, he is not turning them away: the next thing he does is explain the new birth to Nicodemus.
verseByVerse.examples:
The buying and selling were not wicked in themselves, but they had filled the one court where the nations could pray. The searching question is whether anything in the ordinary life of a congregation makes it hard for an outsider to get near God.

The anger of this scene is not at odds with meekness: it is what love does when what it loves is being damaged. But it is no warrant for aggression on God’s behalf. Jesus’ anger is aimed at the dishonouring of God and the shutting out of the powerless, never at a slight to himself (1 Peter 2:23).

The chapter break hides a connection. Verse 25 says he knew what was in man, and the next sentence introduces a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus: the statement and its illustration, side by side.

verseByVerse.quote: The Passover of the Jews was at hand, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem. In the temple he found those who were selling oxen and sheep and pigeons, and the money-changers sitting there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Passover of the Jews was at hand. John mentions three Passovers (2:13; 6:4; 11:55), the main reason the ministry is reckoned at about three years. And the Lord has come to his temple, as Malachi said he would (Malachi 3:1), and the first thing he does there is turn over the furniture.

In the flow. At Cana he turned the water of purification into wine; here he confronts the centre of the whole system of sacrifice, and verse 21 will say that the true temple is his body. The scene also opens the conflict with the Jerusalem leaders that ends at the cross.

In the temple. The trading happened in the outer court, the Court of the Gentiles: animals for sacrifice, sold on the spot to pilgrims. And he found them: he is not told about it; he arrives and looks.

A trade with a rationale. The trade was not obviously a racket. A sacrifice had to be without blemish, and a lamb carried a hundred miles had a poor chance of passing inspection; buying one on site, already approved, was practical.

The money-changers. Every adult male Jew owed an annual half-shekel temple tax. It had to be paid in the coinage of Tyre, required because its silver was reliably pure, even though it carried the image of a pagan god. So pilgrims had to change their money. The changers took a commission, and the trade was probably controlled by, and profitable to, the high-priestly families; later Jewish writings remember them for exactly that.

Rot by convenience. The problem was not that somebody had smuggled something wicked into the temple. It was that a set of reasonable arrangements, each defensible on its own terms, had together turned worship into a transaction, gradually, with nobody deciding it. Institutions do not usually rot by scandal. They rot by convenience. And the heart likes the arrangement. A God who can be dealt with at a counter asks for your money but not for you; pay the fee, perform the rite, and you are free to go. That is religion as a way of keeping God at a safe distance, and it is the opposite of what the temple was built for.

The court of the nations. Now the location, which most readers have never been told. The temple’s courts grew more restricted as you went in: the Court of the Women, then the court for Israelite men, then the priests’ court. The outermost and largest was the Court of the Gentiles, the only place in the building where a non-Jew could come and pray. Beyond it a barrier carried notices warning any foreigner who passed that he would have himself to blame for his death; inscribed stones from it have been dug up. The market was in that court. The one place on earth where a Gentile could come near the God of Israel had been given over to livestock pens and currency tables in festival week.

A house of prayer for all the nations. That is why, at the later cleansing, Jesus cries out Isaiah’s words with the clause we usually leave off: for all the nations (Isaiah 56:7; Mark 11:17). The offence is not merely commerce in a holy place, but that the arrangements of the religious had made it impossible for the outsider to pray. The court the insiders had filled with trade was the court he meant to fill with worshippers from every tribe and tongue.

Is it wrong for churches to sell things or handle money? Not in itself. Churches need money to pay ministers, care for the poor and support missionaries, and Scripture commands generous giving (2 Corinthians 9:7). A bookstall or a collection is not a temple market. The question is whether money and convenience have begun to shape worship and push people out: whether the gospel is ever made to look like something you buy, whether the poor feel unwelcome, whether leaders profit from the flock (1 Peter 5:2). Watch the purpose, not merely the transaction.

In everyday life. The easy application of this passage is about churches selling things, and it lets us think the passage is about somebody else. The harder question is the Court of the Gentiles one: is there anything about the way your church operates, its vocabulary, its arrangements, the things everyone knows and nobody explains, that would make it hard for an outsider to get near God? Nobody in Jerusalem had decided to exclude the nations. They had simply needed the space. Christ made room for you when you were far off; make room for one such person this Sunday.
verseByVerse.note: The trading happened in the outer court. Money-changers exchanged coins into the currency accepted for the temple tax. John places this cleansing early; the other Gospels record one in the last week.

verseByVerse.quote: And making a whip of cords, he drove them all out of the temple, with the sheep and oxen. And he poured out the coins of the money-changers and overturned their tables. And he told those who sold the pigeons, "Take these things away; do not make my Father's house a house of trade."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Making a whip of cords. Some readers enjoy this scene too much, and others are quietly embarrassed by it. The Greek is more restrained than the paintings. He made it of cords, improvised perhaps from rushes or ropes lying about a place full of tethered livestock, and most likely for driving the animals, not for beating people.

He drove them all out. The phrase is followed at once by with the sheep and oxen, which many read as saying who the all were, the animals, though it may include the traders. What the text does make plain is that no one is reported struck: no injury, no arrest, and the authorities who arrive do not accuse him of assault; they ask for his credentials. Whatever happened, it was not a brawl.

The coins and the cages. Look at how the action is graded. The animals are driven out. The coins are poured across the stone floor and the tables turned over. But the pigeon-sellers, whose birds were caged, are told to take them away. He does not tip over their cages, and one likely reason is that pigeons were the offering of the poor, the sacrifice for those who could not afford a lamb (Leviticus 5:7), and released birds do not come back. Even in the middle of it, he will not wreck what the poorest worshippers depended on.

Is this consistent with the gentle Jesus? It is, and the way to see it is to ask what anger actually is. Anger is what love does when what it loves is being damaged. A man who can watch his own child be harmed and feel nothing is not gentle; he is absent. The reason this scene sits so oddly with us is that we have quietly redefined gentleness as the absence of strong feeling, when in Scripture meekness is strength brought under command. Everything here is under command. He does not snatch up a weapon; he stops and makes a whip of cords. Whatever this was, it was not a loss of temper; it was a decision. The Lamb of God has a holy wrath (Revelation 6:16), and it is the same love that weeps over Jerusalem.

What it does not mean. This passage has been used to justify a great deal that has nothing to do with it. It is no warrant for Christians to be aggressive on God’s behalf, still less violent, and no cover for the man whose temper is a standing problem in his household and who has learned to call it righteous anger. Two things separate this from that. Every scrap of it is aimed at the abuse of God’s honour and the exclusion of the powerless, none at a slight to himself; when the injuries were personal he did not open his mouth (Isaiah 53:7; 1 Peter 2:23). And this is the Son acting in his own house with the owner’s authority. If your anger is regularly about your own treatment, this passage is not about you.

Then is anger always wrong for me? No. Be angry and do not sin, Paul writes (Ephesians 4:26). Anger at real evil, at cruelty, injustice, abuse, the dishonouring of God, can be right, and indifference to such things is not a virtue. But our anger is rarely pure, so Scripture surrounds it with fences: be slow to anger (James 1:19–20), do not let the sun go down on it, never take revenge (Romans 12:19), and do not let it harden into bitterness. Ask whose honour your anger is defending. Then bring it to God, act through right channels, and leave vengeance to him.

My Father’s house. Not our Father’s house, but my Father’s house: Jesus claims a unique relationship with God, as he did at twelve in this same building (Luke 2:49). That is what gives him the right to use the whip. He is not a reformer with views about temple administration; he is the Son, dealing with what has been done to his family’s house. A house of trade perhaps echoes Zechariah 14:21: on the day of the LORD there will no longer be a trader in the house of the LORD of hosts. That day has come, and it should sober us as well as thrill us. The one who came to Cana as a guest comes to the temple as its owner, and Malachi, who promised the Lord would come suddenly to his temple, asked in the next breath who could endure the day of his coming (Malachi 3:1–2).

One cleansing or two? John places a cleansing at the start of Jesus’ ministry, the other Gospels one at the end; the details differ, and Jesus may well have done it twice, though John sometimes arranges true events by their meaning and not strictly by date. Either way the point of the scene is untouched. (See Mark 11:15 for the fuller answer.)

For worship. In this chapter the Son holds the whip. Before the Gospel ends, Pilate has him flogged (19:1), and the one who drove the traders from his Father’s house stands silent under the lash, scourged to make a defiled people into a clean house for God. The zeal that would not let his Father be cheapened is the same love that let himself be beaten for those who had cheapened him.

parallels.desc: no longer a trader in the house of the LORD
my Father’s house

verseByVerse.quote: "His disciples remembered that it was written, 'Zeal for your house will consume me.' So the Jews said to him, 'What sign do you show us for doing these things?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
His disciples remembered. The verb comes twice in this chapter, and the two rememberings are not alike. Here the Scripture comes to mind at once, while the coins are still rolling. Later they will remember his saying about the temple of his body, and it will take three years and a resurrection to do it (v. 22).

Zeal for your house will consume me. Psalm 69:9, a psalm of the righteous sufferer often applied to Jesus (15:25; 19:28–29; Romans 15:3). Consume means devour, eat me up. In the psalm the zeal has already consumed the psalmist; what the disciples remember is will consume me. So the sentence is a prediction: this will eat him. The temple authorities will finally move against him, and his zeal for his Father’s house will carry him to his death.

Psalm 69 at the cross. John will reach for this psalm of a man hated without cause again at the cross, when they lift up the sour wine (19:28–29). The zeal and the vinegar come out of the same psalm.

What is zeal, and why do I not seem to have it? What is being described here is not a temperament. Some people are naturally intense and some are not, and the intense ones are not thereby more godly; a great deal of what passes for zeal in religious life is simply a strong personality with a subject. What the disciples saw was not energy. It was a man who could not be indifferent to his Father’s honour because he loved his Father, and the zeal was the shape the love took when the honour was being damaged. So the question to ask is not, am I zealous enough? No one has ever answered that helpfully. Ask instead what it takes to move you. Everybody has something. Find the last thing that genuinely stirred you, that you could not simply let pass, and you have located what you love. And if it is not God’s honour, ask him to grow your love for him, and the zeal will follow.

What sign do you show us for doing these things? By what authority? Prove it with a miracle. The prophets sometimes did symbolic acts; let him prove he is a prophet. And there is an irony in it that only grows as the book goes on: what sign do you show us? is asked in a Gospel built entirely out of signs, by men who, as a body, will be shown sign after sign and refuse to believe.

Querying the credentials. But look carefully at what they are and are not disputing. In John’s account nobody says the market should stay. Nobody defends the money tables or argues that the Court of the Gentiles was the right place for livestock. What is challenged is his standing to do anything about it: not you are wrong, but who authorised you? The safest way to avoid a charge is to query the credentials of whoever brought it.

In everyday life. Jesus’ zeal for his Father’s honour cost him his life, and it was spent for you. You are accepted because of him, so you have no reputation you need to protect. When you are rightly challenged about something wrong in you, resist the urge to query the credentials of the one who said it. Ask first whether it is true.

For worship. The same verse of Psalm 69 goes on: the reproaches of those who reproach you have fallen on me, and Paul says that was Christ (Romans 15:3). He was so jealous for his Father’s name that he let the abuse aimed at heaven land on his own head, and in being consumed he became the house where God and sinners meet.

parallels.desc: zeal for your house has consumed me

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered them, "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up." The Jews then said, "It has taken forty-six years to build this temple, and will you raise it up in three days?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Destroy this temple. The sign he offers: his resurrection. Destroy is a command with the sense of if you destroy. It sounds like a dare, though both sides know they will never pull down Herod’s stonework. But in about three years they will do precisely this to the temple he actually meant, his body (v. 21). “Raise up” (egeirō) is the word for resurrection.

How testimony gets bent. At his trial witnesses say: we heard him say, I will destroy this temple that is made with hands (Mark 14:58), and at the cross the passers-by jeered at him for it (Mark 15:29). He said you destroy. They reported I will destroy. The pronoun was moved, and a prophecy about what they would do to him became a threat about what he would do to them. Little was invented. Something was shifted, and that was enough to hang a capital charge on.

Forty-six years. Herod began rebuilding around 20 BC, which puts this at about AD 27, one of the main fixed points for dating Jesus’ ministry. The work went on until about AD 63, and in AD 70 the Romans burned the temple. They were holding up to the Son of God a building that would stand complete for about seven years. They were not wrong about their temple; forty-six years of it could not be redone in three days. They were wrong about which temple was standing in front of them. He let them destroy the true temple, his body, and on the third day he raised it, never to fall again.

And will you raise it up in three days? They take him literally, and mock. It is the first appearance of a pattern that runs through this whole Gospel. They hear a claim about masonry and answer with a building schedule. In the next chapter a teacher of Israel will hear born again and ask whether a grown man can enter his mother’s womb a second time (3:4). A woman at a well will hear living water and point out that he has nothing to draw with (4:11). A crowd will hear bread from heaven and ask for a permanent supply (6:34). Every time, the misunderstanding takes the same form: the words are taken at the flattest, most literal level, and the flat reading is the one that spares the hearer from having to deal with Jesus himself. The natural mind cannot perceive the things of the Spirit without new birth (1 Corinthians 2:14).

Why did Jesus speak in riddles? Not to hide the truth from honest seekers, but to draw them in and to expose hearts. A saying like this one sticks in the memory and opens up later, which is exactly what happened to the disciples (v. 22). It also sifts the hearers: those who want to understand him keep asking, while those who have already decided against him take the flattest reading and walk away. Jesus never plays games with people who truly want him. When Nicodemus asks, he explains at length. When the disciples ask, he tells them plainly. If something he says puzzles you, do what they did: stay near, keep reading, and ask.
verseByVerse.note: Herod the Great began rebuilding the temple around 20 BC; forty-six years brings us to about AD 27. The work went on for decades more.

parallels.desc: the charge at his trial

verseByVerse.quote: But he was speaking about the temple of his body. When therefore he was raised from the dead, his disciples remembered that he had said this, and they believed the Scripture and the word that Jesus had spoken.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The temple of his body. John’s explanation, and the key. The theme of God’s dwelling place runs the length of the Bible, and this verse is its turning point. In chapter 1 John wrote that the Word dwelt among us (1:14), the language of the tabernacle, the tent where the glory came down. Here the tabernacle has become the temple, the fixed house where God could be met, and John says that house is now a body. Not a building that contains the presence, but a person in whom God is present. Through his death and resurrection Jesus himself becomes the meeting place of God and humanity (4:21–24). Here is the change it makes. In the old temple a worshipper met God by coming to a place, through a priest, with a sacrifice. Now we meet God by coming to a person. When you pray in Jesus’ name and trust his sacrifice, you come as near to God as any high priest behind the curtain, for through him we have access in one Spirit to the Father (Ephesians 2:18).

No temple in the city. For a thousand years God had consented to be met in a house of stone: the smoke, the blood, the courts, the curtain, the one room no one could enter but once a year and never without blood. Then a man stood in the middle of it and said the meeting place was himself; three years later they took him outside the city and killed him, and the curtain of that house was torn in two, from top to bottom (Mark 15:38). The house was never the point. The Son was the point, and the house had been saying so, in stone, for a thousand years. At the close of the Bible John records what was missing from the city that is the end of everything: I saw no temple in the city, for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb (Revelation 21:22). There is no building at the end. There was never going to be.

We are his temple too. And his people, united to him, become God’s temple (1 Corinthians 3:16; Ephesians 2:21–22). The living stones are built on the living cornerstone (1 Peter 2:4–5). Where Christ’s people gather in his name, God dwells; and each believer’s body is a temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19).

Then does it matter where or how we worship? Where, much less than before. Jesus will tell the Samaritan woman that the hour is coming when true worshippers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, not on this mountain or in Jerusalem (4:21–24). No building is holy ground in itself, and you can meet God in a kitchen as truly as in a cathedral. How, very much. We come to God only through Christ, the true temple, and we must worship him as he has revealed himself, not as we invent. And because the church is his temple, gathering with his people is not optional decoration; it is where he has promised to dwell (Hebrews 10:25; Matthew 18:20).

After he was raised. They heard the words with their own ears, and it meant nothing to them for the best part of three years. Then the resurrection made the old sentence clear, as he had promised: the Holy Spirit will bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you (14:26). This verse is that promise working, recorded by a man on the receiving end of it.

For anyone in the middle of something they cannot read. There is a great deal of pressure on Christians to understand what God is doing while he is doing it: to have an account of the illness, the redundancy, the years that went nowhere, the prayer that was not answered. That pressure does not come from this book. The men closest to Jesus, watching the most important events in human history at a distance of a few feet, understood almost none of it until afterwards, and were not disqualified for it. What was asked of them was not comprehension. It was staying near enough to remember.

Scripture and his word. They believed two things with one verb: a sentence he said in a courtyard is placed beside the Old Testament Scriptures as the same kind of word. Jesus’ word has the authority of Scripture.

Which Scripture? John does not name one. Passages such as Psalm 16:10, you will not abandon my soul to Sheol, and Isaiah 53 were among those the apostles later preached, and Jesus himself opened all the Scriptures to them after he rose (Luke 24:27). Their faith was in the whole Old Testament witness to his death and resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).

parallels.desc: they remembered his words

verseByVerse.quote: Now when he was in Jerusalem at the Passover Feast, many believed in his name when they saw the signs that he was doing. But Jesus on his part did not entrust himself to them, because he knew all people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Many believed. Faith produced by spectacle: real, but shallow. Nothing has yet been asked of these people; they have been carried along by a movement that is going well. John is not saying their belief is fake, but untested, and Jesus knows exactly what it is worth.

Did not entrust himself. A play on words English cannot carry. They believed (episteusan) in him, but he did not believe (episteuen), entrust himself, to them: the same verb both times. He did not treat their excitement as a commitment, or open his heart to them as he would to friends (15:15).

What happens to it. In chapter 6 a crowd of the same kind is fed and follows him across a lake; then he says something they find intolerable, and after this many of his disciples turned back and no longer walked with him (6:66). That is this kind of faith meeting the first thing it did not like.

Because he knew all people. This is not cynicism but knowledge. Not all who follow the miracle-worker will follow the crucified one, and many want his blessings without himself.

How do I know my faith is not like theirs? This is a frightening sentence, and it should be handled slowly, because it unsettles people who are already unsettled. If you are troubled by these verses, if you have read them and gone cold and started auditing your own conversion, see that the people being described here were not troubled at all. They were delighted. Nobody in that Passover crowd was lying awake wondering whether their faith would hold, because nothing had yet happened to make them wonder. Anxiety about the reality of your faith is not a symptom of the condition described here. It is nearly always a symptom of caring whether it is real, which is the one thing this crowd conspicuously did not do. Look away from your faith to its object: true faith rests on Christ himself, not on the excitement of signs, and he keeps those who are his (10:28–29).

Same words, different outcome. John uses of these people the same phrase he used of the saved: believed in his name (1:12). The difference does not lie in the words but in what the faith does when it is tested. So Scripture does not ask whether your believing began with the right feeling, but whether you are still holding on to Christ. And those whom God has truly given faith he will keep to the end (Philippians 1:6).

Withholding, not withdrawing. He did not entrust himself to them, but he did not send them away either. The very next thing in this Gospel is that a member of the Jerusalem establishment comes at night with a compliment about signs, and gets the longest and tenderest explanation of the new birth in the Bible. Jesus refuses to be naive about them, but he does not dismiss them.

parallels.desc: I the LORD search the heart

verseByVerse.quote: and needed no one to bear witness about man, for he himself knew what was in man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one to bear witness. This is a Gospel obsessed with witness: the Baptist, the works, the Father and the Scriptures all bear witness, and by chapter 5 Jesus will name them one after another. Everything about himself he was content to have testified to by others. About human beings he needed no one to bear witness, because he already had all the evidence.

He himself knew what was in man. He knows the human heart perfectly, as only God does (1 Samuel 16:7; Jeremiah 17:9–10; Psalm 139:1–4). He knew Nathanael (1:47–48), and will know the Samaritan woman’s past (4:18), and Judas’ betrayal (6:64).

The chapter break in the wrong place. Verse 25 ends with the word man, anthrōpos, and the next sentence John wrote begins: now there was a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus. He knew what was in man, and here comes one: a good, learned, searching member of the ruling council who has understood nothing, and who will be told that what he needs is not more instruction but to be born. His first words, that no one can do these signs unless God is with him, are the sign-based faith of the Passover crowd in the mouth of one of the best-qualified men in Jerusalem.

A comfort and a warning. That Christ knows what is in a man is either the worst news or the best. It is the worst because you can never show him an edited version of yourself, not even the one you tell yourself at three in the morning: he has seen what is really there.

Full-knowledge love. And it is the best news for the same reason, once you know what he did after reading it. The man who knew what was in man went to Jerusalem anyway, into the hands of people whose hearts he had read in full, and died for them. If he had loved us on the strength of a favourable report, the love would be worth nothing, because the report would have been wrong. There was no report. He looked. He knew what was in Judas on the night he dipped the morsel and handed it to him. He knew what was in Peter when he looked at him and called him a rock. He knew what was in the men who would drive the nails, and he did not revise the plan. The cross is not love in ignorance of human sin; it is love offered in full knowledge of it.

If he knows my heart, why should I confess? Because confession is not giving him information; it is agreeing with him. When you confess, you stop hiding and start walking in the light with him (1 John 1:7–9). He already knows; what changes is you. Confession breaks the power of secrecy, humbles pride, and opens you to receive the forgiveness he has promised. It is the difference between a child whose father knows what he did and a child who comes and says so. The father’s knowledge is the same. The relationship is not.

In everyday life. A short question: is there anything you are hoping God has not noticed? Name it, silently, now. Naming it told him nothing he did not know. And the very next chapter contains the words: for God so loved the world. Be honest with him today about what he already knows, and receive what he offers.

parallels.desc: you alone know the hearts of all

2.title: The First Sign: Water into Wine
2.text: <sup>1</sup>On the third day there was a wedding at Cana in Galilee, and the mother of Jesus was there.<sup>2</sup>Jesus also was invited to the wedding with his disciples.<sup>3</sup>When the wine ran out, the mother of Jesus said to him, “They have no wine.”<sup>4</sup>And Jesus said to her, “Woman, what does this have to do with me? My hour has not yet come.”<sup>5</sup>His mother said to the servants, “Do whatever he tells you.”<sup>6</sup>Now there were six stone water jars there for the Jewish rites of purification, each holding twenty or thirty gallons.<sup>7</sup>Jesus said to the servants, “Fill the jars with water.” And they filled them up to the brim.<sup>8</sup>And he said to them, “Now draw some out and take it to the master of the feast.” So they took it.<sup>9</sup>When the master of the feast tasted the water now become wine, and did not know where it came from (though the servants who had drawn the water knew), the master of the feast called the bridegroom<sup>10</sup>and said to him, “Everyone serves the good wine first, and when people have drunk freely, then the poor wine. But you have kept the good wine until now.”<sup>11</sup>This, the first of his signs, Jesus did at Cana in Galilee, and manifested his glory. And his disciples believed in him.<sup>12</sup>After this he went down to Capernaum, with his mother and his brothers and his disciples, and they stayed there for a few days.<sup>13</sup>The Passover of the Jews was at hand, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem.<sup>14</sup>In the temple he found those who were selling oxen and sheep and pigeons, and the money-changers sitting there.<sup>15</sup>And making a whip of cords, he drove them all out of the temple, with the sheep and oxen. And he poured out the coins of the money-changers and overturned their tables.<sup>16</sup>And he told those who sold the pigeons, “Take these things away; do not make my Father’s house a house of trade.”<sup>17</sup>His disciples remembered that it was written, “Zeal for your house will consume me.”<sup>18</sup>So the Jews said to him, “What sign do you show us for doing these things?”<sup>19</sup>Jesus answered them, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.”<sup>20</sup>The Jews then said, “It has taken forty-six years to build this temple, and will you raise it up in three days?”<sup>21</sup>But he was speaking about the temple of his body.<sup>22</sup>When therefore he was raised from the dead, his disciples remembered that he had said this, and they believed the Scripture and the word that Jesus had spoken.<sup>23</sup>Now when he was in Jerusalem at the Passover Feast, many believed in his name when they saw the signs that he was doing.<sup>24</sup>But Jesus on his part did not entrust himself to them, because he knew all people<sup>25</sup>and needed no one to bear witness about man, for he himself knew what was in man.
2.overview:
Two scenes open Jesus’ public ministry, one in a village home and one in the temple, and both announce that something new has come. At a wedding in Cana Jesus turns the water standing in stone jars for Jewish purification into an overflowing supply of the best wine. It is the first of the signs John records: he reveals his glory, and his disciples believe. The prophets pictured the messianic age as a feast overflowing with wine (Isaiah 25:6; Amos 9:13), and the water of the old rites gives way to the wine of the kingdom.

At Passover in Jerusalem Jesus drives the traders from the temple court, and when he is asked for a sign he points to the temple of his body, destroyed and raised in three days. The meeting place of God and people is now Jesus himself. Many in Jerusalem believe because of his signs, but he does not entrust himself to them, for he knows what is in every heart.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–21 — Nicodemus and the New Birth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Nicodemus visits Jesus by night and is told that without a birth from above no one can see God’s kingdom. Jesus explains the birth of water and the Spirit, rebukes Israel’s teacher for not understanding, and points to the Son of Man who must be lifted up like the bronze serpent. The reason is God’s love for the world in the gift of his Son, who came to save, not to condemn; and the light that has come divides those who come to it from those who love the darkness.
verseByVerse.theology:
The new birth is the work of the Spirit, who blows where he wills: no one can produce, control or predict it, and the Spirit gives it to those whom the Father has given to the Son. The lifting up of the Son of Man is the means by which eternal life comes to those who look in faith. God’s motive is love for a world set against him; his means is the gift of his Son; his purpose is salvation, not condemnation. And the light that has come shows each person’s verdict by whether he comes to it or runs from it.

The chapter rules out religious effort as a way in, not because effort is insincere but because flesh, which here means human nature even at its best, cannot give birth to spiritual life.
verseByVerse.examples:
Born again, or born from above, is one of the fullest descriptions of salvation in the New Testament: it names the kind of change (rebirth, not reform), its source (God), and its necessity (without it the kingdom cannot be seen).

Nicodemus is not finished at the end of this conversation. He appears twice more, each time further into the open (7:50–51; 19:39). The man who came at night buried him by day.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews. This man came to Jesus by night and said to him, "Rabbi, we know that you are a teacher come from God, for no one can do these signs that you do unless God is with him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. The chapter of the new birth and of the best-known verse in the Bible. A respected teacher is told he needs not more instruction but a new life only God can give; the Son of Man must be lifted up like the bronze serpent; and the Baptist’s last word is that Jesus must increase.

The link. John has just said that Jesus knew what was in man (2:25), and the next sentence begins: now there was a man of the Pharisees. Same word, back to back. Having told us that Jesus reads the human heart, John opens one up.

A man of the Pharisees. Devout, learned, moral, one of the movement that took God’s law with total seriousness in the details of an ordinary week. John has not chosen a tax collector. If a man could be got into the kingdom by conviction, learning, discipline or religious office, this man is already inside. The point of Nicodemus is not that he is a hypocrite. It is that he is the best that human religion can produce.

A ruler of the Jews. A member of the Sanhedrin, the ruling council of seventy-one. Jesus will call him the teacher of Israel (v. 10).

By night. Perhaps for fear of being seen (12:42; 19:38), calling on the Galilean who had just overturned the temple tables; perhaps for a quiet talk, since later Jewish writings commend study of the law at night. But John rarely mentions night without meaning more. In this Gospel people love the darkness, and the blackest moment is marked with the words: and it was night (13:30). Nicodemus came out of the darkness toward the light, and where he goes from there is the whole of his story.

Three appearances. This is the first of three appearances, each further out into the open. Here he comes at night with a compliment. In chapter 7, when the authorities are moving against Jesus, Nicodemus speaks up, not bravely, but he speaks: does our law judge a man without first giving him a hearing? (7:50–51). He is answered with a sneer (7:52). And after everything, when most of the twelve have scattered and there is nothing left to gain, he comes to a Roman execution site to help bury the body, bringing about seventy-five pounds of myrrh and aloes (19:39), a quantity fit for a king, in front of anyone who cared to look. He seems to have become a believer. The man who came at night buried him in the afternoon. Whatever happened in the conversation that follows did not finish that evening, and it does not seem to have failed.

A teacher come from God. Respectful, and true as far as it goes. The we suggests colleagues who think this and have not come. Calling Jesus a teacher leaves Nicodemus a student, a position he can hold with dignity. What he is about to hear is that he does not need a better teacher. He needs to be born.

More than he knew. Jesus has indeed come from God, but not as prophets and rabbis come. He is the one who descended from heaven (v. 13), the Word who was God (1:1). The teacher of Israel has come to consult a promising colleague, and has in fact come to the one every Scripture he has studied is about (5:39).

Unless God is with him. Every clause of that is true. It is also precisely the position of the Passover crowd who believed because they saw signs, and to whom Jesus did not entrust himself (2:23–24). Nicodemus is that crowd with a doctorate.

Is it wrong to come to Jesus secretly or hesitantly? It is not where anyone should stay, but it is where many begin, and Jesus did not turn Nicodemus away. He received a frightened, half-convinced man at night and gave him his fullest teaching on the new birth. If you are exploring the faith quietly, or a believer still afraid of what others will think, come anyway; he welcomes honest seekers. But do not stay in the dark. Nicodemus’ story moves toward the open, and so should yours. Jesus warns that whoever is ashamed of him and his words, of him he will be ashamed (Luke 9:26). Ask him for courage for the next step into the light.
verseByVerse.note: Nicodemus was a member of the Sanhedrin, the ruling council. Coming by night may have been for secrecy or simply for quiet conversation.

parallels.desc: Nicodemus speaks up in the council
he brings spices for Jesus’ burial

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered him, "Truly, truly, I say to you, unless one is born again he cannot see the kingdom of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Truly, truly. Jesus does not answer the compliment; he answers the need. And he opens with truly, truly (a doubled amen), which in this Gospel only he uses. The prophets said thus says the LORD; he says I say to you, on his own authority.

Unless one is born again. The ESV notes that “again” (Greek anōthen) can also be rendered “from above”. Both are intended: a second birth, and a birth from God. Nicodemus hears only the first, which is not stupidity: his mind has no place for what is being said. A second natural birth would change nothing; flesh would still produce flesh (v. 6). What he needs is not improvement, but a new life given by God.

What does born again mean? It means that God the Holy Spirit gives a spiritually dead person new life, so that he is made alive to God, given a new heart that loves him, and enabled to repent and believe (Ezekiel 36:26; Ephesians 2:4–5). Theologians call it regeneration. It is not turning over a new leaf, having an emotional experience, or joining a particular kind of church. It is something God does in a person, as invisible as conception and as real as birth, and its effects show in a changed life: faith in Christ, love for God and his people, hatred of sin (1 John 5:1; 3:14). Every true Christian is born again; there is no other kind.

He cannot see. Without the new birth a person is blind to the kingdom, even the most religious. And the verb changes: here see, in verse 5 enter. The kingdom is not a locked room he stands outside, rattling the handle. It is a country he cannot even see, which is why argument alone never brings anyone in: he must first be given sight.

The kingdom, twice. The kingdom of God is the headline of Jesus’ preaching in Matthew, Mark and Luke, the subject of many of the parables. In John the phrase appears only here and in verse 5. The great theme of the other three Gospels surfaces once, in a night-time conversation with one man, and is used to tell him that he cannot get in as he is.

The King across the room. Nicodemus cannot see the kingdom, and its King is a few feet away, speaking to him. The birth from above brings people to him: to all who received him, who believed in his name, he gave the right to become children of God (1:12–13). The new birth is not another way in beside Christ. It is God opening blind eyes to see the King.

The wrong category. Nicodemus has spent his life on a project of improvement, and by any available measure it has succeeded. He is not told that he did it badly or must try harder, but that it was the wrong category of thing altogether. You cannot educate your way into a family. A man may study a language for forty years and still not be French. Grace does not improve what we are by nature; it makes us new. It does not help a heart that is already willing; it gives a new heart.

In everyday life. Ask what would have to change for God to be more pleased with you than he is today. If the honest answer is a list, pray more, lose the temper less, be more generous, sort out the thing nobody knows about, then you are answering with the wrong kind of thing, and this verse is aimed at exactly that instinct. Every item on that list may be worth doing. Not one of them is a birth. Bring the list to God, and ask him first for what only he can give.

For worship. The God who said, let light shine out of darkness, has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6). That is what seeing the kingdom is: not a vision of a place but the sight of a face. No one climbed into his family; we were born into it from above, while we were still blind.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “again” (Greek anōthen) can also be rendered “from above.” Nicodemus hears one sense; Jesus means both.

parallels.desc: born of God
born again to a living hope

verseByVerse.quote: Nicodemus said to him, "How can a man be born when he is old? Can he enter a second time into his mother's womb and be born?" Jesus answered, "Truly, truly, I say to you, unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
How can a man be born when he is old? Can he enter a second time into his mother’s womb and be born? Nicodemus takes it literally, or perhaps means: how can someone my age change completely? A whole life of religious habit cannot be undone. His question is not absurd; it is the honest bewilderment of a human mind facing something only God can do. And his own picture answers it: a person cannot cause his own birth. That is the point.

Water and the Spirit. Together they recall Ezekiel’s promise of cleansing and a new heart (Ezekiel 36:25–27): water, cleansing from sin; Spirit, new life; one birth with two aspects. What Jesus presses on Nicodemus is not a rite he has missed but a work of God he cannot perform on himself, and the teacher of Israel should have known it (v. 10).

Ezekiel 36 seen, not only cited. Israel is in exile. The temple is rubble, the land is lost, the name of God has been dragged through the mud of the nations by the very people who carried it, and into that, God says: I will sprinkle clean water on you. I will give you a new heart. I will remove the heart of stone. I will put my Spirit within you. Count the verbs: God is doing all of them. There is not one instruction in the passage. God is not telling a defeated people what to do about their condition; he is telling them what he intends to do about it, while they are in no position to contribute anything at all. The water and the Spirit were promised together, in that order, six hundred years earlier, to people who had proved beyond argument that they could not fix themselves. Nicodemus is being told that the promise has arrived, and that he is one of the people it was made about. And the one telling him is the man on whom the Baptist saw the Spirit come down and remain, he who baptizes with the Holy Spirit (1:33). The God who promised to put his Spirit within his people has come in person to keep his word.

Where Christians differ: “born of water”. Roman Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran and some Anglican teaching take the water to be baptism, and teach that baptism is the means of regeneration (baptismal regeneration). Others take water to mean physical birth, the water of the womb; others take it as John’s baptism of repentance. This commentary’s view: the best reading, in context, is Ezekiel 36: water and Spirit describe one spiritual birth, the cleansing and renewing work of the Spirit. Nicodemus could not have understood a reference to Christian baptism, not yet instituted, and Jesus expected him to understand (v. 10). Baptism is the sign of this new birth, not its cause. The thief on the cross entered paradise without baptism (Luke 23:43).

Then what is baptism for? Baptism is the sign Christ commanded for those who have been born again and believe (Matthew 28:19; Acts 2:38, 41). It pictures what the Spirit has done: washing from sin, burial with Christ and rising to new life (Romans 6:3–4). It is the believer’s public confession of faith and the church’s welcome into its fellowship. So it matters greatly and should not be neglected, but it is not a switch that produces new life. This Gospel says again and again that it is believing that gives life (1:12; 3:15; 20:31). This commentary holds, with the 1689 London Baptist Confession (29.1–2), that baptism belongs to those who profess faith, because in the New Testament it follows hearing and believing (Acts 2:41; 8:12). It honours paedobaptist brothers and sisters, who baptise the infants of believers as the covenant sign that replaced circumcision, and who agree that baptism does not of itself regenerate.
verseByVerse.note: Water and Spirit together recall Ezekiel’s promise of cleansing and a new heart.

parallels.desc: I will sprinkle clean water on you and put my Spirit within you
the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit

verseByVerse.quote: "That which is born of the flesh is flesh, and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Flesh is flesh. Human nature, mortal and fallen, working with its own resources. Like produces like: an apple tree does not, with any encouragement, produce a pear. Religion, morality and effort, however good, are still flesh.

What it does not mean. The sentence is not an insult aimed at the body. Flesh here does not mean the physical as opposed to the spiritual; this is the Gospel that has just said the Word became flesh and meant it as the highest news in the world. It means everything a person is by birth, including the best of it. The intelligence. The moral seriousness. The religious instinct. The genuine longing after God that had a member of the Sanhedrin walking through Jerusalem after dark to find one. All of that is real, and none of it is spirit, and no quantity of it turns into spirit. If the flesh could produce even a little of the life of God, the correct advice to Nicodemus would be to produce more of it, and a great deal of religion gives exactly that advice.

Spirit is spirit. Only the Spirit can produce spiritual life. New birth is not the improvement of the old nature but the creation of a new one (2 Corinthians 5:17), and we do not cooperate in our own birth: the initiative and the power belong to the Spirit. This does not mean that a Christian stops being an ordinary human being with a body and a personality, but that there is now in him a life that comes from God and is alive to God. He can pray as a child to a Father, love what God loves and grieve over what grieves him, because the Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God (Romans 8:15–16).

Spirit and life in his words. Jesus will tie it to himself: it is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh is no help at all; the words he has spoken are spirit and life (6:63). The Spirit brings the dead to life through the words of Christ, as he once called into a tomb and a dead man came out (11:43–44).

For the one who has tried and failed. There is a hard comfort in this for anyone who has spent years trying and getting nowhere. The effort did not fail because there was too little of it. Effort was never the way spiritual life comes. Stop trying to manufacture spiritual life, and ask the Spirit to give it.

For the one raised in a Christian home. Spiritual life cannot be inherited or picked up: not from the family, the church, the years under good teaching, or the Christian vocabulary you can use fluently. Flesh gives birth to flesh in a minister’s house as reliably as anywhere else. If that worries you, take heart: a real love for Christ, however small, a grief over sin, a wish to be his, is not something flesh produces. It is a sign that the gift has come.

Does this mean nothing good can come from an unbeliever? Not in the ordinary sense. Unbelievers can be honest, generous, brave and kind, and we should thank God for it; it is his common grace restraining sin and blessing the world (Matthew 5:45). But none of it is spiritual life, and none of it can make a person right with God or produce love for him. The flesh can build hospitals and write symphonies. It cannot give birth to a child of God. That is why the gospel is not advice for decent people to try harder, but news for dead people that God gives life.

verseByVerse.quote: "Do not marvel that I said to you, 'You must be born again.' The wind blows where it wishes, and you hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You must be born again. The you is plural: through Nicodemus Jesus addresses everyone who has assumed that being properly brought up, taught and serious would be enough. Must: no exceptions.

The wind blows. The ESV notes that the same Greek word (pneuma) means both “wind” and “spirit”, as Hebrew ruach does. So this is more than an illustration. Jesus uses one word for both, and that is his point: no one controls, commands or predicts the wind, or the Spirit. The Spirit is the wind that hovered over the first creation and breathed into the dry bones of Ezekiel’s valley, and he has never asked anyone’s permission to bring the dead to life.

You hear its sound. Wind is not vague. It takes roofs off and puts ships on rocks. What it is not is manageable: you never see it, only what it does. Nicodemus wants to know how. Teachers deal in method; Jesus points him to the wind, not because the new birth is vague, but because there is no method for producing it.

So it is. The new birth comes where the Spirit wills (1:13), and its effects are seen in a changed life. Reformed theology builds on this its teaching that God’s call is effectual: when God calls a person by his Spirit through the gospel, the call does not merely invite; it brings him, giving the very life that answers (6:44; Romans 8:30). This does not mean anyone is dragged in against his will. The Spirit so renews the will that the person comes freely and gladly, wanting Christ for the first time.

The breath of the risen Lord. On the evening of the resurrection Jesus breathed on his disciples and said, Receive the Holy Spirit (20:22). The wind that brings the new birth comes from the one who died and rose, and its first work is always to turn a dead heart toward him (16:14).

So is there nothing I can do? There is no technique that produces the new birth, but that does not leave you idle. Wind is unmanageable and sailors are not therefore idle: they cannot make it blow, and they can put up a sail, and it makes all the difference whether they have. Reading Scripture, hearing it preached, praying, keeping company with God’s people: none of these produces the wind. All of them are sails, the means through which God ordinarily gives new life (Romans 10:17; 1 Peter 1:23). And it does not mean nobody can know whether they have been born again; John wrote a whole letter to settle that question (1 John 5:13). If you want God, ask him; the wanting is itself the breeze.

In everyday life. Pray today, by name, for someone you love who is not yet born again. You cannot make the wind blow, but you can ask the one who sends it.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the same Greek word (pneuma) means both “wind” and “spirit.”

parallels.desc: you do not know the way the spirit comes
come from the four winds, O breath

verseByVerse.quote: "Nicodemus said to him, 'How can these things be?' Jesus answered him, 'Are you the teacher of Israel and yet you do not understand these things?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
How can these things be? Nicodemus’ last words in this conversation, and then he fades from view. His second how is deeper than his first: not mocking disbelief but genuine confusion.

Are you the teacher of Israel. The word the is the sting: not a teacher but the teacher, the man other teachers consulted.

And yet you do not understand these things? The Old Testament had promised the new birth: a new heart and a new spirit (Ezekiel 36:25–27; 11:19), the circumcision of the heart (Deuteronomy 30:6), the new covenant written on hearts, so that no one would need to say, know the LORD, because they all would (Jeremiah 31:33–34), and the valley of dry bones brought to life by the Spirit (Ezekiel 37). All of them say the same thing: Israel’s problem is not information and the solution will not be effort. God himself will have to act. He should have known. A man who had spent a lifetime in those texts had every piece of the puzzle on the table in front of him.

Why he missed it. He knows the verses. What he has never done is apply them to himself, because the promise of a new heart is good news only to a man who has concluded that his own heart is the problem, and Nicodemus has spent his life being told, accurately, that his conduct is exemplary.

How the new heart comes. Nicodemus asks how, and within a few sentences Jesus answers with the cross (vv. 14–15). The new covenant he knew from the prophets would be made in blood, and Jesus is its mediator (Hebrews 9:15). The how of the new birth is not a technique. It is a Person, lifted up for sinners.

I know my Bible well but feel nothing. What should I do? This is a real condition and it deserves to be named rather than scolded. A person can hold correct positions on every disputed doctrine, follow an argument through Romans, spot a bad sermon inside two minutes, and have no living love for God behind any of it. The knowledge is not the problem; Jesus does not tell Nicodemus to read less. But the same equipment that lets a man handle Scripture well can also let him handle it at arm’s length, as a subject to study rather than as God calling him. So read it differently: slowly, prayerfully, asking not what it says but what it says to you, and confessing what it shows you. Ask the Spirit to give you a heart that is moved (Psalm 119:18). And look to Christ, not to your feelings; warmth follows sight of him.

The tone of the rebuke. Jesus asks a question and goes on talking, giving this bewildered official more teaching on the new birth than anyone else in the Gospels receives. The rebuke is real and it is not a rejection. It is what it looks like when the light shines on somebody it intends to keep.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus calls him “the teacher of Israel” — a recognised authority who should have known the prophets’ promises.

verseByVerse.quote: "Truly, truly, I say to you, we speak of what we know, and bear witness to what we have seen, but you do not receive our testimony. If I have told you earthly things and you do not believe, how can you believe if I tell you heavenly things?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
We speak of what we know. The plural may include his disciples or the Baptist, or be Jesus speaking with the authority of heaven. What is certain is that this is eyewitness testimony.

You do not receive. The ESV notes that “you” in these verses is plural: Jesus now addresses the whole group Nicodemus represents. Not cannot understand but does not receive. Testimony is not something you solve. You either take it from the witness or refuse it, and refusing it is not a failure of comprehension but a decision about a person.

Earthly things. Not trivial things, but things that happen down here: a birth, a wind over a field, the Spirit at work in a man in Jerusalem.

How can you believe if I tell you heavenly things? Truths about heaven itself, God’s plan, the Son’s relationship to the Father, which only one from heaven could reveal (v. 13): a descent from heaven, a lifting up, a Son given, the love of God for the world. If they will not accept what God does on earth, where its effects can be seen, they will not accept what he says about heaven.

Should I settle the hard questions before I trust Christ? Not necessarily, and Jesus’ order here is wise. People often want to begin with the furthest questions: predestination and free will, those who never heard, the timetable of the last days, why there is suffering. They are real questions and should not be sneered at, and Scripture says much about them. But look at the order Jesus insists on. He will not take a man to the mysteries of heaven who has not yet dealt with the mystery standing in the room, which is that he needs to be born and cannot arrange it. Settle the plain things first: your need, and Christ’s sufficiency for it. Many hard questions look different from inside the family.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “you” in these verses is plural: Jesus is addressing Nicodemus’s whole circle.

verseByVerse.quote: "No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man. And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up."
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one has ascended. No human being has gone up to heaven to bring back knowledge of God (Deuteronomy 30:12; Proverbs 30:4). Jesus can speak of heavenly things because he has come from heaven (v. 31).

But were not Enoch and Elijah taken up to heaven? They were taken (Genesis 5:24; 2 Kings 2:11), but they did not go up and come back to tell what they had seen. Jesus’ point, in the context of verses 11–12, is that no one has ascended to bring down knowledge of heavenly things; only the one who came from heaven can speak of it.

The Son of Man. The ESV notes that some manuscripts add “who is in heaven”. The KJV and NKJV include the phrase; many of the earliest manuscripts lack it, so most modern Bibles put it in a footnote. If those words are original, they point to the Son’s unbroken communion with the Father even while on earth (1:18).

As Moses lifted up the serpent. Numbers 21:4–9. Near the end of forty years Israel complained about the food, the route, God and Moses in one breath. God sent poisonous snakes, and when the people repented and cried out, he did not remove the snakes. He told Moses to set a bronze serpent on a pole where the whole camp could see it, and anyone bitten who looked at it lived: not by medicine or effort, but by looking in faith at what God provided.

A strange remedy. It is an image, made at the command of the God who had forbidden images for worship, of the very thing that was killing them. And it requires the dying man to do nothing at all: no offering, no journey. A man face down in the sand with poison in him has one thing left that he can do, and it is to turn his head.

The serpent’s afterlife. Israel kept it, and centuries later Hezekiah found them burning incense to it and broke it in pieces (2 Kings 18:4). Even the instrument of God’s mercy will be turned into an idol if it is kept long enough. The look was never meant to stop at the bronze, but to reach the God who gave it.

So must the Son of Man. “Must” (dei): it has to happen, because God has planned it. Given what sin is, there was no other way. The cross is not a tragedy that overtook a good plan; it is the plan, and it was the plan before there was a wilderness or a serpent (Acts 2:23; 1 Peter 1:19–20).

Lifted up. The word (hypsōthēnai) is used of the cross three times in John (here, 8:28 and 12:32–34), with a double meaning: raised off the ground, and exalted. John explains it himself: he said this to show by what kind of death he was going to die (12:33). The cross is his glory and his throne. He is never more visibly the King than when he is nailed up under a placard announcing it.

What hung on the pole. As the serpent, a symbol of the curse, was lifted up, so Jesus, made a curse for us (Galatians 3:13), was lifted up on the cross. To be made a curse means that he took the place of the condemned: the sentence God’s law pronounces on lawbreakers fell on him, so that it would not fall on those who trust him (Deuteronomy 21:23; Galatians 3:10–13). Centuries after the wilderness the Son of Man hung on a Roman cross outside the city, and what hung there was our sin. Not his own; he had none. All of it, laid on one body, in daylight, where the whole camp could see (2 Corinthians 5:21). He became, in our place, the curse that was killing us, so that looking at him would be the end of it. And those who look to him in faith will live.

What does it mean to look to Christ? To look is to trust: to turn away from every other hope and rest your whole weight on Christ crucified for you. It is not a feeling you must work up or a degree of understanding you must reach. The dying Israelite did not need to understand bronze or theology; he needed to believe God’s word and turn his eyes. So it is for you. Look to Christ when you first come to him, and keep looking: when guilt accuses, when temptation bites, when death comes near. Turn to me and be saved, all the ends of the earth (Isaiah 45:22).

In everyday life. If you feel that your sin is the thing killing you, you are not being melodramatic; it is what the passage says is happening. The instruction is not to fight the snake, or explain how you came to be bitten, or demonstrate improvement first. It is to look, and God deliberately made the remedy the one thing a dying man can still manage. Today, when the old guilt bites, look again at the cross.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add “who is in heaven.” In John, “lifted up” means both the cross and his exaltation.

parallels.desc: the bronze serpent on a pole
he said this to show by what kind of death he was going to die

verseByVerse.quote: "that whoever believes in him may have eternal life."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever believes in him. Whoever means anyone: not whoever understands, for Nicodemus is proof that understanding is not the entrance, and not whoever qualifies. The dying Israelite did not have to comprehend the bronze; he had to trust that the God who told him to look meant it. The KJV adds should not perish here, borrowed from verse 16; the earliest manuscripts do not have it.

May have eternal life. The first appearance of the phrase that will become the Gospel’s whole purpose, and it arrives attached to a snake on a pole. Eternal life (zōē aiōnios) is the life of the age to come, unending. But the word life matters more: zōē, the life that was in the Word from the beginning (1:4). It is a kind of life, his kind, shared with us: this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent (17:3). It has been given to dying sinners who looked, and it cannot be lost, outlived or buried.

It begins now. The tense is the thing to hold on to. May have is present. Not will receive at death, not will be awarded at the judgment. This Gospel will keep saying it in the present tense until there is no way to miss it: whoever believes has eternal life (6:47); whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life; he does not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life (5:24). Passed. Already. It begins now, at the new birth, and continues for ever. For anyone in Christ, death is not the doorway into eternal life but an interruption in the middle of it.

Where do Jesus’ words end? The ESV notes that some interpreters end Jesus’ words at verse 15, with verses 16–21 as John’s comment. Ancient Greek had no quotation marks. In a red-letter edition the next verse may be printed in red or in black depending on which publisher you happen to be holding. There are reasons for thinking John is now reflecting: the tense shifts to the past, God’s giving of his Son is spoken of as a completed thing, and the phrase only Son is one John uses in his own voice elsewhere (1:14, 18; 1 John 4:9). Others reply that nothing signals a change of speaker. Nothing whatever hangs on it. If John wrote it, it is the Spirit-carried testimony of the apostle who leaned on Jesus’ chest, and it is Scripture. If Jesus said it, it is Scripture. The words are not more true in red ink.

Does eternal life mean I will float in the clouds for ever? No. Eternal life is the life of the age to come, and Scripture pictures that age not as a ghostly existence but as resurrection life in a renewed creation: new heavens and a new earth, where God dwells with his people (Revelation 21:1–4). Believers who die go at once to be with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23), and they will be raised bodily when he returns (5:28–29; 1 Corinthians 15:42–44). At the centre of it all is not a place but a person: we will see him and know him and enjoy him for ever. That knowing begins today.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some interpreters end Jesus’ words at verse 15 and read verses 16–21 as John’s comment.

verseByVerse.quote: "For God so loved the world, that he gave his only Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life. For God did not send his Son into the world to condemn the world, but in order that the world might be saved through him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
