The best-known verse in the Bible. Martin Luther is often credited with calling John 3:16 the gospel in miniature. Its problem is familiarity: a verse can be worn out the way a coin is, still legal tender, with the face rubbed off. So take the words slowly.

For God so loved the world. The ESV notes that verse 16 can also be rendered: For this is how God loved the world. So (houtōs) means in this way, more than so much. The sentence points at something and says, that is how: by giving his Son. The verse does not merely tell us how great the love is. It shows us, by pointing to the gift.

The world. This is the word that has been quietly sentimentalised. In John, the world is humanity in rebellion against God (1:10): the world that did not know him, that cannot receive the Spirit (14:17), that hates Christ and will hate his people (7:7; 15:18–19). That is the object of the love. Not a world that was lovable and therefore loved; a world that was hostile and loved anyway. Take the sentimental reading and the verse says God cared about a rather nice planet. Take John’s own vocabulary and it says God set his love on the very thing that was set against him. The wonder is not that the world is big, but that it is bad. God loved those who hated him. Nothing in us was the reason for it. The love came entirely from God, and it has never needed anything in us to keep it going.

That he gave his only Son. Gave: in the incarnation, and supremely on the cross. Not only sent, though he did send. To give a thing is to part with it, and the weight of the verse rests on the fact that the Giver did not keep what he gave. His only Son (monogenē): unique, beloved, and not created (1:14, 18). The KJV’s only begotten renders the same word; most scholars now take it to mean one of a kind, and both renderings confess a Son who is uniquely and eternally the Father’s. The Father had one Son, eternally his, his delight before there was a world, and put him into the hands of a race that did not know him or receive him. Abraham was told to take his son, his only son Isaac, whom he loved (Genesis 22:2), and at the last moment his hand was stopped and a ram was provided. On Golgotha no hand stopped the Father’s. He did not spare his own Son (Romans 8:32), because this time the Son was the Lamb.

Should not perish. Perish (apolētai) means be destroyed, be lost for ever, and it is stated without softening. This is not a verse about improving lives. It is a rescue verse, and rescue implies something to be rescued from.

Does perish mean simply ceasing to exist? No. Some have taught that the lost are finally annihilated, but Scripture speaks of the wicked going away into eternal punishment as the righteous go into eternal life, with the same word for both (Matthew 25:46), and of a destruction that is everlasting and conscious, away from the presence of the Lord (2 Thessalonians 1:9; Revelation 14:11). To perish is to be lost: ruined, cut off from God, under his wrath for ever (v. 36). That is a terrible truth, and it is told here not to frighten us for its own sake but to show the size of the rescue. God gave his Son so that we need not perish.

Not to condemn. The purpose of his first coming was salvation, not judgment (12:47), and salvation through him alone (14:6; Acts 4:12). It is a statement of purpose, not a denial that judgment exists, as the next sentence proves. A lifeboat does not go out to drown anybody. That the drowning is real is why it was launched.

Where Christians differ: God’s love and the extent of the atonement. Some take this verse to prove that Christ died equally for every individual, making salvation possible for all: this is the Arminian view, which holds that God’s choosing rests on faith he foresees, and many faithful Christians hold it or something near it. This commentary’s view: the verse teaches God’s love for a rebellious world, the gift of his Son, and the promise of life to everyone who believes. It is the foundation of the free offer of the gospel to all people: anyone who believes will be saved. It does not say Christ died in the same way for every individual. Elsewhere John shows that Christ lays down his life for his sheep (10:11, 15), and that those who believe are those the Father gives him (6:37, 44). Both truths stand: the gospel is offered to all, and those who believe are saved by a Saviour whose death secured their salvation. Reformed theology calls this definite (or particular) atonement: Christ died to save, and surely saves, those the Father gave him. Believers who read these verses differently are brothers to be heard, and all agree that whoever believes will not perish.

Is it not cruel for a father to send his son to die? Only if the Son were an unwilling third party. But he is not a victim the Father sacrifices to spare himself. Father and Son are one God, and the Son goes willingly: no one takes his life from him; he lays it down of his own accord (10:18). Nor does the Father give up something he cares little for. He gives what he loves most (Romans 8:32). The cross is not God making someone else pay so that he need not. It is God himself, in the person of his Son, bearing the judgment his own holiness requires, because he would rather suffer than lose us.

Can I tell anyone that God loves them? Yes, and you should, with care. God’s goodness and kindness extend to every person he has made (Psalm 145:9; Matthew 5:44–45), and his offer in the gospel is sincere to all: he takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but would rather they turn and live (Ezekiel 33:11). So you may say to anyone: God so loved the world that he gave his Son, and if you believe in him you will not perish; come to him, and he will not turn you away (6:37). What you should not do is tell someone that God loves them in a way that makes no claim on them, or that they are safe without Christ. The love of John 3:16 is a love that calls rebels to believe.

In everyday life. Say the verse about yourself, out loud, with your own name where the world stands. It was not written to be agreed with as a general truth. It was written to be believed by somebody. Then think of one person who needs to hear it, and pray for a chance to tell them.

For worship. The Father gave the Son, and the Son gave himself. Paul, who had once hated his name, wrote it in the first person: the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me (Galatians 2:20). The love of John 3:16 is wide enough for the world and personal enough to have a single name on it.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that verse 16 can also be rendered “For this is how God loved the world” — the stress is on the manner of his love.

parallels.desc: your son, your only son

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever believes in him is not condemned, but whoever does not believe is condemned already, because he has not believed in the name of the only Son of God. And this is the judgment: the light has come into the world, and people loved the darkness rather than the light because their works were evil."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not condemned. No condemnation, now or ever (5:24; Romans 8:1). The verdict is settled. The Light came into a world that loved the dark, and he did not come to condemn it. He came to bear its condemnation.

Condemned already. Everything turns on one word, and it is the word that frightens people: already. It is more merciful than it sounds. The point is not that unbelief is their only sin, but that they are already under condemnation for their sin, and by refusing Christ, they refuse the only rescue. They remain where they are (v. 36). The verse is not saying that a sentence is passed on people the moment they hear about Christ and decline. It is saying the sentence was passed long before, and that the arrival of Christ is not what put anyone in danger. He walked into a situation that was already lost. Nobody was standing in neutral territory waiting to see how they felt about him.

A rescue, not an examination. So the gospel is not an examination a person might fail but a rescue a person might refuse. If it were an examination, Christ’s coming would add a danger. Because it is a rescue, he is the only way out of a danger that was already there. That is why not believing in the name of the only Son of God is the final sin: it refuses the only cure.

How strong must my faith be? This verse does real damage in the hands of the wrong reader. There are people who read condemned already and immediately begin auditing themselves for whether they have believed hard enough or sincerely enough to have crossed the line. Read the sentence again. The condemnation attaches to one thing only: not believing in the name of the only Son of God. It is not measuring the quality of anyone’s faith. It is distinguishing between those who have come to him and those who have not. A weak hand on a strong rope is not the same as no hand at all, and this verse is about which rope, not about the strength of the grip. Weak faith in a strong Saviour saves.

This is the judgment. Judgment (krisis) is the verdict, the dividing line: not a throne or a book opened, but a person arriving. The light is Jesus (1:9), and the judgment is what people do when he comes.

Loved the darkness. The real reason for unbelief is not lack of evidence but love of sin. People do not reject Jesus because they cannot believe, but because they will not give up the darkness. So the judgment is not only something done at the end. It is already showing now. God’s verdict will make public what each person had already chosen to love, which is why the last day can be perfectly just, and no one will be surprised by it. The verb matters. Not tolerated the darkness, not drifted into it. Loved it. This is not a verdict on every honest questioner; Nicodemus came with questions and Jesus welcomed him. It names the root of the world’s refusal, and each of us can recognise it in himself.

Because their works were evil. This locates the real difficulty exactly where Nicodemus has been told it is. If unbelief were an information problem it could be solved by teaching, and he of all people would already be safe. It is a problem of what we love. And love cannot be argued into a person; a new heart has to be born.

What of those who have never heard of Christ? This verse describes everyone apart from him: no one is saved another way (14:6; Acts 4:12). Those who never hear are not condemned for rejecting a message they never received, but for their sins against the light they had (Romans 1:20; 2:12). That is why Paul asks how they are to believe in him of whom they have never heard (Romans 10:14). The answer is not speculation but mission. And we may trust that the Judge of all the earth will do what is right (Genesis 18:25), including with infants who die before they can hear: the Reformed confessions teach that elect infants dying in infancy are saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when and where he pleases (the Westminster Confession 10.3; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 10.3). Parents who have lost a little one may rest their grief with that Judge, whose tenderness to children Jesus showed when he took them in his arms and blessed them (Mark 10:16).

parallels.desc: no condemnation

verseByVerse.quote: "For everyone who does wicked things hates the light and does not come to the light, lest his works should be exposed. But whoever does what is true comes to the light, so that it may be clearly seen that his works have been carried out in God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hates the light. Exposed (elenchthē) means convicted, shown for what one is. The instinct needs no teaching: a child who has broken something goes quiet and moves toward the door. The edited version we give at dinner parties, the friendships kept carefully shallow, are developments of the same reflex: stay where the lighting is favourable.

Avoidance feels like busyness. This is where the verse becomes uncomfortable, because avoidance of the light is not usually experienced as avoidance. It is experienced as being busy: as not having time to pray, or finding a book of the Bible dull, or preferring to read about the faith rather than sit still before God. The man in this verse is not shaking his fist. He simply does not come. Not every dry season is avoidance, though: tiredness, grief and depression can make prayer heavy for people who love the light dearly. The mark of this verse is unwillingness, not difficulty, and anyone grieved by his own coldness is already turned toward the lamp.

Whoever does what is true. Literally, whoever does the truth. In Scripture truth is something a person can do: integrity, being in reality what one appears to be. So the two groups are not the clever and the stupid, or the religious and the irreligious, but those who will come out into the open and those who will not.

Carried out in God. His works were done by God’s grace and in union with him, and the light shows it. Perhaps an encouragement to Nicodemus, who had come by night: come into the light.

Exposed and not ashamed. The next chapter shows what coming to this light looks like. A Samaritan woman with five husbands behind her is told the whole of it, and she runs into her town saying, come, see a man who told me all that I ever did (4:29). The light is not a searchlight hunting criminals, but the face of the Saviour, who exposes in order to heal.

What it does not mean. This pair of verses can be read as saying that good people come to Christ and bad people avoid him, which would undo the whole chapter. But his works have been carried out in God: whatever is found in the light was put there by the one holding the lamp. Even what the light finds in God’s children is never flawless; it is accepted because the Son obeyed perfectly in their place, and his obedience is counted as theirs (Romans 5:19). This is not salvation by works. It shows which way real faith moves: toward the light.

How do I come into the light in practice? By refusing to hide from God or from his people. Begin with honest confession to God, naming what you have done rather than speaking of it vaguely (1 John 1:9). Read Scripture in a way that lets it search you, not only inform you (Hebrews 4:12). Where there is a sin that has a grip on you, tell a mature, trusted Christian, and let them pray with you and ask you about it (James 5:16). Put right what can be put right. None of this earns forgiveness; Christ has done that. It is simply what it looks like to live as a forgiven person who no longer needs the dark.

For worship. He was exposed for us. At the cross the soldiers divided his garments (19:23–24), and the Light of the world hung stripped in the open, bearing the shame our hiding had earned. He clothes with his own righteousness those who come out of the dark (Isaiah 61:10). The Lord was uncovered in the light so that we could stand in it clothed.

parallels.desc: expose the works of darkness

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–36 — John's Final Testimony: The Bridegroom's Friend
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus and his disciples baptise in the Judean countryside while John, still free, baptises at Aenon near Salim. When John’s disciples complain that everyone is going to Jesus, John answers that a person receives only what heaven gives: he is the friend of the bridegroom, whose joy is complete when he hears the groom’s voice, and Jesus must increase while he decreases. The closing verses give the reason: the one from heaven is above all, speaks the words of God, has the Spirit without measure, and holds all things in his hand, so that to believe in him is life and to refuse him is to remain under God’s wrath.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Baptist’s last words in this Gospel (if the closing verses are his) sum up its theology: Jesus comes from above, speaks the words of God, gives the Spirit without measure, and holds in his hands both eternal life and God’s wrath. There is no middle ground. The Baptist who began by pointing to the Lamb of God ends by declaring the eternal stakes of the decision about him.

The wrath remains: it does not arrive but stays where it already was. That is also where the mercy lies, because what remains can be lifted, and this chapter has already said how.
verseByVerse.examples:
He must increase, but I must decrease is the mark of all genuine ministry: a minister who builds his own kingdom rather than Christ’s has misunderstood the calling.

The words were not sentimental. Within months John was in prison, doubting, and then executed; yet Jesus called him the greatest born of women (Matthew 11:11). So this is the passage for anyone being replaced. The decrease is bearable, and even a completed joy, only because of who fills the space.

verseByVerse.quote: After this Jesus and his disciples went into the Judean countryside, and he remained there with them and was baptizing. John also was baptizing at Aenon near Salim, because water was plentiful there, and people were coming and being baptized.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Into the Judean countryside. An early Judean ministry, recorded only in John. Jesus leaves the centre, where he had the attention of a member of the Sanhedrin, and goes to the fields, where the water is.

Baptizing. Jesus himself did not baptise, but his disciples did (4:2). The disciples handled the water, the sign; the Lord kept for himself the giving of what it signifies, the new birth by the Spirit (1:33).

At Aenon near Salim. The location of Aenon (springs) near Salim is uncertain, perhaps in the Jordan valley, or in Samaria.

Water was plentiful. Plenty of water suggests immersion, though it is not conclusive; it is first a logistical remark about crowds.

Two ministries, no rivalry. Two ministries at once, in the same region, and neither man treats the other as competition. The only people in this passage worried about the arrangement are the followers, which is how it usually goes.

How should I think about other churches in my town? As fellow workers, where they preach the same gospel. Christ has one church, gathered in many congregations, and the success of a faithful church down the road is a gain for the kingdom, not a loss for yours. Name them in your prayers, speak well of them, and rejoice when people are converted there. That does not mean every difference is unimportant; where the gospel itself is denied, love must speak plainly. But most of our rivalries are not about the gospel at all. They are about numbers, style and pride, and those are not worth one moment of the Spirit’s grief.
verseByVerse.note: The location of Aenon (“springs”) near Salim is uncertain.

verseByVerse.quote: (for John had not yet been put in prison)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not yet put in prison. The other Gospels begin Jesus’ Galilean ministry after John’s arrest (Mark 1:14). John explains that this Judean ministry came earlier, overlapping with John’s.

An eyewitness filling the gap. This aside reads like the remark of someone who knows the order of events, which fits this Gospel’s claim to rest on an eyewitness (21:24).

A shadow across the parenthesis. The reader is told in passing how this ends. The man about to say he must increase, but I must decrease is a few months from a cell and not long from an executioner. He spoke those words not from a settled retirement but on a downward slope.

Forerunner to the end. John went before Jesus in birth, preaching and baptising, and in suffering too: Elijah had already come and they did to him whatever they pleased, and so also the Son of Man would suffer (Matthew 17:12–13). The King who followed him would go further into the dark than John ever went: under the wrath of God for sinners.

Do the Gospels contradict each other on the order of events? No. They complement one another. Each Gospel writer selected and arranged true events for his purpose, and John, probably writing last, often fills in what the others pass over: an early Judean ministry, several visits to Jerusalem, long conversations. Here he even points out for us where his account joins theirs. Apparent differences in order usually arise because one writer groups events by theme while another follows the calendar more closely. Not every question of order has a certain answer, and believers can say so honestly while trusting that the accounts are true. Reading the four together does not weaken our confidence in them; it gives us a fuller picture of one Lord, from four angles, resting on eyewitness testimony.
verseByVerse.note: The other Gospels begin Jesus’ Galilean ministry after John’s arrest; John fills in an earlier period.

verseByVerse.quote: Now a discussion arose between some of John's disciples and a Jew over purification. And they came to John and said to him, "Rabbi, he who was with you across the Jordan, to whom you bore witness — look, he is baptizing, and all are going to him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A discussion arose … over purification. Perhaps about John’s baptism compared with Jesus’, or with Jewish washings. The argument that produces the New Testament’s great statement about humility began as a dispute about whose water counted. This Gospel has kept returning to the question of cleansing since the six stone jars at Cana. The answer is not a better rite but a person, the Son who would himself make purification for sins (Hebrews 1:3).

He who was with you. They do not name Jesus. Every word is the language of a threatened camp: he who was with you treats him as a junior member of John’s movement, and to whom you bore witness implies that he owes his success to John’s recommendation.

All are going to him. Jealousy, and all is not true, since John is still baptising crowds. All is what anxiety says, the arithmetic of a man watching numbers move the wrong way. And look, the smallest word in the sentence, gives it away: they are directing his attention, as one does when a person is failing to be as alarmed as the situation warrants.

Loyal and wrong. The saddest thing is that they are being loyal, out of real affection. That is how the ugliest instincts in church life often present themselves: not as jealousy but as concern, about standards, about a church down the road that seems to be doing rather well. John is not comparing at all, because he settled who Jesus is at the Jordan. While his disciples counted heads, John looked at the Lamb, and there was nothing left to count. Christ is the end of all our comparisons.

How do I deal with jealousy of other Christians? Name it honestly as sin, not as concern, and confess it to God. Then fight it with truth. Remember that their gifts and fruit were given from heaven (v. 27), so envying them is a complaint against God. Remember that you are one body, so their gain is yours (1 Corinthians 12:26). Thank God for them specifically, out loud, and pray for their further blessing; envy rarely survives sincere intercession. And look again at Christ, because jealousy grows where we have stopped being satisfied in him.

verseByVerse.quote: John answered, "A person cannot receive even one thing unless it is given him from heaven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not even one thing. Everything comes from God: John’s ministry, Jesus’ ministry, every gift, every success. The sentence is absolute, and the temptation is to hear it as modesty and move on. Not most things. Not the important things. Not one (1 Corinthians 4:7).

It cuts both ways. Applied to the case in hand it cuts in two directions at once. If Jesus is drawing the crowds, heaven gave him the crowds, so envying him is a complaint against God. If John’s numbers are falling, heaven arranged that too, so the decline is something God has assigned, to be accepted. And if John ever had a crowd, that was given as well, so it was never his to lose. Envy always requires a sense of ownership: the assumption that a thing was mine, or ought to have been. Take away the ownership and there is nothing for envy to attach to. A man cannot be robbed of what he was only ever handed. The same truth cuts against taking credit: the intelligence, the temperament, even the capacity to work hard, were all given.

The Gift from heaven. The greatest thing ever received from heaven was a few miles away: God gave his only Son, the true bread from heaven (6:32). Even the Son, as the one sent, lives as one who receives from the Father (5:26; v. 35). If the Son himself delights to receive, no servant of his has anything that was not handed to him.

If everything is given, does my effort not matter? It matters greatly, and it too is given. Paul says he worked harder than any of the apostles, and in the same breath, though it was not I, but the grace of God that is with me (1 Corinthians 15:10). God gives gifts so that we will use them diligently, and he holds us accountable for what we do with them (Matthew 25:14–30). The point of this verse is not that we should be passive, but that we should be humble and content: working hard with what we have been given, without pride when it prospers or envy when others prosper more.

For worship. Even the receiving is given. No one can come to me, Jesus says, unless it is granted him by the Father (6:65). The Father gave the Son, and then gave the empty hands that take him and the faith that holds on. We have nothing we did not receive, and so nothing to boast of except the Giver.

parallels.desc: what do you have that you did not receive?

verseByVerse.quote: "You yourselves bear me witness, that I said, 'I am not the Christ, but I have been sent before him.' The one who has the bride is the bridegroom. The friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly at the bridegroom's voice. Therefore this joy of mine is now complete."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am not the Christ. John has said it since chapter 1 (1:20, 23), and it has never once sounded like a disappointment. He can watch the crowd leave without panic because he never mistook himself for the reason they came.

The bridegroom. In the Old Testament, God is the bridegroom of his people (Isaiah 54:5; 62:5; Hosea 2:19–20). Jesus is the bridegroom; his people are the bride (Mark 2:19–20; Ephesians 5:25–32; Revelation 19:7; 21:2). John is quietly applying to Jesus the role that belongs to the LORD himself. The LORD who betrothed Israel to himself in faithfulness has come in flesh to claim his bride from every nation at the cost of his own blood.

The friend of the bridegroom. Like a best man, he often helped arrange the wedding and brought the bride to the groom. His joy was to see the marriage happen, not to take the bride for himself, and the moment the bridegroom’s voice was heard, his work was over.

Rejoices greatly. The Greek doubles it: he rejoices with joy. This is not resignation dressed up, but the gladness of somebody whose work has succeeded, and whose success takes the form of being no longer required.

This joy of mine. The Greek tense describes a thing brought to fullness and staying full, and he says it at the very moment the crowds are moving to Jesus. He is not managing a loss. He is at the height of his life.

The bride is not the audience. If Jesus is the bridegroom, there is a bride. The people baptised in that river, and those who would follow for two thousand years, are not the crowd at the wedding. They are the one being married.

What does it mean that the church is Christ’s bride? It means that Christ loves his people with the faithful, exclusive, self-giving love of a husband, and has bound himself to them by covenant for ever. He gave himself up for her, to make her holy and present her to himself in splendour (Ephesians 5:25–27). It means the church belongs to him, not to its leaders; ministers are at most the friends of the bridegroom. And it means our story ends with a wedding: the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:7–9). If you are in Christ, you are not merely a guest at that feast. You are part of the bride.

In everyday life. If you teach, lead, parent or befriend people in the faith, ask whose voice they are learning to love: yours, or the bridegroom’s? Your task is to bring them to him and step back. The next time someone you have helped grows close to Christ in a way that no longer needs you, let it complete your joy rather than diminish it.
verseByVerse.note: The friend of the bridegroom arranged the wedding and brought bride and groom together — his joy was the groom’s joy.

parallels.desc: as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride

verseByVerse.quote: "He must increase, but I must decrease."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He must increase. On most readings the Baptist’s last recorded words in this Gospel (some think he speaks on to verse 36). Must (dei) is the word Jesus used of the Son of Man who must be lifted up (v. 14): the rise of one and the shrinking of the other belong to one plan of God, which John has no say over. The first clause is the one that matters; the second simply follows from it. Christ is increasing still: his kingdom spreading, his name honoured among the nations, his glory filling more of the earth until it covers it as the waters cover the sea (Habakkuk 2:14).

But I must decrease. Not reluctantly, but gladly, the motto of every true servant of Christ. John is like the moon, which has no light of its own: when it fades, that is not a tragedy but the arrival of morning.

What I must decrease came to. He said it, and then it happened, and not gently. Herod arrested him for telling the truth about a marriage. From a cell he sent to ask whether Jesus was the one who was to come, or whether they should look for another (Matthew 11:2–3), which is not the question of a man serenely fulfilled. And he was beheaded without trial, to keep a promise made in front of dinner guests.

The greatest, wobbling. And Jesus’ verdict came while he was in that cell, doubting: among those born of women there has arisen no one greater than John the Baptist (Matthew 11:11). The man who arranged his whole existence around becoming unnecessary seems to have wobbled at the end, and was called the greatest anyway.

Does decreasing mean I must think nothing of myself? No. John did not despise himself; he knew exactly who he was, the voice, the friend of the bridegroom, and he did that work with courage. Decreasing is not self-hatred or false modesty. It is the gladness of seeing Christ honoured more than yourself, and the willingness to be forgotten if he is remembered. The decrease is bearable, and in fact a completed joy, solely because of who is filling the space. Nobody in Scripture is ever asked to shrink for the sake of shrinking. You are asked to make room for him, and in him you will find yourself more truly than you ever could by holding on (Matthew 16:25).

In everyday life. This is the verse for anyone being replaced: by the younger colleague who is plainly better at it, the role handed on, the children who no longer ring, the body doing less than it did. The world has no account of these except loss. Make John’s words your prayer today: Lord, may you increase, and may I decrease; and remember that the one who must increase went lower for you than any slope can take you.

verseByVerse.quote: "He who comes from above is above all. He who is of the earth belongs to the earth and speaks in an earthly way. He who comes from heaven is above all. He bears witness to what he has seen and heard, yet no one receives his testimony."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who is speaking? Verses 31–36 may be John the Baptist’s words continuing, or the Gospel writer’s reflection; the Greek has no quotation marks, and the same uncertainty arises earlier in this chapter about where Jesus’ words to Nicodemus end. John moves from reporting a voice to adding his own without announcement, because in his mind the two are saying the same thing. Either way the words explain why Jesus must increase, and their authority is unaffected.

Above all. Jesus, from heaven, is supreme over all. The first half of the verse states the principle underneath everything in this chapter. Where a person comes from decides the authority he speaks with.

He who is of the earth. John the Baptist, and every human teacher. If it is the Baptist speaking, the man Jesus would call the greatest born of women places himself among those of the earth without complaint. He is being accurate about the one distinction that matters: not between a great man and a small one, but between everyone born here and the one who came from somewhere else. The best teacher in Israel and the last of the prophets are both of the earth. Only one person in the passage came down.

What he has seen and heard. Jesus speaks from direct knowledge of heaven (v. 11), as no other teacher can. He came down from that height to speak to us of what he had seen, and all truth is safe in his mouth.

No one receives. A general rejection (1:11), not literally no one, as the next verse shows. It is not a statistic but a lament. The testimony is perfect; the evidence was never the problem.

If Jesus is above all, how should I weigh other voices? Every other voice is of the earth, however wise, and must be tested by his. That includes teachers you admire, traditions you love, experts, your own feelings, and the spirit of the age. Many of them say true and useful things, and we should listen with humility. But when they contradict what Christ has said in his word, he wins, every time (Galatians 1:8). That is what sola Scriptura means in practice: not that only the Bible is useful, but that only the Bible, as the word of the one from above, has the final say.

parallels.desc: you are from below, I am from above

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever receives his testimony sets his seal to this, that God is true."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sets his seal. Some do receive it. A seal pressed into wax by a signet ring was the ancient equivalent of a signature on a contract: this is mine, I stand behind it. Setting a seal was not an opinion. It was a commitment.

That God is true. To believe Jesus’ testimony is to affirm that God is truthful, since Jesus speaks God’s words (v. 34). So faith, in this verse, is not first a feeling or even first a benefit received. It is a signature. To believe Christ is to put one’s name to the claim that God tells the truth, and to do it in advance of much of the evidence, since a great deal of what God has said has not happened yet. And to refuse it is to call God a liar (1 John 5:10). If God has testified about his Son and a man declines the testimony, there is no third position available. That removes the idea that unbelief is always a modest, humble position. It is a verdict, and it is a verdict about somebody’s character. That does not make every doubter dishonest; it means the question is finally personal: whether God can be trusted.

The Son the Father sealed. The image has a deeper layer in this Gospel. Jesus says of himself that on him God the Father has set his seal (6:27): the Father has certified the Son, by the Spirit who came down and remained on him at the Jordan (1:32–33), by the works he gave him to do, and finally by raising him. So the believer’s seal is a countersignature. God has already signed his name to his Son, and faith adds its own underneath, agreeing that what the Father says about Jesus is true. And a seal works both ways: believers are themselves sealed with the promised Holy Spirit (Ephesians 1:13). The one who signs his name to God’s truthfulness discovers that God has already signed his name to him.

What if I believe but still have doubts? Then you are like many in Scripture: the father who cried, I believe; help my unbelief (Mark 9:24), the psalmists who asked how long, John the Baptist in his cell. Doubt is not the opposite of faith; unbelief is. Faith is trusting God’s word while questions remain. So bring your doubts to God honestly, take them to his word, talk to mature believers, and keep doing what faith does: praying, gathering, obeying. Your seal is not on the strength of your feelings but on the truthfulness of God, and he does not change when you waver (2 Timothy 2:13).
verseByVerse.note: To set one’s seal to something is to certify it as true.

parallels.desc: let God be true

verseByVerse.quote: "For he whom God has sent utters the words of God, for he gives the Spirit without measure. The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The words of God. Jesus’ words are God’s words (7:16; 12:49–50; 14:10). Not in the partial, occasional manner of the prophets, but fully.

Without measure. Prophets received the Spirit in measure, for particular tasks. The Greek does not supply the subject: the Father gives the Spirit to the Son without measure, as at the Jordan (1:32–33; Isaiah 11:2), or the Son gives the Spirit without measure, as the one who baptizes with the Holy Spirit (1:33). Both are true, and in that order: out of the fullness that rests on him, the Son gives, so that what reaches the believer is not a diluted portion.

The Father loves the Son. The eternal love within the Trinity (5:20; 17:24), before anything was made: the oldest fact in existence, and everything in this chapter flows from it.

All things into his hand. All authority (13:3; Matthew 28:18), including salvation and judgment. It is what love does: the Father withholds nothing from the Son. And it is the same hand out of which, in chapter 10, no one is able to snatch his sheep (10:28–29). What has been put into that hand includes people, and nothing has ever been taken out of it.

Can I be sure I am safe in his hand? If you belong to Christ, yes. The Father has given all things into the Son’s hand, including those who come to him, and Jesus says of them: I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand (10:28). Your security does not rest on the strength of your grip but on his. You will still stumble and doubt, but the one who holds you is the one who loves the Father and does his will, and it is the Father’s will that he should lose nothing of all that he has been given (6:39). That is not a licence to drift. It is the ground on which a trembling believer can stand.

For worship. The love that holds the universe together passed between the Father and the Son before there were any creatures, and in the upper room the Son asked that this very love might be in his people: that the love with which you have loved me may be in them, and I in them (17:26). The oldest love there is has been opened, and there is room inside.

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life; whoever does not obey the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains on him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Has eternal life. The chapter that began with new birth ends with the sharpest possible alternative: eternal life or the abiding wrath of God.

Whoever does not obey the Son. The two halves deliberately do not match. We expect believes and does not believe; John writes believes and does not obey (apeitheō, refuses to be persuaded). John is not smuggling works into salvation. Faith in Christ is obedience to God’s command (1 John 3:23), and the unbelief in question is not an intellectual position politely held but a refusal of one who has a right to be obeyed.

The wrath of God remains. Wrath (orgē) is God’s settled, holy opposition to sin, and this is its only appearance in John’s Gospel. All people are already under it because of sin (Ephesians 2:3), and it remains on those who refuse the only one who can remove it. Nothing arrives; the wrath remains, the same truth as condemned already (v. 18). Christ bore God’s wrath for those who believe (Romans 5:9; 1 Thessalonians 1:10).

The abiding word. The verb is menō. It first appeared when the Spirit came down and remained on Jesus (1:32–33), and it will run to the vine: abide in me, and I in you (15:4). Something abides on everyone. On Christ, the Spirit rests. On those who are his, he himself abides. And on the one who refuses him, the wrath he was born under simply stays where it was.

How can a God of love have wrath? Because his love is holy. Wrath in God is not a mood that flares and fades; it is his steady, just opposition to evil, the right response of perfect goodness to what destroys his creatures and defies his glory. A God who felt nothing about cruelty, abuse and lies would not be loving; he would be indifferent. And the cross shows the two together: God’s love provided what his justice required, when Christ bore the wrath we deserved as our substitute (Romans 3:25–26; 1 John 4:10). The same chapter that speaks of wrath speaks of a love that gave its only Son. The love is the way out of the wrath.

What it does not mean. This verse frightens people, and some of them are the wrong people. It is not addressed to the Christian who has bad days, or doubts, or a faith that feels thinner than he wishes. The one described here is not struggling with the Son; he is declining him. And the whole sentence turns on a present-tense contrast, has eternal life against remains, which means the two conditions are the two states people are in this evening. If wrath remains rather than arrives, then it can be lifted rather than merely postponed, and this chapter has already said how. It was lifted the way the poison was lifted in the desert: not by the dying man’s exertion but by his looking at something raised up on his behalf.

For worship. In the garden, as they came to arrest him, Jesus said to Peter, shall I not drink the cup that the Father has given me? (18:11). It was the cup of the wrath that remains on the unbelieving, and he drank it to the bottom, so that for those who believe in the Son not a drop is left. The chapter that began with a man coming in the dark ends with the wrath of God, and between them stand the Son given and the Son lifted up. Worthy is the Lamb who drank the cup so that it would never be ours.

parallels.desc: the wrath of God is revealed

3.title: You Must Be Born Again
3.text: <sup>1</sup>Now there was a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews.<sup>2</sup>This man came to Jesus by night and said to him, “Rabbi, we know that you are a teacher come from God, for no one can do these signs that you do unless God is with him.”<sup>3</sup>Jesus answered him, “Truly, truly, I say to you, unless one is born again he cannot see the kingdom of God.”<sup>4</sup>Nicodemus said to him, “How can a man be born when he is old? Can he enter a second time into his mother’s womb and be born?”<sup>5</sup>Jesus answered, “Truly, truly, I say to you, unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.<sup>6</sup>That which is born of the flesh is flesh, and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit.<sup>7</sup>Do not marvel that I said to you, ’You must be born again.’<sup>8</sup>The wind blows where it wishes, and you hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit.”<sup>9</sup>Nicodemus said to him, “How can these things be?”<sup>10</sup>Jesus answered him, “Are you the teacher of Israel and yet you do not understand these things?<sup>11</sup>Truly, truly, I say to you, we speak of what we know, and bear witness to what we have seen, but you do not receive our testimony.<sup>12</sup>If I have told you earthly things and you do not believe, how can you believe if I tell you heavenly things?<sup>13</sup>No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man.<sup>14</sup>And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up,<sup>15</sup>that whoever believes in him may have eternal life.<sup>16</sup>“For God so loved the world, that he gave his only Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life.<sup>17</sup>For God did not send his Son into the world to condemn the world, but in order that the world might be saved through him.<sup>18</sup>Whoever believes in him is not condemned, but whoever does not believe is condemned already, because he has not believed in the name of the only Son of God.<sup>19</sup>And this is the judgment: the light has come into the world, and people loved the darkness rather than the light because their works were evil.<sup>20</sup>For everyone who does wicked things hates the light and does not come to the light, lest his works should be exposed.<sup>21</sup>But whoever does what is true comes to the light, so that it may be clearly seen that his works have been carried out in God.”<sup>22</sup>After this Jesus and his disciples went into the Judean countryside, and he remained there with them and was baptizing.<sup>23</sup>John also was baptizing at Aenon near Salim, because water was plentiful there, and people were coming and being baptized<sup>24</sup>(for John had not yet been put in prison).<sup>25</sup>Now a discussion arose between some of John’s disciples and a Jew over purification.<sup>26</sup>And they came to John and said to him, “Rabbi, he who was with you across the Jordan, to whom you bore witness—look, he is baptizing, and all are going to him.”<sup>27</sup>John answered, “A person cannot receive even one thing unless it is given him from heaven.<sup>28</sup>You yourselves bear me witness, that I said, ’I am not the Christ, but I have been sent before him.’<sup>29</sup>The one who has the bride is the bridegroom. The friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly at the bridegroom’s voice. Therefore this joy of mine is now complete.<sup>30</sup>He must increase, but I must decrease.”<sup>31</sup>He who comes from above is above all. He who is of the earth belongs to the earth and speaks in an earthly way. He who comes from heaven is above all.<sup>32</sup>He bears witness to what he has seen and heard, yet no one receives his testimony.<sup>33</sup>Whoever receives his testimony sets his seal to this, that God is true.<sup>34</sup>For he whom God has sent utters the words of God, for he gives the Spirit without measure.<sup>35</sup>The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand.<sup>36</sup>Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life; whoever does not obey the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains on him.
3.overview:
Nicodemus, a Pharisee on the ruling council, comes to Jesus at night with a compliment, and Jesus answers that no one can see the kingdom of God unless he is born again, or born from above (the Greek word means both). This birth is of water and the Spirit, the cleansing and new heart God promised through Ezekiel, and it is as free and unmanageable as the wind. The Son of Man must be lifted up as Moses lifted up the bronze serpent, so that whoever believes may have eternal life, because God so loved the world that he gave his only Son.

Those who refuse him are condemned already, because they love the darkness. In the second half of the chapter John the Baptist, told that everyone is going to Jesus, rejoices like the bridegroom’s friend. The chapter ends with the choice that runs through the whole Gospel: eternal life for whoever believes in the Son, and God’s wrath remaining on whoever will not obey him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–42 — The Woman at the Well
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the road through Samaria Jesus rests at noon by Jacob’s well and asks a Samaritan woman for a drink. He offers her living water that becomes a spring of eternal life, then brings up her husbands, answers her question about the right mountain for worship, and tells her that he is the Messiah. She leaves her jar and brings her town, while Jesus tells his puzzled disciples that his food is to do his Father’s will and that the fields are already ripe for harvest. Many Samaritans believe, and confess him as the Saviour of the world.
verseByVerse.theology:
The living water Jesus offers is not a religious programme or a moral reform; it is the life that is in himself. He does not merely point to the source of life; he is the source. John himself explains the image later: the rivers of living water are the Spirit (7:38–39). So the gift at the well is the new birth Nicodemus could not grasp, now pictured as a spring.

Worship in spirit and truth does not mean heartfelt worship as opposed to formal worship. It means worship made possible by God’s Spirit and shaped by the truth, and in this Gospel the truth is a person, Jesus himself (14:6). And the decisive clause is that the Father is seeking such worshippers (v. 23). We usually think of worship as our search for God; here God is the one out looking, which is what the chapter has been showing since verse 4, when Jesus had to pass through Samaria.
verseByVerse.examples: The five husbands need more care than they often get. John never calls this woman immoral, and a woman could not ordinarily divorce in that world, so five marriages may mean five times widowed or five times sent away. We are not told, and it matters to say so, because women have sat through sermons on this chapter and been handed a shame the passage never assigns.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Jesus learned that the Pharisees had heard that Jesus was making and baptizing more disciples than John (although Jesus himself did not baptize, but only his disciples),
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Nicodemus was a man, a Jew, a respected teacher, who came by night; the Samaritan woman is an outsider with a broken history, met at noon. Both need exactly the same gift, and only one of them goes home and tells a town. Then a royal official takes Jesus at his bare word. The Son of God crosses every barrier to find his worshippers, and the faith he looks for believes his word.

The setting. Jesus travels north from Judea to Galilee through Samaria, the hostile country between, and the first half of the chapter happens at a single well outside Sychar, under Mount Gerizim.

The Pharisees had heard. Just before, John’s disciples came to him upset that all are going to Jesus. Now the same report reaches the Pharisees, who had already sent men to investigate John (1:24). The same news reaches two groups. It makes John’s disciples jealous, though John himself refuses to share their jealousy; it makes the Pharisees start watching Jesus.

Making and baptising more disciples than John. The news itself was numbers: not doctrine, not a healing, a count of disciples. When religious authorities measure ministries by headcount, they are already treating the kingdom of God as one organisation competing with others. John the Baptist had already given the right response to the same figures: he must increase, but I must decrease (3:30).

Jesus himself did not baptise. John makes more exact what he wrote at 3:22: it was the disciples who did the baptising. There is no record of Jesus baptising anyone with his own hands, so no group of Christians could ever claim a superior baptism from Jesus himself. Paul was relieved to have baptised almost nobody at Corinth for the same reason (1 Corinthians 1:13–17).

Why did he leave? Not in fear. This is a man who had recently cleared the temple courts in front of these same authorities. He goes because a clash now would come too soon. Everything in this Gospel moves towards his hour, the time the Father has set for his death, and it has not yet come (2:4; 7:30). There is a kind of courage that consists of walking away from a fight you could win, at a moment of your own choosing, because the fight is not the point.

Does it matter who baptises me? No. The power of baptism does not lie in the minister, however gifted or famous, but in Christ, who commanded it, and in the faith of the one who is baptised into him. Jesus deliberately left the water to his disciples so that no one would treasure a baptism for the hand that gave it. If you were baptised as a believer by an ordinary pastor in an ordinary church, you were baptised into exactly the same name as those who were baptised by Peter or by the disciples on the Jordan. Thank God for the man who baptised you, but do not boast in him.

verseByVerse.quote: he left Judea and departed again for Galilee. And he had to pass through Samaria.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He had to pass through Samaria. It is often said that strict Jews went round Samaria by the Jordan valley, though Josephus says Galilean pilgrims usually took the direct route, about three days. So the road through Samaria was the quicker one, not the only one, and when John writes that Jesus had to go this way, he is saying more than a fact about maps.

The word of divine necessity. The word is edei, it was necessary, and this Gospel uses it for things settled in heaven: you must be born again (3:7); so must the Son of Man be lifted up (3:14). The necessity that put him on that road is the same that put him on the cross. There was a woman, and a town, that the Father had prepared to hear him.

The whole chapter is an appointment. A woman is going to walk out to a well at the hottest hour of the day, on an errand she has run a thousand times, and find that the shortest route between Judea and Galilee has been redrawn in heaven so that a tired man would be sitting on the wall when she arrived.

Who were the Samaritans? Their Jewish neighbours called them half-breeds and heretics, but that is an enemy’s description, not a fair one. When Assyria destroyed the northern kingdom in 722 BC it deported the leading families and resettled foreigners in the land, and the population that resulted was mixed in blood and in religion (2 Kings 17:24–41). By Jesus’ day they held to the five books of Moses and nothing else, no prophets and no psalms, and they worshipped on Mount Gerizim rather than in Jerusalem. The hostility had recent history in it: in the late second century BC the Jewish ruler John Hyrcanus marched north and destroyed the Samaritan temple on Gerizim. Its ruins stood on the mountain above the well.

Does every detour in my life have a purpose like this? This verse does not promise that every closed door has a well and a waiting woman behind it, or that you will be told the reason. It does say that the God who arranges routes is not confined to the ones that look sensible, and that at least once in history the pointless-looking detour was the whole plan. Scripture says more broadly that God works all things together for good for those who love him (Romans 8:28). So hold your detours with open hands. You may never see the reason this side of glory, but you are not on the road by accident.

For worship. The Son did not drift into Samaria. He was sent there by the same love that sent him into the world. Long before the woman left her house that morning, the Father had set her name on his Son’s road, and the Son walked it gladly, though his own people avoided it. We worship not a God who waits behind a wall for the clean and the qualified, but one who must go through Samaria, because he will not leave his sheep in enemy country.
verseByVerse.note: Samaria lay between Judea and Galilee. Many Jews travelled round it by the Jordan valley; the direct route went through it.

parallels.desc: Philip preaches in Samaria

verseByVerse.quote: So he came to a town of Samaria called Sychar, near the field that Jacob had given to his son Joseph. Jacob's well was there; so Jesus, wearied as he was from his journey, was sitting beside the well. It was about the sixth hour.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A town of Samaria called Sychar. Probably near ancient Shechem, at the foot of Mount Gerizim, close to the modern city of Nablus.

Jacob’s field. The geography is thick with covenant memory, and John names Jacob twice in two verses. This is the field Jacob bought outside Shechem when he came back from Paddan-aram, one of the only pieces of the promised land a patriarch ever owned outright (Genesis 33:18–20). It is the plot he willed to Joseph (Genesis 48:22), and it is where Joseph’s bones were finally buried after being carried out of Egypt and round the wilderness for forty years (Joshua 24:32). It is where Israel stood and swore that they would serve the LORD (Joshua 24), and where the kingdom tore in half a few generations later (1 Kings 12). There is hardly a square yard of ground in Israel more layered with promise, oath-taking and failure, and it is in Samaria, in enemy country.

Jacob’s well was there. Still shown near Shechem, one of the most certainly identified sites in the Gospels, it goes down more than a hundred feet through rock.

Wearied. The verb means worn out by labour, the exhaustion that comes from work rather than lack of sleep. He is truly human: tired here, thirsty in verse 7, and hungry, as the disciples’ errand implies (v. 8). The Word made flesh (1:14) gets tired. This is the Gospel that opened by saying all things were made through him (1:3). Four chapters in, he is too worn out to walk on and has to sit down. John sets the two facts side by side and feels no need to explain either away: Jesus is truly God and truly man, and any picture of him that drops one of the two has stopped listening to John. The one who made the stars sat down because his legs ached. And the tired man on the wall of the well is the same Lord who neither slumbers nor sleeps, who upholds the universe by the word of his power.

Beside the well. Literally on the well, on the low stone wall around its mouth. A Jewish traveller has sat down on the wall of a Samaritan well with nothing to draw with.

The sixth hour. Noon: the worst part of the day to be walking or fetching water. Women usually drew water in the cool of morning or evening, and together. A woman coming alone at noon was probably avoiding the others, though John does not say so, and we should hold that guess lightly.

From this well to the cross. There is a line running from this well to the end of the book. The man sitting here with no bucket is about to offer a stranger water that ends thirst for ever. Fifteen chapters later he will hang on a cross, and almost the last thing he says before it is finished is I thirst (19:28). He ended thirsty: the living water he offers her freely cost him the cross.

Was Jesus really tired, if he was God? Yes. The eternal Son took to himself a true body and a reasonable soul (the Westminster Shorter Catechism, Q. 22), with the common weaknesses of our nature, yet without sin (the Westminster Confession 8.2; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 8.2), and in that nature he truly grew weary, hungry and thirsty. His divine nature did not become tired, and it was not turned into something less than God; but the person who sat on the well was the Son of God, and his weariness was his own. This is not a weakness in the gospel. It is its glory. A Saviour who only seemed human could not stand in our place, and he could not sympathise with our weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15).

In everyday life. A word to the reader who is simply tired: not spiritually dry, tired, with the day still eight hours long. There is no rebuke here and no instruction to push through. The Son of God sat down on a wall because he could not go on, and the most important conversation in the chapter happened while he was in that condition. Exhaustion is not a lapse in discipleship. Sit down if you must, and let him use you there.
verseByVerse.note: Jacob’s well is still shown near Shechem (modern Nablus) at the foot of Mount Gerizim. The ESV notes that the sixth hour was about noon, the heat of the day.

parallels.desc: Jacob buys land at Shechem
Joseph buried there

verseByVerse.quote: A woman from Samaria came to draw water. Jesus said to her, "Give me a drink."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A woman from Samaria. Alone, at noon, and unnamed. John never tells us her name, and she becomes one of the most remembered people in the Bible.

Give me a drink. Count what is wrong with this scene by the standards of the day, because the list is longer than we feel it. He is a man, alone, speaking to a woman, alone, in an isolated place. Rabbinic caution about this was severe; there were teachers who held that a man should not greet a woman in public. He is a Jew asking a Samaritan for water, which raises a question of ritual cleanness that she will name herself, since the vessel is hers and strict Jews regarded Samaritan vessels as unclean. And he is asking a favour of somebody with nothing, which is not how benefactors behave. He breaks three barriers, sex, race and religion, in four words, and offers no explanation for any of it.

He begins by asking. The first thing the Son of God says to her is a request for help. She is not approached as a case or a project, but as the person by the well with the rope. He who owns the cattle on a thousand hills and the waters under the earth stood at a Samaritan well and asked a sinner for a cup. He made himself dependent, here on a woman with a rope, and later on borrowed boats, borrowed rooms and a borrowed tomb. The Lord who could have commanded the water to rise asked her for it instead, because he had come for her, and not for the water.

It was not a technique. A favour asked to open a conversation is a manoeuvre, and people can smell it. He was genuinely thirsty, and the request, being true, did what no strategy could have done.

What he did not open with. Not her history, which he already knew in full. Not her theology, which was defective. Not her nationality. Every one of those comes up later in the conversation, and not one of them is the doorway.

How do I start a conversation about Christ without it feeling artificial? Begin where Jesus began: with honesty and ordinary common ground. Nearly all our discomfort comes from arriving as the one with all the answers, which sets up a transaction where one party is deficient and both know it. This conversation starts from the other end. The most common ground between two human beings is not that one is right; it is that both need things. Be genuinely interested in the person, accept their help when you need it, and let real questions come. Do not hide that you are a Christian, and do not force the subject; pray for the moment and take it when it comes, as Jesus does in verse 10.
verseByVerse.note: A Jewish teacher would not normally speak with a woman in public, still less a Samaritan.

parallels.desc: meetings at a well

verseByVerse.quote: (For his disciples had gone away into the city to buy food.) The Samaritan woman said to him, "How is it that you, a Jew, ask for a drink from me, a woman of Samaria?" (For Jews have no dealings with Samaritans.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciples had gone. So the conversation was private. And a party of Jewish men buying food in a Samaritan town is already looser about boundaries than the custom.

How is it that you, a Jew, ask for a drink from me, a woman of Samaria? Her reply is not a rebuff and it is not bitterness. It is astonishment, and notice how she puts it: you, a Jew; me, a woman of Samaria. In one breath she names everything that stands between them. She has spent her life on the wrong side of a line she did not draw, and here is somebody standing on the other side of it asking for a drink.

No dealings. Some understand the verb as do not use vessels in common with Samaritans, which fits the scene exactly: her surprise is not that a Jew has spoken to her, but that he proposes to drink from her jar. Hatred ran deep on both sides; a Samaritan village would later refuse Jesus, and James and John wanted to call down fire on it (Luke 9:52–54).

The crack through which grace enters. Contempt she could have handled. Contempt is familiar, and she knows how to brace herself against it. What she has no defence against is a Jewish man asking her for a favour. The contempt she had braced herself for did not come, so she is off balance and talking. Many people outside the faith already know what they expect from Christians; they expect contempt and have braced themselves against it. The most disarming thing we can offer is not a better argument. It is for the contempt they expected not to be there.

Does this mean Christ does not care about truth, only about kindness? No. In a few verses he will tell her plainly that the Samaritans worship what they do not know (v. 22). He crosses the barrier of contempt, not the barrier of truth. What he refuses is the hatred, the ritual separation and the assumption that she is beneath him. What he never gives up is the truth about God and about her life. The church needs both: no wall of contempt around itself, and no blurring of the gospel. Love that hides the truth is not love, and truth spoken with contempt is rarely heard.

For worship. Christ is our peace, who has made us both one and has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility (Ephesians 2:14). It began here, at a well, with a cup. He went to the cross to make one new people out of enemies, and every church where former enemies share the Lord’s Table is a monument to what he began beside Jacob’s well.
verseByVerse.note: Samaritans were a mixed people descended from Israelites and settlers brought in by Assyria; Jews and Samaritans had centuries of hostility. The ESV notes that the last sentence may mean Jews did not share vessels with Samaritans.

parallels.desc: the settling of Samaria

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered her, "If you knew the gift of God, and who it is that is saying to you, 'Give me a drink,' you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water."
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you knew the gift of God. The gift is eternal life, given by the Spirit and found in Christ himself (3:16; Romans 6:23). It is free: it cannot be earned or bought.

Who it is. She does not know what is on offer, nor who is offering it. The second matters most, because a promised gift is worth only as much as the giver’s power to give it, and she is looking at a tired man with no bucket.

You would have asked him. That is all. Not you would have qualified, or made amends first, or got the mountain question right. The only thing standing between this woman and living water, on Jesus’ own account, is that it had not occurred to her to ask, and it had not occurred to her because she did not know who she was talking to. Her difficulty is not that she is unworthy; her history is about to be laid out and it changes nothing. It is not that she is a Samaritan; that barrier has already been crossed. Ignorance, not unworthiness, is what keeps her poor. And he does not lecture her about it. He tells her, in stages, until she asks.

Living water. The one asking for water is the one who gives it. Living water (hudōr zōn) ordinarily meant running water, a spring, as opposed to the still water of a cistern or well. So she thinks he is offering her running water from some spring, just as Nicodemus took born again to mean a second physical birth.

What is the living water? In the Old Testament God himself is the fountain of living waters, whom his people forsook for broken cisterns (Jeremiah 2:13; 17:13). Living water pictures the life and the Spirit that God pours out on his people (Isaiah 44:3; 55:1; Ezekiel 47; Zechariah 14:8). And John tells us in so many words what Jesus means: standing in the temple at the feast, Jesus promises rivers of living water to whoever believes, and John adds that he said this about the Spirit (7:37–39). The gift at the well is nothing less than the Spirit of God dwelling in a person, the same new birth from above that Nicodemus could not grasp, now pictured as a spring. For you, it means that God himself comes to live in you, and from the inside he gives you a new love for him, an understanding of his word and the power to turn from sin (Ezekiel 36:27; Galatians 5:22–23). And Jesus gives the Spirit; he is the fountain.

Then why do so few people ask? Because they do not know the gift or the giver. Many people who stay away from Christ are not refusing living water; they think they are refusing a set of rules, a dull institution or a moral lecture. That is why Christian witness must keep pointing to who Jesus is and what he gives. When people truly see him, the asking follows.
verseByVerse.note: “Living water” normally meant fresh, flowing water from a spring, as opposed to still water in a cistern.

parallels.desc: the fountain of living waters

verseByVerse.quote: The woman said to him, "Sir, you have nothing to draw water with, and the well is deep. Where do you get that living water? Are you greater than our father Jacob? He gave us the well and drank from it himself, as did his sons and his livestock."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nothing to draw water with. Travellers carried a leather bucket and a rope; Jesus had none, and the well is deep. Her objections are the sensible ones of a competent person. She takes him literally, as Nicodemus did (3:4).

Our father Jacob. The Samaritans claimed the patriarchs as their own, which Jews disputed. In one phrase she has half crossed the boundary she raised: they have the same forefather, and she is standing on his land.

Are you greater than our father Jacob? An ironic question, expecting the answer no. The answer is yes. Jacob gave a well; Jesus gives living water. Jacob dreamed of a ladder between heaven and earth; Jesus is the ladder (1:51). John loves this kind of irony. It is exactly the shape of the question the crowd will ask about Abraham in chapter 8, to which Jesus answers that before Abraham was, I am (8:53–58). The Gospel keeps putting the true answer in the mouths of people who mean it as an impossibility. Jacob dug a hole, and it was a good hole, and his descendants were still drawing from it nearly two thousand years later. The man she is talking to made the water.

Her literalism is the staircase. He does not correct her about the bucket. He takes the difficulty she has raised and uses it as the next step up.

What do I do with objections that seem to miss the point? Take them seriously, as Jesus does. A question that sounds naive or off-target is very often the real question, held at the only end the person can currently reach. Do not mock it or brush past it. Answer honestly what can be answered, and then use it, as Jesus does, to lift the conversation toward who he is. Patient, respectful answers to plain questions have led more people to Christ than clever arguments.
verseByVerse.note: The well is deep, said to be over 100 feet.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to her, "Everyone who drinks of this water will be thirsty again."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thirsty again. A strange thing to say to a woman with a jar in her hand. It sounds mild, but it covers everything. He is not saying that Jacob’s water is bad, only that no drink of it lasts.

It is simply true. Every good thing available to a human being works on the same cycle: it satisfies, the satisfaction wears off, and the need returns at full strength and slightly sooner than last time. The meal, the holiday, the promotion, the applause, the relationship. None of them fails. They all work exactly as advertised, and then they stop working, and the stopping is not a fault in them. The eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing (Ecclesiastes 1:8). Human beings have a thirst no earthly thing can quench, because we were made for God.

Thirst is not the sin. Say it plainly to the reader who keeps going back to the same well and hates himself for it, whether the well is a bottle, a screen, a person he should have stopped calling, or the approval of someone whose opinion he cannot get out from under. The verse does not rebuke the thirst. God made us to thirst; the ache is not evidence that something has gone wrong with you. What the verse says is that the well you keep returning to has never once promised to give what you keep hoping it will. It gives what it has. It gives it every time. And the interval between drinks gets shorter, which is the mechanism of every addiction there has ever been.

He does not despise the well. He asked for a drink from it. The problem was never that people love good things too much, but that they ask of them what they were never built to carry.

If I am a Christian, should earthly pleasures stop satisfying me? They should satisfy you more truly, not less, because you no longer need them to be God. A Christian can enjoy a meal, a friendship or a holiday as a gift from the Father, give thanks, and let it go when it ends, because his soul is not hanging on it. What changes is not that the gifts taste of nothing, but that their running out is no longer a disaster. The danger comes when we start asking a gift to do what only the Giver can do.

In everyday life. Take the thing you were most sure would settle you, the thing you believed ten years ago would mean you had arrived. Suppose you got it. Did the wanting stop, or did it change address? That is not cynicism about good gifts; it is evidence about what kind of creature you are. Name the well you keep going back to, and bring that thirst to Christ.

For worship. God did not make us small enough to be filled by the world. He made us for himself, as Augustine confessed, and nothing less than himself will ever fill us. When we had forsaken the fountain for cisterns that hold no water, he came himself to the well and offered us the fountain again.

verseByVerse.quote: "'but whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never be thirsty again. The water that I will give him will become in him a spring of water welling up to eternal life.' The woman said to him, 'Sir, give me this water, so that I will not be thirsty or have to come here to draw water.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Never be thirsty. A strong double negative in the Greek: never, ever. A door closing on the whole cycle of drinking and thirsting again.

A spring of water. Then the image changes in a way that should stop the reader, because it stops being about drinking at all. He does not say the water will keep her topped up, or that she may come back whenever she runs low. He says the water he gives becomes in him a spring. The one who drinks becomes a source. That is the difference between a well and a spring. A well is a hole where water is stored; it has to be gone to, lowered into, hauled out of, and it is finite. A spring is water arriving from underneath, under its own pressure. The picture is not of a reservoir carefully managed. It is of something that will not stay down. He does not hand out cups; he opens springs.

Welling up. The word (hallomenou) means leaping, springing up; it is used of the lame man leaping in the temple (Acts 3:8). This is the life of the Holy Spirit within the believer (7:38–39), an inner source of life that never runs dry, rising toward its goal: eternal life.

Sir, give me this water. She still misunderstands: she wants to be spared the daily trip, and perhaps the shame of coming alone at noon. But she has asked for it anyway, which is more than Nicodemus managed. She misunderstands and yet holds out her hand, and in this Gospel that is better than understanding and not asking.

He does not correct her yet. He lets her ask for the right thing for the wrong reason, and goes on. No one comes to him with perfectly pure motives, and he has never yet sent anyone away until their motives were right.

Why, then, do believers still thirst for God? The Psalms are full of it: as a deer pants for flowing streams, so pants my soul for you, O God (Psalm 42:1). The thirst that ends is the thirst of emptiness, the restless search for something to fill the soul. The Christian has found the spring; it is in him. But a spring is drawn on every day, and Jesus goes on inviting his own: if anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink (7:37). The longing believers feel is not the old emptiness. It is the appetite of those who have tasted and want more, and it will be fully satisfied when we see him face to face (Revelation 7:16–17).

What if I feel dry, not like a spring at all? Feelings rise and fall; the spring is not your feelings but the Spirit himself, and he does not leave the believer (14:16). Dry seasons come to all God’s children, through tiredness, sorrow, sin or simply God’s wise testing. In them, keep to the means by which the Spirit refreshes his people: his word, prayer, the Lord’s Supper, the fellowship of the church. Confess any sin you know of. And keep asking. The promise does not depend on how full you feel today, but on the faithfulness of the one who gave it.

In everyday life. If you belong to Christ, the source is already inside you. Begin the day not by hauling up your own resources but by asking the Spirit to rise in you, for patience with the children or joy in a dull task.

parallels.desc: like a spring of water whose waters do not fail

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to her, "Go, call your husband, and come here." The woman answered him, "I have no husband." Jesus said to her, "You are right in saying, 'I have no husband';"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Go, call your husband. The turn is so abrupt that it is worth asking why he makes it. They have been talking about water and eternal life; she has just asked for the gift. Instead of giving it, he says: go and fetch your husband. It is not a change of subject. It is the point at which the conversation stops being about a topic and becomes about her. Everything up to here could be discussed in general terms: thirst in general, life in general, a gift available to whoever wants one. The moment he mentions her husband, it is about one particular woman and her history, and she can no longer keep it at a safe distance. She cannot receive living water without facing her thirst, and her sin. Jesus goes straight to the wound.

Where the difficulty lies. Many people find Christianity beautiful and are never once cornered by it, because they only ever discuss it as something about people in general. What changes everything is never a doctrine. It is always a sentence like go, call your husband, a sentence about you.

I have no husband. Four words that are entirely true and are being used to hide something. It is not a lie. It is an accurate sentence deployed as a wall, a half-truth to close the subject.

You are right. He does not knock the wall down. He agrees with it, and then says the thing the wall was built to keep out. When people expose us, they usually start with what we got wrong; Jesus starts with what she got right. It is the difference between being caught out and being told the truth by somebody plainly on your side.

Why does Christ bring up my sin if salvation is a free gift? Because the gift is for sinners, and no one drinks who will not admit they are thirsty. Jesus does not raise her history to make her earn the water, but so that she will know he is offering it to her, the real woman, and not to an idealised version of her. A gospel that never touches your actual life cannot save your actual life. Repentance is not a price paid for grace; it is the hand opening to receive it. When Christ puts his finger on something, it is because he means to heal it.

In everyday life. Is there a question you are keeping Christ from asking, a subject you steer around in prayer the way she steered around her household? Name it to him today; he raises it only to heal it.

verseByVerse.quote: "for you have had five husbands, and the one you now have is not your husband. What you have said is true."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You have had five husbands. He had never met her and he knows every year. In that culture a woman could not ordinarily divorce her husband, while a husband could dismiss a wife for very little. So five marriages may mean five times widowed, or five times sent away: a life of things done to her at least as much as by her.
