Not your husband. She was living with a man without marriage. This is the one irregularity Jesus names outright, and it is a real one: the present arrangement is not a marriage in God’s sight. That may be why she came to the well alone at noon.

How much do we actually know? It is worth being honest about how much the text supplies, because a great deal has been built on very little. John never calls this woman immoral, and Jesus never tells her, as he tells the man at the pool, to sin no more (5:14). The town listens to her and comes out at her word (vv. 29–30, 39), which is not how a town treats a woman it has entirely cast out. There are women who have sat through sermons on this chapter and heard themselves described, divorced not by their choosing, widowed young, or long ago abandoned, and been handed a shame the passage never assigns. What the passage does assign is this: Jesus knew every year of her history before she said a word, asked her for a drink anyway, gave her the plainest statement of his identity in the Gospels, and sent her back to tell her town who he was.

Are the five husbands a symbol? Some have read them as an allegory: Assyria resettled Samaria with people from five foreign cities, each bringing their own gods (2 Kings 17:24–31), so the five husbands stand for false worships and the sixth for corrupt Samaritan religion. It is ingenious, but John gives no hint of it, the numbers do not work cleanly, and above all it dissolves a real woman into a symbol, which is the very thing this passage refuses to do to her. She is not a diagram of Samaria. She is somebody with five marriages behind her and a man in the house now, standing in the heat with a jar.

What you have said is true. Jesus exposes her without contempt. He tells the truth, and in telling it shows that he knows her completely and is still speaking to her. The gentleness is not softness about sin: the one speaking is the holy God in human flesh, whose eyes are too pure to look on evil (Habakkuk 1:13), and the wonder is that holiness so pure came close enough to ask her for a cup.

What if I am living in a situation like hers? Then hear both halves of this verse. Christ knows your situation completely, and he does not pretend it is right: living together outside marriage is not what God designed, and he calls you out of it, into marriage or into chastity. But he says it while offering you living water, not while slamming a door. Come to him as you are; he will not send you away. Talk honestly with a pastor about the steps to take. And if your story is one of being left, widowed or divorced against your will, know that this verse does not lay at your feet a shame that belongs to others.

For worship. Five marriages had ended, and the man in the house had not married her. Then, at a well, the kind of place where Isaac’s bride was found and Jacob met Rachel, she met the Bridegroom (3:29), who came to give, not to take. He knew the whole history before she spoke, and it did not alter the offer by a drop. The Lord who searches the heart is the Lord who died for what he finds there.

parallels.desc: he knew what was in man

verseByVerse.quote: The woman said to him, "Sir, I perceive that you are a prophet. Our fathers worshiped on this mountain, but you say that in Jerusalem is the place where people ought to worship."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A prophet. Only a prophet could know such things. Her understanding is growing: from a Jew (v. 9), to sir (v. 11), to a prophet, and soon to the Christ (v. 29).

This mountain. Mount Gerizim rose directly above the well; she could have pointed at it. Israel was told to pronounce the blessings there (Deuteronomy 11:29; 27:12), and the Samaritan copy of the law even named it as the place for the altar. On its summit lay the rubble of their temple, torn down by John Hyrcanus. The disagreement she raises is a ruin she can see, and the people who made it are this man’s people.

But you say Jerusalem. Is she changing the subject to avoid her sin, or asking sincerely? Both readings are possible, and the honest thing is to hold them together.

It may be deflection. A man has just named the most painful arrangement in her life, and within one sentence she is discussing which religion is right. A large, impersonal question has turned up just when the small personal one became unbearable. Religion is uncommonly good for this. Arguing is a great deal easier than being known.

It may be entirely genuine. Standing before somebody who has just proved he can see, she asks where a sinner should go to find God and forgiveness, and takes the only chance she may ever get.

Jesus does not force a verdict. He answers the question with the fullest teaching on worship in the Gospels, which is what he would do if it were sincere, and the only thing that would have helped if it were not. He is after the person, and he will follow her down any road she takes until she finds herself in front of him. And the argument, he is about to say, is over, and neither side won it.

What should I do when someone turns a personal conversation into a religious debate? Answer the question briefly and honestly, as Jesus does, and then bring it back to the person and to Christ. Do not get drawn into a long argument about church history, other religions or the hypocrisy of Christians while the real matter waits. You might say: that is a fair question, and here is a short answer; but can I ask what you make of Jesus himself? Winning a debate of this kind rarely wins the person.
verseByVerse.note: “This mountain” is Mount Gerizim, where the Samaritans worshipped; a Samaritan temple had stood there until the Jews destroyed it more than a century before.

parallels.desc: the blessing on Mount Gerizim
the place the LORD will choose

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to her, "Woman, believe me, the hour is coming when neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem will you worship the Father."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woman, believe me. The same courteous address he used to his mother (2:4; 19:26): he speaks to a Samaritan at a well with the same respect he shows his own mother. And believe me asks for trust before he says the thing that will cost her her side of the argument.

The hour is coming. The new age Jesus is bringing through his death and resurrection. In John the hour is always tied to his glorification (12:23; 17:1) and to the gift of the Spirit.

Neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem. Neither. Not your mountain is wrong and ours is right, which was the whole dispute. The argument is not settled; it is made obsolete. Jesus himself is the new temple (2:19–21), and after his resurrection God can be worshipped anywhere, through him. Within about forty years the Jerusalem temple would be rubble too, as the one on Gerizim already was.

The Father. The first time in this conversation he uses the name. She asked where; he answers who, with the family name. Worship in the new age is the worship of children.

The end of holy places. What is dismantled here is older than the Samaritan question: the assumption, held by most religions and sitting deep in human instinct, that God is more available in some places than others. That there is a spot, the spot has to be reached, and getting there is most of the work. It survives in people who would deny holding it: the sense that prayer counts more in a church building than in a car, that the same words weigh more before six in the morning than at eleven at night, the low-grade grief of coming home from a place where God seemed close. This verse says the mountain has been closed, and that everyone who cannot get to the holy place, the housebound, the shift worker, the mother of small children, the prisoner, has not been kept away from anything at all.

Does this mean church buildings and gathering on Sunday do not matter? Gathering matters; the place does not. Christ abolished holy geography, not the holy assembly. Believers are commanded not to neglect meeting together (Hebrews 10:25), and the gathered church is where the word is preached and the Supper shared. But the building is a roof, not a temple. God is not more present in the sanctuary than in your kitchen; he is present with his people, wherever they meet in Christ’s name. Love your church’s gathering because God’s people are there, not because the bricks are holy.

Is this not what people mean by spiritual but not religious? Only half. Jesus does abolish the holy place, but he does not make worship private or shaped by taste. In the next breath he says the Samaritans worship what they do not know, that salvation is from the Jews, and that the Father must be worshipped in truth (vv. 22–24), and in this Gospel the truth is Jesus himself (14:6). He removed the location, not the object or the way. A spirituality that builds its own picture of God has not left the mountain behind; it has built a new one inside the self, and it is just as unable to bring a sinner to the Father.

parallels.desc: in every place incense will be offered to my name

verseByVerse.quote: "You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know, for salvation is from the Jews. But the hour is coming, and is now here, when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, for the Father is seeking such people to worship him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You worship what you do not know. One clause keeps the passage from being turned into a mere lesson in tolerance. Everything else here is so generous that it is tempting to conclude Jesus is indifferent to the disagreement. He is not. The Samaritans had kept only the five books of Moses, and the result was a God known in outline, a knowledge incomplete and distorted.

Salvation is from the Jews. He does not call Samaritan religion a different route up the same mountain. God revealed himself to Israel, and the Messiah came from Israel according to the flesh (Romans 9:4–5). He does not flatter her; he tells her the truth.

From, not for. Salvation comes from the Jews; it was never for the Jews alone. So the same sentence takes away any boasting. Israel’s privilege was not something to keep but something to pass on. Israel was the well the water came through, and a well does not congratulate itself on the water.

And is now here. He has said the hour is coming (v. 21); now he adds that it is here. The new worship is beginning at this well, in this conversation, in the presence of Jesus.

In spirit and truth. In spirit: from the heart, by the Holy Spirit, who gives new birth (3:5). In truth: according to God’s revelation of himself, now fully given in Jesus, who is the truth (14:6).

The Father is seeking. This turns ordinary religious instinct upside down. We assume worship is what we do to find God; here God is the one out looking. She came to fetch water and found somebody already sitting there who had come by a road his countrymen avoided. The verse is happening as he speaks it. Not that God needs our worship (Acts 17:25); he seeks us for our good and his glory. He sought Adam in the garden, he sought Israel in Egypt, he sought this woman at the well, and he sought you. We love because he first loved us, and we worship because he first came looking.

Is it narrow to say other religions do not know God? It is honest, and it is what Jesus says. Many religions contain true things about right and wrong, and every person has some knowledge of God from creation and conscience (Romans 1:19–20). But saving knowledge of God comes only through his own revelation, given to Israel and fulfilled in Christ, and no one comes to the Father except through him (14:6). To say otherwise would not be kind; it would be leaving people at a dry well. And see the spirit in which Jesus says it: sitting with a Samaritan, asking for her help, offering her the gift. Truth about other faiths should always come with that kind of love.

What if I do not feel like much of a worshipper? Take heart from the last clause. You may have spent years with a low sense that the singing does not move you, that your prayers are dutiful, that others plainly have something you do not. This verse does not tell you to try harder to find God. It says the Father is out looking for worshippers. The search that matters is the one conducted from his end, and it has a far better record than ours. True worship is not measured by the strength of your feelings, but by whether you come to the Father through the Son, trusting what he has revealed.
verseByVerse.note: The Samaritans accepted only the five books of Moses.

parallels.desc: out of Zion shall go the law

verseByVerse.quote: "God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God is spirit. One of the great definitions of God in John’s writings, with God is light (1 John 1:5) and God is love (1 John 4:8).

What it does not say. Not God is a spirit, one item in a category of ghostly beings. Nor that God is vague, a force or an impersonal energy. The God described here talks, seeks, loves, and is called Father in the same breath.

What it does say. God has no body and is not in one place rather than another. He is everywhere present, not confined to a mountain or a temple (1 Kings 8:27; Acts 17:24–25). A temple can be burned and a mountain captured, and Gerizim had been. None of that touches him, because he was never on it. He is infinite, eternal and unchangeable, filling heaven and earth, dwelling in light unapproachable, and nearer to each of us than our own breath. And this God, who needs no house, has made his home in the hearts of those who believe.

Must worship in spirit and truth. Worship must match the nature of the one worshipped. If God were local, worship would be a matter of arriving. Since he is not, it is a matter of what kind of person you are before him, and everyone is before him all the time.

Not sincerity against ritual. The phrase is often misread as heartfelt against formal. That is not quite it. Spirit here is the Holy Spirit, the one Jesus described to Nicodemus as the agent of the new birth and has just pictured as a spring inside a person. Truth is not mere sincerity either; in this Gospel truth is a person before it is a quality: I am the way, and the truth, and the life (14:6). So worship in spirit and truth means worship enabled by God’s own Spirit and shaped by God’s own revelation in his Son. Both halves are gifts. Neither is a technique. And it cuts both ways. It rules out worship that is correct and dead, the right words in the right order with nobody home. And it rules out worship that is warm and invented, deeply felt and directed at a God assembled from preference. Truth without Spirit is a corpse. Spirit without truth is a mood.

Where Christians differ: how should we worship? Some traditions emphasise elaborate liturgy, ritual and visual symbols; others, free and spontaneous worship. Lutherans and Anglicans have generally held that churches may use what Scripture does not forbid; Reformed churches, that they should use only what it commands. This commentary’s view: Reformed churches have drawn from this verse, among others, what is called the regulative principle: worship should be shaped by what God has revealed in his word, not by human invention, and offered from the heart by the Spirit. External forms matter less than the heart, but worship must be true to Scripture: the reading and preaching of the word, prayer, singing, the sacraments. Held charitably toward brothers who differ in practice.

What does this mean for how a church worships? It removes sacred places, not the gathered church (Hebrews 10:25). In truth means worship shaped by what God has revealed in Scripture; the Reformed tradition has expressed this as the principle that worship should include only what God commands (the Westminster Confession 21.1; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 22.1). In spirit means worship from the heart, by the Spirit’s work. Neither rules out order or form, a planned service or a written prayer; both rule out empty ritual on one side and worship invented to please ourselves on the other.

If God is spirit, how could Jesus be God in a body? God in his own being is spirit and has no body. In the incarnation the eternal Son did not turn into matter or stop being spirit; he took a true human body and soul into union with himself (1:14). So the invisible God is seen in Jesus (1:18; 14:9). This is not a contradiction of God is spirit but the wonder of it: the God who cannot be confined to a mountain chose to dwell among us in the flesh, so that we might know him and worship him in truth.

In everyday life. Ask what is left of your worship when the service is dull, the preacher poor and the room cold. That residue is the part that was in spirit and truth; the rest was the building.

verseByVerse.quote: "The woman said to him, 'I know that Messiah is coming (he who is called Christ). When he comes, he will tell us all things.' Jesus said to her, 'I who speak to you am he.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
I know that Messiah is coming. With only the five books of Moses, the Samaritans had no royal prophecies of David’s line. They looked for the prophet like Moses into whose mouth God would put his words (Deuteronomy 18:15–18); later Samaritan writings call him the Taheb, the restorer.

He will tell us all things. They expected a teacher who would settle everything, including the mountain. So her sentence is quietly poignant: one day somebody will come who can sort this out. Whether she is putting the matter off or simply longing, she leaves it all to someone still to come, while he is standing three feet from her.

I who speak to you am he. Literally, I am, the one speaking to you (egō eimi): an ordinary way of saying that is me, but also the first use of the weightiest phrase in this Gospel. I am echoes the name God gave Moses at the bush (Exodus 3:14), and Jesus will use it of himself again and again (6:20; 8:58).

To her, first. He has spoken with a member of the ruling council by night without ever saying this; his disciples have been with him for months. And the first time in John that Jesus plainly says he is the Messiah, he says it to a Samaritan woman with a broken past, alone, in the heat. Not to the Sanhedrin. Not to Nicodemus.

Why does Jesus say so openly here what he hides elsewhere? The Samaritans expected a Messiah who would be a teacher and restorer, not a king leading a revolt. In Galilee and Judea the title would have brought crowds wanting to make him king by force (6:15). In Samaria his open claim carried less political danger, and it could be said plainly.

For worship. A whole people had waited for a prophet like Moses who would one day tell them all things, and the waiting was answered in one sentence to one woman at a well. The voice that once spoke from a burning bush, where Moses hid his face, spoke now from the wall of a well, and she did not need to hide hers. The one she had been waiting for had been waiting for her.
verseByVerse.note: The Samaritans expected a coming prophet like Moses. Jesus’ “I who speak to you am he” is literally “I am, the one speaking to you.”

verseByVerse.quote: Just then his disciples came back. They marveled that he was talking with a woman, but no one said, "What do you seek?" or, "Why are you talking with her?" So the woman left her water jar and went away into town.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They marveled. Not even that she was a Samaritan; simply a woman, when rabbis were expected to avoid talking with women in public. Their surprise is the instinct of every religious person who has quietly ranked people into those worth Christ’s time and those not. Grace upsets the ranking, because none of us earned his time either (Romans 5:8).

The questions nobody asked. John records two questions the disciples did not ask. The first, what do you seek?, is almost the question Jesus himself asked at the start of this Gospel: what are you seeking? (1:38). The disciples do not put it to him, or to themselves. They have learned that he does things they would not have advised, and not yet learned to ask why.

A familiar silence. It is possible to follow Christ for years without ever bringing him the question that is actually there: the prayer not answered, the person not healed, the passage that troubles. This Gospel is full of people who asked him poor questions and got somewhere. Bring your honest questions to him; he is not offended by them.

She left her water jar. She came for water and forgot it, because she had found living water. It is not a symbol she intended; people leave things when something has made the errand irrelevant. And she would have to come back for it. What happened did not remove the daily walk or the heat. It removed whatever reason she had for coming alone. The jar on the wall of the well is a small monument to a soul that had found its spring.

Does this show that women may teach men in the church? Her witness was an invitation, come, see a man, and her neighbours then came to Christ himself and believed because of his word (vv. 39–42). Every believer, man or woman, is to bear witness to Christ like this. The authoritative teaching of the gathered church is a different thing, which Paul reserves for qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12). This commentary holds that view because Paul grounds it in creation rather than local custom (1 Timothy 2:13), though many faithful Christians read the passage differently and deserve a respectful hearing. On any view, Christ honoured this woman’s witness, and a town came to him through it.

verseByVerse.quote: and said to the people, "Come, see a man who told me all that I ever did. Can this be the Christ?" They went out of the town and were coming to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Come, see. The woman who came to the well alone runs to the people, with the words of Jesus and Philip on her lips (1:39, 46).

All that I ever did. Look at what her testimony consists of, because it is a remarkably poor piece of evangelism by any standard we would apply. She has one fact, and it is about herself. She overstates it, all that I ever did, when he had named her marriages and the man in her house. She cannot explain the living water, she has no doctrine of the incarnation, her view of the mountain was the Samaritan one, and he had just set it aside. And the town came out. She does not hide her past. The very thing that made her ashamed becomes her testimony. Notice what she leaves out: she never adds, and he did not despise me. She does not need to, because her whole tone says it. Being completely known had turned out not to be the disaster she would have predicted. That is the entire content of her testimony.

Can this be the Christ? The Greek frames it as a tentative question, something nearer to this could not be the Christ, could it? She does not preach; she invites them to decide for themselves. The tentativeness may be the strength of it. A woman marching back into town with a finished doctrine would be easy to dismiss. A woman asking a question she plainly cannot answer herself, in evident agitation, having left her water jar, is harder to walk past. People argue with a conclusion. They find it harder to argue with somebody who has obviously been changed.

They were coming to him. She did not try to settle the question for them. She brought people to where Jesus was, and stepped aside.

What if I do not know enough to witness? Then you are in exactly her position, and look what God did with it. You do not need a theology degree. You need to know what Christ has done for you and where people can find him. Tell the truth about your own life, invite people to come and see, to read a Gospel, to come to church, to meet him in his word, and let him do the rest. Keep learning, of course, so that you can give a reason for your hope (1 Peter 3:15). But do not wait until you know everything. She knew one sentence, and a town came out.

In everyday life. Write down in one sentence what Jesus has done for you, the plainest, truest sentence you can. Then ask God for one person to say it to this week, and an invitation to add: come and see.

verseByVerse.quote: Meanwhile the disciples were urging him, saying, "Rabbi, eat." But he said to them, "I have food to eat that you do not know about."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rabbi, eat. A town is walking out across the fields toward Jesus because of something that happened while the disciples were shopping, and their contribution to the moment is to press him about lunch.

They are being kind. He had been too tired to walk; they had gone to fetch food; they are now trying to get him to eat it. This is thoughtfulness, and it is completely blind. The largest thing that had happened all day was standing in front of them, and they were looking at a man who had not eaten. That is a fair description of a great deal of church life. The failure is rarely a failure to care. It is that the caring is all practical, the rota, the building, the meal, and the thing God is doing in the room goes unremarked because nobody was looking for it there.

Food you do not know about. As with the water (v. 10), Jesus speaks of a spiritual reality and is misunderstood. It is the second time in this chapter, and the third since Nicodemus heard born again. She said water, and he answered with water that was not water. Now they say eat, and he answers with food they know nothing about. He does not reject the material thing; he takes the ordinary object already in the conversation and uses it as a handle on something the hearer has no other way of reaching. It is not evasion and it is not mysticism. Our words were made for the world we can see, so the only way to speak of the unseen is to borrow them, and that is why almost everyone in this Gospel misunderstands him at first. He pays that cost in nearly every conversation, and never once sounds impatient.

Is it wrong to care about practical things in church? Not at all. Someone has to buy the bread, and the disciples were right to look after their tired Master. Practical service is honoured throughout Scripture (Acts 6:1–6). The danger is only that the practical becomes the whole of what we see. Do the rota and the catering gladly, as service to Christ, but lift your eyes while you do it. Ask, in every meeting and every task: what is God doing here, and with whom?

parallels.desc: man shall not live by bread alone

verseByVerse.quote: So the disciples said to one another, "Has anyone brought him something to eat?" Jesus said to them, "My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Has anyone brought him something to eat? Literal again. It is the most human sentence in the chapter. They are not mocking; they have concluded, reasonably, that somebody must have got there first with a basket, and they are working out the logistics.

My food. His answer redefines what has been sustaining him for the last hour. Not that he did not need food; he did, he was too tired to walk. But there is something that works in him the way food works, and he names it. His deepest satisfaction and sustenance is doing the Father’s will (Deuteronomy 8:3; Matthew 4:4). Talking to this woman had refreshed him more than food. And it is worth pressing this: the Father’s will is described as food, which is to say it feeds rather than costs. That is not how obedience usually feels. We tend to think of doing God’s will as expenditure, drawn from a limited account that has to be topped up later by rest or pleasure. Jesus describes it as something that fills him. Much of what drives us runs the other way: we work in order to be fed, by approval, by success, by the feeling of being needed, and when the praise stops we go hungry. Jesus was fed by the Father’s will itself, so no crowd could fill him up and no rejection could empty him.

To accomplish his work. Accomplish (teleiōsō) means to complete, the same family of words as his cry from the cross: it is finished (tetelestai, 19:30). What he does at this well and at Calvary is one work (5:36; 17:4).

Does this mean I am doing ministry wrongly if it exhausts me? No. The verse has sometimes been used to flog tired people, and it should not be. The man who said this had sat down earlier that day because he could not go on; both facts are in the same chapter on the same afternoon. Weariness in God’s work is normal and honourable, and rest is God’s gift, not a failure (Mark 6:31). What the verse says is that some work, whatever it takes out of the body, puts something back into the soul, and that this is the mark of work done for the Father rather than merely about him.

In everyday life. Compare two things you do for God: one that leaves you flat, and one that tires you and yet you would not give up. The difference is often between a task you took on to be useful and a task the Father actually gave you. The first is a job. The second, in the words of this verse, is food.

For worship. The Son delighted to do his Father’s will, all the way to the cross, where he cried, It is finished. His obedience was never grudging, and it is that perfect, glad obedience that God counts as theirs for all who trust him (Romans 5:19; 2 Corinthians 5:21). And because he finished the work, our obedience can be food too: not a wage we pay, but the joy of children doing the will of a Father who has already given us everything in his Son.

parallels.desc: having accomplished the work

verseByVerse.quote: "Do you not say, 'There are yet four months, then comes the harvest'? Look, I tell you, lift up your eyes, and see that the fields are white for harvest. Already the one who reaps is receiving wages and gathering fruit for eternal life, so that sower and reaper may rejoice together."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four months. Grain sown in winter was harvested in spring, and the saying may have been a proverb for the wait. Harvest is the one thing in farming that cannot be hurried, and Jesus says the wait is over.

White for harvest. Picture what he is looking at: the town coming out across open country toward the well, perhaps in white robes, through the fields (v. 30). He is not offering an image. He is pointing. The harvest is walking toward you while you are asking about lunch. The Lord of the harvest sees fields where we see empty roads. He ripens hearts in secret, by his Spirit, long before we notice.

Already receiving wages. The reward of gospel work is being handed over during the work, and the fruit is gathered for eternal life. This harvest does not rot.

Sower and reaper. In ordinary farming the reaper gets the visible result. Here somebody prayed for years and saw nothing, and somebody else said one sentence and saw a town come out, and the two are paid at the same table.

Does this mean everyone around me is about to believe? No. Jesus is speaking of what God was doing that day in Sychar, and elsewhere he says the labourers are few and that many will reject the word. But the verse warns us that people are usually nearer to believing than we suppose. God has his elect in every place (Acts 18:10), and the Spirit is often at work where we see nothing. The elect are those whom God chose in Christ before the world began, and whom he will surely bring to himself (Ephesians 1:4; John 6:37). So sow widely, pray boldly, and do not write anyone off. The last people anyone expected were already on their way.
verseByVerse.note: Crops were sown in winter and harvested in spring; “four months” was roughly the gap between sowing and harvest, and the saying may have been proverbial.

parallels.desc: the ploughman shall overtake the reaper

verseByVerse.quote: "For here the saying holds true, 'One sows and another reaps.' I sent you to reap that for which you did not labor. Others have labored, and you have entered into their labor."
verseByVerse.commentary:
One sows and another reaps. A proverb, and here it holds true in a direction nobody expects: the disciples will reap a harvest prepared by others.

Others have labored. Who were the others? Samaria has a history, and Jesus is standing in the middle of it. Some of it is very old: Jacob dug the well the disciples are standing beside, Joseph’s bones are buried in the field, Moses sent Israel to that mountain to hear the blessings, and the prophets laboured for centuries. Some of it is recent: John the Baptist had been preaching not far away. And some is a matter of hours: Jesus himself, and a woman who had just gone back to her town and did all the sowing there was time for. The disciples arrive with the shopping and walk into a harvest that centuries of history and one conversation had prepared. And in Acts, Philip, and then Peter and John, would reap in Samaria what Jesus sowed here (Acts 8:4–25).

Somebody always got tired first. The word for laboured is the same root as wearied in verse 6. Every harvest anyone reaps was preceded by exhaustion the reaper did not feel and often never hears about.

Entered into their labor. Every gospel worker builds on others’ work. There is no room for pride (1 Corinthians 3:6–9). Nothing you are reaping is yours. The building was paid for by people who are dead. The doctrine you preach was fought for by people who were burned for it. The person ready to believe in front of you was worked on for years by somebody whose name you will never learn, quite possibly a grandmother who prayed, saw nothing, and died thinking she had failed.

What about the sower who never sees fruit? This is the verse for the discouraged sower: the parent who has prayed for a child for thirty years, the Sunday school teacher who watched most of a generation drift, the missionary who left with almost nothing to report. There is no promise that the sower sees it. There is a promise, one verse earlier, that when it is finally seen, he rejoices with the reaper. God does not forget any seed sown in faith; your labour in the Lord is not in vain (1 Corinthians 15:58). Keep sowing.

In everyday life. Name three people who sowed the gospel in you. If any are still alive, write to one of them this week and thank them. And sow faithfully today, even if others reap.

parallels.desc: cities you did not build
I planted, Apollos watered

verseByVerse.quote: Many Samaritans from that town believed in him because of the woman's testimony, "He told me all that I ever did." So when the Samaritans came to him, they asked him to stay with them, and he stayed there two days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because of the woman’s testimony. John repeats her sentence rather than summarising it, so we know exactly what carried, and it was not a doctrine of the atonement or the two natures of Christ. A town heard a woman say that he knew everything about her, and walked out across the fields to see whether it might be true of them too. What makes the gospel travel is not first the completeness of the account but the evidence that something has happened to the person giving it. Everyone in that town had known the earlier version of her.

They asked him to stay. Stay (meinai) is John’s great word abide. It is one thing to be persuaded about a man; it is another to want him in the house for two days.

Two days. A Jewish rabbi ate Samaritan food, off their plates, under their roofs, for two days, each act carrying a ritual cost in the eyes of the men in Jerusalem. Nothing in the text treats this as remarkable, and that says a great deal. The Son of God was not ashamed to lodge with Samaritans, because they asked him, and he loves to be asked.

Is the later giving of the Spirit in Samaria a pattern for us? In Acts the Samaritans receive the Spirit only after the apostles come. That was a later group, and a special moment in the spread of the church, when God showed that Samaritans were fully included in the one church of the apostles (Acts 8:14–17). These Samaritans in John truly believed, knowing Jesus as the Saviour of the world. Neither passage sets up a two-stage pattern for all believers. Everyone who truly believes in Christ has the Spirit (Romans 8:9).

In everyday life. Ask Christ to stay: in your home, your evenings, your plans. Faith that keeps Christ at the town gate is not yet the faith of Sychar.

parallels.desc: Samaria receives the word

verseByVerse.quote: And many more believed because of his word. They said to the woman, "It is no longer because of what you said that we believe, for we have heard for ourselves, and we know that this is indeed the Savior of the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because of his word. Testimony brings people to Jesus; his word brings them to faith.

No longer because of what you said. This is no insult to her. It is where every true witness hopes to lead: they no longer rely on her account, because they have heard him for themselves. Her task is done.

Saviour of the world. The summit of the episode. Not only the Jewish Messiah, but the Saviour of all peoples, including Samaritans. A saviour rescues from something, and John has already named it: from the judgment that rests on everyone who does not believe, into eternal life (3:16–18, 36). The title appears in the New Testament only here and in John’s first letter (1 John 4:14). And the title had a ring in the first century: inscriptions across the empire honoured emperors as saviour and benefactor. Readers who knew that would hear a title fit for Rome given to a Jewish teacher in a Samaritan village, by Samaritans, outsiders to Israel’s hopes. Outsiders understood what insiders missed. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read the Christ, the Saviour of the world; the earliest lack the Christ, so most modern Bibles omit it.

The ironies stacked in the sentence. The people who confess him are the people a Jew would not share a cup with, and they reach it in two days, when Nicodemus, the teacher of Israel with every advantage, could not follow what Jesus said about being born again. And in the chapter where Jesus has said that salvation is from the Jews, Samaritans are the first to confess a Jew as the Saviour of the world.

Does Savior of the world mean that everyone will be saved? No. It means that Jesus is not the Saviour of Jews only but of Samaritans and Gentiles too, of all who believe, as these Samaritans did. John uses the same title in his letter (1 John 4:14), and Paul calls God the Saviour of all people, especially of those who believe (1 Timothy 4:10). The title speaks of the scope of the offer and the reach of his rule, not of universal salvation.

What if my faith is still borrowed? That is where this whole town started, and where most people start: a parent, a minister, a book. It is a good place to begin and a poor place to remain, because a second-hand faith is only as durable as the person it leans on, and people move away, disappoint and die. The remedy is the one the Samaritans found: hear him for yourself. Read the Gospels as his own words to you, pray to him directly, and sit under the preaching of his word asking him, not the preacher, to speak.

For worship. Caesar claimed the title and is dust; Christ bears it and reigns for ever. One day a great multitude no one can number will stand before his throne and cry that salvation belongs to our God and to the Lamb, and among them will be a town from Samaria and a woman whose name we never learned.

parallels.desc: the Father has sent his Son to be the Savior of the world

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 43–54 — The Official's Son: The Second Sign
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After two days Jesus goes on to Galilee, where the people welcome him because of what they saw him do in Jerusalem. At Cana a royal official from Capernaum begs him to come and heal his dying son. Jesus speaks of a faith that must see signs, then tells the man to go: his son will live. The man believes and goes, his servants meet him with the news, and the timing shows that the fever left at the hour Jesus spoke. He and his household believe. This is the second sign at Cana.
verseByVerse.theology:
The second sign shows faith that believes the word of Jesus before any visible confirmation. In this Gospel faith grows from believing because of signs, to believing his word, to believing in the crucified and risen Lord himself, and each stage is a step deeper into trust in his person.

The two numbered Cana signs (2:11; 4:54) frame everything between them. At the wedding Jesus was present; here he is twenty miles away and only speaks. That is the position of every reader after the ascension: no touch, no visible presence, only his word, and John wrote it down so that people who were never in the room might believe (20:30–31).
verseByVerse.examples:
The official believed before he saw. Everything he came for, Jesus coming down to the house, was refused, and he went home with five words about a child who had been at the point of death when he left. That is the pattern of mature faith: not the absence of evidence, but trust in the word of the one who cannot lie, before the confirming experience comes.

His prayer was not eloquent: one sentence, repeated under pressure. It was answered at once and generously, and nothing suggests Jesus was waiting for a better-formed request. And the answer was not smaller than he asked: the same answer, delivered without the twenty miles.

verseByVerse.quote: After the two days he departed for Galilee. (For Jesus himself had testified that a prophet has no honor in his own hometown.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
No honour in his own country. There is a genuine puzzle in this aside. The proverb says a prophet has no honour in his own country, and John then reports that Jesus went to Galilee, where the Galileans welcomed him. The reason given seems to contradict what follows.

Two solutions. The first is that his own country here means Judea, the land of his birth, and Jerusalem, where he has just been rejected: the temple authorities demanding his credentials, the Pharisees counting his disciples. On this reading the sentence explains why he left Judea. The prophet has no honour where he properly belongs, so he goes north. It also fits John’s habit of using his own for the people who should have received him and did not (1:11). The second is that the welcome in Galilee was no honour at all, and John says as much in the next verse: they welcomed him having seen what he did in Jerusalem. That is enthusiasm for a performer. A prophet is not honoured by a crowd that has come for the signs; he is merely popular, which is a different and less durable thing. The first is the more likely, since John has just shown Jesus rejected in Jerusalem and Galilee does in fact welcome him. Either way the verse does the same work. It casts a shadow over the applause before the applause arrives, so that the reader does not mistake the noise in Galilee for something better than the silence in Judea.

Being liked and being believed. They are not the same, and the first can be an obstacle to the second. A church well thought of in its town is not a bad thing, but it does not prove that the town believes. The Galileans were delighted with him, and chapter 6 will show how long that lasted.

Should I expect rejection from those closest to me? Often, yes, and it should not surprise you. Jesus’ own brothers did not believe in him for a long time (7:5), and he warned that a person’s enemies may be those of his own household (Matthew 10:36). Familiarity can breed a kind of deafness: they knew you before, and find it hard to take seriously what has changed. Keep living faithfully and lovingly among them, speak when there is opportunity, and pray. Jesus’ brothers were in the upper room after the resurrection (Acts 1:14).

verseByVerse.quote: So when he came to Galilee, the Galileans welcomed him, having seen all that he had done in Jerusalem at the feast. For they too had gone to the feast.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Galileans welcomed him. Because of his signs in Jerusalem at the feast (2:23), not because of who he was. This is the sign-faith John introduced at 2:23–25: real as a beginning, insufficient as a foundation.

Set the two receptions side by side. John has arranged them to be compared, and the comparison is uncomfortable. The Samaritans had no signs; no healing or wonder is recorded in that village. They had a woman with a complicated history, one sentence about being known, and two days of listening to him, and they arrived at the Saviour of the world, believing because of his word (v. 41). The Galileans had everything else. They were his own people. They had been up to Jerusalem and seen the signs with their own eyes. They welcomed him warmly. And what they had was an appetite for signs, which he names in a moment (v. 48) and which chapter 6 will test to destruction: after the bread and the fish, many of his disciples turned back and no longer walked with him (6:66).

What separates them. Not information or privilege, but what they were looking for when they came. Spiritual sight is not proportional to religious advantage.

Warm approval with nothing underneath. This is for ourselves rather than for somebody else, because the Galileans are much the easier group to belong to. They were not sceptics or opponents. They were fans. They were pleased he had come, spoke well of him, and turned out when he was in the area. The most dangerous position in this chapter is not hostility. It is warm approval with nothing underneath it. If you wonder whether that describes you, take heart: fans do not lose sleep over whether they truly love him. The concern is itself a sign of life, and the remedy is not anxious self-examination but looking again at Christ.

Is it wrong to come to Jesus because of what he can do for me? It is not wrong to begin there; most of us did, and Jesus welcomed the sick, the hungry and the desperate. The problem is staying there. Faith that wants only his gifts will leave when the gifts seem to stop. Saving faith comes to rest on Christ himself, as Lord and Saviour, and trusts him even when he gives nothing visible. If you came for help, keep coming, and ask him to show you himself, until you would want him even with nothing else.

verseByVerse.quote: So he came again to Cana in Galilee, where he had made the water wine. And at Capernaum there was an official whose son was ill. When this man heard that Jesus had come from Judea to Galilee, he went to him and asked him to come down and heal his son, for he was at the point of death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Cana again. The site of the first sign, and this will be the second (v. 54): John is framing these chapters between two signs at Cana. The Samaritan woman was not looking for Jesus, and he found her; this man comes looking for Jesus and will be given only a word.

An official. A royal official (basilikos), probably serving Herod Antipas: a court appointment, a household, standing. Capernaum lies on the lakeshore; Cana is up in the hills, about twenty miles away, a hard day’s walk and a climb.

He went to him. A courtier left a dying child and travelled all day into the hills on the strength of a report, to beg a travelling teacher to come. Nothing about it is dignified. Every door his rank could open had already been opened; when a man of standing goes personally rather than sending a servant, everything he normally relies on has failed.

Come down. He needs Jesus present. Everything he has seen work, physicians, officials, favours, requires the person to be in the room. He is not lacking faith; he is exercising the only kind he has.

Is this the same as the centurion’s servant in Matthew and Luke? Probably not (Matthew 8:5–13; Luke 7:1–10). Here it is a royal official’s son, at Cana, and the man asks Jesus to come down; there it is a Gentile centurion’s servant, at Capernaum, and the centurion says he is not worthy to have Jesus come under his roof. The likeness is in the healing from a distance, which Jesus did more than once.

Is it wrong to ask God to come and be present in my crisis? Not at all. Many people pray exactly like this: Lord, be in the room at the operation, come to my son. It is what a person asks when they love somebody and are frightened, and the psalms are full of such prayers. What this story does is not rebuke the request but enlarge it. The answer, when it comes, is not smaller than he asked. It is the same answer, delivered without the twenty miles. Christ is not limited by where he is, and by his Spirit he is present with his people everywhere.
verseByVerse.note: The official was probably in the service of Herod Antipas. Capernaum lay down by the lake, about 20 miles from Cana.

parallels.desc: a similar healing of a centurion’s servant

verseByVerse.quote: So Jesus said to him, "Unless you see signs and wonders you will not believe."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Unless you see signs. The you is plural. Jesus is not turning on a frantic father but speaking over his head to the Galileans in general (v. 45), who came out to see whether there would be more signs. The rebuke is aimed mainly at them, not at him.

What was it for? It is a hard thing to have said in one’s hearing when one’s child is dying, and it is worth asking why Jesus said it. The clue is what happens next. Jesus does not, in the end, give this man a sign he can see. He gives him a sentence. The point of verse 48 is that the man is about to be asked to do what the crowd will not: take a word and go, with nothing in his hands. The apparent rebuke sets up the test, and Jesus is testing the official’s faith: will he believe without seeing? The father passes within two verses.

Then are miracles bad for faith? No. John records Jesus’ signs precisely so that we may believe (20:30–31), and Jesus appeals to his works as evidence (10:38; 14:11). Signs are good when they point us to Christ and lead us to trust his word. The weakness Jesus exposes is a faith that will believe only if it keeps seeing: faith in the spectacle rather than in the one who performs it. The signs were given once for all and are written down for us. We do not need fresh ones to believe; we need to believe what has been written.

In everyday life. There is relief here for anyone who has prayed badly under pressure. When something is genuinely at stake, the words go, the composure goes, and what is left is a single sentence repeated. This chapter records such a prayer word for word, and records that it was answered at once and generously. Nothing suggests Jesus was waiting for a better-formed request. He hears the stammered prayer of a frightened parent as clearly as the psalms of the saints.
verseByVerse.note: The “you” here is plural: Jesus speaks to the Galileans in general.

verseByVerse.quote: The official said to him, "Sir, come down before my child dies." Jesus said to him, "Go; your son will live." The man believed the word that Jesus spoke to him and went on his way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before my child dies. It is not an argument. He does not defend his motives or engage with the theology of signs; he says it again. And the word for his son is a diminutive, paidion: my little boy. The rank has fallen off the man entirely.

Go; your son will live. Five words: no journey, no touch, no prayer, no condition attached. The man asked him to come down, and Jesus declines and answers anyway, from twenty miles away.

The man believed the word. He came for one thing, to bring Jesus down to the house, and is sent home without him, with only a sentence about a child who was at the point of death when he left. This is the faith Jesus looks for: believing his word, without a sign.

He went on his way. He did not wait for proof. That is the miracle in this verse, and it happens before the other one is known about. He had no evidence of any kind. There was no way to send word ahead or to hear anything until he arrived, and the arriving would take the rest of that day and into the next. The whole journey home was made on the strength of five words, and every hour of it the alternative explanation was available to him: that he had been fobbed off, that he should have insisted, that a real healer would have come. This is what it looks like when a promise is the only thing in a person’s hands. Not the absence of fear, for there is no reason to think he was calm, but the willingness to act as though the word were true while everything visible is unchanged and the clock is running.

Does this mean that a parent with enough faith can secure healing for a sick child? No. This was a particular word from Jesus to this man: your son will live. We have no such word about every illness, and the faith he commends is trust in what Christ has said, not confidence that he will do what we ask. A parent whose child was not healed did not fail to believe enough. Jesus wept at the grave of a friend he loved (11:35), and his promise to his people is not that no child will die, but that whoever believes in him, though he die, yet shall he live (11:25).

What has Christ actually promised me, then? Far more than one healing. He has promised that whoever comes to him he will never cast out (6:37), that he will never leave nor forsake his people (Hebrews 13:5), that nothing can separate them from God’s love (Romans 8:38–39), that he will raise them on the last day (6:40), and that he is preparing a place for them (14:2–3). These are words as certain as the one spoken at Cana. Faith takes them and walks home on them, often long before the evidence arrives.

Is the official’s faith just wishful thinking? No. Wishful thinking trusts a feeling; this man trusted a person and a sentence, and the sentence could be checked, which is exactly what he did the next day when he asked the hour (v. 52). Faith in the Bible is not believing without reasons. It is resting on someone who has shown himself trustworthy, and staying on his word while the evidence is not yet in. Its strength lies in its object: a weak faith in a reliable Christ saves, and a strong faith in the wrong thing does not.

For worship. His word is enough. The Word who was in the beginning speaks, and it is done. A father turned his back on the healer he had come to fetch and went home with a sentence, and the sentence was worth more than the visit. The grass withers and the flower fades, but the word that sent a man down the hill from Cana stands for ever.

parallels.desc: he sent out his word and healed them

verseByVerse.quote: As he was going down, his servants met him and told him that his son was recovering.
verseByVerse.commentary:
His servants met him. On the road, the next day (v. 52): somebody in that household was so relieved they set off to shorten the wait.

Recovering. Literally, was living: the very word Jesus had used. They think they are reporting an ordinary recovery: the fever has turned.

How God’s answers usually arrive. Not with a label on them. The feared thing does not happen, and from outside it looks like an ordinary good outcome. The father is about to ask one question that turns a recovery into a revelation, and it is a matter of fact: when?

How can I tell whether something was an answer to prayer or just coincidence? Often you cannot prove it, and you do not need to. Scripture teaches that God governs all things, including the ordinary course of events (Matthew 10:29–30), so the recovery that looks natural is still his gift. But it is worth doing what this father did: go back and check. Note what you prayed for and when, and notice what happened. Over time a pattern of God’s faithfulness becomes plain. Give thanks for every mercy without needing to label it a miracle; all good gifts come from above (James 1:17).

verseByVerse.quote: So he asked them the hour when he began to get better, and they said to him, "Yesterday at the seventh hour the fever left him." The father knew that was the hour when Jesus had said to him, "Your son will live." And he himself believed, and all his household.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He asked them the hour. The ESV notes that the seventh hour was about 1 p.m. And one word is easy to read past: yesterday. Capernaum is more than an afternoon’s walk, so unless yesterday means after sunset, when a Jewish day began, the father spent a night on the way. Many see in that a quiet sign of faith, since a man still frightened for his son would hardly have stopped. It is a likely reading, not a certain one.

That was the hour. The hour the fever broke is the hour the words were spoken, twenty miles away. Nothing had touched the boy and nothing had been sent. Not coincidence. The one through whom the fever and the boy and every mile between them had been made simply spoke, and the distance turned out not to matter, because it never had. He does not have to be near a thing to reach it. He is the reason it is there.

He himself believed. A second time. The first (v. 50) was trust in a promise about his son; now John says simply that he believed, and in this Gospel that means trusting Christ himself. Faith in a healer has become faith in his word, and then in him.

All his household. The first household conversion in John (compare Acts 16:15, 34). Not a formula or a guarantee. But consider what they had to go on: a boy who was well, and a father who could tell them the hour.

What if my household has not believed? Then this verse must not be used to reproach you. Plenty of faithful people have households that have not followed, and Jesus himself warned that families would be divided over him (Luke 12:51–53). Salvation is God’s gift, and each person must believe for himself. What this verse does give is hope and a pattern: pray for your whole household by name, live the faith visibly before them, and tell them plainly what Christ has done. God delights to save families, and he is not finished with yours.

Does the household believing support baptising whole households, including infants? Here the household believed; John says so. That is the pattern this commentary takes throughout the New Testament: those who were baptised, or counted as believers, were those who heard and believed (Acts 16:32–34; 18:8). Our paedobaptist brothers, who baptise the infants of believers, read the household passages differently and see in them the covenant inclusion of children, and they hold that view with deep conviction and care for their children’s souls. We honour them as brothers. But this verse, at least, describes a household of believers.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the seventh hour was about 1 p.m.

parallels.desc: he believed, with his entire household

verseByVerse.quote: This was now the second sign that Jesus did when he had come from Judea to Galilee.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second sign. John counts, and then stops; the numbering never resumes. The count ties the two Cana signs together: both at Cana, both after a journey north, both ending in belief (2:11; 4:53).

A frame around the chapters. Between Cana and Cana a member of the ruling council cannot understand the plainest thing, and a Samaritan woman understands enough to fetch a town. The man with everything missed it, the woman with nothing did not, and a royal official closes the section believing on a word alone.

What changes between the first sign and the second. At the wedding he was present and gave an instruction to servants standing there. Here he is twenty miles away and only speaks, and the voice works across a day’s journey as if the journey were not there.

Why does this matter for me? Because this is the position of everyone who follows Christ after the ascension. We are the man on the road home: no touch, no visible presence, no sign before our eyes, only his word and a distance and the walking. The second sign goes further than the first: it rests on a word alone. And John says at the end of his Gospel that he wrote these signs down so that people who were never in the room might believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and have life in his name (20:30–31). That is, so that there could go on being men and women walking home on nothing but his sentence, and finding that the fever had gone at the hour it was spoken.

For worship. Each of Jesus’ signs reveals who he is: the Lord of creation who turned water into wine, the Lord of life who drives out death with a word. The glory that shone at the wedding shone again in a sickroom he never entered. And the same voice will one day speak at every grave, and all who are in the tombs will hear it and come out. Blessed be the Word made flesh, whose glory is full of grace and truth.

parallels.desc: the first sign

4.title: The Woman at the Well
4.text: <sup>1</sup>Now when Jesus learned that the Pharisees had heard that Jesus was making and baptizing more disciples than John<sup>2</sup>(although Jesus himself did not baptize, but only his disciples),<sup>3</sup>he left Judea and departed again for Galilee.<sup>4</sup>And he had to pass through Samaria.<sup>5</sup>So he came to a town of Samaria called Sychar, near the field that Jacob had given to his son Joseph.<sup>6</sup>Jacob’s well was there; so Jesus, wearied as he was from his journey, was sitting beside the well. It was about the sixth hour.<sup>7</sup>A woman from Samaria came to draw water. Jesus said to her, “Give me a drink.”<sup>8</sup>(For his disciples had gone away into the city to buy food.)<sup>9</sup>The Samaritan woman said to him, “How is it that you, a Jew, ask for a drink from me, a woman of Samaria?” (For Jews have no dealings with Samaritans.)<sup>10</sup>Jesus answered her, “If you knew the gift of God, and who it is that is saying to you, ’Give me a drink,’ you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water.”<sup>11</sup>The woman said to him, “Sir, you have nothing to draw water with, and the well is deep. Where do you get that living water?<sup>12</sup>Are you greater than our father Jacob? He gave us the well and drank from it himself, as did his sons and his livestock.”<sup>13</sup>Jesus said to her, “Everyone who drinks of this water will be thirsty again,<sup>14</sup>but whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never be thirsty again. The water that I will give him will become in him a spring of water welling up to eternal life.”<sup>15</sup>The woman said to him, “Sir, give me this water, so that I will not be thirsty or have to come here to draw water.”<sup>16</sup>Jesus said to her, “Go, call your husband, and come here.”<sup>17</sup>The woman answered him, “I have no husband.” Jesus said to her, “You are right in saying, ’I have no husband’;<sup>18</sup>for you have had five husbands, and the one you now have is not your husband. What you have said is true.”<sup>19</sup>The woman said to him, “Sir, I perceive that you are a prophet.<sup>20</sup>Our fathers worshiped on this mountain, but you say that in Jerusalem is the place where people ought to worship.”<sup>21</sup>Jesus said to her, “Woman, believe me, the hour is coming when neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem will you worship the Father.<sup>22</sup>You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know, for salvation is from the Jews.<sup>23</sup>But the hour is coming, and is now here, when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, for the Father is seeking such people to worship him.<sup>24</sup>God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth.”<sup>25</sup>The woman said to him, “I know that Messiah is coming (he who is called Christ). When he comes, he will tell us all things.”<sup>26</sup>Jesus said to her, “I who speak to you am he.”<sup>27</sup>Just then his disciples came back. They marveled that he was talking with a woman, but no one said, “What do you seek?” or, “Why are you talking with her?”<sup>28</sup>So the woman left her water jar and went away into town and said to the people,<sup>29</sup>“Come, see a man who told me all that I ever did. Can this be the Christ?”<sup>30</sup>They went out of the town and were coming to him.<sup>31</sup>Meanwhile the disciples were urging him, saying, “Rabbi, eat.”<sup>32</sup>But he said to them, “I have food to eat that you do not know about.”<sup>33</sup>So the disciples said to one another, “Has anyone brought him something to eat?”<sup>34</sup>Jesus said to them, “My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work.<sup>35</sup>Do you not say, ’There are yet four months, then comes the harvest’? Look, I tell you, lift up your eyes, and see that the fields are white for harvest.<sup>36</sup>Already the one who reaps is receiving wages and gathering fruit for eternal life, so that sower and reaper may rejoice together.<sup>37</sup>For here the saying holds true, ’One sows and another reaps.’<sup>38</sup>I sent you to reap that for which you did not labor. Others have labored, and you have entered into their labor.”<sup>39</sup>Many Samaritans from that town believed in him because of the woman’s testimony, “He told me all that I ever did.”<sup>40</sup>So when the Samaritans came to him, they asked him to stay with them, and he stayed there two days.<sup>41</sup>And many more believed because of his word.<sup>42</sup>They said to the woman, “It is no longer because of what you said that we believe, for we have heard for ourselves, and we know that this is indeed the Savior of the world.”<sup>43</sup>After the two days he departed for Galilee.<sup>44</sup>(For Jesus himself had testified that a prophet has no honor in his own hometown.)<sup>45</sup>So when he came to Galilee, the Galileans welcomed him, having seen all that he had done in Jerusalem at the feast. For they too had gone to the feast.<sup>46</sup>So he came again to Cana in Galilee, where he had made the water wine. And at Capernaum there was an official whose son was ill.<sup>47</sup>When this man heard that Jesus had come from Judea to Galilee, he went to him and asked him to come down and heal his son, for he was at the point of death.<sup>48</sup>So Jesus said to him, “Unless you see signs and wonders you will not believe.”<sup>49</sup>The official said to him, “Sir, come down before my child dies.”<sup>50</sup>Jesus said to him, “Go; your son will live.” The man believed the word that Jesus spoke to him and went on his way.<sup>51</sup>As he was going down, his servants met him and told him that his son was recovering.<sup>52</sup>So he asked them the hour when he began to get better, and they said to him, “Yesterday at the seventh hour the fever left him.”<sup>53</sup>The father knew that was the hour when Jesus had said to him, “Your son will live.” And he himself believed, and all his household.<sup>54</sup>This was now the second sign that Jesus did when he had come from Judea to Galilee.
4.overview:
Chapter 3 showed Jesus with a respected Jewish teacher at night; chapter 4 shows him with an unnamed Samaritan woman at noon. Tired and thirsty at Jacob’s well, he asks her for a drink, crossing the barriers of race, sex and religion at once, and offers her living water, a spring of eternal life within. He gently brings her history into the light, answers her question about where to worship with the news that the Father now seeks worshippers in spirit and truth, and tells her plainly that he is the Messiah.

She leaves her water jar and brings her town, and many Samaritans believe, first through her word and then through his, and confess him as the Saviour of the world. Back in Cana a royal official begs Jesus to come and heal his dying son; Jesus only speaks, the man believes and goes, and the fever leaves at that very hour. Together the stories show the gospel crossing every boundary, and faith growing from hearing about him to trusting his word.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–18 — The Healing at the Pool of Bethesda
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A healing at the pool of Bethesda, given to a man who did not ask and did not know who healed him, becomes a dispute about the Sabbath, and the dispute becomes the first plot against Jesus’ life. His answer, that his Father is working and so is he, is heard rightly as a claim to be equal with God.
verseByVerse.theology:
The opposition shows what Jesus was claiming. When he defends his Sabbath work by appeal to his Father’s, the leaders understand him to claim equality with God, and he does not correct them; the discourse that follows explains the claim rather than withdrawing it. Teachers of the day already agreed that God keeps working on the seventh day, giving life and judging, and Jesus goes on to claim exactly those two works (vv. 21–22).

Those who wanted him dead were not offended by his ethics; they understood him to be saying that God was his own Father in a way true of no one else.
verseByVerse.examples:
The healing shows how grace comes: the man did not ask, did not know who Jesus was, and showed no faith before he was healed.

Jesus’ question, whether he wants to be healed, speaks to anyone who long ago stopped asking God for something, and invites us to bring it to him plainly. And the mat carried through the city is a reminder that grace received is meant to be seen, not left discreetly at the pool.

verseByVerse.quote: After this there was a feast of the Jews, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem. Now there is in Jerusalem by the Sheep Gate a pool, in Aramaic called Bethesda, which has five roofed colonnades.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. John 5 is a turning point. A Sabbath healing, given unasked to a man with no recorded faith, leads to the first plot against Jesus’ life, because the leaders rightly hear him making himself equal with God. A man who could do nothing was made whole; the best-taught men in the nation had every witness and would not come.

A feast of the Jews. Unnamed; perhaps Pentecost, Tabernacles or Purim. John normally names the feasts, so we cannot date the chapter precisely.

By the Sheep Gate. The Sheep Gate was in the north wall, near the temple (Nehemiah 3:1), and its name suggests it was where sheep for sacrifice were brought in. The healing happens beside the gate of the sacrificial lambs, in the presence of the Lamb of God.

A pool, in Aramaic called Bethesda. The ESV notes other spellings in the manuscripts (Bethzatha, Bethsaida). Bethesda may mean house of mercy: a colonnade full of blind, lame and paralysed people waiting for water that mostly did not come. That was either the bitterest name in Jerusalem or a prophecy, and on this day it turned out to be the second: the house of disappointment became what its name had promised, because the Lord of mercy himself had come to it.

Which has five roofed colonnades. For a long time this description was treated as proof that the writer did not know Jerusalem: a four-sided pool needs four colonnades, not five, and no such structure was known. Then it was dug up. Excavations near the Church of St Anne uncovered a double pool north of the temple, with colonnades on the four outer sides and a fifth across the partition between them, though details of the layout are still debated. The writer knew the city in a detail that was later lost. That does not prove the miracle, and it should not be overstated, but it removes a confident objection. And has is present tense, which may suggest John wrote before AD 70, or may simply describe the scene vividly.

Does archaeology prove the Bible true? It cannot prove the miracles or the gospel; those rest on the testimony of God in his word, received by faith through the Spirit. But archaeology has again and again confirmed the Bible’s places, names and details, and has often embarrassed confident critics, as it did here. That matters. Christianity is not a set of timeless ideas detached from history; it stands or falls on real events in real places. When the details John mentions in passing turn out to be accurate, it is a reasonable confirmation that he is telling the truth about the larger things as well.
verseByVerse.note: The Sheep Gate was in the north wall, near the temple. The ESV notes that some manuscripts read Bethsaida. Archaeologists have uncovered twin pools there with colonnades on four sides and one across the middle.

parallels.desc: the Sheep Gate

verseByVerse.quote: In these lay a multitude of invalids — blind, lame, and paralyzed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A multitude of invalids. Paralysed is literally withered. They are the very conditions Isaiah promised would be reversed when God came: then shall the lame man leap like a deer (Isaiah 35:5–6), and the ones Jesus listed for the Baptist: the blind see, the lame walk (Matthew 11:4–5). These are exactly the people the promised Messiah was to heal, and the colonnade is full of those still waiting.

He walks into it. The Son of God, in a city full of holy places, spent part of a feast day where untreated suffering was most concentrated. Where suffering gathers, he does not withdraw.

Textual note. The ESV notes that some manuscripts, followed by the KJV and NKJV, add the end of verse 3 (waiting for the moving of the water) and verse 4, about an angel who stirred the water, so that the first person to step in was healed. It is missing from the earliest and best manuscripts and was probably added to explain verse 7, reflecting popular belief. That is why the verse numbers jump from 3 to 5. Some think the pool was fed by an intermittent spring that bubbled up, which people believed had healing power. Nothing is lost by its absence: the man trusted the water and its legend; Jesus ignored the water entirely and healed with a word.

Does a missing verse mean the Bible is unreliable? No. We have thousands of manuscripts of the New Testament, far more and far earlier than for any other ancient book, and comparing them lets scholars see clearly where a later copyist added a note. Modern Bibles are open about these places, as the ESV is here. No doctrine of the faith depends on a disputed verse. The very fact that we can identify such additions shows how well God has preserved his word.

A mercy for the quickest. Whatever was true about that water, the belief around it had a cruel shape: whoever gets in first is healed. It was a mercy available to the quickest, the people who needed it least, and closed to the man who had been there longest. Jesus does not touch the water, carry the man to it or make him first. He heals him where he lies, and the whole business of stirred water and racing to it no longer matters. That is the difference between a mercy you have to qualify for and a mercy that comes to where you are.

In everyday life. Every town has its colonnade: the care home, the hospital ward, the street where people sleep. The people there are not a problem to be managed but the very ones Jesus walked towards, and his servants find, often to their surprise, that he is already there.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 4, about an angel stirring the water and the first one in being healed, a popular belief explaining why the sick waited there.

verseByVerse.quote: One man was there who had been an invalid for thirty-eight years. When Jesus saw him lying there and knew that he had already been there a long time, he said to him, "Do you want to be healed?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
An invalid for thirty-eight years. It is longer than many people lived then. If he was struck down at twenty, he is nearly sixty, and he has spent his whole adult life on a mat beside a pool, watching other people get well. The number may echo Israel’s thirty-eight years in the wilderness (Deuteronomy 2:14), but John does not say so, and the link is better held loosely.

When Jesus saw him. Out of the multitude, Jesus chose this one; the man did not ask. Why this man? John does not explain. Grace is sovereign: God gives his kindness freely, as he chooses, not as a wage for anything he finds in us (Romans 9:16). And Jesus knew that he had already been there a long time, without being told (2:25).

Do you want to be healed? The strangest thing Jesus says in the chapter. To a man who has lain beside a healing pool for thirty-eight years it sounds almost like an insult. Of course he wants it. And yet Jesus does not ask this of everyone he heals, so it is meant for this man and this history. Something happens to a want that has been disappointed for thirty-eight years. It does not stay a clean, sharp thing. It goes quiet, gets managed, and turns into a routine: the same spot, the same hours, the same near misses, until the waiting is the life. That is not weakness of character; it is what happens to human beings, and it happens fast. Perhaps he had given up hope, or grown used to his condition and the life of a beggar. Healing would mean new responsibilities. So the question is not cruel. It is the most respectful thing in the passage. Jesus wakes him to desire. He asks a man who has not been asked anything in decades what he actually wants.

What if I have stopped hoping for something? This question is for you too: the marriage that has been like this for years, the child who does not call, the sin confessed so often the confessing has gone hollow, the prayer abandoned around the fifth year of praying it. The question is not a rebuke for having stopped hoping. It is an invitation to say aloud what would be different if God moved, which is harder than it looks. God may answer as you ask, or differently, or in his own time; but he invites you to bring the desire to him honestly rather than bury it. Hope in God is never foolish, even when hope in the circumstance has worn thin.
verseByVerse.note: Thirty-eight years may echo Israel’s thirty-eight years of wandering before entering the land (Deut 2:14), though John does not draw the link.

parallels.desc: thirty-eight years until that generation perished

verseByVerse.quote: The sick man answered him, "Sir, I have no one to put me into the pool when the water is stirred up, and while I am going another steps down before me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sir, I have no one. The loneliest words in the chapter. What he names as his problem is not his legs. It is that in thirty-eight years, in a colonnade full of people, at the season of a feast, nobody had stayed close enough to put him in the water. The Greek is bare: a man I do not have. The paralytic in Mark had four friends (Mark 2:3); this man had none. He is surrounded by people and alone, a common kind of alone.

Another steps down before me. He has tried, more times than he could count, and every time someone quicker got in first. Thirty-eight years of nearly.

He does not answer the question. Asked whether he wants to be well, he describes the system and his place at the bottom of it. Not one word is untrue and not one word is an answer: after thirty-eight years his hope has shrunk to an explanation of why nothing can change. He does not know who is speaking to him (v. 13); his hope is in the water. He is talking to the answer while explaining why there isn’t one.

Why does Jesus heal someone who showed no faith? Because grace does not wait for us to be ready. This healing is a picture of how God saves: not because we reached the water first, or had the right friends, or even knew who he was, but because Christ came to us and spoke. Faith is the hand that receives Christ, and God gives that hand too (Ephesians 2:8). In this man’s case the healing came first and the knowing later. That should encourage you to pray for people who seem to have no faith at all. Christ can begin where there is nothing.
