For worship. When there was no man to help, the Son of Man came, the friend of the friendless, the one who stays when everyone else has stepped down before us. He was himself forsaken by all his friends, so that no one who trusts him need ever say again, I have no one.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to him, "Get up, take up your bed, and walk." And at once the man was healed, and he took up his bed and walked. Now that day was the Sabbath.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Get up, take up your bed, and walk. Three commands, all impossible, given before there is any evidence that he can obey. Take up your bed: the word is krabattos, a poor man’s mat, the pallet a beggar rolls under his arm. His word gives the power to obey. No pool, no stirring, no help needed.

At once. After thirty-eight years, instantly, with no touch and no prayer: grace arriving unrequested at a man who had given up asking, which is why Bethesda has so often been read as a picture of the gospel.

The mat. A healed man walking away is a private mercy. A healed man carrying his bed through the city is a public claim, the evidence held up in both arms. Jesus tells him to carry the mat, on the Sabbath, in Jerusalem, at a feast, past the authorities. That is deliberate, and the rest of the chapter follows from it.

Now that day was the Sabbath. John withholds it until after the healing, so that the reader feels the joy first and the objection second. Jesus knew what day it was, and his answer in verse 17 shows he chose it.

Must Christians, then, keep the Sabbath? Christians differ here, and both views are held by faithful believers. Many Reformed Christians, following the Westminster Confession, hold that the fourth commandment still binds, the day of rest now kept on the Lord’s Day, the first day of the week, and kept with joy as a day for worship and works of mercy (Westminster 21.7–8). (The 1689 London Baptist Confession says the same, 22.7–8.) Others read the Sabbath as fulfilled in Christ, the true rest (Hebrews 4:9–10), so that no day binds the conscience (Colossians 2:16–17; Romans 14:5–6), while still gathering gladly on the first day, the day of resurrection. This commentary’s view: the second fits the New Testament best: the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, and the Lord’s Day is a gift, gladly set apart for worship, fellowship and rest, not the fourth commandment moved to Sunday, and no one may bind another’s conscience over it. The first view is held by many godly brothers and deserves respect. Both agree with what this passage plainly teaches: the day was never meant to forbid mercy, and Jesus is Lord of it.

In everyday life. It is possible to be genuinely helped by Christ and entirely discreet about it, to leave the mat at the pool. He told this man to pick it up. Is there some evidence of his grace in your life that you have kept out of sight?

For worship. He speaks, and the dead legs stand; he commands, and the thing commanded is done. The word that called the world out of nothing called a withered man off his mat. And he chose the Sabbath, the day of God’s rest, to give a man the first true rest he had known in thirty-eight years.
verseByVerse.note: The bed was a light mat. Carrying a load on the Sabbath was forbidden by tradition, drawing on the prophets.

parallels.desc: a similar command to a paralytic
bear no burden on the Sabbath

verseByVerse.quote: So the Jews said to the man who had been healed, "It is the Sabbath, and it is not lawful for you to take up your bed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the Jews said. In John, the Jews often means the Jewish religious authorities in Jerusalem, not the Jewish people as a whole. Jesus, his disciples and the healed man were all Jews.

Not lawful. The Mishnah, written down around AD 200 but preserving older tradition, lists carrying an object from one domain to another among the thirty-nine kinds of forbidden work (Mishnah Shabbat 7:2).

Be fair to them first. They were not inventing a rule out of nothing. The prophets had been explicit: take care, and do not bear a burden on the Sabbath day or bring it in by the gates of Jerusalem (Jeremiah 17:21–22). Jeremiah names the city and the gates. He was forbidding the traffic of trade on God’s day, loads carried in to be bought and sold (Nehemiah 13:15–19 shows the same abuse); a healed man carrying his own mat home was never what he had in view. These men are standing in that city, watching a man carry a load, and they have a text. So this is not a case of religious people making things up. It is something more uncomfortable and far more common: people applying a real command of God, in a situation it was never written for, and being badly wrong while sounding entirely correct.

Seeing only the rule. Look at what their sentence leaves out. A man who has been paralysed for thirty-eight years is walking through Jerusalem carrying his own bed, and all they have to say is a rule. Not one question about how, not one word to him about what has happened. They see the mat, the mat is against the rules, and the man holding it is invisible. It is what happens when rules become the only thing we see by, so that everything is either kept or broken. A miracle walks past and is processed as an infringement. And there is a reason the heart prefers the rule. Rules you can keep give you a sense of control and of standing before God: you know where you are, and you know you are doing well. A grace that comes unasked to a man who had kept nothing threatens that whole arrangement, because it says that God’s best gift is not earned, and so cannot be earned by us either.

Lord of the day they were guarding. The Sabbath these men were defending was God’s sign of the rest he would give his people, and the giver of that rest had just given it. The one load the man lifts that day is the proof that his real burden has been taken away. The men at the gate see the Sabbath command broken; they are looking at what it pointed to, walking past them on two healed legs.

Does this mean rules do not matter? No. God’s commands are good, and Jesus never broke the law of God. What he exposed was a way of handling God’s law that loses sight of its purpose: love for God and neighbour (Matthew 22:37–40). The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath (Mark 2:27). The problem was not that they cared about obedience, but that they cared about their reading of a rule more than about the man in front of them and the God who had just healed him. Keep God’s commands; but never let your system of applying them blind you to his mercy.

In everyday life. Think of the last time something happened in a Christian setting outside your expectations: a convert with a chaotic life, someone doing good work with theology you would want to correct. What was your first reaction? Discernment is a duty. But these men’s first reaction was a rule, and the second, joy at what God had done, never came.
verseByVerse.note: In John, “the Jews” often means the Jewish religious authorities.

verseByVerse.quote: But he answered them, "The man who healed me, that man said to me, 'Take up your bed, and walk.'" They asked him, "Who is the man who said to you, 'Take up your bed and walk'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man who healed me. His logic is sound: someone with the power to end thirty-eight years of paralysis with a word plainly has standing to say what may be carried and when. That is not an evasion but an argument. What he lacks is a name.

Who is the man who said to you? Read the two sentences side by side and see what each party seizes on. He says: the man who healed me. They say: the man who said to you. They repeat his sentence with the healing surgically removed. Not who healed you, but who told you to break the rule. They are not interested in the miracle, only the offence. They have edited it out on the spot, which is how an inconvenient fact gets dropped from a discussion.

The right question for the wrong reason. Yet who is the man? is the question this whole Gospel exists to answer. They ask it to identify a suspect. But they ask it.

Be gentle with the healed man. He has had his legs for perhaps an hour, does not know who healed him, and is questioned by the most powerful men in the city about a rule he broke because he was told to. People are often hard on him for later naming Jesus to the authorities, and some of it may be fair. But not everyone is at his best in that position.

What do I say when I am challenged about my faith and do not know much yet? Say what you know, as this man did. You may not be able to answer every question, but you can say what has happened to you and who did it. The man born blind in chapter 9 said: one thing I do know, that though I was blind, now I see (9:25). That is enough to begin with. Then go and learn more, so that next time you can say more. And do not be ashamed to say, I do not know the answer to that yet, but I will find out.

For worship. Who is the man? His enemies asked it to name a suspect, and every page of this Gospel answers it: the Word made flesh, the Lamb of God, the Lord who heals. At the last they answered it themselves without knowing, with a title fixed above his head on a cross: Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews (19:19).

verseByVerse.quote: Now the man who had been healed did not know who it was, for Jesus had withdrawn, as there was a crowd in the place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus had withdrawn. Healed without knowing his healer: grace before knowledge. He was gone before a crowd could gather around the miracle, as he will be again (6:15), the opposite of what anyone building a following would do. The Lord does good to those who do not even know his name, and is content to be unrecognised in his kindness. But he does not stay hidden for ever; in the next verse he comes looking.

Set him beside the man born blind. The contrast is deliberate. That man is interrogated by the same authorities and grows sharper with every round, is thrown out of the synagogue, and then, found by Jesus, worships (9:38). This man is asked one question and produces a name. One received his sight, lost his standing and gained Christ. This one received his legs and told the authorities who had done it.

A mercy received is not conversion. The healing did not, as far as we are told, save him. Every physical mercy in the Gospels is real, and none of them is automatically anything more. A marriage restored, a diagnosis reversed, a job that came in time: each may be a genuine gift from God and leave the recipient where they were.

Can someone receive God’s blessings and still not be saved? Yes, sadly. God is kind to all; he sends rain on the just and the unjust (Matthew 5:45), and many received healing from Jesus without following him (Luke 17:17–18). Blessings are meant to lead us to repentance (Romans 2:4), but they do not save by themselves. Only faith in Christ unites us to him. So do not measure your standing with God by your circumstances, good or bad. Ask instead: do I know him, trust him and follow him?

verseByVerse.quote: "Afterward Jesus found him in the temple and said to him, 'See, you are well! Sin no more, that nothing worse may happen to you.' The man went away and told the Jews that it was Jesus who had healed him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus found him. The man had gone to the temple, perhaps to give thanks, walking where for years he could only have been carried. And the finding is deliberate: Jesus had slipped away, and now he goes looking for a man who does not know his face. The healing was the beginning of the errand, not the end. He comes back for people: for the blind man after he is thrown out (9:35), and for Peter on a beach after the denials (21:15).

See, you are well! Jesus does not say all illness is punishment for sin (9:3), but warns this man that sin has worse consequences than paralysis: eternal judgment. And the order matters: the mercy came first, unasked, and the command follows it. He is not told to stop sinning so that he may be helped; he has been helped, and now he must turn from sin. He loves us too well to heal our bodies and leave our souls in danger: his warnings are as much mercy as his miracles.

Am I ill because of something I did? Many readers carry that question quietly for years. John himself settles the general question four chapters on. The disciples see a man born blind and ask who sinned, this man or his parents, and Jesus rejects the premise: neither (9:3). Illness is not a scoreboard. In a world under the curse, bodies fail, and you cannot read a person’s sins off their illness. Job’s friends built a theology on the opposite assumption, and God told them they had not spoken rightly of him (Job 42:7). Sometimes a particular sin does bring particular harm, and then repentance is the path. But you must not assume your suffering is punishment. If you are in Christ, the punishment for your sin was borne at the cross, and whatever you suffer now comes from a Father’s hand.

So what is Jesus saying here? Not that this man’s thirty-eight years were a sentence served, but the thing any of us most needs to hear on the far side of a mercy: there is something worse than thirty-eight years on a mat. He has given the man his legs; now he warns him about his soul, in the temple, where the man has rightly come. Taken at that level the warning stops sounding cruel and becomes kind. Sin is worth abandoning not because it made you ill, but because judgment is real, and the body you have just got back will not last for ever either.

He told the Jews. Why? Perhaps naively, perhaps to protect himself, perhaps as testimony; John does not say, and it is wise not to judge him harshly. But the effect is plain: from then on the authorities pursued Jesus (v. 16).
verseByVerse.note: Jesus does not say all illness is punishment for sin, but warns that sin leads to worse than illness.

parallels.desc: go, and from now on sin no more

verseByVerse.quote: And this was why the Jews were persecuting Jesus, because he was doing these things on the Sabbath. But Jesus answered them, "My Father is working until now, and I am working."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Persecuting Jesus. The tense means they kept on persecuting, and the cause was a pattern, not one incident. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, add here that they sought to kill him; the earliest do not, and John says it in verse 18 anyway.

My Father is working until now. A staggering claim, and sharper than it looks, because it lands inside a debate the rabbis were already having. God rested on the seventh day (Genesis 2:2–3), but Jewish teachers, as rabbinic writings later record, knew that God does not down tools on the seventh day: children are born and people die on the Sabbath, and giving life and judging the dead were the standard examples of divine work that never stops. One recorded answer was that God is exempt: the whole universe is his house, so he may work in his own home on his own day. Jesus takes that exact exemption and applies it to himself. He does not merely argue that mercy is allowed on the Sabbath. He claims for himself the exemption that belongs to God alone, because the work he does is God’s work. And he spends the next dozen verses on those two works: giving life and executing judgment. And my Father: not our Father. A unique relationship.

The rest of God and the work of God. The rest God took on the seventh day was rest from making the world, not from upholding it. Every heartbeat since has been his work. There has not been an hour when God was not sustaining the universe, and the reason anything exists this morning is that he is holding it in being. And Jesus does what the Father does: he holds the stars in their places and a healed man on his feet with the same hand.

Who actually kept the Sabbath that day? Consider what happened. A man who had not stood for thirty-eight years stood. He had spent every seventh day of nearly four decades lying on a mat beside a pool, and on this one he walked home. If any human being in Jerusalem entered into rest that day, it was him. The one accused of breaking the Sabbath is the only person in the story who gave anyone a Sabbath, and the men defending the day spent it drawing up charges. The day was made as a mercy, a weekly memorial of a God who finished his work. To turn it into an instrument for keeping a healed man from carrying his bedding is not strictness. It is a misreading of what the day was for.

Is God really working all the time, even in the boring parts of my life? Yes. My Father is working until now. God does not take weekends off from caring for his creation or his children. He is at work in the dull Tuesday as much as in the dramatic answer to prayer, upholding all things by the word of his power (Hebrews 1:3), working all things for the good of those who love him (Romans 8:28), and completing the good work he began in you (Philippians 1:6). You may not see it. But you are never in a moment that God has left unattended.
verseByVerse.note: Jewish teachers recognised that God keeps working on the Sabbath, sustaining the world; Jesus claims the same right.

parallels.desc: lord even of the Sabbath

verseByVerse.quote: This was why the Jews were seeking all the more to kill him, because not only was he breaking the Sabbath, but he was even calling God his own Father, making himself equal with God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seeking all the more to kill him. The first time John mentions the plot, and the thread runs on through the Gospel (7:1, 19; 8:37; 11:53). He healed a man who had been on the ground for thirty-eight years, and they began to plan his death.

His own Father. His own (idion): personally, in a way no one else could. Jews called God Father collectively, the Father of the nation. To speak of God as one’s own Father, in a way that made his working and God’s working the same working, was a different kind of sentence altogether.

Making himself equal with God. They understood him perfectly. John reports it flatly as what was happening: the narrator agrees with their reading of the words, not with what they did about it. Either Jesus was a blasphemer, or he is God. He does not deny it; the discourse that follows explains it.

The people who understood him best. This closes off one of the most popular ways of handling Jesus: the idea that he was a teacher of ethics whose followers later inflated him into something divine. The people who wanted him dead were the ones who understood him best. They were not offended by his ethics; nobody organises an execution over the golden rule. They killed him for who he said he was, and this verse is where the plot to kill him begins. A sceptic may reply that John wrote late and put the claim in Jesus’ mouth. But the earliest Gospel tells the same story: Mark has the scribes call him a blasphemer for forgiving sins, which only God can do (Mark 2:7), and the high priest condemn him for blasphemy at his trial (Mark 14:61–64).

Two charges, neither right as they put it. He was not breaking the Sabbath, only their reading of it; he never once broke the law of God. And he was not making himself equal with God: he was stating what was already the case, a larger claim altogether.

In the flow. The whole chapter turns on verse 18: everything after it is Jesus’ answer to this one charge, and he does not retract it but unfolds it. John opened by saying that the Word was God (1:1) and will close with Thomas saying, my Lord and my God (20:28); here, halfway between, the enemies of Jesus state the same truth as an accusation.

If Jesus is equal with God, why does he pray to the Father and obey him? Because within the one God there are three persons, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, equal in power and glory, and distinct in how they relate to one another (Westminster Confession 2.3; 1689 London Baptist Confession 2.3). The Son is fully God, and he is also the Son: from all eternity he shares one life, one will and one love with the Father. And in the work of salvation, becoming man, he took the form of a servant, humbled himself, and became obedient to death (Philippians 2:6–8). So his prayers and obedience do not make him less than God. They show us God the Son living out, in our nature, the love and unity he has always shared with the Father.

For worship. The charge sheet, when it was finally drawn up, said that he made himself the Son of God (19:7). It was the only accusation ever brought against him that was true, and true in a sense the prosecution never suspected, since he had not made himself anything. He had come from his Father’s side, and he was on his way back to it by way of the cross they were preparing for him. He claimed equality with God and died for the claim, and the empty tomb was the Father’s verdict that every word of it was true.

parallels.desc: you, being a man, make yourself God

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–47 — The Son's Authority: Witness and Judgment
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus answers the charge. The Son acts in perfect union with the Father; he gives life and will judge, so that all may honour him as they honour the Father. Whoever hears and believes has already passed from death to life, and at the last day all the dead will hear his voice. Then he calls four witnesses, and the trial turns on the accusers.
verseByVerse.theology:
The discourse claims for the Son the two works that belong to God alone, giving life and judging, and the honour that belongs to God alone. No one can honour God while declining Christ. The four witnesses are not offered as proofs that force belief; that the leaders reject them shows the state of their hearts.

The Son has life in himself as the Father does (v. 26): not life on loan, as every creature has it, but his own, with nothing behind it that could fail. That the Father granted it describes the eternal relation of Father and Son, not an event in time. And verse 29 does not teach salvation by works, since verse 24 gives life to whoever hears and believes: the good and evil done are the evidence of a life that had or had not crossed from death to life.
verseByVerse.examples:
The claims of this discourse leave no middle ground: a man who says he will raise the dead and judge the world is either deluded or who he says he is. And the judgment of the last day is already being decided in each person’s response to him now (vv. 24, 28–29).

The chapter also names three ways of being religious without coming to Christ: enjoying a faithful preacher for a while without following where he points (v. 35); studying Scripture as if life were found in the text rather than in the one it points to (v. 39); and living for the approval of one’s own circle rather than the glory that comes from the only God (v. 44).

verseByVerse.quote: "So Jesus said to them, 'Truly, truly, I say to you, the Son can do nothing of his own accord, but only what he sees the Father doing. For whatever the Father does, that the Son does likewise. For the Father loves the Son and shows him all that he himself is doing. And greater works than these will he show him, so that you may marvel.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nothing of his own accord. Not weakness, but unity. Jesus answers the charge of verse 18 not by denying it but by explaining it: the Son never acts independently of the Father. It sounds like a limitation, but it is the strongest claim in the paragraph. Anyone can act independently of God; every one of us does it hourly, and that is what sin is. Only one person can say that he never has, and that everything he does is what he sees the Father doing, continuously and without deviation, which no prophet ever said.

The workshop. There may well be a picture underneath this. In that world a trade passed from father to son by watching: a boy stood in his father’s shop and learned by seeing it done. The claim is both homely and enormous. Then look at what is made in this workshop: raising the dead and judging the world, work that no human being can do.

For whatever the Father does, that the Son does likewise. Whatever: everything, not approximately but exactly. Only one who is God can do everything God does.

The Father loves the Son. The verb here is philei; in 3:35 the same love is agapa, and John uses the two interchangeably. What matters is what that love does: it shows the Son everything and holds nothing back. Before the world was made, the Father loved the Son (17:24), and into that eternal love, by grace, God brings his people: he loves them even as he loved the Son (17:23). And the Father will show him greater works than healing a paralysed man: giving life and judging (vv. 21–22).

Where Christians differ: the Son and the Father. Arians (named after a fourth-century teacher who held that the Son was the first and highest creature) and today Jehovah’s Witnesses read “the Son can do nothing of his own accord” as proof that the Son is inferior to the Father. This commentary’s view: the passage teaches that the Son is equal with the Father in nature and power (he does whatever the Father does, gives life, judges, receives equal honour), while distinct in person and relationship (the Father sends; the Son is sent and obeys). This is the doctrine of the Trinity: one God, three persons, equal in power and glory, distinct in relations (Westminster Shorter Catechism 6).

How can I explain the Trinity simply? Start with what the Bible says, not with an illustration. There is one God (Deuteronomy 6:4). The Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God. The three are not the same person: the Father sends the Son, the Son prays to the Father, the Spirit is sent by both. So God is one in being and three in persons. Most illustrations, water and ice and steam, or one man as father, son and husband, end up teaching an old error, that God is one person wearing three masks. It is better to say plainly: this is beyond us, and it is what God has shown us about himself, and it is the most beautiful truth there is, because it means God has always been love.

In everyday life. You cannot do what the Son does, but in him his Father is your Father, and his Spirit is in you. Before the main decisions of today, stop and ask: what is my Father doing here? Do your work as a child learning in your Father’s workshop.

verseByVerse.quote: "For as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he will. For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Father raises the dead. In the Old Testament, only God gives life to the dead (Deuteronomy 32:39; 1 Samuel 2:6; 2 Kings 5:7).

So also the Son. Having claimed to work as his Father works, Jesus now names the two works that Jewish teachers said God never stops doing, giving life and judging, and claims both. To whom he will: by his sovereign choice, spiritual life now (v. 24) and resurrection life at the last day (v. 29). Christians differ over whether that choice rests on faith God foresees (the debate is set out at 6:37); all agree that no one is saved by merit.

To whom he will. Not to whoever qualifies, not to whoever arrives first at the stirring of the water, which is what had kept the man on the mat on the ground. The first half of this chapter demonstrates that clause. Jesus walked into a colonnade of sick people, healed one, and left, and John offers no account of why that man. A Christ who healed everyone at the pool would be easier to admire and would tell us nothing about how mercy actually comes to anyone. What we have is a man who was not first in the queue, had nobody, and got up and walked, because the Son gives life to whom he will.

All judgment to the Son. The final judgment, which belongs to God alone (Genesis 18:25), is given to the Son (Acts 17:31). Every human being will be judged, and the one who judges is the one who was crucified. The judge’s seat is not held by a stranger to human life. The same hands that were pierced will hold the scales of the last day, and the same voice that told a paralysed man to stand will summon the nations.

But Jesus also says he did not come to judge the world. How do these fit? He says it in 3:17 and 12:47, and in 8:15 he says, I judge no one. These fit together. He came the first time to save, not to condemn; the condemnation already rests on those who reject him (3:18). At the end, all judgment is committed to him, and he will judge (v. 27). And in 8:15 he means that he does not judge as they do, by outward appearance and merely human standards.

If the Son gives life to whom he will, is it unfair to those he passes by? No one has a claim on God’s mercy; if we did, it would not be mercy. All of us are sinners deserving judgment, and God would be perfectly just to leave us all to it. That he chooses to save any is pure grace, and that he saves a great multitude is amazing grace (Romans 9:14–16). And the same Christ who gives life to whom he will freely invites all: whoever comes to me I will never cast out (6:37). No one who wants to come is turned away. If you want Christ, that wanting is itself the sign that he is giving you life.

In everyday life. If you are praying for someone who seems far from God, take heart: the Son gives life to whom he will, and no one is too far gone for his voice.

parallels.desc: I kill and I make alive

verseByVerse.quote: "that all may honor the Son, just as they honor the Father. Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Just as they honor the Father. The phrase just as fixes the measure. It does not mean honour him above every other teacher. It means give him the same kind and the same degree of honour as the Father: worship. God will not give his glory to another (Isaiah 42:8). If the Son is to be honoured just as the Father, the Son is God.

The Father wants his Son honoured. It would be natural to assume that any honour paid to the Son is a detour from the Father. The verse says the reverse: the Father has given life and judgment to the Son precisely so that all may honour the Son. To hold back honour from the Son does not protect the Father’s honour.

Whoever does not honor the Son. This closes every exit. There is no arrangement in which a person keeps God and declines Christ (1 John 2:23). That makes Christianity permanently awkward in polite company, and it is better stated than hedged. Many people believe in God, admire Jesus as a moral teacher, and regard his divinity as a later addition. This verse says that arrangement does not exist, not because Christians are narrow, but because the Son himself refuses to be admired as anything less than God.

Is it right to pray to Jesus and sing to him, or only to the Father? It is right to do both. Ordinarily Christians pray to the Father through the Son by the Spirit, since through Christ we have access in one Spirit to the Father (Ephesians 2:18). But Stephen prayed to the Lord Jesus as he died (Acts 7:59), the first Christians called on the name of the Lord Jesus (1 Corinthians 1:2), and all heaven sings to the Lamb (Revelation 5:12–13). Since the Son is to be honoured just as the Father is, worship offered to him is not misdirected. It is exactly what the Father wants.

In everyday life. Listen to how you speak about Jesus when you are not in church: with colleagues, with family, in an argument. It is easy to slide into speaking of him as a figure of great importance rather than a person to be worshipped. Speak of him today as your Lord.

For worship. The Father has decreed that every knee shall bow to the Son, and to the glory of God the Father (Philippians 2:10–11). Honour given to the Son is never stolen from the Father. There is no praise of Christ that needs holding back in case it overshoots. The man who stood bound before a council and was mocked by soldiers is owed the worship of the universe, and one day he will have it.

parallels.desc: no one who denies the Son has the Father

verseByVerse.quote: "Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life. He does not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life. Truly, truly, I say to you, an hour is coming, and is now here, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Has eternal life. Hearing and believing is the way life is received, and the tense is present: already.

He does not come into judgment. No condemnation (3:18; Romans 8:1). This is the strongest assurance in the chapter: not will be acquitted at the judgment, but will not come into it. The verdict was settled at the cross, where Christ took the condemnation in the believer’s place (Romans 8:3). No accusation can reopen the case, because the Judge has given his verdict, and he gave it at the cost of his own life.

Passed from death to life. Perfect tense: has crossed over, and remains on the other side, from spiritual death (Ephesians 2:1) to eternal life. Not is crossing; not will cross when the accounts are settled. The believer is not a candidate for life awaiting a verdict. He is a person who has already emigrated.

An hour is coming, and is now here. Already happening. These dead are not in graves: they are people walking around Jerusalem, spiritually dead and unaware of it, and some are about to hear a voice and start living. In verse 28 he will not add and is now here, and that hour will involve tombs. Two kinds of rising, one spiritual and now, one bodily and still ahead. The same voice does both.

The dead will hear. As Lazarus would hear his voice and come out of the tomb (11:43), so the spiritually dead hear his voice in the gospel and are made alive (Ephesians 2:4–5). This is regeneration, the new birth of 3:3–8: God giving spiritual life to someone dead toward him, so that he now hears, believes and loves what he once ignored. The dead do not cooperate in being raised.

But Paul says we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ. How can believers not come into judgment? Both are true (2 Corinthians 5:10). The believer does not come into judgment in the sense of condemnation (Romans 8:1); that verdict has been given. But his life and work will be reviewed for reward, and some will suffer loss though they themselves are saved (1 Corinthians 3:12–15).

What if I am frightened of the last day? Then hear this verse as Jesus meant it. There is a way of holding the faith in which the whole thing is provisional: a hope that the balance will come out right in the end, with a private suspicion that it may not. This verse rules that out. If you have heard Christ’s word and believe the Father who sent him, the passing has happened. You will stand before Christ, but as one already acquitted, with your sins carried away by him. What remains for you is not a hearing but a homecoming. Your assurance does not rest on the strength of your feelings, but on the word of the Judge himself.

In everyday life. When you share the gospel with someone, remember whose voice gives life. Your task is to speak his word faithfully; his task is to raise the dead.

parallels.desc: dead in trespasses, made alive

verseByVerse.quote: "For as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself. And he has given him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Life in himself. God is self-existent. He depends on nothing; life is his by nature. It is the highest thing said about God in the chapter, and it sounds like philosophy, so put it plainly. Everything that lives has life on loan. A tree has it from the soil and the light, an animal from what it eats, a man from his food and breath and the fact that his heart has not yet stopped, and every one of those supplies can be cut, which is why everything that lives also dies. To have life in himself means to be the one exception: to hold life not as a supply but as his own being, underived, with nothing behind it that could fail. Theologians call this aseity, from the Latin a se, from himself, and it belongs to God alone.

Granted to the Son. The Son too has life in himself: not borrowed, but his own (1:4). At first hearing this sounds like a contradiction, since a life that is granted would seem by definition not to be underived. The church thought long about this and arrived at the right place. Granted does not mean the Son once lacked it. It is not an event in time. The eternal Son receives life eternally from the Father, as the Son eternally comes from the Father. Theologians call this eternal generation, and it means simply this: the Father has always been the Father and the Son has always been the Son. There was never a time when the Son was not (1:1–2), and his being the Son is not a beginning but an eternal relationship. He is not a creature who was given life at some point. He is the Son, and what the Father is, the Son is. And having become man, he has this life as a man too, to give to others.

Because he is the Son of Man. Not, as the argument might lead us to expect, because he is the Son of God. In the Greek there is no the, simply a son of man, which may stress his true humanity as well as recall Daniel 7:13–14, where one like a son of man receives an everlasting dominion. As a man, he can judge humanity fairly, having lived as one of us (Hebrews 4:15). The one who will judge the human race was tired at a well, wept at a grave, and knows from the inside what it costs to be one of the accused.

What difference does it make that God has life in himself? All the difference in the world. Because God depends on nothing, he cannot be worn out, run out or used up. He does not need you, and so his love for you is pure gift, not a deal. And because the Son has life in himself, the life he gives is not a borrowed supply that might run dry. It is his own inexhaustible life. Whoever is joined to him by faith is joined to the one source of life that can never fail, which is why Jesus can promise, because I live, you also will live (14:19).

For worship. The one who holds life in himself took a body that could be killed. Nothing in him required feeding or resting, and he consented to both, and then to the loss of the whole of it. He gave his life away, took it up again, and now gives it to whoever hears his voice.

parallels.desc: one like a son of man given dominion

verseByVerse.quote: "Do not marvel at this, for an hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out, those who have done good to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not marvel at this. The spiritually dead hearing his voice and living is the smaller of the two things. Wait until the graves. This time he says only that an hour is coming, not that it is now here: it is the last day.

All who are in the tombs. The bodily resurrection of all the dead, righteous and wicked: everyone who has ever been buried, in every unmarked place, in the sea and under the ash. And the summons is a voice, the voice of the man who stood in a Jerusalem colonnade and told someone to pick up a mat. And the voice will belong to a man who has been in a tomb himself, and came out, and knows the way.

Life and judgment. Both are raised in the body: the one to eternal life, the other to condemnation.

What it does not mean. Not salvation by good works. In John, the “good” is above all believing in Jesus (6:29), and life comes to whoever hears his word and believes (v. 24). The good and the evil deeds are evidence, not payment: they show whether a life had already crossed from death to life, or had not (Ephesians 2:8–10; James 2:17–18). Nobody is raised to life because their record was good enough, but this Gospel will not let faith be a word said once with nothing following.

One resurrection or two? This verse speaks of one hour in which all who are in the tombs come out, the righteous and the wicked together (compare Daniel 12:2; Acts 24:15). Premillennial Christians (who expect Christ to return before a thousand-year reign on earth) read Revelation 20 as teaching two bodily resurrections a thousand years apart, the first for believers and the second for the rest. The more likely reading is the one this verse gives: a single general resurrection at Christ’s return, with Revelation’s first resurrection referring to the new life believers already share with Christ. This is the amillennial view, which takes the thousand years as a picture of the present age between Christ’s two comings. Many faithful Christians read Revelation 20 otherwise, and the hope they share is the same: Christ will return, raise the dead and judge the world.

How can a loving God raise anyone to judgment? Because he is holy as well as loving, and the two are not rivals. A judge who shrugged at cruelty, betrayal and the abuse of the weak would not be loving; he would be indifferent, and every victim would know it. God takes evil seriously because he takes people seriously. And the verse shows how seriously he takes mercy too: the Judge who will speak at the graves is the one who came first to be judged in our place (v. 24). His offer is real and free, and no one who comes to him will be raised to judgment. Those who come to him will find the Judge is their Saviour.

What will the resurrection body be like? It will be your own body, raised, not a different one, just as Jesus’ risen body bore the marks of the nails (20:27). For believers it will be raised imperishable, glorious and powerful, fitted for the new creation (1 Corinthians 15:42–44), like Christ’s glorious body (Philippians 3:21). The unbelieving dead will also be raised bodily, to face judgment and conscious, eternal punishment (Matthew 25:46). This is why the body matters in the Christian life: what you do with it now is done with something God intends to raise.

In everyday life. Ask what your life would look like to someone who watched it for a year without hearing you say anything about God. Verse 29 is asking whether the crossing has left any tracks. If you see little, do not despair: the tracks are often plainer to others than to ourselves, and life is received by hearing and believing (v. 24), not by the size of the tracks.

parallels.desc: some to everlasting life, some to shame

verseByVerse.quote: "I can do nothing on my own. As I hear, I judge, and my judgment is just, because I seek not my own will but the will of him who sent me. If I alone bear witness about myself, my testimony is not true."
verseByVerse.commentary:
As I hear, I judge. The Son never acts apart from the Father (v. 19), and so his judgment is perfectly just, because it is the Father’s.

Not my own will. Perfect submission (4:34; 6:38). That is the qualification for a judge: not superior intelligence but the total absence of self-interest.

If I alone bear witness. The law required two or three witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15). Jesus accepts the rule, and now calls his witnesses. The vocabulary of witness has run through this Gospel since the Baptist (1:7–8); now the case is formally opened. Not true here means that it would not count as evidence in court, not that it would be false.

But in 8:14 Jesus says his testimony about himself is true. Is that a contradiction? No; each answers a different question. Here he meets them on their own ground: you require corroboration, and you shall have it, and here are the witnesses. In chapter 8 he is answering a challenge to his knowledge, and his point is that he alone knows where he came from and where he is going, so his testimony, whatever a court makes of it, is accurate. One statement is about legal standing; the other is about truthfulness. He does not need corroboration to be right. He offers it because they need it to be persuaded.

He builds a case. He is under no obligation to argue, yet the Son who claims to raise the dead builds a case like a defendant, because the men in front of him will move only on evidence, and he will give them evidence rather than stand on his dignity.

In everyday life. Only one man has ever sought the Father’s will and never his own, and his perfect obedience is counted to all who trust him (Romans 5:19). Because your standing with God rests on his obedience and not on being right, you can be honest about your motives: before you form an opinion of someone today, ask what you stand to gain from it. A judgment with self-interest in it is already bent.
verseByVerse.note: The law required two or three witnesses; a man’s testimony about himself did not count as valid evidence.

verseByVerse.quote: "There is another who bears witness about me, and I know that the testimony that he bears about me is true."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The other witness. Some take the other witness to be John the Baptist (v. 33), but it is most likely the Father, since verse 37 says the Father who sent me has himself borne witness about me. Both point the same way: John spoke because the Father sent him (1:6, 33).

The testimony is true. The Father cannot lie. Jesus is not producing witnesses because he is uncertain. He knows; the case is being built for the benefit of people who do not.

The witnesses. Jesus now calls four witnesses, as in a trial: John the Baptist (vv. 33–35), his works (v. 36), the Father (vv. 37–38), and the Scriptures, including Moses (vv. 39–47).

There is another. He is standing alone in a hostile room: the disciples are not mentioned in this chapter, and the healed man has just identified him to the authorities. The corroboration comes from outside the building, from the one who sent him, and it does not depend on a single person present being persuaded.

How should I argue for the faith with someone who wants proof? From knowledge, not anxiety. Evidence is offered in Scripture constantly and without embarrassment; this Gospel is itself a gathering of evidence, and says so at the end (20:30–31). So give reasons gladly: the eyewitness testimony, the empty tomb, fulfilled prophecy, the changed lives. But there is a way of arguing for Christ that has fear underneath it, and it communicates the fear rather than the case. Jesus never once sounds worried about the verdict. The truth does not depend on your winning the argument. Speak calmly, honestly and kindly, and leave the persuading to God.

In everyday life. If you have to hold a position alone today, in a family, at work, in a church that has gone somewhere you cannot follow, remember this sentence: there is another. It is not an encouragement to be stubborn, but a statement about where the verdict actually comes from.
verseByVerse.note: The other witness is probably the Father (v. 37), though some take it as John the Baptist (v. 33).

verseByVerse.quote: "You sent to John, and he has borne witness to the truth. Not that the testimony that I receive is from man, but I say these things so that you may be saved."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You sent to John. The delegation of 1:19. They cannot dispute his standing, because they investigated him themselves, and John told them, on the record, who he was. Jesus is producing the transcript of their own enquiry.

He has borne witness. He testified that Jesus is the Lamb of God and Son of God (1:29, 34). The tense matters: the testimony stands, still doing its work in a hearing he is not present at. He must increase, but I must decrease (3:30), and by now the decreasing has gone a long way. He is not in the room. His witness is.

Not from man. Having called John, Jesus says at once that his case does not rest on him. Even the greatest man born of women is still a man, and a man’s word is too weak a foundation for who Jesus is.

So that you may be saved. He mentions John for their sake, because they respected him. Under investigation by men already trying to work out how to kill him (v. 18), he says the reason he is bothering is not to win his own acquittal but to win them: a man on trial for his life, telling the court his defence is being offered for their benefit. While they plotted his death, he argued for their life.

Does my witness matter if I never see results? Yes. Faithful testimony goes on working after the person who gave it can no longer give it: in rooms they never entered, in arguments they did not know were happening, long after they have been forgotten by everyone but God. John was probably in prison, perhaps already dead, when Jesus cited him. Your words to a child, a friend or a colleague may be called as evidence by the Spirit years from now. Speak truly, and leave the timing to God.

In everyday life. Even Jesus’ hard words are spoken so that people may be saved. When you have to say something hard to someone this week, check your motive first. Are you speaking so that they may be saved, or so that you may be right?

verseByVerse.quote: "He was a burning and shining lamp, and you were willing to rejoice for a while in his light."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A burning and shining lamp. A lamp, not the light itself (1:8). The word is lychnos, the ordinary oil lamp you carry into a room after dark. Burning: with zeal; shining: giving light. A lamp truly alight, but still only the thing you use until morning. And the tense is past: by now John was probably in prison.

For a while. Literally, for an hour. The whole country went out to the Jordan (Matthew 3:5), and it lasted about as long as such things last. They did not follow where he pointed: enthusiasm without repentance. The lamp had been admired and put out, and here stands the daylight it was lit for, and they are trying to work out how to kill him.

Enjoying is not following. There is a way of consuming preaching as an experience: hearing a man who is genuinely alight, feeling something, discussing it warmly, and being at the end of the season exactly where you started. The enjoyment is not fraudulent, which is what makes it dangerous. It feels like following, and it is only enjoying.

Is it wrong to have a favourite preacher? Not in itself. God gives gifts to his church, and it is right to thank him for preachers who help you. But the Corinthians turned admiration into parties, I follow Paul, I follow Apollos, and Paul rebuked them (1 Corinthians 3:4–7). The test of a good preacher is that, like John, he is a finger aimed at Christ, and the test of a good hearer is that he follows where the finger points. If you would stop going to church when your favourite preacher leaves, it may be the lamp you love and not the light.

For worship. Christ is the light; every faithful preacher is only a lamp lit by him, burning for a while and then put out. The lamps pass, but the light of the world shines on, and the city to come has no need of sun or moon, for the glory of God gives it light, and its lamp is the Lamb.

parallels.desc: I have prepared a lamp for my anointed

verseByVerse.quote: "But the testimony that I have is greater than that of John. For the works that the Father has given me to accomplish, the very works that I am doing, bear witness about me that the Father has sent me. And the Father who sent me has himself borne witness about me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Greater than that of John. First, the works that the Father has given him to accomplish, culminating in the cross (17:4; 19:30). Not works he chose as demonstrations, but works handed to him as an assignment, to be finished, the same word as in 4:34. The healing at the pool was not an improvisation. It was an item on a schedule, and so was every other sign in this book, and so was the last one.

The works bear witness. The works show who he is (10:25, 37–38; 14:11), and they outrank the Baptist for a simple reason. John’s testimony was a man’s word, and men have been wrong. A man who had been on the ground for most of his life is walking through Jerusalem carrying his bed, and the fact does not depend on anyone’s credibility. Either it happened or it did not.

The Father has borne witness. Perfect tense: a lasting testimony. When did it happen? He does not say here, and the Gospel offers several answers: the Spirit descending and remaining at the Jordan, which the Baptist saw and reported (1:32–34); the Scriptures, which he is about to name; and most simply the works themselves, since it is the Father who gives them.

A cumulative case. Each witness on its own could be argued with. Together they make a strong case, and in this room the problem was not a shortage of evidence, which is why the next verse turns from the evidence to the men.

Where can I see Jesus’ works today? In the written record first, given for this very purpose (20:31). But also in what he goes on doing by his Spirit through his church: sinners converted, drunkards made sober, enemies reconciled, the dying unafraid, the gospel spreading through every nation as he said it would. These are not new revelations, and they do not replace Scripture; but they are the living fruit of the finished work, and they bear witness too. Look for them, and tell others what you have seen.

parallels.desc: the Father’s voice at the baptism

verseByVerse.quote: "His voice you have never heard, his form you have never seen, and you do not have his word abiding in you, for you do not believe the one whom he has sent."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Never heard, never seen. Here the discourse turns, and it should be felt as an insult before it is understood as a diagnosis. He is telling the most religiously accomplished men in the nation, whose lives were organised around the word of God, that they have never heard God’s voice, never seen his form, and do not have his word living in them. At Sinai, Israel heard God’s voice and saw no form (Deuteronomy 4:12); his likeness is now visible in Jesus (14:9). The invisible Father, whose voice no sinner could bear and whose form no eye has seen, has shown his face in Jesus Christ.

But Israel heard God’s voice at Sinai, and Moses saw his glory. What does Jesus mean? Jesus is not denying that; he is saying that these hearers have not truly heard or seen, since his word does not abide in them (v. 38). And no one has seen the Father as he is (1:18; Exodus 33:20); the appearances of God in the Old Testament were real but partial, and many believe they were appearances of the Son himself.

His word abiding in you. The phrase looks ahead to the vine (15:4, 7). What these men lack is not information about God, which they had in quantity, but God’s word taking up residence. It is possible to know the whole text and never have it live in you.

You do not believe. The proof: when the Word of God stood in front of them they did not recognise him. The Father makes himself known through the Son, so trying to know God while bypassing Jesus is not another road to God. It does not reach him.

The trial has changed sides. It opened with Jesus in the dock; now the men who convened the hearing are being examined. And the finding against them is not that they weighed the evidence wrongly. The evidence was never the problem.

Why do good arguments sometimes change nothing? Because the difficulty is not always in the evidence. Anyone who has argued about the faith with someone they love knows the experience of watching a good case land on nothing. It is tempting to conclude that a better argument would have done it. Sometimes that is true, and the argument is worth improving. But this verse says there is a condition in which no quantity of evidence will be enough, because the problem lies in the heart. Knowing that keeps a person praying for someone, and not merely preparing for the next conversation. Only God can open the heart (Acts 16:14).

parallels.desc: you heard the sound of words, but saw no form

verseByVerse.quote: "You search the Scriptures because you think that in them you have eternal life; and it is they that bear witness about me, yet you refuse to come to me that you may have life."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You search the Scriptures. They studied the Old Testament with great diligence; later Jewish tradition remembers scribes counting its letters. They were serious Bible students.

Command or statement? It can be read as a command, Search the Scriptures, as the King James Version has it, and searching is rightly commended elsewhere (Acts 17:11). But the context favours a statement: they were searching, and missing the one the Scriptures spoke of.

In them. A saying attributed to Hillel runs: the more study of the law, the more life (Mishnah Avot 2:7). The sentence turns on a preposition they got wrong: in them. The life was understood to be located in the text, obtainable by handling it. Jesus does not deny that the Scriptures give life. He denies that the life is in the text itself, and not in the one it points to.

They bear witness about me. The purpose of Scripture is to point to Christ (Luke 24:27, 44). The Scriptures are the fourth witness in his case, and no one calls a witness so that the court may admire the witness.

You refuse to come. The problem was their will: not you cannot, not you have not understood, but you refuse. Men bent over scrolls for a lifetime, tracing every promise of the one who was to come, and he stands in the room, having just healed a man in front of them. The distance between the text and the person was a few feet, and they would not cross it.

How does you refuse to come fit with No one can come to me unless the Father draws him? The inability is not that people want to come and are prevented, but that their wills are bound by love of themselves and their own glory (v. 44). They cannot because they will not, and that is why they are responsible. Only the Father’s drawing changes the will (6:44).

Am I in danger of reading the Bible like this? This is aimed at people who read their Bibles, so it is better felt than pointed at someone else. A person can conduct a serious study of Scripture as a closed system: to enjoy tracing themes, resolving difficulties, the satisfaction of a passage finally coming clear, and for the whole exercise to end in itself. The pleasure is real; it feels like devotion; and it can go on for years without once arriving at a person. The remedy is not to study less but to study prayerfully, asking at every passage: what does this show me of Christ, and how will I come to him because of it?

In everyday life. After the last passage you studied, did you end up knowing something, or wanting him? Both can be good. Only one is what the text was for.

verseByVerse.quote: "I do not receive glory from people. But I know that you do not have the love of God within you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I do not receive glory from people. He seeks his Father’s glory (7:18; 8:50). He has no stake in their good opinion, so his assessment of them is not coloured by what he needs from them, and a man who wants nothing from you is the only one who can tell you the truth about yourself.

The love of God within you. Love for God, or God’s love: the Greek permits both, and in this Gospel the two are never far apart. Despite their religiousness, they did not love God; if they did, they would love the one he sent (8:42). They are not mainly failing a logical test but a love test. To have the love of God within you is for God himself to have become your joy, so that you are glad when he is honoured and grieved when he is not (Matthew 22:37), the one thing no amount of religious activity can counterfeit.

Why this sentence is frightening. It is frightening precisely because these men would have passed every other test. Attendance, orthodoxy, knowledge of the text, moral seriousness, faithful keeping of the feasts: all in order. What was missing does not show up on any of those instruments. And it explains the whole chapter. They had watched a man paralysed for decades get up and walk, and their first and only response was a rule about carrying. Nothing in them leapt. A person who loves God is not able to watch God do something and feel only procedural concern; the loving gets in the way. Their reaction was not a failure of information. It showed accurately what was in them: no love for God to be stirred.

What if I fear this describes me? Then take an honest comfort from it. The men in this passage were entirely untroubled by the question. That a verse like this makes you anxious shows that you care about loving God, and they did not. And the remedy, if it is needed, is not to work up an affection. Love for God is not manufactured by an effort of will. It is what happens when a person actually sees him, which is precisely what Jesus spent this chapter offering. We love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19). Look at his love for you in Christ, and ask the Spirit to pour God’s love into your heart (Romans 5:5).

verseByVerse.quote: "I have come in my Father's name, and you do not receive me. If another comes in his own name, you will receive him. How can you believe, when you receive glory from one another and do not seek the glory that comes from the only God?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
In my Father’s name. He comes with his Father’s authority, representing him, and he is rejected: his own people did not receive him (1:11).

Another in his own name. False messiahs who came on their own authority were often welcomed; in AD 132 Simon bar Kokhba led a disastrous revolt, and Rabbi Akiba is said to have hailed him as Messiah. A man who comes sent by God, pointing away from himself, asks us to submit to God’s choice, not our own. A man who comes on his own authority lets his followers feel they have picked their own leader, and that flatters them.

Glory from one another. The root of their unbelief: love of human praise (12:42–43). Glory here means reputation, the opinion others hold of you. So the sentence describes a closed economy. These men held a currency they issued to each other: standing, deference, the seat at the front, the title in the street, the respect of colleagues who were the only people qualified to grant it. And that currency had a fatal property. It could only be earned from the people inside the system, which means it could only be kept by not leaving. Belief in Jesus would have cost every one of them everything the system paid. A man cannot pursue two kinds of honour issued by different authorities that exclude each other. He will take the one he is nearer to.

And do not seek the glory that comes from the only God? God’s approval is the only honour that matters. The way out is in the same verse. He does not tell them to want no approval at all. He tells them they are seeking it from people who have nothing lasting to give. The glory that comes from the only God is real, and Christ will one day say to his servants, well done. He refused the glory men offered and received the glory the Father gave, and now he shares it with those who trust him: the glory that you have given me I have given to them (17:22).

Is it wrong to care what people think of me? Not entirely: a good name is valued (Proverbs 22:1), but people’s opinion must not decide what you will say and do about Christ (Proverbs 29:25), and in Christ God’s approval is already yours. (See Luke 16:14 for the fuller answer.)

In everyday life. Think of the decisions you would make differently if nobody you respected ever found out: what you would say in a meeting, which opinion you would voice, whether you would mention Christ in a particular room. That gap shows how much you live for the approval of others, the glory from one another of verse 44. But in Christ the only God has already given you his approval, and it is not withdrawn when you fail.

parallels.desc: Theudas and Judas the Galilean

verseByVerse.quote: "Do not think that I will accuse you to the Father. There is one who accuses you: Moses, on whom you have set your hope. For if you believed Moses, you would believe me; for he wrote of me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will not accuse you. The reversal is complete. They convened this hearing and have been the prosecution throughout. Now the defendant says he will not prosecute. For one second it sounds like mercy, and then the sentence finishes.

One who accuses you. Moses, the giver of the law they trusted, the name that gave them standing, will be their prosecutor. The law they thought would save them will condemn them (Romans 3:19–20). Yet the curse that Moses pronounced on all who break the law, Christ bore himself, becoming a curse for us (Galatians 3:13).

He wrote of me. Moses wrote of Christ: the seed of the woman (Genesis 3:15), the offspring of Abraham (Genesis 22:18), the Passover lamb (Exodus 12), the bronze serpent (Numbers 21:9; John 3:14), the prophet like Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15–18). And the claim is larger than a few predictions: the whole body of his writing was about him, the tabernacle and the glory that filled it, the priest who went in with blood once a year, the rock that gave water, each written by a man who saw only part of what he was describing.

What Moses was for. So the disagreement in this room is not between a Jewish teacher and a Christian innovation, but about what Moses was for. Jesus does not set Moses aside as a preliminary stage. He claims him as his own witness and tells the men holding the scrolls that they have misread the author they built their lives on.

Did Moses really write the first five books? Jesus treats it as settled that Moses wrote (compare Mark 12:26; Luke 24:27, 44), and he means the books of the law. That need not mean Moses wrote every line: the account of his death (Deuteronomy 34) was plainly added by another hand, and many believing scholars allow for some later editing; but Jesus treats the law as Moses’ own testimony. Where did Moses write of him? Beyond the pictures already named, in the ruler from Judah (Genesis 49:10), and above all in the prophet like Moses: the LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me (Deuteronomy 18:15).

parallels.desc: a witness against you

verseByVerse.quote: "But if you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words? They claimed to honour Moses, but did not truly believe what he wrote. If they will not believe the written Scriptures they revere, they will not believe Jesus’ spoken words. Faith in Scripture and faith in Christ stand or fall together. Jesus places his own words alongside Scripture. The chapter ends on a question, and it is left unanswered, which is the point, since the answer would have to come from the men it was asked of. The logic is simple. Moses wrote of Christ. They do not believe Christ. Therefore they do not, in any sense that matters, believe Moses, whatever they think they are doing when they read him.

The problem is not the medium. People who will not be persuaded by Scripture are not waiting for a better delivery. They had the writings, the works, the Baptist, the Father’s testimony, and the man himself, available for questions.

Stand back and see the whole chapter. It opened with a man who could not get himself to the water, who had nobody, and he was made whole. It closes with the most scripturally literate men in the nation, who had every witness heaven could produce, and would not come. The man on the mat had no friends, no theology, and a voice telling him to stand up, and he got up; the men with all the evidence stayed sitting down. Between the two lies the sentence that explains both: the Son gives life to whom he will.

Should I trust the Old Testament as much as the words of Jesus? Yes. Jesus puts Moses’ writings and his own words side by side, and treats doubting one as the road to doubting the other. He believed the Old Testament to be the word of God, quoted it as settling arguments, and said Scripture cannot be broken (10:35). The whole Bible is one book with one Author and one subject. The Old Testament is not a lesser Bible to be outgrown; it is the testimony to Christ that Jesus himself used. Read both Testaments with the same trust, because the Lord you love trusted both.

5.title: The Son Has Life in Himself
5.text: <sup>1</sup>After this there was a feast of the Jews, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem.<sup>2</sup>Now there is in Jerusalem by the Sheep Gate a pool, in Aramaic called Bethesda, which has five roofed colonnades.<sup>3</sup>In these lay a multitude of invalids—blind, lame, and paralyzed.<sup>5</sup>One man was there who had been an invalid for thirty-eight years.<sup>6</sup>When Jesus saw him lying there and knew that he had already been there a long time, he said to him, “Do you want to be healed?”<sup>7</sup>The sick man answered him, “Sir, I have no one to put me into the pool when the water is stirred up, and while I am going another steps down before me.”<sup>8</sup>Jesus said to him, “Get up, take up your bed, and walk.”<sup>9</sup>And at once the man was healed, and he took up his bed and walked. Now that day was the Sabbath.<sup>10</sup>So the Jews said to the man who had been healed, “It is the Sabbath, and it is not lawful for you to take up your bed.”<sup>11</sup>But he answered them, “The man who healed me, that man said to me, ’Take up your bed, and walk.’”<sup>12</sup>They asked him, “Who is the man who said to you, ’Take up your bed and walk’?”<sup>13</sup>Now the man who had been healed did not know who it was, for Jesus had withdrawn, as there was a crowd in the place.<sup>14</sup>Afterward Jesus found him in the temple and said to him, “See, you are well! Sin no more, that nothing worse may happen to you.”<sup>15</sup>The man went away and told the Jews that it was Jesus who had healed him.<sup>16</sup>And this was why the Jews were persecuting Jesus, because he was doing these things on the Sabbath.<sup>17</sup>But Jesus answered them, “My Father is working until now, and I am working.”<sup>18</sup>This was why the Jews were seeking all the more to kill him, because not only was he breaking the Sabbath, but he was even calling God his own Father, making himself equal with God.<sup>19</sup>So Jesus said to them, “Truly, truly, I say to you, the Son can do nothing of his own accord, but only what he sees the Father doing. For whatever the Father does, that the Son does likewise.<sup>20</sup>For the Father loves the Son and shows him all that he himself is doing. And greater works than these will he show him, so that you may marvel.<sup>21</sup>For as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he will.<sup>22</sup>For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son,<sup>23</sup>that all may honor the Son, just as they honor the Father. Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him.<sup>24</sup>Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life. He does not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life.<sup>25</sup>“Truly, truly, I say to you, an hour is coming, and is now here, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live.<sup>26</sup>For as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself.<sup>27</sup>And he has given him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man.<sup>28</sup>Do not marvel at this, for an hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice<sup>29</sup>and come out, those who have done good to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment.<sup>30</sup>“I can do nothing on my own. As I hear, I judge, and my judgment is just, because I seek not my own will but the will of him who sent me.<sup>31</sup>If I alone bear witness about myself, my testimony is not true.<sup>32</sup>There is another who bears witness about me, and I know that the testimony that he bears about me is true.<sup>33</sup>You sent to John, and he has borne witness to the truth.<sup>34</sup>Not that the testimony that I receive is from man, but I say these things so that you may be saved.<sup>35</sup>He was a burning and shining lamp, and you were willing to rejoice for a while in his light.<sup>36</sup>But the testimony that I have is greater than that of John. For the works that the Father has given me to accomplish, the very works that I am doing, bear witness about me that the Father has sent me.<sup>37</sup>And the Father who sent me has himself borne witness about me. His voice you have never heard, his form you have never seen,<sup>38</sup>and you do not have his word abiding in you, for you do not believe the one whom he has sent.<sup>39</sup>You search the Scriptures because you think that in them you have eternal life; and it is they that bear witness about me,<sup>40</sup>yet you refuse to come to me that you may have life.<sup>41</sup>I do not receive glory from people.<sup>42</sup>But I know that you do not have the love of God within you.<sup>43</sup>I have come in my Father’s name, and you do not receive me. If another comes in his own name, you will receive him.<sup>44</sup>How can you believe, when you receive glory from one another and do not seek the glory that comes from the only God?<sup>45</sup>Do not think that I will accuse you to the Father. There is one who accuses you: Moses, on whom you have set your hope.<sup>46</sup>For if you believed Moses, you would believe me; for he wrote of me.<sup>47</sup>But if you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words?”
5.overview:
The third sign takes place in Jerusalem at the pool of Bethesda. Jesus heals a man who has been an invalid for thirty-eight years, unasked, and tells him to carry his mat on the Sabbath. The authorities object, and when Jesus answers that his Father is working and so is he, they understand him exactly: he is making himself equal with God, and they now seek to kill him.

His reply (vv. 19–47) is one of the fullest statements in the Gospels of who he is. The Son does what the Father does, gives life to whom he will, holds all judgment, and is to be honoured as the Father is. Then, as in a courtroom, he calls his witnesses: John the Baptist, his works, the Father and the Scriptures. The men who searched the Scriptures most carefully would not come to the one they spoke of.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–21 — Feeding the Five Thousand and Walking on Water
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The feeding on the hillside and the crossing of the lake at night form a pair: Jesus provides more than enough from a boy’s lunch and refuses a forced crown, then comes to his disciples over the dark water and tells them who he is.
verseByVerse.theology: Together the two signs show Jesus as Lord of provision and Lord of the sea. His words on the water, “It is I” (v. 20), are the words behind the divine name, and they lead into the first of the great I am sayings later in the chapter. The crowd that wants to crown him misreads the sign: they want the bread without the one who gives it.
verseByVerse.examples: Philip’s sum was correct; his mistake was to answer a question about where with a calculation of how much. And walking on the sea is the most revealing of the nature miracles: in the Old Testament the sea is the realm only God commands (Job 9:8; Psalm 77:19).

verseByVerse.quote: After this Jesus went away to the other side of the Sea of Galilee, which is the Sea of Tiberias. And a large crowd was following him, because they saw the signs that he was doing on the sick.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. John 6 is the chapter of the bread. Near Passover Jesus feeds five thousand, refuses a crown, walks on the sea, and next day explains the sign: he himself is the true bread from heaven, of which the manna was a shadow, his flesh given for the life of the world and received by faith. The crowd thins to a handful, and Peter confesses: Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life.

The only miracle in all four Gospels. Apart from the resurrection, the feeding of the five thousand is the only miracle of Jesus recorded in all four Gospels.

The Sea of Tiberias. Another name for the Sea of Galilee, after the city Herod Antipas built on its western shore around AD 20 and named after the emperor Tiberius.

In the flow. Jesus had just told the leaders in Jerusalem that Moses wrote of him (5:46). Chapter 6 is full of Moses: Passover, a mountain, bread in the wilderness, a crossing of the sea, a grumbling people and a demand for manna. At every point Jesus is shown to be not the one who passes on bread from heaven, but the bread himself. It begins with the largest crowd of his ministry and ends with a handful, and shows that the signs alone do not make disciples.

Because they saw the signs. They followed for the miracles, not for who he was (v. 26), which is a reasonable thing to want and is not yet faith. Between this crowd and the emptying synagogue at the end of the chapter lies no scandal and no change of policy, only a sermon. The crowd shrinks because he explains himself.

Signs point to the one who gives them. In this Gospel a sign is never an end in itself (20:30–31). The healings were the old promises coming true (Isaiah 35:5–6). So the crowd was right to follow the signs and wrong to stop at them: every healing was a finger pointing at the healer, and this chapter is the day he tells them what the finger was pointing at.

He fed them anyway. They were following for the wrong reason, and he fed them anyway. He did not begin by correcting their motives; he began by giving them lunch. He is kind to the ungrateful and generous to the half-hearted. The rebuke comes the next morning.

Is it wrong if I first came to Christ for what I needed from him? No; almost nobody arrives for adequate reasons. People come because something hurts, a marriage is failing, a child is ill, or the fear of dying has become concrete, and every one of those is a version of wanting the loaves. It is where practically everyone starts, and this chapter does not despise it. Jesus received the crowd and fed them. What he will not do is leave anyone there. The question is not why you first came, but whether you are now coming to him for himself.
verseByVerse.note: The Sea of Tiberias is another name for the Sea of Galilee, from the city Herod Antipas built on its western shore and named after the emperor Tiberius.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus went up on the mountain, and there he sat down with his disciples.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus went up on the mountain. The hills east of the lake, and an echo of Moses going up the mountain (Exodus 19; 24).

He sat down with his disciples. The posture of a teacher (Matthew 5:1). But what follows on this mountain is a meal. That is the order the chapter runs on: the bread first and the explanation second, and the crowd delighted by the first is offended by the second. It is possible to enjoy what Christ does and find what he says intolerable.

Withdrawal at both ends. He goes up the mountain before the crowd arrives, and goes up again by himself after they have gone (v. 15), Mark tells us for prayer (Mark 6:46).

Greater than Moses on the mountain. Moses went up to receive what God gave and came down to pass it on; he was faithful as a servant in God’s house (Hebrews 3:5). Jesus goes up and sits, the posture of one with authority of his own, and what follows will come from his own hands. John said it on his first page: the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ (1:17). Moses could only tell Israel where the manna came from. This teacher will feed them himself, and then tell them that he is the bread.
