To soften it would be to say something less true about himself, and he will not lie about who he is or what he has come to do, not even to keep the people who have followed him longest. What makes the saying hard is that it is about a cross: a Messiah whose flesh is given and whose blood is poured out, and a salvation that leaves the sinner nothing to bring but hunger.

What should I do with a teaching of Jesus I find hard to accept? First, make sure it is what he actually teaches, read in its context, and not a distortion. Then ask honestly whether your difficulty is that you do not understand it, or that you do not like it. If the first, study and ask for help. If the second, bring the struggle to Christ himself, as you would to a friend whose judgment you trust more than your own. Many believers have found that the sayings they once resisted became the ones they love most. Faith does not mean pretending something is easy; it means trusting the one who said it.
verseByVerse.note: The remains of a later synagogue at Capernaum stand on the foundations of an earlier one, perhaps the one where Jesus taught.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jesus, knowing in himself that his disciples were grumbling about this, said to them, "Do you take offense at this? Then what if you were to see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Knowing in himself. Jesus knows what is in people (2:24–25); nobody reported it. The knowledge that read the woman at the well is now turned on his own followers as they are quietly deciding to leave. He watched them go before they went.

Do you take offense at this? “Offense” (skandalizō): to trip, to stumble. The cross is the great stumbling block (1 Corinthians 1:23).

Then what if you were to see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before? The sentence is left unfinished in Greek. Two readings are possible. It could mean: if this offends you, how much more will his ascent, the full revelation of his heavenly origin, overwhelm you? Or: when you see him ascend, you will understand that he truly came from heaven, and that his words about his flesh were not about literal eating. In John, his going up includes the cross, resurrection and ascension together (3:13–14; 12:32–34). Either way, the ascension proves his claim that he came down from heaven (vv. 38, 42), and it shows that his flesh would not stay on earth to be literally eaten.

Both readings hold. Either way, where he was before carries the weight. It is the very thing the objectors in verse 42 denied, and he answers by referring, without argument, to the place he came from and is going back to.

Why does the ascension matter to me? Because the one who ascended is now reigning, praying and preparing. He sits at the Father’s right hand as King over all things for the good of his church (Ephesians 1:20–23). He always lives to intercede for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25). He has sent the Spirit (16:7). He is preparing a place for you, and will come again (14:2–3). The ascension means you have a friend at the very centre of all power, wearing your nature, and your life is hidden with him there (Colossians 3:1–3).

verseByVerse.quote: "It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh is no help at all. The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life. But there are some of you who do not believe." (For Jesus knew from the beginning who those were who did not believe, and who it was who would betray him.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is the Spirit who gives life. Life comes from the Holy Spirit, as in the new birth (3:5–8). This is the key to the chapter, where Jesus tells his own disciples what the previous twenty verses were about.

The flesh is no help at all. “Flesh” here means human nature on its own, apart from the Spirit, not Jesus’ own flesh given for the world (v. 51). He has just told them to eat his flesh, and now says flesh is no help at all. That is not a contradiction but a signal, placed where a hearer needs it: they have been thinking in physical, literal terms, and that is the wrong way to take him.

Spirit and life. He does not say his words describe spirit and life. He says they are spirit and life. The saying they have just called intolerable is itself what carries the life, so the way to eat him is to receive what he has said. So eating means believing. That explanation comes from Jesus himself, long before any church had a doctrine of the Supper to defend.

Some of you who do not believe. Said not to the crowd or the authorities but to the people standing closest, some of whom he is telling to their faces that they do not believe.

From the beginning. John’s comment, probably meaning from the start of his ministry. Jesus chose the Twelve knowing what Judas would do (v. 70; 13:18). It is the first mention of the betrayal in this Gospel.

Did Jesus’ knowing make Judas betray him? No. Foreknowledge is not the same as compulsion. John does not say Judas was made to do it; he says Jesus knew. God’s eternal purpose does include even the sins of men, so that the cross came by his definite plan and foreknowledge (Acts 2:23), yet God is not the author of sin, and Judas acted freely and wickedly, and was fully responsible (Westminster Confession 3.1; 5.4; 1689 London Baptist Confession 3.1; 5.4). And the terrible thing about this sentence is not what it does to Judas’s freedom but what it shows of Christ’s patience. He kept a man beside him for years, giving him everything he gave the others, knowing.

In everyday life. Without the Spirit, even the Bible is read and not heard. Before you open Scripture today, pray in one sentence: Holy Spirit, make these words life to me.

For worship. On the evening of his resurrection Jesus breathed on his disciples and said, Receive the Holy Spirit (20:22). His words are not ink but breath: the dead hear the voice of the Son of God and live (5:25). He knew every unbelieving heart in the room, and spoke life into it anyway.
verseByVerse.note: “Flesh” here means human nature on its own, apart from the Spirit.

parallels.desc: the Spirit gives life

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "This is why I told you that no one can come to me unless it is granted him by the Father."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is why I told you. He is quoting himself (v. 44): he repeats the teaching at the very moment it is being proved true, as disciples walk away.

Granted by the Father. “Granted” (dedomenon), given as a gift (Ephesians 2:8; Philippians 1:29). Three times in this chapter: the Father gives (v. 37), draws (v. 44), grants (v. 65). Unbelief is human refusal; faith is God’s gift. Drawing stressed the power required; granting stresses that it was a gift.

No room for pride. Whatever separates those who stay from those leaving, it is not insight, loyalty or a better grasp of the argument: it was granted them. Every believer will say on the last day, not I chose well, but he chose me; not I held on, but I was held.

The comfort in it. If staying were a matter of resolve, every Christian would be one bad season away from the door, and anyone who knows his own resolve would find that terrifying. This verse takes the whole question off that ground. The eleven did not out-endure the others. They were given something, and the giving did not depend on their performance that evening or any evening afterward. Within a year every one of them would run away and one would deny knowing him. They came back, because the one who received them kept them. While I was with them, he would pray, I kept them in your name, and not one of them has been lost except the son of destruction (17:12). That is the part the doctrine explains and self-confidence cannot.

Are those to whom coming is not granted still responsible? Yes. The inability is not like a prison door shut on someone trying to get out; it is a will that does not want to come (5:40). No one is turned away who comes, and no one stays away against his will. God’s gift is mercy, owed to no one; its absence is justice, not cruelty.

In everyday life. The person you find hardest to be patient with looks different once you remember that your faith was granted, not earned.

verseByVerse.quote: After this many of his disciples turned back and no longer walked with him. So Jesus said to the twelve, "Do you want to go away as well?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Many turned back. The turning point of Jesus’ Galilean ministry. The day before, a crowd wanted to make him king (v. 15). “Turned back” literally means went away to the things behind. They had followed for bread and a political Messiah. This is not true believers falling away, but false disciples being revealed (v. 64; 1 John 2:19).

And nothing happened. There was no scandal and no miracle that went wrong. He preached a sermon, and the sermon emptied the room. This is where the faith based on signs at 2:24 and the Galilean welcome of 4:45 were always going to end.

No longer walked with him. A physical description: they stopped travelling in the same direction. Falling away often looks less like a decision than like a road no longer taken.

So Jesus said to the twelve. The first mention of “the twelve” in John.

Do you want to go away as well? The question is framed in Greek to expect a no. Jesus doesn’t beg them to stay or soften his teaching. He tests them, and invites a confession. He does not chase the crowd or send anyone after them. He turns to the twelve, his closest circle, and offers them the door. It is a real question, asked by a man who has just watched a room empty and has nothing left to hold anyone with except himself.

Were these disciples true believers who lost their salvation? Some read them so. But John has already shown that following and believing in a shallow way is not the same as being born again (2:23–25), and Jesus says plainly that some of them did not believe (v. 64). The more likely reading is that they had followed without being given saving faith. As John writes later, they went out from us, but they were not of us (1 John 2:19).

What if someone I love has walked away from Christ? Then this chapter is for you. It happened to Jesus, in his own town, in numbers, on the strength of his own preaching, and it was not evidence that anything had gone wrong in him. It is not necessarily evidence that you failed either. Keep loving them, keep the door open, and keep praying: some who seem to have walked away are wandering believers whom the Shepherd will bring back, like Peter. And the Father who draws can still draw. Leave the final judgment with God, who knows those who are his (2 Timothy 2:19).

For worship. The message was himself, and he would not be less than he is to be more popular. He stood in an emptying synagogue and did not flinch, and the same faithfulness took him to a garden at night, where he said of his friends, let these men go (18:8).

verseByVerse.quote: Simon Peter answered him, "Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simon Peter answered him. Peter speaks for the Twelve, as he does in the other Gospels (Matthew 16:16).

Lord, to whom shall we go? A confession made in a hard hour. His answer is not a compliment, and not a declaration of loyalty. It is a question, and the question is the point. Peter doesn’t claim to understand everything Jesus has said; nothing suggests the twelve understood the discourse any better than the people walking out, who had heard the same sermon. What Peter says is that there is no one else to go to: after all they have seen and heard with Jesus, no other teacher is a real alternative.

Stronger than enthusiasm. A faith held in bewilderment is not a poor one. There is a holding on that survives precisely because it no longer depends on full comprehension: not I understand and therefore I stay, but I have nowhere else to take this, and the words that give life are here.

You have the words of eternal life. Peter has heard v. 63 and believed it. He has just heard the words called a hard saying by men leaving over it, and he calls the same words life. The difference is not that Peter found the saying easier. It is what he concluded about the speaker. Christ alone speaks words that raise the dead and feed the soul for ever.

In the flow. John 5 ended with men who had every witness and would not come (5:40); John 6 ends with a few who have not understood everything and will not leave. The difference is the one the chapter has explained: the Father gives, draws and grants (vv. 37, 44, 65).

What should I do when I have doubts? Do what Peter did: take them to Jesus, not away from him. Doubt is not the same as unbelief; it is often faith struggling. Be honest with God about your questions (the psalms are full of honest complaint), and ask, where else would I go? Every alternative, unbelief, other religions, self-made spirituality, has its own hard sayings, and none offers what Christ does: words of eternal life from one who rose from the dead. Stay close to his word and his people, talk to a mature Christian, and keep coming. Many of the strongest believers have walked through seasons when all they could say was Peter’s question.

parallels.desc: all the words of this Life

verseByVerse.quote: "and we have believed, and have come to know, that you are the Holy One of God." Jesus answered them, "Did I not choose you, the twelve? And yet one of you is a devil."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And we have believed, and have come to know. Both verbs are in the perfect tense: a settled conviction. And the order is the one this Gospel keeps insisting on: believing first, knowing second. The servants filled the jars before they saw the wine; the official walked home before he had news; and these men believed and then came to know.

That you are the Holy One of God. Set apart, the one consecrated and sent by the Father (10:36). Holy is the word God uses of himself (Leviticus 11:44): this man stands wholly on God’s side of that line, pure where we are stained (compare Luke 5:8). And his holiness did not keep him from us; it brought him to us. Textual note: later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read “the Christ, the Son of the living God,” borrowed from Matthew 16:16; the earliest and best read “the Holy One of God,” and the ESV rightly follows them. The title was cried by a demon in a synagogue in this same town (Mark 1:24); Peter now says as a confession of faith what the demon cried out in fear. The words can be perfectly orthodox and mean two different things depending on who says them and why.

Did I not choose you, the twelve? Jesus’ reply both encourages and warns. He chose them, not they him (15:16). Peter has just said the finest thing anyone says in the chapter, on behalf of all of them, at the lowest point of the ministry so far, and the reply must have been very hard to hear. He will not let Peter’s we stand as a count of all twelve. Eleven of them meant it. He does not correct what Peter said about him; he corrects the assumption that Peter spoke for every one of them.

One of you is a devil. “Devil” (diabolos): an adversary. Not that Judas was a demon, but that he was the devil’s tool (13:2, 27). Jesus chose Judas to be an apostle, which is not the same as God’s choosing a person for salvation (17:12). And he says it of a man who at that moment had done nothing publicly wrong, and who had just stayed when others left.

Can a church contain people who are not truly Christians? Yes. The visible church, those who profess faith and gather for worship, has always included some who are not truly born again, as the Twelve included Judas, and as Simon the magician was baptised while still bound by sin (Acts 8:13, 20–23). Only God sees the heart perfectly. That is why churches must preach the gospel to their own members as well as to outsiders, practise loving discipline, and why every believer should examine himself (2 Corinthians 13:5). But it is not a reason for suspicion of everyone. Love believes all things, and we leave the final sorting to Christ.

parallels.desc: Peter’s confession

verseByVerse.quote: He spoke of Judas the son of Simon Iscariot, for he, one of the twelve, was going to betray him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He spoke of Judas the son of Simon Iscariot. “Iscariot” is often taken to mean man of Kerioth, a town in Judea (Joshua 15:25), so Judas was probably the only Judean among the Twelve. Nobody in the room worked out who was meant; at the last supper they will still be asking. John names him here for readers who know how it ends.

One of the twelve. The betrayer was an insider. Jesus knew, and kept him close, and washed his feet (13:5, 26). Judas’ betrayal fulfilled Scripture (13:18; Psalm 41:9), yet he was fully responsible for it (Mark 14:21).

Judas stayed. The crowd leaves, the wider circle leaves, and Judas stays. He heard the hard saying and did not walk out. He stood there when Peter said, to whom shall we go?, and by every visible measure he was one who held on. He remained among the twelve for about another year, was trusted with the money, and had his feet washed by the man he sold. What the verse says without softening is that nearness guarantees nothing. Three years at close quarters with the Son of God, inside the smallest circle, did not produce faith in one man of twelve. The chapter has told us what does: no one can come unless it is granted him by the Father.

Could I be a Judas without knowing it? If you are asking the question in fear, almost certainly not. Consider what the Gospel shows of Judas: until after the betrayal he is never once recorded as troubled about his own state. Anxiety about your own heart, sorrow over sin, longing to love Christ more: these are not the marks being described. The mark of Judas is a man entirely at ease while he loves something more than Christ (12:6). So examine yourself honestly, confess what you find, and then look away from yourself to the Saviour who never casts out anyone who comes. Fear that drives you to Christ is grace, not a sign of reprobation (God’s passing someone by).

For worship. He knew which of the twelve would sell him, and he kept him close. Such is the patience of the Son of God with sinners. The chapter ends where it began, with bread. Five thousand ate it and were hungry again the next morning. One of the twelve ate from the very hands that made it, and starved. But all who come to the living bread are fed for ever.
verseByVerse.note: “Iscariot” is often taken to mean “man of Kerioth,” a town in Judea, but that is uncertain.

6.title: The Bread of Life
6.text: <sup>1</sup>After this Jesus went away to the other side of the Sea of Galilee, which is the Sea of Tiberias.<sup>2</sup>And a large crowd was following him, because they saw the signs that he was doing on the sick.<sup>3</sup>Jesus went up on the mountain, and there he sat down with his disciples.<sup>4</sup>Now the Passover, the feast of the Jews, was at hand.<sup>5</sup>Lifting up his eyes, then, and seeing that a large crowd was coming toward him, Jesus said to Philip, “Where are we to buy bread, so that these people may eat?”<sup>6</sup>He said this to test him, for he himself knew what he would do.<sup>7</sup>Philip answered him, “Two hundred denarii worth of bread would not be enough for each of them to get a little.”<sup>8</sup>One of his disciples, Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother, said to him,<sup>9</sup>“There is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish, but what are they for so many?”<sup>10</sup>Jesus said, “Have the people sit down.” Now there was much grass in the place. So the men sat down, about five thousand in number.<sup>11</sup>Jesus then took the loaves, and when he had given thanks, he distributed them to those who were seated. So also the fish, as much as they wanted.<sup>12</sup>And when they had eaten their fill, he told his disciples, “Gather up the leftover fragments, that nothing may be lost.”<sup>13</sup>So they gathered them up and filled twelve baskets with fragments from the five barley loaves left by those who had eaten.<sup>14</sup>When the people saw the sign that he had done, they said, “This is indeed the Prophet who is to come into the world!”<sup>15</sup>Perceiving then that they were about to come and take him by force to make him king, Jesus withdrew again to the mountain by himself.<sup>16</sup>When evening came, his disciples went down to the sea,<sup>17</sup>got into a boat, and started across the sea to Capernaum. It was now dark, and Jesus had not yet come to them.<sup>18</sup>The sea became rough because a strong wind was blowing.<sup>19</sup>When they had rowed about three or four miles, they saw Jesus walking on the sea and coming near the boat, and they were frightened.<sup>20</sup>But he said to them, “It is I; do not be afraid.”<sup>21</sup>Then they were glad to take him into the boat, and immediately the boat was at the land to which they were going.<sup>22</sup>On the next day the crowd that remained on the other side of the sea saw that there had been only one boat there, and that Jesus had not entered the boat with his disciples, but that his disciples had gone away alone.<sup>23</sup>Other boats from Tiberias came near the place where they had eaten the bread after the Lord had given thanks.<sup>24</sup>So when the crowd saw that Jesus was not there, nor his disciples, they themselves got into the boats and went to Capernaum, seeking Jesus.<sup>25</sup>When they found him on the other side of the sea, they said to him, “Rabbi, when did you come here?”<sup>26</sup>Jesus answered them, “Truly, truly, I say to you, you are seeking me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate your fill of the loaves.<sup>27</sup>Do not work for the food that perishes, but for the food that endures to eternal life, which the Son of Man will give to you. For on him God the Father has set his seal.”<sup>28</sup>Then they said to him, “What must we do, to be doing the works of God?”<sup>29</sup>Jesus answered them, “This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent.”<sup>30</sup>So they said to him, “Then what sign do you do, that we may see and believe you? What work do you perform?<sup>31</sup>Our fathers ate the manna in the wilderness; as it is written, ’He gave them bread from heaven to eat.’”<sup>32</sup>Jesus then said to them, “Truly, truly, I say to you, it was not Moses who gave you the bread from heaven, but my Father gives you the true bread from heaven.<sup>33</sup>For the bread of God is he who comes down from heaven and gives life to the world.”<sup>34</sup>They said to him, “Sir, give us this bread always.”<sup>35</sup>Jesus said to them, “I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger, and whoever believes in me shall never thirst.<sup>36</sup>But I said to you that you have seen me and yet do not believe.<sup>37</sup>All that the Father gives me will come to me, and whoever comes to me I will never cast out.<sup>38</sup>For I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will but the will of him who sent me.<sup>39</sup>And this is the will of him who sent me, that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me, but raise it up on the last day.<sup>40</sup>For this is the will of my Father, that everyone who looks on the Son and believes in him should have eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day.”<sup>41</sup>So the Jews grumbled about him, because he said, “I am the bread that came down from heaven.”<sup>42</sup>They said, “Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? How does he now say, ’I have come down from heaven’?”<sup>43</sup>Jesus answered them, “Do not grumble among yourselves.<sup>44</sup>No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him. And I will raise him up on the last day.<sup>45</sup>It is written in the Prophets, ’And they will all be taught by God.’ Everyone who has heard and learned from the Father comes to me—<sup>46</sup>not that anyone has seen the Father except he who is from God; he has seen the Father.<sup>47</sup>Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever believes has eternal life.<sup>48</sup>I am the bread of life.<sup>49</sup>Your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, and they died.<sup>50</sup>This is the bread that comes down from heaven, so that one may eat of it and not die.<sup>51</sup>I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever. And the bread that I will give for the life of the world is my flesh.”<sup>52</sup>The Jews then disputed among themselves, saying, “How can this man give us his flesh to eat?”<sup>53</sup>So Jesus said to them, “Truly, truly, I say to you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in you.<sup>54</sup>Whoever feeds on my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day.<sup>55</sup>For my flesh is true food, and my blood is true drink.<sup>56</sup>Whoever feeds on my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him.<sup>57</sup>As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father, so whoever feeds on me, he also will live because of me.<sup>58</sup>This is the bread that came down from heaven, not like the bread the fathers ate, and died. Whoever feeds on this bread will live forever.”<sup>59</sup>Jesus said these things in the synagogue, as he taught at Capernaum.<sup>60</sup>When many of his disciples heard it, they said, “This is a hard saying; who can listen to it?”<sup>61</sup>But Jesus, knowing in himself that his disciples were grumbling about this, said to them, “Do you take offense at this?<sup>62</sup>Then what if you were to see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before?<sup>63</sup>It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh is no help at all. The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life.<sup>64</sup>But there are some of you who do not believe.” (For Jesus knew from the beginning who those were who did not believe, and who it was who would betray him.)<sup>65</sup>And he said, “This is why I told you that no one can come to me unless it is granted him by the Father.”<sup>66</sup>After this many of his disciples turned back and no longer walked with him.<sup>67</sup>So Jesus said to the twelve, “Do you want to go away as well?”<sup>68</sup>Simon Peter answered him, “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life,<sup>69</sup>and we have believed, and have come to know, that you are the Holy One of God.”<sup>70</sup>Jesus answered them, “Did I not choose you, the twelve? And yet one of you is a devil.”<sup>71</sup>He spoke of Judas the son of Simon Iscariot, for he, one of the twelve, was going to betray him.
6.overview:
John sets the feeding of the five thousand near Passover and lets it open into one of Jesus’ longest discourses. After the meal the crowd tries to make him king by force, and he withdraws; that night he comes to his disciples across the stormy lake with words that echo the divine name.

Next day, in the synagogue at Capernaum, he explains the sign. He himself is the true bread from heaven, of which the manna was a picture. All whom the Father gives him will come, none who come will be cast out, and he will raise them up on the last day. The bread is his flesh, given in death for the life of the world and received by faith. Many disciples leave; Peter says there is no one else to go to, though even among the Twelve is one who will betray him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter moves in three stages: Jesus’ refusal to go up on his brothers’ terms (vv. 1–13), his teaching in the temple in the middle of the feast (vv. 14–36), and his invitation on the last day, followed by the failed arrest and the council’s quarrel (vv. 37–52). Behind it all stands the hour of his death, which has not yet come.
verseByVerse.theology: The controversy in John 7 turns on where Jesus comes from and by whose authority he speaks. Asked how he knows the Scriptures without a rabbi, he answers that his teaching is not his own but the Father’s, and that anyone who wants to do God’s will will recognise it. The two questions, where he is from and who gave him authority, are really one: who sent him?
verseByVerse.examples: The Feast of Booths looked back to the wilderness and forward to the day when living waters would flow from Jerusalem (Zechariah 14:8). Jesus stands up at its climax and says that the river flows from him. The officers sent to arrest him came back saying that no one ever spoke like this man (v. 46).

verseByVerse.quote: After this Jesus went about in Galilee. He would not go about in Judea, because the Jews were seeking to kill him. Now the Jews' Feast of Booths was at hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. John 7 and 8 take place at one feast in Jerusalem, and the question running through both is: who is Jesus, and where does he come from? The setting is chosen with care: a week in which the nation camped in shelters of branches to remember God living among them in a tent, poured out water at the altar to remember the rock in the desert, and lit great lamps in the temple court. Into the middle of that week walks the one all three were pointing to.

After this. “After this” covers about six months, from Passover (6:4) in spring to the Feast of Booths in autumn. The hillside crowd of chapter 6 has melted away and many disciples have stopped walking with him (6:66). John records nothing of the summer; what he wants us to see is the next confrontation.

Seeking to kill him. Since the Sabbath healing in Jerusalem (5:18), the authorities had wanted him dead, and everything in this chapter happens with that threat hanging over it. His hour has not yet come (v. 30), and he will not die before the time the Father has set. Yet he is no coward: in the spring he will walk into Jerusalem in the open, knowing what waits for him. He is refusing to die at a time of other people’s choosing. He moves when the Father says, and his moves are never reactions.

The Feast of Booths. The Feast of Booths, or Tabernacles (skēnopēgia, pitching of tents), was the third of the great pilgrim festivals, along with Passover and Pentecost (Deuteronomy 16:16). It came in September or October, at the end of the harvest, and lasted seven days, with an eighth day of solemn assembly (Leviticus 23:33–43). Families built shelters of branches on courtyards and flat roofs and slept in them for the week, remembering the wilderness years when they had nothing and God provided everything. It was the most joyful feast of the year. They kept that feast for more than a thousand years, and in the year John describes, the God they were remembering was walking the roads of Galilee in a body, deciding when to go up to his own festival. He who had led them by cloud and fire now walked by his Father’s word, unhurried and unafraid, towards the feast, and beyond it towards the cross, where the true tabernacle, his body, would be torn down, to be raised again in three days.

The water and the light. By Jesus’ day two ceremonies had been added. Every morning a priest carried water up from the Pool of Siloam and poured it out at the altar, with prayers for rain and songs of joy (Isaiah 12:3). And at night great lamps were lit in the Court of the Women, lighting up all Jerusalem; the sources say there was not a courtyard in the city that did not glow with their light. Jesus will say “come to me and drink” (v. 37) and “I am the light of the world” (8:12) against this background. He is standing in front of the ceremony and saying that it was about him. Zechariah 14, with its living waters flowing from Jerusalem, belonged to this feast: it names Booths as the festival all the nations will one day keep (Zechariah 14:16).

Was Jesus wrong to avoid danger? Should he not have trusted the Father? No. Trusting God has never meant walking carelessly into harm. Jesus refused to throw himself from the temple to prove that God would catch him (Matthew 4:5–7), and here he refuses to throw himself into the hands of men who had already decided to kill him. Paul did the same when he was let down over the wall of Damascus in a basket (Acts 9:25). The question is not whether we take sensible steps to stay safe, but why. Fear says, I must save my life at any cost. Faith says, my life is in the Father’s hands, so I will neither waste it nor cling to it. When the hour came, the same Jesus who avoided Judea set his face to go to Jerusalem, and nothing could turn him back.
verseByVerse.note: The Feast of Booths (Tabernacles) was the joyful autumn harvest festival. For a week people lived in shelters made of branches, remembering Israel’s years in the wilderness.

parallels.desc: the Feast of Booths

verseByVerse.quote: So his brothers said to him, "Leave here and go to Judea, that your disciples also may see the works you are doing. For no one works in secret if he seeks to be known openly. If you do these things, show yourself to the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So his brothers said to him. His brothers were James, Joses, Judas and Simon (Mark 6:3), and Mark mentions sisters as well. Roman Catholic teaching takes them as cousins, and Eastern Orthodox teaching as Joseph’s sons by an earlier marriage, to preserve Mary’s perpetual virginity; but the natural reading is that they were Mary’s later sons (Matthew 1:25; Luke 2:7), and they appear again and again with Mary as her family (Mark 3:31; Acts 1:14).

Your disciples. “Your disciples” may mean the followers in Judea, or those who had turned away (6:66). The phrase is spoken at arm’s length: your disciples, not ours.

No one works in secret. They think like the world: if you want to be famous, go public. Read it as advice rather than villainy; any modern adviser would say the same. That is exactly what is wrong with it. His kingdom does not advance by staged displays for the largest possible audience.

Show yourself to the world. “If” reveals their doubt: they don’t deny the miracles, but they don’t trust him. It is the temptation Satan put to him (Matthew 4:5–7). He had shared the Father’s glory before the world existed (17:5), and he laid it aside so completely that his own brothers thought he needed a publicity campaign. And there is a terrible irony in the words: he will show himself to the world. In this Gospel that is what the cross is: the lifting up, the public display, the moment when he is shown to everybody, written over in three languages for every passer-by to read (19:20). His brothers have named the right event and the wrong method, and they have no idea that the showing they are urging on him will happen at Passover and will kill him.

Does it matter whether Mary had other children? It is not the centre of the gospel, but the plainest sense of the Gospels is that Jesus grew up in a crowded house with brothers and sisters, and Mary is honoured as the mother of our Lord without needing a perpetual virginity. (See Mark 6:3 for the fuller answer.)

In everyday life. Be wary of advice that measures faithfulness by publicity. The pressure is everywhere now: grow the following, post the result, build the brand, be seen. Some visibility is simply the cost of telling people the truth, and nobody should hide a light under a basket. But ask of any plan, in your church or your own heart: is this aimed at making Christ known, or at making me known? The two can look identical from the outside for a long time.
verseByVerse.note: His brothers were James, Joses, Judas and Simon.

verseByVerse.quote: For not even his brothers believed in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not even his brothers. John explains their advice (compare Mark 3:21), in an aside that is among the most useful in the New Testament for a particular kind of grief. These men had lived in the same small house with him for most of their lives, watched him work, eat, sleep and pray, and they did not believe. If moral excellence at close range were enough to produce faith, these four men would have been the first converts in history. Familiarity is the enemy of awe: they knew Jesus the man too well to recognise Jesus the Lord.

But that is not the end of the story. After the resurrection, Jesus appeared to James (1 Corinthians 15:7), and the brothers were among the believers praying in the upper room (Acts 1:14). James later led the church in Jerusalem (Acts 15:13; Galatians 2:9) and is generally held to have written the letter of James, as Judas (Jude) is held to have written the letter of Jude. The scandal of unbelief can be overcome, but only by resurrection: the same power that raised Jesus from the grave raised James from his unbelief.

The case was not closed. Take the person you have most nearly given up on. If this chapter had been the last word about James, every reasonable observer would have concluded the case was closed: a lifetime of evidence, no result. It was about six months from being reopened, and nothing in the meantime looked like progress. The worst week of all, the week his brother was crucified, was the week that, as far as we can tell, led to James’ conversion.

My family has watched my life for years and still does not believe. Have I failed them? Not necessarily. The most compelling life ever lived was on display in one household for thirty years and did not persuade the people in it. Unbelief is not proof that your witness was poor, and it is not proof that the case for Christ is weak. Faith is not produced by example alone; it is the gift of God, who opens blind eyes when he chooses (6:44). Your example still matters: live in a way that makes the gospel credible, apologise when you fail, keep loving them. But the burden of converting them was never yours to carry. Keep praying, keep loving, and leave the timing with the one who went to see James.

In everyday life. Write down the name of the relative you have quietly stopped praying for, and bring that name back to God today. And if you grew up around Christianity, take the warning: it is possible to have grown up in the very house and still not believe.

For worship. For thirty years the eternal Son let his brothers judge him ordinary, and he never forced their faith. When it came, it came as worship. James, who could have signed himself the brother of the Lord, wrote instead a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ (James 1:1); Jude called himself a servant of Jesus Christ, and only then a brother of James (Jude 1). The brothers who once told him to show himself to the world spent their lives showing him to it. He is patient with the people closest to him, and his patience wins.
verseByVerse.note: James later led the church in Jerusalem, and the brothers were among the believers after the resurrection.

parallels.desc: with Mary and his brothers
he appeared to James

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to them, "My time has not yet come, but your time is always here. The world cannot hate you, but it hates me because I testify about it that its works are evil."
verseByVerse.commentary:
My time has not yet come. “Time” here is kairos, the right moment for a thing. John’s usual word is the hour (hōra), the fixed appointment of his death and glorification, which turns up at Cana (2:4) and in verse 30 and finally arrives in chapter 12 (12:23). Jesus lives by the Father’s timetable, not his brothers’.

But your time is always here. For them any time is fine: they have no mission to fulfil, no appointment they are waiting on, and they are not under threat. He does not mean it as a compliment.

The world cannot hate you. “The world” in John is humanity organised in rebellion against God. It cannot hate them, because they belong to it. Not does not: cannot. They fit; they speak its language and want what it wants. He is telling his brothers that their safety is a bad sign: the world leaves them alone because they are no threat to it. Later he tells his disciples the same truth from the other side: if you were of the world, the world would love you as its own (15:19).

Its works are evil. Light shows up the darkness (3:19–20). People don’t object to Jesus as a teacher of kindness; they object when he says their works are evil. The world tolerates many kinds of religion and moral teaching; it cannot tolerate the claim that its basic direction is sinful and that only grace can save it. The cross is the world’s answer to that testimony. He could have been loved by the world: he had only to stop saying that its works were evil, and it would have praised him to the end. He loved the world too much to flatter it, and he let it hate him to death, so that the people who hated him could be forgiven. The light did not dim itself to be welcome in the dark.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that being disliked is proof of faithfulness. Many Christians are disliked for being rude, ignorant, harsh or politically obnoxious, and that hostility has nothing to do with Christ. The verse names the cause exactly: the world hates him because he testifies that its works are evil. The offence is having the truth told about oneself by someone who loves you enough to tell it. So the test is narrow: not, am I disliked? but, is there anything in my life that would make the world uncomfortable if it were paying attention? A faith with no friction at all may simply be a private faith. It may also be one that has quietly stopped saying the thing that causes friction; and the one who bore the world’s hatred for us gives his Spirit for both courage and love.

Is it not arrogant for Jesus to call the world’s works evil? That charge would stick only if he spoke from a safe height and exempted himself and his friends. He did neither. He says it to the devout and the careless alike, to his own brothers in this verse and to the leaders of the temple in the same chapter, and he says it as the one who has come to carry that evil away. A doctor who tells you the truth about the tumour is not arrogant; the one who hides it to keep you comfortable is cruel. And this doctor pays for the cure himself, with his own life. A teacher who never names evil can never save anyone from it.

But does God not love the world (3:16)? How can the world be the enemy? Both are true, and John holds them together. The world is humanity in rebellion against God, and God loves it anyway, not because it is lovable but because he is love. He loved it enough to send his Son into it, knowing it would hate him. So when Jesus says the world hates him, he is not describing a world God has given up on; he is describing the world he came to save. Christians are called to the same double stance: not loving the world’s rebellion (1 John 2:15), and loving the people caught in it enough to tell them the truth.

parallels.desc: if the world hates you

verseByVerse.quote: "You go up to the feast. I am not going up to this feast, for my time has not yet fully come." After saying this, he remained in Galilee.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You go up to the feast. Jerusalem stands high in the hills, so one always went up to it; the pilgrim psalms are the Songs of Ascents (Psalms 120–134).

I am not going up to this feast. Yet he does go (v. 10); the charge of lying is answered below. Some see a play on “go up”: the same verb is used of his ascending to the Father (20:17). He will not “go up” in that sense, to glory, at this feast.

A charge worth answering. The sentence has been used for centuries to accuse Jesus of lying. The third-century critic Porphyry pressed exactly this point. It can be answered well, because the whole exchange is about how he goes, not whether he travels. His brothers were not offering him a lift to Jerusalem; they were urging a campaign: show yourself to the world (v. 4), go up publicly, with the crowds, and stake your claim. That is the going up he refuses. And John himself supplies the distinction in the very next sentence: when Jesus did go, he went not publicly but in private (v. 10). The man who would shortly refuse to come down from a cross was not a man who trimmed his words to make an afternoon easier.

For my time has not yet fully come. “Fully come” (peplērōtai, been fulfilled). He is not managing his image with a convenient untruth; he is declining a schedule that was not his Father’s.

Textual note. Many manuscripts, including two of the earliest papyri, read “I am not yet going up,” and the KJV and NKJV follow them. Other early manuscripts read “I am not going up,” and most modern Bibles judge this the original, since a scribe was more likely to add “yet” to ease the problem than to remove it. So the honest course is to answer the harder text rather than shelter behind the easier, and as we have seen, the harder text needs no shelter.

If manuscripts differ, can I trust my Bible? Yes. We have far more early copies of the New Testament than of any other ancient book, and comparing them lets scholars see clearly where a copyist slipped or smoothed. The great majority of differences are spelling, word order or small words like this “yet”, and none of them touches any teaching of the faith. This very note shows it: the reading that looks harder is kept precisely because it is harder, which shows that the copyists were not freely inventing but were anxious about every word. Your Bible’s footnotes are not a sign that the text is shaky. They are a sign that it has been handled with great care.

He remained in Galilee. The remaining is not passivity but restraint: the hour has been set from eternity and cannot be rushed by family pressure or popular demand. And when the hour did come, nothing could stop him going up: up to Jerusalem, up onto the cross, up from the grave, and up to the Father’s right hand, where he reigns over every timetable in the world, including yours.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add “yet”: “I am not yet going up.”

verseByVerse.quote: But after his brothers had gone up to the feast, then he also went up, not publicly but in private. The Jews were looking for him at the feast, and saying, "Where is he?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not publicly but in private. The Son of God goes up to his own people’s feast in a stream of pilgrims, unrecognised. And the secrecy is temporary: he goes up hidden in verse 10 and is teaching in the temple courts by verse 14. What he refused was his brothers’ method: the arrival, the entourage, the staged display. Days later he does the most public thing available to a man in Jerusalem, and does it alone.

Looking for him. Two searches run through the chapter: the authorities are looking for him in order to end him, and the crowd because they cannot stop talking about him. He walks through the middle of both.

Where is he? “Where” is a key word in John 7 and 8: where he comes from, and where he is going (vv. 27, 34–35; 8:14, 21). And the question has a coldness to it. They will not use his name. It is the tone of people discussing somebody they have already decided about. Yet beneath the surface it is the deepest question there is: where is God? The answer John gives across twenty-one chapters is that he is here, in this man, at this feast.

The man they cannot find is the tent. The word for the feast comes from the same root as the verb John used in his opening chapter: the Word became flesh and dwelt, literally pitched his tent, among us (1:14). The whole city is sleeping under branches to remember the time God travelled with them in a tent, and the man they are looking for is the tent. He who once filled the tabernacle with a glory so great that Moses could not enter (Exodus 40:35) came up the road dusty and anonymous, so that he could stand among his people and call them to himself. He came close enough to be overlooked.

Is it ever right for a Christian to be secret? Sometimes discretion is wisdom, and Jesus himself shows it here. Believers in hostile countries meet quietly; a Christian may wisely choose not to announce every plan to people who mean him harm (Matthew 10:16–17). But there is a difference between discretion about our movements and silence about our Lord. Jesus hid his journey for a few days; he never hid who he was. If we are hiding our faith because we are ashamed of Christ, that is not wisdom but fear (Mark 8:38). Prudence protects the mission. Cowardice abandons it.

verseByVerse.quote: And there was much muttering about him among the people. While some said, "He is a good man," others said, "No, he is leading the people astray." Yet for fear of the Jews no one spoke openly of him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Much muttering. “Muttering” is the same word as “grumbled” in 6:41 (gongysmos), here meaning whispered debate. It is the word for Israel’s grumbling in the desert, used here of admirers and accusers alike.

Some said, “He is a good man.” A compliment that falls far short (see below). It is the kindly verdict, and the one most people still reach for.

Others said, “No, he is leading the people astray.” “Leading astray” (planaō) was a serious charge: the false prophet who leads Israel away from God was to be put to death (Deuteronomy 13:1–5). Later Jewish writings describe Jesus as one who practised sorcery and led Israel astray, and misleading the nation is among the charges brought against him before Pilate (Luke 23:2). The one thing nobody in this verse says is that he might be telling the truth about himself.

For fear of the Jews. Fear of the leaders silences everyone, and it is not the opposition who are silent. It is the people who think well of him who say nothing. The phrase becomes one of John’s refrains: it is why the blind man’s parents will not answer a straight question (9:22), why Joseph of Arimathea kept his discipleship quiet (19:38). John will name the root: they loved the glory that comes from man more than the glory that comes from God (12:43). Yet the Lord who was mumbled about in the courts of his own temple will one day be confessed aloud by every tongue, to the glory of God the Father (Philippians 2:11).

Why can’t Jesus simply be a good man and a great teacher? Because of what he taught. A good man does not claim to be equal with God, to forgive sins against other people, to be the bread from heaven, or to be the one by whom everyone will be judged. If those claims are false, he is either deceived about himself on a scale no sane good man could be, or he is deceiving others, which is exactly the charge in this verse. The verdicts that take him seriously are that he was deceived, that he was a deceiver, or that he is the Lord. Some reply that the large claims were put in his mouth by the later church; but the earliest sources we have, Mark and the letters of Paul, written within a few decades, already present him forgiving sins and claiming to be the coming judge (Mark 2:5–10; 14:62), and already worship him as Lord (Philippians 2:9–11), so the question cannot be dodged that way. The good teacher who claims nothing is a figure people invented later to avoid having to decide.

Does John’s phrase “the Jews” make his Gospel anti-Jewish? No. John was a Jew, Jesus was a Jew, every disciple and nearly every believer in this Gospel is a Jew, and Jesus says salvation is from the Jews (4:22). In passages like this, “the Jews” plainly means the religious authorities in Jerusalem who opposed him, as the sentence itself shows: the Jewish crowd is afraid of the Jews. The Gospel never gives any warrant for hatred of the Jewish people. Christians who have used it that way have sinned grievously, and contempt for Jews is a denial of the Christ who was born a son of David and wept over Jerusalem.

In everyday life. Recall a recent conversation in which the subject came near enough that you could have said something about him, and you did not. What held you back was probably not persecution but the half-second of awkwardness, the sense of becoming the person who brings that up. The pressure here was far heavier than ours; the mechanism is the same. He was not ashamed to die openly for you, and his Spirit gives the words: next time, say one true sentence about him.

parallels.desc: a prophet who leads you astray
that impostor

verseByVerse.quote: About the middle of the feast Jesus went up into the temple and began teaching. The Jews therefore marveled, saying, "How is it that this man has learning, when he has never studied?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
About the middle of the feast. Around the fourth day of the seven. The timing is deliberate: he let the festival fill up until the crowds were at their largest, and then walked into the busiest place in Jerusalem and began to teach.

Into the temple. Now he appears openly, in the temple courts where rabbis taught. Malachi had promised that the Lord whom you seek would suddenly come to his temple (Malachi 3:1). In the middle of a feast, without announcement, he does, and before long he is exposing the hearts of the men who ran it (v. 19).

How is it that this man has learning, when he has never studied? “Learning” is literally “letters” (grammata), meaning knowledge of the Scriptures and their interpretation. It is not a claim that he was illiterate; Luke shows him handed a scroll in the synagogue and finding his place in it (Luke 4:16–17). “Never studied” means he had not been trained under a recognised rabbi, the way Paul was trained under Gamaliel (Acts 22:3). A teacher was expected to cite his teachers: Rabbi So-and-so said, in the name of Rabbi So-and-so. That is how authority worked, and it is not a foolish system; it is how a community protects itself from anyone who turns up with a private revelation. Jesus quoted no rabbi, and yet he knew the Scriptures more deeply than any of them. They are not sneering, quite. They are trying to account for something that does not fit their categories. The same surprise is expressed about the apostles (Acts 4:13).

Does this mean training does not matter for preachers? No. The system was not wrong to ask where he had studied, and that question has saved the church from a great deal of nonsense. Paul was highly trained, and Scripture requires that elders be able to teach and hold firm to sound doctrine (Titus 1:9; 2 Timothy 2:15). Jesus is unique: his teacher was the Father, which no one else can claim. For everyone else, study is the ordinary way God makes faithful teachers. But the final test is not a certificate. It is whether a teacher’s words agree with Scripture and point to Christ. A trained man can be wrong, and an untrained believer can be right, and both must be weighed by the Word.

For worship. Christ needed no teacher but the Father. The rabbis looked for a chain of teachers behind him and found none, because the chain ended in him: he is the Word who was with God in the beginning, and every true teacher who has ever opened the Scriptures has been borrowing from him. In him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Colossians 2:3), and he gives them freely to fishermen.
verseByVerse.note: “Never studied” means he had not been trained under a recognised rabbi.

parallels.desc: uneducated, common men

verseByVerse.quote: So Jesus answered them, "My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me. If anyone's will is to do God's will, he will know whether the teaching is from God or whether I am speaking on my own authority."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not mine. Jesus answers their question. He did have a teacher: the Father (5:19; 8:28; 12:49). The Son learned in eternal fellowship with the Father, a far greater authority than any line of rabbis. He who is God took the posture of one who listens, receives and passes on, so that what reaches us is nothing less than the Father’s own word.

If anyone’s will is to do God’s will. “Will” (thelē) means wants, wills, desires. The condition for knowing the truth is not first intellectual, but moral and spiritual: a will set on doing what God wants. This answers a question honest people ask: how could I know whether this is true? He offers no argument or sign: willingness first, knowledge second. If a person insists on staying uncommitted while he weighs the evidence, that stance, however honest, keeps him from the one kind of evidence that matters most here.

He will know. The problem with unbelief is not lack of evidence but an unwilling heart (5:40; 8:43–47). That can sound like a cheat, but it is not. Some things can be known while remaining uninvolved, like the boiling point of water; others are only knowable from inside. Nobody has ever learned whether a person is trustworthy by studying them at a distance; you find out by trusting them. To claim that God is known in the second way is not a dodge. It is a claim about what sort of being God is: not an object to be examined but a Lord to be obeyed. And the promise is wide: not if anyone is clever or educated. The condition is a willing heart, not an achievement, and it is open to the least equipped person in the room.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that we can come to faith by our own good will, as if some people are naturally willing. John has just said no one can come unless the Father draws (6:44). The willing heart is itself God’s work. Whoever is of God hears the words of God (8:47). The verse describes how the Father’s drawing works: he gives a heart that wants to obey, and that heart recognises the Son’s teaching as God’s. But it does mean that the person who genuinely wants God’s will will never be left in the dark.

I want to believe, but I still have doubts. Does that mean my will is not set on God? No. Doubt is not the same as unwillingness. Many true believers carry questions for years, and Scripture is full of them (Psalm 73; Mark 9:24). What this verse describes is the person who keeps God at arm’s length so as not to have to obey him. If you want God’s will, even weakly, and you are grieved by your doubts rather than comfortable with them, that wanting is itself his work in you. Bring your questions to him, keep reading his word, and keep obeying what you already know. Light comes along the road of obedience, often more slowly than we would like, but it comes.

In everyday life. Take the one thing you already suspect God wants of you: not a doctrine you are unsure of, but the plain duty you have been avoiding, the apology, the confession, the habit. Do that, in the strength of the Spirit who gave you the wanting. Sometimes the doubt was standing on top of the disobedience, and cannot survive its removal. You will not obey perfectly; the Son did his Father’s will perfectly for you, his obedience is counted as yours, and your halting obedience is accepted in him.

verseByVerse.quote: "The one who speaks on his own authority seeks his own glory; but the one who seeks the glory of him who sent him is true, and in him there is no falsehood. Has not Moses given you the law? Yet none of you keeps the law. Why do you seek to kill me?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seeks his own glory. A test for any teacher: whose glory does he seek? Not eloquence or success, but the direction his ambition points: who is bigger at the end of the sermon?

No falsehood. Jesus seeks only the Father’s glory, and that is the proof of his truthfulness. “Falsehood” here is adikia, unrighteousness. He is not merely claiming to be accurate; he is claiming that there is nothing crooked in him at all, no bent motive under the straight sentence. It is either true or insufferable, and in him it is simply true.

Has not Moses given you the law? Yet none of you keeps the law. Jesus turns to the attack. They pride themselves on Moses, but they don’t keep his law. The change of tone is abrupt. He has been reasoning; now he accuses.

Why do you seek to kill me? The proof: the law forbids murder, and they are planning one. They accuse Jesus of breaking the Sabbath, while they are planning to break the sixth commandment. It is the first time in the chapter that anybody says it out loud. John told the reader at verse 1, but no one in the courts has admitted it, and Jesus puts it in the middle of an argument about Moses, the most pointed place it could go. The charge is not exaggeration. Within months they will do precisely that, and it will be arranged by the men standing in front of him. He is reading their diary aloud.

In the flow. Verse 19 turns the question back on his hearers and leads into verses 21–24, where he defends the Sabbath healing of chapter 5 from their own law: the accused becomes the judge.

How can I tell whether a preacher is seeking his own glory? Watch over time, not over a single sermon, because the test works over years rather than sentences. A man seeking Christ’s glory will make Christ large and himself small in his preaching; he will open the text rather than use it as a launch pad for himself. He will be accountable to others and will not build a ministry that cannot survive without him. He will be glad when someone else is preferred, slow to defend his own reputation, and quick to admit when he is wrong. Be wary of the teacher whose stories are mostly about himself, who cannot take correction, or whose church seems to exist to display him. And turn the test on yourself: when you serve, whose name do you most want remembered?

For worship. There has only ever been one teacher in whom there was no falsehood at all. Every word he spoke aimed at his Father’s glory, and the Father answered by glorifying him (17:1). The men who held Moses in their hands and murder in their hearts stood before the only man who ever kept the law perfectly, and he kept it for them, all the way to the cross they were planning for him.

verseByVerse.quote: The crowd answered, "You have a demon! Who is seeking to kill you?" Jesus answered them, "I did one work, and you all marvel at it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You have a demon. “Have a demon” was a way of saying mad (10:20); the same charge returns in 8:48, 52. On the crowd’s part this is not so much hostility as alarm. Pilgrims who know nothing of the leaders’ plot hear a teacher say people are trying to murder him and conclude he is unwell. Anyone who names what the room has agreed not to see is usually called mad; it is the cheapest response available. In this case the man was entirely correct.

Who is seeking to kill you? They don’t know. The leaders do (v. 25). It is worth keeping the two groups apart in this chapter, because John does. The crowd here is the festival pilgrims: ignorant, volatile and mostly well disposed. “The Jews”, in John’s shorthand, generally means the Jerusalem leadership, the men in verse 1 who had already decided. When the crowd asks who is seeking to kill him, they are telling the truth; they do not know. The reader has been told in the chapter’s first sentence, and so watches the exchange knowing what the crowd does not know.

One work. The “one work” is the healing at the pool on the Sabbath (5:1–9), which started the plot to kill him. “Marvel” here means they are disturbed and shocked by it, not admiring. His reply goes straight past the insult. The Holy One, on whom the Spirit rested without measure, heard his own people say he had a demon, and he did not answer evil for evil. And count how long ago that was: chapter 5 was at an unnamed feast, chapter 6 at Passover, and this is Tabernacles. Many months on, they are still on it. The word “one” shows how far out of proportion the grievance is. A single act of kindness to a man who had been ill for thirty-eight years has produced a settled determination to kill the one who did it, and the grievance has outlasted the memory of everything else he has done.

How should I respond when people think my faith is foolish or unhinged? Much as Jesus did: without panic and without retaliation. He did not argue about whether he was mad; he went straight back to the real issue. When people call your faith foolish, do not take the bait of defending your sanity or your intelligence. Gently bring the conversation back to Christ himself: what he did, what he said, why it matters. Paul was told he was out of his mind and answered with courtesy and the truth (Acts 26:24–25). And remember that if they said it of the Master, they will say it of his servants (15:20). It is not a sign you have failed. It may be a sign you have been clear.

In everyday life. Most of us carry a grievance like this somewhere: one act, by one person, still held against them months or years later, while everything else they have done is forgotten. Grudges grow in the dark. Brought to the God who has dropped every charge against you, they can be seen for the size they really are, and let go.
verseByVerse.note: The “one work” is the healing at the pool on the Sabbath.

verseByVerse.quote: "Moses gave you circumcision (not that it is from Moses, but from the fathers), and you circumcise a man on the Sabbath."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses gave you circumcision. Jesus argues from their own law, in a standard rabbinic form his opponents would have recognised instantly.

Not that it is from Moses, but from the fathers. Circumcision was given to Abraham (Genesis 17:10–12), centuries before Moses, and the law confirmed it (Leviticus 12:3). The obligation they allow to override the Sabbath is older than the Sabbath laws of Sinai. He is showing them that they already know how to rank two commandments when they seem to collide.

You circumcise a man. The law said a boy must be circumcised on the eighth day. If the eighth day fell on a Sabbath, circumcision went ahead, even though it was work. The rabbis agreed, and the Mishnah says everything needed for circumcision may be done on the Sabbath. Jesus is not proposing a novelty; he is taking their own ruling and asking why it stops where it does.

What kind of thing wins. Circumcision overrides the Sabbath because it marks a child as belonging to God. The rule they already accept is not a technicality. It is about mercy. When a rule and a person’s standing before God seem to collide, the person wins. Jesus is about to apply that to a man who had been on a mat for thirty-eight years, and it is their principle, not his.

Does this mean God’s commandments can be broken when they clash? No. God’s law does not contradict itself; the problem lies in how men had applied it. The Sabbath was never meant to forbid works of necessity and mercy, and even the confessions that keep Sunday as the Christian Sabbath, the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, say so plainly, permitting works of necessity and mercy (Westminster 21.8; 1689 22.8). Jesus is not setting one command against another. He is showing that the command, rightly understood, always had room for love. When we feel that obeying God and loving people are in conflict, the answer is not to drop one but to look again at what God actually commanded.

For worship. The Lord who reasoned so patiently about the eighth-day sign had received it himself: Luke tells us he was circumcised as a boy of eight days (Luke 2:21), marked with the covenant he had made with Abraham. And what the sign promised, he gives: a circumcision made without hands, the putting off of the body of the flesh by the circumcision of Christ (Colossians 2:11), so that people from every nation are marked as God’s own, not by a knife but by his death and rising.
verseByVerse.note: Circumcision on the eighth day went ahead even when that day was a Sabbath. It began with Abraham, before Moses.

verseByVerse.quote: "If on the Sabbath a man receives circumcision, so that the law of Moses may not be broken, are you angry with me because on the Sabbath I made a man's whole body well? Do not judge by appearances, but judge with right judgment."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Light and heavy. The argument goes from lesser to greater, a standard rabbinic method, which they called light and heavy. If it is right to perform circumcision, which affects one part of the body, on the Sabbath...

Are you angry with me because on the Sabbath I made a man’s whole body well? ...how much more right is it to make a whole man well? Some rabbis themselves argued that if circumcision, involving one member, overrides the Sabbath, saving a life overrides it too. Jesus takes the argument further: healing fits the very purpose of the Sabbath, a day of rest and restoration.

Right judgment. “Appearances” (opsis) means what is seen on the surface: they see only that he worked on the Sabbath. Right judgment looks at what was really done, and why, as God looks on the heart (1 Samuel 16:7). This verse is regularly quoted as if it said the opposite of what it says. It is a command to judge. Jesus is in the middle of telling a crowd that their verdict on him is wrong, and his complaint is not that they judged but that they judged badly.

So am I allowed to judge people or not? Yes and no, and Jesus’ two sayings fit together once you notice what each is about. Judge not, that you be not judged (Matthew 7:1) forbids the judgment that sets itself up as final, condemns the person, and applies to others a standard the speaker exempts himself from; it is followed at once by the log in one’s own eye. This verse requires the judgment that looks past the surface to the substance. The first forbids condemning. The second commands discerning. A Christian must tell right from wrong, truth from error, and a wolf from a sheep. What he must never do is sit in God’s seat over another person’s soul, or judge by rumour, appearance or prejudice.

Where Christians differ: the Sabbath today. Jesus never abolished the Sabbath in the Gospels, but showed its true purpose. Some Christians keep a strict Saturday or Sunday Sabbath; others see no special day at all. This commentary’s view: the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, our rest (Hebrews 4:9–10; Colossians 2:16–17). The Lord’s Day, the first day, when Christ rose, is a privilege for Christians, set apart gladly for worship, fellowship and rest, not as a binding law with rules about work, and with works of mercy always in place; no one may bind another’s conscience about it (Romans 14:5). The view of the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, that the Lord’s Day is the Christian Sabbath under the fourth commandment (Westminster 21.7–8; 1689 22.7–8), is held by many godly brothers and deserves respect.

What does keeping the Lord’s Day look like in practice? Begin with what it is for: meeting the risen Christ with his people. So put gathered worship at the centre and arrange the rest of the day around it, rather than fitting church into a busy Sunday. Rest from your ordinary work where you can, not as a rule to earn favour but as a gift that says your life does not depend on your labour. Make room for what refreshes the soul: the word, prayer, family, hospitality, visiting the lonely or the sick. Works of mercy and necessity are always in place: nurses, carers and parents of small children are not breaking anything. And do not make the day a burden for others; Jesus came to free the Sabbath from that.

parallels.desc: judge righteously

verseByVerse.quote: Some of the people of Jerusalem therefore said, "Is not this the man whom they seek to kill? And here he is, speaking openly, and they say nothing to him! Can it be that the authorities really know that this is the Christ?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people of Jerusalem. Not the pilgrims, but locals who know the plot the crowd denied (v. 20), watching a man the leaders want dead teach in the temple courts untouched.

Speaking openly. “Openly” is parrhēsia, saying everything without holding back, the word used of the crowd in verse 13: no one spoke openly of him. The people who admire him whisper; the man they want dead speaks freely in the temple.

Can it be that the authorities really know that this is the Christ? The Greek form expects the answer no. They are half joking, half wondering. “The Christ” (ho Christos), the Messiah, the anointed king. Their reasoning is not stupid. If the authorities wanted him, and he is standing in public, and nothing is happening, then something must have changed, and the only explanation they can think of is that the rulers have quietly come round.

The restraint nobody can see. They are wrong, and John will supply the reason four verses later: no one laid a hand on him, because his hour had not yet come (v. 30). The inaction they are trying to explain is a restraint nobody in the story can see. That is the shape of a great deal of providence, God’s unseen hand governing great events and small, so that not even a sparrow falls apart from your Father (Matthew 10:29). Things do not happen, and everyone constructs a reason; the real reason is not available to the people looking for it.

verseByVerse.quote: "But we know where this man comes from, and when the Christ appears, no one will know where he comes from."
verseByVerse.commentary:
We know. They know he is from Nazareth in Galilee. And “we know” carries the deepest irony in the chapter, because they do not know. John’s readers have known since the first verse that he comes from the Father’s side, and that the true answer to where he is from is a place none of them has considered.

No one will know. Some expected the Messiah to appear suddenly from hiding. Jewish writings speak of the Messiah being hidden until God revealed him. Others knew he would come from Bethlehem (v. 42). The crowd uses both traditions against him within fifteen verses. Here he is disqualified because his origin is known. In verse 42 he is disqualified because it is the wrong one. Any candidate who satisfied the second would fail the first.

The irony. They know neither his birthplace, Bethlehem, nor his true origin, the Father. Using two objections that cancel each other out is a recognisable human habit, not a peculiarly Jewish one. When a conclusion has been reached in advance, the reasons arrive afterwards and do not need to be consistent with each other, since their job is not to establish the conclusion but to protect it.

So where did Jesus come from? Three answers, all true. As a man, he was born in Bethlehem, the town of David, as Micah foretold (Matthew 2:1–6), and grew up in Nazareth, which is why he was called a Nazarene. As the Son, he came from the Father, with whom he was before the world began (1:1; 17:5). And he came into the world by the Holy Spirit, conceived in the womb of the virgin Mary (Luke 1:35). His enemies knew only the town where he grew up. Faith knows all of them: the eternal Son, born of a woman, raised in a despised village, so that no one could say God had come too high for them to reach.

For worship. The one whose goings forth are from of old, from ancient days (Micah 5:2), consented to have a hometown that people could sneer at. He came from the Father’s side to a carpenter’s house, and let men think they had him summed up. They did not know that the man in front of them had made the hills that Nazareth stood on.
verseByVerse.note: Some expected the Messiah to appear suddenly from hiding.

verseByVerse.quote: "So Jesus proclaimed, as he taught in the temple, 'You know me, and you know where I come from. But I have not come of my own accord. He who sent me is true, and him you do not know. I know him, for I come from him, and he sent me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Jesus proclaimed. “Proclaimed” (ekraxen, cried out): a loud, public, solemn declaration (v. 37; 12:44). He raises his voice in the temple courts.

You know me. It can be read as a concession, yes, you know the human facts and they are correct as far as they go, or with an edge, as near to sarcasm as he comes: so you know me, do you? The sentence that follows tips it toward the second. Whatever they know, it has left them ignorant of the one thing that would explain him: he has not come of his own accord, but was sent.

Him you do not know. “True” (alēthinos): genuine, real. To reject the Son is to show you do not know the Father (8:19; 15:21). He tells a courtyard of devout people, at their own feast, that they do not know God, not imperfectly but at all, and that he does. A man may say a great deal about God in that building and survive it; this is the charge they will not forgive.

I know him. Jesus knows the Father because he came from the Father’s presence. The ground he gives is not experience but origin: he started with God, as God (1:1, 18). No prophet, priest or rabbi had ever stood in the Father’s presence and come out to tell us what he saw. He came out shouting it in the temple, and then he opened the way into the Father’s presence with his own blood, so that people who did not know God could be brought home to him.

In the flow. The crowd has just said they know where he comes from (v. 27). Jesus says they know only the half that matters least: he comes from the Father who sent him. Everything else in John 7 and 8 rests on this claim, and the attempt to arrest him in the next verse shows they understood how much he was claiming.

Can someone be sincerely religious and still not know God? Yes, and this verse is the proof. These men prayed, fasted, studied Scripture and kept the feasts, and Jesus says they did not know the one they worshipped. Knowing God is not the same as being religious. Eternal life is to know the only true God and Jesus Christ whom he has sent (17:3), and no one comes to the Father except through the Son (14:6). That is not a reason to sneer at sincere people of other faiths or none, but it is a reason not to leave them where they are. And it is a question to ask ourselves, gently and honestly: do I know God through Christ, or do I only know the religion?

In everyday life. Knowing God comes through knowing the Son. If God feels distant or unreal to you, look at Jesus: read a Gospel, slowly, and ask at each page, so this is what God is like. Then talk to him about what you see.

verseByVerse.quote: So they were seeking to arrest him, but no one laid a hand on him, because his hour had not yet come. Yet many of the people believed in him. They said, "When the Christ appears, will he do more signs than this man has done?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
His hour had not yet come. Now the word John has been holding back returns: not kairos, the right moment of verse 6, but hōra, the appointment of his death, resurrection and return to the Father (2:4; 8:20; 12:23; 13:1; 17:1). That hour is the cross, and it will not come until chapter 12. What protects him here is not a bodyguard but an appointment with his own execution that has not yet fallen due. He is safe because his death is fixed for another day.

Does this mean nothing bad can happen to me until my work is done? Not quite, and it is worth being honest about what the verse promises. It does not say God’s servants are always preserved until they have done everything we think they should do; Stephen was stoned early in his ministry, and John the Baptist was beheaded on a whim at a party. What it says is narrower, harder and more solid: nothing whatever happens outside the Father’s timing, including the things that look like defeat. The same providence that kept hands off Jesus in this verse will hand him over in chapter 18, and it is the same providence doing the same loving work. Your days are written in his book (Psalm 139:16). No accident, no enemy and no illness can shorten them by an hour.

Many believed. In John, belief can be shallow (2:23–25; 8:30–31), but here it is a start. In a chapter of hostility and arrest warrants, faith is quietly spreading.

When the Christ appears, will he do more signs than this man has done? They reason from the signs. This is not the deepest faith, but signs are meant to lead to faith (20:30–31). Their reasoning is modest and mostly right: could anyone do more than this? It is not a complete confession. It is not nothing.
