Is faith that starts from miracles real faith? It can be the beginning of real faith, and Jesus does not despise it. He does not break a bruised reed (Matthew 12:20). John himself wrote down the signs so that we may believe (20:31). But faith that only wants more signs, and stops at what Jesus can do, has not yet reached who he is. The crowd in chapter 6 wanted more bread and walked away when he offered himself. True faith moves from the works to the person: from what he did, to trusting him, loving him and following him when there are no signs at all. Whatever first drew you to Christ, the question is whether you have come to rest in him.

parallels.desc: his hour had come

verseByVerse.quote: The Pharisees heard the crowd muttering these things about him, and the chief priests and Pharisees sent officers to arrest him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowd muttering. What actually triggers the warrant is telling. Not the teaching, not the Sabbath argument, not the claim in verse 29 to have come from God. It is verse 31: the muttering of the crowd, the fact that people are starting to believe. The Pharisees move when the numbers move. What got reported was not a sermon but the mood of ordinary people, which tells you what they feared to lose: their grip on the people. When religion becomes a position to protect, the coming of God himself feels like a threat, and the people who should have been first to welcome him are the first to send for the police.

The chief priests and Pharisees. Two groups who normally disagreed. The chief priests were mostly Sadducees, the priestly aristocracy who controlled the temple and denied the resurrection (Acts 23:8); the Pharisees were the lay party of strict law-keeping. Together they made up much of the Sanhedrin, and in this Gospel they act together only to deal with him (11:47, 57; 18:3). Opposition to Christ unites people who cannot stand each other, as it will unite Herod and Pilate (Luke 23:12).

Officers to arrest him. The officers were the temple police, Levites who kept order in the temple under the chief priests. The rulers of the temple sent officers against the Lord of the temple. They set out with a straightforward job, and they will come back empty-handed, saying that no one ever spoke like this man (v. 46).
verseByVerse.note: The officers were the temple police.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus then said, "I will be with you a little longer, and then I am going to him who sent me. You will seek me and you will not find me. Where I am you cannot come."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will be with you a little longer. About six months remained before the cross. He answers a warrant for his arrest by announcing his travel plans, and the effect is to take the whole confrontation out of their hands. They think they are deciding whether he stays. He tells them he is leaving anyway, shortly, and for somewhere they cannot follow.

Going to him who sent me. Jesus speaks of his death, resurrection and ascension as a going home to the Father (13:1, 3; 16:5, 28). He is not driven out; he goes.

You will not find me. A solemn warning: there will come a time when it is too late. Compare Proverbs 1:28 and Isaiah 55:6: seek the Lord while he may be found. It is addressed to men holding an arrest warrant, who will one day want what he offered and find the offer withdrawn. That is not a threat aimed at the worried. It is a fact aimed at the comfortable.

Where I am you cannot come. Not “where I will be” but “where I am”: he speaks as the one who already belongs to the Father’s presence. Unbelievers cannot follow him there (8:21). He says something similar to the disciples later (13:33), but with a promise: you will follow afterwards (13:36; 14:3).

I am frightened that it may be too late for me. Is this verse about me? If you are troubled by it, that trouble is itself the evidence that it is not describing you. The seeking that fails in this verse is not the seeking of the frightened; it is the seeking of men who refused him to his face, and who would one day want rescue without wanting him. Scripture never shows a penitent sinner coming to God and finding the door shut. The whole burden of this Gospel is the opposite: whoever comes to me I will never cast out (6:37), said to a crowd that mostly walked away. While you are alive and can call on him, the door is open. Call on him now.

In everyday life. If there is something you have been meaning to settle with God, a sin to confess, a step of obedience, a first prayer, do not leave it for a better week.

For worship. He went home to the Father by way of the cross, and he did not go alone. The place where his enemies could not come is the place he has gone to prepare for his friends (14:2–3). To unbelief he says, where I am you cannot come; to faith he says, I will come again and take you to myself, that where I am you may be also. The same words that warn the proud are the hope of every believer.

verseByVerse.quote: The Jews said to one another, "Where does this man intend to go that we will not find him? Does he intend to go to the Dispersion among the Greeks and teach the Greeks? What does he mean by saying, 'You will seek me and you will not find me,' and, 'Where I am you cannot come'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Where does this man intend to go that we will not find him? They misunderstand again, thinking only of earthly places.

Does he intend to go to the Dispersion among the Greeks and teach the Greeks? The Dispersion (diaspora) means the Jews living scattered outside the land of Israel, in the cities of the Greek-speaking world. Probably more Jews lived outside the land than in it. They mockingly suggest he will go and teach Gentiles, something no respectable Jerusalem teacher would do. They are making his words sound absurd: either the man is talking nonsense, or he means something ridiculous, like going off to the scattered communities in foreign cities and teaching foreigners.

The irony. Their mocking guess was prophetic. Through his apostles, Jesus did go to the Dispersion and teach the Greeks. The gospel went from Jerusalem to the synagogues of the Dispersion and then to the Gentiles (Acts 11:20; 13:46), carried above all by Paul, a Pharisee trained in Jerusalem, and the letters of James and 1 Peter are addressed to the Dispersion. John was probably writing for readers who lived in those cities. When they reached this sentence, they were reading a mocking question that had turned into their own address.

Enemies who say more than they know. It is not the only time opponents of Jesus say more than they know. It will happen again at 11:50, when Caiaphas remarks that it is better for one man to die for the people, and John stops the story to point out that he was prophesying without the least idea of it. The people most determined to stop him are being used, and their own sentences are being taken up and made true in a sense they would have found intolerable. The Lord of history takes even the sneers of his enemies and writes them into his plan. A taunt in the temple became a map of the mission, and the scattered nations heard the voice that Jerusalem refused.

What does he mean by saying...? They cannot understand, because they are thinking on the wrong level. And look at what they do with his words. They quote them back, both halves, in full: you will seek me and you will not find me, and where I am you cannot come. Men who are dismissing something do not usually repeat it that carefully. It is the behaviour of people worrying at a sentence they cannot get out of their heads. They have no idea what it means, they are certain it is nonsense, and they cannot leave it alone.
verseByVerse.note: The Dispersion means the Jews living scattered outside the land among the nations.

verseByVerse.quote: On the last day of the feast, the great day, Jesus stood up and cried out, "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture has said, 'Out of his heart will flow rivers of living water.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the last day of the feast, the great day. Probably the seventh day, the climax of the water ceremony, though some think the eighth day of solemn assembly. Later Jewish writings describe water carried from Siloam in a golden pitcher each morning and poured out beside the altar, while the people sang the Hallel psalms (Psalms 113–118) and prayed for rain; on the seventh day the priests circled the altar seven times. The ceremony looked back to the water from the rock in the wilderness (Exodus 17:6) and forward to the promised day when living waters would flow out from Jerusalem (Zechariah 14:8, read at this feast) and from the temple (Ezekiel 47:1–12). The rabbis said that whoever had not seen the joy of the water-drawing had never seen joy in his life.

Jesus stood up and cried out. Teachers usually sat. He stands and calls out loudly, just as the water ceremony is ending for another year. Into the silence after the last pouring, a man stands up in the temple courts and shouts. The ceremony had been remembering water from a rock for a nation that would otherwise have died in the desert, and he offers, to anybody at all, what the ceremony had only ever pointed at.

If anyone thirsts. It echoes Isaiah 55:1: come, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters. He is the rock from which the water flows (1 Corinthians 10:4). To come and drink is to believe (6:35). And the terms are as wide as language permits: not if anyone is worthy, or prepared, or knows enough. The only qualification is an appetite, the one thing nobody can manufacture or fake. And everyone in that courtyard knew what it is to be thirsty.

As the Scripture has said. “Heart” is literally “belly” (koilia), the innermost being. No single Old Testament verse says exactly this; Jesus is summing up a theme: Isaiah 58:11 (a spring whose waters do not fail), Ezekiel 47 (the river from the temple), Zechariah 14:8, and the rock in the wilderness. Ezekiel saw the river from under the temple threshold deepening as it ran, ankle-deep, knee-deep, waist-deep, until it was a river no one could cross, and everything it touched lived. He is telling a crowd at that feast that the whole river of promise they had been singing about has arrived, and is standing in front of them.

Rivers. Not a cup, not a well: rivers, plural, more than any single person could ever use. He is thirty-odd years old, has no house, is under an arrest warrant, and will be dead by spring, and in the middle of the greatest festival of his people he offers to be the river. Living water was the everyday phrase for running water, from a spring or a stream, as against still water standing in a cistern, and God calls himself the fountain of living waters (Jeremiah 2:13). Jesus means life that keeps flowing from God himself and never goes stale.

Whose heart? The Greek can be punctuated two ways. Most take it as the believer’s heart: the one who drinks becomes a source of blessing to others (4:14). Others punctuate: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me, and let him drink who believes in me. As Scripture says, out of his heart...” so that the rivers flow from Christ’s heart. Both are true: the water flows from Christ (19:34 shows water flowing from his side), and through the believer to others. The ESV’s reading is natural, and most scholars think it likely. The second reading has real attractions: it fits a ceremony in which water flows from the temple, and Jesus is the new temple (2:19–21). But the difference is smaller than it first appears, since John explains in the next verse that he is speaking of the Spirit, and the Spirit comes from Christ to the believer and then out through him. The spring is Christ either way; the question is only how far downstream the sentence is looking.

In the flow. The chapter reaches its climax. Everything so far has been argument about Jesus; now he stops answering questions and issues an invitation. In 8:12 he takes up the feast’s other great image, the light.

I do not feel thirsty for God. Is this invitation for me? Thirst does not always feel like longing for God. Often it feels like restlessness, boredom, the sense that nothing quite satisfies, or the dull ache after the thing you hoped would fill you has not. Augustine confessed that God made us for himself, so that we find no rest anywhere else, and most restlessness is that thirst in disguise. If you have ever wanted more than this life gives, the invitation is for you. And if you feel nothing at all, come anyway, and ask him to make you thirsty. The invitation is to anyone.

So how do I actually come and drink? To come and drink is to believe: to trust Jesus himself, and to keep trusting him, for what only he can give. In practice it means turning to him in prayer, plainly, as someone who needs him; listening to him in his word, where he speaks; and receiving him in the means he has given, the preaching of the gospel, the fellowship of his people and the Lord’s Supper. Drinking is not a single gulp at conversion. It is a daily return to the spring. When you are dry, do not first try harder. Go back to him and drink again.

In everyday life. Think where you go when you are dry: the screen, the fridge, the shop, the bottle, the approval of others. None of them is the river. When you feel that thirst, pray a single sentence: Lord Jesus, I am thirsty; give me yourself. Then let it flow on to others. Rivers are for giving away.

For worship. The rock was struck in the wilderness and water gushed out for a rebellious people. The true Rock was struck on a hill outside Jerusalem, and from his pierced side came blood and water. The feast poured out one golden pitcher a morning; the river from him has run for two thousand years and never run low. And the offer has not been narrowed since the day it was shouted across the temple courts: if anyone thirsts, let him come.
verseByVerse.note: Later Jewish writings describe water being carried from the pool of Siloam and poured out at the altar each day of the feast. No single verse says these exact words; Jesus draws on several prophecies. The ESV notes a different punctuation that makes Jesus himself the source of the water.

parallels.desc: come to the waters
water flowing from the temple
living waters from Jerusalem

verseByVerse.quote: Now this he said about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive, for as yet the Spirit had not been given, because Jesus was not yet glorified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now this he said about the Spirit. The Old Testament often pictures the Spirit as water poured out (Isaiah 44:3; Ezekiel 36:25–27; Joel 2:28). John stops the story to explain, as he does when a saying would otherwise be misread (2:21; 12:33). The rivers are the Spirit: not an influence but a person. John writes as a man on the other side of Pentecost, describing something that had since happened to him and to everyone reading. Those who believed means every believer, not some special class (Romans 8:9; Galatians 3:2).

For as yet the Spirit had not been given. Literally “for the Spirit was not yet.” Of course the Spirit existed and was active in the Old Testament (Psalm 51:11) and in Jesus’ ministry (1:32). The meaning is that the Spirit had not yet been given in the new covenant way, poured out on all God’s people to dwell in them for ever (14:16–17). Before Pentecost the Spirit came mostly upon prophets, kings and craftsmen for particular tasks. After it he made his home in fishermen, slaves, widows and children, all who believe. The Spirit who hovered over the waters at creation and raised Jesus from the dead has made his home in ordinary believers, and he will never leave.

Because Jesus was not yet glorified. In John, Jesus is glorified in his death, resurrection and ascension (12:23; 13:31; 17:1). The Spirit could not come until Jesus had finished his work and returned to the Father (16:7). The cross opened the way; the exalted Christ poured out the Spirit at Pentecost (Acts 2:33). The river could not flow until the rock had been struck, which is why the invitation of verse 37 was made by a man on his way to a cross. To glorify is to show someone’s true greatness; in John that showing begins, astonishingly, at the cross, where the Son’s love and obedience are displayed most fully (12:23–24), and is completed when the Father welcomes him back to the glory he had before the world existed (17:5).

Where Christians differ: receiving the Spirit. Pentecostal and charismatic teaching often holds that the baptism of the Spirit is a second experience after conversion, marked by speaking in tongues. This commentary’s view: this verse says all who believe receive the Spirit. Every Christian has the Spirit from the moment of faith (1 Corinthians 12:13). There may be many fresh fillings and deeper experiences of the Spirit, but no second class of Christians. The sign gifts of the apostolic age, such as tongues and prophecy, served to confirm the founding of the church and have ceased, while the Spirit himself remains with every believer for ever. The reason given is that Scripture ties those gifts to the apostles and the founding of the church (Ephesians 2:20; Hebrews 2:3–4), and the Scripture they served is now complete. Many faithful brothers and sisters in Pentecostal and charismatic churches read the evidence differently; they love the same Lord and seek the same Spirit, and they deserve to be heard with respect.

How do I know I have the Spirit? Not first by a feeling, but by what the Spirit does. He brings you to confess that Jesus is Lord and to mean it (1 Corinthians 12:3). He makes Christ precious to you (16:14). He teaches you to call God Father and to trust him as his child (Romans 8:15–16). He makes you hate sin and fight it, and he grows his fruit in you, slowly: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness (Galatians 5:22–23). If you trust Christ, the Spirit lives in you, whether or not you have had any dramatic experience. Weak faith is still Spirit-given faith.

What does it mean to be filled with the Spirit? It means to be more and more under his influence, as a sail is filled by the wind. Paul commands it as a continuing thing, be filled (Ephesians 5:18), and he shows its marks in the next verses: worship, thankfulness and humble service in home and church. It is not a second level of Christian, and it is not measured by how dramatic your experiences are. You seek it by keeping in step with him: reading the word he inspired, praying, confessing sin quickly, obeying what he shows you, and asking. Jesus promised that the Father gives the Holy Spirit to those who ask him (Luke 11:13).

In everyday life. If you believe in Christ, the Spirit lives in you. You are not waiting for him; ask him to fill you and flow through you. Before the hard conversation, the temptation or the task beyond you, pray simply: Holy Spirit, you live in me; help me now.

verseByVerse.quote: When they heard these words, some of the people said, "This really is the Prophet." Others said, "This is the Christ." But some said, "Is the Christ to come from Galilee?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
This really is the Prophet. “The Prophet” is the prophet like Moses whom Moses promised (Deuteronomy 18:15–18; compare 1:21; 6:14). Some Jews thought of the Prophet as distinct from the Messiah; Jesus is both (Acts 3:22).

Is the Christ to come from Galilee? The Greek expects the answer no. John knows the answer and does not stop to give it; he lets the objection stand. All through this Gospel people reject Jesus on grounds that would have collapsed under one honest question, and as far as John tells us, nobody asks it.

Why did people expect different figures: a prophet, a Christ? Because the Old Testament promises came in many strands, and few saw how they fitted together. Some looked for the prophet like Moses; some for a king of David’s line; some for a priestly figure; some for all of them, arriving separately. Jesus is all of them in one person: the Prophet who speaks God’s word, the Priest who offers himself, the King who reigns. The Reformers spoke of his threefold office for this reason. The categories built to receive him turned out to be too small one by one, and too confusing all together, until he came and filled them all.

For worship. Moses struck the rock and the people drank, and then he died outside the land, promising another prophet. The crowd saw Moses in Jesus, and they were right, and still short of the truth. Moses gave water; Jesus gives the Spirit. Moses spoke God’s words; Jesus is God’s Word. Moses was faithful in God’s house as a servant, and Christ is faithful over it as a Son (Hebrews 3:5–6).
verseByVerse.note: “The Prophet” is the prophet like Moses whom Moses promised.

verseByVerse.quote: "Has not the Scripture said that the Christ comes from the offspring of David, and comes from Bethlehem, the village where David was?" So there was a division among the people over him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The offspring of David. They were right that the Messiah would be a son of David (2 Samuel 7:12–16; Isaiah 11:1; Jeremiah 23:5).

And comes from Bethlehem, the village where David was? And right that he would come from Bethlehem (Micah 5:2; compare Matthew 2:5–6). These are not men twisting the text. They know it well, they are using it correctly, and they reach a false conclusion, because they have a fact wrong and have not thought to test it.

The irony. They did not know that Jesus had been born in Bethlehem, and was descended from David. John expects his readers to know the story (Matthew 1–2; Luke 2) and to see the irony: they reject him for not meeting the very prophecies he fulfils. It is possible to be a careful reader of Scripture, to quote it accurately, to apply it validly, and still to end up on the wrong side of God: not through bad interpretation but through an assumption underneath it that nobody examined. That he was from Galilee was never checked, because it felt like common knowledge.

A division. “Division” (schisma): Jesus divides people (9:16; 10:19). No one can stay neutral about him. The tear runs through crowds, through the council, and in this chapter through his own family. Jesus said himself that he had not come to bring peace but a sword, and that a man’s enemies would be those of his own household (Matthew 10:34–36). The division is not the goal and it is not the good. It is what happens when a claim this large meets people who are free to refuse it, and the alternative, a Christ small enough that nobody need decide about him, was never on offer.

What if following Christ is dividing my family? It hurts, and Jesus does not pretend otherwise. He knew it from the inside: his own brothers did not believe. First, make sure that the division is over Christ, not over your harshness, pride or a quarrel dressed up as faith. Then stay loving, patient and honest; do not withdraw, retaliate or preach at every meal. Honour your parents and keep your promises where you can do so without denying him (Ephesians 6:2). Keep bringing each of them to God in prayer. And take comfort that the division need not be the last word: the brothers who did not believe in John 7 were praying with the disciples in Acts 1.

For worship. The one they said could not be the Christ was born in the very town they named, of the very line they demanded. God kept his word to David to the letter, in a manger, while the scholars of Jerusalem went on arguing, and the division over his Son is the sign that the Son has come.
verseByVerse.note: They did not know that Jesus had been born in Bethlehem.

parallels.desc: from Bethlehem shall come a ruler

verseByVerse.quote: Some of them wanted to arrest him, but no one laid hands on him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one laid hands on him. Again, as in v. 30. John has told us why: his hour had not yet come. Three attempts (vv. 30, 44, 45), three failures, and John gives the reason only once.

What providence looks like from inside. What is striking is how little there is to see. No lightning, no escape, no crowd parting. Some men in a courtyard felt like seizing a teacher and somehow did not, and if asked they would probably have said the moment passed. The ordinary reasons why a thing did not happen are the means God uses, not an alternative to him. This time the restraint worked at the level of a private impulse, which rose in a man’s mind and did not become an action.

If God restrains evil, why does he not restrain all of it? Scripture does not give us the whole answer, but it gives us enough to trust him. God restrains a great deal of evil we never see, and he permits some evil for purposes we cannot yet see, never approving it, and always turning it to good for those who love him (Genesis 50:20; Romans 8:28). The clearest example is this very story. God held back these hands in the autumn, and in the spring he let wicked hands crucify his Son, because through that greatest evil he was accomplishing the greatest good. If he can do that with the cross, he can be trusted with what he permits in your life.

For worship. No hand could close on him that autumn, because the Father had not yet given him up. In the spring the Son of Man was delivered into the hands of men, as he had said he would be (Mark 9:31), and he went into them willingly, so that his people might be kept in his own. No one will snatch them out of my hand, he said (10:28), and the hand that holds them is the one he let men seize.

verseByVerse.quote: The officers then came to the chief priests and Pharisees, who said to them, "Why did you not bring him?" The officers answered, "No one ever spoke like this man!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The officers. The temple police sent in v. 32 return empty-handed, perhaps several days later. Long enough to hear the invitation of verse 37.

No one ever spoke like this man! An extraordinary admission from men trained to obey orders. They were sent to arrest him, and were arrested by his words. They had heard many teachers in the temple, but never anyone like this (Matthew 7:28–29). An excuse would have been easy: the crowd was too thick, there would have been a riot. Instead they openly admire him in front of the men who ordered the arrest. They make no confession of faith; they simply could not do it, and said why.

The truest sentence in the chapter. The most honest testimony in the chapter comes from men who were not believers and had everything to lose by giving it. No name is preserved; they say the truest sentence in the chapter, are sneered at, and disappear. That is its own small comfort for anyone who has said the right thing once, at cost, and seen nothing come of it. It went into the record. John was still writing it down decades later, and the men who said it had no idea it would outlast the council that mocked them.

What was it about how he spoke? It was not technique. Other teachers quoted authorities; he spoke with his own authority (Matthew 7:29). Other teachers explained God; he spoke as one who had come from him, and his words were spirit and life (6:63). He spoke with perfect truth and perfect love at once, which no one else has managed. He knew what was in a man (2:25), so his words went straight to the heart. And he spoke the Father’s own words (v. 16). When you read the Gospels and find a saying of his lodging in you and refusing to leave, you are feeling what the officers felt.

For worship. The voice that said let there be light spoke in the temple courts in the accent of Galilee, and hardened men sent to bind him went back unable to do it. It called Lazarus out of a tomb; it will call all the dead from their graves (5:28–29); and in between it calls, through the plain reading of his word, sheep who know it and follow (10:27).

verseByVerse.quote: The Pharisees answered them, "Have you also been deceived? Have any of the authorities or the Pharisees believed in him?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Have you also been deceived? “Deceived” (planaō): led astray, the same word as v. 12. This is not a request for reasons. It is a warning shot, and its purpose is to make the officers feel foolish. Nobody so much as answers what they said, that no one ever spoke like this man.

Have any of the authorities or the Pharisees believed in him? The argument from authority: none of the experts believe, so it must be false. A familiar argument to this day. The irony: one of them is about to speak up (v. 50), and later Joseph of Arimathea, a member of the council, will be revealed as a secret disciple (19:38), and many priests will believe (Acts 6:7). The claim is not that Jesus is wrong. It is that no one who matters thinks he is right. And it is aimed at policemen, who are being asked whether they propose to set their judgment against that of the learned. It is designed to remind them of their place, and it works: nothing more is heard from the officers. Meanwhile Nicodemus is sitting in that chamber while the question is put as though it answered itself, and both he and Joseph will carry the body of Jesus the following spring.

Consensus is evidence about people. Consensus is not nothing, and a wise reader does not despise it; the church has generally been right to be suspicious of the man who alone sees the truth. But what most people think tells you about the people, not about whether the thing is true, and its worth depends entirely on whether the people are free to say what they think. In this room they were not, and the proof is that the one sympathiser present could manage only a question about procedure.

Should I ignore scholars and experts when they reject Christianity? No. Listen to them, learn from them, and take their arguments seriously; many scholars are believers, and honest scholarship has served the church well. But look at what kind of claim is being made. A sentence that begins, most educated people do not believe, is a statement about people, not an argument about the evidence. Ask what the actual reasons are, and weigh them. Remember too that every generation has its consensus, and the consensus of one century is often the embarrassment of the next. The question is not who believes, but whether it is true. Look at Christ yourself, and read the evidence for the resurrection with your own eyes.

parallels.desc: many even of the authorities believed

verseByVerse.quote: "But this crowd that does not know the law is accursed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This crowd that does not know the law. Religious leaders despised ordinary people who did not know the details of the law and its oral traditions. They called them the “people of the land” (am ha’aretz), and some rabbinic sayings warn against eating with them or marrying their daughters. The phrase hardened into something like a caste: people who could not be relied on to tithe or keep the purity rules.

Is accursed. The law did pronounce a curse on those who did not keep it (Deuteronomy 27:26). The irony again: the very leaders who know the law are breaking it, as Nicodemus will point out in the next verse. This is the class judgment of the educated on the uneducated, delivered as a theological verdict.

The people who got closest. And it is aimed at the people who had got closest to the truth in this chapter. The crowd is confused, divided and working from bad information. They are also the ones asking whether this might be the Christ. It is the pattern of the whole Gospel: a Samaritan woman hears one of the plainest statements of his identity (4:26), fishermen stay when the theologians leave, a blind beggar will out-argue the council. And the men who know most about God’s law say, in the same breath, that nobody who matters believes in him and everybody else is cursed.

Does this mean knowledge is dangerous and I should not study? No. Knowledge of God’s word is a great gift, and Scripture urges us to grow in it (2 Peter 3:18). The problem in this verse is not knowledge but pride: knowledge without love puffs up (1 Corinthians 8:1). The test is what your learning does to the way you see other believers. If it makes you more patient, more humble and more delighted when an untrained Christian sees something true, it is doing its proper work. If it makes you contemptuous, it has become the thing in this verse. Study hard, and stay low.

For worship. The rulers called the crowd accursed. Christ became a curse for them, and for us, hanging on a tree, so that the blessing of Abraham might come to the people of the land and the Gentiles alike (Galatians 3:13–14). He did not curse the ignorant; he taught them, healed them and died for them. The despised people of the land turned out to be the people of his heart.
verseByVerse.note: Religious leaders despised ordinary people who did not know the finer points of the law.

parallels.desc: cursed be anyone who does not confirm the words of this law

verseByVerse.quote: Nicodemus, who had gone to him before, and who was one of them, said to them, "Does our law judge a man without first giving him a hearing and learning what he does?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nicodemus, who had gone to him before. Nicodemus was a member of the council, the man who came to Jesus by night (3:1–2), and his presence answers their question (v. 48): here is one of the rulers at least open to Jesus.

Does our law judge a man without first giving him a hearing and learning what he does? He doesn’t defend Jesus outright, but appeals to justice. The law required a fair hearing (Deuteronomy 1:16–17; 17:4). The men who boast of knowing the law are condemning a man without trial. Nicodemus exposes them with their own law. It is easy to be disappointed that he says so little, but be accurate about the risk he was taking. He has just heard the room agree that no authority believes in Jesus and that anyone who does is deceived. Speaking at all marks him as a possible sympathiser, and the sneering reply he gets shows he was heard exactly that way. The sneer shows what going further would cost him. And on the merits he is entirely right. It is the only legally correct sentence spoken in the chamber, and it comes from the one man there who has actually met him.

The shape of his story. Three appearances: by night with a question (3:1–2); here, with a cautious objection about procedure; and finally at the cross, in daylight, in public, carrying about seventy-five pounds of myrrh and aloes to bury a condemned man (19:39), a quantity fit for a king, at the moment when being associated with him could not possibly have looked worse. The journey took perhaps two years, and nobody in that room would have picked him out as a future disciple. Grace was not in a hurry, and it did not let go.

Is it all right to be a secret or cautious believer? A cautious beginning is not the same as settled secrecy. Nicodemus’ first steps were small, and Jesus did not despise them; many true believers begin quietly. But John does not leave him there, and neither should we stay there. Jesus warns that whoever is ashamed of him, he will be ashamed of (Mark 8:38), and John says sadly of some rulers that they believed but did not confess him, because they loved human praise (12:42–43). If you are a quiet believer, ask what the next honest step is: telling one friend, joining a church, being baptised. Faith that is real grows towards the light.

In everyday life. Nicodemus said little here, but he said something. In the meeting where someone is being talked about unfairly, the one sentence may be simply: should we not hear his side first? It costs something to say it, and the Lord who bore so patiently with Nicodemus will strengthen you for it.
verseByVerse.note: Nicodemus was a member of the council.

parallels.desc: inquire diligently

verseByVerse.quote: They replied, "Are you from Galilee too? Search and see that no prophet arises from Galilee." They went each to his own house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Are you from Galilee too? They don’t answer his point. They mock him: are you one of these northern peasants too? Nicodemus asked a question about legal procedure. Nobody answers it. This is not a rebuttal but a way of putting a man in a category so that nothing he says needs weighing.

Search and see. “Search” means search the Scriptures. They were wrong: the prophet Jonah came from Gath-hepher in Galilee (2 Kings 14:25), and Isaiah had promised that a great light would shine in Galilee of the nations (Isaiah 9:1–2; Matthew 4:15–16). Gath-hepher is only a few miles from Nazareth. The men who dismissed the crowd as ignorant of the law (v. 49) get a fact about the prophets wrong, because they are angry, and never notice.

Textual note. One early papyrus reads “the Prophet” here, meaning the prophet like Moses would not arise from Galilee, which would make their claim less obviously false. The ESV follows the majority of manuscripts.

They went each to his own house. The council breaks up without decision. This sentence (v. 53) begins the passage about the woman caught in adultery (7:53–8:11), which the ESV places in brackets. The earliest and most reliable manuscripts do not contain it, and some place it elsewhere (after Luke 21:38, for example). Its style is unlike John’s, and the KJV prints it because it follows later manuscripts. It is very likely a true story about Jesus preserved in the church, but not originally part of John’s Gospel. The ESV keeps it with a note, and we comment on it in chapter 8 with that caution.

The flattest sentence in the chapter. No verdict, no arrest, no resolution, while the man they were discussing, as the bracketed story goes on to say, went out to the Mount of Olives. They went each to his own house. He had no house to go to. The Son of Man had nowhere to lay his head (Luke 9:58).

Why does my Bible put brackets here, in the middle of a scene? Because the passage that begins with this sentence and runs to 8:11 is the one the brackets surround, and it opens at the last verse of a chapter. That is why the bracket in your Bible seems to start in an odd place. The brackets are not a sign that the translators are hiding anything; they are telling you honestly what the manuscripts show. The story itself is very probably a true memory of Jesus, and it may be read and treasured as one, provided no doctrine is made to rest on it alone.

In everyday life. When you notice yourself answering a point by attacking the person who made it, stop. Ask whether what they said is true. Anger made these scholars forget their own Bibles; wait until you are calm before you answer.
verseByVerse.note: They were wrong: the prophet Jonah came from Gath-hepher in Galilee. The ESV notes that the earliest manuscripts do not include 7:53–8:11 and brackets the passage.

parallels.desc: Jonah son of Amittai, of Gath-hepher
Galilee of the nations

7.title: Rivers of Living Water
7.text: <sup>1</sup>After this Jesus went about in Galilee. He would not go about in Judea, because the Jews were seeking to kill him.<sup>2</sup>Now the Jews’ Feast of Booths was at hand.<sup>3</sup>So his brothers said to him, “Leave here and go to Judea, that your disciples also may see the works you are doing.<sup>4</sup>For no one works in secret if he seeks to be known openly. If you do these things, show yourself to the world.”<sup>5</sup>For not even his brothers believed in him.<sup>6</sup>Jesus said to them, “My time has not yet come, but your time is always here.<sup>7</sup>The world cannot hate you, but it hates me because I testify about it that its works are evil.<sup>8</sup>You go up to the feast. I am not going up to this feast, for my time has not yet fully come.”<sup>9</sup>After saying this, he remained in Galilee.<sup>10</sup>But after his brothers had gone up to the feast, then he also went up, not publicly but in private.<sup>11</sup>The Jews were looking for him at the feast, and saying, “Where is he?”<sup>12</sup>And there was much muttering about him among the people. While some said, “He is a good man,” others said, “No, he is leading the people astray.”<sup>13</sup>Yet for fear of the Jews no one spoke openly of him.<sup>14</sup>About the middle of the feast Jesus went up into the temple and began teaching.<sup>15</sup>The Jews therefore marveled, saying, “How is it that this man has learning, when he has never studied?”<sup>16</sup>So Jesus answered them, “My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me.<sup>17</sup>If anyone’s will is to do God’s will, he will know whether the teaching is from God or whether I am speaking on my own authority.<sup>18</sup>The one who speaks on his own authority seeks his own glory; but the one who seeks the glory of him who sent him is true, and in him there is no falsehood.<sup>19</sup>Has not Moses given you the law? Yet none of you keeps the law. Why do you seek to kill me?”<sup>20</sup>The crowd answered, “You have a demon! Who is seeking to kill you?”<sup>21</sup>Jesus answered them, “I did one work, and you all marvel at it.<sup>22</sup>Moses gave you circumcision (not that it is from Moses, but from the fathers), and you circumcise a man on the Sabbath.<sup>23</sup>If on the Sabbath a man receives circumcision, so that the law of Moses may not be broken, are you angry with me because on the Sabbath I made a man’s whole body well?<sup>24</sup>Do not judge by appearances, but judge with right judgment.”<sup>25</sup>Some of the people of Jerusalem therefore said, “Is not this the man whom they seek to kill?<sup>26</sup>And here he is, speaking openly, and they say nothing to him! Can it be that the authorities really know that this is the Christ?<sup>27</sup>But we know where this man comes from, and when the Christ appears, no one will know where he comes from.”<sup>28</sup>So Jesus proclaimed, as he taught in the temple, “You know me, and you know where I come from. But I have not come of my own accord. He who sent me is true, and him you do not know.<sup>29</sup>I know him, for I come from him, and he sent me.”<sup>30</sup>So they were seeking to arrest him, but no one laid a hand on him, because his hour had not yet come.<sup>31</sup>Yet many of the people believed in him. They said, “When the Christ appears, will he do more signs than this man has done?”<sup>32</sup>The Pharisees heard the crowd muttering these things about him, and the chief priests and Pharisees sent officers to arrest him.<sup>33</sup>Jesus then said, “I will be with you a little longer, and then I am going to him who sent me.<sup>34</sup>You will seek me and you will not find me. Where I am you cannot come.”<sup>35</sup>The Jews said to one another, “Where does this man intend to go that we will not find him? Does he intend to go to the Dispersion among the Greeks and teach the Greeks?<sup>36</sup>What does he mean by saying, ’You will seek me and you will not find me,’ and, ’Where I am you cannot come’?”<sup>37</sup>On the last day of the feast, the great day, Jesus stood up and cried out, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink.<sup>38</sup>Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture has said, ’Out of his heart will flow rivers of living water.’”<sup>39</sup>Now this he said about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive, for as yet the Spirit had not been given, because Jesus was not yet glorified.<sup>40</sup>When they heard these words, some of the people said, “This really is the Prophet.”<sup>41</sup>Others said, “This is the Christ.” But some said, “Is the Christ to come from Galilee?<sup>42</sup>Has not the Scripture said that the Christ comes from the offspring of David, and comes from Bethlehem, the village where David was?”<sup>43</sup>So there was a division among the people over him.<sup>44</sup>Some of them wanted to arrest him, but no one laid hands on him.<sup>45</sup>The officers then came to the chief priests and Pharisees, who said to them, “Why did you not bring him?”<sup>46</sup>The officers answered, “No one ever spoke like this man!”<sup>47</sup>The Pharisees answered them, “Have you also been deceived?<sup>48</sup>Have any of the authorities or the Pharisees believed in him?<sup>49</sup>But this crowd that does not know the law is accursed.”<sup>50</sup>Nicodemus, who had gone to him before, and who was one of them, said to them,<sup>51</sup>“Does our law judge a man without first giving him a hearing and learning what he does?”<sup>52</sup>They replied, “Are you from Galilee too? Search and see that no prophet arises from Galilee.”<sup>53</sup>[[They went each to his own house,
7.overview:
Six months after the feeding of the five thousand, the Feast of Booths (Tabernacles) arrives: the joyful autumn festival when Israel lived in shelters of branches to remember the wilderness, and prayed for rain. Jesus’ unbelieving brothers urge him to go to Jerusalem and show himself; he refuses to move on their timetable, then goes up privately. Halfway through the feast he teaches in the temple, and the crowd cannot agree about him: a good man, a deceiver, mad, the Prophet, the Christ. The authorities send officers to arrest him.

On the last great day of the water ceremony, Jesus stands and invites anyone who thirsts to come to him and drink. John explains that he meant the Spirit, who would be given once Jesus was glorified. The officers come back without him, and when Nicodemus asks for a fair hearing he is mocked. Through the whole chapter runs one question: where does Jesus come from?

8.title: The Light of the World

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–30 — Light in the Darkness: The Second I AM
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: This first section has two parts: the bracketed story of the woman brought to Jesus in the temple at dawn (7:53–8:11), and Jesus’ claim to be the light of the world, the dispute over his testimony, and his warning that unless they believe that he is who he says, they will die in their sins (vv. 12–30).
verseByVerse.theology: The chapter is full of courtroom language and the bare words I am, the name of the God who spoke to Moses. Jesus says that he judges no one (v. 15), and also that his judgment is true (v. 16). The two belong to different times: he came first to save, and he will come again to judge, and those who trust him now will face no condemnation then, because he bore it at the cross.
verseByVerse.examples: She goes free not because the law is set aside, but because the one who alone had the right to condemn her would shortly bear the penalty himself. Every Christian stands where she stood.

verseByVerse.quote: but Jesus went to the Mount of Olives. Early in the morning he came again to the temple. All the people came to him, and he sat down and taught them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. John 8 continues the confrontation at the Feast of Booths and climbs higher than anything Jesus has yet said. It opens with the bracketed story of a woman caught in adultery, whom Jesus neither condemns nor excuses. Then comes the second great I am, I am the light of the world, and an argument about witness, freedom and true parentage. Three times Jesus uses the bare words I am, the name God gave himself at the burning bush, and the third time his hearers pick up stones. The chapter begins with a sinner who deserved stoning and was spared, and ends with the sinless one nearly stoned himself: the whole gospel in miniature.

A textual note first. The story of the woman caught in adultery (7:53–8:11) is printed in brackets in the ESV. The earliest and best Greek manuscripts do not have it; the early church fathers who commented on John verse by verse pass straight from 7:52 to 8:12; and where the story does appear in later manuscripts, it wanders: after 7:36, after 7:44, at the end of John, or after Luke 21:38. Its style is more like Luke’s than John’s, and most scholars, conservative evangelicals included, conclude that it was not part of John’s original Gospel; the KJV, following later manuscripts, prints it without brackets. Yet many believe it records a true event from Jesus’ life, preserved in the church’s memory. Because Scripture is God’s word as originally given, the church should not build doctrine on this passage alone; but what it shows of Jesus is taught elsewhere in Scripture too.

How could such a thing happen? A reader who has been told a passage may not be original usually wants to know. The evidence is not evenly balanced. The great fourth-century manuscripts do not have these verses, and neither do the earliest papyrus copies of John. Where later manuscripts do carry the passage, they cannot agree where to put it, and a floating passage is a strong sign of one that was added rather than removed. Many of the manuscripts that include it also mark it with the little symbols scribes used for doubtful material. They knew. And yet almost nobody thinks the story was invented. It was known very early in the Latin-speaking churches, and Jerome says he found it in many manuscripts. Augustine suggested that some men of little faith had removed it, fearing it would give their wives licence to sin. Whether or not that is the reason, it is the kind of story that would be uncomfortable to keep and hard to imagine anyone making up. It is very probably a true memory of Jesus that circulated on its own and was written into John’s Gospel at a point where it fitted.

Should I be shaken by the brackets in my Bible? No. The brackets are the church showing its working, in public, about twelve verses out of some eight thousand in the New Testament. Nothing in them is a hidden embarrassment; it is printed in your Bible with an honest note precisely so that you can see it. And nothing is lost either way. The passage teaches nothing that the rest of Scripture does not teach plainly: the same Lord who says neither do I condemn you here says it in substance on every page of the Gospels, and calls sinners to leave their sin everywhere. So it may be read, treasured and preached as a faithful record of Jesus, with the caution that no doctrine should rest on it alone.

The Mount of Olives. Jesus spent nights on the Mount of Olives during his time in Jerusalem (Luke 21:37), across the Kidron Valley, on the hillside where, months later, he would pray in agony and be arrested. The council had gone each to his own house (7:53).

All the people came to him. While the leaders plot, ordinary people come, and the temple becomes again at daybreak a house of teaching.

He sat down. Sitting was the posture of a teacher, and of authority. He is not a guest in the temple but its Lord, teaching in his Father’s house.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus spent nights on the Mount of Olives during his time in Jerusalem. Teachers sat to teach.

verseByVerse.quote: The scribes and the Pharisees brought a woman who had been caught in adultery, and placing her in the midst they said to him, "Teacher, this woman has been caught in the act of adultery."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The scribes and the Pharisees. The scribes were the experts in the law; John never uses the word elsewhere, another sign of the passage’s different origin.

Caught in adultery. Where is the man? Adultery is not committed alone. The law required both to die (Leviticus 20:10; Deuteronomy 22:22). His absence suggests a set-up: the men about to quote Moses have already broken the law they cite by leaving one of the two guilty people at home. That missing man tells you what this really is: they have chosen the defendant who is easier to drag in and whose life matters less to them. It is also, in the oldest and most familiar way, a woman made to carry in public a shame that a man is quietly allowed to walk away from.

In the midst. In a ring of men, in the temple courts at dawn, she is not brought to a court but to a lesson, and made the visual aid. And this is how every one of us stands before God’s judgment: no cover, no defence, fully seen.

Teacher. There is no doubt of her guilt. They open with the title of respect, spoken by men who have arranged the one situation in which they think any answer will destroy him.

Why does Jesus never mention the missing man? He does not need to. Everyone present could count. By refusing to play the part they had written for him, he declines to complete a sentence that was never being passed honestly, and he refuses to let the law of God be used as a stone in somebody else’s fight. The missing man stands as a silent witness against the accusers. And it is a warning for every age: when a community is fierce about one person’s sin and silent about another’s, according to who is more convenient to blame, it is not defending holiness. It is using it.

In everyday life. You stand only because Christ refused to use your sin against you. So watch for the moment in a conversation when someone else’s failure becomes useful to you: to win an argument, to look better, to settle a score. Put it down.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now in the Law, Moses commanded us to stone such women. So what do you say?" This they said to test him, that they might have some charge to bring against him. Jesus bent down and wrote with his finger on the ground.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses commanded us. Stoning was specified for a betrothed woman (Deuteronomy 22:23–24), and the man was to die with her (Leviticus 20:10). They quote half the law. Men this careless about the letter are not the guardians of it they claim to be.

So what do you say? The trap. If Jesus says, “Let her go,” he contradicts Moses and loses his standing as a teacher of the law. If he says, “Stone her,” he loses his reputation as the friend of sinners, and he defies Rome, which did not allow the Jews to carry out death sentences (18:31). Either way, they have a charge.

To test him. The woman is not a person to them but a prop, and that is exploitation of a cruel kind.

He wrote on the ground. What did he write? We are not told, and guesses abound: the sins of the accusers, the law requiring both parties, a line from the prophets. Perhaps the point is simply that he refuses to be rushed.

The one guess worth knowing. One suggestion depends on where this scene sits rather than on imagination. Jeremiah says that those who turn away from the LORD shall be written in the earth, for they have forsaken the LORD, the fountain of living water (Jeremiah 17:13). The fountain of living water is the very thing Jesus had stood up and shouted about on the last day of the feast (7:37–38). If that is what his finger traced in the dust, the accusers were watching their own verdict being written while they waited for his. It cannot be proved and should not be preached as certain.

The posture. What can be said with confidence is the posture. He is asked to pronounce a death sentence, and his first act is to go down: to stoop into the dirt of the courtyard while a woman stands in the middle of a circle of men. Whatever he wrote, he had put himself lower than everyone present, including her.

In everyday life. When you are pushed for an instant answer by someone who has already decided what they want you to say, you are allowed to pause. Stoop before you speak: pray, think, and let the heat go out of the moment.

For worship. The Lawgiver himself was crouched in the dust of his own temple, and the men quoting his law at him did not know it. He had come down to the ground to keep that law in every point for people who had broken it, and in the end he would be lifted up from the ground to bear its curse (Galatians 3:13).
verseByVerse.note: The law required both the man and the woman caught in adultery to be put to death; the man is missing. Rome did not allow the Jewish authorities to carry out executions, so the question was a trap either way.

parallels.desc: both of them shall die

verseByVerse.quote: And as they continued to ask him, he stood up and said to them, "Let him who is without sin among you be the first to throw a stone at her." And once more he bent down and wrote on the ground.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Without sin among you. Under the law the witnesses were to throw the first stones (Deuteronomy 17:7). They had to be honest witnesses, for the law gave a false witness the very penalty he had sought for another (Deuteronomy 19:16–19). Jesus turns the light on the accusers: are they fit to carry out God’s judgment? What he does not do matters as much. He does not deny the law, dispute the facts, or make a speech about mercy. He hands them the stones and attaches the condition the law already contained. No answer could keep closer to the law, and it empties the courtyard. In a group that had arrived with a woman and without the man, it would have landed like a hand on the shoulder.

Once more he bent down. He leaves them with their consciences. Having said the one sentence, he goes back to the ground and gives them the freedom to leave without being stared at. The genius of grace is that it does not humiliate even the accusers; it invites them to look at themselves.

So does a church or a court have to be sinless to deal with sin? No. If that were the rule, no human court could ever sit and no church could ever discipline anyone, and Scripture commands both. Judges and elders act as servants of God’s justice, not as people claiming to be better than the accused (Romans 13:4; Galatians 6:1). What this verse demands is honesty: that those who judge are not guilty of the same thing, are not using the process for their own ends, and come to it knowing their own need of mercy. A pastor confronting a sin, a parent correcting a child, a court sentencing a crime, can all do right, provided they do it with clean hands and a humble heart.

In everyday life. The last time you were quite certain somebody else was in the wrong, would your certainty have survived being asked, in front of witnesses, whether you were clear of the same thing? Remember the one who had every right to throw a stone at you and did not.
verseByVerse.note: Under the law the witnesses were to throw the first stones.

parallels.desc: the hand of the witnesses first against him

verseByVerse.quote: But when they heard it, they went away one by one, beginning with the older ones, and Jesus was left alone with the woman standing before him. Jesus stood up and said to her, "Woman, where are they? Has no one condemned you?" She said, "No one, Lord." And Jesus said, "Neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Beginning with the older ones. The oldest have the longest memories of their own sins, or simply the wisdom to know they are guilty. Stones are put down, one by one. Every one of them had come in sure that he stood on the right side of the law, and every one left knowing, at least for a moment, that he stood where she stood. That is the hardest discovery a religious person can make: that his record has not made him safe, and that he needs the same mercy as the sinner he came to accuse.

Left alone with the woman. Augustine’s famous phrase: two were left, misery and mercy. The only one without sin, the only one with the right to throw the stone, remains.

Woman, where are they? Has no one condemned you? “Woman” is a respectful address (2:4). The question is gentle, almost wondering. The trap has collapsed, and what remains is a woman, a silence, and mercy.

Neither do I condemn you. Jesus, who is without sin, does not condemn her. Not because her sin doesn’t matter, but because he came not to condemn the world but to save it (3:17). And how can the holy one release the guilty? Because he himself would bear her condemnation on the cross (Romans 8:1–3). This is not leniency: he does not say the charge was false or the law harsh. Everyone else had merely lost the right to throw; he had the right and declined to use it. This is mercy from the judge’s seat, and it costs him. Within months the man who said neither do I condemn you was under condemnation himself, outside the city, with the sentence being carried out on him. She walked out of that courtyard alive because somebody else did not.

Sin no more. Grace and holiness together: he calls it sin, and tells her to leave it. He does not say, “Sin no more, and then I won’t condemn you.” He says, “I don’t condemn you; now go and sin no more.” Grace is the root of obedience, not its reward. The change of life follows an acquittal; it does not purchase one. And grace does not leave people where it finds them. The instruction is real, and it is addressed to a real situation she has to go home to.

Was she forgiven if she had not repented? The story does not tell us what was in her heart, and we should not invent it. What it shows is the order of grace: Jesus speaks mercy and then calls for a changed life, and that call is itself a call to repent. Elsewhere Scripture is plain that forgiveness is received through repentance and faith (Luke 24:47; Acts 3:19). The point here is not that repentance is unnecessary, but that it is not the price. No one earns the verdict by changing first. We come to Christ as we are, receive his mercy, and his mercy sends us out to live differently.

What if I keep falling into the same sin after being forgiven? Then come back, as often as you need to. Go and sin no more is a real command, and Christ means it to be obeyed. But it is the command of the one who has already said, I do not condemn you, and that verdict is not withdrawn when you stumble (1 John 1:9–2:1). Fight the sin, seriously: cut off what feeds it, tell a trusted believer, ask for help. And when you fall, do not hide from him, which is what shame always urges. Run to him. The freedom to obey grows out of being forgiven; it never grows out of the fear that he might stop forgiving you.

For worship. She had been marched in by a ring of men and stood in the middle; she walked out alone, through an open court, with no one holding her arm. That is how the Lord releases sinners: not on probation, not under watch, but sent home with a verdict that will never be reopened, because the one who spoke it was going to answer for it himself.

parallels.desc: no condemnation

verseByVerse.quote: Again Jesus spoke to them, saying, "I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life." So the Pharisees said to him, "You are bearing witness about yourself; your testimony is not true." Jesus answered, "Even if I do bear witness about myself, my testimony is true, for I know where I came from and where I am going, but you do not know where I come from or where I am going.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Again Jesus spoke to them. John’s original narrative picks up from 7:52: still the Feast of Booths, still in the temple.

In the flow. Verse 12 follows straight on from the last day of the feast: there Jesus offered living water (7:37–38); here he offers light. The rest of the chapter tests the claim, and chapter 9 acts it out, as he gives sight to a man born blind while the men who claim to see remain in the dark (9:41).

I am the light of the world. The second great “I am” saying (after 6:35). The lamps of the feast recalled the pillar of fire that led Israel through the wilderness (Exodus 13:21). Jesus is the true light, not just for Israel but for the world (1:4–9; Isaiah 42:6; 49:6). Light in Scripture means God’s presence, truth, holiness, salvation (Psalm 27:1).

Beside the cold lamps. John tells us where he was standing eight verses later: in the treasury (v. 20), in the Court of the Women, which is where the great lampstands of the feast had been lit every night. The sources describe four enormous golden lampstands, so tall that young priests climbed ladders to fill them, while men danced with torches through the night. Now the feast is probably over, and the lamps are out and cold. A man stands in that court, beside the extinguished stands, and says, I am the light of the world. As with the water, he waits until the ceremony has finished and says that the thing it pointed at is standing in front of them, and does not go out. He was the light of the pillar of fire, the glory over the tabernacle, the radiance that filled Solomon’s temple, and now he stood in the temple in a body, beside the cold lamps, offering himself to everyone.

Will not walk in darkness. As Israel followed the pillar of fire. Darkness in John means sin, ignorance and death (1:5; 3:19; 12:35). And the promise is not first that we will see everything, but that we will have him with us. The verb is about walking, not seeing. Israel did not get a map in the wilderness; they got a pillar of fire that moved, and followed it one night at a time. And the one who follows will have the light of life, the light that gives life (1:4).

Your testimony is not true. They object on legal grounds: self-testimony was not accepted. Jesus himself had granted the principle (5:31). The objection is not stupid, and readers notice the apparent clash with chapter 5.

My testimony is true. The principle is meant for ordinary witnesses. Jesus is unique. He alone knows the truth about himself. And he is not withdrawing what he said in chapter 5 but denying that he is alone, which is exactly what he says next: it is not I alone who judge, but I and the Father (v. 16).

Where I came from and where I am going. He knows his origin and his destiny; they do not. No human can verify his testimony from outside; only God can, and he does (v. 18).

What does it mean in practice to follow the light? It means trusting Jesus and going where he leads, one step at a time, by his word. It does not mean you will always see far ahead, or understand why things happen. It means you will not be left in the darkness of sin, confusion about God, or hopelessness about death. Practically: read his words and do what they say; when you face a choice, ask what honours him and obeys him; when you sin, bring it into the light quickly rather than hiding it (1 John 1:7). Following the light is less like being given a floodlight and more like being given a lamp for your feet (Psalm 119:105).

In everyday life. Name the area of your life that feels darkest at the moment: a decision, a grief, a secret. Bring it to him in prayer today, and take one step of obedience in it, however small. The light comes to the one who follows.

For worship. The lamps of the feast burned for a week and were put away for a year. The light who spoke in the treasury that morning has never been put away. The darkness tried to put him out on a cross and could not; the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it (1:5). And at the end the city of God will need no sun or moon, for the glory of God gives it light, and its lamp is the Lamb (Revelation 21:23).
verseByVerse.note: At the Feast of Booths great lamps were lit in the temple courts. This is the second of Jesus’ “I am” sayings in John.

parallels.desc: a pillar of fire to give them light
a light for the nations

verseByVerse.quote: "You judge according to the flesh; I judge no one. Yet even if I do judge, my judgment is true, for it is not I alone who judge, but I and the Father who sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You judge according to the flesh. By human standards, by appearances (7:24), from a merely human point of view. They looked at a Galilean with no credentials and drew the obvious conclusion, which was wrong.

I judge no one. Not that Jesus never judges (5:22, 27), but that he did not come to judge as they do, nor was judging the purpose of his first coming (3:17; 12:47). The two fit together once you see the timing: in his first coming anyone who meets him meets him as Saviour. The judging is real, it is his, and it is kept for the last day. He who will sit on the throne at the last came the first time to stand in the dock. The one who will judge the living and the dead was judged by men who judged according to the flesh, and he let them do it, so that his people could stand in the last judgment without fear.

My judgment is true. His judgment is God’s judgment, for the Father and the Son act together (5:30).

If Jesus will judge everyone, why does God seem to let things go now? Because the court has not yet sat, and the delay is grace. The reason a person is not being judged today is not that God has grown relaxed about sin. It is that he is patient, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance (2 Peter 3:9). The interval is given to be used: for the unbeliever to turn, and for the believer to call others to turn. It is also a comfort to anyone who has been wronged and has seen no justice. Nothing has been forgotten. The judge is Christ, and his judgment is true.

verseByVerse.quote: "In your Law it is written that the testimony of two people is true. I am the one who bears witness about myself, and the Father who sent me bears witness about me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In your Law. The law required two or three witnesses to establish a matter (Deuteronomy 17:6; 19:15). “Your Law” does not distance Jesus from the law; it emphasises that they are the ones who claim to live by it. There is a quiet authority in it: very well, let us proceed by your own procedure. A prophet says, thus says the LORD. This is the Lord of the law himself, agreeing to be tried by its rules.

The Father who sent me. On any ordinary reading it is an outrageous answer: the two-witness rule exists so that no man’s account of himself need be taken on trust, and he satisfies it by calling a witness nobody else can call and nobody present can cross-examine. But the second witness had already testified, publicly, three ways: in the works he gave Jesus to do (5:36), in the Scriptures (5:39), and at the Jordan (1:32–34). All of them had the Scriptures, and many had seen the works.

But how can I believe a witness I cannot see? In the same way these men were meant to: through the testimony he has given. The Father’s witness is not hidden. It is in the works of Jesus, recorded so that you may believe (20:31); in the Scriptures, which from Moses onwards point to him (5:39, 46); and supremely in the resurrection, by which God declared him to be his Son (Romans 1:4). And the Spirit himself bears witness, opening our eyes to see what is there (15:26; 1 John 5:6–10). You are not asked to believe without evidence. You are asked to receive the evidence God has given, rather than demanding a different kind on your own terms.

For worship. Two witnesses, and both of them God. At the Jordan the Father’s voice owned him as his beloved Son (Matthew 3:17); at the empty tomb the Father spoke again, louder, by raising him from the dead. The God who cannot lie has told us who Jesus is, and in telling us he has shown us what he is himself: a Father who delights in his Son, and gives him to the world.

parallels.desc: two or three witnesses

verseByVerse.quote: They said to him therefore, "Where is your Father?" Jesus answered, "You know neither me nor my Father. If you knew me, you would know my Father also." These words he spoke in the treasury, as he taught in the temple; but no one arrested him, because his hour had not yet come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Where is your Father? They want to see this second witness. Perhaps it is also a sneer at the rumours about his birth (v. 41). On its face the question is fair: he has named a second witness, and in any human court the next step is to ask to see him.

You know neither me nor my Father. They cannot see the Father because they don’t know the Son. He does not produce the Father, offer a sign, or argue. The witness they want to examine is not someone who can be summoned into the courtyard, and the only access to him is through the man they are cross-examining.

You would know my Father also. To know Jesus is to know the Father (14:7–9). This is one of John’s plainest statements that Jesus is the revelation of God, and that every other road to the Father is closed (14:6). It should be stated without softening: there is no way to know God that goes around Jesus: not through sincerity, not through the law these men administered, not through the temple they were standing in. We do not have to climb up to heaven to find out what the Father is like; the Son came down, and stood among the offering boxes, and said, know me and you will know him. Every glimpse of the Father we will ever have, in this age and the next, will be in the face of Jesus Christ.

In the treasury. The treasury was probably in the Court of the Women, where thirteen trumpet-shaped offering boxes stood. It was among the busiest places in the temple, and where he would later sit and watch a widow put in two small coins (Mark 12:41–44). He is standing where Israel brought its gifts to God when he says that they do not know God.

No one arrested him. The boldest claims are made in the busiest place, to the men who wanted him dead, and still no one could touch him.

What about people who love God but do not believe in Jesus? Jesus’ words are hard and clear: to know the Father you must know the Son, and to reject the Son is to show that you do not know the Father (5:23; 1 John 2:23). Many people are sincere, devout and morally serious without Christ, and we should respect their seriousness and treat them with love. But sincerity is not the same as knowing God, and Scripture says there is salvation in no other name (Acts 4:12). That is not a reason for pride; it is a reason for urgency and tenderness, because the God they are looking for has come in Jesus, and they need to hear of him.

In everyday life. When you catch yourself picturing God as harsh, distant or indifferent, set that picture beside the Jesus of the Gospels: crying out to the thirsty, touching the leper, weeping at a grave. Whoever has seen him has seen the Father (14:9), so let the Son correct the picture.
verseByVerse.note: The treasury was probably in the Court of the Women, where the offering chests stood.

verseByVerse.quote: So he said to them again, "I am going away, and you will seek me, and you will die in your sin. Where I am going, you cannot come." So the Jews said, "Will he kill himself, since he says, 'Where I am going, you cannot come'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am going away. As in 7:33–34, he is going to the Father, and where he is going they cannot come: heaven is closed to those who reject the one who opens it.

You will die in your sin. The most frightening sentence in the chapter. To die in your sin is to die unforgiven, still carrying your guilt, and so to face God’s judgment with it. Isaiah saw the holy God and cried out that he was lost (Isaiah 6:5); to come before that holiness with every sin still on your account is the most fearful thing that can happen to a human being (Hebrews 10:31). The warning of 7:34 comes back with its reason added: they will not find him, and so they will die in their sin.

One root, many fruits. “Sin” is singular here: the root sin of unbelief (16:9), which verse 24 names as not believing that he is who he says. In verse 24 the word is plural: the sins that flow from that root. There is one thing fundamentally wrong with these men, and everything else follows from it. Every sin will be brought into the light at the judgment, and none will be overlooked. But the decisive matter is a person’s relation to Christ, because he is the only one who can take sins away. To refuse him is to keep every sin one has ever committed.

Will he kill himself? A worse misunderstanding than in 7:35. Suicide was thought to send a person to the lowest depths of Hades, so they mean, perhaps, that he is going where they would never go. The irony is deep: Jesus will lay down his life, of his own will (10:17–18), but not as they imagine, and it will be they who put him to death. They have guessed, in mockery, that he intends to die by his own decision. They are wrong about the manner and the motive, and right about the fact. Once again his enemies prophesy without knowing it.

Can a believer die in his sin? No. A believer dies in the Lord (Revelation 14:13), with every sin forgiven, because Christ has borne them. Dying in your sin means dying without Christ, still carrying your guilt. If you trust him, even weakly, even with sins you are still fighting, you will not die in your sin; you will die forgiven, and wake in his presence. The warning is for those who refuse him. For those who come to him, the promise of 6:37 stands: he will never cast them out.

In everyday life. Do not carry your sin to the grave. If there is anything you have never brought to Christ, bring it today.

verseByVerse.quote: He said to them, "You are from below; I am from above. You are of this world; I am not of this world. I told you that you would die in your sins, for unless you believe that I am he you will die in your sins."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You are from below; I am from above. Two realms, two origins (3:31). He is not insulting them. He is explaining why the conversation keeps failing: two parties are using the same words, and one of them came from somewhere else.

That I am he. “That I am he” is literally “that I am” (egō eimi), with nothing added. This is the divine name. In Exodus 3:14 God revealed himself as “I am who I am,” and in Isaiah the Lord says again and again, “I am he” (Isaiah 41:4; 43:10, 13, 25; 46:4; 48:12), using in the Greek Old Testament the same words Jesus uses here. Jesus is claiming to be the God of Israel, come in the flesh. To be saved, one must believe that he is who he says he is. Salvation is not faith in faith, or vague faith in God, but faith in Jesus as Lord and God (20:28).

The bare name. Translators rightly supply the pronoun, but the bare form is what the hearers got, the form God used at the bush. It comes back at verse 28, and at verse 58 it will nearly get him stoned. And the condition is as narrow as anything he ever said: not, unless you live well, or keep the law, which these men did with great rigour, but unless you believe that I am. There is no version of this in which the identity of Jesus is an optional extra on top of a decent life. He has made it the point on which everything turns, in the temple, in public, and the men listening understood him perfectly.

Where Christians differ: is Jesus God? Jehovah’s Witnesses, Unitarians and others teach that Jesus is a created being, a lesser god or a great prophet. This commentary’s view: Jesus here claims the divine name, and makes faith in it necessary for salvation. With 1:1, 5:18, 8:58, 10:30 and 20:28, John teaches plainly that Jesus is God the Son, one with the Father. This is not a secondary doctrine: unless you believe, you die in your sins.

Does this warning fall on people who have never heard of Jesus? This verse is spoken to men who had heard the claim plainly and were rejecting it, so its first force falls on everyone who has heard. Their danger was not ignorance but refusal: the one they rejected was standing in front of them. But Scripture as a whole is clear that salvation comes only through conscious faith in Christ: there is no other name under heaven by which we must be saved (Acts 4:12), and people cannot believe in one of whom they have never heard (Romans 10:14). That is why the church is sent to the nations. God is just, and no one will be condemned for rejecting a Christ they never heard of, but for real sins against the light they had (Romans 1:20; 2:12). And the Reformed churches have held that elect infants who die in infancy are saved by Christ through the Spirit. The right response is not to speculate but to go, and send, and pray.

In everyday life. When you say the creed, or sing that Jesus is Lord, do not let the words slide past. Jesus is God: the one who loves you is the I AM.

For worship.
