If I tell the truth, why do you not believe me?<sup>47</sup>Whoever is of God hears the words of God. The reason why you do not hear them is that you are not of God.”<sup>48</sup>The Jews answered him, “Are we not right in saying that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?”<sup>49</sup>Jesus answered, “I do not have a demon, but I honor my Father, and you dishonor me.<sup>50</sup>Yet I do not seek my own glory; there is One who seeks it, and he is the judge.<sup>51</sup>Truly, truly, I say to you, if anyone keeps my word, he will never see death.”<sup>52</sup>The Jews said to him, “Now we know that you have a demon! Abraham died, as did the prophets, yet you say, ’If anyone keeps my word, he will never taste death.’<sup>53</sup>Are you greater than our father Abraham, who died? And the prophets died! Who do you make yourself out to be?”<sup>54</sup>Jesus answered, “If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing. It is my Father who glorifies me, of whom you say, ’He is our God.’<sup>55</sup>But you have not known him. I know him. If I were to say that I do not know him, I would be a liar like you, but I do know him and I keep his word.<sup>56</sup>Your father Abraham rejoiced that he would see my day. He saw it and was glad.”<sup>57</sup>So the Jews said to him, “You are not yet fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham?”<sup>58</sup>Jesus said to them, “Truly, truly, I say to you, before Abraham was, I am.”<sup>59</sup>So they picked up stones to throw at him, but Jesus hid himself and went out of the temple.
8.overview:
The chapter opens with the story of the woman caught in adultery (7:53–8:11), which the earliest manuscripts of John do not contain. It very probably preserves a true memory of Jesus. The accusers leave one by one, and Jesus neither condemns the woman nor excuses her sin.

The rest of the chapter continues Jesus’ teaching at the Feast of Booths. He calls himself the light of the world, and the argument that follows is about who vouches for him, where he comes from, what real freedom is, and who his hearers’ father really is. It ends with his plainest claim to be God, that before Abraham was, he is, and they pick up stones. Because the chapter has been used to fuel hatred of Jews, it needs care: Jesus speaks as a Jew to particular opponents who were seeking to kill him, and his words warn every religious person, not one people.

9.title: The Man Born Blind

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–41 — Sight and Blindness: The Light of the World at Work
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter has five scenes: the healing (vv. 1–7), the neighbours (vv. 8–12), the first questioning by the Pharisees and the summons of the parents (vv. 13–23), the second questioning and the man’s expulsion (vv. 24–34), and Jesus finding him, followed by his words about sight and blindness (vv. 35–41).
verseByVerse.theology: Physical sight and spiritual sight run side by side through the chapter. The man born blind is a picture of every person by nature, needing God to open his eyes; the Pharisees are blind precisely because they are sure they see (v. 41). The one who knows he cannot see can be given sight; the one who insists he sees stays blind.
verseByVerse.examples: The healed man’s words about Jesus grow under pressure: the man called Jesus (v. 11), a prophet (v. 17), from God (v. 33), and at last Lord, with worship (v. 38). The questioning meant to break his testimony drives him further into faith. The leaders cast him out (v. 34), and Jesus finds him (v. 35).

verseByVerse.quote: As he passed by, he saw a man blind from birth. And his disciples asked him, "Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. John 9 records what is usually counted as the sixth sign in John’s Gospel, and it acts out what Jesus has just said: I am the light of the world (8:12; 9:5). A man born blind receives his sight and comes to see who Jesus is, while the leaders, who claim to see, grow blind. The man’s understanding of Jesus grows step by step until he worships him as Lord; the leaders end with we see, the one claim that keeps them blind. And Jesus does the seeking from first to last.

He saw a man blind from birth. Jesus sees him first. The man asks for nothing; grace takes the initiative. Blind from birth: this is the only healing in the Gospels of someone born with his condition. Medically it was hopeless, and it is a picture of the spiritual blindness we are all born with (2 Corinthians 4:4). Spiritual blindness does not mean we cannot be religious; it means we can look straight at Jesus and see nothing worth worshipping, until God shines in our hearts the light of the knowledge of his glory in the face of Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6). The verse just before this chapter says that Jesus hid himself and went out of the temple (8:59). If the scenes follow closely, he has just escaped being stoned, and on the way out he stops for a beggar. That is how grace always begins: not with our seeking, but with his seeing. Before we ever looked for him, he had already looked on us and loved us.

Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind? Many assumed that disability was punishment for a particular sin. If born blind, either his parents had sinned (Exodus 20:5 was misapplied), or he had sinned in the womb, which some rabbis, in writings later than the New Testament, thought possible (citing Jacob and Esau struggling, Genesis 25:22). Job’s friends made the same mistake. The disciples did not invent this idea; it was what they had been taught, and most people still think the same way. When something terrible happens, the mind goes looking for the cause in the sufferer: what did they do, what did I do, what am I being punished for?

A man turned into a case. They discuss him in front of him as a theological problem, which is presumably what had happened to him all his life; nobody in the verse speaks to him. That is the other reason people still ask the question. Once we have explained someone’s suffering, we feel we have dealt with it, and nothing more is asked of us. The disciples want an explanation that would let them walk on. Jesus refuses their explanation, and then puts his hands in the dust of the road to heal the man.

Is my suffering a punishment for my sins? Not in the way the disciples meant. All suffering exists because we live in a fallen world, and sometimes a particular sin does bring painful consequences: drunkenness ruins a liver, lies ruin a friendship. But Scripture refuses to let us read every illness, disability or loss as God’s verdict on someone’s private sin (Luke 13:1–5; Job 42:7). If you are a Christian, your punishment was borne by Christ; there is now no condemnation (Romans 8:1). Your Father may discipline you in love (Hebrews 12:6), but discipline is the training of a child, not the sentence of a judge. So when trouble comes, do not torment yourself trying to find the sin that caused it. Bring it to God, ask him what he wants to do in it, and trust him.

In everyday life. When you see someone suffering, do not ask first whose fault it is; ask what God might do, and what you might do. Someone you know who is disabled, ill or struggling is more often talked about than talked to; Christ saw you before you asked for anything, so go and speak to them this week, as a person, not a case.
verseByVerse.note: Many assumed that disability was punishment for a particular sin, even a parent’s.

parallels.desc: the son shall not suffer for the iniquity of the father

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered, "It was not that this man sinned, or his parents, but that the works of God might be displayed in him. We must work the works of him who sent me while it is day; night is coming, when no one can work."
verseByVerse.commentary:
It was not that this man sinned, or his parents. Jesus rejects the simple link between a particular sin and a particular suffering. All suffering exists because of the fall (Romans 8:20–22), and some suffering is the direct result of a particular sin (5:14; 1 Corinthians 11:30). But not all, and here there is no such link.

That the works of God might be displayed. Jesus moves from cause to purpose: not why, but what for. That does not make the suffering less real, but it gives it meaning.

Did God blind a baby to set up a miracle? A parent will read this verse differently from a commentator, and the question has to be met. Put like that it sounds intolerable, and no one should pretend otherwise. Two things need saying. First, the verse says less than the objection assumes. It does not say God caused the blindness in order to show off. It says the works of God will be displayed in this man, and the display, when it comes, is that Jesus gives him his sight, then goes looking for him after he has been thrown out, and gives him himself. Whatever the years cost, the man ends the chapter seeing, worshipping, and known to the Son of God, which is more than the men who questioned him ever got. Second, the Greek can be punctuated differently, so that the words about God’s works begin the next sentence: neither this man nor his parents sinned; but that the works of God might be displayed in him, we must work the works of him who sent me. On that reading Jesus is not giving a reason for the blindness at all, but turning from the cause of the blindness to the work that must be done. The ESV’s reading is the more natural Greek, and it means that God had a purpose in this man’s blindness from the start. But on either reading the comfort stands: God does not waste the suffering of those he loves.

In the flow. Jesus’ answer is the key to the chapter: everything that follows is the works of God being displayed in this man. And the deepest work of God is that you believe in him whom he has sent (6:29), so the display is finished not at the pool but in verse 38, when he falls down before Jesus.

While it is day. “We”: Jesus includes his disciples in the mission. “Must” (dei): it is God’s will, and so it has to be done. “While it is day”: while the opportunity lasts. The disciples asked about the past; Jesus answers with what God intends to do now, and then he goes to the blind beggar and does it.

Night is coming, when no one can work. For Jesus, the night is his death; for us, it is our death or his return. The night came for Jesus at the cross, and through it he brought the morning that will never end. The servant who knows the time is short neither coasts nor panics; he does today’s work.

How can I believe my suffering has a purpose when I cannot see it? You may not see it yet, and you may not see all of it in this life. This man was blind for many years before anyone explained anything, and the explanation, when it came, was not a theory but a person. What Scripture promises is not that every sorrow will make sense to us now, but that God works all things together for good for those who love him (Romans 8:28), and that our light and momentary affliction is preparing an eternal weight of glory (2 Corinthians 4:17). Hold on to what you know of his character, revealed in Christ, while you wait for what you cannot yet see of his purpose. And look for the works of God in small things now: comfort given, faith deepened, others helped through what you have suffered (2 Corinthians 1:3–4).

In everyday life. Stop asking only why, and start asking what for. Take the hardest thing in your life right now and pray: Father, display your works in this.

verseByVerse.quote: "As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world." Having said these things, he spit on the ground and made mud with the saliva. Then he anointed the man's eyes with the mud
verseByVerse.commentary:
As long as I am in the world. The claim of 8:12, now about to be shown in action: the light of the world gives light to a man who has never seen it. He does not mean that the world will go dark when he leaves it: he had told his disciples that they too are the light of the world (Matthew 5:14). They carry his light on.

Mud with the saliva. Saliva was widely believed to have healing power, and Jesus used it elsewhere (Mark 7:33; 8:23). But there may be more. God formed man from the dust of the ground (Genesis 2:7), and this man’s eyes had never worked from the beginning; there was nothing to repair. So the hands that once made dust into a man make dust into eyes: creation rather than medicine. The God who said let there be light made light enter eyes that had never known it. Kneading mud was also one of the kinds of work the rabbis’ rules forbade on the Sabbath (v. 14).

He anointed the man’s eyes. Jesus healed by a word constantly, even from miles away (4:50). Here he uses his fingers and wet earth: perhaps to engage the man’s faith by sending him to wash, perhaps as a deliberate challenge to the Sabbath traditions. The man can only feel a stranger’s fingers putting wet earth on his face. If God’s work in your life has felt less like a miracle and more like being roughly handled, you are in this man’s company: for him too the process was messy, and he had no idea what was happening while it went on.

Does God still heal today? Yes, God can and does heal, in answer to prayer and through the ordinary means of doctors and medicine, which are also his gifts (James 5:14–16). He is the same Lord. But the sign-miracles of Jesus and his apostles were given to confirm who he was and to launch the church, and Scripture does not promise that every believer who prays in faith will be healed now. Christians differ here: many faithful believers expect gifts of healing to continue in the church, while this commentary, with many Reformed churches, holds that the apostles’ sign-gifts ceased with them; both agree that God still hears and answers prayer for the sick. Paul left Trophimus ill (2 Timothy 4:20) and lived with his own thorn (2 Corinthians 12:7–9). So pray boldly for healing, use every good means, and trust God with the answer. The final healing of every believer is certain, at the resurrection, when he will make all things new.
verseByVerse.note: Saliva was widely believed to have healing power. Kneading mud counted as work on the Sabbath under the traditions.

parallels.desc: the LORD God formed the man of dust

verseByVerse.quote: and said to him, "Go, wash in the pool of Siloam" (which means Sent). So he went and washed and came back seeing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The pool of Siloam. The pool lay at the south end of the city, fed by Hezekiah’s tunnel, cut through solid rock to bring the Gihon spring inside the walls (2 Kings 20:20); its remains, a large stepped pool, were uncovered in 2004. Isaiah speaks of the waters of Shiloah (the same name as Siloam) that flow gently, a picture of God’s quiet help, which Judah refused (Isaiah 8:6). At the feast just past, the golden pitcher had been filled here every morning (7:37), and now Jesus sends a blind man to the same pool. Like Naaman told to wash in the Jordan (2 Kings 5:10), the man must obey.

Which means Sent. John explains the name (from the Hebrew shalach, to send), which he rarely does with places. Sent is this Gospel’s own word for Jesus, the one the Father sent (v. 4). A man is sent by the Sent One to a pool called Sent, and comes back seeing.

Came back seeing. Simple obedience, immediate result. He walks, probably across much of the city, with mud on his face, at the word of a voice he does not recognise. And no promise was attached: Jesus did not say, and you will see. He said, go and wash.

Does God heal through my obedience, or is it all grace? It is all grace, and grace works through obedience. The man did not heal himself by walking to Siloam; the power was entirely Christ’s. But Christ chose to give his gift through the man’s act of trusting obedience. That is the pattern of the Christian life: God works in you, both to will and to work (Philippians 2:13), and you work out what he works in. The water did not have the power, and the walking did not earn the sight. But a man who refused to go would have stayed blind. So do what Christ says, not to earn his gift, but because the gift comes along the road of trust.

In everyday life. Consider the clear instructions Scripture gives without any explanation of what they will accomplish: to forgive, to give, to confess, to rest. If we will obey only once we have been told how it will work, we are not obeying; we are bargaining. This man had mud on his eyes and a direction, and that was enough.

For worship. Judah once refused the waters of Shiloah that flow gently, and put its hope in kings. Now that gentle help has come in person. The Son moves through the streets of Jerusalem unhurried and unspectacular, and he is enough; no one who comes to him blind goes away the same. The pool was only named Sent. He is the Sent One himself.
verseByVerse.note: The pool of Siloam lay at the south end of the city, fed by Hezekiah’s tunnel.

parallels.desc: Hezekiah brought water into the city
the waters of Shiloah

verseByVerse.quote: The neighbors and those who had seen him before as a beggar were saying, "Is this not the man who used to sit and beg?" Some said, "It is he." Others said, "No, but he is like him." He kept saying, "I am the man."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Is this not the man who used to sit and beg? A blind man had few options but begging. His neighbours knew him only as the blind beggar. Nobody uses his name: John never gives it in the whole chapter, and neither do his neighbours. To them he was simply his blindness.

He is like him. The change is so great they hardly recognise him. What stands before them looks like him and does not behave like him: upright, moving freely, meeting their eyes.

I am the man. The phrase is egō eimi (I am), used here in its ordinary sense: it’s me. He has to keep saying it, because they will not have it.

The same man, made new. The change is total, yet he is still the same man: Christ did not replace him, but gave him his eyes. The Lord does not discard what he redeems. His own risen body was the same body, bearing the marks of the nails, and yet Mary at the tomb did not at first know him (20:14–16, 27). The Saviour who rose as himself, changed and still himself, will transform our lowly bodies to be like his glorious body (Philippians 3:21).

If I am a new creation, why do I still feel so much like my old self? Because God remakes you without replacing you. You are still you: your history, your personality, your memories. What has changed is your standing with God, the life of the Spirit in you, and the direction you are now facing (2 Corinthians 5:17). The old habits and feelings do not all vanish at once; the new nature grows over a lifetime, often slowly (Romans 12:2). Like this man, you may find that others notice the change before you do. Do not measure your new birth by how new you feel this morning. Measure it by Christ, who has made you his, and keep walking in the light.

parallels.desc: they recognized him as the one who sat begging

verseByVerse.quote: So they said to him, "Then how were your eyes opened?" He answered, "The man called Jesus made mud and anointed my eyes and said to me, 'Go to Siloam and wash.' So I went and washed and received my sight."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man called Jesus. The question how runs through the chapter (vv. 15, 19, 26), and so does the growth of the man’s answer to who: the man called Jesus (v. 11), a prophet (v. 17), one from God (v. 33), and at last the Son of Man, Lord, worshipped (vv. 35–38). His sight was given in a moment; his understanding grows step by step. Here he has only the name, reported the way you would report a stranger’s.

I received my sight. He tells it plainly, without interpretation. And the versions get shorter rather than longer: here a full sentence with the name and the instruction, to the Pharisees a dozen words (v. 15), under real pressure only the core (v. 25). Invented stories tend to grow in the telling. This one gets shorter. And this is a beggar, whose living had depended on telling his story well. Given a real audience for the first time, he tells it plainly.

I do not have a dramatic testimony. Do I have anything to say? Yes. Your testimony is not the story of how bad you were, or how sudden your conversion was. It is what Jesus has done for you, and that is never small. This man’s first testimony was three plain sentences, and it set off an investigation that ran the length of a chapter and defeated the best-trained men in Jerusalem. If you were raised in a Christian home and cannot remember not believing, your testimony is that God kept you and opened your eyes early. Say it in your own words: what Christ is to you, what he has forgiven, what he has changed, why you trust him. That is enough.

For worship. The beggar said the name the way one reports a stranger’s, and without knowing it he said everything. The name Jesus means the LORD saves. Heaven had chosen that name before Mary’s child was born (Matthew 1:21), and here Jesus had lived up to it on a blind man’s eyes, before the man knew what the name meant. Jesus is content to be known at first only by his name, and he patiently teaches its meaning himself, until each of his people knows it as the name above every name.

verseByVerse.quote: They said to him, "Where is he?" He said, "I do not know." They brought to the Pharisees the man who had formerly been blind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Where is he? I do not know. The crowds at the feast had asked the same question (7:11), and where Jesus is, and where he comes from, runs through chapters 7 to 9. The man has never seen him. When he came back seeing, Jesus had gone, and he will not meet him until verse 35. So the whole defence he is about to make, against trained interrogators and at the cost of his place in the community, is made for a man he could not pick out of a crowd. He has no relationship with Jesus yet. He has an event and a name.

The Lord no one can trap. At the feast his enemies hunted him and could not lay a hand on him, because his hour had not yet come (7:30; 8:20); a beggar who could hunt no one will be found by him. Jesus is never where men can corner him and always where his sheep need him. His absence in these verses is not neglect; it leaves the man, for a while, to stand on what Christ has done before he knows who Christ is. We are not held by the strength of our grip on Christ, but by the strength of his grip on us.

They brought him to the Pharisees. Perhaps they wanted an official ruling, because it was a Sabbath. The referral is not obviously hostile: an unexplained healing was a religious matter, and taking it to the authorities is what a careful neighbourhood would do. It turns into an interrogation because the Pharisees have their authority to lose if Jesus is from God. The man goes willingly, assuming that people who ask questions want answers; he will learn otherwise, and learning it is what makes him a disciple.

What if I believe, but there is still so much about Jesus I do not know? You are where this man was. A great deal of real faith begins with something that happened before there was much understanding to attach it to: a prayer answered, a word that struck home, a sense of being found. The understanding comes later, often through trouble, as it did for him. Do not despise your beginnings, and do not stay in them. Ask to know him better, read his word, and expect to grow. And take comfort: you may not yet know where Jesus is in every situation, but he always knows where you are.

verseByVerse.quote: Now it was a Sabbath day when Jesus made the mud and opened his eyes. So the Pharisees again asked him how he had received his sight. And he said to them, "He put mud on my eyes, and I washed, and I see."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now it was a Sabbath day. John holds this detail back until now. As in 5:9, it is a Sabbath healing. The rabbis’ tradition listed thirty-nine kinds of work forbidden on the Sabbath, and kneading was one; making mud counted as kneading. Some also forbade putting saliva on the eyes, and they debated whether healing was allowed at all when life was not in danger. A man blind from birth was in no danger; he could have waited until sundown.

He chose this on purpose. He could have spoken a word, as he usually does, and no rule would have been touched. He chose the one method that would cross their Sabbath rules in a way nobody could miss. The man’s eyes matter; but Jesus is also deliberately forcing the question of who has authority over the Sabbath, as he did in chapter 5 with a man and his mat: my Father is working until now, and I am working (5:17). The God who rested on the seventh day after making the world was at work on this seventh day making a new creation, and he is still at work, until the day when all his people enter his rest.

And I see. No name, no instruction, no explanation. His answer is shorter because he is getting impatient, not because he is hiding anything: he gives the one fact nobody can argue away.

Did Jesus really break the Sabbath? He broke the rules the teachers had added to it, which forbade kneading and healing, not God’s command. The law of Moses never forbade doing good on the Sabbath, and Jesus taught that works of mercy were always lawful (Matthew 12:12). He is Lord of the Sabbath (Mark 2:28). The Pharisees’ premise, that he did not keep the Sabbath, was false.

In everyday life. Don’t let human rules stand between people and the mercy of God. Ask whether any expectations in your church, or your own heart, make it harder for hurting people to come to Christ. Keep what God commands. Hold everything else loosely.

verseByVerse.quote: Some of the Pharisees said, "This man is not from God, for he does not keep the Sabbath." But others said, "How can a man who is a sinner do such signs?" And there was a division among them. So they said again to the blind man, "What do you say about him, since he has opened your eyes?" He said, "He is a prophet."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not from God. Some start from their Sabbath rule, and so the miracle must be explained away. Others start from the miracle, which is a fair argument. The difference is which of the two they treat as beyond question.

A division among them. Division (schisma, a tear): Jesus divides people wherever he goes (7:43; 10:19), and now even the Pharisees are split. It is a small mercy: some of the men whose job was to guard the people from false prophets were following the evidence, and said so. A man may belong to a body that has made up its mind and still think for himself.

What do you say about him, since he has opened your eyes? They ask the man himself, perhaps hoping he will help their case. A council of trained men cannot agree, and asks the opinion of the man they are examining. It is asked dismissively, and it is the question that starts him thinking.

He is a prophet. His second step. Nobody taught him; he has reasoned it out under questioning. His faith is being built by the very process designed to dismantle it, and he is more right than he knows. Moses had promised a prophet like himself, whom Israel must hear (Deuteronomy 18:15), and the crowds at the feast had been asking whether Jesus was the Prophet (7:40). The beggar has said the smallest true thing about Jesus, and it leads on to the greatest: the prophets carried God’s words, but Jesus is himself the Word of God (1:1). A beggar called him a prophet and was right. Heaven calls him Lord, and is right.

What if I start from the wrong fixed point? Everyone starts somewhere. These Pharisees had made their own reading of the Sabbath the one thing that could not be questioned, and so they could not see God at work in front of them. Christians can do the same with a tradition, a political view, a favourite teacher or a past experience. The test is whether you will let Scripture and the facts of what Christ has done correct your fixed point, or whether you explain away anything that does not fit. Hold firm to what God has clearly said. Hold everything else humbly, ready to be corrected.

parallels.desc: a prophet who gives a sign

verseByVerse.quote: The Jews did not believe that he had been blind and had received his sight, until they called the parents of the man who had received his sight and asked them, "Is this your son, who you say was born blind? How then does he now see?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
They did not believe. The Jews here means the same Pharisees, the leaders. They cannot find a fault in the man’s account, so they deny that he was ever blind.

Until they called the parents. The parents are the best witnesses, and the summons is also a tactic. They have a witness who will not budge; they want one who will, and parents have more to lose.

Is this your son, who you say was born blind? How then does he now see? Three questions: is he your son, was he born blind, and how does he see? And the wording quietly plants a doubt. Not, who was born blind, but, who you say was born blind. Before a single answer is given, the blindness has been turned from a fact into something the family merely claims, and then it is the family that is investigated. The Pharisees never actually say the man is lying. People still do this, and it does not even take malice.

The sign they could not undo. The same method would be used on the greatest sign of all. When the tomb was found empty, the chief priests, Matthew tells us, did not deny it was empty; they paid the guards to say the disciples had stolen the body (Matthew 28:11–15). Make the witnesses the question, and nobody has to face the fact itself. But the risen Christ, like the seeing beggar, kept standing in front of people, and no investigation has put him back in the tomb. The Light cannot be argued out of the room; it only shows more clearly the more closely it is examined.

How should I handle evidence that is inconvenient? Honestly. The tempting move, when a fact threatens something we have decided, is to turn it into somebody’s opinion and then question the person. The honest move is to look at the fact itself. That applies to the evidence for Christ, which deserves to be weighed rather than waved away. It also applies to Christians, when something we do not want to hear comes to light: a hard passage of Scripture, a just complaint against us, a wrong done in our church. Truth is never the enemy of faith. The God of truth is not served by anyone’s refusal to look.

verseByVerse.quote: His parents answered, "We know that this is our son and that he was born blind. But how he now sees we do not know, nor do we know who opened his eyes. Ask him; he is of age. He will speak for himself."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Our son, born blind. They answer the first two questions plainly. Under pressure, they confirm the two facts that make the miracle undeniable, and the claim that the blindness was invented dies in their answer.

We do not know. They avoid the third. They probably did know; their son must have told them. They are afraid.

Ask him; he is of age. A son was regarded as of age at about thirteen, able to give legal testimony, and this man was an adult. So they shift the danger onto him, at the moment he most needs someone beside him.

Be fair to them. The parents are often spoken of with contempt, and that is too harsh. They had raised a blind child in a world with no provision for one, in a society that had already decided someone’s sin was responsible; the disciples’ question in verse 2 is what these two had been hearing about themselves all his life. Now the authorities were in effect asking them to risk being put out of the synagogue (v. 22). They did not lie, and they did not stand by their son, and John records it without comment.

The one who stood alone. Within months the same pressure fell on Jesus himself, and those closest to him did what these parents did. Matthew and Mark tell us that when he was arrested all the disciples left him and fled (Matthew 26:56; Mark 14:50), and he stood before the high priest with no friend beside him. He bore that loneliness on purpose. The Son was left standing alone, so that none of those he came for would ever finally stand alone.

I have gone quiet about Christ when I should have spoken. Is that the end of me? No. If you have gone quiet when the subject came up at work, or let a remark pass, or answered a direct question with something technically true and deliberately empty, that is the same failure as theirs, and Scripture records it honestly but without harshness. See what does not happen to these two. They are not cursed or written off. Peter would do far worse within months, three times, out loud, and be given breakfast on a beach and a commission (21:15–19). The failure is real, and it need not be final. Underneath most of our silences is the fear of man, which needs the approval of the people in the room more than it needs God’s, and it lays a snare (Proverbs 29:25). The cure is not more willpower but a larger sight of the approval you already have in Christ. Confess it to the Lord, ask for courage, and take the next opportunity he gives you.

In everyday life. Look for the believer near you who is paying a price for faithfulness: the colleague who refused to lie, the relative who has been shut out. Stand next to them this week, in some visible way.

For worship. For my father and my mother have forsaken me, but the LORD will take me in (Psalm 27:10). A grown son stood alone before a hostile court, and the Lord was already on his way to him. He receives those whose own families stepped back. He restores those who stepped back themselves. And he has never once said of any of his people, Ask him; he is of age.
verseByVerse.note: A son was regarded as of age at about thirteen.

verseByVerse.quote: (His parents said these things because they feared the Jews, for the Jews had already agreed that if anyone should confess Jesus to be Christ, he was to be put out of the synagogue. Therefore his parents said, "He is of age; ask him.")
verseByVerse.commentary:
Put out of the synagogue. His parents spoke as they did because they feared the Jews, meaning the leaders. Being put out of the synagogue (aposynagōgos, 12:42; 16:2) meant exclusion from the community. Some scholars argue this reflects a later period, after AD 70, but local exclusion could already happen in Jesus’ lifetime; Luke 6:22 records him warning of it.

What it cost. The synagogue was not a church one might change. It was the school, the court, the welfare system and the register of who belonged. Exclusion could mean that no one would trade with you, marry your children or sit with you: not embarrassment but the removal of every relationship the family had.

Already agreed. The decision had been taken in advance, before this man’s case came up. The investigation in this chapter was never really an investigation. And though the man never says Christ, only a prophet and from God, the policy seems to be applied to him anyway (v. 34).

Confess Jesus to be Christ. To confess is to declare openly that he is the Messiah, Israel’s anointed King. But the Christ himself would be put out before any of his followers were. He was rejected by the leaders of his people, led out of the city, and suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood (Hebrews 13:12). Every disciple since who has been shut out for his name finds Christ already there, outside with him. The one who was put out for us has made a home for us that no council can shut.

What if confessing Christ would cost me my family or my job? Then you are in the company of this man, and of believers in many countries today for whom it is exactly that costly. Jesus does not hide the price: whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me (Matthew 10:37). But he also promises that no one who leaves home or family for his sake will fail to receive a hundredfold now, in the family of his church, and eternal life in the age to come (Mark 10:29–30). Count the cost honestly. Seek wisdom about how and when to speak, and the support of other believers. But do not deny him. What you lose for Christ, you never lose for ever.
verseByVerse.note: Being put out of the synagogue meant exclusion from the community’s worship and social life.

parallels.desc: they will put you out of the synagogues

verseByVerse.quote: So for the second time they called the man who had been blind and said to him, "Give glory to God. We know that this man is a sinner." He answered, "Whether he is a sinner I do not know. One thing I do know, that though I was blind, now I see."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Give glory to God. This was a solemn formula for putting a man on oath to tell the truth, especially to confess wrongdoing, as Joshua said to Achan (Joshua 7:19). Here it means: admit this was a fraud. Achan confessed under that formula and was put to death, because the holy God had been robbed (Joshua 7:20–25). These men use the language of God’s holiness to frighten a beggar, and never ask whether they themselves stand before the holy God.

We know that this man is a sinner. They have settled the matter: a Sabbath-breaker is a sinner. The verdict is announced before the testimony is taken.

Whether he is a sinner I do not know. He will not be drawn into an argument he is not equipped to win. He refuses to give an opinion he does not have, and that honesty is rare in a man under pressure.

One thing I do know. John Newton echoed it in Amazing Grace. It is the shortest form his story has yet taken, and unbreakable. They can outrank him, out-argue him and out-quote him. They cannot make him doubt that he was blind yesterday.

Glory given without knowing it. They told him to give glory to God, and he did, more truly than they meant. In this Gospel the glory of God is seen in the works of the Son (2:11; 11:4, 40), and the plainest way to glorify God is to say what his Son has done. The beggar tells the truth about Jesus, and so honours the Father; the men demanding glory for God are refusing it to the one in whom God’s glory shines (8:54).

Is my experience enough to prove Christianity is true? It is part of your witness, but it is not the whole case, and this man shows why. His experience is where he stands; it is not where he stops. In verse 33 he reasons from Scripture and history to a conclusion about who Jesus is. Experience can be misread, and people of other faiths also report experiences. The Christian faith rests on what God has done in history, above all the death and resurrection of Christ, and on what he has said in Scripture. Your experience of his grace is the personal confirmation of that public truth. So tell what has happened to you, and point beyond yourself to the Christ it all depends on.
verseByVerse.note: “Give glory to God” was a solemn call to tell the truth.

parallels.desc: give glory to the LORD and tell me now what you have done

verseByVerse.quote: They said to him, "What did he do to you? How did he open your eyes?" He answered them, "I have told you already, and you would not listen. Why do you want to hear it again? Do you also want to become his disciples?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
You would not listen. They go over it again, looking for a contradiction, and he is growing bolder. The exasperation is genuine, and funny: he has worked out that they hope the story will come out differently the second time. These men have working eyes and ears and are getting nothing through either.

The disciple sounds like his Master. You would not listen: Jesus had said the same to the same men only days before. Why do you not understand what I say? It is because you cannot bear to hear my word (8:43). The beggar never heard that sentence, yet he is already being treated as his Lord was treated, and answering as his Lord answered. If they persecuted him, they will persecute his people too (15:20). The road of the disciple is the road Christ walked first.

Why do you want to hear it again? There is a mischievous edge to it. He knows the answer before he asks.

Do you also want to become his disciples? A daring, ironic question. The Greek form expects the answer no. And “also” implies that he himself is, or is becoming, one. It is sarcasm, and it is also, accidentally, evangelism: the first invitation in the chapter, issued by a beggar to the council’s investigators. Up to now he has been reporting. Here he takes sides. And look at what has produced this. Not a conversation with Jesus, whom he has still never seen. Not teaching. Being pushed. Every question they ask drives him one step further into a position he had not held before, and by the end of the interview he is a disciple of a man he could not recognise.

How can opposition make faith stronger? Because it forces us to decide what we really believe, and to lean on God rather than on comfort. Peter says that trials test faith as fire tests gold (1 Peter 1:6–7), and James that testing produces steadfastness (James 1:2–4). This man had faith the size of a name when the questioning began, and a clear confession when it ended. It is not that hardship automatically strengthens faith; sometimes it shakes it. But God uses it, for those who keep turning to him, to burn away what is false and make the real thing plain. If your faith is under pressure now, do not assume it is failing. It may be growing.

For worship. The Lord who chooses what is weak in the world to shame the strong had put his wit in a beggar’s mouth and his courage in a beggar’s heart. The man did not yet know who Christ was, and already the life of Christ was showing in him. He does not only rescue his people; he makes them like himself, so that the world, questioning them, finds itself hearing him.

verseByVerse.quote: And they reviled him, saying, "You are his disciple, but we are disciples of Moses. We know that God has spoken to Moses, but as for this man, we do not know where he comes from."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they reviled him. “Reviled” (eloidorēsan): abused, insulted. They began with an investigation, moved to intimidation, and end by shouting at a beggar.

Disciples of Moses. They set Moses against Jesus. But Moses wrote of Jesus (5:46), so their claim defeats itself: anyone who meets the one Moses wrote about and refuses him is no longer following Moses. The pronouns draw a line: you are his; we are Moses’. And there is a warning in the boast. The name of Moses has become a badge of being on the right side, and religion used that way is the hardest blindness to cure, because it looks like sight.

We know that God has spoken to Moses. That much was true (Exodus 33:11). But for them God’s speaking lies in the past and is finished. The man in front of them is evidence that God has acted today, and their thinking has no room for that.

We do not know where he comes from. The question of his origin again. Earlier they claimed to know where he came from (7:27); now they say they do not. They mean that he has no credentials. In fact they have named their own problem: they do not know that he came from God.

Is the Old Testament still for Christians, or has Jesus replaced Moses? Jesus has not replaced Moses; he has fulfilled him. The whole Old Testament is God’s word and points to Christ (Luke 24:27, 44). Its promises are kept in him, its sacrifices fulfilled in his once-for-all death, its moral law written on our hearts by the Spirit. The Pharisees’ error was not loving Moses too much but reading him without Christ, so that the book meant to lead them to Jesus became a wall against him. Read the Old Testament gladly, as Christian Scripture, and ask in every part how it leads you to the one Moses wrote about.

verseByVerse.quote: The man answered, "Why, this is an amazing thing! You do not know where he comes from, and yet he opened my eyes. We know that God does not listen to sinners, but if anyone is a worshiper of God and does his will, God listens to him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
An amazing thing. The beggar becomes the teacher, amazed that the experts cannot see the obvious. The Lord who hid these things from the wise and revealed them to little children gave a beggar the clearest reasoning in the room.

We know that God does not listen to sinners. He turns their “we know” back on them. This was a common Jewish belief, drawn from Scripture: God does not hear the prayers of the wicked who cling to their sin (Psalm 66:18; Proverbs 15:29; Isaiah 1:15). It does not mean God never hears a repentant sinner’s prayer (Luke 18:13–14). In the man’s argument it means that God would not answer an impostor’s prayer by doing what Scripture reserves for God himself, opening the eyes of a man born blind. He argues from a belief they share with him, which is why they cannot answer it.

A sentence that needs a guard. Lifted out of this courtyard and read as a rule about prayer, these words have frightened people badly. They are the healed man’s words, a new believer arguing from the common piety of his day, not a formula handed down from heaven. Even the psalm behind it says something narrower: if I had cherished iniquity in my heart, the Lord would not have listened (Psalm 66:18). The word is cherished. What closes God’s ear is not the presence of sin in a person but his fondness for it: the man who hugs his sin and demands God’s help at the same time.

God listens to him. So, he concludes, Jesus must be a godly man whom God hears. He is more right than he knows. There is one man whom the Father always hears (11:42), the one who always does what pleases him (8:29), the true worshipper the Father has been seeking. And sinners are heard at all only through that man, whose perfect obedience is counted as theirs.

I am a sinner. Will God listen to my prayers? Yes. The plainest answer is a story Jesus told. A tax collector stood far off, would not lift his eyes, beat his breast and prayed for mercy as a sinner, and Jesus said that man went home justified (Luke 18:13–14). Justified means declared right with God by God himself: his sin forgiven, his record settled, his standing accepted, not because of his prayer but because of the mercy he asked for. God listened to a sinner, at the very moment he called himself one. If you have been afraid that your sin has stopped God’s ears, see which way the fear runs. The person whose sin has closed God’s ear is not troubled about it. The trouble you feel is not evidence that he has stopped listening. It is very often the first evidence that he has already begun to work. Come to him through Christ, honestly, and he will hear you.

In everyday life. Is there a sin you are holding on to while asking God for help? The Son has already borne it; let it go, and pray.

parallels.desc: if I had cherished iniquity, the Lord would not have listened

verseByVerse.quote: "Never since the world began has it been heard that anyone opened the eyes of a man born blind. If this man were not from God, he could do nothing."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Never since the world began. He is right. The Old Testament has spectacular healings: Elijah and Elisha each raised a dead child, and Naaman’s leprosy went. But no one anywhere in Scripture before this opens the eyes of someone blind from birth. The Old Testament reserves the opening of blind eyes to God himself (Psalm 146:8; Exodus 4:11), and promises it as a sign of the days when the Messiah would come (Isaiah 29:18; 35:5; 42:7). So the beggar’s argument is an accurate survey of the record, from a man who had listened to a great deal of Scripture in the synagogue he was about to be thrown out of. The sign says that God himself is at work, and the Messiah has come. The promised new age had begun, and the God who made the eye had come to give it sight.

If this man were not from God. His third step: Jesus is from God. The question they cannot answer, the beggar answers. He does not say Jesus is the Messiah, which he has no way yet of knowing; he claims only the least that the evidence proves, and it is enough to end the argument. It leaves them nothing to attack except him.

How should I think about the evidence for Christ? Like this man: clearly, honestly, and from the facts. Christianity does not ask you to switch off your mind. The signs were written so that you may believe (20:30–31), and the risen Christ was seen by many witnesses, most of them still alive when Paul wrote (1 Corinthians 15:3–8). Weigh the evidence: the Old Testament promises, the life and claims of Jesus, the empty tomb, the transformation of the disciples. Evidence alone does not save; the Spirit must open the heart. But God uses evidence, and a mind that reasons honestly from what Christ has done will find that it points to God, even while some questions remain.

parallels.desc: the eyes of the blind shall be opened

verseByVerse.quote: They answered him, "You were born in utter sin, and would you teach us?" And they cast him out. Jesus heard that they had cast him out, and having found him he said, "Do you believe in the Son of Man?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
You were born in utter sin. They go back to the disciples’ mistaken assumption (v. 2): your blindness proves you were born in sin. In admitting he was born blind, they finally admit the miracle. And yet the irony is that it is true of all of us: we are all born in sin (Psalm 51:5), they too. What the disciples raised as a puzzle, these men use as a weapon.

And would you teach us? Pride: a beggar cannot teach scholars. They never manage to say, you are wrong. They say, who do you think you are? They have lost the argument, so they fall back on their rank. This is what happens when a man’s position becomes the one thing he cannot afford to lose: he no longer weighs what is said, only who says it. Such a heart cannot be taught by the gospel, which always comes from below: in a manger, from a cross, through a beggar.

They cast him out. Out of the room, and probably out of the synagogue (v. 22). He has lost his community and standing for confessing Jesus: a man with new eyes and nothing else.

Having found him. Rejected by the religious leaders, the man is found by the Good Shepherd, who calls his own sheep by name and leads them out (10:3–4). Jesus never casts out anyone who comes to him (6:37); those cast out for his sake, he gathers in. The words having found him suggest that Jesus went looking. The man could not have gone looking for a face he had never seen; while he stood in the street with nowhere to go, he was already being sought. The one who saw the man first, when he was blind and begging and unaware anyone was there, came back and found him again the moment the world had finished with him. That is the whole Gospel in one man’s afternoon. The Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost, and he has never stopped looking for those that everyone else has thrown away.

In the flow. Chapters 9 and 10 are joined more tightly than the chapter division suggests. They cast him out (exebalon, vv. 34–35); a few sentences later the good shepherd brings out all his own (10:4), with the same verb. The Pharisees threw the man out of their fold; the Shepherd was bringing him out of it.

Do you believe in the Son of Man? “Son of Man” is Jesus’ favourite title for himself. It comes from Daniel 7:13–14, where one like a son of man comes before God and receives a kingdom that will never end. Jesus is asking a man who has just been stripped of his standing in Israel whether he will believe in the one to whom every kingdom is finally given.

Textual note. Later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read “Son of God.” The earliest and best manuscripts read “Son of Man,” and a scribe is more likely to have changed it to the more familiar confession than the other way round. The meaning is not changed: in John the Son of Man is the one who comes from heaven (3:13).

I have been rejected by a church or by Christians. Has Christ rejected me? No. Sometimes believers are put out unjustly, as this man was, and Christ sees it and comes looking for them. If you have been wronged by a church, bring it to him; he is the Good Shepherd, and he has not cast you out. At the same time, be honest: sometimes church discipline is a loving and right response to unrepented sin (Matthew 18:15–17), meant to bring a person home, not to destroy them. Whatever has happened, do not let the failures of Christians keep you from Christ, and do not give up on his people. Seek a faithful church where you can be known and cared for.

In everyday life. Who has been pushed out of the circles you move in: the family, the friendship group, the church? Christ went looking for you; go and look for them.
verseByVerse.note: “Son of Man” is Jesus’ favourite title for himself.

parallels.desc: brought forth in iniquity

verseByVerse.quote: He answered, "And who is he, sir, that I may believe in him?" Jesus said to him, "You have seen him, and it is he who is speaking to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And who is he, sir, that I may believe in him? Sir (kyrie) can mean sir or Lord. He commits before he knows the answer: not, tell me who he is and I will consider it, but, I am ready to believe and need only the name. And he is speaking to a stranger, because he has never seen the face.

You have seen him. Since the pool this man has seen his neighbours, his parents and the council, but never this face. The eyes he is using to look at Jesus were made by the man he is looking at, out of dirt.

He who is speaking to you. As Jesus revealed himself to the Samaritan woman (4:26). Twice in this Gospel Jesus states his identity outright to one person, without being pressed, and both times to someone with no standing at all. The men who run the temple, who kept demanding that he speak plainly, never once heard it put to them as simply as this.

How does Jesus reveal himself to people today? Through his word, by his Spirit. He no longer stands in the street to be seen with physical eyes; he speaks in Scripture, in the preaching of the gospel, and the Spirit opens hearts to see him there (Romans 10:17; 2 Corinthians 4:6). That is not second best. Jesus said that those who have not seen and yet believe are blessed (20:29). If you want to know him, go where he speaks: read a Gospel, sit under faithful preaching, and ask him to show himself to you. Like this man, you may find he has been speaking to you all along.

For worship. Moses asked to see God’s glory and was shown only his back. A beggar who had lost everything was shown the face. The only Son, who is at the Father’s side, has made him known (1:18), and he makes him known still, not to those who are sure they already see, but to those who ask, Who is he, Lord? We shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2), and the first face of the age to come will be the face that sought us when we could not seek him.

parallels.desc: I who speak to you am he

verseByVerse.quote: He said, "Lord, I believe," and he worshiped him. Jesus said, "For judgment I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lord, I believe. Now “Lord” (kyrie) in its full sense, the last step of his confession.

And he worshiped him. Worshiped (prosekynēsen): bowed down before him. In John this word is used only of worshipping God (4:20–24; 12:20). Jesus accepts it, because he is God: the man ends on his face. A beggar in a Jerusalem street was the first in this Gospel to fall down before him, and he will not be the last.

Textual note. A few early manuscripts lack “He said, ‘Lord, I believe,’ and he worshiped him. Jesus said.” Many scholars think the words are original: they are found in the great majority of manuscripts, including very early ones, and the omission may be accidental.

For judgment I came into this world. Jesus did not come to condemn (3:17), but his coming brings a separation. The giving of sight itself divides people: the man who knew he was blind can see, and the men who were certain they could see have spent the chapter proving they cannot. Nobody was condemned by a new verdict. They were exposed by a light, which is what light does.

In the flow. Verse 39 gathers up the Gospel so far: the light came and his own did not receive him (1:9–11); people loved the darkness (3:19). Chapter 9 is that sentence acted out in a single day, and in chapter 12 John will explain the leaders’ blindness from Isaiah 6 (12:37–41).

That those who do not see may see. Those who know they are blind and come to him are given sight; those who are sure they already see are left in their blindness (Isaiah 6:9–10; Matthew 11:25).

Is it right to worship Jesus? Yes, and this verse is one of the plainest reasons. Scripture forbids worshipping anyone but God (Exodus 20:3–5; Matthew 4:10), and when Cornelius bowed before Peter, or John before an angel, they were told at once to stand up (Acts 10:25–26; Revelation 22:8–9). Jesus never says that. He receives this man’s worship, and Thomas’ confession, my Lord and my God (20:28), because he is God the Son. The Father wills that all should honour the Son just as they honour the Father (5:23). So Christians rightly pray to Jesus, sing to him and bow before him, together with the Father and the Spirit, one God.

For worship. On his face in a Jerusalem street, a man just thrown out of the house of worship worshipped. He had found the true temple standing in front of him in a body. The council kept the building; the beggar had the Lord of it.

verseByVerse.quote: Some of the Pharisees near him heard these things, and said to him, "Are we also blind?" Jesus said to them, "If you were blind, you would have no guilt; but now that you say, 'We see,' your guilt remains."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Are we also blind? The Greek form expects the answer no. Surely not us? They are not asking; they are inviting a denial, and they ask because they have understood him perfectly well.

If you were blind, you would have no guilt. If they knew themselves to be blind and came to him for sight, their sin would be forgiven; or, if they truly had no opportunity to see, they would be less guilty. The mercy is real, but no one in that crowd is in that position.

Your guilt remains. Remains (menei): stays, abides. The most dangerous condition is not blindness but the proud claim to see. A man who knows he cannot see will ask for help; a man who is sure he can see will not, and there is nothing further to be done for him while he goes on saying it (compare Revelation 3:17). The last word of the chapter is John’s word for abiding, but here it is guilt that stays, as at 3:36: the wrath of God remains on him. Sin has only two ways to go. It remains, or it is carried away by the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world (1:29). The men who said we see kept theirs.

Two kinds of blind men. That is the chapter in one line. One of them said, I do not know, twice (vv. 12, 25), and ended on his face worshipping. The others said, we know (vv. 24, 29), and we see (v. 41), and ended with nothing but the verdict they had passed on him. They would rather be blind than be taught by a beggar.

How do I know whether I am one of those who think they see? Ask whether you are still teachable. The Pharisees could not be taught by anyone below them. Ask when you last changed your mind about something because Scripture corrected you, or when you last let a doctrine you hold be questioned by someone with less standing than you. Ask whether you pray for light, or assume you already have it. This test is meant to catch the confident, not to crush the anxious. If you are worried that you might be blind, and want Christ to open your eyes, that very worry shows you are not where these men were. The humble cry, Lord, that I may see, is the cry he always answers.

For worship. Every one of us was born on the wrong side of this verse, blind and sure we could see. If any of us now see, it is not because we were humbler than the Pharisees, but because the Light of the world came close enough to touch us, and showed us our blindness before he cured it. Even knowing that we are blind is his gift. The light that exposes is the light that heals, and he never shines it on his own people to shame them, only to bring them home.

parallels.desc: a guide to the blind

One thing I do know, that though I was blind, now I see.”<sup>26</sup>They said to him, “What did he do to you? How did he open your eyes?”<sup>27</sup>He answered them, “I have told you already, and you would not listen. Why do you want to hear it again? Do you also want to become his disciples?”<sup>28</sup>And they reviled him, saying, “You are his disciple, but we are disciples of Moses.<sup>29</sup>We know that God has spoken to Moses, but as for this man, we do not know where he comes from.”<sup>30</sup>The man answered, “Why, this is an amazing thing! You do not know where he comes from, and yet he opened my eyes.<sup>31</sup>We know that God does not listen to sinners, but if anyone is a worshiper of God and does his will, God listens to him.<sup>32</sup>Never since the world began has it been heard that anyone opened the eyes of a man born blind.<sup>33</sup>If this man were not from God, he could do nothing.”<sup>34</sup>They answered him, “You were born in utter sin, and would you teach us?” And they cast him out.<sup>35</sup>Jesus heard that they had cast him out, and having found him he said, “Do you believe in the Son of Man?”<sup>36</sup>He answered, “And who is he, sir, that I may believe in him?”<sup>37</sup>Jesus said to him, “You have seen him, and it is he who is speaking to you.”<sup>38</sup>He said, “Lord, I believe,” and he worshiped him.<sup>39</sup>Jesus said, “For judgment I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind.”<sup>40</sup>Some of the Pharisees near him heard these things, and said to him, “Are we also blind?”<sup>41</sup>Jesus said to them, “If you were blind, you would have no guilt; but now that you say, ’We see,’ your guilt remains.
9.overview:
Jesus has just called himself the light of the world (8:12); now he gives sight to a man blind from birth, the sixth sign in John. The disciples ask whose sin caused the blindness; Jesus answers that it happened so that God’s works might be displayed in him. He spreads mud on the man’s eyes and sends him to wash in the pool of Siloam, which means Sent, and the man comes back seeing. A string of questionings follows: the neighbours, the Pharisees, the frightened parents, and the man again, until the leaders throw him out.

Along the way the man’s understanding of Jesus grows until, when Jesus finds him, he calls him Lord and worships him. The Pharisees go the other way, from confident sight to blindness. The chapter shows what conversion is, and how religious certainty can keep a person from seeing.

10.title: The Good Shepherd

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–21 — The Good Shepherd Lays Down His Life
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus contrasts the true shepherd, who comes in by the door and calls his own sheep by name, with thieves who climb in another way. He is the door, through whom the sheep are saved, and the good shepherd, who lays down his life for them of his own accord and will gather other sheep into one flock.
verseByVerse.theology: The shepherd picture draws on the whole Old Testament: God as the shepherd of his people (Psalm 23; Ezekiel 34), the promised shepherd from David’s line (Ezekiel 34:23–24; Jeremiah 23:4). Jesus takes all of it to himself. He is the door, the only way to God; the good shepherd, who gives rather than takes; and the one who lays down his life freely, as no hired hand would. The picture cannot be understood apart from the cross.
verseByVerse.examples: The sheep hear his voice, and that recognition is a gift, not an achievement. They know the shepherd’s voice because they are already his, and not one the Father has given is lost. The Pharisees cannot hear because they are not his sheep (v. 26); the church hears because the Shepherd has given her ears.

verseByVerse.quote: "Truly, truly, I say to you, he who does not enter the sheepfold by the door but climbs in by another way, that man is a thief and a robber. But he who enters by the door is the shepherd of the sheep."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. The Pharisees have just thrown out a sheep of God’s flock, the man born blind (9:34), and Jesus has gone and found him; now he tells them who the true shepherd is. The men listening to this picture of the sheepfold are the men who have just thrown a sheep out of theirs. Behind the chapter lies Ezekiel 34, where God condemns the shepherds of Israel who fed themselves and not the flock, and promises to shepherd his sheep himself. Jesus says, in effect: I am that shepherd. The chapter begins with a beggar thrown out of a synagogue and ends with the Son of God holding his people in hands no power in the universe can open.

Truly, truly, I say to you. The solemn double Amen that Jesus uses when he is about to say something that carries his full authority. The prophets said, thus says the LORD. Jesus says, I say to you: he speaks with God’s own authority.

By another way. Knowing two kinds of first-century sheepfold makes the whole passage clear. The first is the one described here: a walled enclosure in or near a village, often a courtyard beside a house, holding the flocks of several families overnight, with a solid door and a man paid to watch it. The second kind, described by travellers in the region in later centuries and very likely as old as the trade, was used out in the hills: a rough circle of piled stones with a gap and no door at all, because the shepherd lay down across the gap and slept there. Nothing came in or went out except over him. He was the door.

That man is a thief and a robber. The two words are not synonyms. A thief (kleptēs) works by stealth: he wants the animals and would rather not be seen. A robber (lēstēs) is a bandit with violence in hand, the word John uses of Barabbas (18:40). Jesus has in mind, first, the Pharisees who have just cast out the man born blind. Every generation of the church has met both kinds, and the marks are the same: the man did not come in by the door, and he is interested in what he can get out of the sheep.

By the door. The true shepherd comes openly, with the right to be there. He does not need to climb, because the door belongs to him; he does not need to hide, because he has nothing to take. He came as the prophets said he would, born in David’s city, announced by the forerunner, doing in public the works the Scriptures said the Messiah would do. He walked in by the door his Father had built for him over a thousand years of promise.

How do I tell whether a leader has come in by the door? Ask three questions. First, does he come through Christ and his word, or around them? A true shepherd sends you to Christ and is content to be measured by Scripture; a false one needs you to depend on him, his special insight or his new revelation. Second, is he accountable? Doors have keepers. A man who answers to no elders, no church and no one but himself has climbed the wall, however gifted he is (1 Timothy 3:1–7; 1 Peter 5:1–4). Third, what is he taking? Watch where the money, the admiration and the control flow. A shepherd spends himself on the sheep; a thief spends the sheep on himself.
verseByVerse.note: A sheepfold was a walled enclosure where several flocks might be kept overnight, with a single doorway.

parallels.desc: the false shepherds of Israel

verseByVerse.quote: "To him the gatekeeper opens. The sheep hear his voice, and he calls his own sheep by name and leads them out. When he has brought out all his own, he goes before them, and the sheep follow him, for they know his voice."
verseByVerse.commentary:
To him the gatekeeper opens. The gatekeeper knows the true shepherd and lets him in. Some have said he is the Father, the Spirit or John the Baptist, but not every detail of a parable stands for something, and it is wise not to press this one. The point is that Jesus is not an intruder. Heaven opens to him.

By name. The detail is drawn from life. Shepherds in that world led their flocks rather than drove them, and often had names for their sheep, given for a marking, a habit, an injury. Several flocks are mixed in the fold overnight. In the morning a shepherd stands at the door and calls, and out of the mass his own animals detach themselves and come. His own (ta idia) is a warm phrase, they belong to him, as God said to Israel, I have called you by name, you are mine (Isaiah 43:1).

Leads them out. The word (exagei) is used of God leading Israel out of Egypt. And John has just shown it happening. The synagogue authorities threw the man born blind out of their fold; Jesus went and found him (9:35). What looked like being thrown out was really being led out to freedom. Christ always calls his sheep out of somewhere and towards pasture (v. 9).

He goes before them. A dog behind a flock drives it; the animals move because something is pressing them from the rear. This is the opposite. The sheep move because somebody they trust is already moving, and every step of the road he asks them to walk he is walking a few paces ahead. There is no stretch of the road he has not already covered, including death itself, which he went through entirely alone so that nobody following him would ever have to face it alone.

Does Jesus really know me by name, among so many? Yes, and the number is no strain on him. Human attention is divided because we are finite; his is not. The Shepherd who calls the stars by name (Psalm 147:4) knows the hairs of your head (Matthew 10:30). You are not a case number in a vast administration of souls. He knows your history, your temperament, the sin you are fighting and the sorrow you have not told anyone, and he calls you as you are. On days when you feel invisible to everyone, including the church, you are not invisible to him.

In everyday life. Whatever is waiting for you this week, a hard conversation, a hospital appointment, a decision you dread, he has gone ahead of you into it. You are following someone who is already there. Listen for his voice in his word before you walk into the day.
verseByVerse.note: Shepherds in the East led their flocks rather than drove them, and named their sheep; the sheep knew their shepherd’s call.

parallels.desc: who shall go out before them and bring them in

verseByVerse.quote: "A stranger they will not follow, but they will flee from him, for they do not know the voice of strangers." This figure of speech Jesus used with them, but they did not understand what he was saying to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A stranger they will not follow. The healed man would not follow the Pharisees; he had heard the voice that opened his eyes, and after that their voices did not sound like his. What protects the sheep is not constant watchfulness but knowing his voice well. There is a voice in this world that the sheep cannot finally mistake, because it is the voice that called them into being and called them out of the dark. Ten thousand strangers have spoken since, clever and confident and sometimes in his name, and his flock has gone on recognising him.

The way to know a forgery. The way to recognise a false teacher is not first to study false teaching, which is endless and endlessly inventive. It is to know the real voice so well that the wrong one grates, and that is a matter of hours spent in the Gospels rather than hours spent on the internet. Bank staff, it is often said, learn to spot forged notes by handling genuine ones.

They will flee from him. The sheep’s safety consists in moving away, quickly, without an argument; they do not assess the stranger’s credentials or give him a hearing out of politeness. Not every voice claiming to speak for God deserves a debate. Some of them deserve a closed door (2 John 10).

This figure of speech Jesus used with them. The word is paroimia: a proverb, a veiled saying, a picture with something hidden inside it.

They did not understand. It is the same failure as Nicodemus over the new birth (3:4), the Samaritan woman over living water (4:15), the crowd over the bread of life (6:34), and the disciples over his food (4:33). These are Israel’s trained teachers of Scripture, and the picture they cannot follow is a picture of them. They miss it, and in missing it they prove the point: they are not his sheep, and his voice sounds to them like noise.

Christians do get deceived, so what does this promise mean? It means that the elect, those God has chosen as his own, will not be finally and fatally led away from Christ, not that no believer is ever confused. Sheep can be frightened, scattered and misled for a time; Paul had to write to the Galatians because true believers had been bewitched (Galatians 3:1). But the Shepherd guards his own, and they come back to his voice. This is a comfort, not a licence for carelessness. The same apostle who recorded that the sheep will flee from strangers tells us to test the spirits (1 John 4:1), and the means by which the Shepherd keeps his sheep from deception is precisely their knowing his word. So if you have been taken in by something, do not conclude you were never his. Go back to the voice, and let it correct you.

verseByVerse.quote: So Jesus again said to them, "Truly, truly, I say to you, I am the door of the sheep. All who came before me are thieves and robbers, but the sheep did not listen to them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am the door of the sheep. This is the third great I am saying, after the bread of life (6:35) and the light of the world (8:12). Here the hill fold without a gate explains the picture: the shepherd’s own body closed the gap. The two images that look like a muddle (how can he be both the shepherd and the door?) are one image seen at two hours of the day. He leads them out in the morning; he lies across the entrance at dusk. Anything that wants them must get past him first. On a Friday outside Jerusalem the wolf came, the shepherd died in the doorway, and not one sheep was lost. There is only one way into God’s flock, and he is it (14:6).

All who came before me are thieves and robbers. Taken on its own, the sentence would include Moses, Samuel and every prophet, and that cannot be meant by a man who has said that Moses wrote about him (5:46) and that Abraham rejoiced to see his day (8:56). The prophets pointed to him; they did not come instead of him. He means those who claimed to be saviours apart from him. Gamaliel names two such men, Theudas and Judas the Galilean (Acts 5:36–37). They all came for themselves.

Is Jesus really the only way? Yes. He does not say he is a door, one entrance among many, but the door. That is not narrowness on his part but reality: there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5), and there is no other name under heaven by which we must be saved (Acts 4:12). Salvation comes through conscious faith in him. That is exactly why the church sends missionaries, because the door must be shown to those who have not yet heard of it (Romans 10:14–15). But the other half of the picture is just as important: the door is open. The same verse that excludes every other way invites everyone to this one. And it is not arrogant to say so. It would be arrogant if Christians had found the door by their own cleverness or goodness. To point to a door you did not build, and went through only because you were called, is the humblest thing a sinner can do.

In everyday life. Most of us have little doors we are tempted to use instead of him: being good enough, being busy enough in church, having grown up in it, feeling the right things. Come to God today the only way anyone has ever come, through Christ, and come with nothing in your hands.
verseByVerse.note: This is the third of Jesus’ “I am” sayings in John.

verseByVerse.quote: "I am the door. If anyone enters by me, he will be saved and will go in and out and find pasture. The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy. I came that they may have life and have it abundantly."
verseByVerse.commentary:
If anyone enters by me, he will be saved. The offer is open to anyone at all, and the only way in is one person, Christ.

In and out. To go in and out is a Hebrew way of speaking of living in safety, coming and going without fear. Moses asks God for a leader who will go out and come in before the people, so that the congregation of the LORD may not be as sheep that have no shepherd (Numbers 27:17), which is exactly what a shepherd does. So the promise is not that the sheep will be shut in somewhere safe. It is freedom of movement under protection: a door that opens both ways, with somebody trustworthy standing in it. Salvation is not a cage, and the sheep do not merely survive; they feed.

The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy. That is all he ever does, and each step is worse than the last: he takes, he kills, he ruins. Nowhere in the list is the word give. False shepherds use the flock for themselves, and behind every false shepherd stands the one who was a murderer from the beginning (8:44).

Abundantly. “Abundantly” (perisson) means over and above, overflowing. Jesus gives not just survival but the fullness of eternal life, which is to know the only true God and Jesus Christ whom he has sent (17:3). This is the bright side of the cross: not merely rescue from death but the gift of life, not merely pardon but adoption, not merely forgiveness but an inheritance. He did not come to take a little less from us than the thief; he came to give more than we could hold, and the cost of the giving was his own life.

What it does not mean. This verse is a favourite of the prosperity gospel, which reads it as a promise of health, money and success, on the reasoning that an abundant life must mean an abundance of things. The word says nothing whatever about possessions, and the context rules them out. The verse sits one sentence away from a shepherd being killed. The abundance on offer is defined by the man offering it, and what he is about to hand over is his life. The apostles who first carried the promise were beaten, imprisoned and killed. Paul lists what his own abundant life came to, beaten, shipwrecked, cold, hungry, in prison (2 Corinthians 11:23–27), and then counts everything as loss for the surpassing worth of knowing Christ (Philippians 3:8). Abundant life is life with God, rich in him, whatever our circumstances (Philippians 4:11–13).

Then why does my Christian life feel so ordinary? Because abundance here is measured by what you have in Christ, not by how vivid each day feels. A child of a king is no less an heir on a wet Monday than on his coronation day. The life Jesus gives is real now: forgiveness that is complete, a Father who hears, the Spirit within, a people to belong to, and a future that cannot be taken. But much of it is still hidden with Christ (Colossians 3:3–4), and some of it you have hardly begun to draw on. If your life with God feels thin, the answer is not to look for a new experience but to go back to the pasture: his word, prayer, the Lord’s Table, the company of his people. Sheep that are fed grow strong slowly.
verseByVerse.note: “Go in and out” is a Hebrew expression for living in safety.

parallels.desc: this is the gate of the LORD

verseByVerse.quote: "I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep. He who is a hired hand and not a shepherd, who does not own the sheep, sees the wolf coming and leaves the sheep and flees, and the wolf snatches them and scatters them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
