I am the good shepherd. The fourth I am saying. The adjective kalos carries the sense of fine, noble, attractive; the nearest English is probably the model shepherd, the one every other shepherd should be measured against. And the claim is enormous. In the Old Testament the shepherd of Israel is God himself: the LORD is my shepherd (Psalm 23:1); he will tend his flock like a shepherd, he will gather the lambs in his arms (Isaiah 40:11). In Ezekiel 34 God promises two things that seem to pull apart. He will shepherd his people himself (34:11–16), and he will set over them one shepherd, his servant David (34:23). Jesus is both: God himself come to find his sheep, and David’s son set over them.

Lays down his life. Shepherds did risk their lives against wild animals and thieves: David fought a lion and a bear for his father’s flock (1 Samuel 17:34–36). But the point of David’s story is that he won and lived. A dead shepherd is a failure. So the sentence turns the whole trade upside down. Every other shepherd risks his life in order to save the flock, and the saving depends on his surviving. This one saves the flock by dying: his death is not a risk he runs but the way he saves them.

For the sheep. The little word is hyper: on behalf of, and where one dies so that others live, in their place. This is substitution. The sheep were under a sentence they could not bear, and he stepped between them and it.

What does it mean that he died in my place? It means that the punishment your sins deserved fell on him instead of you. God’s justice is not set aside at the cross; it is carried out, on the Shepherd. He was pierced for our transgressions, the LORD laid on him the iniquity of us all (Isaiah 53:5–6), and he bore our sins in his body on the tree (1 Peter 2:24). This is called penal substitution: penal because it is a penalty, substitution because it is borne by another. For you it means that God will never punish you for a sin Christ has already paid for. When guilt accuses you, do not answer it with your record. Answer it with his death.

Who does not own the sheep. The hired hand is the right contrast, rather than the thief. He is not wicked. He simply does the sensible thing: a wolf arrives, the animals are not his, and no wage is worth being killed for. Against him the good shepherd is not a better employee but a different kind of person altogether. And the reason the hired hand runs is stated plainly: he does not own the sheep. The good shepherd does: they are his, given to him by the Father (v. 29), and losing one would be losing his own. The cross is not something imposed on Jesus from outside. It is the act of the owner, who would rather die than lose one of his own.

The wolf snatches them. The wolf stands for anything that attacks God’s people: false teachers, whom Paul calls fierce wolves that will not spare the flock (Acts 20:29), persecutors, and the devil himself. Remember the verb snatches (harpazei). It comes back in verse 28, where Jesus says that no one will snatch his sheep out of his hand.

For worship. The God of Psalm 23 did not stay at a safe distance with a rod and a staff. He went down into the valley of the shadow of death himself, all the way into the dark, so that his sheep could walk through it and fear no evil.
verseByVerse.note: Shepherds risked their lives against wild animals and thieves.

parallels.desc: David rescues a lamb from a lion

verseByVerse.quote: "He flees because he is a hired hand and cares nothing for the sheep. I am the good shepherd. I know my own and my own know me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He flees because he is a hired hand and cares nothing for the sheep. His failure is not that he steals, betrays or misleads. He runs, at the one moment when staying is the only thing that matters. There has never been a moment when the Good Shepherd was absent from his flock because it had become too dangerous to stay. He stayed in Gethsemane while the disciples slept, stayed before the high priest while Peter warmed himself at the fire, and stayed on the cross until it was finished (19:30). It is a warning for every pastor: shepherd the flock of God that is among you, not for shameful gain, but eagerly (1 Peter 5:2–4). And it is a warning for every parent, elder and friend whose care quietly evaporates when caring becomes costly. The hired hand’s real master is his own comfort, and a man who serves his comfort always runs when the wolf comes.

I know my own and my own know me. The verb know (ginōskō) means more than information. It is the knowledge of love and relationship, as when God says to Israel, you only have I known of all the families of the earth (Amos 3:2). Jesus knows his own personally, and has always known them: the Lord knows those who are his (2 Timothy 2:19). And they know him. Knowing him means trusting him, speaking to him in prayer, listening to him in his word, and finding over the years that he is who he said, the way a wife knows her husband and not only facts about him (Philippians 3:10).

The order of the knowing. He does not say my own know me, and I know them. His knowing of you comes first and holds the relationship together, and it does not rise and fall with how well you know him. Your grasp of him will always be partial in this life. His grasp of you is complete.

What should I do if my pastor behaves like a hired hand? First be fair: pastors are frail men, and tiredness, mistakes or a different style are not the same as not caring. Pray for him, and speak to him directly and kindly if something troubles you (Matthew 18:15). If the problem is real and continues, take it to the other elders, who are there to guard the flock. But if a leader is abusing anyone, spiritually, emotionally, physically or sexually, that is not a matter for patience. It must be reported, to the church’s leaders and, where the law is broken, to the authorities, and the vulnerable must be protected. The Good Shepherd’s care for the sheep never covers for the wolf.

In everyday life. Is there someone in your church whom you have quietly left for someone else to care about? Be there for them this week. None of us stays as faithfully as he did, but he stayed in our place, and his perfect obedience, not ours, is counted as ours (Romans 5:19). That is the ground on which we go back and try again.

parallels.desc: woe to my worthless shepherd
the Lord knows those who are his

verseByVerse.quote: "just as the Father knows me and I know the Father; and I lay down my life for the sheep. And I have other sheep that are not of this fold. I must bring them also, and they will listen to my voice. So there will be one flock, one shepherd."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Just as the Father knows me and I know the Father. This is the largest claim in the discourse. The mutual knowing of the shepherd and the sheep is compared to the mutual knowing of the Father and the Son. It is not a faint likeness: the words are just as, and he uses the same expression when he prays that his people may be one just as the Father and he are one (17:21–23). The closeness between Christ and a Christian is modelled on the closeness between the Father and the Son.

Where Christians differ: for whom did Christ die? Many godly Christians believe Christ died equally for every person, making salvation possible for all (1 Timothy 2:6; 1 John 2:2). This commentary’s view: here Jesus lays down his life for the sheep, and in v. 26 tells some hearers they are not his sheep; his death was designed to save, and actually saves, those the Father has given him (6:37–39; 17:9), while the offer goes to all and his death is enough for all. (See 2 Corinthians 5:14 for the fuller answer.)

Then can I tell anyone that Christ died for them? You can tell everyone, with full sincerity, that Christ is offered to them, that his death is enough for any sinner, and that whoever comes to him will never be cast out (6:37). That is how the apostles preached: they did not first work out who the elect were; they called all people everywhere to repent and believe (Acts 17:30). The moment someone trusts Christ, he may say with Paul, he loved me and gave himself for me (Galatians 2:20). Definite atonement, the teaching that Christ died to save his sheep in particular, does not make the invitation less real. It makes it certain that the invitation will not be refused by everyone, because the Shepherd has sheep and his death will bring them home.

Other sheep. The other sheep are Gentiles who would believe. Verse 16 uses two different words, which the KJV translated with the same word. A fold (aulē) is a pen, a set of walls, and this fold is Israel, with its law and its temple. A flock (poimnē) is the animals themselves. Jesus does not say the other sheep will be brought into this pen. He says there will be one flock under one shepherd. Before they have heard of him, they are already his sheep, because the Father has given them to him. God told Paul in Corinth, I have many in this city who are my people (Acts 18:10), before most of them had believed.

I must bring them also. “Must” (dei): it is certain, it is the Father’s plan. Not I hope to. The Shepherd had already settled it.

And they will listen to my voice. Not might, but will. His voice will reach them through the gospel, preached by his servants, and they will respond: as many as were appointed to eternal life believed (Acts 13:48).

What it does not mean. Mormon teaching claims that the other sheep were people in the Americas whom Christ visited after his resurrection. But the context is Israel’s fold and those outside it, the Gentiles, whom Jesus would gather through the preaching of the apostles (11:52; 17:20), into one flock, not two churches with two scriptures.

So there will be one flock, one shepherd. Jews and Gentiles together, one people of God, the dividing wall broken down (Ephesians 2:14–16). The church is one not because it has one organisation but because it has one Shepherd.

If the sheep will certainly come, why should I evangelise? Because the way he brings them is through his voice, and his voice is heard in the gospel his people speak. They will listen to my voice is a promise about the means as well as the result: how are they to hear without someone preaching? (Romans 10:14). Election, God’s choosing of his people before they ever chose him, is not a reason to keep quiet; it is the reason evangelism is not hopeless. Paul stayed eighteen months in Corinth because God had many people there. So speak of Christ to your neighbour with confidence. You do not have to know whether he is one of the other sheep. You only have to let him hear the voice.

In everyday life. If you came into the faith from outside, the wrong background, the wrong family, arriving late and by a side door, you are exactly the kind of person Jesus spoke of in advance. You are not an afterthought or a second tier. Before there was a church in Rome or Corinth or anywhere beyond Judea, the Shepherd stood in the temple and spoke of sheep he already owned on the far side of the world.
verseByVerse.note: The “other sheep” are Gentiles who would believe.

parallels.desc: I will set up over them one shepherd, my servant David

verseByVerse.quote: "For this reason the Father loves me, because I lay down my life that I may take it up again. No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord. I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it up again. This charge I have received from my Father."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this reason the Father loves me, because I lay down my life. The Father has always loved the Son, before the foundation of the world (17:24). So the Son does not earn that love by dying. Rather, the Father delights to see his eternal love returned in perfect obedience, as a father’s face lights up when his son freely does the very thing the father longed for.

That I may take it up again. His death is not the end. He lays down his life with the purpose of taking it up again in the resurrection. The cross and the empty tomb belong to one plan.

Of my own accord. Few statements in the Bible are plainer that the death of Jesus was not merely something that happened to him. Judas will decide to sell him, the council will decide to condemn him, Pilate will decide to hand him over, and soldiers will decide where to put the nails. Every one of those is a real human decision, and none of them is the deepest reason he died. At the arrest the soldiers fall back at his word (18:6). On the cross he bows his head and gives up his spirit (19:30). The soldiers thought they had arrested him, Pilate thought he had judged him, the priests thought they had finished him, and all the while the Son of God was laying down what he alone had the right to lay down.

I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it up again. The word is exousia, the right and the power to act. A man might conceivably give his life away. Nobody has ever had the right to pick it back up. That changes how we see the resurrection. It is not a rescue, not the Father arriving to undo a disaster, but the second half of one continuous act by the same person. He had said the same at the start of his ministry: destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up, and he was speaking of his body (2:19–21).

But does not Scripture say the Father raised him? Yes: God raised him up (Acts 2:24; Romans 6:4), and the Spirit gives life to mortal bodies (Romans 8:11). There is no contradiction. The Father, the Son and the Spirit act together in all God’s works. The Son took up his life again by the authority the Father gave him, as the next clause says, and by the Spirit’s power. One God raised Jesus from the dead, and each person of the Trinity was at work in it.

Voluntary is not the same as easy. To say the death was voluntary is not to say it was painless, or that his humanity was a costume, or that Gethsemane was theatre. The man who says no one takes it from me is the same man who will be in agony and ask for the cup to pass. Both are true. Keep only the first and you have a Jesus who never really suffered; keep only the second and you have a victim who was overwhelmed. He was neither.

This charge I have received from my Father. His death and resurrection are the Father’s command, freely obeyed. The most voluntary act in history was also an act of obedience, and only in Jesus are the two so perfectly joined.

If no one took his life, are those who killed him not guilty? They are guilty. Peter holds both truths in one sentence: he was delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, and you crucified and killed him by the hands of lawless men (Acts 2:23). God’s sovereign purpose never makes human sin innocent, and human sin never defeats God’s purpose. That is a comfort for your own life too. The wrongs done to you are truly wrong, and God will judge them, yet none of them is outside his hand, and he can work even them for good (Genesis 50:20).

In everyday life. When you are tempted to think that Jesus’ love for you was reluctant, a grim duty he could not escape, remember this verse. He was not trapped; he chose you with open eyes. And when you are called to lay something down for others, you do not do it alone: the Spirit who raised him from the dead now lives in you (Romans 8:11), and by him you can give freely, as he did.

verseByVerse.quote: There was again a division among the Jews because of these words. Many of them said, "He has a demon, and is insane; why listen to him?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
There was again a division among the Jews because of these words. The word is schisma, a tear, the word for cloth pulled apart, and this is the third time in four chapters (7:43; 9:16; here).

Many of them said, He has a demon, and is insane; why listen to him? The charge has two halves that do not usually go together. He has a demon: that is the spiritual accusation, made again and again (7:20; 8:48, 52). And is insane: that is different, a claim that he is out of his mind. They reach for both at once, which is what people do when a claim is too great for them to face. A man who says he will lay down his life and take it up again does sound mad, unless he is God.

Why listen to him? This part of their sentence shows most about them. It is not an argument; it is advice to stop listening. And it is still the surest way to protect an opinion: do not answer the claim, just persuade people it is not worth hearing.

There is no middle ground. The famous choice between madman, liar and Lord is set out most starkly here, because the people present understood the options exactly. A man saying what Jesus had just said about laying down his life and taking it up again is not a great moral teacher who has been misunderstood. He is possessed, or deranged, or telling the truth. The usual modern reply is different: that sayings like this are legend, put on his lips later. That is a fair question about whether the Gospels are reliable, and it has to be weighed on that ground; but it is not the same as calling him a good teacher who meant something smaller.

What if my faith divides my own family? It is painful, and it is not a sign that you have failed. Jesus said it would happen (Matthew 10:34–36), and he never once softened his words to prevent division. Make sure the offence they feel is the offence of Christ and not of your manner: be patient, humble, honest, and kinder than you have to be (1 Peter 3:15–16). Do not argue every meal; let them see the change. Keep loving them, keep praying for them, and remember that in this very crowd the same words that drove some to say why listen drove others to ask whether a demon can open the eyes of the blind. Families divided over Christ are often families on the way to him.

verseByVerse.quote: Others said, "These are not the words of one who is oppressed by a demon. Can a demon open the eyes of the blind?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not the words of one who is oppressed. They are judging by what his words are like. They have heard him speak of a shepherd laying down his life, and it does not sound like a man with a demon.

Can a demon open the eyes of the blind? They point back to the man born blind, and their reasoning is sound. Opening blind eyes is God’s work: the LORD opens the eyes of the blind (Psalm 146:8). Whatever the enemy of souls does, he does not open eyes. The three verbs of verse 10 are his: steal, kill, destroy. He has never restored anything. Every genuine healing in the Gospels is evidence that the power behind it is God’s, not the devil’s.

The man who is not in the room. The blind beggar is not in the courtyard, and John never mentions him again, yet his healed eyes are still bearing witness. For some in the divided crowd the argument is settled by the fact that a man who had never seen can see. What God has done in you may also be speaking to people you will never meet.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–42 — I and the Father Are One
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At the winter Feast of Dedication the leaders corner Jesus in Solomon’s colonnade and demand a plain answer. He points to his works, speaks of the sheep the Father has given him, and says that he and the Father are one. When they reach for stones, he answers from Psalm 82, then withdraws beyond the Jordan.
verseByVerse.theology: I and the Father are one is the high point of the shepherd discourse. The oneness includes unity of purpose but goes further: it is a oneness of divine nature, and his hearers rightly take it as a claim to be God (v. 33). He argues from the lesser to the greater: if Scripture can call human judges gods, how much more can the one the Father consecrated and sent be called the Son of God? The defence does not shrink the claim; it enlarges it.
verseByVerse.examples: Beyond the Jordan, many believe because John’s witness has been borne out by Jesus’ works. The chapter ends not with hostility in Jerusalem but with a harvest by the river, a reminder that God often gathers his people far from the places that look most important.

verseByVerse.quote: At that time the Feast of Dedication took place at Jerusalem. It was winter, and Jesus was walking in the temple, in the colonnade of Solomon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Feast of Dedication. The Feast of Dedication (Hanukkah) celebrated the rededication of the temple in 164 BC by Judas Maccabeus, after Antiochus IV Epiphanes had defiled it with an altar to Zeus and the sacrifice of pigs. It lasted eight days, in December, with lamps lit in homes; Josephus calls it Lights. Two months earlier, at the Feast of Booths, Jesus had stood among the great lamps of the temple courts and said, I am the light of the world (8:12). Now he walks through the temple during the festival of lamps. The lamps of Hanukkah were lit for a temple that would be destroyed within forty years of this winter. The one walking through its colonnade was the true temple, the dwelling of God among men, and the true light, of which those lamps were only a reminder. His light does not come from a jar of oil that might run dry, but from the eternal life of the Father, and the darkness has not overcome it (1:5).

A feast about bad shepherds. Hanukkah commemorated a rescue from bad shepherds: from Antiochus, but also from Israel’s own high priests, Jason and Menelaus, who bought their office from the Greek rulers and handed God’s people over to them. That is exactly Ezekiel’s charge (Ezekiel 34:2). The men Jesus has just called thieves and hired hands are keeping a festival that exists partly because their predecessors were exactly that.

The colonnade of Solomon. A covered portico along the east side of the temple courts, sheltered from the winter wind. The early church later met there (Acts 3:11; 5:12), so that the place where Jesus was surrounded and nearly stoned became the place where his people gathered openly in his name.

If the Maccabees are not in our Bible, how do we know this history? From 1 and 2 Maccabees, Jewish books written in the second and first centuries BC, and from the historian Josephus. Roman Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include the books of Maccabees, but Protestant churches, following the Hebrew canon that Jesus and the apostles used, do not treat them as Scripture (the Westminster Confession 1.3; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 1.3). They are valuable history, like any reliable ancient record, but they do not carry God’s authority. Jesus’ presence at the feast does not make it a command for Christians. He was a faithful Jew keeping a national festival of thanksgiving, and he used it to show who the true temple and the true light are.
verseByVerse.note: The Feast of Dedication (Hanukkah) celebrated the re-dedication of the temple in 164 BC, after Antiochus IV had defiled it. It fell in December. Solomon’s colonnade ran along the east side of the temple courts.

parallels.desc: Solomon’s Portico

verseByVerse.quote: So the Jews gathered around him and said to him, "How long will you keep us in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly." Jesus answered them, "I told you, and you do not believe. The works that I do in my Father's name bear witness about me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gathered around. The verb (ekyklōsan) means surrounded, hemmed in, as in the Greek of Psalm 22:16: a company of evildoers encircles me.

How long will you keep us in suspense? Literally, how long will you lift up our soul? The phrase can be taken two ways. It can mean keeping someone hanging; it can also carry the sense of vexing or provoking them, how long will you annoy us? Either way there is a complaint inside it: this is your fault. We would have settled the matter long ago if you had been clearer.

Tell us plainly. They want a political statement they can either rally to or report to the Romans. At a feast that remembered Judas Maccabeus, the word Christ meant a liberator with a sword. That is exactly why Jesus avoided the title Messiah in public: when a crowd tried to make him king by force, he withdrew (6:15). He would not let them fill the word with the wrong meaning.

I told you. He has said I am the bread of life, I am the light of the world, before Abraham was, I am, I am the door, I am the good shepherd, and I lay down my life that I may take it up again. They have already reached for stones once (8:59), which is not the behaviour of people who found him vague. The problem is not clarity but unbelief.

The works bear witness. Then he does something generous, and points them to events: water made wine, a dying boy healed by a word, five thousand fed, a beggar with new eyes walking around Jerusalem. He is offering them the lowest rung on the ladder. Believe the evidence if you cannot yet believe the man.

In the flow. The question asked here in public, whether he is the Christ, is the one the other Gospels record at his trial before the council (Mark 14:61), and the charge of that trial, blasphemy, comes here in verse 33. In this Gospel Jesus is on trial from chapter 5 onward, in the open, before the people. So by the time he is arrested, the reader has heard the whole case, and knows that the verdict was reached against the evidence.

Why did Jesus not simply say, Yes, I am the Messiah? Because the word in their mouths meant something he was not. To them the Messiah was a national liberator who would drive out Rome; to say yes plainly would have confirmed that error, and handed them a political charge. Instead he told them who he was in fuller terms than the title: the Son who does his Father’s works, the shepherd of Ezekiel 34, the one who is before Abraham. When he did say it plainly, it was to a Samaritan woman (4:26) and, at the end, put under oath before the high priest (Matthew 26:63–64; Mark 14:61–62), when there was no longer any danger of the word being mistaken for a rebellion. He is the Christ, but on his own definition.

In everyday life. If you are praying for someone who keeps asking for proof, pray not mainly for better arguments but for opened eyes.

verseByVerse.quote: "but you do not believe because you are not among my sheep. My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You are not among my sheep. This is the sentence in the chapter most likely to frighten a reader who is already frightened, and it needs handling with care. Look at the order. Jesus does not say, you are not my sheep because you do not believe, but you do not believe because you are not my sheep. Being his sheep comes first; believing follows. Who his sheep are is settled by the Father’s gift (v. 29; 6:37). This is election: God’s free choice, before the world began, of a people to be his own, not because of anything in them but because of his love (Ephesians 1:4–5). It does not remove their guilt: they do not believe because they will not (5:40). But it explains why some believe and others do not.

Where Christians differ: does faith make us his sheep, or does being his sheep produce faith? Arminian Christians read the verse the other way round: people are not his sheep because they do not believe, and they could have believed if they would; God’s choice follows his foreknowledge of their faith. Many godly believers read it so, out of a real concern for human responsibility and the sincerity of the gospel offer. This commentary’s view: Jesus says the opposite order. You do not believe because you are not among my sheep. Belief is the mark of the sheep, not the way of becoming one: all that the Father gives me will come to me (6:37), and as many as were appointed to eternal life believed (Acts 13:48). God’s choice is unconditional, resting on his own grace and not on anything foreseen in us (Ephesians 1:4–5; Romans 9:11–16). And yet these hearers were fully responsible for their unbelief, for they refused to come (5:40). Scripture holds both together, and so must we.

Who is being addressed. Read cold, at three in the morning, the verse becomes: what if I am not one? What if the reason faith is hard is that I was never given any? So look first at who Jesus is speaking to. These are men who have watched the signs for a long time, who have had the claims stated to their faces repeatedly and plainly, who have already reached for stones once, and who are at this moment trying to extract a sentence they can use at a trial. Jesus is not describing a person who is anxious about whether he belongs. He is describing men who are entirely untroubled and have made up their minds.

The mark of a sheep. He gives the mark in the next breath, and it is not a feeling. They hear; they are known; they follow. The sheep in this picture are not described as confident, and nothing in the passage suggests they can tell by looking inward. He knows them as his own (v. 14), and faith shows itself in following.

What if I am afraid I am not one of his sheep? Then do not ask whether you feel like a sheep. Ask what you have done with the voice. A person who has heard something in Christ that will not let him go, and who keeps turning back to him after every failure, is following, and that is the evidence this passage offers. Then do the plainest thing of all, which no doctrine of election has ever qualified: come to him. Nobody who came to him was ever turned away on the grounds of not being on a list; whoever comes to me I will never cast out (6:37). The anxiety that says perhaps I am not one is answered the same way it has always been. Come, and find out.

If they could not believe, how can they be blamed? Because their inability was not a lack of opportunity or evidence but a refusal. They did not want him. No one is kept from Christ against his will while longing to come; the trouble with the fallen heart is precisely that it does not want to come (5:40; 3:19). God is not unjust in leaving people to the choice they themselves love. The wonder is not that some are left, but that any are drawn, and that he draws such people as us.

verseByVerse.quote: "I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand. My Father, who has given them to me, is greater than all, and no one is able to snatch them out of the Father's hand."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I give them eternal life. Present tense: a gift already handed over, not a prize at the end.

They will never perish. The Greek (ou mē apolōntai eis ton aiōna) is as emphatic as the language gets: a double negative, strengthened by a phrase meaning for ever. It is the same construction as whoever comes to me I will never cast out in chapter 6 (6:37). Eternal life that could end would not be eternal.

No one will snatch them. The verb (harpazō) is the one from verse 12, where the wolf snatches: a word for violent seizure. What is denied is not that anything will try, but that anything will succeed.

The Father’s hand. Then the second hand. The same promise is made twice, by two persons, about the same sheep, and the reason given is not the sheep’s grip but the Father’s greatness. Two hands hold the sheep, and neither hand is yours.

A textual note. The Greek of verse 29 is genuinely uncertain. The manuscripts divide between my Father, who has given them to me, is greater than all, and what my Father has given me is greater than all. Translations differ and both readings are defensible. Nothing in the assurance depends on which is right; on either reading the sheep are held by someone nothing can overpower.

Where Christians differ: can a believer be lost? Some argue that while no one else can snatch the sheep, a sheep may choose to leave. Earnest believers hold this, often out of a real concern that grace should not be abused. This commentary’s view: “no one” includes the sheep themselves, and Jesus says plainly that his sheep will never perish. The sheep are kept not by their own grip on Christ but by his grip on them (Romans 8:38–39; Philippians 1:6; 1 Peter 1:5). This is the perseverance of the saints. Those who fall away for good show that they were never his sheep (1 John 2:19). True sheep may stray and stumble, but the Shepherd brings them back.

The preservation of the saints. The perseverance of the saints, the teaching that true believers continue in faith to the end, could as well be called their preservation, since the verse puts the holding in his hand rather than in theirs (the Westminster Confession 17.1). They persevere because they are preserved, and they are preserved because the one who holds them is greater than all. This is the will of him who sent me, that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me, but raise it up on the last day (6:39).

Against presumption. This is said of sheep who hear and follow (v. 27). It is not a guarantee attached to a decision made once at fifteen and then abandoned, and the New Testament is not shy about people who went out from us because they were not of us (1 John 2:19). Anyone who says, I am safe, so I can live as I like, has not heard the Shepherd’s voice in this verse at all.

Against despair. The fear is usually not that something will snatch, but that the sheep will wander off, which sheep famously do. And the answer to that is in the Shepherd’s own words in another Gospel: he leaves the ninety-nine and goes after the one that is lost until he finds it, and when he has found it he lays it on his shoulders, rejoicing (Luke 15:4–5). The promise that they will never perish covers every way of perishing, including their own wandering.

What about Christians who fall into serious sin? A true believer can fall badly and for a time, as David did with Bathsheba and Peter did by the fire. Sin does real damage: it grieves the Spirit, darkens assurance, harms others and brings the Father’s discipline (Hebrews 12:5–11; Westminster 17.3; 1689 17.3). But a sheep of Christ will not be left there. The Shepherd pursues, convicts and restores, as he restored Peter on the shore (21:15–19). So if you have fallen, do not reason that you are lost; reason that he is coming after you, and turn back to him now. And if you feel no grief at all about a sin you are living in, take that as a serious warning, and come to him today. But if you are troubled by this very question, the trouble is itself a sign of the Shepherd’s voice at work in you.

What if someone I love has walked away from the faith? Grieve and pray, and do not give up. You cannot see the heart, and you do not know the end of the story. Some who wander are sheep who will be brought back, sometimes after many years; others, Scripture says, were never truly his (1 John 2:19), and only God knows which. Your part is not to pronounce, but to love, to keep the door open, to speak of Christ when there is an opening, and above all to bring him or her to the Shepherd in prayer. He goes after the lost one, and he is better at finding than we are at waiting.

For worship. The one who said these words was months from having those hands opened with nails, and the holding did not stop. There is no wolf strong enough, no night long enough, no wandering far enough to take one sheep out of the hands of God.

parallels.desc: there is none that can deliver out of my hand

verseByVerse.quote: "I and the Father are one." The Jews picked up stones again to stone him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I and the Father are one. The Greek word for one here (hen) is neuter: one thing, one in nature. It is not the masculine form (heis), which would mean one person. I and the Father are two, and the verb are is plural; but they are one thing, one in being. The verb keeps them distinct, and the one keeps them undivided. Here, for the Father and the Son, is the heart of the doctrine of the Trinity: distinct persons, one God.

Two errors settled at once. The word one rules out the view that the Father and the Son are merely two names or modes of one individual, a view the early church met in Sabellius and which is taught today by Oneness Pentecostalism. John has already told us that the Word was with God (1:1), and you cannot be with yourself. It equally rules out the opposite error, pressed by Jehovah’s Witnesses, that the Father and the Son are one only in the sense that their wills agree. Men do not pick up stones over a shared policy. They tell us themselves what they heard, two verses on: you, being a man, make yourself God.

Where Christians differ: is this only unity of will? Some say this means only unity of will and purpose, as believers are to be one (17:22). This commentary’s view: it includes unity of purpose, but cannot stop there. The hearers took it as a claim to be God, and Jesus did not correct them; instead he went on to say the Father is in him and he in the Father (v. 38). Believers share a unity of love; the Son shares the Father’s very being (1:1; 5:18).

Stones again. They understood exactly what he meant (v. 33). The first attempt (8:59) followed before Abraham was, I am; this one follows I and the Father are one. What the church later put into the creeds was not an invention of the fourth century. It was already sitting in a sentence spoken in a temple colonnade in winter, by a man about to be stoned for saying it.

How can three persons be one God without contradiction? Because one and three are not said in the same sense. God is one in being: there is one divine nature, one will, one power, one glory. He is three in person: the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are truly distinct, relating to one another in love (17:24). A contradiction would be one God who is three Gods, or one person who is three persons. The Trinity is neither. We cannot picture it fully, and every illustration fails somewhere, which is what we should expect if God is greater than his creation. But we do not believe it because we can picture it. We believe it because the Son himself stood in the temple and said both I and the Father, and are one.

In everyday life. When you pray to Jesus, you are not praying to a lesser being who will pass the message on. And when you feel unsure of the Father’s love, look at the Son: the Father is not different from him. They are one.
verseByVerse.note: “One” is neuter in Greek: one in nature and purpose, not one person.

parallels.desc: the LORD is one

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered them, "I have shown you many good works from the Father; for which of them are you going to stone me?" The Jews answered him, "It is not for a good work that we are going to stone you but for blasphemy, because you, being a man, make yourself God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have shown you many good works from the Father; for which of them are you going to stone me? A calm, ironic question with stones raised above him, and more than sarcasm. The adjective is kala again, the word from the good shepherd: fine, noble, beautiful works. He is asking men holding rocks to name the beautiful thing they object to, and it forces them to state their actual charge, which they do, accurately: not a good work, but blasphemy, for which stoning was the law’s penalty (Leviticus 24:16).

You, being a man, make yourself God. If they had misheard a lesser claim, a prophet, a teacher, a man specially favoured, Jesus could have corrected them in one sentence and saved his life. He does not; he goes on to say the Father is in him and he in the Father (v. 38). They understood his words as a claim to deity, and he let the understanding stand.

The direction is reversed. They understood his claim correctly. Their mistake was to think that a man was making himself God. The truth is the opposite: he was God, making himself man (1:14; Philippians 2:6–7). And they are right about the man too. His humanity was standing in front of them, tired and dusty and not yet fifty (8:57). What they could not do was hold the two together: a man, and God.

Did Jesus ever actually claim to be God? Yes, and his enemies are the clearest witnesses. People sometimes say the idea that Jesus is God was invented by the church later. John wrote decades afterwards, but the earliest Gospel, Mark, already has him forgiving sins and condemned for blasphemy (Mark 2:5–7; 14:61–64), and Paul’s letters, earlier still, call him Lord and pray to him (1 Corinthians 16:22; Philippians 2:6–11). And here, during his lifetime, men who heard him tried to kill him for exactly that claim, and he did not withdraw it. He forgave sins as only God can (Mark 2:5–7), took the divine name I am (8:58), received worship (20:28), and said that to see him is to see the Father (14:9). A man who said these things and was not God would not be a good teacher. The only reason to worship him is that he is who he said.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered them, "Is it not written in your Law, 'I said, you are gods'? If he called them gods to whom the word of God came — and Scripture cannot be broken —"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Is it not written in your Law, I said, you are gods? “Law” here means the whole Old Testament, as often in John. The quotation is from Psalm 82:6. The psalm calls Israel’s judges “gods” because they represented God’s justice, exercising his authority among his people (compare Exodus 21:6; 22:8–9, where the KJV, among others, takes elohim to mean the judges).

Read the whole psalm. God puts the gods on trial: they judge unjustly and will not defend the weak and the fatherless (82:2–4). Then the sentence falls: nevertheless, like men you shall die (82:7). The psalm calls them gods, and then sentences them to die like men, which shows that they are not gods at all. The word is a title of office, men entrusted with God’s authority to judge, and the point of the psalm is to strip it off them.

To whom the word of God came. The argument goes from the lesser to the greater: if mere human judges can be called gods, how can it be blasphemy for the one the Father consecrated and sent to call himself the Son of God? His hearers did not take it as a retreat. They do not put the stones down; they try again to arrest him (v. 39). The claim of verse 30 stands.

Where Christians differ: who are the gods of Psalm 82? Some scholars read them as heavenly beings, the spiritual powers set over the nations, judged by God for their injustice. Others read them as Israel’s human judges. This commentary’s view: the second is more likely. Jesus’ argument is that the word of God came to them (v. 35), and the psalm says they will die like men (Psalm 82:7), which fits human rulers far better. They were called gods because they held God’s authority, and judged because they abused it.

Scripture cannot be broken. He rests his argument on a single word in a short psalm, and says that word cannot be set aside. This is one of the foundations of the doctrine of the inerrancy and authority of Scripture: because it is God’s own word, Scripture is true in all it affirms and binds all who hear it. Jesus himself held this, and his followers can hold no lower view than their Lord’s.

What it does not mean. This verse has been wrenched a long way from its meaning. “You are gods” is quoted by Mormonism to teach that faithful men and women may themselves become gods, and by Word of Faith teachers to tell congregations they are little gods with creative power in their mouths. But the psalm is a charge against those judges, not a promise; to quote it as a promise of divinity is to mistake the accusation for a reward. Nor is Jesus saying he is a god only in the sense the judges were. He is arguing from their own Scripture that calling himself the Son of God cannot be blasphemy in itself, and then he goes further than the judges ever could: the Father is in me and I am in the Father (v. 38). No creature is ever promoted to be God.

What are we promised instead? Something better than the counterfeit and different in kind: not deity by nature, but adoption by grace. We become children of God (1:12), sharers in his life and holiness, and one day we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2). Sons, not gods. The offer of godhood was first made in a garden by someone else (Genesis 3:5), and it has never once been kept.

If Scripture cannot be broken, what about the parts that seem to contradict each other? Take them seriously and humbly, as Jesus took Scripture. Most apparent contradictions dissolve with careful reading: different writers choosing different details, rounding numbers, arranging events by theme rather than strict order, or using words in different senses, as Paul and James do with justify. Some remain hard, and it is honest to say so. But a difficulty we cannot yet solve is not an error we have proved. When you meet one, look at a good study Bible or commentary, ask your pastor, and hold on to the Lord’s own conviction while you wait for light.

For worship. The eternal Word stood under the written word and rested his whole defence on one phrase of an old psalm. And he alone does what the judges of Psalm 82 failed to do: he defends the weak and the fatherless, and he will judge the earth in righteousness. Arise, O God, the psalm ends, for you shall inherit all the nations (82:8). In him, God has arisen.
verseByVerse.note: The psalm calls Israel’s judges “gods” because they represented God’s authority. “Your Law” here means the Scriptures as a whole.

parallels.desc: “I said, ‘You are gods’”

verseByVerse.quote: "do you say of him whom the Father consecrated and sent into the world, 'You are blaspheming,' because I said, 'I am the Son of God'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Consecrated. The verb is hagiazō: to set apart as holy, to sanctify, to dedicate. And the feast they are standing in is the Feast of Dedication, in Greek ta enkainia, the renewing, in Hebrew Hanukkah, which means exactly that: dedication. They are keeping the festival of an altar defiled, rebuilt and set apart again for God, and Jesus says: the Father has consecrated me.

The true temple. He has already told them he is the true temple (2:19–21), the holy place where God dwells; now he tells them, during the feast of the temple’s reconsecration, that the consecration they are commemorating has been fulfilled in a person.

Sent into the world. Sending implies somewhere to be sent from. Consecrated before he was sent: he existed with the Father before coming. It is the thing they have denied all along. Those two words, consecrated and sent, contain the incarnation, God the Son coming into the world as a man, stated in the middle of a legal defence.

You are blaspheming, because I said, I am the Son of God? The argument against the charge is simple. Blasphemy is a man claiming for himself a place God has not given him. But if the Father himself set the Son apart and sent him, then the Son is only reporting what the Father has done, and the accusation collapses. It collapses not because the claim is smaller than they thought, but because the Father himself stands behind it.

Christians are called sanctified too, so is it the same thing? It is related, and the difference matters. Jesus was consecrated as the holy Son, set apart for his mission, with no sin to be cleansed from. We are sinners made holy because of him. In his prayer he says, for their sake I consecrate myself, that they also may be sanctified in truth (17:19). He set himself apart for the cross so that we could be set apart for God. Your holiness is borrowed from his, and the Spirit is working it out in you day by day.

parallels.desc: before you were born I consecrated you

verseByVerse.quote: "If I am not doing the works of my Father, then do not believe me; but if I do them, even though you do not believe me, believe the works, that you may know and understand that the Father is in me and I am in the Father."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then do not believe me. He begins by handing them a test that could destroy him. If the works are not there, he says, you are entitled to dismiss me. Jesus invites testing; he does not ask for blind faith.

Believe the works. Start anywhere. He is not standing on his dignity or requiring that they come to him by the front door of full faith; he is trying to get them in by any opening still ajar. The works are evidence (14:11).

The Father is in me. The goal he names is not mere agreement but knowledge: know, and understand. He wants them to arrive at the very thing they are about to try to arrest him for. And no judge of Psalm 82 could have said this. The Father and the Son dwell in each other; later theologians call it perichōrēsis, the mutual indwelling of the persons. It is the deepest statement of their oneness (14:10–11; 17:21).

Is it all right to believe because of evidence, rather than simply by faith? Yes. Biblical faith is not believing without reasons; it is trusting God on the basis of what he has shown. Jesus himself points to his works, John writes his Gospel so that by reading the signs we may believe (20:31), and the resurrection was proved by many proofs (Acts 1:3). Evidence alone cannot change a heart; only the Spirit can do that, as these hearers show. But the Spirit uses evidence. So do not be ashamed of asking questions, and do not despise friends who need reasons. Point them to the works, and pray that the Spirit will open their eyes to the one who did them.

Counting the works. When Christ no longer seems real to you and you feel little love for him, this verse allows a smaller step: look at what he has actually done. Not what you feel about him; the record. Faith that has lost its warmth can still count the works, and this passage says that is a legitimate place to stand while the rest comes back.

verseByVerse.quote: Again they sought to arrest him, but he escaped from their hands. He went away again across the Jordan to the place where John had been baptizing at first, and there he remained.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He escaped from their hands. Yet another failed attempt in this Gospel (7:30, 44; 8:20, 59; 10:31), and John’s only explanation for any of them is that his hour had not yet come. No one can snatch the sheep out of his hand (v. 28); and no one can seize him out of the Father’s plan. The withdrawal is not retreat from danger: no mob in Jerusalem could hurry him to the cross a day early, and no fear could keep him from it a day late.

Where John had been baptizing. This is Bethany beyond the Jordan (1:28), where this Gospel started: the Baptist standing in the water, pointing at Jesus and saying, behold, the Lamb of God. The public ministry, which opened there, now closes there, at the spot where the first two disciples turned and followed him. He will cross the river again to walk to the tomb of Lazarus at Bethany (11:7), and from there to his own tomb.

He remained there. After a winter of stones and interrogations he goes back to the river and stays put. What happens next is the raising of Lazarus and then the last week. It is worth noticing that there was a quiet stretch before it, and that he took it.

Is it cowardice for a Christian to step back from conflict or rest? No, not when it is done for the right reasons. Jesus withdrew more than once, not from fear but because his hour had not come, and he took his disciples apart to rest (Mark 6:31). Courage is not the same as walking into every fight, and faithfulness is not the same as never stopping. Withdrawing is wrong when it means abandoning a duty God has given you, as the hired hand did. It is right when it means waiting for God’s time, guarding your soul, or refusing to let other people’s hostility set your agenda. Rest is not desertion. It is often preparation.
verseByVerse.note: “Across the Jordan” is Bethany beyond the Jordan, where John had baptized.

verseByVerse.quote: And many came to him. And they said, "John did no sign, but everything that John said about this man was true." And many believed in him there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John did no sign. Many came to him there, away from the leaders. What they said is said of nobody else in the New Testament, and it is said of the man Jesus called the greatest born of women (Matthew 11:11). No miracle, not one healing, nothing that would have drawn a crowd on its own account. His greatness was in his witness.

Everything that John said was true. And here, probably after his death (the other Gospels report it before the feeding of the five thousand), in the place where he had worked, ordinary people say it. They had remembered, and when the one he pointed to came back to that stretch of river, they knew him because of what a dead man had told them. He had called him the Lamb of God (1:29), the one who would baptise with the Spirit (1:33), the Son of God (1:34), and every word had proved true. It is a beautiful epitaph, and the best thing that can be said of any servant of Christ: what he said about Jesus was true.

Many believed in him there. Jerusalem, with the temple and the scholars and the festivals, produced stones. The riverbank, where John’s witness had prepared the ground, produced believers. It also closes a circle. The prologue said John came as a witness, that all might believe through him (1:7). Here, after the Baptist’s death, at the place where he worked, that purpose is fulfilled. Christ let his greatest prophet die in a prison cell without seeing this fruit, and then he walked back to the very riverbank where that prophet had preached and gathered the harvest himself.

Should I expect miracles to confirm my witness? No, and this verse is a great relief. The greatest of the prophets did no sign at all, and his witness bore fruit years later. The miracles of Christ and the apostles had a special purpose: to confirm the new revelation as it was given (Hebrews 2:3–4). This commentary holds, charitably, that the sign gifts of that foundational age have ceased, while God still answers prayer and can heal as he wills. Many brothers and sisters see this differently, and we honour them. But on any view, the ordinary means God uses to bring people to faith is the faithful word of witness, spoken plainly and backed by a life. You do not need a sign. You need to tell the truth about Jesus.

10.text: <sup>1</sup>“Truly, truly, I say to you, he who does not enter the sheepfold by the door but climbs in by another way, that man is a thief and a robber.<sup>2</sup>But he who enters by the door is the shepherd of the sheep.<sup>3</sup>To him the gatekeeper opens. The sheep hear his voice, and he calls his own sheep by name and leads them out.<sup>4</sup>When he has brought out all his own, he goes before them, and the sheep follow him, for they know his voice.<sup>5</sup>A stranger they will not follow, but they will flee from him, for they do not know the voice of strangers.”<sup>6</sup>This figure of speech Jesus used with them, but they did not understand what he was saying to them.<sup>7</sup>So Jesus again said to them, “Truly, truly, I say to you, I am the door of the sheep.<sup>8</sup>All who came before me are thieves and robbers, but the sheep did not listen to them.<sup>9</sup>I am the door. If anyone enters by me, he will be saved and will go in and out and find pasture.<sup>10</sup>The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy. I came that they may have life and have it abundantly.<sup>11</sup>I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.<sup>12</sup>He who is a hired hand and not a shepherd, who does not own the sheep, sees the wolf coming and leaves the sheep and flees, and the wolf snatches them and scatters them.<sup>13</sup>He flees because he is a hired hand and cares nothing for the sheep.<sup>14</sup>I am the good shepherd. I know my own and my own know me,<sup>15</sup>just as the Father knows me and I know the Father; and I lay down my life for the sheep.<sup>16</sup>And I have other sheep that are not of this fold. I must bring them also, and they will listen to my voice. So there will be one flock, one shepherd.<sup>17</sup>For this reason the Father loves me, because I lay down my life that I may take it up again.<sup>18</sup>No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord. I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it up again. This charge I have received from my Father.”<sup>19</sup>There was again a division among the Jews because of these words.<sup>20</sup>Many of them said, “He has a demon, and is insane; why listen to him?”<sup>21</sup>Others said, “These are not the words of one who is oppressed by a demon. Can a demon open the eyes of the blind?”<sup>22</sup>At that time the Feast of Dedication took place at Jerusalem. It was winter,<sup>23</sup>and Jesus was walking in the temple, in the colonnade of Solomon.<sup>24</sup>So the Jews gathered around him and said to him, “How long will you keep us in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly.”<sup>25</sup>Jesus answered them, “I told you, and you do not believe. The works that I do in my Father’s name bear witness about me,<sup>26</sup>but you do not believe because you are not among my sheep.<sup>27</sup>My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.<sup>28</sup>I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand.<sup>29</sup>My Father, who has given them to me, is greater than all, and no one is able to snatch them out of the Father’s hand.<sup>30</sup>I and the Father are one.”<sup>31</sup>The Jews picked up stones again to stone him.<sup>32</sup>Jesus answered them, “I have shown you many good works from the Father; for which of them are you going to stone me?”<sup>33</sup>The Jews answered him, “It is not for a good work that we are going to stone you but for blasphemy, because you, being a man, make yourself God.”<sup>34</sup>Jesus answered them, “Is it not written in your Law, ’I said, you are gods’?<sup>35</sup>If he called them gods to whom the word of God came—and Scripture cannot be broken—<sup>36</sup>do you say of him whom the Father consecrated and sent into the world, ’You are blaspheming,’ because I said, ’I am the Son of God’?<sup>37</sup>If I am not doing the works of my Father, then do not believe me;<sup>38</sup>but if I do them, even though you do not believe me, believe the works, that you may know and understand that the Father is in me and I am in the Father.”<sup>39</sup>Again they sought to arrest him, but he escaped from their hands.<sup>40</sup>He went away again across the Jordan to the place where John had been baptizing at first, and there he remained.<sup>41</sup>And many came to him. And they said, “John did no sign, but everything that John said about this man was true.”<sup>42</sup>And many believed in him there.
10.overview:
The Pharisees have just thrown out the man born blind, and Jesus has found him. Against those false shepherds Jesus describes himself in two pictures from village life, the door of the sheepfold and the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep, with Ezekiel 34 in the background, where God promises to shepherd his flock himself through his servant David.

Two months later, at the winter Feast of Dedication, the leaders demand that he say plainly whether he is the Messiah. He speaks of the sheep no one can snatch from his hand or the Father’s, and says that he and the Father are one. They take up stones for blasphemy; he answers from Psalm 82, then withdraws across the Jordan, where many believe in him.

11.title: The Resurrection and the Life

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–44 — Lazarus Raised: The Sign That Decides
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Lazarus of Bethany falls ill, and Jesus, who loves the family, waits two days before going back to Judea. He meets Martha and then Mary in their grief, weeps, and at the tomb prays to the Father and calls the dead man out.
verseByVerse.theology: The miracle looks ahead to Jesus’ own resurrection and, through it, to the raising of all who are in him. I am the resurrection and the life (v. 25) is a claim not only about what Jesus can do but about who he is: the source of the life of the age to come, already present. Those who believe in him will never die, not because they escape physical death but because they have already passed from death to life (5:24).
verseByVerse.examples: Jesus weeps (v. 35) while knowing he is about to raise Lazarus. His tears are true compassion, not ignorance of the outcome. God in the flesh does not watch human sorrow from a distance; he enters it and weeps in it before he conquers it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now a certain man was ill, Lazarus of Bethany, the village of Mary and her sister Martha. It was Mary who anointed the Lord with ointment and wiped his feet with her hair, whose brother Lazarus was ill.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. The raising of Lazarus is the seventh sign in John’s Gospel, as the signs are usually counted, and the climax of them all. It shows that Jesus is the resurrection and the life, with power over death itself, and it is the turning point that leads to the cross: because of it the council decides Jesus must die (v. 53). He loves a family, delays on purpose, walks back into danger, weeps at a grave he is about to empty, and is angry at death. Then he calls a dead man by name, and the dead man comes out.

The setting. Jesus is at this moment in Bethany across the Jordan, where the Baptist worked (10:40; 1:28). The message reaches him there about a man in Bethany near Jerusalem, on the Mount of Olives (v. 18). The whole chapter is the journey from one Bethany to the other: from the place where his ministry began to a tomb two miles from the city that will kill him.

Lazarus of Bethany. “Lazarus” is a short form of Eleazar, meaning God helps, and the chapter will show what that name means when God’s help arrives in person and calls the sick man’s name. This is very probably the household Jesus stayed in when he came to Jerusalem (Luke 10:38; Mark 11:11). So the illness is not a case. It is somebody’s brother, in a house Jesus loved. The eternal Son, who has the Father’s love from before the world began, chose a house in a village and three friends to love. He let himself be fed and housed and grieved over, and when the illness came to that house it came to him.

It was Mary who anointed the Lord. John identifies Mary by an act she has not yet performed in his story; the anointing comes in the next chapter (12:1–8). And so from the first verses the shadow of Jesus’ burial falls across the illness of his friend.

Is this Mary the sinful woman of Luke 7, or Mary Magdalene? No. Luke 7:36–50 describes an earlier and different anointing, in Galilee, by an unnamed woman known as a sinner, in the house of a Pharisee. Mary of Bethany anointed Jesus at Bethany days before his death (12:1–8). Mary Magdalene is a third woman, from Magdala in Galilee, from whom Jesus had cast out seven demons (Luke 8:2). Later tradition merged the three, but the Gospels keep them distinct, and it is worth keeping them distinct, because each of them is a separate testimony to his grace.

Did Jesus really need friends? He did not need them as God, who is complete in himself. But he was truly man, and a true man is made for friendship. He chose to have a home where he was welcome, people he loved by name, a table where he could rest. That is no weakness. It is a picture of what he is: the Son of God who has come near enough to be your friend (15:15). And it is a dignity he gives to ordinary Christian hospitality. A house where Christ is loved and his people are welcome is doing something he himself valued.
verseByVerse.note: Bethany was a village on the Mount of Olives, about two miles east of Jerusalem. John mentions Mary’s anointing ahead of time; it comes in chapter 12.

parallels.desc: Martha and Mary

verseByVerse.quote: So the sisters sent to him, saying, "Lord, he whom you love is ill." But when Jesus heard it he said, "This illness does not lead to death. It is for the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified through it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He whom you love is ill. The message is short, and it is a model of how to pray. There is no request in it. They state the situation and the relationship and stop. Their confidence is not in having framed the request correctly. It is in the fact that he loves their brother, and that he will know what to do with that information. “Love” here is phileō, the love of friendship; two verses later John uses agapaō, with no clear difference of weight.

This illness does not lead to death. A bereaved reader will stop at this sentence, because Lazarus dies. The Greek is pros thanaton: toward death, in the direction of death. He is not predicting whether the man’s heart will stop. He is saying where the illness is aimed and what it ends in. Its final outcome is not death but resurrection.

For the glory of God. As with the man born blind (9:3), the purpose is God’s glory. And the glory of God is the glory of the Son: the Father is honoured when the Son is honoured (5:23). The Son will be glorified by the miracle, and also by the death it will bring him to (v. 53; 12:23). The sign that shows his glory is also the sign that sends him to the cross.

If I pray for healing and the person dies, did God fail? No, and this verse should not be used to promise what it does not promise. Christians die of their illnesses, and this text has been quoted over sickbeds in a way that later looked like a broken promise. What it actually says is stranger and better: that for those who belong to him, an illness can pass straight through death and still not have death as its destination. God may heal, and we should ask him to. But his answer is never limited to the two choices of healing or failure. For a believer, death is not God’s defeat but the doorway to his presence and the road to resurrection. Pray boldly, and leave the shape of the answer to his love.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus. So, when he heard that Lazarus was ill, he stayed two days longer in the place where he was.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus. John is careful to say it before he tells us of the delay, so that we cannot misread the delay as indifference.

So he stayed two days longer. The little word “so” is the hinge of the chapter, and it should be felt as a shock. The delay is the consequence of the love, not a suspension of it. He meant to give them something far greater than a healing: a resurrection, and a deeper knowledge of who he is. The Lord who stayed two days beyond the Jordan was not careless of Bethany; he was carrying the whole of it in his heart, and walking toward it on his own schedule.

The arithmetic. When Jesus arrives, Lazarus has been in the tomb four days (v. 17). The journey from Bethany beyond the Jordan to Bethany near Jerusalem probably took about a day. Before that, he waited two days. Before that, the messenger had to travel the same road, probably another day. Lazarus may well have died soon after the messenger set out, before the message ever reached Jesus. The two days did not cause the death, but they ensured that no one could doubt he was truly dead.

The comfort for if only. There is a form of bereavement that spends years on the timing: if the appointment had been a week earlier, if we had gone straight to the hospital, if the prayer had started sooner. This passage puts a family in exactly that position, lets them say the sentence twice (vv. 21, 32), and quietly shows that the sums never worked: no hurrying would have brought him there in time. He allowed a death he could have prevented, in a family he loved, in order to give them and everybody watching something a healing could not have given. John does not pretend the four days were anything but painful.

Why does God delay answering my prayers? Scripture does not give a single reason for every case, but this chapter gives us the deepest one: his delays are governed by love, not neglect. Sometimes he waits because he intends to give something greater than what we asked. Sometimes the waiting itself is shaping us, teaching us to trust him rather than our timetable. Often we will not know why until later, and some things not until we see his face. What you can know now is the sentence John put first: Jesus loved them. Read every delay in your life with that sentence in front of it, and keep praying.

verseByVerse.quote: Then after this he said to the disciples, "Let us go to Judea again." The disciples said to him, "Rabbi, the Jews were just now seeking to stone you, and are you going there again?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let us go to Judea again. Not let us go to Lazarus, which is what the errand is, but Judea, where men had tried to stone him. And he does not go alone or send them: they are going into it together. The road to Bethany was the road to Calvary, and he took it with his eyes open, having counted the cost.

Seeking to stone you. The disciples are not being cowardly. The authorities had tried, twice, in a matter of months (8:59; 10:31, 39), the last time at the Feast of Dedication not long before.

And are you going there again? The word “again” appears twice, once in Jesus’ mouth and once in theirs. For him it is a return to unfinished business. For them it is the second time into a place that nearly killed him. That is often how God’s call sounds. He who gives it sees the whole picture; those who receive it can see only what happened last time.

The shape of costly obedience. It rarely looks like heroism. More often it looks like this walk back to Judea: a hospital visit that may be awkward, a conversation that may be costly, a return to a place where you were once hurt.

Should I take risks for Christ, or be prudent? Both, in their place. Prudence is not sin; Jesus himself withdrew when his hour had not come (10:40; 11:54), and he told his disciples to flee from one town to the next under persecution (Matthew 10:23). But prudence becomes sin when it is used to excuse disobedience. The question is not, is this safe? but, is this where he is going? If Christ calls you to a costly duty, to love someone difficult, to speak truth, to serve in a hard place, the danger is not a reason to refuse. And if he has not called you, there is no virtue in seeking danger for its own sake.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered, "Are there not twelve hours in the day? If anyone walks in the day, he does not stumble, because he sees the light of this world. But if anyone walks in the night, he stumbles, because the light is not in him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Are there not twelve hours in the day? The picture depends on a fact of life before street lighting. The daylight hours were counted as twelve, from sunrise to sunset, whatever the season, so the hours were longer in summer and shorter in winter. When the light went, work stopped, and a man walking a stony Judean track after dark would fall. So the claim is about allotted time. Jesus’ day is the appointed time of his ministry (9:4), and it cannot be cut short until it is finished. He is not saying the danger is imaginary. He is saying the clock is not kept by the men holding the stones.

He does not stumble. The one who walks in God’s will walks safely. The disciples’ safety on this road is not a matter of the route but of whom they are following.

The light is not in him. The picture moves from the sun outside to a light inside a person. In this Gospel that light is Jesus himself (1:4–5; 8:12), and whoever does not have him stumbles (12:35).

The hard edge of the picture. Twelve hours is a fixed allowance. It cannot be shortened by enemies, and it cannot be extended by carefulness either. He is telling them that safety cannot be manufactured by choosing a different road, and that the only truly dangerous position is to be walking somewhere he is not going.

Does this mean nothing bad can happen to me if I obey God? No. It is not a promise of long life or freedom from harm. Jesus’ own twelve hours had only weeks left to run, and, by early tradition, many of the men listening would die violently for him. It is a promise that the ending is not in the hands of whoever is throwing the stones. Your days are written in God’s book (Psalm 139:16), and nothing can cut them short before he says. That frees you from two fears: the fear that your enemies control your life, and the fear that you must control it yourself by endless caution.
verseByVerse.note: The daylight hours were counted as twelve, from sunrise to sunset.

verseByVerse.quote: After saying these things, he said to them, "Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep, but I go to awaken him." The disciples said to him, "Lord, if he has fallen asleep, he will recover."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Our friend Lazarus. Not my friend, which he might have said about a man the disciples barely knew. He includes them in the friendship before he tells them the man is dead.

Fallen asleep. Sleep was a common picture of death for believers (Matthew 9:24; Acts 7:60; 1 Thessalonians 4:13–14). The noun built from it is koimētērion, a sleeping place, and that is where our word cemetery comes from. Sleep is not a nicer word for extinction; it is a claim about what death now is for those who belong to him. Sleep is temporary, and it ends in the ordinary way: somebody says your name, as is about to happen at the mouth of a cave.

I go to awaken him. The language is domestic, the ordinary language of rousing someone in the morning: to him a resurrection is going in to wake somebody up.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the soul sleeps unconscious between death and resurrection, as some teach. Sleep describes the body’s rest and the certainty of waking. The believer’s spirit goes at once to be with Christ (Luke 23:43; Philippians 1:23; 2 Corinthians 5:8). The dead in Christ are conscious and at rest with him, waiting for the resurrection of the body (the Westminster Confession 32.1).

He will recover. They take it literally, and with some relief: sleep is a good sign in illness, so if he is sleeping he is turning the corner, and there is no need to walk into Judea. The literal meaning is the one that suits them, as it often suits us.

What actually happens when a Christian dies? The body is buried and returns to dust, but the person, the soul, is immediately with Christ, made perfect in holiness, in conscious joy, awaiting the redemption of the body (Westminster 32.1; 1689 31.1). There is no purgatory and no unconscious waiting. Then, when Christ returns, the body will be raised, transformed and reunited with the soul, never to die again (1 Corinthians 15:42–44, 51–53). So when a believer dies, we may say truly that he has fallen asleep, and truly that he is with the Lord. Both are true, of the body and of the soul.
verseByVerse.note: Sleep was a common picture of death for believers.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Jesus had spoken of his death, but they thought that he meant taking rest in sleep. Then Jesus told them plainly, "Lazarus has died,
verseByVerse.commentary:
They thought he meant sleep. Another of John’s misunderstandings, and John records it in full, writing decades later, with no attempt to make the twelve look better. That is one of the small marks of an honest witness: an inventor of a founding story would have little reason to write his leaders like that.

Lazarus has died. Jesus now speaks “plainly”. The word is parrēsia: openly, without veiling. They had heard sleep as getting better, and rather than let them travel to Bethany with a comfortable misunderstanding, he takes the comfort away and gives them the fact. The Lord who spoke so gently of sleep was not afraid of the word death. He looked at it plainly, called it by its name, and walked toward it, because he had come to deal with it.

How should I speak about death, especially to children? Plainly first, then with hope. Do not let the tenderest words become an anaesthetic that leaves people confused. Children especially can be frightened by vague phrases: gone away, lost, gone to sleep, said without explanation. Say that the person has died, that their body has stopped working and will not work again in this life. Then give the hope, clearly: if they trusted Jesus, they are with him now, and he will raise their body one day. Jesus himself did it in that order. First the fact, then the promise. The picture of sleep can be explained afterwards, when it will mean something.

verseByVerse.quote: "and for your sake I am glad that I was not there, so that you may believe. But let us go to him." So Thomas, called the Twin, said to his fellow disciples, "Let us also go, that we may die with him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Glad that I was not there. He does not say he is glad Lazarus died. He says he is glad he was absent, because his presence would have produced a healing, and a healing would have produced a smaller faith than what is now possible. The disciples already believed (2:11), but faith grows, and they will need more than they have for what is coming in Jerusalem.

In the flow. So that you may believe is the aim of the whole Gospel in miniature (20:31). Within days these men will watch him arrested and killed, and they will need to have seen him empty a grave before they see him laid in one.

Let us go to him. To him, though dead. Jesus speaks of a dead man as someone you can still go to, because to him the dead are not beyond reach.

Thomas, called the Twin. Thomas’s name means twin in Aramaic; Didymus is the Greek equivalent. But there is something twinned in the man himself all through this Gospel. He is the one who says the brave thing and the doubting thing, and both come from the same place: he will not pretend to a confidence he does not have.

That we may die with him. He is remembered for one sentence of doubt after the resurrection (20:24–25), and English has called him “doubting Thomas” ever since. But this is the first time he speaks in the Gospel. He has concluded, reasonably, that going to Judea means execution, and he proposes that they go. That is not doubt. It is loyalty without hope, which is a rarer and harder thing than loyalty with it. He proposes the journey in a flat voice, expecting the worst, because he would rather die with Jesus than live without him. And the one Thomas expected to die with did die, not with them but for them, and then came back through a locked door to show his hands to the man who had followed him in despair.

Is it all right to follow Christ while I am full of doubts and fears? Yes. Jesus did not wait for Thomas to become cheerful before he let him come, and he did not wait for perfect faith before accepting it. He works with what is offered and refines it along the way, as he did with Thomas a few weeks later (20:27–28). What matters is not how confident you feel but where you are walking. Bring your doubts with you, tell him about them honestly, and keep going in the direction he is going. Many of the best saints have followed in a flat voice for long stretches.
verseByVerse.note: Thomas’s name means “twin” in Aramaic; Didymus is the Greek equivalent.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Jesus came, he found that Lazarus had already been in the tomb four days. Bethany was near Jerusalem, about two miles off.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four days. Burial in that world was usually on the day of death; the body was washed, wrapped with spices and laid in a rock tomb within hours, because the climate allowed nothing else. So four days in the tomb is four days from death, and decay would have been well under way. There was also a popular Jewish belief, preserved in later rabbinic writings, that the soul lingered near the body for three days hoping to return, and departed on the fourth when the face became unrecognisable.
