It was a cave, and a stone lay against it.<sup>39</sup>Jesus said, “Take away the stone.” Martha, the sister of the dead man, said to him, “Lord, by this time there will be an odor, for he has been dead four days.”<sup>40</sup>Jesus said to her, “Did I not tell you that if you believed you would see the glory of God?”<sup>41</sup>So they took away the stone. And Jesus lifted up his eyes and said, “Father, I thank you that you have heard me.<sup>42</sup>I knew that you always hear me, but I said this on account of the people standing around, that they may believe that you sent me.”<sup>43</sup>When he had said these things, he cried out with a loud voice, “Lazarus, come out.”<sup>44</sup>The man who had died came out, his hands and feet bound with linen strips, and his face wrapped with a cloth. Jesus said to them, “Unbind him, and let him go.”<sup>45</sup>Many of the Jews therefore, who had come with Mary and had seen what he did, believed in him,<sup>46</sup>but some of them went to the Pharisees and told them what Jesus had done.<sup>47</sup>So the chief priests and the Pharisees gathered the council and said, “What are we to do? For this man performs many signs.<sup>48</sup>If we let him go on like this, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation.”<sup>49</sup>But one of them, Caiaphas, who was high priest that year, said to them, “You know nothing at all.<sup>50</sup>Nor do you understand that it is better for you that one man should die for the people, not that the whole nation should perish.”<sup>51</sup>He did not say this of his own accord, but being high priest that year he prophesied that Jesus would die for the nation,<sup>52</sup>and not for the nation only, but also to gather into one the children of God who are scattered abroad.<sup>53</sup>So from that day on they made plans to put him to death.<sup>54</sup>Jesus therefore no longer walked openly among the Jews, but went from there to the region near the wilderness, to a town called Ephraim, and there he stayed with the disciples.<sup>55</sup>Now the Passover of the Jews was at hand, and many went up from the country to Jerusalem before the Passover to purify themselves.<sup>56</sup>They were looking for Jesus and saying to one another as they stood in the temple, “What do you think? That he will not come to the feast at all?”<sup>57</sup>Now the chief priests and the Pharisees had given orders that if anyone knew where he was, he should let them know, so that they might arrest him.
11.overview:
The raising of Lazarus is the seventh and greatest sign in John, and the event that leads directly to the cross. Jesus delays, returns to Judea despite the danger, tells Martha that he is the resurrection and the life, weeps with Mary, and calls a man four days dead out of his tomb.

Many believe, but the council meets in alarm, and Caiaphas argues that one man should die for the people. John hears in it a prophecy of the cross. From that day they plan to kill him. The one who gives life will give his own.

12.title: The Hour Has Come

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–19 — The Anointing and the Entry
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Six days before Passover, at a dinner in Bethany with Lazarus at the table, Mary anoints Jesus’ feet with costly nard, and Jesus defends her against Judas. The next day the festival crowds go out with palm branches to meet Jesus as he rides into the city on a young donkey, and the Pharisees despair that the world has gone after him.
verseByVerse.theology: Mary’s extravagance is the fitting response to Jesus: Matthew records him calling it a beautiful thing (Matthew 26:10). Judas’ objection sounds pious and is calculated: he uses the language of charity to cover his own greed. The contrast between Mary’s love and Judas’ arithmetic is the contrast between true discipleship and a discipleship that has never left the world’s way of counting.
verseByVerse.examples: The crowd hails Jesus as king, right about the title and wrong about its meaning. Jesus comes on a donkey, fulfilling Zechariah 9:9, the humble king of peace. The disciples understand it only after he is glorified (v. 16), as so often in John: the events become clear in the light of the cross and resurrection, through the Spirit.

verseByVerse.quote: Six days before the Passover, Jesus therefore came to Bethany, where Lazarus was, whom Jesus had raised from the dead. So they gave a dinner for him there. Martha served, and Lazarus was one of those reclining with him at table.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. John 12 closes the first half of the Gospel, the Book of Signs. Jesus is anointed for burial, enters Jerusalem as king, announces that his hour has come, and makes a last appeal to the crowd. From chapter 13 on, Jesus speaks only to his disciples, and then goes to the cross. It is a chapter of fragrance and shouting and a seed falling into the ground.

Six days before the Passover. Probably the Saturday evening before Passover week, after the Sabbath ended. John has started a clock, and it runs to the end of the book. Nearly half this Gospel covers one week.

Jesus therefore came to Bethany. The word “therefore” reaches back to the last verse of chapter 11: the order that anyone who knew where he was should report it. He comes within an hour’s walk of men with a warrant, knowing they are looking for him.

A dinner for him. Mark and Matthew place what is very likely the same dinner in the house of Simon the leper (Mark 14:3). A dinner of gratitude, in the village of resurrection, at the last resting place before Jerusalem.

Martha served. Martha is still serving, as in the one other scene we have of that house (Luke 10:40), now without complaint. Her brother has come back from the dead, and she is in the kitchen. That is not a failure to learn. She is a woman doing what she is good at, for the man who gave her brother back. Service offered in love is worship too.

Lazarus at table. A man who had been dead four days is at dinner, reclining on his elbow as guests did. Resurrection does not produce a spectacle or a ghost. It produces a man having supper with his sisters. And it is a small picture of what is coming: the household of the raised, eating with the one who will himself die and rise.

Did Jesus really spend his last week at dinners? Yes, among other things, and it is not a waste. He taught in the temple, wept over the city, washed feet, prayed in the garden; and he also ate with friends. Table fellowship runs all through the Gospels, and his last free evening before the arrest was spent at a meal (13:1–2). Christians sometimes feel that only overtly religious activity counts. But eating together in gratitude, with Christ honoured at the table, is part of the life of his people, and a foretaste of the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:9).

For worship. With a cross six days away, the Lord of life sat at supper unhurried with a man he had raised. One day all who have been raised by him will recline with him, the dead made alive and eating, in his Father’s house, and he himself will serve them (Luke 12:37).

verseByVerse.quote: Mary therefore took a pound of expensive ointment made from pure nard, and anointed the feet of Jesus and wiped his feet with her hair. The house was filled with the fragrance of the perfume. But Judas Iscariot, one of his disciples (he who was about to betray him), said,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pure nard. Nard was an aromatic oil from a plant grown in the Himalayas, imported from India, and it was very costly. This may have been a family treasure, perhaps put by for her own burial or her dowry. It is worth, as Judas will calculate in a moment, about a year’s wages.

His feet, and her hair. Anointing the head honoured a king; the feet were a servant’s place. And a respectable woman, it is often said, did not let down her hair in public. She gives the most precious thing she owns, in the lowliest way, at the cost of her reputation, without a word.

Feet wiped twice. John uses the same verb for what Mary does here and for what Jesus does in the next chapter. She wiped his feet with her hair; a few nights later he wiped his disciples’ feet with the towel tied round him (13:5). The two scenes belong together. A disciple kneels at his feet in love, and then the Lord kneels at theirs, Judas’s among them, and washes what she only anointed. His is the deeper humbling, the Lord of glory in the servant’s place, and it points to the cross where he would lay down his life to make them clean (13:8–10).

Is this the same anointing as in Matthew and Mark? Very probably yes, one supper, and the differences can be reasonably harmonised. There the woman is unnamed and anoints his head (Mark 14:3); John has the feet. A pound of nard is far more than is needed for either, and Mark describes her breaking the flask and pouring it out; a woman emptying a jar that size over a reclining man will reach both ends of him. She probably did both, and each writer keeps what struck him; John remembers the hair. The host is Simon the leper, and Martha serving fits well enough; John says Lazarus was one of those reclining at table, a guest rather than the householder. The objectors are some in Mark and the disciples in Matthew, while John names the one who started it, as he alone names Peter with the sword and Malchus who lost an ear. And the dates measure different things. John’s six days marks the arrival at Bethany; Mark’s two days (Mark 14:1) dates the chief priests’ plotting, and he tells the anointing there because Judas’s betrayal follows from it. This is not the sinful woman of Luke 7, which was an earlier and different anointing in Galilee. Not every detail can be settled with certainty, but nothing here forces us to doubt either account.

The fragrance of the perfume. Her devotion fills the house, and the story fills the world. Matthew and Mark both record a promise Jesus made about this woman, that wherever the gospel is preached in the whole world, what she has done will be told in memory of her (Mark 14:9). John does not record the promise. He simply keeps it, by telling her story.

But Judas Iscariot. John tells us who Judas is before we hear what he says: the fragrance of devotion and the coldest calculation at one table.

What would extravagant love for Christ look like for me? Rarely a jar of nard, but always something that costs. It might be time given when you have little, money given beyond what is sensible, a reputation risked by being openly his, or a long, quiet service no one sees. The mark of Mary’s act is not its size but its direction: it was all for him, and it was not calculated. Ask what you are keeping back because it is too precious, and whether he is worth more. He is the only one who has ever deserved everything, and the only one who gave everything first.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the pound was a Roman pound, about 11½ ounces. Nard was a costly perfume imported from India. A respectable woman did not normally let down her hair in public.

parallels.desc: a different woman in Galilee

verseByVerse.quote: "Why was this ointment not sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor?" He said this, not because he cared about the poor, but because he was a thief, and having charge of the moneybag he used to help himself to what was put into it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why was this ointment not sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor? The sum is worth converting. The ESV notes that a denarius was a day’s wage; three hundred, once Sabbaths and feasts are taken out, is about a year’s pay for a labourer. So the question is not trivial: a year’s income has just been poured onto somebody’s feet. The objection sounds pious. Mark says some of those present were indignant (Mark 14:4), Matthew that the disciples were (Matthew 26:8); John names Judas as the one who said it. And his arithmetic is correct. If his motive had been what he said it was, his objection would have been a fair one.

Because he was a thief. The moneybag was the common purse, from which the poor were helped (13:29). Judas was the treasurer, and he stole from it. “Used to help himself” is continuous: not once, but habitually, over a long time. Love of money opened the door to his betrayal (Matthew 26:14–15; 1 Timothy 6:10).

The disguise of a good cause. Judas does not argue for theft. He argues for the poor. A concern for the poor can be perfectly genuine, and it can also be the most effective disguise, and from outside the two cannot be told apart. The only person in the room who could tell was the one being anointed.

Why did Jesus choose Judas, and let him keep the money? Jesus knew from the beginning who would betray him (6:64, 70–71), and nothing suggests the theft was hidden from the one who knew what was in man (2:25). He chose Judas so that Scripture would be fulfilled (13:18), and he gave him every privilege of an apostle for three years: his teaching, his miracles, his friendship, his trust. That is the solemn lesson. Judas was not kept out; he was kept close and loved, and he chose silver. Nearness to Jesus, even a ministry in his name, does not save anyone who keeps his heart for something else. And Jesus’ patience with him is a picture of the long patience God shows to every sinner.

How do I guard against the love of money? Give regularly and generously, so that money learns who is master (2 Corinthians 9:6–8). Be open and accountable with money that is not yours: in a church, a charity or a business, never handle it alone. Watch for the moment you begin to justify small dishonesties. Be content with what you have, because he has said, I will never leave you nor forsake you (Hebrews 13:5). And treasure Christ. The cure for loving money is not merely having less of it but loving him more.

For worship. The Lord who knew what was in the bag let Judas carry it for three years and never shamed him before the others. The one Judas valued below a year’s wages was worth more than all the treasure in the world, and he gave himself freely for people who had robbed God.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that a denarius was a day’s wage; three hundred denarii was about a year’s wages.

parallels.desc: Judas had the moneybag

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said, "Leave her alone, so that she may keep it for the day of my burial. For the poor you always have with you, but you do not always have me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Leave her alone. Mary has said nothing, and he speaks for her.

For the day of my burial. Bodies were anointed with spices for burial. The Greek is genuinely difficult, since the ointment has already been poured out and there is nothing left to keep. The best sense is probably that she had been keeping it, that this jar had been put by, and that Jesus is saying she has spent it on the right day. Either way, he sees her act as preparing his body for death. Nicodemus will bring spices (19:39–40), but to a body already dead. Mary does it six days early, while he can still smell it. Her nard prepared his body for the grave; his body, given for us, prepared the way out of ours. Did Mary understand that he would die? Perhaps more than the disciples did. She who sat at his feet may have heard what they missed.

The poor you always have with you. This is often quoted as a shrug, as if nothing can be done about poverty. But Jesus is himself quoting, and the rest of the verse is left off. He is citing Deuteronomy 15:11: for there will never cease to be poor in the land. Therefore I command you, You shall open wide your hand to your brother, to the needy and to the poor, in your land. That there will always be poor people is not a reason to do nothing. It is the reason for the command that follows in the same breath: open your hand. Jesus is not dismissing the poor. There will always be time to help them, and his people must (Galatians 2:10).

You do not always have me. In a few days he would be gone. Devotion to Christ himself comes first; care for the poor flows from it. And remember who raised the objection: Judas had every day of three years to open his hand to the poor, and used the moneybag to fill his own instead.

So should churches spend money on beauty and worship rather than the poor? This verse does not settle that by making the poor unimportant, nor does it license luxury. Mary’s act was unique, a gift to Christ in person before his burial. The lasting principles are these. Christ himself is worthy of our best, and worship is not wasted when it costs. Care for the poor is commanded and must never be neglected; the early church organised it from the start (Acts 6:1–6). The two are not rivals: those who love Christ most will be most generous to the poor, because he is found among them (Matthew 25:40). Be suspicious of any argument, for spending or for saving, that happens to serve the arguer’s own comfort.
verseByVerse.note: Bodies were anointed with spices for burial.

parallels.desc: there will never cease to be poor in the land

verseByVerse.quote: When the large crowd of the Jews learned that Jesus was there, they came, not only on account of him but also to see Lazarus, whom he had raised from the dead. So the chief priests made plans to put Lazarus to death as well, because on account of him many of the Jews were going away and believing in Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Also to see Lazarus. Lazarus has become a living proof, a walking sign.

To put Lazarus to death as well. One of the darkest sentences in the New Testament, and nearly comic in its futility. They are proposing to kill a man who has already been dead once, and got up. The chief priests were mostly Sadducees, who denied the resurrection (Acts 23:8), and a resurrected man was an embarrassment. Rather than believe the evidence, they plot to destroy it. When religion becomes a way of keeping control, even a resurrection stops being good news and becomes a threat to be managed. That danger is not confined to Jerusalem: anyone who wants God on his own terms will find a living Christ inconvenient.

Going away and believing. The problem is not that Lazarus is preaching; not a word of his is recorded anywhere in this Gospel. The problem is that he exists, and his silent, breathing life is a standing testimony to the one who called him out. They plotted to kill Lazarus, but they could not undo the resurrection. The man was alive because the Lord of life had spoken, and no council could reverse that word.

I have no dramatic story, so do I have a testimony? Yes. Lazarus’s entire testimony was that he was alive and people could see him at dinner, and it drew crowds to Christ. Yours is the same in kind: you were dead in sin and are now alive to God (Ephesians 2:4–5), whether your conversion was sudden or so gradual you cannot date it. The evidence is your life now: a love for Christ you did not have by nature, a fight against sin, a hope that death cannot shake. You do not need to have been a criminal or an addict. You need only to say, truthfully and simply, what he has done for you, and let your changed life back it up.

verseByVerse.quote: The next day the large crowd that had come to the feast heard that Jesus was coming to Jerusalem. So they took branches of palm trees and went out to meet him, crying out, "Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, even the King of Israel!" And Jesus found a young donkey and sat on it, just as it is written,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The next day. On the usual reckoning, Palm Sunday.

Branches of palm trees. John is the only Gospel writer who mentions palms, and they were not general festive decoration but a political symbol. Palm branches had become a sign of national victory ever since the Maccabees: when Simon retook the citadel in Jerusalem the people entered with praise and palm branches (1 Maccabees 13:51; 2 Maccabees 10:7). Waving them at a man entering the capital was roughly what waving a national flag at a returning general would be. And going out to meet him (hypantēsis) was how cities greeted a visiting king or conqueror.

Hosanna. “Hosanna” is Hebrew for save us, we pray (Psalm 118:25). By this time it had become a shout of praise, rather as God save the King is a shout of loyalty more than a prayer, but its meaning is a cry for salvation. The blessing is from Psalm 118:26, one of the Hallel psalms sung at Passover and the Feast of Booths, a pilgrim psalm of welcome.

Even the King of Israel! The title is not in the psalm, and it is the whole misunderstanding in a phrase. The psalm is about pilgrims arriving at the temple; they have turned it into a coronation of a national liberator, like the Maccabees. Jesus is king, but not the kind they expect (6:15; 18:36). John has heard the title before, from Nathanael under the fig tree (1:49), and he will see it again, fixed above the cross in three languages as the King of the Jews (19:19–20).

A young donkey. The other Gospels tell how he found it (Mark 11:1–7). The donkey is his answer to the palms. A king coming to a city on a warhorse is coming to take it; a king on a donkey has come in peace. He lets them crown him, and quietly declines the kingdom they have in mind.

Was this the same crowd that shouted Crucify him a few days later? Probably not entirely. The crowd on the road was largely pilgrims and the Galileans and Bethany witnesses who had seen his works; the crowd before Pilate was gathered early in the morning in the city, stirred up by the chief priests (Mark 15:11). But some may well have been in both, and the point stands: popular enthusiasm is fickle. People who wanted a king on their own terms turned against him when he would not be that king. It is a warning against a faith that follows Jesus only while he seems to be giving us what we want.

For worship. The palms on the Jerusalem road were waved for a liberator from Rome, and within the week the city had dropped them. But John saw them again. In his vision of heaven a multitude no one could number, from every nation, stands before the throne with palm branches in their hands, crying that salvation belongs to our God and to the Lamb (Revelation 7:9–10). Every palm the crowd let fall will be lifted again, by people he has truly saved.
verseByVerse.note: Palm branches had become a symbol of national victory and celebration. “Hosanna” means “save, we pray.”

parallels.desc: blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD
branches of palm trees at the Feast of Booths

verseByVerse.quote: "Fear not, daughter of Zion; behold, your king is coming, sitting on a donkey's colt!" His disciples did not understand these things at first, but when Jesus was glorified, then they remembered that these things had been written about him and had been done to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fear not, daughter of Zion. From Zechariah 9:9, with its opening rejoice greatly swapped for the fear not of Isaiah 40:9 or Zephaniah 3:16, the standard word to a frightened Israel. “Daughter of Zion” is Jerusalem. The crowd is exultant and does not need telling to rejoice; they are already doing it, loudly, and about the wrong thing. What they will need in five days, at the cross, is the other word: fear not.

A king of peace. Zechariah goes on to say that this king will cut off the war horse and speak peace to the nations, with a rule from sea to sea (Zechariah 9:10). The King of the universe came into his capital on a borrowed donkey, and the first word of his welcome was fear not. He comes to his people not to terrify but to save, not with chariots but with peace.

They did not understand at first. They were in the procession, two of them had fetched the animal, and they walked into Jerusalem in the middle of the noise, and John says plainly that none of it meant anything to them at the time.

When Jesus was glorified. After the resurrection and ascension, and with the Spirit’s help (14:26), they understood the Scriptures (2:22). Glorified is a large word in John: it takes in his death, his resurrection and his return to the Father as one great event, the moment when who he is was fully shown (7:39; 17:5). Understanding came later: they remembered the same events and at last saw what they meant. Their confusion at the time did not stop the prophecy being fulfilled.

How do we know the apostles did not simply read prophecy into the events afterwards? Because they tell us honestly when they understood, and what they record does not flatter them. Inventors would have been tempted to make themselves wise at the time. Many of the fulfilments were outside anyone’s control: the place of birth, the manner of death, the piercing, the grave. And Jesus himself acted deliberately to fulfil Scripture, as here, showing that he understood his mission in its light. Above all, the resurrection is the key that opened the Old Testament to them, and the resurrection rests on the testimony of many witnesses, more than five hundred of them at one time, most still alive to be questioned when Paul wrote (1 Corinthians 15:3–8). The apostles did not create the pattern. They discovered it, once the risen Lord explained it.
verseByVerse.note: A king riding a donkey came in peace, not on a warhorse.

parallels.desc: your king, mounted on a donkey
fear not, O Zion

verseByVerse.quote: The crowd that had been with him when he called Lazarus out of the tomb and raised him from the dead continued to bear witness. The reason why the crowd went to meet him was that they heard he had done this sign.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Continued to bear witness. The tense is continuous: they had not stopped talking about it.

They heard he had done this sign. John connects the entry directly to Lazarus. The palm branches go back to him: the whole entry, the shouting, the psalm, the improvised coronation, was set off by a resurrection in a village two miles away. The King they hailed had not won a battle. He had emptied a grave, and the only kingdom worth hailing is one whose king has authority over death.

Two crowds. There are two crowds here: one from Bethany, telling what they saw (v. 17), and one from Jerusalem, coming out because they heard (v. 18). The second crowd saw nothing. That is the ordinary way almost every Christian who has ever lived came to faith: not by seeing, but by believing people who did. And it is exactly what Jesus will say to Thomas at the end of the book: blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed (20:29).

Is believing on the testimony of others really enough? Yes, when the testimony is true and comes from God. Most of what any of us know about history, we know from witnesses. The apostles were eyewitnesses who told what they had seen and heard (1 John 1:1–3), wrote it down, and suffered for it. Their testimony is preserved for us in Scripture, and the Holy Spirit himself bears witness through it to our hearts (the Westminster Confession 1.5; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 1.5). Faith is not believing without evidence. It is trusting God’s own testimony, delivered through those he chose, about his Son.

verseByVerse.quote: So the Pharisees said to one another, "You see that you are gaining nothing. Look, the world has gone after him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You are gaining nothing. Frustration, said to one another, which suggests recrimination. The policy is not working, and they are turning on each other.

The world has gone after him. An exaggeration, but a prophetic one. And John opens the very next verse: now among those who went up to worship at the feast were some Greeks. So the Pharisees, complaining bitterly, have accidentally announced what is about to happen. Like Caiaphas, they speak more truly than they know (11:50–51). His enemies said in despair what heaven says in joy: the world has gone after him.

A second irony. The Pharisees think the crowd’s enthusiasm is their defeat. In five days that same city will be shouting for a crucifixion, and the Pharisees will have won everything they wanted. And the world will go after him anyway, by exactly the route they arranged: lifted up on a cross, he will draw all people to himself (12:32).

Is the world really going after him today? More than ever before in history. The church that began with a handful of believers in Jerusalem is now found in almost every nation on earth, and in many places it is growing among the poor and the persecuted. That is not a reason for pride or complacency; there are still many peoples with no church at all. But it is the fulfilment of what the Pharisees feared and what Jesus promised: people from every tribe and language and nation (Revelation 5:9).

In everyday life. You are part of that crowd. Pray this week for one nation where the church is small or suffering.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–50 — The Hour Has Come: Lifting Up the Son of Man
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When some Greeks ask to see Jesus, he declares that the hour of his glory has come, and speaks of the grain of wheat that must die. His soul is troubled, yet he prays that the Father will glorify his name, and a voice answers from heaven. He speaks of the world judged, its ruler cast out, and himself lifted up to draw all people. John explains Israel’s unbelief from Isaiah, and Jesus speaks his final public words.
verseByVerse.theology: The hour is at the centre of John’s Gospel. It is the one event of cross, resurrection and return to the Father, in which the Son of Man is lifted up in humiliation and glorified in the same act. The cross is not the Father’s defeat but his decisive victory, not the Son’s shame but his glory, and it cannot be separated from the resurrection: both belong to the one hour.
verseByVerse.examples: The grain of wheat must fall into the earth and die before it bears much fruit: life through death. The disciple who hates his life in this world, who will not cling to it at the cost of loyalty to Christ, keeps it in a way the self-preserver never can. Our letting go follows his, and the call to follow him is a call to follow him even into death.

verseByVerse.quote: Now among those who went up to worship at the feast were some Greeks. So these came to Philip, who was from Bethsaida in Galilee, and asked him, "Sir, we wish to see Jesus."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some Greeks. John calls them Greeks: Gentiles by birth, not Greek-speaking Jews up for the feast. They had come to worship at the feast, which probably places them among the God-fearers: Gentiles who worshipped the God of Israel without becoming full converts, like Cornelius (Acts 10:2; 17:4). And there was a wall for them. The temple’s outer court was as far as a Gentile could go, and stone notices in Greek and Latin warned that any foreigner who passed the barrier had only himself to blame for the death that followed. That is the position from which they ask their question.

Philip of Bethsaida. Philip has a Greek name, and Bethsaida was a mixed border town near Gentile areas, where Greek would have been spoken daily.

We wish to see Jesus. A request carved on the inside of many pulpits, where only the preacher can see it. They want to see him, which here means to meet him, to come to know him.

What does it mean to see Jesus today? Not a vision, but to know him truly by faith. We see him in the Gospels, where his words and works are written so that we may believe (20:31). We see him in the preaching of his word, when Christ is set before us as crucified (Galatians 3:1). We see him in the Lord’s Supper, which proclaims his death until he comes. And we see something of him in his people, when they love one another as he loved them (13:35). One day we shall see him face to face (1 John 3:2). Until then, every Sunday ought to answer this request.

For worship. They had travelled to a temple whose carved letters told them where to stop, and they asked for the one person who could take them further. The Son they wished to see was himself the true temple, and through his death the dividing wall of hostility came down (Ephesians 2:14), so that Gentiles who once stood outside the inscriptions are brought near by his blood.
verseByVerse.note: These Greeks were probably Gentiles who worshipped the God of Israel, like the centurion Cornelius. Philip had a Greek name.

parallels.desc: other sheep

verseByVerse.quote: Philip went and told Andrew; Andrew and Philip went and told Jesus. And Jesus answered them, "The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Philip and Andrew. Philip is oddly hesitant. He does not take them to Jesus; he tells Andrew, and the two of them go together. Probably that is because they were Gentiles. In Matthew, Jesus says he was sent only to the lost sheep of Israel (Matthew 15:24), and Philip does not know whether this is allowed. Philip is the man who did the arithmetic on the loaves and concluded it could not be done (6:7). Andrew is the man who brought the boy with the lunch anyway (6:8–9), and who brought his brother Peter in the first place (1:41).

The hour has come. The pivot of the Gospel. Jesus’ hour is the time of his death and glorification. Three times John has told us it had not yet come: at Cana (2:4), at the feast when no one laid a hand on him (7:30), in the treasury (8:20). Now the clock strikes, and what makes it strike is not the arrest, the plot or the entry into Jerusalem, but a handful of foreigners asking to see him. Why? Because the Gentiles can only truly see him through his death, when he is lifted up and draws all people (v. 32).

The Son of Man. The title comes from Daniel 7, where one like a son of man is given dominion over all peoples, nations and languages (Daniel 7:13–14). Greeks ask for him, and he answers with the title that has the nations written into it. The Son of Man went to his throne by way of a cross, and the dominion promised to him over every people was bought with his blood.

The cross is the glory. “Glorified” in John takes in the cross, resurrection and return to the Father as one. The cross is not a defeat followed by glory; the cross is itself the glory.

How can a crucifixion be glorious? Because glory in Scripture is the shining out of who God is, and nowhere does that shine more brightly than at the cross. There we see his holiness, which will not overlook sin; his justice, which punishes it fully; his love, which bears that punishment himself for his enemies; and his power, which turns the worst crime in history into the salvation of the world. A crucifixion was meant to be the most shameful death imaginable. God made it the place where he is most honoured. That is why Paul could say, far be it from me to boast except in the cross (Galatians 6:14).
verseByVerse.note: Jesus’ “hour” in John is the time of his death and glorification.

verseByVerse.quote: "Truly, truly, I say to you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit. Whoever loves his life loses it, and whoever hates his life in this world will keep it for eternal life."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth. He answers a request from Gentiles with a fact about farming. They want to see him; he tells them what it will cost to be seen. A seed kept in a jar stays exactly what it is. It remains alone, which is the word he uses, an odd word for a seed and the right word for him. Planted, it dies as a seed, and a plant grows with many seeds. Through his death comes a great harvest of people from every nation, including the Greeks who have just asked to see him. The wall that kept the Gentiles out comes down because the seed goes into the ground.

It bears much fruit. The seed must truly be lost before anything comes up. He is telling them plainly that he is going to die, in the gentlest image available, days before it happens. The grain of wheat fell into the ground outside Jerusalem and lay there until the third day, and from it has come a harvest that fills the earth.

Whoever loves his life loses it. “Life” here is psychē: the self, one’s earthly life. Clinging to your life, living for yourself, is the way to lose everything.

Whoever hates his life. “Hates” is a Hebrew way of saying loves less, prefers something else. Jesus says a disciple must hate his father and mother (Luke 14:26), and God says through Malachi, Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated (Malachi 1:2–3), where the sense is choosing and setting aside rather than malice. It is not self-loathing but ranking Christ above self. The man who holds his life as the thing that must be preserved at all costs will find he could not keep it; the man who holds it loosely, because something matters more, gets it back. Nor is it a way of earning eternal life by giving things up. The grain of wheat that wins the harvest is Christ, not us. Our letting go follows his, and it is possible only because he has already given his life for ours.

What does falling into the ground look like in ordinary life? Usually not martyrdom, but many small deaths. It is giving up the evening you wanted for someone who needs you. It is letting go of a grudge you had every right to hold. It is choosing obedience when it costs a promotion, a friendship or your reputation. It is pouring years into children, a church or a neighbour without seeing the fruit. Each feels like loss, and each is a seed. And ask a plain question: what would you be unable to obey God about, if he asked? Not what you would find hard; what is genuinely not on the table. Whatever that is, it is the part of your life you are still loving in the sense this verse means. Bring it to the one who gave up his life for you before you gave up anything for him.

In everyday life. What are you clinging to? You do not let go by willpower: the Spirit who raised Jesus lives in you (Romans 8:11), and he gives the strength to plant it and wait for the fruit.

verseByVerse.quote: "If anyone serves me, he must follow me; and where I am, there will my servant be also. If anyone serves me, the Father will honor him. Now is my soul troubled. And what shall I say? 'Father, save me from this hour'? But for this purpose I have come to this hour."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He must follow me. Serving Christ means following him, even on the road of the grain of wheat.

Where I am. His servants will be with him in glory (14:3; 17:24), but first they follow him on the road there, and the place he is going in a few days is a cross.

The Father will honor him. Not human glory, but the Father’s approval: the very honour the authorities in verse 43 gave up for the approval of men.

Now is my soul troubled. This is John’s Gethsemane, and it is easy to miss that he has one. John records no agony in the garden, no let this cup pass, no sleeping disciples; when we reach the garden in chapter 18, Jesus walks out to meet the soldiers. The struggle is here, in public, days early. “Troubled” (tetaraktai) means agitated, shaken, like water stirred up. Jesus is truly human and feels the horror of what lies ahead: not just physical death, but bearing the wrath of God against sin (Mark 14:34).

And what shall I say? Father, save me from this hour? The sentence is the whole of Gethsemane compressed. The Greek can be punctuated as a question he considers and rejects, or as a real prayer answered by himself in the next breath. Either way the content is the same as in the garden: a genuine recoil, and a genuine refusal to act on it.

For this purpose I have come. He does not hide the struggle. Standing among Greeks, disciples and a crowd, he says out loud that his soul is in turmoil. Here is the Son of God, entirely certain of the Father’s will, entirely committed to it, and churned up about it, and the trouble does not weaken his obedience by a syllable. Ours wavers at far less, which is why it matters that his did not: by his obedience, offered in our place, the many are made righteous (Romans 5:19).

Is it a sin to feel troubled about what God is asking of me? No. Jesus was troubled, and he never sinned (Hebrews 4:15). Feelings of dread, grief or fear in the face of suffering are part of being human in a fallen world. What matters is what you do with them. Jesus brought his trouble to the Father in prayer, named it honestly, and then chose the Father’s glory over his own escape. You may do the same: tell God exactly how you feel, ask for help, and then say, for this purpose I am here. Obedience does not require that you stop feeling. It requires that you keep going.

parallels.desc: Gethsemane

verseByVerse.quote: "Father, glorify your name." Then a voice came from heaven: "I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again." The crowd that stood there and heard it said that it had thundered. Others said, "An angel has spoken to him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Father, glorify your name. Not save me, but glorify your name, like your will be done in Gethsemane. God’s name in Scripture is more than a label. It is God himself as he has made himself known: merciful and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in steadfast love, and by no means clearing the guilty (Exodus 34:5–7). To ask the Father to glorify his name is to ask that who he truly is be seen and honoured, and Jesus knows where it will be seen most clearly: at the cross.

A voice from heaven. The third time in the Gospels that the Father speaks from heaven, after the baptism (Mark 1:11) and the transfiguration (Mark 9:7).

I have glorified it. He has glorified it in Jesus’ life and signs; he will glorify it again in Jesus’ death and resurrection. The Father is saying: everything up to now, and everything about to happen, are the same work. The Father answered the Son from heaven in the hour of his trouble, and the answer was glory.

Thunder. Others said, An angel has spoken to him. Some heard only noise; others knew it was speech, but not whose. Compare Paul’s companions on the Damascus road (Acts 9:7; 22:9). In the Old Testament, God’s voice is likened to thunder (Psalm 29:3; Exodus 19:19). The sound was real, but they could not receive it as words spoken to them, so it became mere weather, which asks nothing of anyone. That is still a common response to God. People do not deny that something happened; they call it coincidence or psychology, and so need not answer it.

Should I expect God to speak to me with an audible voice? No; that is not how he has promised to guide us. Many sincere Christians see this differently, and God is free to work as he pleases, but the guidance he has promised is his word. The voice from heaven was a rare act at the climax of redemption, to confirm the Son before the cross. God has now spoken to us fully in his Son (Hebrews 1:1–2), and his word is written in Scripture, which is complete and sufficient for all we need for salvation and life (2 Timothy 3:16–17; the Westminster Confession 1.6; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 1.6). The Spirit speaks to us through that word, opening it to our hearts. So when you want to hear God, open the Bible. And when he speaks there, do not file it as thunder.

parallels.desc: the Father’s voice at the baptism and transfiguration

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered, "This voice has come for your sake, not mine. Now is the judgment of this world; now will the ruler of this world be cast out."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For your sake, not mine. Jesus did not need it; he knew the Father’s will, and had said as much at the tomb: I knew that you always hear me (11:42). It was for the crowd, to confirm him.

Now is the judgment of this world. Not at the end of history: now. The trial in which the world condemns Jesus is the trial in which the world is condemned; God overturns its verdict, and its sin is exposed. And the cross shows what a holy God thinks of sin. When the sin of his people was laid on his own Son, he did not spare him (Romans 8:32). If that is what sin cost when it was laid on the Son he loves, no one should imagine it is a small thing to God.

The ruler of this world cast out. “The ruler of this world” is Satan (14:30; 16:11; 2 Corinthians 4:4). The verb is ekballō, the ordinary word for throwing something out, and the word used all through the Gospels for casting out demons: the exorcist’s word, applied to the chief of them. How? By the cross Christ removed the ground of Satan’s accusation, our sin (Colossians 2:14–15; Hebrews 2:14–15; Revelation 12:9–11). Satan still works, but he is a defeated enemy.

The enemy’s own plan. The enemy arranged that execution. He entered Judas (13:27), and he got exactly what he wanted, and it turned out to be the means of his eviction. It is the oldest pattern in Scripture, the thing meant for harm becoming the thing that saves, and here it is at full scale.

Where Christians differ: the binding of Satan. Premillennial Christians, who expect Christ to return before a thousand-year reign on earth, often teach that Satan will be bound only in that future reign. Many godly believers hold this, out of a desire to take prophecy at face value, and some also expect a rapture of the church before it. This commentary’s view: Jesus says Satan is cast out “now,” at the cross. Revelation 20’s binding of Satan describes this present age, in which he can no longer deceive the nations or stop the gospel going to them (Matthew 12:29). This is the amillennial view: the thousand years are the gospel age between Christ’s first and second comings. Christians on every side of this question agree that Christ will return in glory and that Satan’s defeat is certain.

If Satan has been cast out, why is there still so much evil, and why am I still tempted? Because he is defeated but not yet destroyed. Think of a war in which the decisive battle has been won, but the enemy’s forces still fight on in pockets until the final surrender. Satan is still a roaring lion (1 Peter 5:8), still tempting and accusing, and the world still lies under his influence (1 John 5:19). But he cannot stop the gospel, cannot snatch a single sheep from Christ’s hand (10:28), and cannot condemn anyone for whom Christ died (Romans 8:33–34). So resist him, firm in your faith, knowing that the outcome is settled. The day is near when he will be crushed under the feet of the church (Romans 16:20).

For worship. The exorcist’s word was spoken over the prince of demons from a cross, in the very hour of his apparent triumph. The Lamb overcame him, and so do all who belong to the Lamb, by his blood and by the word of their testimony (Revelation 12:11).

verseByVerse.quote: "And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself." He said this to show by what kind of death he was going to die.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lifted up from the earth. This is the third and last of the lifted up sayings in John (3:14; 8:28). In John, “lifted up” means both the cross and his exaltation (Isaiah 52:13). And it is also, brutally and literally, what happened to him: a man raised off the ground on a beam. The two meanings are one movement.

Will draw all people to myself. “Draw” (helkō) is the same verb as 6:44, no one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him: a pulling that succeeds. In context, the Greeks have just asked to see him, and this is the answer to their request: through the cross, Jesus will draw people from every nation. The drawing power lies not in his teaching or his miracles but in the cross: the thing that draws is a man being executed, and it is at his most powerless that he says he will pull the world in.

By what kind of death. John stops to explain, the only time he does so with these sayings, which settles that he means the cross, without cancelling the other meaning. The exaltation and the execution are one event. He was lifted up to die, and he was lifted up to reign, and from that throne he is drawing to himself a people no one can number.

Where Christians differ: does Christ draw every person? Some take “all people” to mean every individual, drawn with a resistible grace, that is, a grace that can be finally refused. Many earnest Christians read it so, out of love for the wideness of the gospel. This commentary’s view: in 6:44 the one who is drawn is raised up on the last day. If every person were drawn in that sense, every person would be saved, which Scripture denies. Here, “all people” means all kinds of people, Gentiles as well as Jews, as the context of the Greeks shows (compare 11:52). The cross draws, effectively, people from every nation.

Does this mean everyone will finally be saved? No. Some have read all as a promise of universal salvation, but this same Gospel records that many turned back (6:66), that some will die in their sins (8:24), and that the word Jesus spoke will judge on the last day (12:48). John does not contradict himself a few verses apart. The barrier between Jew and Gentile is down, and the cross now draws from every nation on earth. It is the same promise as the other sheep who will become one flock under one shepherd (10:16). Everyone who comes to him is drawn, and everyone who is drawn will come.
verseByVerse.note: In John, “lifted up” means both the cross and his exaltation.

parallels.desc: he shall be high and lifted up

verseByVerse.quote: So the crowd answered him, "We have heard from the Law that the Christ remains forever. How can you say that the Son of Man must be lifted up? Who is this Son of Man?" So Jesus said to them, "The light is among you for a little while longer. Walk while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you. The one who walks in the darkness does not know where he is going."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the crowd answered him, We have heard from the Law that the Christ remains forever. Their objection is serious. “The Law” here is the Old Testament, and they can cite it. The promise to David was of a throne established for ever (Psalm 89:36–37); Isaiah’s child would reign from this time forth and for evermore (Isaiah 9:7); Ezekiel’s David would be prince for ever (Ezekiel 37:25); Daniel’s son of man received a dominion that would not pass away (Daniel 7:14). All this is true, but they could not imagine that he would reach that throne through death.

How can you say that the Son of Man must be lifted up? They understand lifted up as death. A dying Messiah made no sense to them; it was exactly the objection Paul would meet for the rest of his life: Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews (1 Corinthians 1:23).

Who is this Son of Man? The honest question. They do not know who he is talking about. They have noticed that he has quietly changed the title. They said the Christ; he said the Son of Man; and they want to know whether these are the same person.

The light is among you. Jesus does not argue; he warns. He is not refusing to answer from impatience. He is telling them that the season for standing about asking questions is nearly over, and the light will shortly go out of the street. Questions can be put off till later; the daylight will not wait.

Lest darkness overtake you. “Overtake” (katalabē) is the same word as 1:5, where the darkness has not overcome the light. Now the darkness will overtake those who refuse the light.

Is it wrong to have unanswered questions before I believe? No. Honest questions are not sin, and many believers carry some for years. But do not make every question a condition of coming to Christ. The crowd’s question had a real answer, the Messiah would reign for ever by dying and rising, but they would only see it if they walked in the light they had. Faith often works that way: you trust what you can see of Christ now, and understanding grows as you follow. Waiting to have everything solved first is itself a choice, and the light does not wait.

parallels.desc: his offspring shall endure forever

verseByVerse.quote: "While you have the light, believe in the light, that you may become sons of light." When Jesus had said these things, he departed and hid himself from them. Though he had done so many signs before them, they still did not believe in him,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sons of light. “Sons of light” is a Hebrew way of saying people who belong to the light and share its character (Luke 16:8; Ephesians 5:8; 1 Thessalonians 5:5). Light in this Gospel is the truth of God shining in Jesus, and those who belong to it stop hiding from it: they come to the light so that what they do may be seen as done in God (3:21). A child of light starts to love honesty, to hate the sin it once covered, and to want what God wants (Ephesians 5:8–9).

He hid himself from them. The light withdraws. This is the last thing Jesus does in front of a crowd in this Gospel; everything after it is private: the supper, the disciples, the arrest, the trials. John used the same phrase at the end of chapter 8 (8:59), and both times it follows a moment when the light was offered and refused.

They still did not believe. John now explains the great mystery of the Gospel: why did Israel, God’s own people, reject their Messiah? The signs were many and clear, from water into wine to a man four days dead walking out of a cave. John writes the verdict flatly, and it warns against assuming that unbelief is always a failure of evidence or presentation.

In the flow. Verse 37 begins John’s closing comment on the first half of his Gospel: he came to his own, and his own people did not receive him (1:11). The second half of the book, from chapter 13, turns to those who did receive him: a few men in a room with their Lord, about to learn what his death means.

Can a person put off believing for too long? Yes, and this verse is a solemn warning. The light was among them, and then it withdrew. Scripture urges, now is the favourable time; now is the day of salvation (2 Corinthians 6:2), because no one is promised tomorrow, and a heart that keeps refusing grows harder. But if you are concerned about your soul and want to come to Christ, that very desire shows the light has not left you. No one who comes to him is turned away (6:37). The danger is not for those who are anxious to come, but for those who are content to wait.

parallels.desc: walk as children of light

verseByVerse.quote: so that the word spoken by the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled: "Lord, who has believed what he heard from us, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?" Therefore they could not believe. For again Isaiah said,
verseByVerse.commentary:
That the word might be fulfilled. Their unbelief did not take God by surprise. John reaches for Isaiah twice to explain what he has just reported, and it matters which parts of Isaiah he takes.

Lord, who has believed what he heard from us, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed? From Isaiah 53:1, the opening line of the great Suffering Servant passage: the chapter about the man despised and rejected, wounded for our transgressions, led like a lamb to the slaughter. The prophet asks who has believed the message about the Servant, and the question has an answer built into it: almost nobody. The prophet who was given the fullest description of the cross in the Old Testament opens it by asking who will accept the report. And the answer, seven centuries later, is a rejected Messiah walking away from a crowd. So the unbelief is not a surprise, and it is not a defeat. It was written into the very passage that describes the whole work. “The arm of the Lord” is God’s power in salvation, revealed in Christ’s signs and in his cross.

Therefore they could not believe. Not merely did not, but could not. It is the hardest phrase in the chapter, and it should not be softened, but it should be read in order. Verse 37 says they did not believe though they had seen everything. Verse 39 says that at a certain point they could not. The inability follows the refusal; it does not come before it. That is the consistent biblical pattern. Pharaoh hardened his own heart through several plagues before the narrative says that God hardened it, though God had told Moses beforehand that he would (Exodus 4:21; 9:12). Romans 1 says three times that God gave them up, to what they had already chosen (Romans 1:24, 26, 28). The judgment is that a man is finally given what he has been insisting on. Isaiah gives the reason in the lines John quotes next: God had blinded their eyes and hardened their heart (Isaiah 6:10).

Does this mean God stops people who want to believe? No. Scripture never shows anyone truly seeking God and being turned away. Behind all human unbelief lies the fallen heart, which does not want God (3:19–20); and God in his justice may confirm a person in the refusal he has chosen. But he never turns away a sinner who seeks him. If you want Christ, that desire is itself evidence of God’s grace at work in you, not of his rejection. Come to him. The doctrine of hardening is a warning to the careless, not a threat to the seeking.

parallels.desc: who has believed what he has heard from us?

verseByVerse.quote: "He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, lest they see with their eyes, and understand with their heart, and turn, and I would heal them." Isaiah said these things because he saw his glory and spoke of him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He has blinded their eyes. From Isaiah 6:10, quoted freely. This passage is quoted in all four Gospels and in Acts (Matthew 13:14–15; Mark 4:12; Luke 8:10; Acts 28:26–27) to explain Israel’s unbelief.

Lest they turn. Hardening is God’s judgment on persistent unbelief (2 Thessalonians 2:11).

What it does not mean. It does not mean God is the author of sin or that they were innocent victims. They had seen and rejected the light (v. 37). Nor does it mean all Israel is hardened for ever: Paul says a partial hardening has come upon Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles comes in (Romans 11:25), and many Jews have believed and will believe.

How far does God’s hand reach in hardening? Some read hardening only as God giving people over to the unbelief they have already chosen, as with Pharaoh. Others, with Romans 9:17–24, see God’s sovereign purpose behind the hardening itself. Scripture holds both: God hardens, and those hardened are responsible, for they loved the glory that comes from man more than the glory that comes from God (v. 43). He never hardens a heart that is seeking him.

He saw his glory. Isaiah 6 is the great vision of the Lord on a throne, high and lifted up, with the seraphim crying, holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts (Isaiah 6:1–5), and John says that glory was Christ’s: the Lord whom Isaiah saw on the throne was the Son. Some take John to mean only that Isaiah foresaw Christ’s glory, but John has just quoted Isaiah 6, and the glory Isaiah saw there was the Lord’s on his throne. This is one of the clearest statements in the New Testament that Jesus is the Lord of the Old Testament, Yahweh himself, and John makes it almost in passing.

High and lifted up. Isaiah saw him high and lifted up (Isaiah 6:1); the same pair of words describes the Servant in Isaiah 52:13, at the start of the passage John has just quoted from; and lifted up is the phrase Jesus has used of himself three times in this Gospel, for the manner of his death. The throne Isaiah saw and the cross John is walking toward are described with the same language. The glory the seraphim could not look at is the glory of a man on a Roman cross outside a city wall, and this Gospel has been saying so since the prologue: we have seen his glory (1:14).

Has God then rejected the Jewish people? No. Paul answers that question directly: has God rejected his people? By no means! (Romans 11:1). There has always been a remnant chosen by grace, and Paul himself was one. Christians hold different views on how Romans 11:25–26 will be fulfilled: some expect a large turning of the Jewish people to Christ before his return, others read all Israel as the full number of the elect from Jews and Gentiles together. But all agree that God’s promises do not fail, that Jewish people are saved in the same way as everyone else, through faith in Jesus the Messiah, and that Christians owe them love, humility and the gospel, never contempt.

Could I be hardened? If you are worried that you might be, that very worry is a sign you are not. Hardened hearts are not anxious about God; they are indifferent. The warning is real, and it is for anyone who has heard the gospel many times and keeps saying not yet. But it is answered in the same way it always has been: turn to Christ today, while it is called today (Hebrews 3:13–15). He has never refused anyone who came.

For worship. When you sing holy, holy, holy, remember whose glory Isaiah saw. He cried woe is me before that throne, and a seraph flew with a burning coal from the altar, and his guilt was taken away (Isaiah 6:6–7). The cleansing Isaiah received at the altar was paid for, in the end, by the King himself, who became the sacrifice every altar pointed to, so that unclean lips like Isaiah’s and ours might be made fit to sing his praise.
verseByVerse.note: Isaiah saw the Lord’s glory in the temple; John says that glory was Christ’s.

parallels.desc: make the heart of this people dull
I saw the Lord, high and lifted up

verseByVerse.quote: Nevertheless, many even of the authorities believed in him, but for fear of the Pharisees they did not confess it, so that they would not be put out of the synagogue; for they loved the glory that comes from man more than the glory that comes from God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Many even of the authorities believed. John uses his full phrase, believed in him; by his own vocabulary these are not mere admirers. Nicodemus and Joseph of Arimathea were probably among these secret believers (19:38–39).

For fear of the Pharisees. Belief without confession. The threat was being put out of the synagogue, the same threat the parents of the blind man feared (9:22).

The glory that comes from man. “Glory” (doxa) here means honour, approval, reputation: Isaiah saw the glory of Christ enthroned; these men preferred the approval of the room. Jesus had made the same charge earlier: how can you believe, when you receive glory from one another and do not seek the glory that comes from the only God? (5:44). So this is not chiefly about cowardice but about whose approval a man is living for. They had arranged their lives around a kind of approval that Jesus was about to cost them.

Is this saving faith? Jesus said that whoever is ashamed of him, he will be ashamed of (Mark 8:38), and that confession with the mouth goes with true belief (Romans 10:9–10). Their faith is at best weak and immature, at worst not real. Joseph and Nicodemus later came out into the open.

Am I saved if I have kept my faith secret? This needs care, because there is a way of preaching these verses that produces despair in exactly the wrong people. Look at who John places in this category elsewhere. Nicodemus came at night, and the same book puts him at the cross with about seventy-five pounds of spices (19:39). Joseph of Arimathea was a disciple, but secretly, for fear of the Jews (19:38), and it was he who went to Pilate and asked for the body when the twelve had scattered. Both men belong to this verse’s category. Both came through. John records the failure and then records what became of them, which is his way of saying that a hidden faith is a dangerous condition, not a settled verdict. If you are hiding your faith, do not conclude you are lost. Conclude that you must come out, and ask Christ for the courage he gave those two men. Start with one person this week.

Naming the cost. More useful than resolving to be braver is to ask what specifically would be lost, and name it precisely: not people might think less of me, but the actual thing, the promotion, the friendship, the family meal, the standing in a particular room. Then ask what it is worth, and whose opinion is being bought with it.

In everyday life. Whose approval do you crave most? In Christ the Father has already welcomed you as his child, so you can afford to lose the room’s. Pick one place where you have kept quiet about Christ, and ask him for an opportunity to speak there.
verseByVerse.note: Nicodemus and Joseph of Arimathea were among these secret believers.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus cried out and said, "Whoever believes in me, believes not in me but in him who sent me. And whoever sees me sees him who sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus cried out. It is a shout, the verb used on the last day of the feast (7:37), much like the cry at the tomb (11:43). The position of these verses is unusual. He hid himself in verse 36; John gave his verdict in verses 37–43; and now, with no sign of a new scene, Jesus speaks again. These final verses (vv. 44–50) are probably a summary of Jesus’ public teaching, perhaps spoken earlier, placed here as his last word to the world.

Not in me but in him who sent me. Not that faith in Jesus is wrong, but that it does not stop with him: it reaches the Father. Faith in Jesus is not a dead end but a window.

Whoever sees me. Jesus is the perfect revelation of the Father (1:18; 14:9). There is no hidden God behind Jesus who is different from him. The one who wept at Lazarus’s grave, washed his disciples’ feet and died for his enemies is not a softer image of a harder God.

Do other religions worship the same God, just without Jesus? No, not according to Jesus. If to see him is to see the Father, then to reject him is to reject the Father; whoever does not honour the Son does not honour the Father who sent him (5:23). People of other faiths may truly know that God exists and that they are accountable to him (Romans 1:19–20), and they are to be treated with respect and love. But the God who is, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, is known and worshipped truly only through his Son (14:6). That is why we share the gospel with them.

In everyday life. When you wonder what God is like, how he feels about you, whether he can be trusted, do not guess: look at Jesus in the Gospels. That is the Father’s face.

verseByVerse.quote: "I have come into the world as light, so that whoever believes in me may not remain in darkness. If anyone hears my words and does not keep them, I do not judge him; for I did not come to judge the world but to save the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have come into the world as light. The prologue said it about him (1:9). And here, in the last thing he says in public, he says it once more, and adds what it is for.

May not remain in darkness. “Remain” assumes that everyone starts in darkness. Darkness here is not a mood. It is life without the knowledge of God: not seeing him truly, loving what he hates, and standing under his judgment without knowing it (3:19; Ephesians 4:18). Faith brings us out.

I did not come to judge the world. His first coming was for salvation; judgment will come at his second (5:22, 27). This is 3:17 again: whatever else is said about judgment, the purpose of his coming never changes.

So does Jesus judge or not? Both, in different senses. He did not come the first time to condemn; he came to save, and anyone who comes to him finds mercy. Yet his coming inevitably divides, because light exposes darkness (3:19–21; 9:39), and on the last day he will sit as judge of all (5:22, 27). The way the two fit is given at once (v. 48). He does not need to pronounce a new sentence on those who reject him; the word they refused will itself be the standard. The purpose of his coming is salvation. Judgment is the consequence of refusing it.

verseByVerse.quote: "The one who rejects me and does not receive my words has a judge; the word that I have spoken will judge him on the last day. For I have not spoken on my own authority, but the Father who sent me has himself given me a commandment — what to say and what to speak."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Has a judge. The phrase “the one who rejects me” means setting aside, disregarding, rather than arguing against. Nobody in John 12 has refuted Jesus. The council admitted the signs, the crowd itself hailed him as king, and the authorities in verse 42 actually believed. What the chapter describes is not defeat by argument but a decision to set the whole thing aside and get on with life. That is how most rejection of Christ happens: not a conclusion reached, but a subject dropped.

The word will judge him. His words themselves will be the evidence. The standard on the last day is a set of sentences spoken publicly, before crowds, written down, and available ever since in a great many languages. To hear the gospel is a great privilege and a great responsibility (Matthew 11:20–24; Hebrews 2:1–3). The gospel is never neutral once it has been heard. It arrives as an offer, and it stays as a standard.

Not on my own authority. His words are the Father’s words, which is why rejecting them is so serious. So to refuse his words is not to disagree with a Galilean rabbi. It is to have been handed, by the Father through the Son, a commandment whose content is eternal life, and to have put it down.

What about those who never heard Christ’s words? They will not be judged for rejecting a message they never received. God judges each person justly, by the light he was actually given, and every person has some light: the witness of creation and of conscience, enough to leave them without excuse (Romans 1:20; 2:14–16). But that light cannot save, because salvation comes only through conscious faith in Christ (Acts 4:12; Romans 10:13–14). Infants who die in infancy and are elect are saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when and where he pleases (the Westminster Confession 10.3; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 10.3). Grieving parents may entrust their little one to the Lord who took children in his arms (Mark 10:16), and to the Judge of all the earth, who always does right (Genesis 18:25). For everyone else, this is why the church sends missionaries: so that those who have never heard may hear the words that give life.

parallels.desc: I will put my words in his mouth

verseByVerse.quote: "And I know that his commandment is eternal life. What I say, therefore, I say as the Father has told me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
His commandment is eternal life. Not his commandment leads to eternal life, which is what we might expect: the commandment is life. The words are the thing itself, as he said in Capernaum when the crowd was leaving: the words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life (6:63). And the life they give is not mere endless existence. It is knowing the Father and the Son he sent (17:3), a life that begins the moment a person believes. So the public ministry ends where the prologue began: in him was life, and the life was the light of men (1:4).

As the Father has told me. Jesus’ last public words in John are complete obedience to the Father; from chapter 13 he is alone with the twelve.

Three years of speaking. He talked to anybody for three years: crowds who wanted bread, a woman at a well at noon, a teacher who came by night, men who picked up stones twice, a beggar the synagogue threw out. And the last thing he says to all of them, at the top of his voice, is that the message was never his own, and that its content is life.

How do I read Jesus’ words so that they give me life? Read them as the Father’s words to you, not as information about the past. Read slowly, a passage at a time, asking what it shows you of Christ and what it asks of you. Read with prayer, asking the Spirit who inspired them to open them to you (14:26). Read with others, in your church, where the word is preached and taught. And obey what you understand; the words of Christ give life to those who keep them, not to those who only admire them (8:51). Life does not come from the reading as a technique. It comes from the living Christ who speaks through what is read.

For worship. The last public word of the Son of God was a word about life, and he went from that street to give it at the cost of his own. Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life (6:68).

Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, even the King of Israel!”<sup>14</sup>And Jesus found a young donkey and sat on it, just as it is written,<sup>15</sup>“Fear not, daughter of Zion; behold, your king is coming, sitting on a donkey’s colt!”<sup>16</sup>His disciples did not understand these things at first, but when Jesus was glorified, then they remembered that these things had been written about him and had been done to him.<sup>17</sup>The crowd that had been with him when he called Lazarus out of the tomb and raised him from the dead continued to bear witness.<sup>18</sup>The reason why the crowd went to meet him was that they heard he had done this sign.<sup>19</sup>So the Pharisees said to one another, “You see that you are gaining nothing. Look, the world has gone after him.”<sup>20</sup>Now among those who went up to worship at the feast were some Greeks.<sup>21</sup>So these came to Philip, who was from Bethsaida in Galilee, and asked him, “Sir, we wish to see Jesus.”<sup>22</sup>Philip went and told Andrew; Andrew and Philip went and told Jesus.<sup>23</sup>And Jesus answered them, “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified.<sup>24</sup>Truly, truly, I say to you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.<sup>25</sup>Whoever loves his life loses it, and whoever hates his life in this world will keep it for eternal life.<sup>26</sup>If anyone serves me, he must follow me; and where I am, there will my servant be also. If anyone serves me, the Father will honor him.<sup>27</sup>“Now is my soul troubled. And what shall I say? ’Father, save me from this hour’? But for this purpose I have come to this hour.<sup>28</sup>Father, glorify your name.“ Then a voice came from heaven: ”I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again.”<sup>29</sup>The crowd that stood there and heard it said that it had thundered. Others said, “An angel has spoken to him.”<sup>30</sup>Jesus answered, “This voice has come for your sake, not mine.<sup>31</sup>Now is the judgment of this world; now will the ruler of this world be cast out.<sup>32</sup>And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.”<sup>33</sup>He said this to show by what kind of death he was going to die.<sup>34</sup>So the crowd answered him, “We have heard from the Law that the Christ remains forever. How can you say that the Son of Man must be lifted up? Who is this Son of Man?”<sup>35</sup>So Jesus said to them, “The light is among you for a little while longer. For again Isaiah said,<sup>40</sup>“He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, lest they see with their eyes, and understand with their heart, and turn, and I would heal them.”<sup>41</sup>Isaiah said these things because he saw his glory and spoke of him.<sup>42</sup>Nevertheless, many even of the authorities believed in him, but for fear of the Pharisees they did not confess it, so that they would not be put out of the synagogue;<sup>43</sup>for they loved the glory that comes from man more than the glory that comes from God.<sup>44</sup>And Jesus cried out and said, “Whoever believes in me, believes not in me but in him who sent me.<sup>45</sup>And whoever sees me sees him who sent me.<sup>46</sup>I have come into the world as light, so that whoever believes in me may not remain in darkness.<sup>47</sup>If anyone hears my words and does not keep them, I do not judge him; for I did not come to judge the world but to save the world.<sup>48</sup>The one who rejects me and does not receive my words has a judge; the word that I have spoken will judge him on the last day.<sup>49</sup>For I have not spoken on my own authority, but the Father who sent me has himself given me a commandment—what to say and what to speak.<sup>50</sup>And I know that his commandment is eternal life. What I say, therefore, I say as the Father has told me.”
12.overview:
Chapter 12 closes the first half of John’s Gospel, the book of signs, and opens the way to the cross. At Bethany Mary anoints Jesus for his burial; the next day crowds hail him as King of Israel as he rides into Jerusalem on a young donkey.

When some Greeks ask to see him, Jesus announces that his hour has come: like a grain of wheat he must die to bear much fruit, and lifted up from the earth he will draw all people to himself. John explains from Isaiah why so many did not believe, and Jesus makes his last public appeal.

13.title: The Foot Washing and the New Commandment

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–20 — The Foot Washing: Love to the End
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At supper, knowing his hour has come and that all things are in his hands, Jesus washes the disciples’ feet. Peter’s protests draw out what the washing means: no one has a share in Christ unless he cleanses him, and the one already bathed needs only his feet washed. Then Jesus explains it as an example for them to follow, and warns that one at his table will turn against him.
verseByVerse.theology: The footwashing is both a moral example (do as I have done) and a picture of the cleansing only Christ gives (if I do not wash you, you have no share with me). The one already bathed needs only his feet washed: the believer is justified once for all, and needs the daily cleansing of confession, not to be justified again.
verseByVerse.examples: Jesus does not wash feet because he has forgotten who he is; he washes feet because he knows exactly who he is (vv. 3–4, 13). Those anxious about their position never serve freely; those who know they are secure in the Father’s love can take the towel without self-protection.

verseByVerse.quote: Now before the Feast of the Passover, when Jesus knew that his hour had come to depart out of this world to the Father, having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end. During supper, when the devil had already put it into the heart of Judas Iscariot, Simon's son, to betray him,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. The second half of John’s Gospel begins here. John’s account of the last evening fills five chapters (13–17), far more than the other Gospels give it. And at the centre of the evening John sets something the other Gospels leave out: the Lord of glory on the floor with a towel round his waist, and the love that put him there.

The setting. It is Thursday evening in an upper room in Jerusalem, at Passover, and before the sun sets again the true Passover Lamb will be dead and buried. Everything John records from here to the end of chapter 17 is said in a few hours, to men who will all run away before morning.

Before the Feast. John says this happened before the Feast, later says the authorities avoided the governor’s headquarters so that they might eat the Passover (18:28), and calls the day of the crucifixion the day of Preparation of the Passover (19:14). Matthew, Mark and Luke present the Last Supper plainly as the Passover meal itself.

Is there a contradiction about the date? The tension is real, but it is smaller than it looks, and most of it dissolves in the wording. The word rendered Preparation is the ordinary Greek term for Friday; it is still the word for Friday in Greek today. So the day of Preparation of the Passover most naturally means the Friday of Passover week, not the day before the meal. And Passover was used loosely for the whole seven-day festival, so to eat the Passover at 18:28 can easily mean the festival meals that followed. Read that way, John and the others agree: the supper was the Passover meal, and Jesus was crucified on the Friday of the feast. A second solution has long been offered, that different groups reckoned the feast a day apart.
