The mother teaching her children the faith, the friend who invites a colleague to church, the believer who gives so a missionary can go, the church member who prays for the lost by name: all of these share in the work of bringing people from death to life. The power is not in you but in the Spirit Christ sends, and in the word. You are not asked to be impressive; you are asked to be a faithful witness.
verseByVerse.note: “Greater works” refers to the worldwide spread of the gospel after the Spirit came.

verseByVerse.quote: "Whatever you ask in my name, this I will do, that the Father may be glorified in the Son. If you ask me anything in my name, I will do it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whatever you ask. This is one of the most quietly resented promises in the New Testament, because someone reading it prayed for something enormous and did not get it. Read as a blank cheque, the sentence is falsified by the life of every Christian who has ever lived, including the men it was spoken to. Paul asked three times for the thorn to be taken away and was refused (2 Corinthians 12:8–9). Jesus himself asked that, if it were possible, the cup might pass, and drank it. So the promise means something other than the flat reading, and the qualification is in the middle of the sentence.

In my name. In the ancient world a person’s name stood for his character and authority; to act in someone’s name was to act as his representative, within his commission. An ambassador can commit his government to anything the government would want and nothing it would not. So praying in Jesus’ name means praying as his representatives, according to his will and for his glory (1 John 5:14). It is not a magic formula; it is to come to the Father on the basis of who Jesus is and what he has done, and to ask what he would ask. We do not approach the throne on our own credit, but on his, and he has never been refused.

That the Father may be glorified. The purpose of prayer stands openly in the sentence as its boundary. The promise is unlimited within it and does not exist outside it.

Ask me. The words mean prayer to Jesus himself, as well as to the Father. Some manuscripts omit me (so the KJV). If it stands, it is remarkable: prayer directed to Jesus, said by Jesus, at a table with Jews who prayed only to God. Prayer to Christ is right, because he is God (Acts 7:59).

What it does not mean. Underneath the blank-cheque reading lies an old idol: a god who signs whatever we write. Prayer in Jesus’ name hands our plans back to a Father wiser than we are, and that is a relief, not a loss.

What about the good prayer that was refused? Something must be said to the person for whom all that is cold comfort, because the honest difficulty is not the greedy prayer. It is the prayer that was plainly good, healing for a child, a marriage saved, a friend brought to faith, that was refused, when the sufferer knows perfectly well it was the kind of thing the Father is glorified by. Two things are true. The first is that Scripture never explains each case. There is no verse that accounts for why one good prayer is answered and another is not, and any commentary that produces a formula is selling something. The second is that the New Testament everywhere assumes the refusals are not indifference. The same Gospel has a man deliberately waiting two days while his friend died (11:6), and the family got more than they asked for and nothing like what they wanted at the time. A refused prayer is heard by a Father who is working a greater good than we can see (Romans 8:28), and who will one day show us why.

In everyday life. Take one thing you are praying for and ask whether Jesus would ask for it and how it would glorify the Father. The prayer may change shape, or you may find you can pray it with new boldness. Then pray it in Jesus’ name, and leave the answer with him.
verseByVerse.note: Praying “in my name” means praying as his representatives, according to his will.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–31 — The Promise of the Spirit and the Peace of Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Love for Jesus shows itself in keeping his word, and he will not leave his people orphaned: the Spirit of truth will be with them for ever, and through him Jesus and the Father come and make their home with them. The Spirit will remind them of all he said. He leaves them his peace and rises to go out and meet the ruler of this world, who has no claim on him.
verseByVerse.theology: The Helper (*paraklētos*, one called alongside) is described four ways in the farewell discourse: the Spirit of truth (14:17), who teaches and reminds (14:26), who bears witness about Jesus (15:26), and who convicts the world (16:8). Each is part of one mission: to apply what Jesus accomplished. He brings no new revelation beyond Jesus, but makes what Jesus said and did present to each generation.
verseByVerse.examples: Not as the world gives. Jesus’ peace, unlike the world’s, holds in the middle of trouble, because it is the wholeness of being right with God and secure in his love. The disciples will need it before the night is over.

verseByVerse.quote: "If you love me, you will keep my commandments. And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Helper, to be with you forever,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you love me, you will keep my commandments. This sets love and obedience in an order worth getting right, because reversed it becomes a machine for producing anxiety. It is a plain future, a statement about what love does, not a test love must pass. Love shows itself in obedience (vv. 21, 23; 1 John 5:3). Keep means guard, treasure, obey. The Spirit who is given writes the law on the heart, creating the desire to obey that the law alone could not create.

Another Helper. The word has no good English equivalent: Helper, Comforter, Advocate, Counsellor, Paraclete (the ESV margin gives Advocate or Counselor). Paraklētos means, literally, one called alongside. In ordinary Greek it was a legal term: the friend you brought to court with you, not so much a hired advocate as somebody of standing who stood at your side and spoke for you. Comforter has weakened badly; it once carried the sense of strengthening (Latin fortis, strong).

Another. The word is allon: another, and the context makes it another of the same kind. Jesus has been their Helper; the Spirit will be another like him. John calls Jesus himself a paraklētos (1 John 2:1): you are losing me, and you are getting one exactly like me. This also shows that the Spirit is a person, not a force: Jesus would not compare himself to a power. And the Trinity is here: the Son asks, the Father gives, the Spirit comes, the whole Trinity bending toward eleven frightened men, and toward every believer since.

To be with you forever. They have had Jesus in the flesh for a few short years and are losing him tonight. What is coming has no term on it at all.

What if I do not feel that I love Jesus enough to obey him? Then start where the love starts: not with your love for him, but his for you. We love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19). Love for Christ grows as you look at what he has done, so read the Gospels, sit at the cross, and remember your forgiveness. Then obey in the small thing in front of you, even without strong feeling. Obedience is often how love is learned, as a child learns love for a parent partly by trusting and doing what he says. And the Helper is given precisely because you cannot do this alone. Ask him for love, and he gives it (Romans 5:5).
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “Helper” can also be rendered “Advocate” or “Counselor.” “Another” implies one like Jesus himself.

parallels.desc: an advocate with the Father

verseByVerse.quote: "even the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive, because it neither sees him nor knows him. You know him, for he dwells with you and will be in you. I will not leave you as orphans; I will come to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit of truth. He is the Spirit who brings and teaches the truth, and the truth is Christ (15:26; 16:13). The unbelieving world, which neither sees him nor knows him, has no capacity to receive him (1 Corinthians 2:14), because spiritual sight requires the new birth he creates.

With you and in you. Two prepositions mark the change of an age: with you now, in the person of Jesus; in you after Pentecost. The Spirit had always been at work: he came upon judges and prophets and kings, and rested on Jesus without measure. But in the old covenant he came and went, and came on particular people for particular tasks. What is promised here is permanent residence in ordinary believers, which is precisely what Ezekiel and Joel had said would mark the last days (Ezekiel 36:27; Joel 2:28–29).

Not as orphans. Orphans (orphanous) means bereaved children, and disciples whose teacher had died were sometimes called orphans. So he is naming exactly what they are about to be, and denying it. By tomorrow evening they will look like a school whose master has been executed; he tells them in advance that the appearance will be false.

I will come to you. Not I will send help, but I will come: in the resurrection appearances (v. 19), and by the Spirit, who brings Christ’s own presence (v. 23). The coming of the Spirit is the coming of Christ himself to his people, by another route.

For the one who has lost the person who explained things. There is a particular loneliness that belongs to people who have lost the one who made the world make sense: a parent, a mentor, a pastor. This verse was spoken to eleven men about to be exactly that, by the man they were about to lose, and what he promised was not a replacement but his own return.

How do I know the Spirit is in me? Not chiefly by unusual feelings, but by what he does: he makes you confess Jesus as Lord, call God Father, love Christ and his people, and hate your sin; and anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him (Romans 8:9). (See Acts 2:33 for the fuller answer.)
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “and is in you.”

verseByVerse.quote: "Yet a little while and the world will see me no more, but you will see me. Because I live, you also will live. In that day you will know that I am in my Father, and you in me, and I in you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The world will see me no more. After his death the world will not see him again until he returns; the disciples will see him in the resurrection appearances, and by faith.

Because I live. The ground is stated as a fact, and the consequence follows from it and not from anything about the disciples. I live is present tense: he is the living one, even facing death. His resurrection life is the source and guarantee of theirs, both now in the new birth and at the last in the resurrection of their bodies.

Where assurance rests. That is where a Christian’s assurance finally rests. The question is not whether my faith is strong enough to survive, or whether my grip will hold. It is whether he is alive. If the answer to that is yes, the rest follows by the logic of this verse, and the strength of my grip is not what holds me.

In that day. That day is the day of resurrection and Pentecost. Three circles of union run from the life of God outward: the Father and the Son, the believer in the Son, the Son in the believer. We are drawn into the fellowship of the Trinity (17:21–23). And it will be known only in that day, not by argument, when the Spirit comes and the whole evening becomes clear.

What does it mean to be in Christ? It means that by faith, through the Spirit, you are joined to him so closely that what is true of him becomes true of you. His death counts as your death to sin, his righteousness as your righteousness, his life as your life, his Father as your Father (Romans 6:4–11; 2 Corinthians 5:21). It is not a feeling, though it brings feelings; it is a fact God has made. Every blessing of salvation comes to you in him (Ephesians 1:3). And because it is his work, it does not come undone. The branch does not hold the vine; the vine holds the branch.

For worship. He said I live on the night before he died, and it was true even then. Glory to the living one, who died and is alive for evermore and holds the keys of Death and Hades (Revelation 1:18), so that the grave of every believer is a locked room whose key is in the Saviour’s hand.

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever has my commandments and keeps them, he it is who loves me. And he who loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him." Judas (not Iscariot) said to him, "Lord, how is it that you will manifest yourself to us, and not to the world?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Has my commandments and keeps them. To have his commandments is to know them; to keep them is to do them. Love for Christ is not sentiment but allegiance expressed in the pattern of a life.

Loved by my Father. The chain of love here does not run the way religion expects. Read carelessly it is a transaction. It cannot be, because the same Gospel has already said the Father loved the world first (3:16), and John’s letter will make it explicit: we love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19). What is described is not the beginning of the Father’s love but its answering movement. Somebody who has come to love Christ finds himself inside a love that was there before he arrived, and now comes toward him in a particular and personal way.

Manifest myself. Manifest (emphanisō) means make visible, show plainly. It is a promise of something experienced rather than merely believed, and it is the reason Judas asks his question.

Judas (not Iscariot). This Judas is Judas the son of James, probably the Thaddaeus of Matthew and Mark’s lists (Luke 6:16; Matthew 10:3). By the time John writes, the name is a byword for treachery, and his parenthesis is a small mercy toward a man who did nothing wrong and had his name ruined by somebody else.

Lord, how is it that you will manifest yourself to us, and not to the world? He is not being slow. He expects the Messiah to show himself publicly to the world. If the Messiah is going to make himself plainly visible, surely that is a public event; the whole point of the messianic hope was a disclosure the nations could not miss. Why only to them?

Why does Jesus seem more real to some Christians than to me? Part of the answer is in this verse: he shows himself to those who love him and keep his word. Closeness to Christ grows along the path of obedience and his word, not by waiting for a special experience. Where there is unconfessed sin, neglect of Scripture, or a divided heart, the sense of his presence often fades. But not every dry season is caused by sin; godly believers have walked through long stretches of darkness while trusting him (Isaiah 50:10). Keep reading, keep praying, keep obeying, and keep company with his people. He has promised to make himself known, and he keeps his promises.
verseByVerse.note: This Judas is Judas the son of James, probably the Thaddaeus of Matthew and Mark.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered him, "If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him. Whoever does not love me does not keep my words. And the word that you hear is not mine but the Father's who sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
If anyone loves me. Jesus answers Judas indirectly, and the condition is repeated for the third time in this chapter. Whatever else this indwelling is, it is not available to mere admiration.

Make our home with him. One word turns the whole chapter round, and it is invisible in English. Home is monē, the singular of the rooms of verse 2. So the chapter has two dwelling places pointing in opposite directions: Jesus goes to prepare a dwelling for us in the Father’s house, and meanwhile the Father and the Son come to make their dwelling in us. The God whom heaven cannot contain has chosen to make his home in sinners who love his Son. One day we will go to live with him; already he has come to live with us.

The answer to Judas. How will he manifest himself to us and not to the world? By moving in. The disclosure is not a display the nations could photograph; it is the Father and the Son taking up residence in a person, which is a thing only that person and God can know.

We. Father and Son together, by the Spirit: in the same discourse the Spirit is given to be with them for ever (v. 16) and to be in them (v. 17), so all three are described in one chapter as taking up residence in ordinary people. The whole Trinity dwells in the believer. Every believer is a temple of God (1 Corinthians 3:16; 6:19). The holy God now lives in sinners he has cleansed: both the deepest comfort and the most searching call to holiness (2 Corinthians 6:16–7:1).

The dwelling moves into people. God dwelt in a tent, then a temple, from which the glory departed (Ezekiel 10); then the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (1:14). Now the dwelling moves again, into people.

Not mine but the Father’s. The other side. To reject Christ’s word is to reject the Father’s. The stakes of hearing the gospel are as high as its source.

If God lives in me, why do I still sin so much? Because the house is being renovated while he lives in it. God does not wait for a believer to be perfect before he moves in; he moves in to make him holy. His presence is the reason you now hate your sin and fight it, which you did not before. Your body is his temple (1 Corinthians 6:19), so sin is now a grief to him (Ephesians 4:30), and that should make you serious. But it is not a reason to doubt that he dwells in you. He has not moved in to move out again: the work he began in you he will finish (Philippians 1:6).

In everyday life. Ask what in your life you would be ashamed for the Father and the Son to see: the screen, the grudge, the habit. Clear one room today, not to earn his presence but because he is already there.

parallels.desc: my dwelling place shall be with them

verseByVerse.quote: "These things I have spoken to you while I am still with you. But the Helper, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things and bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
While I am still with you. They have heard much they do not yet understand. But the Helper, the Holy Spirit, will be sent by the Father in the Son’s name: as the Son’s representative, to continue his work.

Teach and remind. The second verb is the more remarkable: a promise about memory, made to men who had misunderstood much of what they were told. As far as we know, nothing had been written down; the teaching of Jesus existed in the memories of eleven frightened men who would have to hand it on.

The promise that grounds the New Testament. The promise is especially to the apostles, and it is the basis of the New Testament: the Gospels rest on the memory of men whom the Spirit helped to remember, by his work of inspiration (2 Peter 1:21), and the letters come from men whom he taught. John, writing decades later, reproduces long discourses, exact phrases, the fragrance of the ointment, the number of the water jars. Detail alone does not prove an eyewitness, and some scholars take the discourses as the church’s later reflection; John’s own claim is that the Spirit reminded rather than invented, and the church received his Gospel as the testimony of one who was there (21:24).

Where Christians differ: the Spirit’s teaching today. Some claim the Spirit gives new revelation today, beyond Scripture. Most who speak of such words do not mean to add to the Bible, and many test what they hear by it; the real question is whether such words carry God’s authority. This commentary’s view: the promise is first to the apostles, and was fulfilled in the New Testament, which is complete and sufficient (Jude 3; 2 Timothy 3:16–17). The Spirit still teaches every believer, not by new revelation, but by illuminating the Scripture he inspired. The canon is closed; the Spirit opens our eyes to it.

The boundary. The Spirit does not bring new material. Everything in the two verbs is tethered to what Jesus said: teaching all things, and reminding of all that I have said to you. Every claim to fresh revelation that adds to or contradicts these books has this verse against it. The Spirit is not a source of information beyond Christ, nor is he an idea; his work is to make what Christ said land in a person who has read it many times without it moving anything.

Does the Spirit still guide me personally? Yes, but through his word, not beside it. He gives wisdom as you study Scripture, pray and take counsel (James 1:5); he brings to mind what you have read when you need it; he convicts, comforts and directs your heart along the lines Scripture has drawn. What you should not do is treat impressions, dreams or inner nudges as new words from God that bind you or others. Test every impression by Scripture, and where Scripture leaves a choice open, choose wisely and in faith, trusting God’s providence. A feeling may be from the Spirit, but only the Bible is certainly from him.

verseByVerse.quote: "Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you. Not as the world gives do I give to you. Let not your hearts be troubled, neither let them be afraid. You heard me say to you, 'I am going away, and I will come to you.' If you loved me, you would have rejoiced, because I am going to the Father, for the Father is greater than I."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you. Peace (shalom) was how a Jew said goodbye at a door, and still is. And leave is what a man does in a will. He is dying tomorrow and disposing of his estate, and this is what is in it. His peace is wholeness, right relationship with God, the calm that comes from reconciliation (Romans 5:1; Philippians 4:7), bought at the cross by the one who bequeaths it. No thief can steal it and no storm can reach it, because it was purchased by his blood and kept in the Father’s hands.

Not as the world gives. The world’s peace is the absence of trouble, sought in control: money, health, the children settled, our reputation safe. It lasts only as long as the circumstances do, which is why it leaves us anxious even while we have it. He is distinguishing a bequest from a pleasantry. What he bequeaths is not a quiet life. Within hours the men receiving it will scatter into the dark. It means that the thing which makes a person whole, being right with God, has been settled elsewhere and cannot be reached by circumstances. Christ’s peace holds in the middle of trouble (16:33).

Neither let them be afraid. The chapter returns to its start. He has been talking for a whole chapter and the fear is still in the room, so he says it again, and adds the word for what they are actually feeling.

You would have rejoiced. His going is gain for him: return to glory.

For the Father is greater than I. How can this be, if the Son is equal with God (5:18; 10:30)? Not greater in nature or being, but greater in position: in his incarnation and earthly mission, the Son took the role of a servant, and the Father sent him. Now he returns to the glory he had with the Father (17:5). In the work of salvation he willingly came as the one the Father sent and obeyed him, even to death (5:19, 30; Philippians 2:6–8). That submission belongs to his mission, not to any inferiority of nature, and it shows that order and equality are not rivals.

Where Christians differ. Arians in the fourth century (followers of Arius, who taught that the Son was the first and highest created being), and Jehovah’s Witnesses today, cite this verse to show that the Son is a lesser being. This commentary’s view: the same Gospel calls him God (1:1; 20:28). This verse speaks of his incarnate state, as the one sent; greater refers to role and position, not essence. A son can be equal to his father in nature and still honour his father as the head of the house. Athanasius and the Nicene Creed held both truths together.

Four answers to the Arian reading. This was an anchor text of Arius, and it is the verse a Jehovah’s Witness is most likely to open at your door. First, look at what the sentence is for: a reason he gives his friends to be glad. Nobody offers a confession of inferiority as consolation. Second, the word is greater, not better: the language of position, as a king is greater than his son without being more human. Third, and decisively, the same book tells us the Word was God (1:1), that Jesus said I and the Father are one (10:30) and before Abraham was, I am (8:58), and closes with Thomas saying to him, my Lord and my God, uncorrected (20:28). Fourth, he is hours from the cross, having taken the form of a servant though he was in the form of God (Philippians 2:6–7); a man on his way to be crucified saying the Father is greater is telling you where he has placed himself, not what he is: greater in office, equal in nature. And there is tenderness in it: where he is going is better, and if they loved him they would be glad for him.

How do I keep Christ’s peace when life is falling apart? By remembering where it is kept. His peace does not live in your circumstances, so circumstances cannot take it; it lives in your standing with God, which he has settled by his blood. When fear rises, bring it to him in prayer with thanksgiving, and the peace of God will guard your heart (Philippians 4:6–7). Fill your mind with what is true. Keep company with believers. And do not mistake feeling shaken for having lost his peace: Jesus himself was troubled in spirit while perfectly at peace with the Father. The storm may be loud; the anchor still holds.
verseByVerse.note: “Peace” (shalom) was the everyday greeting and farewell. “The Father is greater” speaks of the Son in his humble human state, not a lesser divine nature.

parallels.desc: the LORD give you peace

verseByVerse.quote: "And now I have told you before it takes place, so that when it does take place you may believe. I will no longer talk much with you, for the ruler of this world is coming. He has no claim on me,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before it takes place. He did the same with the betrayal (13:19): he foretells the event so that, when it comes, it confirms their faith instead of destroying it. The disciples will endure the passion with greater faith because they remember these words.

The ruler of this world is coming. Satan comes through Judas and the soldiers (13:27; 18:3), through the temple police and the cohort with lanterns.

He has no claim on me. Literally, in me he has nothing. The enemy will search this man and find nothing belonging to him: no handhold, no debt, no compromise. That is the claim of sinlessness stated in its most practical form, and it is what makes the next three days work.

The sting with nothing to inject. Everyone else who has ever died had something in them that death could rightly claim. Hebrews describes the devil as the one who has the power of death (Hebrews 2:14), and Paul puts the mechanism plainly: the sting of death is sin (1 Corinthians 15:56). On Jesus he has no claim. So Jesus does not die because Satan has power over him, but freely, for love of the Father. When they come for him in the garden, they are arresting a man over whom they have no rights whatever, and he goes anyway. The spotless Lamb walked into the enemy’s hour with nothing in him for the enemy to seize, and laid down his life of his own accord.

Does the devil have a claim on me? If you are in Christ, no. His accusations are real, and some of them are true, but they have no legal force, because Christ has paid the debt in full and cancelled the record that stood against you, nailing it to the cross (Colossians 2:14). Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies (Romans 8:33). When the accuser reminds you of your sins, agree that they were real, and then point him to the cross where they were punished. He has nothing in Christ, and you are in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "but I do as the Father has commanded me, so that the world may know that I love the Father. Rise, let us go from here."
verseByVerse.commentary:
As the Father has commanded me. The voluntary obedience of the Son is the world’s lesson in what love for the Father looks like.

That I love the Father. The only place in the Gospels where Jesus says in so many words that he loves the Father, and it is a startling reason to give for a crucifixion. The cross is a ransom, a substitution, a victory, and here he names it as a demonstration of his love for his Father, put on where the world can see it. The love between the Father and the Son, from all eternity, was displayed before the world on a Roman gallows.

Rise, let us go from here. There is a real puzzle here, better faced than ignored: three more chapters of discourse follow before anybody actually leaves. Chapter 18:1 says that when Jesus had spoken these words, he went out with his disciples across the brook Kidron. Some think they left here, with chapters 15–17 spoken on the way to the garden, perhaps passing vines (15:1); others that they rose but lingered, as people do about to part. Many scholars see a seam where the discourse once ended; that would not make the words less his, and the author left them.

Not the words of a victim. He is the one who ends the meal, opens the door, and sets off toward the garden where he knows Judas will bring the soldiers, because he told him to go and do it quickly. Nobody fetches him from the room; he goes out to meet them, in love, not under compulsion.

Why did Jesus have to obey the Father, if he is equal with him? Because in the plan of salvation the Son freely took the place of the servant, as the second Adam who would obey where the first disobeyed (Romans 5:19). His obedience is not the obedience of an inferior being but the willing obedience of a Son who shares the Father’s will and delights in it. And it was for us: his perfect obedience in life and death is counted to everyone who trusts him. When you obey God, you are not earning his favour; you are walking in the steps of the Son whose obedience has already won it for you.
verseByVerse.note: Some think they left the upper room here, with chapters 15–17 spoken on the way; others that they rose but stayed.

If it were not so, would I have told you that I go to prepare a place for you?<sup>3</sup>And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and will take you to myself, that where I am you may be also.<sup>4</sup>And you know the way to where I am going.”<sup>5</sup>Thomas said to him, “Lord, we do not know where you are going. How can we know the way?”<sup>6</sup>Jesus said to him, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.<sup>7</sup>If you had known me, you would have known my Father also. From now on you do know him and have seen him.”<sup>8</sup>Philip said to him, “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us.”<sup>9</sup>Jesus said to him, “Have I been with you so long, and you still do not know me, Philip? Whoever has seen me has seen the Father. How can you say, ’Show us the Father’?<sup>10</sup>Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me? The words that I say to you I do not speak on my own authority, but the Father who dwells in me does his works.<sup>11</sup>Believe me that I am in the Father and the Father is in me, or else believe on account of the works themselves.<sup>12</sup>“Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do; and greater works than these will he do, because I am going to the Father.<sup>13</sup>Whatever you ask in my name, this I will do, that the Father may be glorified in the Son.<sup>14</sup>If you ask me anything in my name, I will do it.<sup>15</sup>“If you love me, you will keep my commandments.<sup>16</sup>And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Helper, to be with you forever,<sup>17</sup>even the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive, because it neither sees him nor knows him. You know him, for he dwells with you and will be in you.<sup>18</sup>“I will not leave you as orphans; I will come to you.<sup>19</sup>Yet a little while and the world will see me no more, but you will see me. Because I live, you also will live.<sup>20</sup>In that day you will know that I am in my Father, and you in me, and I in you.<sup>21</sup>Whoever has my commandments and keeps them, he it is who loves me. And he who loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him.”<sup>22</sup>Judas (not Iscariot) said to him, “Lord, how is it that you will manifest yourself to us, and not to the world?”<sup>23</sup>Jesus answered him, “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him.<sup>24</sup>Whoever does not love me does not keep my words. And the word that you hear is not mine but the Father’s who sent me.<sup>25</sup>“These things I have spoken to you while I am still with you.<sup>26</sup>But the Helper, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things and bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you.<sup>27</sup>Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you. Not as the world gives do I give to you. Let not your hearts be troubled, neither let them be afraid.<sup>28</sup>You heard me say to you, ’I am going away, and I will come to you.’ If you loved me, you would have rejoiced, because I am going to the Father, for the Father is greater than I.<sup>29</sup>And now I have told you before it takes place, so that when it does take place you may believe.<sup>30</sup>I will no longer talk much with you, for the ruler of this world is coming. He has no claim on me,<sup>31</sup>but I do as the Father has commanded me, so that the world may know that I love the Father. Rise, let us go from here.
14.overview:
Jesus has just told his friends that he is leaving, that one of them will betray him and that Peter will deny him. Into their fear he says: “Let not your hearts be troubled.” He is going to prepare a place for them in his Father’s house and will come again for them. Thomas’s question draws out that he is himself the way to the Father, and Philip’s that whoever has seen him has seen the Father.

The second half promises the Holy Spirit as “another Helper”, through whom Jesus himself comes to them, and in whom the Father and the Son make their home with those who love him. He leaves them his peace, and goes out to the cross so that the world may know that he loves the Father. The Trinity is not argued here but lived: Father, Son and Spirit all make their home with the believer.

15.title: The True Vine

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–17 — Abide in Me: The Vine and the Branches
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus is the true vine and his Father the vinedresser, who removes fruitless branches and prunes fruitful ones. The disciples must stay joined to him, his words in them, and so live in his love, share his joy, and love one another. He calls them friends, chosen and appointed to bear fruit that lasts.
verseByVerse.theology: Jesus is the vine Israel was always meant to be: the true Israel, the faithful Son, who bears fruit that lasts. A branch does not manufacture fruit; it bears what the life of the vine produces in it.
verseByVerse.examples: You did not choose me, but I chose you (v. 16). Their following is traced back to his choosing, which does not make them passive: they are appointed to go and bear fruit. But the initiative and the guarantee of their fruitfulness rest with the one who chose them.

verseByVerse.quote: "I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinedresser. Every branch in me that does not bear fruit he takes away, and every branch that does bear fruit he prunes, that it may bear more fruit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. John 15 teaches what life in Christ looks like after he has gone. First, the vine and the branches: union with Christ, from which all fruit flows (vv. 1–17). Then the world’s hatred, which his people must expect (vv. 18–27). Underneath all of it is the vine himself, the true Israel, through whom the life of God flows into ordinary people and makes them fruitful.

The setting. Jesus has just said, Rise, let us go from here (14:31), so these words may be spoken as they leave or on the walk toward the Kidron valley, in the last hours before his arrest.

I am the true vine. The seventh and last of the great I am sayings in John. The force of true lands only once you know what the vine had always meant: a familiar picture of Israel, planted by God but fruitless (Psalm 80:8–16; Isaiah 5:1–7; Jeremiah 2:21; Ezekiel 15; Hosea 10:1). In Isaiah’s song the vineyard yielded wild grapes (Isaiah 5:2). So when a Jew heard vine, he heard a story that had gone wrong: a people planted with every advantage who produced nothing worth picking.

True, not derivative. The word alēthinē does not mean truthful. Here it means real as against derivative: the genuine article of which the others were copies, the same word John used of the true light (1:9) and the true bread (6:32). Everything that vine was meant to be and never was, Jesus is: the real Israel, the faithful Son, who bears the fruit Israel did not. So a place among God’s people no longer comes by birth, nation or ceremony, but by being united to Jesus through faith, so that a Gentile who trusts him is as much a branch as any son of Abraham (Galatians 3:29).

The golden vine. They may even have been able to see one. Josephus describes a vine of gold above the entrance to the temple sanctuary, with clusters as tall as a man, and the Mishnah adds that worshippers gave golden leaves and grapes to hang on it as offerings. It cannot be proved that they passed it, and it does not need to be; but a man saying I am the true vine under a golden one worth a fortune would not have needed to explain himself.

My Father is the vinedresser. Vinedresser (geōrgos) means farmer, gardener. The Father tends the vine. Nothing happens to the branches by accident; every cut is made by the Father’s hand.

He takes away. In context, Judas is the clearest example: outwardly attached to Christ, a disciple, but never truly united to him by faith. Some take takes away (airei) as lifts up, as trailing branches are lifted off the ground, but it is probably wrong: verse 6 describes the same kind of branch being thrown out, withering, gathered and burned, which is not what happens to a branch that has been tied up.

Can a believer be cut off? The branch taken away is one that bears no fruit at all, and v. 6 shows what becomes of it. It was attached to the vine outwardly, but never drew life from it; it is a professing, not a living, branch (compare 1 John 2:19). If you are anxious that this describes you, the anxiety is itself a sign of life: a branch with no sap in it does not care whether it bears fruit.

He prunes. Pruning hurts, but it makes a vine more fruitful. The Father uses trials, discipline and his word to cut away what hinders fruit (Hebrews 12:5–11). This second knife falls on the healthy branch; it is not punishment but cultivation. God sometimes cuts away what is good to produce what is better, and removes what is comfortable to make room for what is fruitful. No cut is careless, no season is wasted, and no living branch is ever thrown away.

How do I know whether I am being pruned or punished? If you belong to Christ, the Father’s knife on your life is never punishment in the sense of paying for your sins, because Christ has borne that punishment in full (Romans 8:1). What you experience is a Father’s discipline, which is always for your good, that you may share his holiness (Hebrews 12:10). Sometimes he removes a sin; sometimes he removes a comfort, a plan, a reputation, or even a good thing that had become too large in your heart. You may not know the precise reason for each cut. You can know the purpose: more fruit, more likeness to Christ, more joy in him. Ask him what he is teaching you, and trust the hand that holds the knife.
verseByVerse.note: The vine was a familiar picture of Israel, planted by God but often fruitless; Jesus is the true vine. This is the seventh of his “I am” sayings in John. Vinedressers cut away dead wood and pruned living branches hard.

parallels.desc: a vine brought out of Egypt
the vineyard that yielded wild grapes
discipline yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness

verseByVerse.quote: "Already you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you. Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit by itself, unless it abides in the vine, neither can you, unless you abide in me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Already you are clean. The eleven have been cleansed by receiving his word in faith (13:10); Judas has gone. And there is wordplay between verses 2 and 3 that no English version can carry: he prunes, kathairei; you are clean, katharoi. Same root: the pruning is not primarily about productivity but cleansing.

The knife is the word. That locates the pruning somewhere unexpected: not only in circumstances, though God certainly uses those, but in the word landing on a person and taking something off him (Hebrews 4:12).

Abide in me. Now the command, and the keyword of the chapter: abide (menō), remain, stay, live in. It is both a command and a promise: abide in me is the command, and I in you is the promise that Christ lives in the one who stays.

What abide means. It is not a mystical exercise. Menō is the ordinary word for staying: the disciples asked where he was staying and then stayed with him (1:38–39); he stayed two days in Samaria (4:40); he remained beyond the Jordan (10:40). It means to go on being where you already are. The command is not get in; the branches are already in the vine. The command is: do not go anywhere.

How do we abide? The chapter supplies the content rather than leaving it vague. By keeping his word in us (v. 7): Scripture staying resident rather than visited. By resting in his love (v. 9): staying inside his love rather than trying to earn it. By keeping his commandments (v. 10): doing what he said. And by prayer, which runs through all three. So abiding turns out to consist of ordinary things done continuously. Nothing there requires a special temperament or technique. It is the difference between a branch attached to a vine and a branch lying on the ground, and the branch does not achieve it. It simply does not detach.

Unless it abides in the vine. A branch does not produce fruit by effort but by staying connected to the life of the vine. This is the dependence that pride always resists and grace always establishes. All the life is his, all the fruit is his, and all the glory is his, and he shares it with branches that could produce nothing on their own.

What does abiding look like on a busy day with no time for long devotions? It looks like staying turned toward Christ in the ordinary hours. Begin the day with even a few verses, read with attention, and carry one with you. Speak to him briefly and often: before the meeting, in the queue, when you are tempted, when you are glad. Obey him in the small next thing. Remember, when guilt or worry rises, that you are loved and forgiven in him. Abiding is not measured by the length of your quiet time but by whether you are depending on him or on yourself. Longer times with the Scriptures and prayer feed it, and you should make room for them, but a branch abides all day, not only in the morning.

parallels.desc: the washing of water with the word

verseByVerse.quote: "I am the vine; you are the branches. Whoever abides in me and I in him, he it is that bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing. If anyone does not abide in me he is thrown away like a branch and withers; and the branches are gathered, thrown into the fire, and burned."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You are the branches. He says it again, plainly, and promises much fruit. What is the fruit? Christlike character, the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22–23); obedience (v. 10); love (v. 12); joy (v. 11); answered prayer (v. 7); and people brought to Christ (4:36; Romans 1:13).

Apart from me you can do nothing. The most absolute statement of dependence in the Gospel: nothing of spiritual value. The separated branch does not produce diminished fruit; it produces none. Humbling, and encouraging: with him, by the Spirit through whom his life flows into us, everything he calls us to is possible (Philippians 4:13).

Thrown away like a branch. Vine wood is useless for building, and pruned branches were burned because they were good for nothing else (Ezekiel 15:2–5). The gathering into the fire is a picture of final judgment (Matthew 13:40–42) of the branch that seemed to be in the vine but had no living connection, finally revealed and removed.

Can a branch in Christ be cut off and burned? That answer should not be given quickly, because the words are severe and a reader may be frightened by them, and the difficulty is real. Verse 2 says every branch in me that does not bear fruit he takes away. In me. How can a branch be in Christ and be cut off and burned, when the same Lord said five chapters earlier that no one is able to snatch them out of his Father’s hand (10:29)?

The vine was always mixed. The picture itself supplies the answer. In the Old Testament the vine is Israel, full of people who belonged to the covenant community outwardly, carried its sign in their bodies, kept its feasts, and were not the true people of God at all. One of the Twelve has just gone out into the night to sell him (13:30). Judas was a branch in every visible sense, called, trusted with the common purse, and he bore nothing, because there was nothing in him to bear with. John gives us the category plainly in his letter: they went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would have continued with us (1 John 2:19).

No sheep prised from his hand. So the two sayings stand together without strain. The fruitless branch is not a sheep prised out of the Shepherd’s hand; it is a branch tied on to the vine that never drew a drop of sap from it. Union with Christ that is real produces fruit, always, however slowly and however little: that is what the passage means by fruit, not a level of achievement but evidence of life.

Where Christians differ: can a true believer be cut off? Some take this to teach that genuine Christians can lose their salvation if they stop abiding. This commentary’s view: the branches burned are those who never truly abide, like Judas, and the warning is one of God’s means of keeping his people abiding. (See Romans 11:22 for the fuller answer.)

The Arminian reading. Arminian Christians (who hold that saving grace can be resisted and a true believer can finally fall away) read this as a warning that a true believer can be cut off and lost (compare Hebrews 6:4–6). They are right that the warning is real. But the passage does not set it against the Shepherd’s promise; it is one of the means by which Christ keeps the true branches abiding.

If this frightens you. To the person genuinely alarmed by this verse: the very desire to abide is sap moving. Christ did not tell his friends this to leave them measuring themselves for the fire; the command in the passage is not examine yourself but abide in me, and abiding is not an achievement to be pulled off. It is a staying put. Stay where you are, in him, and the fruit is his business, not yours.

How much fruit must I see to be sure I am a true branch? There is no quota. Jesus speaks of fruit, more fruit and much fruit (vv. 2, 5), which means growth, not a fixed measure. Look for the kind of thing the chapter names, not for impressive results: a real love for Christ and his word, a hatred of your sin and a willingness to fight it, love for his people, and some desire that others know him. Those may be small and mixed with much weakness, but they are signs of sap. And do not base your assurance chiefly on your fruit. Base it on Christ’s promise to keep his sheep, and on the Spirit’s witness that you are God’s child (Romans 8:16); then let the fruit confirm what the promise declares.
verseByVerse.note: Vine wood is useless for building; pruned branches were burned.

parallels.desc: the wood of the vine

verseByVerse.quote: "If you abide in me, and my words abide in you, ask whatever you wish, and it will be done for you. By this my Father is glorified, that you bear much fruit and so prove to be my disciples."
verseByVerse.commentary:
My words abide in you. You cannot abide in Christ while ignoring his word; Scripture filling the mind and heart is how he dwells richly in us (Colossians 3:16).

Ask whatever you wish. This is the second of three prayer promises in chapters 14 and 15, and the conditions accumulate: in my name (14:13–14); here, abiding and his words abiding; at verse 16, being chosen and sent. The boundary here is the most searching: not a formula appended to a request but a condition about where the person praying is living.

The prayers change before the answers do. A person saturated in what Christ said begins, over time, to want different things, so that the wishing itself has been under instruction. The wishes are genuinely the person’s own; they have simply stopped being arbitrary.

By this my Father is glorified. The vine’s purpose is the vinedresser’s glory. To glorify God is not to add anything to him but to make his worth visible, as a heavy crop shows the skill of the gardener. When a harsh man grows gentle or a fearful woman grows brave, people see what kind of God has been at work (Matthew 5:16).

Prove to be my disciples. More literally, and become my disciples: discipleship is something one grows into, not only a status secured at the start. Fruit does not earn the title; it is how the title becomes visible.

How can I let Christ’s words abide in me, if I struggle to read the Bible? Start small and steady rather than large and occasional. Read a short passage, perhaps a few verses of a Gospel, at the same time each day. Read it twice, slowly, and ask: what does this show me of Christ, and what does it ask of me? Choose one sentence to carry with you, and say it to yourself during the day. Listen carefully to the preaching on Sunday and talk about it afterwards. Learn a verse by heart each week. If reading is hard for you, listen to Scripture read aloud. The aim is not to finish a plan but to let his words take up residence.

verseByVerse.quote: "As the Father has loved me, so have I loved you. Abide in my love. If you keep my commandments, you will abide in my love, just as I have kept my Father's commandments and abide in his love."
verseByVerse.commentary:
As the Father has loved me. The comparison is easy to read past. The measure of Christ’s love for us is not a great deal, or more than you know, but the love the Father has had for the Son from before the foundation of the world (17:24). We are loved with the love the Father has for his only Son, and that love will not run dry, because it springs from God himself. Nothing we do began it, and nothing can exhaust it.

Abide in my love. The phrase can be heard as a threat: stay in it or you will fall out of it. Read it against the picture. A branch does not generate the sap; it lives in a supply that is already flowing. Abiding in his love is not maintaining his affection at a certain level, which is impossible and was never asked; it is remaining inside something that is there whether one feels it or not.

If you keep my commandments. Obedience is how we stay in his love, not to earn it but to enjoy it.

As I have kept my Father’s commandments. Nobody supposes the Son earns the Father’s love by good behaviour. His obedience is the form of a love that was never in question, and the disciples’ obedience is being described in the same way. Obedience is love’s response, not love’s price. And his keeping was perfect where ours never is (1 John 1:8). That perfect obedience is counted as ours (Romans 5:19), so a branch that keeps his commands only haltingly still abides in a love that rests on his record, not its own.

Does God love me less when I disobey? No. His love for his children rests on Christ, not on their performance, and it does not rise and fall with your week (Romans 8:38–39). But your enjoyment of his love can be clouded by sin, as a child who has disobeyed may avoid his father’s eyes even while his father loves him as much as ever. The way back is not to make up for it first, but to come home: confess, receive his forgiveness, and walk with him again. You do not obey to get into his love; you obey because you are in it, and obedience keeps you in the warmth of it.

parallels.desc: keep yourselves in the love of God

verseByVerse.quote: "These things I have spoken to you, that my joy may be in you, and that your joy may be full. This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
That my joy may be in you. Not joy in general but a joy that belongs to him, the joy of the Son in the Father’s love and in doing his will, and the man handing it over will be dead by tomorrow afternoon. So it is not a mood produced by favourable circumstances. Hebrews describes the same thing from the far side: for the joy that was set before him he endured the cross, despising the shame (Hebrews 12:2).

Full. Filled up, brought to the brim (compare 1 John 1:4). The Christian life is not grim duty; obedience and joy go together. And he has gone through death to make sure that one day our joy will be full, brim full, for ever.

For the believer who does not feel joyful. There is a reader for whom this verse is an accusation. Christians told they ought to be joyful, who are not, conclude that something is defective in them, which is often untrue and always unhelpful, particularly for people whose flatness is a matter of temperament, exhaustion or illness rather than of the soul. Look at where the joy is located. It is his, and it arrives by abiding. It is not summoned up, and it has nothing to do with being naturally cheerful. Some of the most joyful Christians in history, Charles Spurgeon among them, fought long battles with depression. And this is not said at a wedding, but in a room somebody has just walked out of to fetch soldiers.

How can I have joy and sorrow at the same time? Because Christian joy is deeper than mood. Paul describes himself as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing (2 Corinthians 6:10). Joy in this sense is the settled gladness of knowing that you are loved by God, forgiven in Christ, and kept for glory, and it can sit underneath real grief like the deep water under a stormy surface. You do not have to pretend to be happy at a graveside or in a hospital ward. You can weep, and still know that the One who loves you is risen and that the end of the story is good. That is his joy in you.

This is my commandment. The new commandment of 13:34, repeated, now on the ground of the vine: branches in the same vine are branches in relationship with each other.

verseByVerse.quote: "Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends. You are my friends if you do what I command you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Greater love has no one than this. This sentence is carved on many war memorials, and it belongs there. A man who dies to bring his friends out is doing what Christ himself calls the greatest love there is, and no Christian should be grudging about it.

Greater than the greatest. But the verse says something the memorials cannot. He is defining the ceiling of human love and then going beyond it the following afternoon. Paul: one will scarcely die for a righteous person, but God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us (Romans 5:7–8), and a few lines later, while we were enemies (5:10). Christ exceeds the soldier’s love, because his friends at that moment were not behaving like friends. One had sold him, one would deny him three times before dawn, and the rest would run. He calls them friends anyway, and the word is not sentimental: philoi, from the affectionate verb, the word the sisters used of Lazarus (11:3). The love that went beyond the highest human love has found us, and it will never let us go.

If you do what I command. The condition sounds like a friendship on probation, and the next verse forbids that reading: he has already called them friends (v. 15). The conditional describes the shape of the friendship rather than its price: not that obedience makes us his friends, but that it shows we are. And the command is given by somebody who is about to obey a harder one: he asks nothing of them that he is unwilling to do first.

Can I really call Jesus my friend? Yes, and with wonder, because he calls you that first. Friendship with Christ does not make him less than Lord; you are friends of the King, not his equals. So the friendship is full of reverence as well as warmth. But it is real: he has laid down his life for you, he has told you the Father’s plans, he hears you, he is for you. You may speak to him with the openness of a friend, bring him your troubles without performance, and trust his loyalty when you feel least loyal yourself. What a friend we have in Jesus is sentimental only if it forgets the cross; remembered there, it is the plain truth.

In everyday life. Think of someone in your church who needs a friend who will lay something down for them, time, comfort, convenience, money, and lay one thing down for that person this week, quietly, for Christ’s sake.

parallels.desc: he laid down his life for us

verseByVerse.quote: "No longer do I call you servants, for the servant does not know what his master is doing; but I have called you friends, for all that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you. You did not choose me, but I chose you and appointed you that you should go and bear fruit and that your fruit should abide, so that whatever you ask the Father in my name, he may give it to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
No longer servants. Every great figure of the Old Testament is a servant. Moses my servant, David my servant: it was the highest title a Jew could aspire to, and he takes it off them, for a precise reason: a slave is told what to do and not why.

I have called you friends. In the whole Old Testament only Abraham is called the friend of God (2 Chronicles 20:7; Isaiah 41:8; taken up in James 2:23), and of Moses alone it is said that the LORD spoke to him face to face, as a man speaks to his friend (Exodus 33:11). Two men in two thousand years, and God shared his plans with them (Genesis 18:17). Now Jesus calls all his disciples friends. The promotion is in disclosure: not easier commands, but the reasons, as he has been doing all evening. They are still his servants (v. 20; Romans 1:1), but more than servants: trusted friends.

All, and yet more to come. Jesus says he has made known all that he has heard from his Father, yet soon says he still has many things to say to them, but they cannot bear them now (16:12). He has told them all they need as his friends; the rest the Spirit will bring out after his glory, through the apostles (16:13).

You did not choose me. In that culture, as far as we can tell, disciples usually chose their rabbi, and at least two of these men had first followed John the Baptist (1:35–40). Jesus reverses it. That is a blow to pride and a relief to the anxious: the one who chose them knew exactly whom he was choosing. We did not find him; he found us. The Bible’s word for this is election: God choosing people for himself before they had done anything good or bad, out of his own love and not for their worth (Ephesians 1:4; Romans 9:11).

Is I chose you about salvation, or about the apostles’ office? In the first place it is the choosing of the Eleven for their mission, that you should go and bear fruit; Judas, too, was chosen as an apostle (6:70). But it rests on the same truth that runs through John, that those who come to Christ come because the Father gave them and drew them (6:37, 44). So it is rightly applied to every believer: our faith began with his choice. It reflects the deeper truth of election to salvation (13:18; 17:6; Ephesians 1:4). Our salvation starts with his choice, not ours. We chose him only because he first chose us.

Does election make my choice meaningless? No. You really did repent and believe; no one did it for you, and it was truly your act. Election explains why you did. Left to ourselves we would never have chosen him (6:44), so behind your choosing lies his, which made it possible and certain. That does not make you a puppet; it makes you a rescued sinner. And it brings two great gifts: humility, because you cannot boast about having chosen well, and security, because what began with his choice does not depend on the strength of yours.

Appointed to bear fruit. Election in this verse runs straight out into mission, and the last word about the fruit is the chapter’s keyword, abide. Fruit that stays.

Whatever you ask the Father. Prayer is connected with fruitful mission. Those whom he has chosen and sent pray in his name, and the Father answers them.
verseByVerse.note: Abraham and Moses were each called the friend of God.

parallels.desc: Abraham, my friend
as a man speaks to his friend

verseByVerse.quote: "These things I command you, so that you will love one another."
verseByVerse.commentary:
These things I command you. The sentence closes the first half of the chapter by naming what all of it was for: the vine, the pruning, the abiding, the joy, the friendship, the choosing were all aimed at love among his people. The world will hate them (v. 18); they must love one another.

Not where we would have put the emphasis. We might land on the upward direction: know him better, pray with confidence. He says the point of the whole thing is that they should love each other. Good doctrine always runs out into love: election produces humility, grace produces gratitude, and both produce the servant-hearted love of the community of the chosen.

Love that flows from the vine. Fruit is not extracted from a branch by exhortation; it comes from the life flowing into it. The love these men are to have for one another is Christ’s own love passing through them. He loved them first, he is about to lay down his life for them, and the sap of that love is what will turn eleven quarrelling men into a family.

To these men, that night. Luke tells us that at this supper they had argued about which of them was the greatest (Luke 22:24), and within hours they would all abandon him and then spend the weekend locked in a room together, with Peter’s failure in the middle of it. He gives the command anyway, for the third time that evening (13:34; 15:12).

What if the Christian I find hardest to love has really wronged me? Then love will look like forgiveness, and forgiveness is not pretending the wrong did not happen. It means you do not hold it against him or seek to pay him back, because Christ has not held your sins against you (Ephesians 4:32). It may mean a hard conversation (Matthew 18:15), and where there is abuse or danger it means protection and, where needed, the involvement of church leaders and the authorities; love never requires you to stay in harm’s way. But it does mean praying for him, refusing bitterness, and being ready for reconciliation when there is repentance. Ask Christ for his love, because yours will run out.

In everyday life. If anything is still unresolved from your last disagreement with a fellow believer, take a step toward peace this week: a message, a call, an apology for your part, a prayer for his good.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–27 — The World's Hatred and the Spirit's Witness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The world will hate the disciples because it hated Jesus first and because he chose them out of it. Its hatred is without excuse, since he spoke and did works no one else did. But the Spirit of truth, whom Jesus will send from the Father, will bear witness about him, and so will they.
verseByVerse.theology: The world’s hostility to the church is not an accident to be explained away but follows from the conflict between the kingdom of God and a world in rebellion against him. Jesus promises not a strategy to remove it but the Spirit, who bears witness about Jesus alongside the disciples who were with him from the beginning.
verseByVerse.examples: If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you (v. 20). This is both warning and honour: to suffer for Christ is to share in his sufferings. The disciple should not manufacture hostility, but when it comes for Christ’s sake he may take it as confirmation, not contradiction, that he belongs to Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "If the world hates you, know that it has hated me before it hated you. If you were of the world, the world would love you as its own; but because you are not of the world, but I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
If the world hates you. The change of subject is abrupt and deliberate: from love (vv. 9–17), without a pause, to hatred (vv. 18–25). The community commanded to love one another will need to, because nobody outside it will. The world in John is humanity in rebellion against God. That does not mean the planet, or people as such, for God so loved the world (3:16). It means human life arranged without God: its approval, its values and its loyalties, wherever they are found, including in religion. And the word is not dislike but hatred.

It has hated me before. The world’s hatred is first directed at Christ, and the disciples share in what he suffered because they share his name (1 Peter 4:12–14).

The world would love its own. The logic is oddly comforting once it is seen. The hostility is not evidence that something has gone wrong with the disciples; it is evidence that they no longer belong to the system that is doing the hating. Belonging elsewhere is the whole cause.

I chose you out of the world. They now belong to another kingdom (17:14–16), with different loyalties and a different love, and the world resents it. Their chosenness is the source of both their dignity and their danger. The world’s hatred cannot reach the love that chose us; it can only confirm whose we are.

Two guards. This passage is misused in both directions. The first is against manufacturing persecution: much of what Christians suffer in comfortable countries is the consequence of being rude, ill-informed or needlessly provocative. Peter drew the line himself: let none of you suffer as a murderer or a thief or an evildoer or as a meddler (1 Peter 4:15). Being disliked for being disagreeable is not sharing in the sufferings of Christ. The second is against the opposite error: many Christians are imprisoned, dispossessed and killed today, and a church that reads verse 18 as a metaphor for social awkwardness has excluded much of its own family. The comfortable believer should neither invent a persecution nor conclude the verse is spent, but pray for the persecuted church.

Should I try to be liked by unbelievers, or expect to be hated? Neither as a goal. Aim to be faithful to Christ and kind to people, and leave the reaction to God. Scripture tells us to live such good lives among unbelievers that they may see our good deeds (1 Peter 2:12), to be wise toward outsiders and gracious in speech (Colossians 4:5–6), and to live peaceably with all as far as it depends on us (Romans 12:18). Many unbelievers will respect, even love, a gentle and honest Christian. But when faithfulness to Christ costs you their approval, do not trade him for it. Being hated is not a mark of holiness in itself; being hated for his name is.

verseByVerse.quote: "Remember the word that I said to you: 'A servant is not greater than his master.' If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you. If they kept my word, they will also keep yours. But all these things they will do to you on account of my name, because they do not know him who sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A servant is not greater than his master. The word he tells them to remember is one he said earlier that evening, at the basin (13:16), where it was an argument for washing feet. Here the other edge is out: if the master is hunted, no servant should expect to be exempt. The same proverb produces humility in one direction and realism in the other.

If they persecuted me. The church shares her Lord’s experience (Acts 9:4; 2 Timothy 3:12), because the world sees in her something of him.

They will also keep yours. The parallel runs both ways. The verse is not a prediction of universal hostility but that the disciples’ reception will mirror his, and his was mixed. A Samaritan village believed; some of the authorities believed and would not say so. His reception included Nicodemus and a beggar who worshipped him (9:38).

On account of my name. Persecution of the church is ultimately aimed at Christ himself, and its root is ignorance of the true God (16:3). They are being hit by something aimed past them. And the ignorance is not innocent: they have had the opportunity to know and refused.

How should I respond when I am treated badly for being a Christian? Remember that you are sharing your Master’s lot, and that it is an honour (Acts 5:41; Matthew 5:11–12). Do not repay evil for evil or insult for insult, but bless (1 Peter 3:9). Pray for those who mistreat you, as Jesus did on the cross. Speak the truth gently and stand firm without bitterness. Use lawful protections where you have them, as Paul did (Acts 22:25). And keep on with the work: some who now oppose you may later keep the word, as Saul of Tarsus did.

verseByVerse.quote: "If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have been guilty of sin, but now they have no excuse for their sin. Whoever hates me hates my Father also."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They would not have been guilty. He cannot mean they would have been innocent. Paul spends three chapters establishing that the whole world is guilty before God (Romans 1–3), and John himself has already had Jesus say that people loved the darkness rather than the light (3:19). What is meant is the specific sin the chapter is about: rejecting God’s Son with the evidence in front of them. That sin was not available before he arrived. A man cannot refuse a person he has never met.

Responsibility tracks light. The principle underneath runs right through the Bible: privilege increases responsibility (9:41; Luke 12:47–48). The position of the well-informed is more dangerous, not safer. A person who has grown up hearing the gospel and can predict the sermon is in this verse’s territory.

No excuse. Excuse (prophasin) means pretext, a cloak: the plausible cover story. What his coming did was not to create the guilt but to remove the covering that had made it deniable.

Whoever hates me hates my Father also. There is no loving the Father while hating the Son (5:23; 1 John 2:23). It is 14:9 turned round: if seeing him is seeing the Father, then hating him is hating the Father. It closes off a common position, held sincerely by many: that one may honour God and set Jesus aside as a good man the church has exaggerated. There is no God available behind Christ to be respected while Christ is declined.

What about religious people who worship God but reject Jesus? This verse speaks to them with great seriousness and great love. Many sincerely believe they honour God while rejecting Jesus as the Son. But Jesus says that the Father and the Son cannot be separated: to refuse the Son is to refuse the Father who sent him (5:23). That is why Christians must lovingly and humbly tell their Jewish, Muslim and other religious neighbours about Christ, not to win an argument but because there is no other way to the God they seek. We should honour their sincerity and their questions, and never despise them, while still saying plainly who Jesus is.

In everyday life. If you have grown up in church, ask honestly whether you have ever personally come to Christ, or only been near him. If not, come today; he casts out no one who comes (6:37). If you have, thank God for the light you were given, and ask what he wants you to do with it this week.

verseByVerse.quote: "If I had not done among them the works that no one else did, they would not be guilty of sin, but now they have seen and hated both me and my Father. But the word that is written in their Law must be fulfilled: 'They hated me without a cause.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The works that no one else did. His works were unique (9:32), a category of evidence the council itself conceded in closed session (11:47).

Seen and hated. Seeing and hating: the clearest evidence of the depth of sin. When perfect goodness came among them, the world’s enmity against God became fully visible.

Written in their Law. Their Law here means the Scriptures as a whole, including the Psalms. He has used the phrase before (8:17; 10:34), and it is not a repudiation of Scripture: he quotes it as authoritative, so that the court’s own law testifies against the verdict. The words come from Psalm 35:19 and 69:4, laments of David hated by enemies without reason. Psalm 69 also supplies the zeal for the house (2:17) and the sour wine on the cross (19:28–29). Even their hatred fulfilled Scripture.

Without a cause, and as a gift. Without a cause is dōrean. It means gratuitously, for nothing. The same word appears in Romans 3:24: we are justified by his grace as a gift, dōrean, freely, for nothing. The world’s hatred of Christ was unearned, and the sinner’s acquittal is unearned, and they meet at the same cross, and the free gift wins. He received hatred he had done nothing to deserve; the people who hated him receive a righteousness they have done nothing to deserve.

Why would anyone hate Jesus? Because his light exposes what we love in the dark (3:19–20). He was kind, but he was also holy, and his holiness told people the truth about themselves. He claimed authority over their lives, their religion and their future. He would not be used. People who wanted a different kind of God found in him the real one, and resisted. The same thing happens in every heart before the Spirit changes it: we may admire Jesus at a distance, but when he comes close and claims us, the natural heart pushes him away. That is why new birth is necessary (3:3).

In everyday life. When you are treated unfairly today, remember that the Lord was hated without cause, and was silent like a lamb. Then remember that you were loved without cause, and let that shape how you answer.
verseByVerse.note: “Their Law” here means the Scriptures as a whole, including the Psalms.

parallels.desc: those who hate me without cause

verseByVerse.quote: "But when the Helper comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness about me. And you also will bear witness, because you have been with me from the beginning."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the flow. The promise of the Spirit arrives in the middle of a warning about hatred: the case against Christ looks lost, so Jesus names his witnesses, and the defence is given the last word.

When the Helper comes. Here paraklētos has its courtroom sense most clearly, for the Helper is also the Advocate: in a hostile world, the Spirit stands alongside the persecuted church and speaks for Christ. And in this verse the Son sends him, where earlier that evening the Father was said to send him (14:16, 26). Both send.

Who proceeds from the Father. Proceeds (ekporeuetai) means goes out from, comes forth. Most take it of the Spirit’s mission; theologians have also seen in it his eternal relationship to the Father.

The phrase that divided the church. The Nicene Creed, as agreed in the fourth century, said the Spirit proceeds from the Father, in the words of this verse. And the same verse holds the other half of the later argument: whom I will send to you from the Father. The East protects the Father as the single source within the Godhead; the West protects the Son’s full involvement. Both are defending something the verse says. And on Easter evening the risen Son will breathe on the disciples and say, receive the Holy Spirit (20:22).

Where Christians differ: does the Spirit proceed from the Son? The Western church added to the Nicene Creed that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son (filioque). The Eastern Orthodox church rejected the addition, and it was a major cause of the split of 1054. This commentary’s view: the Western confession, held by the Reformed churches (the Westminster Confession 2.3; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 2.3), is right in substance: the Spirit is the Spirit of the Son as well as of the Father (Galatians 4:6; Romans 8:9), and the Son sends him, as here. Yet the matter is subtle, and should be held humbly, with respect for Eastern brothers and sisters who confess the same Trinity.

He will bear witness about me. The Spirit’s great work is to point to Christ (16:14). He does not draw attention to himself; he is the floodlight that shines on the Son.

You also will bear witness. Two witnesses, the requirement of the law that runs through this Gospel (8:17). And the qualification for the human half is purely factual: not eloquence or bravery, neither of which they were about to prove, but that they were there. Their eyewitness testimony (Acts 1:21–22), preserved in Scripture, is the foundation of the church (Ephesians 2:20). And the Spirit still bears witness through every believer who speaks of Christ.

The pressure taken off. The Spirit’s witness is the one that convinces; the disciples’ job is to say what they saw. Nobody is asked to produce faith in anybody. And you have been with me from the beginning was said to eleven men who would, before the night was over, all be somewhere else. He sent them anyway.

I was not an eyewitness, so how can I bear witness? By passing on faithfully what the eyewitnesses saw, and by telling what Christ has done for you. The apostles’ testimony is written down for you (20:31; 1 John 1:1–3), so you do not need to invent anything; you point people to it. And you can say, as the healed blind man did, what you know: I was blind, now I see (9:25). The Spirit uses that ordinary testimony. You are not responsible for convincing anyone. You are responsible for being honest and clear about Jesus, and leaving the convincing to the Spirit who loves to glorify him.

For worship. The Spirit of truth has one subject, the Son, and every heart that has seen the glory of Jesus has seen it by his light. The world has never silenced the witness of eleven frightened men, because behind their weak words stood the Spirit who will not let Christ be forgotten. Glory to the Father who sends, the Son who is shown, and the Spirit who shows him.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “Helper” can also be rendered “Advocate” or “Counselor.”

parallels.desc: we are witnesses, and so is the Holy Spirit

15.text: <sup>1</sup>“I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinedresser.<sup>2</sup>Every branch in me that does not bear fruit he takes away, and every branch that does bear fruit he prunes, that it may bear more fruit.<sup>3</sup>Already you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you.<sup>4</sup>Abide in me, and I in you.
