As the branch cannot bear fruit by itself, unless it abides in the vine, neither can you, unless you abide in me.<sup>5</sup>I am the vine; you are the branches. Whoever abides in me and I in him, he it is that bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.<sup>6</sup>If anyone does not abide in me, he is thrown away like a branch and withers; and the branches are gathered, thrown into the fire, and burned.<sup>7</sup>If you abide in me, and my words abide in you, ask whatever you wish, and it will be done for you.<sup>8</sup>By this my Father is glorified, that you bear much fruit and so prove to be my disciples.<sup>9</sup>As the Father has loved me, so have I loved you. Abide in my love.<sup>10</sup>If you keep my commandments, you will abide in my love, just as I have kept my Father’s commandments and abide in his love.<sup>11</sup>These things I have spoken to you, that my joy may be in you, and that your joy may be full.<sup>12</sup>“This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you.<sup>13</sup>Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends.<sup>14</sup>You are my friends if you do what I command you.<sup>15</sup>No longer do I call you servants, for the servant does not know what his master is doing; but I have called you friends, for all that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you.<sup>16</sup>You did not choose me, but I chose you and appointed you that you should go and bear fruit and that your fruit should abide, so that whatever you ask the Father in my name, he may give it to you.<sup>17</sup>These things I command you, so that you will love one another.<sup>18</sup>“If the world hates you, know that it has hated me before it hated you.<sup>19</sup>If you were of the world, the world would love you as its own; but because you are not of the world, but I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you.<sup>20</sup>Remember the word that I said to you: ’A servant is not greater than his master.’ If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you. If they kept my word, they will also keep yours.<sup>21</sup>But all these things they will do to you on account of my name, because they do not know him who sent me.<sup>22</sup>If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have been guilty of sin, but now they have no excuse for their sin.<sup>23</sup>Whoever hates me hates my Father also.<sup>24</sup>If I had not done among them the works that no one else did, they would not be guilty of sin, but now they have seen and hated both me and my Father.<sup>25</sup>But the word that is written in their Law must be fulfilled: ’They hated me without a cause.’<sup>26</sup>“But when the Helper comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness about me.<sup>27</sup>And you also will bear witness, because you have been with me from the beginning.
15.overview:
Israel was God’s vine, planted and tended by him but so often fruitless. Jesus now says, “I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinedresser.” His disciples are the branches, and all their fruit comes from abiding in him: apart from him they can do nothing. Abiding means living in his love, keeping his word, and loving one another as he has loved them. He calls them friends, and reminds them that he chose them and sent them to bear lasting fruit.

The second half turns from love within the church to hatred from the world. The world hated him first, without a cause, and his servants should expect the same. Yet they will not be alone: the Spirit of truth will bear witness about Jesus, and they too will bear witness, because they have been with him from the beginning.

16.title: The Spirit and the Joy of the Disciples

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — The Spirit Convicts the World
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus forewarns the disciples of persecution so that it will not trip them. His going, which grieves them, is for their good, because then he will send the Helper, who will convict the world and lead the apostles into all the truth about Christ.
verseByVerse.theology: The Spirit convicts the world on three counts: sin (its refusal to believe in Jesus), righteousness (Jesus vindicated by his return to the Father), and judgment (the ruler of this world condemned at the cross). This conviction is not coercion but illumination: the Spirit opens eyes to what is true. The gospel is not an optional improvement but rescue from real condemnation.
verseByVerse.examples: He will guide you into all the truth (v. 13). The promise was first to the apostles, and was fulfilled in the New Testament. The Spirit does not add to it, but still opens believers’ eyes to the word he inspired (1 Corinthians 2:10–13). So the church, reading the Spirit’s word with prayer and humility, can come to the truth Jesus promised.

verseByVerse.quote: "I have said all these things to you to keep you from falling away. They will put you out of the synagogues. Indeed, the hour is coming when whoever kills you will think he is offering service to God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. John 16 completes Jesus’ farewell teaching. He warns of persecution, explains why his going is good for them, describes the Spirit’s work in the world and in the church, and promises that their sorrow will turn to joy. It ends with one of the great promises of Scripture: I have overcome the world. Spoken to men about to scatter, it is the voice of a Victor who has not yet fought and has never doubted the outcome.

The setting. The words follow straight on from 15:27, late on Thursday night; within hours he will be arrested, and these men will be asked whether they know him.

To keep you from falling away. Falling away (skandalisthēte) is to be tripped, to catch your foot on an obstacle you did not see, not formally to renounce the faith; and the obstacle Jesus has in mind is persecution arriving without warning.

The stumbling-block placed in view. He removes it by putting it in the road ahead where they can see it. Suffering predicted by the one you follow is different from suffering that seems to prove he was not in control.

They will put you out of the synagogues. As had already happened to the man born blind (9:22, 34). For a Jew of that day, it meant being cut off from community, worship, family and livelihood.

Offering service to God. The English softens the word, and it is chilling. Service (latreia) is worship, the technical term for what went on in the temple (Romans 12:1). The killing will be performed as an act of worship, by men who go home believing they have pleased God. Religious zeal without the knowledge of God can become murderous. Stephen was the first recorded to die this way (Acts 7:58–60).

The case study who became an apostle. Paul had been such a man. He hunted Christians sincerely, convinced he ought to oppose the name of Jesus (Acts 26:9–11). That is the hope inside the warning: the first man to fulfil this prophecy on a large scale ended up writing a large part of the New Testament. Nothing in verse 2 puts a person beyond the reach of grace.

Why does God let his people be persecuted at all? Scripture does not give a complete explanation, but it gives enough to trust him. Suffering for Christ joins us to him and makes us share his path (Philippians 3:10; 1 Peter 4:13). It purifies faith like fire refining gold (1 Peter 1:6–7). It bears witness to the world, as the blood of martyrs has so often been seed for the church. And it is temporary, while the glory to come is eternal and far outweighs it (Romans 8:18; 2 Corinthians 4:17). None of this makes persecution good in itself. But God never wastes the sufferings of his people, and he holds the persecutors, too, in his hand.
verseByVerse.note: Paul had been such a man, persecuting believers as a service to God.

parallels.desc: Paul’s zeal as a persecutor

verseByVerse.quote: "And they will do these things because they have not known the Father, nor me. But I have said these things to you, that when their hour comes you may remember that I told them to you. I did not say these things to you from the beginning, because I was with you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They have not known the Father. The diagnosis is the most important sentence in the passage: religious violence is not caused by too much God but by not knowing him. That cuts against a common modern account, which holds that strong conviction is itself the danger. The men who will kill his followers as an act of worship do not know God too well; they do not know him at all.

A usable test. Any conviction that makes a person willing to destroy someone in God’s name has, by that fact, revealed itself as ignorance of the God who sent his Son to be destroyed rather than to destroy. And the test reaches the respectable as well as the violent. Contempt offered as zeal, the cold shoulder and the cutting remark made in God’s name, grow from the same root: religion used to prove oneself right, instead of knowledge of the God who justifies the ungodly (Romans 4:5).

When their hour comes. The hour of the persecutors. When it comes, the memory of these words will confirm faith: this is what he said would happen.

Not from the beginning. While he was with them, the hostility was aimed at him. Matthew records earlier warnings (Matthew 10:17–22), but what is new tonight is that he is leaving, and the blows will now land on them. There is information God holds back, and the holding back is not deception. It is timing.

Does this mean every religious person who opposes Christians does not know God? It means that no one who truly knows the Father will persecute those who belong to his Son. People may disagree with Christians, even sharply, for many reasons, and many in other religions are sincere and morally serious. But Jesus says the deepest reason for hostility toward him and his people is not knowing the Father as he has revealed himself in the Son. That is a reason for compassion, not contempt: they need what we have been given, the knowledge of God in the face of Jesus Christ. And Christians must apply the test to themselves first: the church has sometimes persecuted in God’s name, and every time it did, it was failing to know him.

parallels.desc: I had acted ignorantly in unbelief

verseByVerse.quote: "But now I am going to him who sent me, and none of you asks me, 'Where are you going?' But because I have said these things to you, sorrow has filled your heart."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But now I am going to him who sent me, and none of you asks me, Where are you going? The apparent contradiction should be dealt with directly, because a careful reader trips on it. Peter had asked precisely that three chapters earlier: Lord, where are you going? (13:36). Thomas had asked something very close (14:5). The resolution is in what is happening in the room: none of you asks me, now, at this moment. Peter asked earlier and did not want the answer; he immediately turned the conversation to his own loyalty. They had asked only about the separation, not about where he was going and why it would be good. Nobody is asking now, and the rest of the sentence says why. They are thinking only of their loss.

Sorrow has filled your heart. That is a real observation about grief. Sorrow closes questions down.

What Jesus does not do with it. He does not tell them to stop being sad, or hurry past it. He names it, and takes responsibility for having caused it. Then he gives them the one thing that will turn it round: not an argument but a fact about the Spirit.

Is it wrong for a Christian to grieve deeply? No. Jesus did not rebuke these men for their sorrow, and he himself wept at a grave (11:35). Paul did not tell the Thessalonians to stop grieving, only not to grieve like those who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13). Grief is love feeling the weight of loss, and the Psalms give us words for it. What faith adds is not the removal of sorrow but a window in it: the knowledge that God is doing something we cannot yet see, and that the story does not end here. So grieve honestly, bring your grief to the Lord, and let others carry it with you. In time, ask him to show you what he is doing.

verseByVerse.quote: "Nevertheless, I tell you the truth: it is to your advantage that I go away, for if I do not go away, the Helper will not come to you. But if I go, I will send him to you. And when he comes, he will convict the world concerning sin and righteousness and judgment:"
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is to your advantage that I go away. The most counterintuitive sentence of the farewell discourse. The verb, sympherei, is the word Caiaphas used: it is better for you that one man should die for the people (11:50), cold political arithmetic in a council chamber. Caiaphas meant: better for us that he dies. Jesus means: better for you that I go. What Caiaphas meant as murder God meant as salvation, and what the disciples felt as loss God meant as gain.

The Helper will not come. Why could the Spirit not come while Jesus was here? Directly: the Spirit is sent by the glorified Son, and John has already told us that the Spirit was not yet given because Jesus was not yet glorified (7:39). The cross, resurrection and ascension come first, then Pentecost (Acts 2:33): the Spirit applies the finished work, and there was nothing to apply until the work was done.

A distribution of his presence. Implied, and this is the part that touches the disciples’ grief: a body is in one place. The Spirit is with every believer everywhere, always, and within them. What is coming is not a replacement for his presence but a distribution of it. The arrangement they are grieving was the inferior one. He goes away in order to come nearer.

Did Old Testament believers not have the Spirit? They did: David prayed take not your Holy Spirit from me (Psalm 51:11), and they too were born of God, as Jesus implies when he rebukes Nicodemus, Israel’s teacher, for not understanding the new birth (3:10). What came at Pentecost was the Spirit poured out on all God’s people, dwelling in them permanently, on the ground of Christ’s finished work. That is what Jesus means: the Spirit as the promised gift of the new covenant could not come until he had gone.

He will convict the world. Convict (elenxei) is a courtroom word: to cross-examine, to bring to light, to prove a case. The Spirit proves the world wrong on three counts. The world thinks it has judged Jesus; the Spirit turns the case around.

Would it not be better to have Jesus here in person? It feels that way, and Jesus says plainly that it is not. If he were here in the flesh, he could be in only one place; you might live your whole life without getting near him. By the Spirit he is with every believer, in every place, at every hour, and not beside you only but within you. The disciples who walked with him in Galilee often misunderstood him; after Pentecost the same men understood and preached with boldness. You are not a second-class Christian for living after the ascension. You live in the age Jesus called better.

parallels.desc: they were cut to the heart

verseByVerse.quote: "concerning sin, because they do not believe in me; concerning righteousness, because I go to the Father, and you will see me no longer;"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not making people feel bad. Convict does not mean to make somebody feel bad, and to confuse the two does real harm. The Spirit shows a person what is true; the accuser presses him about what he is. The one produces clarity and moves toward a remedy; the other produces a fog of general unworthiness and moves nowhere at all.

Concerning sin. Not sins, plural, catalogued, but the root: the world’s great sin is not first its immorality but unbelief (3:18–19), and every other sin is fruit of this tree. This is how conviction began at Pentecost: “cut to the heart” over the one they crucified (Acts 2:36–37).

Concerning righteousness. This is the difficult clause. Jesus was tried, convicted and executed as a blasphemer and a criminal. The ascension is the appeal court, overturning the sentence: his return to the Father, in resurrection and ascension, proves that he was righteous (Acts 2:24, 32–36; 1 Timothy 3:16). So the Spirit convinces people that Jesus was in the right, and that their own righteousness is worthless. And the righteousness of Christ, now accepted in heaven, is the righteousness God gives to all who believe (Romans 3:21–22). For the believer this changes everything: God does not weigh our better days against our worse ones and hope they balance. He counts Christ’s perfect record as ours the moment we trust him, so that we stand before him accepted as Christ is accepted (2 Corinthians 5:21). That is what justification means: God declaring the guilty righteous because of Christ. The Judge who was judged is the righteousness of all who believe in him.

And you will see me no longer. The phrase belongs to the argument: the vindication is invisible. Nobody watched the Father receive him. The Spirit’s work is to convince the world of a verdict handed down out of sight.

How can I tell the Spirit’s conviction from false guilt? The difference is practical. Conviction from the Spirit is specific: it names a thing, and it can be dealt with, and there is a door out of it marked with the name of Christ. The other kind is vague, cumulative, and always about the whole self rather than an act, and it never once suggests anything to do. If what you are hearing has no exit, it is not this verse. When the Spirit convicts, he leads you to confess and to trust Christ’s blood (1 John 1:9), and then he lifts the burden. When the accuser speaks, he tells you that you are beyond help. Answer him with the cross.

parallels.desc: raised for our justification

verseByVerse.quote: "concerning judgment, because the ruler of this world is judged. I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Concerning judgment. The tense is what matters: the ruler of this world is judged, already, said before the cross, about the cross. The world judged Jesus, but it was Satan who was judged there (12:31); the Spirit publishes a verdict already entered. The prince of this world was cast out at the very cross where he thought he had won, and his sentence stands. When the world looks as though the enemy is winning, the question of who governs was settled on a Friday afternoon and nothing since has reopened it. The Spirit convinces people that the world’s verdicts are wrong and God’s judgment is certain (Acts 17:31).

You cannot bear them now. One of the kindest sentences in the Gospel. Bear is to carry a weight: he has more to say, and he stops, because he can see the limit of what they can carry tonight. This is why the New Testament contains more than the Gospels: the apostles’ letters unfold what Jesus began to teach.

Measured to our strength. If you suspect that God is expecting more of you than you can manage, this verse has him doing the arithmetic in the other direction: measuring what he says against what they can carry, and stopping short. The Spirit will bring it later; nothing is permanently withheld, but postponed to a point where it will help rather than crush. Mighty to defeat the devil, tender toward the weak: that is our Lord.

If Satan is already judged, why is there still so much evil? Because his sentence has been passed but not yet fully carried out. At the cross Christ disarmed him and broke his claim on God’s people (Colossians 2:15; Hebrews 2:14–15), and the gospel now goes out to the nations, freeing his captives. He still prowls like a lion (1 Peter 5:8), but on a chain, and his time is short. At Christ’s return the sentence will be executed in full, and he will be cast out for ever (Revelation 20:10). We live between the verdict and the execution. That is why we fight, and why we fight without fear.

verseByVerse.quote: "When the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all the truth, for he will not speak on his own authority, but whatever he hears he will speak, and he will declare to you the things that are to come. He will glorify me, for he will take what is mine and declare it to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Into all the truth. A promise first to the apostles. Guide (hodēgēsei) comes from the word for a road: what a guide does for a traveller who does not know the country. All the truth means not chemistry or astronomy but the truth about God, salvation and the meaning of Jesus. This was fulfilled in the writing of the New Testament.

No new country. This verse needs a boundary, because it has been claimed by every movement that ever wanted to add something to Scripture. A guide does not invent the terrain. He takes people over ground that is already there. So the church tests every claim to a fresh word from the Spirit by the word the Spirit has already given, and finds in it everything needed to make us wise for salvation and equipped for every good work (2 Timothy 3:15–17). (On words from the Spirit today, see 14:26.)

Not on his own authority. Jesus states the limit himself. The Spirit does not bring a different message from the Son, any more than the Son brought a different message from the Father. He is not a second source. He reports.

The things that are to come. Not a promise of prediction to individual believers about their futures, but most naturally the things the apostles would be given to understand and write: the meaning of the cross, the shape of the age, the end.

He will glorify me. The Spirit shines the spotlight on Jesus, not on himself, and this is one of the surest tests of any spiritual claim. So the question to ask of anything that claims the Spirit is not whether it is impressive or emotional, but something much harder to fake: does it make much of Christ? His great delight is to take what is Christ’s and show it to us, until our hearts burn with the glory of the Son.

The Spirit who stands out of the light. Much that has gone under the Spirit’s name fails that test, because the attention settles on the phenomenon or on the man producing it. The Spirit does not seek his own glory: he is the one who habitually stands slightly out of the light and points.

Is this a promise to every believer, or to the apostles? In the first place it is to the apostles, who received the Spirit’s guidance into all truth and wrote it down in the New Testament. Believers today share in the promise through their word, as the Spirit opens our eyes to it (1 Corinthians 2:12–13). It is not a promise of new revelation beyond Scripture.

If the Spirit guides into truth, why do Christians disagree? Because the Spirit’s guidance into all the truth was given infallibly to the apostles, and what he gave them is in Scripture without error. Our reading of it is not infallible. We are sinners, limited in knowledge, shaped by our backgrounds, and sometimes stubborn. Where Scripture is clear, on Christ, the gospel and the way of salvation, true believers broadly agree, and that agreement is itself the Spirit’s work. Where we differ, the remedy is to go back humbly to the text, to pray, to listen to the church’s wiser teachers, and to love those with whom we disagree. The Bible is the judge, not our impressions.

verseByVerse.quote: "All that the Father has is mine; therefore I said that he will take what is mine and declare it to you. A little while, and you will see me no longer; and again a little while, and you will see me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
All that the Father has is mine. One of the largest claims in the Gospel, dropped in casually. Not all that the Father has given me, the language of a servant entrusted with an estate, but all that the Father has. No creature could say it. The Father, the Son and the Spirit share all things (17:10).

He will take what is mine. The Spirit takes from the Son, and everything the Father has belongs to the Son, so what the Spirit brings to the church is drawn from the whole wealth of God. There is no smaller supply reserved for people at this end of the chain. In Christ we have all, because in him we have God.

A little while. His death, in a few hours.

And again a little while. His resurrection, on the third day. Some also see a reference to his second coming. The second little while runs to the third day, and behind it, arguably, the whole age of the church. That elasticity is how the New Testament speaks about the interval: yet a little while, and the coming one will come and will not delay (Hebrews 10:37), written nearly two thousand years ago.

What does it mean for me that all the Father has belongs to Christ? It means that in Christ you lack nothing that you truly need. Every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places is yours in him (Ephesians 1:3); his righteousness, his sonship, his inheritance, his access to the Father are shared with you. Paul could say that all things are yours, and you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s (1 Corinthians 3:21–23). When you feel spiritually poor, the remedy is not to look for some other source, a technique or an experience, but to look to Christ, in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden (Colossians 2:3). The Spirit’s work is to show you what is already yours.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–33 — Sorrow Turned to Joy: I Have Overcome the World
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The disciples are puzzled by the little while. Jesus tells them their grief will turn to joy, as a woman’s labour gives way to the joy of a child, and that they will pray to a Father who himself loves them. When they declare that now they believe, he warns that they will scatter, and ends with peace in him and victory over the world.
verseByVerse.theology:
The second half of the chapter turns on time. Jesus speaks of what is coming as already settled: the ruler of this world is judged, and I have overcome the world, in the perfect tense, before the arrest. The church lives inside an outcome settled but not yet visible.

So the childbirth image governs the section: pain that turns out to have been the way the joy came. And prayer in Jesus’ name belongs here, not as a technique for extracting outcomes, but as the asking of people whose end is secured. Its stated goal in verse 24 is fullness of joy.
verseByVerse.examples:
In the world you will have tribulation (v. 33) stands against every version of Christianity that promises exemption. And it sits beside in me you may have peace without contradiction: two locations, and a believer is in both at once.

No one will take your joy from you (v. 22) is not a promise of cheerfulness. The joy is grounded in his seeing them, not in their managing to feel anything, which is why no one can confiscate it.

verseByVerse.quote: So some of his disciples said to one another, "What is this that he says to us, 'A little while, and you will not see me, and again a little while, and you will see me'; and, 'because I am going to the Father'?" So they were saying, "What does he mean by 'a little while'? We do not know what he is talking about."
verseByVerse.commentary:
What is this that he says to us? The disciples are puzzled, and whisper among themselves. John has recorded something almost comic and entirely human. They repeat the riddle back to each other, word for word, as though saying it again might help. They add the other thing he said, about going to the Father, in case it is a clue.

What does he mean by a little while? We do not know what he is talking about. And then they give up. An honest admission of confusion. The repetition of the phrase shows how much it bothered them. They could not imagine death and resurrection. And notice that they do not ask him. He is sitting there. They discuss it among themselves in what was probably an audible mutter, and John says he knew they wanted to ask, which means nobody did. Why not? Probably the same reason anybody sits on a question in a room where the mood has turned: it has been a long evening, they have already been told one of them is a traitor and that Peter will deny him, and asking would mean admitting in front of the others that they had not followed.

They had understood very little. After years of the best teaching ever given, on the final evening they cannot make out what he means: not the footwashing, not the vine, not the going away. Whatever is required to follow him, comprehension on the night is evidently not it. He did not wait for their comprehension before he loved them, died for them, and sent them.

The riddle answered by his own body. The puzzle they could not solve was not a puzzle of words. A little while, and you will see me no longer, was Friday’s tomb; again a little while, and you will see me, was Sunday’s garden. What changed these men was not a clearer sentence but Easter, and then the Spirit. Christ is himself the meaning of what he says, and those who cannot follow the words are carried through by the deed.

John’s own voice inside it. John was at the table that night (13:23), perhaps among the men muttering, and decades later he could have made the disciples look wiser. Instead he preserves the flat admission in the first person plural: we do not know what he is talking about.

Is it wrong to have doubts and questions about the faith? Questions are not the same as unbelief. These men loved Jesus and were confused, and he did not reject them for it. Thomas doubted, and Jesus came to meet him (20:27). The Psalms are full of honest questions put to God. What matters is where you take them. Bring them to Christ in prayer, to his word, and to mature believers, rather than nursing them in private or letting them harden into a reason to walk away. Some questions will be answered as you grow; some will wait for glory. Faith is not the absence of questions but trust in the Lord while you ask them.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus knew that they wanted to ask him, so he said to them, "Is this what you are asking yourselves, what I meant by saying, 'A little while and you will not see me, and again a little while and you will see me'? Truly, truly, I say to you, you will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice. You will be sorrowful, but your sorrow will turn into joy."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus knew. He answers the question they did not put, but not with the explanation they were after. They wanted the timetable decoded; he tells them instead what it is going to feel like, which is the thing they will actually need.

You will weep and lament. Weep is the ordinary word for shedding tears; lament is formal mourning, the wailing at a funeral. And at the cross the disciples will mourn while his enemies celebrate. Not only grief, but grief while other people were pleased.

Your sorrow will turn into joy. Not followed by joy, not replaced by joy, but turned into joy. The thing they wept over on the Friday is the thing the church has sung about ever since (Galatians 6:14). Nothing was deleted; the same event changed meaning.

A better promise. It does not say the bad thing will be compensated for later by a good thing, but that the bad thing will turn out to have been the good thing, seen from the wrong end. The disciples on the Saturday did not need a timetable. They needed to have been told, by somebody who knew it would happen, that what they were feeling was not the end of the story.

Does this mean every sorrow of mine will become joy? For the believer, yes, in God’s time, though not always in the way or on the timetable we would choose. God works all things together for good for those who love him (Romans 8:28), and the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory to be revealed (8:18). Some sorrows are turned within this life: a loss that later bears fruit, a trial that deepens faith. Others will be turned only when Christ returns and wipes away every tear (Revelation 21:4). But nothing a Christian suffers is wasted or final. The cross is the proof: if God could turn that into joy, he can turn yours.

For worship. The Man who made this promise walked into the sorrow first, and on the third day his own anguish was turned, not erased: the risen Lord still bore his wounds, and he showed his friends his hands and his side, and then they were glad (20:20). The scars that were the world’s triumph became the sight that filled them with joy. He does not ask us to forget the Friday. He shows us his hands.

parallels.desc: weeping may tarry for the night, but joy comes with the morning

verseByVerse.quote: "When a woman is giving birth, she has sorrow because her hour has come, but when she has delivered the baby, she no longer remembers the anguish, for joy that a human being has been born into the world. So also you have sorrow now, but I will see you again, and your hearts will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Her hour has come. That is his word, running through this Gospel since Cana and meaning, almost throughout, the cross. He now lends it to a woman in labour. It is an Old Testament picture for the pains that come before God’s new age (Isaiah 26:17–19; 66:7–14).

The pain is the way the joy arrives. Childbirth says that the pain is not incidental to the joy but is the way the joy arrives. Nobody gets the child by another route. The cross is the birth pang of the new creation.

She no longer remembers the anguish. The clause can be overstated: no mother forgets that labour hurt. What is meant is that the pain stops being the thing the day is about. It is displaced by something in the room that was not there before.

I will see you again. He will come to them in the resurrection (20:20), and the direction matters: not you will see me, as in verse 16, but he will see them. The joy is grounded in his looking at them, not in their managing to catch sight of him.

No one will take your joy. Not nothing: no one, and in a chapter that has just said the ruler of this world stands judged, that includes him. Joy grounded in the risen Christ cannot be taken away by persecution, loss or death; the apostles rejoiced after being flogged (Acts 5:41).

But I have lost my joy; was it taken? The joy itself, rooted in the risen Christ, cannot be taken, but your sense of it can be clouded: by sin, by sorrow, by exhaustion, by illness, by spiritual attack. David prayed, restore to me the joy of your salvation (Psalm 51:12), which shows that a true believer can lose the feeling and still have the salvation. Go back to the source. Confess any known sin. Rest your body if it is worn out. Get help if you are ill. Look again at the risen Christ in the Gospels, and keep company with his people. The joy has not been stolen; it is waiting where it always was, in him.

verseByVerse.quote: "In that day you will ask nothing of me. Truly, truly, I say to you, whatever you ask of the Father in my name, he will give it to you. Until now you have asked nothing in my name. Ask, and you will receive, that your joy may be full."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You will ask nothing of me. That day is after the resurrection, and English uses one word for two things. Ask here is erōtaō, which here means to ask a question, as in v. 19 (it can also mean to request, as in 14:16). They will no longer be confused, because the Spirit will teach them.

Whatever you ask of the Father. This ask is aiteō, to petition. So the sentence is not saying that prayer to Jesus will cease, but that the questions will stop. The interrogation ends; the asking begins. After Easter they ask about the timing once, and then go and preach (Acts 1:6–8). A new way of prayer opens: directly to the Father, in the name of the Son.

Until now you have asked nothing in my name. Prayer in Jesus’ name is new, made possible by his death and exaltation as our mediator (Hebrews 4:14–16). The disciples had prayed, but not yet on the ground of the Son’s completed work.

That your joy may be full. Prayer is presented not as a duty but as the pathway to the full joy Jesus has been promising throughout this discourse.

At full stretch. The promise must be handled honestly, because every Christian who has prayed for long has asked and not received: a parent for a dying child, a wife for twenty years for a husband who never turns. Left unqualified, the sentence hands such people a false hope or a private verdict on their own faith.

Not a formula. First, in my name means asking as his representative, for what he himself would ask (see 14:13–14): this is the confidence that we have toward him, that if we ask anything according to his will he hears us (1 John 5:14). The promise is not that God will do our will if we invoke the right name, but that he will not refuse his own.

The prayer he did not press. Second, Jesus had prayed such a prayer himself: now is my soul troubled. And what shall I say? Father, save me from this hour? And then he answered his own question: but for this purpose I have come to this hour (12:27). He raises the request and declines to press it, because there was something he wanted more. That is praying in his name from the inside. The Father did not save him from that hour, and the whole world was saved through it.

The stated end is joy. The stated end is joy, not delivery of goods. Some prayers God grants outright; some he answers with something better than we had the wit to ask for; and some he answers with himself, which is why saints who received almost nothing they asked for have so often been the gladdest people in the room. The prayer unanswered in the form we wanted has been taken up by a Father who is committed to the fullness of our joy and not merely to the shortening of our discomfort.

How do I pray in Jesus’ name in practice? Come to the Father as his child because of Christ, not because of your own record. Bring what is on your heart honestly; you do not have to tidy it first. Ask yourself whether what you are asking fits what Jesus loves and what Scripture promises, and let that shape your request. Pray for his kingdom and his glory first, as he taught in the Lord’s Prayer, and then for your daily needs without embarrassment. End with in Jesus’ name, not as a password but as a confession: I come only through him. Then trust the Father with the answer.

verseByVerse.quote: "I have said these things to you in figures of speech. The hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in figures of speech but will tell you plainly about the Father. In that day you will ask in my name, and I do not say to you that I will ask the Father on your behalf;"
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have said these things to you in figures of speech. Figures of speech (paroimiai) are veiled sayings, pictures: the same word John used of the shepherd discourse that nobody followed (10:6). The vine, the woman in labour, the shepherd, the bread: figures that point beyond themselves.

Plainly about the Father. After the resurrection, through the Spirit, the meaning of every figure will be plain, and the questions of the last night will stop.

I do not say that I will ask. The delicate clause sounds at first like a withdrawal of the intercession, and it is not. Hebrews says he always lives to make intercession (Hebrews 7:25), Paul that he is at the right hand of God interceding for us (Romans 8:34), and John’s own letter calls him our advocate with the Father (1 John 2:1). What he dismantles is a picture of prayer extracted by a sympathetic mediator from a reluctant judge. The Son’s mediation is not distance but access; the name of Jesus opens the door, and does not stand between the one praying and the Father. He says at once why that picture is wrong: the Father himself loves them (v. 27).

If the Father loves me, why do I need Jesus as mediator at all? Because the Father’s love for sinners is holy love. He loves us, and he will not pretend our sin is nothing. In Christ, love found a way to be just and to justify (Romans 3:26): the Father gave the Son, and the Son bore our sins, so that we could come near. Christ’s mediation is not the cause of the Father’s love but its gift. The Son did not die to make the Father love us; the Father sent the Son because he already loved us (3:16). So we need Jesus, and we need not fear the Father. Through the one we come confidently to the other.

In everyday life. If you tend to pray to Jesus but avoid addressing the Father, as though he were sterner, begin your prayer today with Father, and speak to him as a loved child.

verseByVerse.quote: "for the Father himself loves you, because you have loved me and have believed that I came from God. I came from the Father and have come into the world, and now I am leaving the world and going to the Father."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Father himself loves you. The emphatic himself is doing deliberate work: not because Jesus asks him to, but directly, without anything having to be arranged. Loves is phileō, warm affection. The Father sent the Son because he loved the world (3:16).

A common distortion. The picture of a severe Father and a merciful Son standing between us and him has no basis in this Gospel (14:9), and it makes prayer a kind of legal manoeuvre. There is nobody to be got round.

Because you have loved me and have believed that I came from God. Their love and faith are the evidence that they belong to the Father’s family, and themselves the fruit of his love.

Does the Father’s love, then, depend on ours? No. We love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19). Jesus is speaking of the Father’s fatherly delight and fellowship with those who love his Son (compare 14:21, 23), not of the love that chose them before they loved. Their love for Jesus is itself the fruit of God’s love, and the Father rejoices in it.

I came from the Father. The whole of Jesus’ mission in one sentence, in four movements: his pre-existence with the Father, the incarnation, the cross, and the resurrection and ascension. A creed before there were creeds, said at a supper table, and the disciples’ response is the first sign all evening that something has got through. The Son came down from the Father’s side into our world, walked our roads, went to our cross, and returned to the Father, all to bring us into the love that was there before the world began.

How can I believe the Father loves me when I feel so far from him? Look not first at your feelings but at what he has done. The Father sent his Son into the world for you; that is how you know the love of God (1 John 4:9–10). He has given you his Spirit, who cries Abba, Father, in your heart (Galatians 4:6), even when your own voice is weak. He has adopted you, and a father does not disown his child on a bad day. Feelings of distance are real and painful, and the Psalms are full of them, but they are not the measure of his love. The cross is. Speak to him as Father even when it feels hollow, and let his word, not your mood, tell you who you are.

verseByVerse.quote: His disciples said, "Ah, now you are speaking plainly and not using figurative speech! Now we know that you know all things and do not need anyone to question you; this is why we believe that you came from God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now you are speaking plainly. Touching and slightly absurd: they say it after a sentence arguably no plainer than anything else he has said that evening. They have not solved the riddle; something has simply landed, and the relief in their voices is audible.

You know all things. What has convinced them is not the vine or the Spirit but that he answered the question they had not asked aloud (v. 19). It is a real thing to have noticed, and it is a very small basis for what is coming.

This is why we believe. A real confession, but their confidence is ahead of their understanding. The faith they express is genuine but not yet refined by the fire of the passion.

Lighter than it feels. Faith attaches itself to the evidence in front of it: an answered prayer, a coincidence too neat to dismiss. None of that is false. It is simply lighter than it feels, and the weight it will have to carry is not known in advance. Jesus does not disparage their confession. He asks one question about it, and then tells them what will happen before dawn.

Is my faith real if it is weak and untested? Yes. These men truly believed, and Jesus prayed for them as those the Father had given him (17:6–8). Weak faith in a strong Saviour saves, because it is the Saviour who saves, not the strength of the faith. But faith grows by being tested, and God will test it, not to break it but to deepen it (1 Peter 1:6–7; James 1:2–4). So do not despise your faith for being small, and do not trust it for being fervent. Trust Christ, and let him strengthen it through the trials he sends.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered them, "Do you now believe? Behold, the hour is coming, indeed it has come, when you will be scattered, each to his own home, and will leave me alone. Yet I am not alone, for the Father is with me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do you now believe? The Greek can be read as a question or a flat statement, so now you believe, and either way there is no mockery in it. Not doubting their faith, but warning them of its weakness. He does not say they are wrong. He says what their believing is about to do.

You will be scattered. The language is Zechariah’s: strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered (Zechariah 13:7; Matthew 26:31). And the detail is what makes it hurt: each to his own home. They will simply go back to where they came from, individually, the way people do when something ends.

And will leave me alone. All of them would run. The specificity of the prediction is its own kind of mercy: Jesus is not surprised by their failure; he has accounted for it in advance.

Yet I am not alone. The Father never leaves him (8:29). This sentence has to be handled with great care, because it stands a few hours from a cry that appears to contradict it. What then of his cry from the cross that God had forsaken him (Mark 15:34)? Both are true, and the church has generally held them together rather than choosing. The abandonment at Golgotha is real: it is the sin-bearing, the cup, the thing he asked to be spared. Yet even there the Father’s love for the Son never ceased, and the unity of the Trinity was never broken. It is the Son experiencing, in our place, the one thing he had never known. Jesus could still say my God and, at the end, Father, into your hands (Luke 23:46).

Why the words here are not made false. What happens on the Friday is the specific, temporary, substitutionary exception, and it fell on him precisely so that it would never fall on them.

What if I feel completely alone? Then you are in the place where Jesus has been, and where he has promised to meet you. He knows what it is to have every friend go home. And he knows, in a way nobody else ever will, what it is to bear the Father’s turning away, which means that the promise I will never leave you nor forsake you (Hebrews 13:5) is not a slogan. It cost something to be able to say it. If you are in Christ, the Father is with you as he was with his Son, and he will never forsake you, because the forsaking was borne for you. Tell him how alone you feel. Then reach out to his people; loneliness often lies to us about who would gladly come.

For worship. The Shepherd did not stop loving the sheep he knew would scatter. He went on alone to bear the stroke Zechariah foretold, and to drink a cup no friend could share. Then he came back, and found them behind locked doors, and stood among them and said, Peace be with you (20:19). The flock that ran has been gathering ever since, around the Shepherd who was left alone so that none of his own ever will be.

parallels.desc: strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered

verseByVerse.quote: "I have said these things to you, that in me you may have peace. In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
That in me you may have peace. The purpose of the whole farewell discourse is peace, and the location comes first: not in circumstances, but in me, the preposition of the vine chapter. The peace does not depend on the world outside, because it is not stored there.

In the world you will have tribulation. Tribulation (thlipsis) is pressure, distress, affliction: the same word used of the woman in labour in verse 21. And the verb is not might, but will (Acts 14:22).

Two locations. The two prepositions stand side by side. In me, peace. In the world, tribulation. Both are true at once of the same people, which is why a Christian life so often feels like two contradictory reports about the same afternoon.

I have overcome the world. Take heart (tharseite) means be courageous. And the tense is the thing: I have overcome (nenikēka) is a completed victory with lasting effect, said before the arrest, the trial and the nails. By the cross and resurrection he has defeated sin, death and Satan. John uses its noun in his letter: this is the victory that has overcome the world, our faith (1 John 5:4). His people share in his victory (Revelation 3:21).

The order of the verse. The trouble is guaranteed, the peace is available, and the outcome was settled before the fight started. He does not promise to remove the tribulation; he tells them where the peace is kept and who has already won. Anxiety often demands a life it can control and keep free of trouble, and Jesus never offers that. He offers himself, and a victory that does not depend on our keeping anything under control.

Before the prayer. The next words out of his mouth are a prayer. By any measure that evening he had overcome nothing yet. The crowds were gone, the traitor was out arranging the arrest, the eleven were about to scatter to their own homes, and he himself would be dead within a day. And he says it in the perfect tense, finished, standing, done, with the whole of it still in front of him, because he had never once been in any doubt about how it ends.

If Jesus has overcome the world, why do I keep losing? Because the victory is his before it is yours, and you are living in the time between the decisive battle and the final peace. The world still presses, sin still wounds, and you will sometimes fall. But the outcome is not in doubt, because it does not rest on your strength but on what he has already done. Your faith joins you to the Victor (1 John 5:4–5), and he will finish the work he began. So fight, but fight from victory, not for it. When you fall, get up in his strength, not yours. The last chapter is already written, and in it the Lamb has conquered.

In everyday life. When trouble comes today, say both halves of the verse: in the world I have tribulation; in him I have peace. Then do the next right thing with the courage his Spirit gives.

parallels.desc: the victory that has overcome the world

16.text: <sup>1</sup>“I have said all these things to you to keep you from falling away.<sup>2</sup>They will put you out of the synagogues. Indeed, the hour is coming when whoever kills you will think he is offering service to God.<sup>3</sup>And they will do these things because they have not known the Father, nor me.<sup>4</sup>But I have said these things to you, that when their hour comes you may remember that I told them to you. “I did not say these things to you from the beginning, because I was with you.<sup>5</sup>But now I am going to him who sent me, and none of you asks me, ’Where are you going?’<sup>6</sup>But because I have said these things to you, sorrow has filled your heart.<sup>7</sup>Nevertheless, I tell you the truth: it is to your advantage that I go away, for if I do not go away, the Helper will not come to you. But if I go, I will send him to you.<sup>8</sup>And when he comes, he will convict the world concerning sin and righteousness and judgment:<sup>9</sup>concerning sin, because they do not believe in me;<sup>10</sup>concerning righteousness, because I go to the Father, and you will see me no longer;<sup>11</sup>concerning judgment, because the ruler of this world is judged.<sup>12</sup>“I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now.<sup>13</sup>When the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all the truth, for he will not speak on his own authority, but whatever he hears he will speak, and he will declare to you the things that are to come.<sup>14</sup>He will glorify me, for he will take what is mine and declare it to you.<sup>15</sup>All that the Father has is mine; therefore I said that he will take what is mine and declare it to you.<sup>16</sup>“A little while, and you will see me no longer; and again a little while, and you will see me.”<sup>17</sup>So some of his disciples said to one another, “What is this that he says to us, ’A little while, and you will not see me, and again a little while, and you will see me’; and, ’because I am going to the Father’?”<sup>18</sup>So they were saying, “What does he mean by ’a little while’? We do not know what he is talking about.”<sup>19</sup>Jesus knew that they wanted to ask him, so he said to them, “Is this what you are asking yourselves, what I meant by saying, ’A little while and you will not see me, and again a little while and you will see me’?<sup>20</sup>Truly, truly, I say to you, you will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice. You will be sorrowful, but your sorrow will turn into joy.<sup>21</sup>When a woman is giving birth, she has sorrow because her hour has come, but when she has delivered the baby, she no longer remembers the anguish, for joy that a human being has been born into the world.<sup>22</sup>So also you have sorrow now, but I will see you again, and your hearts will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you.<sup>23</sup>In that day you will ask nothing of me. Truly, truly, I say to you, whatever you ask of the Father in my name, he will give it to you.<sup>24</sup>Until now you have asked nothing in my name. Ask, and you will receive, that your joy may be full.<sup>25</sup>“I have said these things to you in figures of speech. The hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in figures of speech but will tell you plainly about the Father.<sup>26</sup>In that day you will ask in my name, and I do not say to you that I will ask the Father on your behalf;<sup>27</sup>for the Father himself loves you, because you have loved me and have believed that I came from God.<sup>28</sup>I came from the Father and have come into the world, and now I am leaving the world and going to the Father.”<sup>29</sup>His disciples said, “Ah, now you are speaking plainly and not using figurative speech!<sup>30</sup>Now we know that you know all things and do not need anyone to question you; this is why we believe that you came from God.”<sup>31</sup>Jesus answered them, “Do you now believe?<sup>32</sup>Behold, the hour is coming, indeed it has come, when you will be scattered, each to his own home, and will leave me alone. Yet I am not alone, for the Father is with me.<sup>33</sup>I have said these things to you, that in me you may have peace. In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world.”
16.overview:
Jesus warns his disciples plainly so that persecution, even persecution in God’s name, will not make them fall away. His going fills them with sorrow, but it is for their good, for unless he goes the Helper will not come. The Spirit will convict the world concerning sin, righteousness and judgment, and will guide the apostles into all the truth, glorifying Christ.

Then Jesus speaks of “a little while”, and with the picture of a woman in labour promises that their grief will be turned into a joy no one can take. They will pray to the Father in his name, for the Father himself loves them. He foretells that they will scatter and leave him alone, yet he is not alone. His last words before his prayer are a promise for every age: “In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world.”

17.title: The High-Priestly Prayer

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–26 — Jesus Prays for Himself, the Disciples, and All Believers
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The prayer moves outward in three circles. Jesus asks to be glorified in the hour that has come, and defines eternal life as knowing the Father and the Son he sent. He asks that the disciples be kept, made holy by the word, and sent into a hostile world as he was sent. Then he prays for every later believer: that they may be one, so that the world may believe, and that they may be with him to see his glory. It ends with the Father’s love, and the Son himself, dwelling in his people.
verseByVerse.theology: The prayer recalls the high priest entering the Most Holy Place on the Day of Atonement. Jesus is both priest and sacrifice: he intercedes for his people while preparing himself for the offering that will accomplish what he asks. What he asks for them, protection (v. 11), joy (v. 13), holiness (v. 17) and unity (vv. 21–23), is what the church still lives on.
verseByVerse.examples: That they may be one, as we are one (v. 22): the unity Jesus prays for is patterned on, and drawn from, the unity of the Father and the Son. It is a shared life of love and purpose, not one organisation. It is also how the world is meant to see the truth (vv. 21, 23), so a church at war with itself undercuts its own witness. In Jesus’ prayer, unity and mission belong together.

verseByVerse.quote: When Jesus had spoken these words, he lifted up his eyes to heaven, and said, "Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son that the Son may glorify you, since you have given him authority over all flesh, to give eternal life to all whom you have given him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. John 17 is often called Jesus’ high priestly prayer: he prays as the great High Priest for his people before offering himself as their sacrifice. Like the high priest who carried the names of the tribes on his heart into the holy place (Exodus 28:29), Jesus carries his people before the Father. He prays for himself (vv. 1–5), for his disciples (vv. 6–19), and for all who will believe through them (vv. 20–26). It is his longest recorded prayer, and it lets us overhear the conversation within the Trinity, spoken aloud in his friends’ hearing within the hour of his arrest.

He lifted up his eyes to heaven. Eyes open, head up, looking: a common Jewish posture in prayer; the bowed head and closed eyes are a later Christian habit, good in its place but not a biblical instruction. He did the same at the tomb of Lazarus (11:41). This is not a man with his face in his hands, but a man looking his Father in the face on the last evening of his life.

The Son who looks up and the sinner who cannot. Set beside him the one man in the Gospels who could not do it: the tax collector in the parable, who would not even lift up his eyes to heaven, but beat his breast (Luke 18:13). Both were heard: a Son who looks up because he has every right to, and a sinner who cannot because he has none, and the Father receives them both, the second because of the first.

Father. Six times in this prayer he says it, and twice with an adjective: Holy Father at verse 11 and righteous Father at verse 25, forms of address found nowhere else in the Bible. It is the family word he taught his disciples, qualified only where the petition needs it.

The hour has come. The hour so long awaited closes a thread that has run the whole length of the book. Three times it was not yet: at Cana to his mother (2:4), and twice when men tried to seize him and could not (7:30; 8:20). Then, from the arrival of the Greeks onward, it has come (12:23, 27; 13:1; and here). For three years the not-yet was a protection; no hand could touch him before his Father’s time. The first thing he does with the news is pray.

Glorify your Son. Not a selfish prayer. The Son asks to be glorified in his death, resurrection and exaltation, so that he can glorify the Father. Their glory is one, and the glorifying begins not on a throne but on a cross. In this Gospel the lifting up on the cross is the beginning of the lifting up to glory (3:14; 12:32–33). The Father’s glory is the shining out of who he is, and nowhere does he show what he is more fully than in the hour when he gives his Son for sinners. The Son is asking to be the place where that is seen.

Authority over all flesh. All humanity answers to the Son (Matthew 28:18). The man about to be bound and led from court to court is the one to whom every human being in those courts already answers. He holds authority over every human being who has ever lived, and he uses it to give life.

All whom you have given him. The Father’s giving of a people to the Son runs right through this prayer (vv. 2, 6, 9, 24). His authority is universal; his saving gift is particular. Before anything was made (v. 24; Ephesians 1:4), the Father and the Son agreed together on the rescue of a particular people, the Father giving them and the Son undertaking to save them, so that every believer’s salvation was planned in love before he existed. Some read given as those the Father foresaw would believe. But Jesus will say, I am not praying for the world but for those whom you have given me (v. 9), which shows that the giving is the Father’s choice, not merely his foresight. And none of those given will fail to receive what the Son was given authority to give (6:37–39).

If some are given, can I know whether I am one of them? You do not find out by looking into the secret counsel of God; you find out by coming to Christ. The same Jesus who spoke of those the Father gives him said in the same breath, whoever comes to me I will never cast out (6:37). The giving is the hidden root; the coming is the visible fruit. Nobody has ever come to Christ and been turned away because his name was missing from a list. If you are coming to him, trusting him, wanting him, that is how the Father’s gift shows itself in a human life. Election is not a wall to keep anyone out. It is the reason anyone comes in at all.

In everyday life. Pray with your eyes on the Father, not on yourself. Before you bring him a list, say his name the way a child does, and remember who taught you to say it. When the hour you have been dreading arrives, speak to your Father first, and ask that he be glorified in it.
verseByVerse.note: John 17 is often called Jesus’ high priestly prayer: he prays for himself, his disciples and all future believers.

verseByVerse.quote: "And this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent. I glorified you on earth, having accomplished the work that you gave me to do."
verseByVerse.commentary:
That they know you. Verse 3 is the nearest thing to a definition of eternal life anywhere in Scripture, and it is not the definition most people carry. Not living for ever, nor going to heaven when you die, though both are true. Eternal life is knowing, and the verb (ginōskō) here means the knowledge of a person rather than of a subject (Jeremiah 31:34; Hosea 6:6). It is the word of the new covenant promise: they shall all know me.

Eternal life has already begun. First, eternal life has already started for anyone who has it. Because it is a relationship, it begins when the relationship does, the moment we come to know God, and dying does not interrupt it. That is precisely what he told Martha at the tomb: everyone who lives and believes in me shall never die (11:25–26). It grows for ever, but it does not wait.

What makes eternal life eternal. Second, and more searching: endless existence without God, every faculty intact, would not on this verse’s terms be life at all. What makes eternal life eternal is not the length of it but who is in it. Heaven without God would be a long exile; a cell with God in it is already the beginning of heaven.

The only true God. This verse is sometimes used against the deity of Christ, as though the only true God excluded Jesus. But the sentence makes knowing Jesus Christ part of the definition of eternal life, standing in the same clause and joined by and to knowing the only true God. No monotheist would put a creature there. He does not deny his own deity by calling the Father the only true God; he denies the idols. The Son is included within the one true God (1:1). And John, who wrote this sentence, wrote in his letter of the Son: “He is the true God and eternal life” (1 John 5:20), using the same two words. The verse distinguishes the Father from the Son, which orthodoxy has always done. It does not divide them.

Jesus Christ. This is the only place in the Gospels where Jesus uses the full name Jesus Christ of himself. Some think John has phrased his Lord’s words for readers a generation later, which would be in keeping with how he writes. Nothing turns on it.

Having accomplished the work. The verb means completed, finished, from the same family as the cry “It is finished” (19:30). He speaks from the threshold of the cross as though it were behind him, because his obedience was already settled: there was no part of the Father’s will he would leave undone. Every hour of thirty-odd years was offered to the Father without a single failure. No other human being has ever been able to say, I glorified you on earth, without needing to add a confession.

How do I actually get to know God better? The same way you come to know anyone: by listening to him, speaking with him, and spending time in his company. He speaks in Scripture, so read it not only to learn facts but to meet him; ask as you read, what does this show me of God and of Christ? Speak to him in prayer, honestly, as a child does. Meet him with his people at his table and under his preached word. And obey what you learn, because Jesus said the one who keeps his commands is the one to whom he shows himself (14:21). Knowledge of God grows slowly, like a friendship, and it grows most in the hard seasons when he is all you have.

Is it not narrow to say eternal life comes only by knowing Jesus Christ? It is narrow in the way any true answer is narrow. If eternal life is a relationship with God, the question is not which religion is most sincere but whether God can be known at all, and Jesus says he is known in the one he sent (14:6). Every other road asks us to climb up to God by devotion or goodness, which favours the disciplined and the respectable and leaves everyone else without hope. This road is open to the worst sinner, and closed only to the person who insists on coming as anything other than a receiver. A door that only God could open, held open to anyone who will come, is not arrogance. It is mercy.

For worship. The God who made the galaxies has made himself knowable, and the knowing of him is life itself. He did not leave us to guess at him. He sent his Son, the only man who could tell the Father that he had glorified him on earth with nothing left undone, and that finished obedience is credited to people whose obedience is full of holes. To know the only true God in the face of Jesus Christ is to have begun a life that will outlast the stars, because the One we know has no end.
verseByVerse.note: “Know” in the Bible means a personal relationship, not mere information.

parallels.desc: that he understands and knows me
“It is finished”

verseByVerse.quote: "And now, Father, glorify me in your own presence with the glory that I had with you before the world existed. I have manifested your name to the people whom you gave me out of the world. Yours they were, and you gave them to me, and they have kept your word."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The glory that I had with you. No prophet ever prayed anything like it. Moses asked to see God’s glory; this is a man asking for his own back. And the claim inside the request is the whole of the Prologue in a single clause: he had glory, with the Father, before there was a world to have it in. It is one of the clearest statements of Christ’s eternal pre-existence. God says he will not give his glory to another (Isaiah 42:8). So the Son is not another; he is God.

With you. The same thought as 1:1: glory possessed alongside the Father when nothing else existed. The Son did not begin at Bethlehem. He came from somewhere, and he is about to go back. Before the first star burned, the Son was face to face with the Father in a glory no creature had seen.

The glory set down. In the incarnation he veiled that glory: he did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself (Philippians 2:6–7). Now he asks for it back, and asks to return to it now in his human nature as well. The one who goes back to the Father’s presence goes back with hands that were pierced and a body that was raised. Our flesh has entered that glory in him.

Did Jesus stop being God when he laid his glory aside? No. He did not lay aside his deity; he laid aside the open display of it. He remained what he always was while becoming what he was not, a man. The emptying of Philippians 2 is explained by the next words, taking the form of a servant: he emptied himself by adding, not by subtracting. So even in the manger and on the cross he was the eternal Son, upholding all things (Hebrews 1:3). The glory was hidden, as the sun is hidden behind cloud. At times it broke through, at Cana, on the mountain, at the tomb of Lazarus. Here he asks for the cloud to be taken away.

Your name. The name is God’s character, all that he is (1:18). The whole ministry of Jesus, teaching, signs, foot-washing and finally the cross, is the disclosure of the Father’s name.

Yours they were, and you gave them to me. They belonged to the Father before they belonged to the Son. Chosen before they came (6:37; Ephesians 1:4), they are first the Father’s and then, by gift, the Son’s. Election is the Father’s prior claim on the people the Son will redeem.

They have kept your word. This is startlingly generous. Eleven men who have understood very little all evening, who, Luke tells us, argued that same night about which of them was the greatest (Luke 22:24), who will soon run into the dark, and one of whom will deny knowing him three times before the cock crows. And his report to his Father: not they are trying, but they have kept your word.

How he measures his people. He is not blind, and he is not flattering. He is describing them as what they had become by receiving his word, which is a different measurement from the one we habitually run on ourselves.

Does this mean my sin does not matter to him? No. He grieves over it and he will deal with it; after the resurrection, beside the Sea of Galilee, he will restore Peter by name, and it will hurt (21:15–17). But he does not define his people by their failures. He defines them by what grace has made them: people who have received his word and are his. That should make you more serious about sin, not less, because you are being treated as something better than your worst nights. And it should silence the voice that tells you that your stumbles prove you were never his.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now they know that everything that you have given me is from you. For I have given them the words that you gave me, and they have received them and have come to know in truth that I came from you; and they have believed that you sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything is from you. The teaching, the signs, the authority, the men themselves. Nothing in the ministry of Jesus came from him acting on his own, apart from the Father (5:19), and the disciples have finally grasped it, on the last night, not long before their nerve fails them.

Given, received, known, believed. The chain runs Father to Son, Son to disciples, and through them to us. Faith begins by receiving: not by inventing God’s word or improving it, but by taking what is handed over.

Knowing before believing. Knowing comes before believing here. They came to know that I came from you: his origin. They believed that you sent me: his commission. The recognition of who he is precedes the trust in what he was sent to do, and both rest on words that were handed over rather than worked out. In his report to the Father all four verbs are completed actions, credited in full; he knew what the next few hours would show, and he still said it.

Two errors corrected at once. Faith is not a leap in the absence of content, nor a conclusion of unaided reasoning, since the words came from outside. Christian faith is neither blind nor self-made. It is the open-eyed reception of what God has said.

My faith feels nothing like as solid as that. Does it count? Yes. The disciples’ faith that night was real, and within an hour it was shaking badly. Jesus called it faith anyway, because faith is measured by its object, not by its strength. A trembling hand that grasps a strong rope is as safe as a steady one. If you have received his words as true, if you believe that Jesus came from God and that the Father sent him to save sinners, you have the faith this verse describes, however weak it feels. Feed it with the same words that created it, and ask him, as a father once did, to help your unbelief (Mark 9:24).

verseByVerse.quote: "I am praying for them. I am not praying for the world but for those whom you have given me, for they are yours. All mine are yours, and yours are mine, and I am glorified in them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am praying for them. I am not praying for the world. It is the coldest-sounding sentence in the warmest chapter in the Bible. Jesus’ high priestly intercession here is particular: for those the Father has given him. That does not mean he never prayed for unbelievers (Luke 23:34), or that we should not (1 Timothy 2:1). But his intercession as High Priest, which secures salvation, is for his own (Hebrews 7:25; Romans 8:34). His sacrifice and his intercession have the same scope. He prays for those for whom he dies, and he dies for those for whom he prays. Reformed readers see here strong support for definite atonement: that when Christ died he intended actually to save a particular people, those the Father had given him, and not merely to make salvation possible for everyone and then wait to see who would take it. His death and his prayers aim at the same people, and they do not miss (10:11, 15). Many faithful Christians read the matter differently, holding that Christ died for every person alike and pointing to verses such as 1 John 2:2; they are brothers in the same gospel, and the question is how to hold those verses together with this prayer, where the High Priest’s pleading has a definite people in view.

What the sentence is. Three things help. First, a statement about the scope of this petition, not about the heart of the one praying. He is asking for something specific, that these men be kept, and that what he is about to do for them be applied to them, and the world that is rejecting him cannot be the subject of that request.

The world in the same prayer. Second, the same prayer turns to the world twice, a few verses on: so that the world may believe that you have sent me (v. 21); so that the world may know (v. 23). The unity he asks for is asked for the world’s sake. He prays for his church in order to reach the world.

Father, forgive them. Third, within hours the man who said I am not praying for the world would be praying, out loud, from a cross, for the men driving the nails: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34). (These words are missing from some early manuscripts of Luke, but many scholars judge them original and most Bibles print them.) That is not indifference. So the verse says that there is a particular intercession which has a particular object, and the object is the people the Father gave him. This is the High Priest with the names on his breastplate. He is praying for named individuals, and the naming is the comfort rather than the offence.

For they are yours. He pleads for them on the ground that they belong to the Father. The argument is the argument of a son to a father: these are yours; take care of what is yours.

All mine are yours, and yours are mine. Any of us could say the first half; nobody else can say the second. Yours are mine is a claim to hold the Father’s property as one’s own (16:15). Luther is said to have observed that no creature could utter it. It is the language of perfect equality, spoken quietly as a matter of course. All that the Father has is his, and all that he has he spends on the people he was given.

I am glorified in them. Their existence is his ongoing glory: an exhibition of what grace produces in those who receive it. The eleven are not much to look at tonight, and he says he is glorified in them anyway, as a craftsman is honoured by the work still on his bench.

Is Jesus praying for me now? Yes, if you are his. He always lives to make intercession for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25), and Paul names it as one of the reasons no one can condemn us: Christ Jesus is the one who died, was raised, is at the right hand of God, and indeed is interceding for us (Romans 8:34). His intercession is not a nervous pleading with a reluctant Father; it is the risen Son presenting his finished sacrifice for the people it was offered for, and asking for what it purchased. It is never refused. On the days you cannot pray, he is not silent.

Then should I pray only for Christians? No. The Son’s high priestly intercession is unique to him, and it is not our pattern for every prayer. We are told to pray for all people, kings and those in authority included (1 Timothy 2:1–4), to pray for our enemies (Matthew 5:44), and to plead for the lost as Paul did for Israel (Romans 10:1). We do not know who the Father has given to the Son, so we pray for everyone and preach to everyone, trusting that he will call his own through those prayers and that preaching.

verseByVerse.quote: "And I am no longer in the world, but they are in the world, and I am coming to you. Holy Father, keep them in your name, which you have given me, that they may be one, even as we are one. While I was with them, I kept them in your name, which you have given me. I have guarded them, and not one of them has been lost except the son of destruction, that the Scripture might be fulfilled."
verseByVerse.commentary:
No longer in the world. He speaks as if already gone, and he knows exactly what a hostile world will cost them. Everything he now asks for them is asked with that picture before him: his friends left behind, in enemy country.

Holy Father. He has been saying Father all evening. Here he adds holy, and the reason is in the petition attached: he is asking that these men be kept in a world that is unholy, and that they be made one. The God whose presence on Sinai could not be approached without washing and warning (Exodus 19:10–13) is Father to men like the eleven: that is grace. Keep means guard, protect, preserve. (Where the ESV reads your name, which you have given me, the KJV, following later manuscripts, reads those whom thou hast given me; the earliest manuscripts speak of the name given to the Son.) In your name means by the power of who you are, and in loyalty to your revealed character. This is the basis of their perseverance: those whom God has given to Christ will be kept in faith to the end. They may stumble badly, as Peter did that very night, but they will not finally fall away, because the one who began a good work in them will bring it to completion (Philippians 1:6).
