Our perseverance is not the story of how tightly we held on. It is the story of a Father who keeps, and a Son who guards, and a name that has never once failed those who are kept in it.

Which you have given me. The Father has given the Son his name: the divine name (Philippians 2:9–11). The Son keeps his people by the same name in which he reveals the Father, the name above every name.

That they may be one. The goal of their preservation is unity modelled on the Trinity: not organisational sameness, but the unity of shared life, love and purpose that the Father and Son have always had.

The son of destruction. The Greek plays on one root (apōleto, apōleias): Not one was lost except the son of lostness. “Son of destruction” is a Hebrew way of describing one who belongs to destruction and is destined for it; the phrase turns up once more in the New Testament, for the man of lawlessness (2 Thessalonians 2:3). It is Judas. He was never one of those truly given; he was lost because he never truly belonged (6:64, 70).

That the Scripture might be fulfilled. The Scripture Jesus means is probably the psalm he quoted of Judas earlier that same evening: “Even my close friend in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me” (Psalm 41:9). Jesus did not fail to keep him; Judas’s end shows his own guilt and God’s sovereign purpose, both together.

Was Judas free? The hard question must not be dodged. Two things have to be held, and the New Testament holds them both without visible strain. Judas is never once described as a victim. He is called a thief who helped himself to the money bag (12:6), Satan enters him after he takes the morsel (13:27), and Peter says he turned aside to go to his own place (Acts 1:25): his own, chosen, fitting. Nothing in any account treats him as a man who wanted otherwise. And equally, Scripture had said it would happen, and Peter at Pentecost says the whole event went forward according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, in the same breath as you crucified and killed him by the hands of lawless men (Acts 2:23). What Scripture never does is derive one from the other. It does not say Judas betrayed him because it was written; it says it was written, and he did it, and both are true. Anyone who claims to have resolved that has almost certainly done so by quietly dropping one half.

Could I be the one exception, like Judas? The verse is not given to help us classify anybody, still less to frighten the trembling. It is given to explain why the keeping did not fail: I have guarded them, and not one of them has been lost. The exception is the man who was never inside the guarding in the first place. Judas loved money, kept his heart closed, and never came to Jesus in sorrow; even his remorse took him away from Christ rather than to him (Matthew 27:3–5). If you fear that you might be a hypocrite and run to Christ with that fear, you are doing the one thing Judas never did. The sheep who worry that they are goats are seldom goats. Bring your fear to the Shepherd, and let his keeping be your confidence.
verseByVerse.note: “Son of destruction” describes one destined for destruction — Judas.

verseByVerse.quote: "But now I am coming to you, and these things I speak in the world, that they may have my joy fulfilled in themselves. I have given them your word, and the world has hated them because they are not of the world, just as I am not of the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
My joy fulfilled. He is praying, they are listening, and he says he prays aloud for their sake (15:11). It is a genuine prayer, and he wanted them to overhear it.

Overheard love. Consider the difference between somebody telling you that they value you, and overhearing them say it to a third party when they did not know you were listening. The second is the one that lands. Everything in it about their being given to him, kept, loved and sent, they heard him say to his Father, and they were meant to spend the rest of their lives remembering what he said about them when he was talking to God. John did remember, and wrote it down, so that we could overhear it too.

My joy. Joy has come up again and again in the last hour (15:11; 16:20–24; and here). He keeps returning to it on the worst night of his life. And it is his joy he gives: not a mood they must manufacture, but the joy of the Son in the Father’s love and in doing the Father’s will. That joy did not leave him in the garden. It was the joy set before him for which he endured the cross (Hebrews 12:2). The world can take a great deal from the people of God, but it cannot reach the joy that lives in the heart of the Son, and that is the joy he has given.

The world has hated them. The sober half. The word they received sets them apart, and draws the world’s hatred. He does not pray it away; he states it as the present condition and moves on.

Not of the world. Their origin is now from above, like his (3:3). The new birth has made them citizens of another country, and the world can sense it. They are hated not because they are odd but because they belong to the one the world rejected.

Why does the world hate Christians, and what if I am not hated? The world’s hatred is first a hatred of Christ, and it falls on his people because they carry his word (15:18–20). It does not always look like persecution; often it is scorn, exclusion, or simply being left out. And many Christians in many places live quietly with kind neighbours, which is a mercy to be thankful for, not a sign of failure. But if your faith never costs you anything, it is worth asking whether anyone can see it. Do not court hostility by being unpleasant; Peter says we should suffer as Christians, not as wrongdoers or meddlers (1 Peter 4:15–16). Simply be faithful, and let the response be his business.

In everyday life. Take the joy he gives into the place where you are least welcome as a Christian: the office where your faith is mocked, the family gathering where it is ignored. Joy is not denial of the hostility; it is a deeper possession that the hostility cannot reach.

verseByVerse.quote: "I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you keep them from the evil one. They are not of the world, just as I am not of the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not out of the world. This verse settles what a Christian is to do with the world by refusing both of the available shortcuts, for his people must stay in the world for their mission (v. 18). The first shortcut is withdrawal: the compound, the Christian bubble, the instinct to arrange a life in which one need never deal with anybody who does not already agree. It is not wicked, usually driven by a desire not to be defiled; but he declines to ask for it, though the men he loved were about to be hunted.

From the evil one. The evil one is Satan (1 John 5:18–19), and the danger is not the world itself but the one who works in it. The Greek could also be rendered from evil, as in the Lord’s Prayer (Matthew 6:13). Either way, behind the evil stands the evil one, and the Father’s keeping is the answer to his strategy.

Protection, not exemption. Not that nothing will happen to them: a great deal did, and, as early tradition tells it, most of them died for it. But that the one who wants them will not get them. Satan may sift them like wheat (Luke 22:31); he will not keep them. A Christian can lose his job, his health, his life for Christ, and lose nothing that the evil one was after.

In, not of. The second shortcut is assimilation, and this verse blocks it. Staying in the world is not the same as belonging to it. The position he prays for is the uncomfortable middle. Its practical shape is not withdrawal from the neighbours but a difference in what one is loyal to, which is much harder to arrange and impossible to fake. They are citizens of heaven on embassy in the world.

Where Christians differ: separation from the world. Some Christians have sought holiness by withdrawing from society; others have so blended in that no difference remains. This commentary’s view: Jesus prays for neither. His people are to live in the world, engaged in its life, but distinct in character and loyalty, kept by God from evil. Not monasteries, nor conformity, but holy presence.

So is it wrong to protect my children or avoid certain places? No. Wisdom is not withdrawal. Parents rightly guard young children from what would harm them, and every Christian should flee situations that feed his own particular temptations (2 Timothy 2:22). The question is direction and purpose. Are you sheltering in order to grow strong enough to go out, or hiding so that you never have to? Christian schooling, careful choices about entertainment, a decision not to take a job that would compromise you: none of these is the error Jesus refuses. The error is a life that has no unbelieving friends, no presence among the lost, and no intention of having any. He sends his people in, and he keeps them while they are there.

For worship. The Son who had every reason to ask that his friends be taken out of danger asked instead that they be kept in it. And through two thousand years of hostility his church has never been taken out of the world nor swallowed by it. The evil one is strong, but he has never yet taken from the Father one whom the Father was asked to keep. Our safety is not distance from danger. It is the hand of God.

parallels.desc: deliver us from evil

verseByVerse.quote: "Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth. As you sent me into the world, so I have sent them into the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sanctify them. Sanctify is not first a moral word. Hagiazō means to set apart for a purpose: it is what was done to vessels, to a day, to a priest. The moral content follows from the setting apart rather than the other way round: a thing devoted to God must then be fit for him. So to sanctify is both a status (set apart, 1 Corinthians 6:11) and a process (made holy, 1 Thessalonians 5:23). The petition is not first make them better but make them yours, for this work, which is exactly why the next verse is about being sent.

Your word is truth. Not your word is true, which would be a claim about accuracy, though it is accurate. Your word is truth: a noun, not an adjective. It is the thing reality is measured by. We grow in holiness as we are shaped by God’s word (Psalm 119:9, 11; Ephesians 5:26; 2 Timothy 3:16–17). When your feelings, your culture or your own reasoning disagree with what God has said, it is not his word that must give way. It is the fixed point, and everything else is checked against it (Isaiah 40:8).

The answer is a book. The instrument named for the sanctifying is that word: not an experience, not a technique, not a decision. When growth has stalled we look for a new method; this verse points somewhere quieter and more effective, the same place the pruning came from in chapter 15: you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you (15:3). The Spirit sanctifies, and the sword he uses is the word of God (Ephesians 6:17).

As you sent me. The Son’s mission is the pattern for the church’s (20:21). This is John’s Great Commission, which he will say to their faces on Easter evening. The church is sent as the Son was sent, which meant coming all the way in, living among people at their level, and being at their disposal. Of course the church does not atone; that work is his alone. But it goes as he went: humbly, truthfully, and at cost.

What if reading the Bible feels dry? It sometimes will, and the word works anyway. Much of what nourishes us does so without our feeling it; nobody remembers last month’s meals, but they are why you are alive. Keep reading, and read more of it at a time so that you see its shape. Read it with others, ask questions of it, hear it preached, and pray before you open it: open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of your law (Psalm 119:18). Read it to meet Christ, not only to tick a box. And remember that sanctification is the Father’s work in answer to the Son’s prayer. You are not making yourself holy by effort; you are putting yourself where he has promised to work.
verseByVerse.note: To sanctify is to set apart for God and make holy.

parallels.desc: your law is true

verseByVerse.quote: "And for their sake I consecrate myself, that they also may be sanctified in truth. I do not ask for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
I consecrate myself. Verse 19 has the priest and the sacrifice in one sentence. Consecrate is the same word as sanctify in verse 17, and Jesus was already holy. Here he means he sets himself apart for the sacrifice, as a priest was consecrated and as an offering was consecrated (Exodus 28:41; Deuteronomy 15:19). He dedicates himself to death for their sake (hyper, on their behalf and in their place). In the old ritual the priest and the animal were consecrated and the priest offered the animal; here one person does all of it to himself, for other people, the night before it takes effect.

That they also may be sanctified. Their being set apart depends on his: he goes first, and what he does to himself is the reason the thing can be done to them at all. We are sanctified by the will of God through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all; by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified (Hebrews 10:10, 14).

How can my holiness depend on his? Because holiness is first a belonging and only then a likeness. By his death Christ has set you apart for God once and for all; you were washed, you were sanctified (1 Corinthians 6:11). That is finished, and it cannot be undone by a bad week. Out of that settled status comes the daily growth in holiness, as the Spirit uses the word to make you in practice what Christ’s sacrifice has already made you in standing. So you do not fight sin in order to become God’s; you fight it because you already are his, and you fight it with the confidence of someone whose victory was bought before the battle started.

Those who will believe. Now Jesus prays for us. In one sentence it opens out to the whole church, in every century. If you believe, Jesus prayed for you that night.

Through their word. The chain is specified. The eleven spoke, people believed and spoke, and it has not stopped. And the word is still theirs: the apostolic word we have in the New Testament, which is why the church has always measured its preaching by Scripture. So everything that follows, the unity, the glory given, being loved as the Son is loved, being with him where he is, is not asked for the apostles alone. It is asked for the ordinary Christian who has never seen a miracle and finds prayer difficult.

How can he have prayed for me if I did not exist yet? Because he is the eternal Son, and he knew the people the Father had given him before the foundation of the world (v. 24; Ephesians 1:4). He named you in the only way a person can be named who does not yet exist, those who will believe in me, and the Father, who knows every one of them, heard the request as a request for each. And he did not merely foresee you. He prayed for you, and then he went out and made it possible.

For worship. Nobody has ever been prayed for like that. With the arrest drawing near, the Son of God spent his last quiet on strangers who had not been born. And the One who prayed for them set himself apart, priest and lamb in one, and walked out into the night to be the offering that would make them holy. Every believer since has been brought near to God on that prayer and that blood, and the High Priest who prayed it has never stopped praying.

parallels.desc: sanctified through the offering of his body

verseByVerse.quote: "that they may all be one, just as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be in us, so that the world may believe that you have sent me. The glory that you have given me I have given to them, that they may be one even as we are one,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
That they may all be one. This is the verse on which the whole question of a divided church turns, and three answers have been given to it. Rome reads the prayer as asking for one visible institution under one visible head, and takes the existence of separated churches as the standing wound this prayer was meant to prevent. The ecumenical movement read it as a mandate to merge structures. And a good many Protestants have read it as a prayer for an invisible unity only, on the comfortable assumption that since all true believers are already one in Christ, our visible divisions cost nothing.

As you, Father, are in me. The prayer itself rules out each of the three readings. Against the single-institution and merger readings, look at the pattern Jesus gives. The unity he asks for is modelled on the life of the Trinity, where the persons are genuinely distinct and the unity is one of love, life and will rather than of administration. Nothing in that picture requires a single earthly organisation, and the apostolic churches of the New Testament were plainly many congregations, not one structure.

That they also may be in us. Christian unity is rooted in union with the Father and the Son. It is not first something we build but something we are brought into. That is why it is precious and breaking it serious.

So that the world may believe. Unity is a witness. And here is the answer to the invisible-only reading: a unity the world cannot see cannot persuade the world of anything. Whatever this unity is, it must show. The harder and better answer: it is not a summons to dissolve our confessions into one institution, and it is not permission to be comfortable about our divisions. It asks for a love between Christians that outsiders can actually observe and cannot account for: believers who honour one another across the lines, refuse to caricature, and are visibly glad of grace wherever it appears (13:35). Every time two estranged believers are reconciled, the world catches a glimpse of what God is like.

Unity and truth in one prayer. Four verses earlier Jesus asked, sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth (v. 17). Unity and truth are petitions of one prayer and cannot be traded against each other. A unity bought by agreeing to say less than the gospel says is not the answer to this prayer but a counterfeit of it, and the Reformers, who did not leave lightly, understood that. Neither does unity in the truth excuse needless division among true believers. What is asked is that those who hold the truth should stop treating each other as enemies. And it searches the heart: much division among believers is not a stand for truth at all, but the old idol of being right, and being seen to be right, dressed up as zeal.

The glory that you have given me. The glory of the Son, revealed in his life and above all in the cross, he shares with his people. Given is past tense, before the cross, to eleven men who were about to run. So it is no reward. The prayer says what it is for in the same breath: that they may be one even as we are one. The glory given is the shared life that produces the unity. Not radiance, not status, not visible splendour, but a share in what the Father and the Son have between them.

When should I leave a church, and when should I stay? Stay through disagreements over secondary matters, through disappointing preaching, through personalities that grate; those are the very places where the unity Jesus prayed for is proved. Leave, peaceably and without slander, when a church abandons the gospel itself, denies the authority of Scripture, or will not deal with serious sin or abuse, and only after you have raised your concern honestly with its leaders. Even then, do not burn the bridge; you may be leaving brothers and sisters you will spend eternity with. And never leave a church simply to escape a person you have refused to forgive.

Can I be united with Christians whose baptism or church order differs from mine? Yes, in the deepest sense, and in more practical ways than many think. A Baptist and a Presbyterian who both trust Christ alone are already one in the Father and the Son. They may not be able to form one congregation, because each must act on his convictions about baptism with a clean conscience. But they can pray together, honour each other’s ministers, share platforms for the gospel, help each other’s churches in need, and speak of each other with warmth. This commentary holds believer’s baptism, and holds it alongside a glad affection for paedobaptist brothers (those who baptise the infants of believers) who love the same Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: "I in them and you in me, that they may become perfectly one, so that the world may know that you sent me and loved them even as you loved me. Father, I desire that they also, whom you have given me, may be with me where I am, to see my glory that you have given me because you loved me before the foundation of the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Perfectly one. Perfectly means brought to completion, the word family of accomplished (v. 4) and of It is finished (19:30). What his finished work secured, his people grow into.

Loved them even as you loved me. Two clauses here are among the hardest things in the Bible to believe about oneself. The first: even as you loved me, the same comparison he used at 15:9, now made to the Father in prayer, which means it is not a figure of speech aimed at encouraging anybody. He is telling the Father what is the case. The Father loves believers as he loves the Son. Not that we are equal to the Son, but that we are loved with the same love, because we are in him.

The measure of the Father’s love. Most Christians will affirm that God loves them, and most, if pressed, would describe that love as something a good deal cooler than the love of the Father for the Son: a settled goodwill, perhaps a determination to put up with them. This verse forbids it. The measure is not a lot; the measure is the love that has existed between the Father and the Son from before the world was made, and the sentence has no qualifier in it anywhere.

How can God love me like that when I am so sinful? Because he does not love you on the strength of what you are in yourself. He loves you in his Son. You have been united to Christ by faith, clothed in his righteousness, adopted into his sonship (Galatians 4:4–7). When the Father looks at you he sees you in the Beloved (Ephesians 1:6), and the love that rests on the Son rests on you there. Your sin is real, and it grieves him; but it was laid on Christ and punished in him, so it cannot shut you out of the love that Christ enjoys. You will not feel this every day. It is true every day.

I desire. The second is verse 24, and the verb changes. Everything up to now has been asking. Here it is thelō, I will: not a request but the confident will of the Son, in perfect agreement with the Father. And what he uses it for is not deliverance, or vindication, or a shorter road. He uses it to ask that the people he is leaving should end up where he is (14:3). He spends that confident will not to escape the cross but to secure our company.

To see my glory. Heaven is seeing Christ’s glory. This is the second time in this prayer he has looked back before the world existed: first to ask for his glory back (v. 5), now to say why the Father gave it. God did not need to create to have someone to love. He is love, from all eternity (1 John 4:8). Before light and time there was a Father loving a Son, and this prayer asks that a crowd of latecomers be brought in to watch. We will see the glory of the Son with our own eyes, and we will not grow tired of looking.

What will heaven actually be? Before it is a place of rest or reunion, it is being with Christ and seeing him. Everything else follows from that. The reunions are real, the end of pain is real (Revelation 21:4), the renewed creation is real; but the centre is the face of the Lamb (Revelation 22:4). Paul said to depart and be with Christ is far better (Philippians 1:23), and John said that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2). If heaven seems vague or dull to you, it is usually because Christ seems vague to you now. Get to know him here, and you will long to see him there.

In everyday life. Say it to yourself before you get out of bed: the Father loves me as he loves his Son. A person who knows he is loved like that does not need to win every argument or be noticed in every room.

verseByVerse.quote: "O righteous Father, even though the world does not know you, I know you, and these know that you have sent me. I made known to them your name, and I will continue to make it known, that the love with which you have loved me may be in them, and I in them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
O righteous Father. This is the second and last of the qualified addresses (v. 11). It is the word for a judge who gets the verdict right, used as every human court he will stand in before morning is about to withhold one. The courts of men will condemn him; the righteous Father will raise him.

I know you. Three groups: the world that does not know God, the Son who knows him perfectly, and the disciples who know that the Son came from him. The only way out of the first group into the third is through the second. Nobody comes to know the Father except through the Son who knows him (Matthew 11:27).

I will continue to make it known. Two tenses, and the future is the striking one. He said at verse 4 that he had accomplished the work he was given, and here he says the making known continues. Both are true: the accomplishing is the cross, and the disclosing does not stop at the cross. It goes on through the Spirit, through the word, through the preaching of the church, and it is going on now, wherever the gospel is read.

That the love may be in them. The prayer ends where all the purposes of God end: the love of the Father for the Son dwelling in believers, and Christ himself dwelling in them. Not that they may know about the love, but that the love itself, the actual love of the Father for the Son, should be located inside them. The eternal love that flowed between the Father and the Son before there was a world has been poured into the hearts of sinners.

And I in them. The prayer ends without a petition. He does not close with a request or a summary; he ends by naming a destination, and the destination is not a place. After four chapters of farewell the final word is a preposition and a pronoun: in them. Not to a system, not to an institution, not even to heaven considered as a location, but to the Son of God taking up residence in ordinary people.

In the flow. The next sentence has him crossing the Kidron (18:1). Everything he has just asked, keeping, holiness, unity, the Father’s love in his people, he goes out to secure by being arrested, condemned and lifted up.

What does it mean in practice that Christ is in me? It means you are never alone and never left to your own resources. By his Spirit the risen Christ lives in every believer (Romans 8:9–10; Galatians 2:20; Colossians 1:27). That is why you can love people you could not love by nature, endure what would otherwise crush you, and keep praying when prayer feels empty: the life of Christ is working in you. You will not usually feel it as a sensation. You will see it, over years, in a growing likeness to him and a love for him that was not there before. It is also why you can face death calmly: what is in you cannot die.

Yours they were, and you gave them to me, and they have kept your word.<sup>7</sup>Now they know that everything that you have given me is from you.<sup>8</sup>For I have given them the words that you gave me, and they have received them and have come to know in truth that I came from you; and they have believed that you sent me.<sup>9</sup>I am praying for them. I am not praying for the world but for those whom you have given me, for they are yours.<sup>10</sup>All mine are yours, and yours are mine, and I am glorified in them.<sup>11</sup>And I am no longer in the world, but they are in the world, and I am coming to you. Holy Father, keep them in your name, which you have given me, that they may be one, even as we are one.<sup>12</sup>While I was with them, I kept them in your name, which you have given me. I have guarded them, and not one of them has been lost except the son of destruction, that the Scripture might be fulfilled.<sup>13</sup>But now I am coming to you, and these things I speak in the world, that they may have my joy fulfilled in themselves.<sup>14</sup>I have given them your word, and the world has hated them because they are not of the world, just as I am not of the world.<sup>15</sup>I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you keep them from the evil one.<sup>16</sup>They are not of the world, just as I am not of the world.<sup>17</sup>Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth.<sup>18</sup>As you sent me into the world, so I have sent them into the world.<sup>19</sup>And for their sake I consecrate myself, that they also may be sanctified in truth.<sup>20</sup>“I do not ask for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word,<sup>21</sup>that they may all be one, just as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be in us, so that the world may believe that you have sent me.<sup>22</sup>The glory that you have given me I have given to them, that they may be one even as we are one,<sup>23</sup>I in them and you in me, that they may become perfectly one, so that the world may know that you sent me and loved them even as you loved me.<sup>24</sup>Father, I desire that they also, whom you have given me, may be with me where I am, to see my glory that you have given me because you loved me before the foundation of the world.<sup>25</sup>O righteous Father, even though the world does not know you, I know you, and these know that you have sent me.<sup>26</sup>I made known to them your name, and I will continue to make it known, that the love with which you have loved me may be in them, and I in them.”
17.overview:
Before going out to Gethsemane, Jesus lifts his eyes to heaven and prays aloud. Since the sixteenth century this has been called his “high-priestly prayer”: like the high priest on the Day of Atonement, he prays for himself, for his priests (the apostles), and for the people. It lets us hear the Son speaking to the Father on the night before the cross.

Every Christian is in view in this prayer, and Christ’s intercession continues for them in heaven (Hebrews 7:25).

18.title: The Arrest, the Denial, and the Trial Before Pilate

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–27 — Gethsemane, the Arrest, and Peter's Denial
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The arrest in the garden across the Kidron, the hearing before Annas, and Peter’s three denials, which John sets side by side with Jesus’ own questioning, so that we watch the disciple fail outside while his Lord stands firm inside.
verseByVerse.theology: I am he, in Greek *egō eimi*, is the divine name Jesus has been claiming throughout this Gospel (8:58). At it armed men fall to the ground. He gives himself up not because he is overpowered but because he chooses to: the Shepherd lays down his own life for the sheep (10:11, 18). The arrest is at once his most vulnerable moment and his most sovereign act.
verseByVerse.examples: Peter’s denials come at a charcoal fire among the servants and officers, three times as Jesus had said, and then the rooster crows. What fails here is self-confident discipleship, faith leaning on its own courage rather than on Christ. His restoration in chapter 21 will be built on a different foundation: the love and prayer of his Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: When Jesus had spoken these words, he went out with his disciples across the brook Kidron, where there was a garden, which he and his disciples entered. Now Judas, who betrayed him, also knew the place, for Jesus often met there with his disciples.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. John’s account of the arrest and trials shows Jesus in complete control. He goes out to meet his captors, they fall before him, he protects his disciples, and before Pilate he is the one who judges. Meanwhile Peter denies him three times. The King goes to the cross as the Lord who lays down his life of his own accord (10:18). Every power in Jerusalem will take its turn with him, and each will think it is deciding his fate; none of them is.

Across the brook Kidron. The Kidron Valley lies east of the city, below the Mount of Olives. John calls it a cheimarros, a winter torrent, a stream bed that runs only after rain. There is a tradition, impossible to verify, that the blood of the temple sacrifices was channelled down into it, which at Passover would have been the blood of thousands of lambs. Whether or not that is so, the Lamb of God now crosses it on his way to his own death.

The king who crossed the Kidron weeping. There is an Old Testament scene underneath this crossing. A thousand years earlier another king went out of Jerusalem, betrayed: “And all the land wept aloud as all the people passed by, and the king crossed the brook Kidron” (2 Samuel 15:23). David is fleeing Absalom, going up the Mount of Olives weeping, head covered and feet bare. The man who had betrayed him was Ahithophel, his own counsellor, the friend whose advice had been “as if one consulted the word of God” (2 Samuel 16:23). When his counsel was not followed, he hanged himself (2 Samuel 17:23). The Son of David now walks the same ground with the opposite purpose. David went over it to save his life. This King goes over it to lay his down.

A garden. Matthew and Mark call it Gethsemane, “oil press” (Mark 14:32), an olive grove across the valley on the Mount of Olives. John alone calls it a garden (kēpos), and he will use the word again: in the place where he was crucified there was a garden (19:41). John does not spell out an echo of Eden, but many readers have heard one: a garden, where Adam fell; a garden, where the second Adam is arrested; and a garden, where he will be buried and rise. The story that went wrong in a garden is being put right in one.

Judas also knew the place. The place was not discovered. It was known, because it was theirs, and the only reason Judas could find him in the dark is that he had been welcome there. That is the pattern of all intimate betrayal: the enemy uses knowledge gained in trust. And Jesus did not change his habits that night; he went where Judas would find him. Nothing forced him; love led him.

Was it right for Jesus to walk into danger like that? Yes, because his hour had come and his Father had sent him to this. For three years he had withdrawn when men tried to seize him early (7:30; 10:39), because his time was not yet. Now it was, and to avoid the garden would have been to refuse the cup. That is very different from courting danger or despising one’s life. Jesus is not teaching us to put ourselves in harm’s way for the sake of it; ordinary prudence is right for us, as it was for him in the years before. He is showing us a Saviour who laid down his life when it was required, and not one moment before or after.

In everyday life. If one of the places where you have known Christ’s company has become the place of a wound, a betrayal in the fellowship, a hurt in the church, remember that your Lord knew that too. He did not stop going to the garden because Judas knew it. Do not abandon the places of fellowship because one person abused them.
verseByVerse.note: The Kidron Valley lies between Jerusalem and the Mount of Olives; it is usually dry except in the rainy season. Matthew and Mark name the garden Gethsemane.

parallels.desc: David, betrayed, crosses the Kidron weeping

verseByVerse.quote: So Judas, having procured a band of soldiers and some officers from the chief priests and the Pharisees, went there with lanterns and torches and weapons. Then Jesus, knowing all that would happen to him, came forward and said to them, "Whom do you seek?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
A band of soldiers. Two things about the arresting party are absurd. The first is the size. The band was a cohort (speira), a tenth of a Roman legion, nominally six hundred men, though probably only a detachment was sent. So the Romans were involved from the start. With them came the temple police (“officers”). All this, at night, for a man who had taught openly in the temple every day and could have been taken there at noon (18:20).

With lanterns and torches. The second is the equipment. It is Passover, which falls at full moon. They have come out on the brightest night of the month, carrying fire, to look for the light of the world, and they will not find him until he steps out and tells them where he is.

Knowing all that would happen. Not was found, not was seized: he went out to them. The whole passion in this Gospel is governed by that verb. And he knew all of it: the ropes, the slap, the flogging, the nails. Some courage depends on not knowing how bad it will be; this is the rarer kind. He walked out of the trees toward the torches with the whole of the following day already in view.

Whom do you seek? It is the first thing he says in the passion narrative, and it echoes the first words Jesus speaks in this Gospel, what are you seeking?, asked of two men following him (1:38). He will ask it again of Mary at the tomb (20:15). The book opens with him asking what people want, the arrest opens with the same question put to men with weapons, and the resurrection morning opens with it put to a weeping woman. The hunters are asked to name their quarry, as though he were in charge of the proceedings, which he is.

Did Jesus really know everything that would happen? Yes. As the eternal Son he knows all things, and in his human mind he had been given to know his path in detail; he had predicted his betrayal, his handing over to the Gentiles, the mocking, the flogging and the cross (Mark 10:33–34). That is what makes his going forward so astonishing. Nothing took him by surprise. And it is a comfort for us: the Christ who goes before you into your sufferings is not improvising. He knows the road you are on, and he walked a harder one with his eyes open.

For worship. The hunted one is the great Seeker. Men came with torches to find him, and he let himself be found, because he had come to look for people who were not looking for him. The Lamb went to the altar on his own feet, and his searching love found us in our darkness long before we lifted a lantern toward him.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the “band of soldiers” was a cohort, a tenth of a Roman legion — Roman troops joined with the temple police.

verseByVerse.quote: They answered him, "Jesus of Nazareth." Jesus said to them, "I am he." Judas, who betrayed him, was standing with them. When Jesus said to them, "I am he," they drew back and fell to the ground.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am he. Jesus of Nazareth is a man from a despised village (1:46), the name that will be nailed above his head in three languages (19:19). His reply is barer in Greek than the English can be: two words, egō eimi, with no he. (The ESV notes that it is literally “I am”.) On one level, it simply means I am the one. But John’s readers have heard Jesus use these words as the divine name (8:24, 28, 58). They are the words that made them pick up stones at 8:58, and they echo what God said out of the bush (Exodus 3:14).

Judas was standing with them. John will not let it pass. In the middle of the sentence about the divine name, he records where the man was standing: among the soldiers.

They fell to the ground. They could not take him unless he let them (10:18). And when they went down, Judas, standing among them, presumably went down too. The great I AM who spoke to Moses from the fire stood among the olive trees in a carpenter’s body, and the soldiers of the strongest empire on earth could not stay on their feet before his name.

What the falling is and is not. It is not a rescue or a threat; the soldiers get up and do their job. It is a demonstration placed where the reader most needs it. From here to the end of the book, everything done to him is done by other people: he is bound, struck, tried, flogged, sentenced, nailed. John puts one moment at the front of that sequence in which an armed cohort goes over backwards at two words, so that nobody afterwards can say he was overpowered.

Why did they fall? Was it a miracle? John does not explain the mechanism, and we should not invent one. He simply records that when the Son of God spoke his name, armed men could not stand. Some have suggested shock or confusion, but that would not explain why soldiers who had come for this very purpose went down together. The plain sense is that for a moment the majesty of who he is broke through, as it did on the mountain of transfiguration, and creatures fell before their Creator. The day is coming when every knee will bow at that name (Philippians 2:10). In the garden, a company of armed men bowed early.

In everyday life. When Christ seems weak in your world, mocked at work, ignored in the news, outvoted in the culture, remember the garden. He has never been overpowered, only patient. Let that steady you, and humble you when you think his cause depends on your cleverness.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “I am he” is literally “I am” here and in verse 8 — the words of the divine name.

parallels.desc: my adversaries stumble and fall

verseByVerse.quote: So he asked them again, "Whom do you seek?" And they said, "Jesus of Nazareth." Jesus answered, "I told you that I am he. So, if you seek me, let these men go."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So he asked them again. He is directing his own arrest, identifying himself a second time to men who have just been knocked down by the first.

Let these men go. It is a condition. He is negotiating, at the moment of his arrest, with a cohort that has just been knocked off its feet, and the only thing he asks for is that his friends be allowed to walk away. Not a hearing, not fair treatment, not time: he uses the one piece of leverage he has to get them out of the garden (10:11–12).

And it worked. Every one of the eleven survived that night, which is not what usually happened to the followers of an executed insurrectionist. He had prayed earlier that night, out loud where they could hear, that the Father would keep them (17:12). Here he is making it true himself, with soldiers in front of him. The prayer and the answer to the prayer are the same person. He asked the Father to keep them, and then kept them, and the keeping cost him the thing he was keeping them from.

Is this really a picture of the cross? Yes, and John means it to be. The arrest is not the atonement; that happens on the cross, where Jesus bears God’s wrath for sin. But the garden shows its shape in advance: the Shepherd stepping between his sheep and the danger, accepting what was coming for them so that they can go free. At the cross he does the same thing before a far greater judgment. The law’s sentence against his people falls on him, and they are released. Whenever you feel the accusation of your sins, hear him say to it: if you seek me, let these go.

verseByVerse.quote: This was to fulfill the word that he had spoken: "Of those whom you gave me I have lost not one." Then Simon Peter, having a sword, drew it and struck the high priest's servant and cut off his right ear. (The servant's name was Malchus.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
To fulfil the word. Jesus’ words are fulfilled like Scripture, because they are Scripture. The word is from 17:12 (and 6:39). John applies a saying about eternal security to physical safety on one night: not a misapplication but a window. The man who will not let them be arrested in a garden is the same man who will not let them be lost at the end, and the second promise is made credible by watching him keep the first.

Simon Peter, having a sword. Only John names Peter as the swordsman. Peter acts as he promised (13:37), bravely and foolishly, against a cohort. But be fair to him: hopelessly outnumbered, he drew anyway. It is not cowardice, and the same man will be denying everything before morning, which tells you something uncomfortable about how little courage in one form predicts courage in another.

The servant’s name was Malchus. An eyewitness detail: if, as many think, John is the other disciple who was known to the high priest (18:15), he knew the household, and the other Gospels say only that someone struck the servant of the high priest. John gives the wounded man a name, and he will mention him again when a relative of his recognises Peter at the fire (18:26). To Peter he was a target. To Jesus, as Luke the doctor tells us, he was a man to be healed (Luke 22:51), and so the last healing before the cross was done for an enemy, mending what a disciple had broken.

What Peter got wrong. Peter’s fault was not his courage but his reading of the situation. He had heard about the cup and the hour and the Good Shepherd laying down his life, and he arrived at the garden believing his job was to stop it. Ask what you are currently defending God from. If the answer involves preventing something he has already said he intends to do, a loss, a humbling, a door closing, then the sword is out, and the most likely outcome is somebody else’s ear.

How can I tell whether my zeal is Peter’s sword? Ask three questions. Is it in line with what Christ has actually said, or with what I assume he must want? Am I using the weapons he gave, truth spoken in love, prayer, patient witness, or the world’s weapons of force, manipulation and contempt? And who is getting hurt? Zeal that wounds the people Christ came to save, or that would have kept him from the cross, is zeal without knowledge (Romans 10:2). Real zeal for Christ looks like his own: it is willing to suffer, quick to heal, and never needs to win by cutting someone down.
verseByVerse.note: Only John names Peter as the swordsman and Malchus as the servant.

verseByVerse.quote: So Jesus said to Peter, "Put your sword into its sheath; shall I not drink the cup that the Father has given me?" So the band of soldiers and their captain and the officers of the Jews arrested Jesus and bound him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Put your sword into its sheath. His kingdom does not advance by the sword (v. 36; Matthew 26:52), and he has to rescue his disciples not only from the soldiers but from themselves.

Shall I not drink the cup that the Father has given me? The “cup” pictures the suffering and judgment the Father had appointed for him. In the Old Testament the cup is often the cup of God’s wrath (Psalm 75:8; Isaiah 51:17; Jeremiah 25:15). That wrath is no sudden flare of irritation. It is the holy resistance of a pure God to evil, his just response to sin (Romans 1:18), and it would be a lesser God who looked at the world’s cruelty and felt nothing. Jesus will drink the cup of God’s anger against sin, so that his people never have to. The other Gospels record his prayer in the garden, “remove this cup” (Mark 14:36); John gives us his resolve: shall I not drink it? And notice whose cup it is: the cup the Father has given. Not Judas’s cup, not Caiaphas’s, not Pilate’s. Behind every human hand that night stands the Father’s purpose, and the Son receives it from him.

Where is Gethsemane? The word cup prompts a question about what John has not told us. All three of the other Gospels place at this spot the most famous prayer ever prayed in a garden: Jesus falling on his face, in anguish (Luke’s detail of sweat like drops of blood is missing from some early manuscripts), asking that the cup might pass, and the disciples asleep a stone’s throw away. John gives us none of it. He brings Jesus across the Kidron, and the next thing that happens is that Judas arrives with lanterns. He is not concealing the anguish, and the proof is that he assumes it here. Jesus speaks of the cup the Father has given him as of something already settled between them; you cannot resolve a struggle you never had, and the sentence only makes sense if there was one. John has written the agony in his own place and his own way. He put it in chapter 12, in daylight, in public, before a crowd: now is my soul troubled, and shall I ask to be saved from this hour? No, for this purpose I have come to this hour (12:27). That is much the same prayer, the same request raised and the same refusal to press it, only moved out of the dark and into the open where everyone could hear.

Both pictures are needed. The others show us a man overtaken by horror and holding on; John shows a man walking into it with his eyes open. The church needs both. Take John without the others and you may forget what it cost him. Take the others without John and you may forget that nobody took his life from him.

Did Jesus resist the Father’s will in the garden? No. In Gethsemane his human soul shrank from the cup with all the horror of a holy man facing the wrath of God against sin, and he said so honestly. But every time he said it he added, not my will, but yours, be done (Luke 22:42). To feel the full weight of something terrible and still embrace God’s will is not resistance; it is the deepest obedience there is. And it means that when you pray in agony, asking God to take something away while longing to do his will, you are not sinning. You are praying the way your Lord prayed.

And bound him. The captain is a chiliarchos, commander of a thousand, a senior Roman officer. They bind the one who had just floored them, and he lets them. There was a man in Israel’s memory who had been bound by his father and laid on wood on a mountain, and who, Jewish tradition said, was old enough to have resisted and did not (Genesis 22:9). Tradition called it the Akedah, the Binding, and some linked it with Passover. Isaac was released and a ram was found. This time the ropes stay on.

For worship. The cup was ours. We filled it with every sin we ever committed, and the Father put it into the hands of his Son, and the Son did not set it down. Shall I not drink it? he asked, and on the next afternoon he drank it to the bottom, so that not one drop of wrath is left for those who are his. What remains for us is another cup altogether, the cup of blessing at his table (1 Corinthians 10:16), filled not with anger but with the new covenant in his blood.
verseByVerse.note: The “cup” pictures the suffering and judgment the Father had given him to bear.

verseByVerse.quote: First they led him to Annas, for he was the father-in-law of Caiaphas, who was high priest that year. It was Caiaphas who had advised the Jews that it would be expedient that one man should die for the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
First they led him to Annas. Annas had been high priest from AD 6 to 15, until the Romans removed him, but five of his sons and his son-in-law Caiaphas held the office after him, so for roughly half a century the high priesthood was a family business run out of one house. Many Jews still regarded him as the true high priest, since the office was meant to be for life (Luke 3:2). Only John records this preliminary hearing.

Father-in-law of Caiaphas. The family dominated the temple, and it is often thought that they profited from its trade, the very trade Jesus had disrupted (2:13–16). So Jesus is taken first not to a court but to the house of the man whose family had the most to lose. Annas holds no office; it is a private call before anything official begins.

Expedient that one man should die. The verdict was decided before the trial (11:49–52), and John told us then that Caiaphas spoke a prophecy he did not know he was uttering. Now the prophet is the presiding judge, accomplishing his own prophecy without understanding it. One man did die for the people, and for children of God scattered through every nation and century, and we are among them.

A night of irregularities. Jewish law as later written down forbade capital trials at night, forbade them on the eve of a festival, required a day to elapse before a death sentence, and required the court to sit in its own chamber. Every one appears to be broken in the next few hours. How much of that later law was in force in the AD 30s is disputed; but the men conducting this are the guardians of the law, and they are working in the middle of the night in a private house.

Why did God let such corrupt men hold the high priesthood? Because he was bringing the old priesthood to its end and replacing it with a better one. The very men who should have recognised the Lamb of God handed him over, and in doing so fulfilled the purpose of the priesthood without knowing it: a sacrifice was offered for the people. God often lets human corruption run its course in order to show that salvation comes from him and not from human institutions. The true High Priest stood bound before the false ones, and within days the temple curtain would be torn in two (Matthew 27:51).
verseByVerse.note: Annas had been high priest from AD 6 to 15; five of his sons and his son-in-law Caiaphas held the office after him, and he remained the power behind it. Only John records this first hearing.

parallels.desc: the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas

verseByVerse.quote: Simon Peter followed Jesus, and so did another disciple. Since that disciple was known to the high priest, he entered with Jesus into the courtyard of the high priest, but Peter stood outside at the door. So the other disciple, who was known to the high priest, went out and spoke to the servant girl who kept watch at the door, and brought Peter in.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simon Peter followed. Brave, after the others had fled (Mark 14:50). He fails in a place most of the others never went.

And so did another disciple. He is often thought to be the beloved disciple, John himself (20:2), which fits the way this Gospel refers to its author in the third person and never by name. The difficulty is the next clause: he was known to the high priest, and a Galilean fisherman’s acquaintance with the household of Annas is not obvious. Perhaps through business or family; some think he is someone else entirely. The Gospel does not say.

Into the courtyard. A large house with a central courtyard, which Annas and Caiaphas may have shared. Whoever the other disciple was, he used his access to bring Peter in.

A door opened in kindness. The man with the connections brings his friend inside, and inside is where Peter will fail. The kindness was real; left in the street, Peter might have gone home. That is not a reason to be careful about kindness. It is a reason to be honest about how failure arrives: seldom through malice, often through a door somebody opened for us out of love. And the door is kept by a servant girl, whose idle question will bring down the most famous denial in history.

Two men through one gate. John sets Master and disciple in the same courtyard on purpose. Jesus goes in bound, under guard, knowing exactly what is about to happen at the fire; Peter goes in free, confident and unaware. One will be questioned and tell the truth; the other will be questioned and lie. The Lord did not go in to keep Peter from falling that night. He went in to be condemned in Peter’s place, and he had already prayed, as Luke records, that Peter’s faith would not fail (Luke 22:32).

Should I avoid places where I might be tempted? Often, yes, and with no shame in it. Scripture tells us to flee youthful passions (2 Timothy 2:22) and to make no provision for the flesh (Romans 13:14). But Peter’s problem was not that he went into the courtyard; following his Lord into danger was right. His problem was that he went in sure of his own strength, having brushed aside the warning (13:37–38). Go where Christ calls you, even into hard places. But go praying, aware of your weakness, and leaning on him, not on your record of loyalty.
verseByVerse.note: The “other disciple” is often thought to be the beloved disciple, John.

verseByVerse.quote: The servant girl at the door said to Peter, "You also are not one of this man's disciples, are you?" He said, "I am not." Now the servants and officers had made a charcoal fire, because it was cold, and they were standing and warming themselves. Peter also was with them, standing and warming himself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You also are not one of this man’s disciples, are you? She frames the question so that it invites a no. She is not accusing him; she is a girl at a door, making conversation, probably without much interest either way. “Also” means like the other disciple, whom she knows to be one of them and who has come to no harm.

I am not. No threat has been made. And Peter, who a few hours ago swung a sword at an armed man’s head in the dark, says ouk eimi, I am not. The contrast with the garden is deliberate (vv. 5, 6, 8). The Lord named himself and a cohort went over backwards; the disciple denies who he is to a girl minding a gate.

A charcoal fire, because it was cold. Jerusalem can be cold on spring nights. The word (anthrakia) appears only here and in 21:9, where the risen Jesus cooks breakfast and restores Peter beside another charcoal fire. The risen Lord may have lit the second to heal what the first had witnessed. For now Peter stands with the enemies of Jesus, among the officers who arrested his master, at their fire, getting warm.

How denial usually happens. Denial is rarely dramatic. It is much more often what Peter does here: taking the answer somebody has already assumed, because correcting them would be awkward and nothing much seems to be at stake. It costs nothing at the time, which is why it is so easy. Underneath it is the fear of man, the wish to be accepted by the people round the fire, and Scripture calls that fear a snare (Proverbs 29:25). The cure is not a stronger will but a greater fear: the fear of the Lord, whose opinion matters more than any circle we want to belong to.

Is keeping quiet about my faith the same as denying Christ? Not always. There is a time to keep silence and a time to speak (Ecclesiastes 3:7), and not every conversation calls for a testimony. Wisdom, tact and timing are not cowardice. But silence becomes denial when someone asks you directly, or assumes something false about you, and you let it stand to protect yourself. The test is the motive. Am I silent because this is not the moment, or because I am ashamed of him? If it is shame, Jesus’ words apply: whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, of him will the Son of Man be ashamed (Mark 8:38). Ask him for courage before the question comes. And if you have already failed in exactly this way, remember that the man who stood at this fire was restored by the same Lord and sent out to preach.
verseByVerse.note: Jerusalem, high in the hills, can be cold on spring nights. John mentions a charcoal fire again when Peter is restored.

verseByVerse.quote: The high priest then questioned Jesus about his disciples and his teaching. Jesus answered him, "I have spoken openly to the world. I have always taught in synagogues and in the temple, where all Jews come together. I have said nothing in secret."
verseByVerse.commentary:
About his disciples and his teaching. Annas, called high priest by courtesy, fishes for evidence. It is a security official’s question, looking for sedition or false teaching.

Which high priest is this? John calls both Annas and Caiaphas high priest. Annas had held the office and still bore the title, and many read v. 19 as his questioning, with Jesus then sent to Caiaphas (v. 24). Others read vv. 19–23 as Caiaphas. The first is the more likely.

Why John leaves out the trial before the council. Matthew and Mark record a full session of the Sanhedrin with witnesses and the verdict of blasphemy. John has none of it, and sends Jesus on to Caiaphas in a single sentence (v. 24). The likeliest reason is the one that explains most of John’s omissions: the other accounts were long in circulation and he supplies what they lacked. Nobody else records the Annas hearing.

He would not name them. Jesus answers only about his teaching, not one word about the disciples. He has just got them out of the garden; he is not going to name them in a courtyard. Meanwhile, a few yards away, one of those disciples is refusing to name him. The Shepherd who has nothing to hide hides his sheep.

Openly to the world. The word for openly (parrhēsia) is the one John uses of speaking with boldness, in public, without concealment, and it can be checked.

Nothing in secret. This does not deny that Jesus taught the Twelve privately (chapters 13–17). His private teaching explained the same message he preached openly (Mark 4:34); there was no secret doctrine for insiders.

The God who did not speak in secret. Jesus is using the language of the God of Israel. Through Isaiah the Lord had said, I did not speak in secret, in a land of darkness (Isaiah 45:19), setting himself against the idols and oracles with their hidden whispers. Now the prisoner says the same of his own ministry, because he is the Word made flesh (1:14). Annas wants secrets. He is standing before the one in whom God has hidden nothing he means his people to know.

Is there any hidden teaching for advanced Christians? No. Christianity has no secret inner doctrine reserved for an elite. Every generation has had teachers claiming special knowledge beyond the Bible, from the Gnostics of the second century to modern movements promising a deeper revelation, and every one is answered by this verse. What Jesus taught he taught openly, and what the apostles received they wrote down for the whole church (1 John 1:3). The deepest things of God are in the same Scriptures that a child can read. Growth in Christ is not access to hidden knowledge; it is going further into what has been openly given.

parallels.desc: I did not speak in secret

verseByVerse.quote: "Why do you ask me? Ask those who have heard me what I said to them; they know what I said." When he had said these things, one of the officers standing by struck Jesus with his hand, saying, "Is that how you answer the high priest?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why do you ask me? Ask those who have heard me. Under Jewish law, a case should be established by witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15), and later Jewish tradition would not let the accused be made to testify against himself. Jesus calls for a proper trial. The hearing is already procedurally compromised, and he says so.

Struck with his hand. The word (rhapisma) can mean a blow with a rod, but probably means an open-handed blow across the face, illegal and humiliating. It is not mainly a way of causing pain. It is the standard gesture for putting an inferior back in his place.

Is that how you answer the high priest? Showing off to his master. The officer explains himself in exactly those terms. So the first violence done to Jesus is not judicial and not even angry. It is an act of etiquette enforcement by a junior official who thought the prisoner’s tone was wrong. This is the man through whom all things were made, standing bound in a courtyard, being corrected on his manners by a member of the temple staff.

I gave my back. Isaiah had described it, and the wording is worth having beside the scene: “I gave my back to those who strike, and my cheeks to those who pull out the beard; I hid not my face from disgrace and spitting” (Isaiah 50:6). The verbs are active. The Servant is not overwhelmed; he presents himself. The face that was slapped in Annas’s courtyard is the face we will see in glory, and the shame he carried there is the reason we will be able to look on it without shame.

Why did God allow his Son to be humiliated like this? Because our sin is not only guilt but shame, and he came to bear both. We dishonoured God; the Son received dishonour. We exalted ourselves; he was struck and put in his place. Hebrews says he endured the cross, despising the shame (Hebrews 12:2), and the shame began here, with a slap from a servant. And in John’s account the first blow does not come from Roman soldiers but from a servant of the temple, in the high priest’s own house: he came to his own, and his own people did not receive him (1:11). If you carry shame, for what you have done or for what was done to you, look at this courtyard. Your Lord has stood in it. He knows what it is to be treated as worthless by those who should have honoured him, and he bore it so that you could be clothed with honour as a child of God.

parallels.desc: you shall not revile God, nor curse a ruler

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered him, "If what I said is wrong, bear witness about the wrong; but if what I said is right, why do you strike me?" Annas then sent him bound to Caiaphas the high priest.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If what I said is wrong, bear witness about the wrong; but if what I said is right, why do you strike me? Calm and dignified. The reply shows what to do with an injustice, and most of us have only two settings. He does not absorb it silently, and he does not retaliate. He states the principle: there are two possibilities, and the blow is wrong under both. If what he said was wrong, produce the evidence; that is what a court is for. If it was right, the blow has no justification at all. Either way the officer has skipped the only step that mattered. And he does not appeal to who he is. He could have. The argument he uses is one that would protect any prisoner in any courtyard.

Turning the other cheek. Jesus does not literally turn the other cheek here (Matthew 5:39), but neither does he retaliate. Turning the other cheek means refusing revenge, and it evidently permits a man to say plainly that what has just been done to him was unjust.

Entrusting himself to him who judges justly. Peter wrote about it afterwards: “when he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly” (1 Peter 2:23). The last clause is the mechanism. It is possible to say plainly that a thing is unjust and still not fight it, provided one genuinely believes there is a court that will sit later. Every injustice ever done to his people will one day be put right in a court that cannot be rigged, presided over by the one who was struck in Annas’s house.

Sent bound to Caiaphas. The formal trial before the council is described by the other Gospels (Mark 14:53–65). Nothing has been established and no charge produced; he is simply moved on, still bound, in a process decided long before (11:53).

When should I speak up against wrong done to me, and when should I stay silent? Speak when truth or justice needs it, calmly, without insult or threat, as Jesus did here and as Paul did when he appealed to his rights as a Roman citizen (Acts 16:37; 22:25). Use the proper channels: a complaint, a court, the elders of the church; and if you are being abused, tell someone and get safe, because Scripture never asks you to stay under harm. Stay silent when speaking would only be revenge, self-display, or a fight for your pride. In both cases, the heart beneath is the same: you entrust yourself to God, who judges justly, and you refuse to repay evil for evil (Romans 12:17–19).

verseByVerse.quote: Now Simon Peter was standing and warming himself. So they said to him, "You also are not one of his disciples, are you?" He denied it and said, "I am not." One of the servants of the high priest, a relative of the man whose ear Peter had cut off, asked, "Did I not see you in the garden with him?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Warming himself. John has interleaved the scenes deliberately: Peter denies (vv. 15–18), Jesus is questioned and struck (vv. 19–24), Peter denies twice more (vv. 25–27). Both men are being asked who they are. One says no; the other will not name a single one of his disciples. Our salvation has never depended on the faithfulness of the one by the fire. It depends on the faithfulness of the one inside, who kept his silence about Peter and went on to die for him.

The second denial. The pressure rises: not a servant girl at a gate but several men at the fire at once (they said to him), with the same expected-no form of question.

A relative of Malchus. Another eyewitness detail, and the danger is real: this man saw him with the sword.

Did I not see you in the garden with him? The Greek expects the answer yes. That is a different order of danger. This man was there. He has a family grievance and an eyewitness identification, and Peter is standing in the household of the injured party warming his hands.

Before we feel superior to Peter. By the third question Peter had something to be afraid of; the first denial cost him nothing, the third might have cost his life. Nothing suggests any of us would have done better, and the others are not in the courtyard at all.

Courage in the wrong form. The questioner remembers the ear. Peter’s one act of courage that night has become the evidence against him, and the thing he did to prove his loyalty is what makes him identifiable when he wants to deny it. Bravery in the wrong form does not bank anything for later.

In everyday life. Peter’s first lie made the second necessary, and the second made the third almost automatic. If you have told a small untruth to avoid embarrassment this week, go back and correct it before it grows. You can do it without dread: the Lord who told the truth inside while Peter lied outside kept the law perfectly in your place, and his record, not yours, is your standing before God.

verseByVerse.quote: Peter again denied it, and at once a rooster crowed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter again denied it. Matthew and Mark say he swore and called down curses (Mark 14:71). John says nothing else. No weeping, no look, no comment. The worst night of Peter’s life is reported in a handful of words, and then the narrative simply moves to Pilate.

A rooster crowed. Exactly as Jesus said (13:38). Luke supplies what happened next: “And the Lord turned and looked at Peter” (Luke 22:61). Then Peter remembered the saying of the Lord, and he went out and wept bitterly (Luke 22:61–62). The crow did not condemn him. It reminded him that the worst moment of his life had been foreseen by the man he had just disowned, and had not stopped him being at that supper, or having his feet washed, or being prayed for by name.

The mercy hidden in the prediction. That is why Jesus made it. A failure your Lord described to your face beforehand is inside the story rather than the end of it. If you carry a particular memory, Christ knew about it before it happened; and in Peter’s case he announced it, washed the man’s feet anyway, prayed for him by name, arranged his escape from the garden, and on the third day sent word specifically to him through the messenger at the tomb: “go, tell his disciples and Peter” (Mark 16:7).

The four accounts. The Gospels name different questioners, a servant girl, another girl, the bystanders, and in John alone a relative of Malchus, and they place Peter differently in the courtyard. They agree on three denials and the rooster. Questions were flying round a crowded fire. Mark adds that the rooster crowed twice (Mark 14:72).

The fire still to come. John, who leaves the weeping out here, has not forgotten. He will tell of Peter’s restoration (21:15–19): three questions of love to match the three denials, and a man given his work back. There is no failure of ours that his faithfulness has not already outrun.

Judas and Peter. Both failed Jesus that night, and John has shown us both at close range. Judas went out into the night (13:30); Peter wept and would be brought back. What separated them was not that one sin was large and the other small. It was Christ. Jesus had prayed for Peter (Luke 22:32), and Peter was among those the Father had given the Son, of whom he had just told the Father that not one had been lost except the son of destruction (17:12).

Can a Christian who has denied Christ be forgiven? Yes. Peter is the proof, and he became the preacher of Pentecost. Jesus’ warning that he will deny before the Father whoever denies him (Matthew 10:33) speaks of a settled, final rejection of Christ, the life that disowns him and never returns. It does not speak of a believer who falls in weakness and comes back weeping. The warnings of Hebrews 6 describe those who fall away for good, not those who are grieved by their fall; if you are troubled that you have denied him, that very trouble shows the Spirit is still at work in you. Confess it, as plainly as Peter wept over it, and believe that the blood of Jesus cleanses from all sin (1 John 1:7–9).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28–40 — The Trial Before Pilate: What Is Truth?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Roman trial begins. John moves Pilate back and forth between the accusers outside and the prisoner inside, and at its centre puts the conversation the accusers never heard: about a kingdom not of this world, and about truth.
verseByVerse.theology: Are you the King of the Jews? is the question of this trial, and the title Pilate later fixes over the cross (19:19) will turn out to be the truest sentence anyone writes that day. Jesus’ kingdom is not from this world: it does not advance by the sword, as Peter learned, or by political force. It advances by the witness of the one who is the truth. Pilate asks what truth is while standing in front of the answer.
verseByVerse.examples: The Barabbas exchange is the gospel in miniature: the guilty goes free and the innocent is condemned. Barabbas was exactly what Jesus’ accusers had claimed Jesus was. In choosing him the crowd chose the liberation it wanted, political and violent, and rejected the one it needed, which only a substitute could win.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they led Jesus from the house of Caiaphas to the governor's headquarters. It was early morning. They themselves did not enter the governor's headquarters, so that they would not be defiled, but could eat the Passover. So Pilate went outside to them and said, "What accusation do you bring against this man?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
To the governor’s headquarters. The governor’s headquarters is the praetorium: either Herod’s old palace near the city’s western wall or the Antonia Fortress at the corner of the temple. Pilate, governor of Judea from AD 26 to 36, normally lived in Caesarea, but came to Jerusalem at feasts to keep order. John builds it like a drama in scenes, with Pilate going out to the accusers and in to the prisoner and out again, never settling.

It was early morning. Roman officials began work at dawn. The night’s proceedings have produced a prisoner and no case, and the leaders want the matter finished before the festival crowds wake.

So that they would not be defiled. Entering a Gentile house was thought to make a Jew ritually unclean, barred from the festival meals of that day. So they stand in the street and make Pilate come out. The irony is crushing: men who will not step over a threshold because of a ceremonial rule are arranging a judicial killing on the other side of it (Matthew 23:24).

A conscience pointed at the wrong object. The mechanism is not hypocrisy in the crude sense of knowing better and pretending. These men were sincere about the purity rule, which is what makes it frightening. A real conscience about small things can stay in perfect working order while the large thing goes past unnoticed.

Eat the Passover. This raises a famous question. The other Gospels present the Last Supper as a Passover meal (Mark 14:12–16); here, the Passover seems still to come. The answer below is the likeliest harmonisation, not a certainty.

Where Christians differ: the date of the Passover. Some say John has moved the date for theological reasons, so that Jesus dies as the lambs are slaughtered; others that different groups followed different calendars. This commentary’s view: “eat the Passover” can refer to the whole seven-day feast of Unleavened Bread, which was also called Passover (Luke 22:1), including the festal offering eaten on the next day (2 Chronicles 30:22). The Last Supper was a Passover meal, and the leaders here wished to stay clean for the feast’s continuing meals. The Gospels do not contradict one another.

What accusation do you bring against this man? Pilate starts a formal Roman trial. And Pilate goes out to them, which is the first move of the trial and sets its direction. A Roman governor was not obliged to conduct business in the street to accommodate the religious sensibilities of a subject people. He does it anyway, and by the end of the morning he will have conceded everything. When authority loses the will to be just, it becomes the instrument of injustice, however correct its procedures appear.

Clean for the feast, outside the Lamb’s door. Jesus is handed over on the day of Preparation (19:14), and not a bone of his is broken (19:36), the rule for the Passover lamb (Exodus 12:46). The men guarding their purity for the Passover meal are delivering up the Passover Lamb himself: Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed (1 Corinthians 5:7). They would not cross a Gentile threshold to stay clean. He would cross from heaven to earth, and into death, to make the unclean clean.

How do I know if I am straining gnats and swallowing camels? Look at where your conscience is loudest. If you are troubled about small matters of practice, the right wording, the right music, the right habits, while untroubled by bitterness, greed, a harsh tongue or an unreconciled brother, the scale is wrong. Jesus did not say the small things do not matter; he said these you ought to have done, without neglecting the others (Matthew 23:23). Ask God to recalibrate you by his word, especially by the weightier matters of justice, mercy and faithfulness, and ask a trusted friend where they think your blind spot lies.

For worship. The Lamb was handed across the threshold the priests would not cross, into Gentile hands, and so the Lamb of Israel was slain by Jew and Gentile together, for Jew and Gentile together. The wall they guarded so carefully that morning he broke down in his flesh (Ephesians 2:14), and now the unclean of every nation are made clean and welcomed to his feast.
verseByVerse.note: The governor’s headquarters is the praetorium. Entering a Gentile’s house would make them ritually unclean for the festival.

verseByVerse.quote: They answered him, "If this man were not doing evil, we would not have delivered him over to you." Pilate said to them, "Take him yourselves and judge him by your own law." The Jews said to him, "It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death."
verseByVerse.commentary:
If this man were not doing evil. Their first answer is not an answer, and Pilate notices. They do not name a charge; they are asking a Roman court to ratify a verdict already reached without hearing the grounds for it.

Judge him by your own law. Procedurally correct, and an attempt to get rid of the case. Rome generally left internal religious matters to local courts.

Not lawful for us. Now they show their real goal: in Judea Rome kept the power of capital punishment for itself. Stephen was stoned (Acts 7), but that was mob action, distinct from a formal judicial execution, which in a Roman province was reserved to the governor. What they are saying is not that killing him is impossible but that killing him legally requires Pilate.

Why does John keep saying the Jews handed Jesus over?
