He uses the phrase for the Jerusalem leaders and those who followed them, not for the whole people; Jesus, his disciples and the first believers were all Jews. Pilate himself says Your own nation and the chief priests (18:35). The guilt for the cross belongs to those who planned it, to Pilate who allowed it, and, in the deepest sense, to all of us whose sins put him there. Peter says the Jerusalem crowd and their rulers acted in ignorance (Acts 3:17), and the gospel was preached to them first. The charge of collective Jewish guilt, used to justify persecution, has no ground in John or anywhere in Scripture.

A prisoner with no charge. They cannot name a crime because there is none to name. Jesus had asked them openly, Which one of you convicts me of sin? (8:46), and no one had answered. Now they have nothing better to bring the governor. The sinless one stands at the door of the praetorium, and the emptiness of their case is the first testimony of the morning to what Pilate will say three times: I find no guilt in him. The Passover lamb had to be without blemish (Exodus 12:5), and the men handing him over are proving, without meaning to, that he is.
verseByVerse.note: Rome kept the power of capital punishment for itself in Judea.

parallels.desc: Stephen stoned by a mob

verseByVerse.quote: This was to fulfill the word that Jesus had spoken to show by what kind of death he was going to die. So Pilate entered his headquarters again and called Jesus and said to him, "Are you the King of the Jews?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
By what kind of death. John’s note turns the whole exchange. Stoning was the Jewish penalty for blasphemy; being “lifted up” meant crucifixion, the Roman penalty (3:14; 8:28; 12:32–33). If the council had been able to act alone, he would have been stoned. A jurisdictional technicality is the means by which the manner of his death was secured.

Hanged on a tree. Being hanged on a tree meant being under God’s curse (Deuteronomy 21:23; Galatians 3:13). Paul builds on it: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13). He had to die that way, under that sentence, and the men insisting on the correct paperwork were arranging it.

What does it mean that Christ became a curse? It means he stood where the law’s judgment falls. The law pronounced a curse on everyone who does not keep it (Galatians 3:10), and that is all of us. On the cross the Father treated his Son as the bearer of that curse, not because Jesus had sinned, but because our sin was laid on him (2 Corinthians 5:21). The tree was the outward sign of the inward reality: the Holy One under God’s judgment in our place. So the curse is not merely lessened for the believer. It has been exhausted on Christ, and the blessing of Abraham comes to us instead (Galatians 3:14).

Are you the King of the Jews? The charge is now political. Luke says they accused him of forbidding tribute to Caesar and claiming to be Christ a king (Luke 23:2). In Greek, Pilate’s “you” is emphatic, placed first: su, you? This beaten, bound man? A king? It is contemptuous, and understandably so. In front of him is a man in his thirties, unarmed, tied up, handed over by his own nation’s leadership, with no supporters visible anywhere in the building. Pilate has spent years managing real insurgencies in this province, and he has seen what a claimant to a throne looks like. This does not.

The only charge that could interest Rome. That is why the question sits at the centre of the trial. It is the only charge that could interest a Roman court, treason, a rival king, and everything the priests want depends on making it stick. Blasphemy, which Pilate would have thrown out, surfaces only later (19:7). They were right that he was a king, and wrong about what kind, and Pilate is about to be right for the wrong reasons and write it on a board (19:19).

In the room they would not enter. The one conversation in which Jesus explains himself happens in a room the accusers refused to enter. Pilate meanwhile goes out (v. 29), comes in (v. 33), goes out again (v. 38), and never settles anywhere, not even with his own verdict.
verseByVerse.note: Stoning was the Jewish penalty for blasphemy; being “lifted up” pointed to Roman crucifixion.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered, "Do you say this of your own accord, or did others say it to you about me?" Pilate answered, "Am I a Jew? Your own nation and the chief priests have delivered you over to me. What have you done?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do you say this of your own accord, or did others say it to you about me? The prisoner starts interrogating the judge. If Pilate means a political rebel king, the answer is no. If he means the Messiah, the answer is yes. That is not evasion. It is the question that separates two entirely different conversations, and in effect it is an offer: the offer he made to Nicodemus and the woman at the well and the man born blind, extended to the Roman prefect of Judea in the early morning. He was the one on trial, and he spent his breath trying to reach his judge.

Am I a Jew? Contempt. Why would a Roman care about Jewish religious ideas? And it is a self-revealing sentence. He is declining to be personally involved. Whatever this is about, it is not his world and he does not intend to enter it. The effect is to shut the door on the only conversation in the room that could have done him any good.

Your own nation. Immediately after refusing to be interested, Pilate does still want to know. That is the tragedy of Pilate: he is not a monster and not stupid. He asks good questions and repeatedly declines to stay for the answers. He knows he is being used, and says so. And he goes through with it anyway, which is the difference between seeing a thing clearly and being willing to pay for acting on it. What he would not pay was his standing with Caesar, and when the crowd later cries that releasing this man would make him no friend of Caesar, that settles it (19:12). Many who see clearly enough who Jesus is are held back by the same thing: not a lack of evidence, but the fear of what following him would cost.

Can I keep Jesus at arm’s length, like Pilate? You can try, and many do: interested in him as a historical figure, a moral teacher, a subject for discussion, but unwilling to let the question become personal. Jesus will not leave it there. He asked Pilate, in effect, are you asking this for yourself? and he asks every reader the same. Neutrality about Christ is not available, because he claims to be the King to whom every person will answer (Acts 17:31). Pilate tried to be a spectator at his own trial of Jesus, and ended as the man whose name is spoken in every recitation of the Creed: suffered under Pontius Pilate.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered, "My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting, that I might not be delivered over to the Jews. But my kingdom is not from the world." Then Pilate said to him, "So you are a king?" Jesus answered, "You say that I am a king. For this purpose I was born and for this purpose I have come into the world — to bear witness to the truth. Everyone who is of the truth listens to my voice."
verseByVerse.commentary:
My kingdom is not of this world. The preposition is ek, out of, from. It is a statement about origin, not about location. His kingdom does not come from this world or work the way the world’s kingdoms do: its source is heaven, and its power is truth, not swords. Its territory is very much this world, which is why he is standing in a Roman courtroom.

Why the preposition matters. Read as a statement about location, the sentence becomes a charter for a Christianity that concedes the actual world to other powers and retreats into private religion, the arrangement every tyranny has been happy to grant the church. Read as a statement about origin, it says something far more disturbing to Pilate: there is a kingdom operating in his province whose authority did not come from Rome, does not depend on Rome, and will outlast Rome. Rome has fallen. His kingdom has spread to every nation by nothing but the word of the cross and the power of the Spirit, and it will stand when every throne on earth is dust.

My servants would have been fighting. Jesus gives evidence Pilate can check: exactly one sword had been drawn in the garden, and its owner had been told to put it away. The absence of a fight is the proof of the kingdom’s origin. Every time the church has reached for the sword to advance the faith, and it has, it has contradicted the sentence its Lord spoke at his own trial.

So you are a king? Pilate seizes on the word, and Jesus answers, You say that I am a king: a cautious yes. He is a king, though not in Pilate’s sense, and his kingdom’s origin is God.

Born, and came. A man born, and one who came from elsewhere: incarnation in a phrase. It is the only time in this Gospel he speaks of his birth.

To bear witness to the truth. He conquers by testimony. He describes himself to the governor as a witness, which is the humblest possible job description, and it is the one that gets him killed.

Listens to my voice. His subjects are those who hear him, as the sheep hear the shepherd (10:27), and the sentence is an invitation even to Pilate.

In the flow. Nathanael hailed him as King of Israel (1:49); the crowd tried to make him king by force (6:15); he rode in as Zechariah’s king (12:13–15). Now he tells a Roman what kind of king he is, and Pilate will write the title over the cross (19:19–20): this King is never more truly enthroned than when he is lifted up.

Where Christians differ: the kingdom and the state. Some have sought to establish Christ’s kingdom by political power or force; others have concluded that faith has nothing to say to public life. This commentary’s view: Christ’s kingdom advances by the word and Spirit, not by the sword. The church must not use the state’s weapons to spread the gospel. Yet Christ is king over all, and his truth addresses rulers too, as here.

Does this mean Christians may never fight? Some Christians, pacifists, read it so, and their earnest witness against violence deserves respect. But Jesus is speaking of his kingdom: it will never be advanced by force. That does not abolish the state’s God-given sword (Romans 13:4), nor forbid a Christian to serve as a soldier or police officer (Luke 3:14), nor to defend life. The church must never use force to spread the gospel; a Christian citizen may share in the just defence of others.

What does it mean to be of the truth? It means to belong to the truth rather than merely to hold opinions about it: to have been born of God, so that his voice is recognised as the voice of home. Jesus is not saying that some people are naturally better at truth than others. He is saying that those whom God has drawn will hear the Shepherd when he speaks (6:44–45; 10:26–27). In practice it shows in a willingness to be corrected by Christ, to come to the light even when it exposes you (3:21), and to keep listening to his word when it is unwelcome. If his voice is the one you want to hear above all others, you are of the truth.

In everyday life. In your workplace, your vote, your conversations about public life, refuse the weapons of slander, manipulation and contempt even when your cause is right. The King you serve won without them.

parallels.desc: the good confession before Pontius Pilate

verseByVerse.quote: Pilate said to him, "What is truth?" After he had said this, he went back outside to the Jews and told them, "I find no guilt in him. But you have a custom that I should release one man for you at the Passover. So do you want me to release to you the King of the Jews?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
What is truth? There are two ways to say it. It can be a sneer: the tired cynicism of a career official who has watched every faction in a difficult province dress up its interests as principle, and who has concluded that truth is a word people use when they want something. That is the usual reading and it fits the man. It can also be genuine, and something in the scene allows it. He has just been told by a bound prisoner that there is such a thing as truth and that men can be of it. Pilate may be, for one moment, actually asking. Either way, the Truth is standing in front of him (14:6).

He did not stay. What settles it is not the tone but the timing: whatever he meant by it, he did not wait. Francis Bacon wrote: “What is truth? said jesting Pilate, and would not stay for an answer.” He asked the largest question a person can ask, in the presence of the only one who could have answered it, and left the room. Many still ask the question without wanting the answer.

How do I answer a friend who says there is no such thing as truth? Gently, and with a question of your own. Is that statement true? If it is, there is at least one truth; if it is not, there is no reason to believe it. Then move from argument to a person. Christianity does not claim merely to have found some true ideas; it claims that the Truth became a man, lived, died and rose, and that his resurrection is a public fact that can be examined (1 Corinthians 15:3–8). Invite your friend to read one of the Gospels with you. Pilate’s problem was not lack of evidence; it was that he would not stay for it. Ask your friend to stay.

I find no guilt in him. This is the first of three times (19:4, 6). Three times the Roman court, in the person of its highest local representative, returns a verdict of not guilty, and three times it proceeds anyway. The innocent will die for the guilty. He was declared innocent three times by the court that crucified him, so that we who are guilty might be declared righteous by the court of heaven.

A custom. Immediately after acquitting him, he does not release him but offers a deal, which means that from this moment Jesus is no longer being tried. He is being negotiated over. No source outside the Gospels attests this amnesty, though governors are known to have released prisoners to please a crowd. Offering them the King of the Jews, he is trying to wriggle out and mocking the leaders with the title.

verseByVerse.quote: They cried out again, "Not this man, but Barabbas!" Now Barabbas was a robber.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not this man, but Barabbas! Mark says Barabbas had committed murder in an insurrection (Mark 15:7). So the man the crowd asks for is a real one: an armed nationalist with blood on his hands, of exactly the kind Rome crucified in batches, and of exactly the kind Jesus had been accused of being.

Son of the father. His name means “son of the father” (bar abba). Some early manuscripts of Matthew call him Jesus Barabbas (Matthew 27:16–17), which, if it stood, would mean Pilate asked the crowd to choose between Jesus son of the father and Jesus who is called Christ. The evidence is divided. But the scene makes the point the name suggests: a guilty son of a father goes free, and the innocent Son of the Father dies.

Barabbas was a robber. The word (lēstēs) means bandit, insurrectionist, the word used of the thieves and robbers in 10:1, 8, who climb into the sheepfold by another way. It is what Josephus calls the insurgents of the period. They chose the robber over the Good Shepherd, the kind of liberation, violent and political, that Rome could crush, and refused the liberation no power can overcome.

The exchange acted out. What happens next is the doctrine of substitution acted out in a courtyard, once, in front of witnesses, before anybody had a word for it. One man guilty of insurrection and murder, one declared innocent by the judge: the guilty man walks out of a Roman prison free while the innocent one is taken away to the cross that had been prepared. Barabbas is the first person whose life was saved by Jesus’ death in a literal sense. Every believer can read his own case into that morning.

What became of him. Nothing is recorded of what became of Barabbas. He walks out of history. He did not choose it, did not deserve it, and as far as we know never thanked anybody. That is the exchange: not a bargain, not a reward, not a transaction anybody entered into, but a guilty man’s sentence served by an innocent one, arranged by people who were trying to do something else entirely, on the morning of the Passover.

Was Barabbas saved? Scripture does not tell us, and we should not guess. His release was physical; he was spared a Roman cross, which is not the same as being forgiven by God. To be saved from the judgment of God a person must trust in the one who took his place (3:16, 36). Barabbas is a picture of substitution, not proof that everyone it pictures receives it. That is why the picture ends with a question for us rather than for him: you have heard that Christ died in the place of sinners; have you received him as dying in yours?

Is it just for an innocent man to be punished in place of the guilty? It would be unjust if the substitute were unwilling, or a third party dragged in against his will, or if the judge simply waved the guilt away. None of those is true at the cross. The Son came willingly (10:18); the Judge whose law was broken is the same God who provides the substitute (Romans 3:25–26); and the Son is united to his people as their head, so that what he does, he does as one of us and for us. Barabbas’s release was an injustice by Pilate. Our release is the justice of God satisfied by the love of God, so that he is both just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus. To justify means to declare a person righteous in God’s court: not to make him better by degrees, but to pronounce the verdict in his favour, because his penalty has been borne and Christ’s righteousness is counted as his (Romans 4:5; 2 Corinthians 5:21).

In everyday life. You are Barabbas. When someone wrongs you, remember how much you were released from, and let that make you quick to forgive.

For worship. Barabbas walked out of the prison into the morning light, and the Lord of glory walked out of the praetorium toward the cross Rome kept for men like Barabbas. Every rebel who trusts in Christ goes out through that same door. The prison stands open because the cross was occupied, and the one who hung there was the King of the Jews, our substitute.
verseByVerse.note: Mark says Barabbas had committed murder in an insurrection; “robber” was often used for violent rebels.

18.text: <sup>1</sup>When Jesus had spoken these words, he went out with his disciples across the brook Kidron, where there was a garden, which he and his disciples entered.<sup>2</sup>Now Judas, who betrayed him, also knew the place, for Jesus often met there with his disciples.<sup>3</sup>So Judas, having procured a band of soldiers and some officers from the chief priests and the Pharisees, went there with lanterns and torches and weapons.<sup>4</sup>Then Jesus, knowing all that would happen to him, came forward and said to them, “Whom do you seek?”<sup>5</sup>They answered him, “Jesus of Nazareth.” Jesus said to them, “I am he.” Judas, who betrayed him, was standing with them.<sup>6</sup>When Jesus said to them, “I am he,” they drew back and fell to the ground.<sup>7</sup>So he asked them again, “Whom do you seek?” And they said, “Jesus of Nazareth.”<sup>8</sup>Jesus answered, “I told you that I am he. So, if you seek me, let these men go.”<sup>9</sup>This was to fulfill the word that he had spoken: “Of those whom you gave me I have lost not one.”<sup>10</sup>Then Simon Peter, having a sword, drew it and struck the high priest’s servant and cut off his right ear. (The servant’s name was Malchus.)<sup>11</sup>So Jesus said to Peter, “Put your sword into its sheath; shall I not drink the cup that the Father has given me?”<sup>12</sup>So the band of soldiers and their captain and the officers of the Jews arrested Jesus and bound him.<sup>13</sup>First they led him to Annas, for he was the father-in-law of Caiaphas, who was high priest that year.<sup>14</sup>It was Caiaphas who had advised the Jews that it would be expedient that one man should die for the people.<sup>15</sup>Simon Peter followed Jesus, and so did another disciple. Since that disciple was known to the high priest, he entered with Jesus into the courtyard of the high priest,<sup>16</sup>but Peter stood outside at the door. So the other disciple, who was known to the high priest, went out and spoke to the servant girl who kept watch at the door, and brought Peter in.<sup>17</sup>The servant girl at the door said to Peter, “You also are not one of this man’s disciples, are you?” He said, “I am not.”<sup>18</sup>Now the servants and officers had made a charcoal fire, because it was cold, and they were standing and warming themselves. Peter also was with them, standing and warming himself.<sup>19</sup>The high priest then questioned Jesus about his disciples and his teaching.<sup>20</sup>Jesus answered him, “I have spoken openly to the world. I have always taught in synagogues and in the temple, where all Jews come together. I have said nothing in secret.<sup>21</sup>Why do you ask me? Ask those who have heard me what I said to them; they know what I said.”<sup>22</sup>When he had said these things, one of the officers standing by struck Jesus with his hand, saying, “Is that how you answer the high priest?”<sup>23</sup>Jesus answered him, “If what I said is wrong, bear witness about the wrong; but if what I said is right, why do you strike me?”<sup>24</sup>Annas then sent him bound to Caiaphas the high priest.<sup>25</sup>Now Simon Peter was standing and warming himself. So they said to him, “You also are not one of his disciples, are you?” He denied it and said, “I am not.”<sup>26</sup>One of the servants of the high priest, a relative of the man whose ear Peter had cut off, asked, “Did I not see you in the garden with him?”<sup>27</sup>Peter again denied it, and at once a rooster crowed.<sup>28</sup>Then they led Jesus from the house of Caiaphas to the governor’s headquarters. It was early morning. They themselves did not enter the governor’s headquarters, so that they would not be defiled, but could eat the Passover.<sup>29</sup>So Pilate went outside to them and said, “What accusation do you bring against this man?”<sup>30</sup>They answered him, “If this man were not doing evil, we would not have delivered him over to you.”<sup>31</sup>Pilate said to them, “Take him yourselves and judge him by your own law.” The Jews said to him, “It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death.”<sup>32</sup>This was to fulfill the word that Jesus had spoken to show by what kind of death he was going to die.<sup>33</sup>So Pilate entered his headquarters again and called Jesus and said to him, “Are you the King of the Jews?”<sup>34</sup>Jesus answered, “Do you say this of your own accord, or did others say it to you about me?”<sup>35</sup>Pilate answered, “Am I a Jew? Your own nation and the chief priests have delivered you over to me. What have you done?”<sup>36</sup>Jesus answered, “My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting, that I might not be delivered over to the Jews. But my kingdom is not from the world.”<sup>37</sup>Then Pilate said to him, “So you are a king?” Jesus answered, “You say that I am a king. For this purpose I was born and for this purpose I have come into the world— to bear witness to the truth. Everyone who is of the truth listens to my voice.”<sup>38</sup>Pilate said to him, “What is truth?” After he had said this, he went back outside to the Jews and told them, “I find no guilt in him.<sup>39</sup>But you have a custom that I should release one man for you at the Passover. So do you want me to release to you the King of the Jews?”<sup>40</sup>They cried out again, “Not this man, but Barabbas!” Now Barabbas was a robber.
18.overview:
John’s account of the arrest and trials shows Jesus not as a victim but as the one in control. In the garden he steps forward to meet his captors, and they fall at his word; he secures his disciples’ release and goes willingly to drink the cup his Father has given him. Bound, he is questioned by Annas, while in the courtyard outside Peter denies him three times.

At dawn he is brought to Pilate. The leaders who will not enter a Gentile house are handing over the true Passover Lamb. Before the governor Jesus speaks of a kingdom not of this world and of the truth he came to bear witness to. Pilate finds no guilt in him and still bargains him away, and the crowd asks for Barabbas. The judge is on trial before the truth, and fails.

19.title: The Crucifixion and Burial of Jesus

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — The Crown of Thorns and the Cross
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The sentence and the crucifixion. Pilate’s attempts to release Jesus fail one by one until the threat about Caesar settles it. Jesus carries his own cross to Golgotha, and Pilate refuses to change the title over it.
verseByVerse.theology: Behold the man (v. 5) and Behold your King (v. 14) are Pilate’s two presentations of Jesus, each truer than Pilate knows. Here is humanity’s representative, the man who is also the King. Pilate intends mockery; God intends revelation. The crown of thorns and the purple robe are parodies of kingship that are true of the King who reigns from the cross.
verseByVerse.examples: Crucified between two others (v. 18): the innocent numbered among the guilty. The title in Aramaic, Latin and Greek makes the proclamation universal. The chief priests want it turned into a mere claim; Pilate refuses: What I have written, I have written.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Pilate took Jesus and flogged him. And the soldiers twisted together a crown of thorns and put it on his head and arrayed him in a purple robe.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. John 19 tells of Jesus’ sentence, crucifixion, death and burial. John presents the cross as the King’s enthronement: crowned, robed, proclaimed king in three languages, lifted up. And it is the Passover sacrifice: he dies on the day of Preparation in Passover week, no bone broken, offered sour wine on hyssop. At the centre stands his cry: It is finished. Everything in this Gospel has been moving here, and John tells it with a restraint that makes every detail weigh.

Flogged him. Roman flogging used a whip weighted with bone or metal. It tore the flesh to ribbons, and sometimes killed the prisoner before crucifixion. This one comes in the middle of the trial, before any sentence, and Luke supplies Pilate’s reasoning in his own words: I will therefore punish and release him (Luke 23:16, 22).

A compromise worse than a miscarriage. Pilate has found no guilt, and he is trying to give the crowd something short of a death: the manoeuvre of an official who knows what justice requires and is looking for a cheaper alternative. It did not work, and it is in some ways worse than a straightforward miscarriage: a savage punishment inflicted on a man he has publicly declared innocent, not as a sentence but as a bargaining position.

A crown of thorns. The Greek word is not diadēma, the usual word for a king’s crown. What they twist together is a stephanos, a word used above all for the victor’s wreath, given to the winner of the games or to a general on his return. They meant it as a joke. Within days the man wearing it will be seen to have won, and the word they chose is the one the New Testament uses for the crown he will give away: the crown of life, of righteousness, of glory that does not fade (James 1:12; 2 Timothy 4:8; 1 Peter 5:4).

The thorns of the curse. Thorns were part of the curse on the ground after Adam’s sin (Genesis 3:18). A handful of it is pressed onto his head by men who are laughing. The King bears on his head the sign of God’s just sentence on a world gone wrong through sin, so that those who trust him receive blessing instead: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (Galatians 3:13).

A purple robe. Purple was the colour of royalty, made from costly dye; this was perhaps an old soldier’s cloak. The soldiers are doing theology without knowing it: robing the King and crowning him for his throne.

Why did Jesus have to suffer so much? Would his death alone not have been enough? Scripture does not treat his sufferings as a mere preliminary to the real work. His whole humiliation, the flogging, the mockery and the pain as well as the death, was part of his obedience and his bearing of our sin. Isaiah links the wounds themselves to our healing (Isaiah 53:5), and Peter says he bore our sins in his body on the tree (1 Peter 2:24). The suffering also shows us what sin is: not a small fault but a thing that, when it fell on the holy Son, looked like this. And it means that there is no pain you can suffer that he has not entered. He is a High Priest who can sympathise with our weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15).

In everyday life. When you suffer in your body, tell the Lord who was flogged. You do not have to explain pain to him.

For worship. The King’s first crown was made of thorns. He wore it without complaint for people who had brought thorns into the world. The head they mocked is crowned now with many diadems (Revelation 19:12), the royal crowns they would never have given him, and he wears them still bearing the marks of the first. There is no crown in heaven that was not won under that one.
verseByVerse.note: Roman flogging used a whip weighted with bone or metal. Purple was the colour of royalty.

verseByVerse.quote: They came up to him, saying, "Hail, King of the Jews!" and struck him with their hands. Pilate went out again and said to them, "See, I am bringing him out to you that you may know that I find no guilt in him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hail, King of the Jews! A parody of “Hail, Caesar!” These are probably auxiliary troops in Roman service, and they mock him with the truth. Without anybody intending it, the mockery stages a coronation: robe, crown, acclamation and homage, every element of an accession present and inverted. Heaven will one day ring with the same acclamation, sung in earnest by people from every nation.

I find no guilt in him. The second declaration of innocence (18:38). The horror is quiet and official: the verdict is innocent, and the prisoner has just been flogged. To Pilate the beating is not a sentence but an offer, and he wants the crowd to notice his fairness in the very sentence in which he produces a man he has had beaten half to death for no offence.

Why does God let people mock Christ, then and now? Because he is patient, and because he is not threatened. The mockery of the soldiers was not a defeat for God; it was the means by which the King was led to his throne. The mockery of today, the jokes, the contempt, the casual blasphemy, is no more a threat to his reign than theirs was. God is giving time for repentance (2 Peter 3:9), and some of the mockers will be his. Mark tells us that a Roman centurion, watching him die, confessed him as the Son of God (Mark 15:39). When you hear Christ mocked, grieve, speak up where you can with grace, and pray for the mocker. He may yet kneel.

In everyday life. Watch for the Pilate in yourself: the wish to be seen as fair while doing the unjust thing. If you have harmed someone and are now asking others to admire your reasonableness, stop, and put it right; the King who took those blows has borne that sin too, so you can own it without fear.

verseByVerse.quote: So Jesus came out, wearing the crown of thorns and the purple robe. Pilate said to them, "Behold the man!" When the chief priests and the officers saw him, they cried out, "Crucify him, crucify him!" Pilate said to them, "Take him yourselves and crucify him, for I find no guilt in him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold the man! In Latin, Ecce homo, and few scenes in the Gospels have been painted more often. What Pilate means by it is entirely cynical: look at the state of him; this is your dangerous insurgent. He is betting that the sight will make them stop wanting him dead. But the sight of suffering does not reliably produce pity, and here it produces a howl.

The true man. But John hears more. Here is the man: the true human being, the second Adam, the Son of Man (Daniel 7:13), suffering for all. Behind the words may be heard Zechariah’s behold, the man whose name is the Branch (Zechariah 6:12), a man crowned as a priest on his throne. What is being pointed at is not a specimen of suffering but the human race’s representative, who stands in for others, so that what he does counts for them: as by Adam’s disobedience the many were made sinners, so by Christ’s obedience the many will be made righteous (Romans 5:19). The curse that fell on the first Adam is sitting on the second’s head in the form of thorns. God’s verdict on humanity and his answer to it stand in one figure.

Crucify him, crucify him! The chief priests and officers lead the shout. We should resist the instinct to distance ourselves from it too quickly. This is what happened when God became visible and stood in front of a crowd at close range without power: not indifference, not confusion, but a demand that he be removed. Anyone who has wondered why God does not simply show himself finds at least part of an answer in this verse, and it is not a comfortable one. Here is everything humanity was meant to be, beaten and robed in mockery, and here is everything humanity has become, howling for his death. Pilate’s reply is his third declaration of innocence, and a taunt: he knows they cannot legally crucify.

Would I have shouted with the crowd? In one sense, yes. Not because you would have been in Jerusalem that morning, but because the same heart that shouted is in every one of us by nature: the heart that wants God out of the way when he comes too close (Romans 8:7). That is why the cross is not only something done by them; it was done for our sins, and in that sense by us. But the gospel does not leave you in the crowd. The man they rejected prayed for those who crucified him (Luke 23:34, words missing from some early manuscripts but printed in most Bibles), and about three thousand people in that same city were baptised seven weeks later (Acts 2:23, 36–41). The shout of crucify him is answered by the cry of it is finished.

parallels.desc: no beauty that we should desire him

verseByVerse.quote: The Jews answered him, "We have a law, and according to that law he ought to die because he has made himself the Son of God." When Pilate heard this statement, he was even more afraid.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We have a law. The law against blasphemy (Leviticus 24:16): their law, which a Roman court had no business enforcing. They had spent the morning translating a religious conviction into a political one because that was the only version Rome would hear. Now, frustrated, they revert to the real one, and hand Pilate a problem he has no competence to judge.

The Son of God. The real charge comes out (5:18; 10:33). All morning it has been the charge of kingship; now they say what the council had actually condemned him for. They are right that he had claimed it, and had understood him exactly (8:59; 10:31). The only question is whether it is true. The eternal Son, who had been with the Father before the world existed, stood in a governor’s court accused of being exactly who he was.

Even more afraid. He was already uneasy, and John has not said so until now. Something about this prisoner has been unsettling him since the first interview. Matthew says his wife had warned him of a dream: have nothing to do with that righteous man (Matthew 27:19). Romans believed in sons of gods: Augustus was officially called son of the deified Julius. And every Roman knew stories of gods walking about in disguise and of what happened to men who mistreated them without recognising them. What if this man really was one?

Did Jesus really claim to be God? Yes, and his enemies understood it better than many modern readers. He claimed God as his own Father in a way that made himself equal with God (5:18). He said, before Abraham was, I am (8:58). He said, I and the Father are one, and they took up stones because, as they said, you, being a man, make yourself God (10:30–33). He accepted Thomas’s confession, my Lord and my God (20:28). He did not die for claiming to be a good teacher; he died for claiming to be the Son of God. As C. S. Lewis argued, a man who said these things would be deluded, a deceiver, or the Lord he claimed to be. The resurrection settled which.

In everyday life. If he is the Son of God, then everything he says has the authority of God, including what he says about your money, your marriage, your fears and your sins. Bring the area where you have treated his words as optional under his claim today, trusting the Spirit he has given you to work in you both the will and the doing (Philippians 2:13).

parallels.desc: whoever blasphemes the name of the LORD shall surely be put to death

verseByVerse.quote: He entered his headquarters again and said to Jesus, "Where are you from?" But Jesus gave him no answer. So Pilate said to him, "You will not speak to me? Do you not know that I have authority to release you and authority to crucify you?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Where are you from? Not his hometown; Pilate knows that (Luke 23:6–7). He means: who are you, really? It is the great question of John’s Gospel, asked before by the crowd who said they knew where he came from and therefore he could not be the Christ (7:27), and by the Pharisees who said they did not know where he came from (9:29). Now a Roman asks it, frightened, in a private room, and it is the right question at last.

No answer. After a night of speaking, the one question that goes to the centre is met with silence. This is the Servant of Isaiah: he was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth (Isaiah 53:7). And Pilate had already heard the truth (18:37) and walked out before the answer. A man who leaves before the answer to one question does not get an answer to the next.

The answer John has already given. The reader has had the answer since the first verse of the book. He is the Word who was with God and was God (1:1), come from the Father into the world (16:28). The prisoner in the purple robe is the one through whom Pilate, Rome and the stone pavement under their feet were made (1:3). He is from the Father’s side, and he has come to take sinners back there with him (14:3).

What if God is silent when I ask him something? There are people who have asked God something real, not idly, not to score a point, and received nothing. Not a refusal. Silence. The temptation is to conclude either that nobody is there, or that the asking was somehow disqualified. This verse establishes that the silence of God is not always what it appears. Jesus’ silence was not indifference; the man in front of Pilate was at that moment on his way to dying for sinners. The nearest thing to an answer Pilate was ever going to get was standing there in a purple robe with his hands tied. That does not explain any particular silence, and it is not offered as an explanation. It establishes something narrower and worth having: a silent Christ and an absent Christ are not the same thing. Keep praying, keep reading his word, and remember that he has already given his clearest answer at the cross.

Do you not know that I have authority to release you and authority to crucify you? Pilate falls back on his power. He thinks he holds Jesus’ life in his hands. It is the response of small authority everywhere to being ignored. He has just been frightened. Now he reaches for rank. Power has seldom been so mistaken about itself.

For worship. Christ was silent before his judge, so that we might have something to say before ours: he died for me. He held his peace so that we could have peace. And the one who would not answer Pilate answers every sinner who comes to him: whoever comes to me I will never cast out.

parallels.desc: he opened not his mouth

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered him, "You would have no authority over me at all unless it had been given you from above. Therefore he who delivered me over to you has the greater sin." From then on Pilate sought to release him, but the Jews cried out, "If you release this man, you are not Caesar's friend. Everyone who makes himself a king opposes Caesar."
verseByVerse.commentary:
From above. The word for from above is one this Gospel has used before, and it is not the obvious one. It is anōthen, the word that baffled Nicodemus in chapter 3. Here there is no ambiguity, and the claim is enormous. All human authority is delegated by God (Romans 13:1). God has ordained this hour (Acts 2:23; 4:27–28). Pilate thinks he is in charge; Jesus tells him he holds real power, and that it is on loan. The Father had given Pilate his authority, the Son had given himself into his hands, and the whole of that terrible morning was moving according to a purpose formed before the world began.

The greater sin. It is singular, he who delivered me, most probably Caiaphas (some think Judas, or the leaders as a group), who had the Scriptures, the office, and full knowledge of what he was doing, as against a Gentile administrator out of his depth. Pilate is guilty, but less so. There are degrees of sin (Luke 12:47–48). Scripture consistently weighs guilt by the light received, which is uncomfortable for the well-taught and merciful toward the ignorant.

Comfort under bad authority. There is comfort here for anyone under an authority that is behaving badly, and it must not become a defence of tyranny. It does not say that what Pilate is about to do is right: somebody has the greater sin, which means sin is being committed and measured. It says that the power being abused is borrowed and bounded, and that the man wielding it will answer for how he used what he was lent.

Not Caesar’s friend. This is the sentence that ends the trial. Friend of Caesar was an honorary title for loyal officials, and the emperor Tiberius was suspicious and quick to punish disloyalty. Pilate’s record was poor: he had provoked riots with the emperor’s image in Jerusalem, had probably been overruled by Tiberius after the Jewish leaders complained over his head, and within a few years would be sent to Rome to answer for a massacre in Samaria. The men making the threat know his file. Everything before this, the acquittals, the fear, the attempts to release him, collapses the moment his career is named.

If God is in control, was Pilate really to blame? Yes. God’s sovereignty never excuses human sin. Pilate’s authority came from above, but his decision to condemn an innocent man to save his own position came from his own heart, and Jesus calls it sin. Peter holds both together in one sentence: Jesus was delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, and you crucified and killed him by the hands of lawless men (Acts 2:23). God ordained the end; the men who did it did what they wanted, and they are answerable. That is not a puzzle to be solved by dropping one half. It is the comfort of the believer: even the worst human choices cannot escape God’s purpose.

Must I obey authorities who act unjustly? In general, yes, in everything lawful, because their authority is from God (Romans 13:1–7; 1 Peter 2:13–17), and that includes respecting rulers we did not vote for and employers we do not admire. But obedience has a limit: when a ruler commands what God forbids, or forbids what God commands, we must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29). Christians may also use lawful means to resist injustice: appeal, protest, the ballot, the courts. And abuse in a home or a church is never to be submitted to; get help and get safe. Above all, remember that every ruler is lent his power and will answer for it.
verseByVerse.note: “Friend of Caesar” was an honorary title for loyal officials; the threat was that Pilate would be reported to the emperor.

parallels.desc: there is no authority except from God

verseByVerse.quote: So when Pilate heard these words, he brought Jesus out and sat down on the judgment seat at a place called The Stone Pavement, and in Aramaic Gabbatha. Now it was the day of Preparation of the Passover. It was about the sixth hour. He said to the Jews, "Behold your king!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The judgment seat. The bēma was the raised platform from which a Roman official gave formal sentence. It stood at the Stone Pavement, in Aramaic Gabbatha, perhaps meaning a raised place: an eyewitness detail. The irony is that Jesus is the true Judge (5:22, 27). Pilate sits on the seat of judgment over the one before whose judgment seat Pilate himself will one day stand (2 Corinthians 5:10).

The day of Preparation. The regular term for Friday (v. 31; Mark 15:42): the Friday of Passover week, and John wants us to see the Passover Lamb (1:29).

But was the Last Supper a Passover meal? Matthew, Mark and Luke say it was (Mark 14:12–16), while John seems to put the Passover a day later (13:1; 18:28). Some think different groups followed different calendars that year, or that Jesus held the meal early. The more likely answer is that the day of Preparation of the Passover means the Friday of Passover week, the day of preparation for the Sabbath (compare 19:31; Mark 15:42), and that in 18:28 the Passover means the meals of the festival week. On that reading the Supper was a Passover meal, and Jesus died on the Friday of Passover. It is not the only careful answer, and believers who hold every word of the Gospels true still weigh these options.

It was about the sixth hour. About noon by Jewish reckoning. Mark says he was crucified at the third hour, about 9 a.m. (Mark 15:25), and the trial cannot be running three hours after the crucifixion. Two reasonable answers are offered. The first is that John is counting hours the Roman civil way, from midnight, so that his sixth hour is about six in the morning. The second is that the day was divided into rough quarters, and each writer named the marker nearest the event, for a morning that ran somewhere between the two. John writes about the sixth hour; nobody in that courtyard had a watch.

The day, not the clock. If John is using Roman hours, a neat correspondence with the midday slaughter of the lambs should be held lightly. What matters does not depend on the hour: Jesus was condemned and killed on the day of Preparation, in the week when the Passover lambs of that feast were sacrificed. John says so twice, and the symbolism he is pressing rests on the day, not on the clock.

Behold your king! Pilate mocks the Jews, and speaks the truth. Still thorn-crowned and purple-robed, this is what the King of the new covenant looks like: enthroned in suffering, crowned with the curse.

In the flow. The trial has been about one question since Pilate first asked, Are you the King of the Jews? (18:33), and here it reaches its climax. From here the chapter carries two threads to their end: the King enthroned on a cross, and the Lamb sacrificed in Passover week.
verseByVerse.note: The judgment seat was the raised platform from which a Roman official gave judgment. The ESV notes that the sixth hour was about noon; Mark gives the third hour for the crucifixion — times were approximate and may be reckoned differently.

verseByVerse.quote: They cried out, "Away with him, away with him, crucify him!" Pilate said to them, "Shall I crucify your King?" The chief priests answered, "We have no king but Caesar." So he delivered him over to them to be crucified. So they took Jesus,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Away with him! Total rejection, and Pilate twists the knife.

We have no king but Caesar. It is said by the chief priests: not the crowd, not a hothead, but the men whose office existed to represent Israel before God. Israel longed for the Messiah, the son of David, to rule under God its King. Now, to get rid of Jesus, they renounce both.

What Israel was. Israel was a nation founded on the conviction that its true King was God. When the people first asked Samuel for a king, the LORD’s verdict was that they had rejected him from being king over them (1 Samuel 8:7). Gideon refused a crown on exactly that ground: the LORD will rule over you (Judges 8:23). And this is said at Passover, which celebrated deliverance from a pagan king, in Jerusalem, a few hundred yards from the temple, by the priesthood, about the emperor of the occupying army, in order to secure the execution of their own Messiah. In rejecting Jesus they reject God. Some forty years later Caesar’s soldiers burned the temple to the ground.

Does this mean God has rejected the Jewish people? No. This verse has been used badly, and the guard must be stated. It is a sentence spoken by a group of officials in a particular courtyard on a particular morning, and it is not a verdict on a people. The Gospel’s author, its subject, Jesus’ mother and every one of his apostles were Jews, and Paul says plainly that God has not rejected his people (Romans 11:1–2). Christians hold different views on what Romans 11 promises for Israel’s future, but none of them gives any ground for contempt. What this verse is, is a warning about religious leadership, and it lands nearest those who most resemble the men who said it: people who know the Scriptures, hold religious office, and find the real King inconvenient.

There is always a Caesar. Something can always be appealed to as the real authority when the true King is inconvenient: career, safety, respectability, a group’s approval. The chief priests did not stop believing in God that morning. Under pressure, they named somebody else as the one whose displeasure they could not risk.

Delivered him over. To them means to their will; Roman soldiers carried it out (v. 23). The verb is weighted. Judas delivered him to the priests, the priests delivered him to Pilate, Pilate delivers him to be crucified. And behind them all stands another delivering: he who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all (Romans 8:32).

In everyday life. Finish this sentence honestly: the thing I could not bear to lose, even for Christ, is.... Whatever fills the gap is the Caesar you are tempted to bow to. Bring it to him today, and say aloud that he is your King.

For worship. His own priests disowned the King, and he did not disown them. They chose Caesar to be rid of him. Within weeks thousands in the same city bowed to him as Lord and Christ (Acts 2:36), and before long a great many of the priests became obedient to the faith (Acts 6:7). Caesar’s throne is dust. His stands, and its gates are still open to those who once cried, Away with him.

parallels.desc: they have rejected me from being king over them

verseByVerse.quote: And he went out, bearing his own cross, to the place called The Place of a Skull, which in Aramaic is called Golgotha. There they crucified him, and with him two others, one on either side, and Jesus between them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bearing his own cross. Condemned men carried their own crossbeam to the place of execution. The upright post usually stood there already. The other Gospels tell us Simon of Cyrene was made to carry it behind Jesus (Mark 15:21; Luke 23:26). Nobody need be wrong: after a night of blows and a Roman flogging, men often could not finish the walk. John, whose whole passion narrative insists that nothing was taken from Jesus and everything was given, records that he went out carrying it himself.

Isaac and the wood. John may be recalling Isaac carrying the wood up Mount Moriah for his own sacrifice (Genesis 22:6). Abraham said God would provide the lamb. Here the Father provides the Lamb, and the Lamb carries the wood. There was no ram in the thicket to take his place, because he was the provision.

Outside the camp. He went outside the city, as the sin offering was burned outside the camp (Leviticus 16:27). Hebrews makes a doctrine of it: Jesus suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood, so let us go to him outside the camp and bear the reproach he endured (Hebrews 13:12–13). To sanctify means to make holy: to cleanse sinners and set them apart as God’s own, fit to come into his presence.

Golgotha. Perhaps a rocky hill shaped like a skull, or a place of execution. “Calvary” comes from the Latin calvaria, skull. The Church of the Holy Sepulchre probably marks the site, just outside the city wall of that time, and beside a road, because public execution was meant to be seen.

There they crucified him. Not one of the four Gospels describes the physical process; every first-century reader knew what the words covered. Crucifixion was the most cruel and shameful death Rome could inflict, reserved for slaves and rebels. Nails were driven through his hands and, it seems, his feet (20:25; Luke 24:39; the word for hand can include the wrist); the victim died slowly, of exhaustion, shock and laboured breathing, often over days. Cicero said the very word “cross” should be far from a Roman citizen’s thoughts. The evangelists want us to see not the gore but the meaning.

Jesus between them. Numbered with the transgressors (Isaiah 53:12). The three crosses are Isaiah’s sentence carried out by a Roman work detail with no idea what they were doing. They crucified the Lord of glory between two thieves, and he hung in the middle, where sinners are, so that sinners could be brought to where he is.

What does it mean for me to take up my cross? Not to carry his cross; that was his alone, and no one can share the work of atonement. But Jesus said that anyone who would follow him must deny himself, take up his cross daily and follow (Luke 9:23). To carry your cross is to accept, for his sake, the cost of belonging to him: the loss of approval, the death of your own way, the hardships that come from obedience. It is not every misfortune, a bad back or a difficult neighbour, though he helps with those too. It is the shame and loss that come because you are his. And it is always carried following him, which means it leads, as his did, through death to resurrection.
verseByVerse.note: Condemned men carried their own crossbeam to the place of execution; Simon of Cyrene was later made to carry it. Golgotha is Aramaic for “skull.”

parallels.desc: Isaac carries the wood

verseByVerse.quote: Pilate also wrote an inscription and put it on the cross. It read, "Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews." Many of the Jews read this inscription, for the place where Jesus was crucified was near the city, and it was written in Aramaic, in Latin, and in Greek.
verseByVerse.commentary:
An inscription. The charge was usually written on a board (titulus) and carried before the condemned man or hung around his neck, then nailed to the cross. The crowd would know what the state was punishing, which makes this one remarkable. Matthew calls it the charge against him (Matthew 27:37), yet it names no deed, only a person and a title. The only crime it can point to is being who he is, and Pilate had three times said he found no guilt in him.

The King of the Jews. The charge was meant to mock and warn: this is what happens to would-be kings. But it proclaims the truth: on the cross, Jesus is enthroned as King. The Latin initials INRI (Iesus Nazarenus Rex Iudaeorum) appear on many crucifixes. Pilate meant ironic humiliation; he wrote the gospel.

In Aramaic, in Latin, and in Greek. The King is announced to the whole world. Aramaic (literally Hebrew, as older translations have it), the language of home and street; Latin, the language of the army and the law; Greek, the common language of trade and learning. So the first public proclamation of the kingship of Jesus was in three languages, official, posted over his head beside a main road at the busiest time of the Jewish year, and paid for by the Roman government. That proclamation has never been taken down.

Is Jesus King now, or only when he returns? Now. He was enthroned at the cross and the resurrection, and he is seated at the Father’s right hand, reigning until all his enemies are put under his feet (1 Corinthians 15:25; Ephesians 1:20–22). Matthew records the risen Lord’s own claim to all authority in heaven and on earth (Matthew 28:18). His reign is hidden now, exercised through his word and Spirit as he gathers his people from every nation, and it will be visible to all when he returns. That is why the church can be confident in every age and every place. The board over the cross was not a joke that came true later. It was true when it was nailed up.

In everyday life. Pray today for Bible translators, for missionaries learning a hard tongue, for a church whose language you do not speak. The cross was first proclaimed in three languages. It will finally be praised in all of them.
verseByVerse.note: Aramaic was the local language, Latin the language of Roman government, Greek the common language of the eastern empire.

verseByVerse.quote: So the chief priests of the Jews said to Pilate, "Do not write, 'The King of the Jews,' but rather, 'This man said, I am King of the Jews.'" Pilate answered, "What I have written, I have written."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not write The King of the Jews. The chief priests are humiliated: the sign says that the Jews’ king has been crucified. They want the statement turned into a quotation, the claim of a dead pretender: an old way of disposing of a truth without denying it outright.

What I have written. Pilate, who has spent the morning conceding everything, refuses. The perfect tense, twice: it stands written and it will go on standing. It is probably not conscience. It reads like a man who has been pushed around all morning and finds one thing he can refuse: a small, safe, spiteful assertion of the authority he failed to use when it mattered.

God served by a governor’s irritation. Like Caiaphas (11:51), Pilate testified to the truth without meaning to. God’s purposes at Calvary were served by a governor’s petty irritation, as by soldiers gambling and a priest’s political calculation. The only official document we know the crucifixion of Jesus Christ produced, the one legal text, in three languages, over his head, unretracted, says that he is the King. God’s word stands written.

The proverb. Quod scripsi, scripsi passed into proverb, usually quoted admiringly. It was said by somebody who had been moved on every question that mattered, about a notice, after the nails were in.

How do people today turn the truth into a quotation? Every time Jesus’ claims are reported as merely what he said, or what his followers believed, so that nobody has to reckon with whether they are true. It is the way of much modern talk about religion: Christians believe that Jesus is Lord, rather than Jesus is Lord. That can be honest description, and in the right setting it is fair. But watch for it in your own heart: the habit of holding Christ’s words at arm’s length, as interesting claims, rather than receiving them as the truth about the world. Scripture does not say he said he was King. It says he is.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–42 — The Death and Burial of Jesus
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At the cross: the soldiers and the seamless tunic, the women who stayed and the mother given a home, the thirst and the last word, then the spear, the eyewitness’s testimony, and the burial. Four times in a few verses John notes that Scripture was fulfilled.
verseByVerse.theology: It is finished stands at the centre of John’s account. It announces a completed action whose effects remain: the work of redemption is done and needs no addition. Salvation is received, not achieved.
verseByVerse.examples: The beloved disciple who stood at the cross with the women is a model of discipleship under pressure: present where the cost was highest. He saw the blood and water from the soldier’s spear, the sign that Jesus truly died, and testifies that what he saw is true, so that we also may believe.

verseByVerse.quote: When the soldiers had crucified Jesus, they took his garments and divided them into four parts, one part for each soldier; also his tunic. But the tunic was seamless, woven in one piece from top to bottom, so they said to one another, "Let us not tear it, but cast lots for it to see whose it shall be." This was to fulfill the Scripture which says, "They divided my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots." So the soldiers did these things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four parts. The four shares suggest a squad of four soldiers; the clothes of the condemned were the executioners’ perk. The items were perhaps the outer cloak, the belt, the sandals, the head covering. One item is left over. Jesus was probably crucified naked, as the condemned usually were, the final humiliation.

The tunic was seamless. This was the inner garment. Some note that, according to Josephus, the high priest’s robe was woven in one piece (compare Exodus 28:32). Readers since the early centuries have seen the garment of the priest preserved whole on the body of the priest, or the unity of the church; it is an echo rather than an argument. John does not explain; he points to the fulfilment of Scripture.

To fulfil the Scripture. The verse is Psalm 22:18. (In verse 16 of that psalm, the Hebrew of the line about hands and feet is uncertain: most Hebrew manuscripts read like a lion, while the ancient Greek translation and some Hebrew evidence point to pierced, which the ESV follows.) Written about a thousand years earlier, centuries before crucifixion is known to have been practised, the psalm contains a line that had no obvious application to anything: they divide my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots. It reads like Hebrew poetry saying one thing twice. At Golgotha it turns out to be two things, and the reason they did both is a technical accident of weaving.

In the flow. Here John begins a run of four fulfilments of Scripture in a few verses: the garments here, the thirst (v. 28), the unbroken bones (v. 36) and the pierced side (v. 37). The trial has shown human beings doing what they chose; the cross shows God doing what he had said.

Psalm 22 read whole. It opens with the cry Jesus quotes from the cross. It has men mocking and wagging their heads; it has hands and feet pierced; it has bones out of joint and a tongue sticking to the jaw; and it ends, unaccountably, in worldwide praise, with all the families of the nations worshipping and a people yet unborn told that he has done it. Christians from the first have found it very hard to read as coincidence.

Did the Gospel writers simply make the story fit the psalm? It is a fair question, and the answer lies in what they could not have invented. Dividing a prisoner’s clothes was routine for Roman execution squads, done in public in front of a crowd, and John says he stood at the cross himself (19:26, 35). More than that, nobody inventing a Messiah would have given him a cross. A crucified Christ was a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Gentiles (1 Corinthians 1:23); the first Christians did not choose the story because it suited them. They told it because it happened, and then found, to their astonishment, that God had written it down a thousand years before.

So the soldiers did these things. They noticed none of it: four men gambling at the foot of a cross, entirely at liberty, fulfilling to the letter a poem they had never read. They gambled for his last possession while he was purchasing an inheritance for his people, and the naked King on the cross clothes sinners with the garments of salvation and the robe of righteousness (Isaiah 61:10).

Was Psalm 22 really about Jesus, or about David? Both, in their proper order. David wrote out of his own suffering, and the psalm makes sense in his life. But it goes far beyond anything David endured: the piercing, the stripping, the casting of lots, and above all the ending, where the sufferer’s deliverance brings the ends of the earth to worship God. David was a prophet and knew that God had promised a greater Son (Acts 2:30–31). The Spirit who moved him to write was speaking of the sufferings of Christ and the glories to follow (1 Peter 1:11). So Jesus could take its first line on his lips as his own, and John could see its details fulfilled at the foot of the cross. The psalm was always his.
verseByVerse.note: The four shares suggest a squad of four soldiers; the clothes of the condemned went to them.

parallels.desc: they divide my garments among them

verseByVerse.quote: but standing by the cross of Jesus were his mother and his mother's sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene. When Jesus saw his mother and the disciple whom he loved standing nearby, he said to his mother, "Woman, behold, your son!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Standing by the cross. Probably four women: his mother; her sister (perhaps Salome, mother of James and John, Mark 15:40; Matthew 27:56, which would make John Jesus’ cousin); Mary the wife of Clopas; and Mary Magdalene, from whom Jesus had cast seven demons (Luke 8:2). The men who had sworn the night before to die with him are absent, except one, and the ones standing near enough for him to see are women with no power to do anything at all.

Being there. That is worth saying to anybody who has ever stood beside a suffering they could not fix. These women had no standing and no ability to intervene. What they could do was be there, close enough for him to see them. In those hours it was the one thing anybody could do for him, and John records their names.

A sword through her soul. Simeon’s prophecy to Mary is fulfilled: a sword will pierce through your own soul also (Luke 2:35). She has had some thirty years to wonder what he meant, and she is finding out. And the son she watches die is dying for her too. She had rejoiced in God her Saviour when she first carried him (Luke 1:47); now she stands beneath the cross as one of those he is saving, and in the hour he bears her sins he also provides for her body. If you have stood beside a child’s suffering or buried a son or daughter, you are not alone at that place: the mother of the Lord stood there, and her Son saw her.

Woman, behold, your son! The disciple whom he loved is the only one of his male followers John places at the cross. “Woman” is not cold but respectful, and John brackets the ministry with it: Cana, where the hour had not come (2:4); Golgotha, where it has. In his agony, he provides for his mother, as the eldest son should; his brothers did not yet believe (7:5). Even on the cross, he keeps the fifth commandment. The Son of God, bearing the sins of the world, turned his eyes from the weight of the cross to the face of his mother and made sure she would have a home. Such is the heart of our Saviour: never so taken up with saving the world that he forgets the one standing in front of him.

Where Christians differ: Mary at the cross. Roman Catholic teaching sees here Mary made the spiritual mother of all believers, and sometimes speaks of her as co-redemptrix, sharing in Christ’s saving work. This commentary’s view: the plain meaning is that a loving son provides a home for his widowed mother. Christ alone is the Redeemer, and his sacrifice needs no human partner (1 Timothy 2:5; Hebrews 10:14). Mary is honoured as a believer and the mother of our Lord, but she is not a mediator. This also suggests that Mary had no other sons who believed at that time, but it does not prove she had no other sons at all (Mark 6:3).

Does this make Mary the spiritual mother of all believers, as Roman Catholic teaching holds? The text shows a son providing for his widowed mother, and the disciple taking her to his own home (v. 27). Nothing gives her a role in the church’s salvation or prayers. Mary is honoured as the mother of the Lord and a believer among believers (Acts 1:14), but Christ alone is our mediator. Many Roman Catholic friends honour Mary out of real love for her Son, and that love deserves respect even where we must differ.

What if my own family does not believe? Jesus knows what that is like; his brothers did not believe in him at the time (7:5), and he still loved and provided for his own. Keep loving them, honour your parents, and pray for them patiently. Do not make them feel they are a project. The brothers who doubted came to faith after the resurrection: James became a leader of the Jerusalem church, and both he and Jude wrote letters in the New Testament (Acts 1:14; 15:13). And in the meantime, the church becomes family to you, as the beloved disciple became a son to Mary.

In everyday life. Jesus kept the fifth commandment perfectly in your place, where your own honouring has fallen short. So look after your parents gladly, especially in their need. And when someone you love is suffering and you cannot fix it, do not stay away for fear of being useless. Be there.

parallels.desc: a sword will pierce your own soul

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said to the disciple, "Behold, your mother!" And from that hour the disciple took her to his own home. After this, Jesus, knowing that all was now finished, said (to fulfill the Scripture), "I thirst."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, your mother! A new family is formed at the cross. He had brothers; under any ordinary reckoning the eldest son’s responsibility passes to the next son. He passes it instead to a disciple. It is a statement about what the new family is founded on, and it is not blood. So the believers in your church are your family in Christ, bound to you by his blood rather than by birth, and that bond will outlast every earthly one. Jesus had said it plainly: whoever does the will of God is his brother and sister and mother (Mark 3:35).

To his own home. Tradition says she later lived with him in Ephesus. It is the first act of the church, performed while its Lord was still dying, and it consists of somebody taking a widow in (James 1:27).

Knowing that all was now finished. The word is the same as in v. 30: everything the Father gave him to do was complete, except his final words and death. On a cross every breath was a labour, and what he does with that breath is domestic: settling who will look after his mother.

I thirst. The Scriptures are Psalm 69:21 and Psalm 22:15. The thirst was not staged for a quotation: the man had been flogged and had lost blood for hours, and dehydration is one of the ways crucifixion kills. What John means is that he knew what he was doing when he said it aloud. He is not manufacturing a fulfilment; he is naming, in the last minutes, the one thing left on the list.

The fountain thirsts. The giver of living water (4:14; 7:37), who promised a woman at a well that she would never thirst again, died thirsty. Every drink of grace we have ever taken was paid for by that thirst.

Did Jesus suffer as God or as man? He suffered as the one person who is both. God in his divine nature cannot suffer or die; the eternal Son did not cease to uphold the universe on the cross. But the Son took a true human nature, body and soul, and in that nature he truly thirsted, bled and died. Because it was the Son of God who suffered in that nature, Scripture can say God purchased the church with his own blood (Acts 20:28). So the thirst on the cross was not play-acting by a divine being in a costume. It was the real thirst of a real man, who was also God.

For worship. The Lamb died thirsty, so that a multitude no one can number will never thirst again. And because he thirsted there, the Lamb in the midst of the throne will be the shepherd of his people, guiding them to springs of living water, while God wipes away every tear from their eyes (Revelation 7:16–17).

parallels.desc: my tongue sticks to my jaws

verseByVerse.quote: A jar full of sour wine stood there, so they put a sponge full of the sour wine on a hyssop branch and held it to his mouth. When Jesus had received the sour wine, he said, "It is finished," and he bowed his head and gave up his spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sour wine. Cheap, vinegary wine (oxos), the soldiers’ drink. Not the drugged wine he refused earlier (Mark 15:23).

On a hyssop branch. Hyssop was the plant used to sprinkle the blood of the Passover lamb on the doorposts (Exodus 12:22), and in purification (Psalm 51:7). It is not an obvious thing to hold a soaked sponge up with, and John very likely wrote hyssop because he knew what it was for: at the moment the true Passover Lamb is dying, a stalk of it is lifted to his mouth. John records it and says nothing, which is his habit.

It is finished. One word in Greek: tetelestai. Perfect tense: finished, and remaining finished, a thing completed with results that stand. The verb turns up in business papyri for a tax or debt paid, and it is often said that receipts were marked with it to mean “paid in full”; however that may be, the New Testament uses the same verb for paying a tax (Matthew 17:24; Romans 13:6). Not “I am finished,” which is what a dying man says, but “It is finished”: the subject is the work the Father gave him (4:34; 17:4), not the man. The sacrifice for sin is complete, the debt is paid, the prophecies are fulfilled.

In the flow. This is the word the whole Gospel has been moving toward. John opened the upper room by saying he loved his own to the end (13:1), and the word for end belongs to the same family as finished. What follows in the chapter, the spear, the witness and the burial, establishes that he truly died, and chapter 20 will show that the finished work has been accepted.

The guard this word sets. If the work is finished, nothing can be added to it: not by penance, not by devotion, not by a lifetime of good behaviour, not by anything a person does on their worst day or their best. The commonest form of Christian misery is the suspicion that something is still outstanding. This word was cried from a cross to settle it.

He bowed his head. A dying man’s head falls when he dies. John has him bow it first, as one lying down to rest, and then give up his spirit; the verb is one of handing over, of giving something into someone’s keeping. The Good Shepherd had said, no one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord (10:18), and this is the sentence where he does it. Luke records his last words, “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!” (Luke 23:46).

Nothing was taken. The clothes were taken from him that afternoon, and the freedom, and the reputation, and the blood. His life he handed over, at a moment of his choosing, having first said that the account was settled.

Where Christians differ: what happened at the cross? Some say Christ’s death was mainly an example of love, or a victory over evil powers, and reject the idea that he bore God’s punishment for our sin. This commentary’s view: Christ’s death was a victory and an example, but at its heart it was penal substitution: he bore the penalty of our sins in our place (Isaiah 53:5–6; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Galatians 3:13; 1 Peter 2:24). That is why “It is finished” can mean “paid in full.” Nor does the Mass repeat or re-present the sacrifice; it was offered once for all, finished (Hebrews 9:25–28; 10:10–14).

Was Jesus really forsaken by the Father? Yes, in the sense Scripture means, and it was the deepest part of his suffering. On the cross he cried, My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? (Mark 15:34). The Father did not stop loving his Son; the Son was never more pleasing to him than in this obedience. But as the sin-bearer, Christ endured the Father’s judgment on sin and the withdrawal of the felt comfort of his presence, the experience of the condemned. The union of the Trinity was not broken. What he bore was the forsakenness that our sins deserved, so that we would never be forsaken (Hebrews 13:5). John records the end of it: when the wrath was exhausted, he cried, it is finished, and committed his spirit to his Father.

If it is finished, why do I still struggle with sin and suffering? Because what was finished is the payment, not yet the whole renewal. The work that saves you is complete: your guilt is paid, your standing with God secure, your future certain. Nothing you suffer is punishment for sins Christ has paid for; it is a Father’s training (Hebrews 12:5–11). But the application of that finished work goes on: the Spirit is making you holy, and the creation still groans until Christ returns (Romans 8:18–23). You fight sin not to finish what he left undone, but because he has finished it, and the victory he won guarantees yours.

In everyday life. Most of us keep trying to add something to the cross: the extra effort to feel forgiven, the penance of self-punishment, the sense that God is still waiting for you to make it up to him. Name it, and say the word aloud. Confess the sin, receive the forgiveness, and get up and serve him out of gratitude, not to pay a debt that has been cancelled.

For worship. Glory to the Lamb who did not die defeated. No priest’s work was ever done: they stood day after day offering the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins (Hebrews 10:11). He offered one sacrifice for sins for all time, and said so, with hyssop at his lips. Then he bowed his head and gave his spirit into his Father’s hands, and he lives to make sure that not one of those he paid for is ever charged again.
verseByVerse.note: Hyssop was the plant used to sprinkle the blood of the Passover lamb. “It is finished” is a cry of completion, not defeat.

parallels.desc: a bunch of hyssop

verseByVerse.quote: Since it was the day of Preparation, and so that the bodies would not remain on the cross on the Sabbath (for that Sabbath was a high day), the Jews asked Pilate that their legs might be broken and that they might be taken away. So the soldiers came and broke the legs of the first, and of the other who had been crucified with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not on the Sabbath. The law forbade leaving a hanged body overnight (Deuteronomy 21:22–23), and the coming Sabbath made it urgent. The Romans often left bodies on crosses for days as a warning, but in Judea they seem generally to have respected Jewish custom. The same officials go back to the same governor a second time in one day. The first request was for a death. The second is to have it hurried up so as not to spoil the evening.

The curse taken down before nightfall. The law they invoke says why the body must come down: a hanged man is cursed by God, and the land must not be defiled (Deuteronomy 21:23). The leaders do not know that the man on the middle cross is bearing that very curse, not for any crime of his own but for the sins of his people, as Paul would write, becoming a curse for us so as to redeem us from the curse of the law (Galatians 3:13). The law wanted the curse over by nightfall, and his was (2 Corinthians 5:21).

A high day. The weekly Sabbath falling within the festival, especially solemn: hence the pressure to have the bodies down, and the speed of the burial. The Lord of the Sabbath died on the eve of the Sabbath, so that his body would rest in the tomb on the day God rested from his works.

That their legs might be broken. Breaking the legs (crurifragium) with a heavy mallet sped death. A man could breathe, it is commonly thought, only by pushing himself up on his feet. It is the same irony as the governor’s doorstep that morning (18:28): men who would not enter a Gentile house in case it barred them from a meal are, that afternoon, arranging for the legs of living men to be shattered so that the evening’s observance is not spoiled.

What about the thief who believed?
